title: La Morte D'Arthur
author: Rob McArthur
description: Arthur's Britain from the young king's crowning through the Grail's terrible light to the last battle on Salisbury Plain, told in encounters inspired by Sir Thomas Malory.

entries.body:
The snow has barely melted from the churchyard at Carleon when the news runs through every inn and hall in Logres: the boy who drew the sword from the stone has been crowned. His name is Arthur. He is fifteen years old, his beard has not yet come in, and eleven kings have already sworn they will not kneel to him.

At Pentecost the young king holds his first great feast. The hall is half built and the roof lets in the rain, but the tables groan. An old man in a wet grey cloak sits at the king's elbow and eats nothing. "That is Merlin," a squire whispers to you, "and he knew the king would win before the king did."

When the meat is cleared, Arthur climbs onto his own table so that everyone can see him. "I will not ask you to love me," he says. "I am too young to be loved. I will ask you to swear. Never to do outrage nor murder. To give mercy to any who ask it. To help ladies, damsels and widows in their need. Never to fight in a wrongful quarrel for any law or any gold." He looks down the long hall, from the lords at the high table to the knights crowded by the door. "Who will swear with me?"

King Lot of Orkney's herald does not wait to hear the answers. He is already on his horse.

Each Knight chooses how to answer the young king:

Those who kneel and swear the oath before the Bishop of Canterbury, meaning every word, gain 1 Rank of Divinity.

Those who swear it loudly, with an eye on the queen's ladies watching from the gallery, gain 1 Rank of Romance.

Those who swear it with their fingers crossed beneath the table, and slip out afterwards to find King Lot's herald in the stable yard, gain 1 Rank of Villainy.

notes: The Knight with the fewest Ranks of Renown may draw 1 Quest Card

entries.body:
You come upon a king sitting on a milestone with a long roll of parchment across his knees, reading it aloud to his horse. He is a big, sunburnt man with a gold circlet pushed back on his head like a farmer's hat.

"Good knight!" he calls. "You may be able to help me. I am Bagdemagus, King of Gore, and I have been passed over for the Round Table three Pentecosts running. Three! Men half my age sit there now." He shakes the parchment. "So I have bought a list of adventures from a pedlar at Sarum. Forty adventures, a penny each. The first one says there is a knight in a copper tower two leagues from here who keeps a lady in a cage. If I free her, they will have to give me a seat." He squints at you. "Unless you mean to free her first. Is that it? Are you after my adventure?"

responses.label: You may ride with King Bagdemagus to the copper tower and help him free the lady.
You may challenge King Bagdemagus to a joust for the right to the adventure.
You may ask the king how a man comes to be passed over three times.

entries.body:
As you ride along the cliffs near Tintagel in a hard wind, you see a man in old-fashioned armour standing at the edge, looking out to sea. The rain passes straight through him.

"Do not be afraid," he says, without turning. "I have been dead a long while and have lost the knack of hurting anyone. I am Uther, who was called Pendragon. I was king here once." His voice is tired. "I took a woman from her husband by a trick of Merlin's, and got a son on her the same night her husband died. I never told her I was sorry. I never told the boy anything at all. Now he is king, and I cannot leave this cliff until one of them hears it from me." He turns at last. His face is Arthur's face, older and harder. "Will you carry it for me?"

responses.label: You may carry King Uther's apology to the court at Camelot.
You may pray over the ghost of King Uther and try to lay him to rest here.

entries.body:
You come upon a small abbey in a fold of the hills, with an iron bell that rings by itself as you pass. The monks bring you in to see their oldest brother, who is lying on a bed beside the altar.

He is the oldest man you have ever seen. His skin is as thin as candle-smoke and his eyes are milky white. A crown lies on the altar beside him, black with age. "I am Evelake," he says, in a voice like dry leaves. "I was a king in Sarras across the sea, and I came to this island with Joseph of Arimathea when your grandfathers' grandfathers were children. I pressed too near the holy vessel and was struck blind. I asked God to let me live until I could touch the knight who will see it. I have been asking for three hundred years." A hand like a bundle of twigs lifts toward you. "Come here. Let me touch your face."

responses.label: You may kneel and let King Evelake touch your face.
You may ask the old king to tell you of Joseph and the vessel.
You may take the ancient crown from the altar while the monks are at prayer.

entries.body:
As you ride through a village at noon, the people scatter from you, crossing themselves. Only one man stays in the market square: a stooped king in a stained purple cloak, standing in full sunlight. He casts no shadow.

"You see it too," he says bitterly. "I am Carados of the Marches, and my people think I am a ghost. Three nights ago a piper came to my hall and played so sweetly that I danced until dawn. When the sun came up, my shadow was dancing after him down the road, and it has not come back." He shudders. "My steward has taken the keys. My wife will not let me into her chamber. My own dogs howl at me. A king without a shadow, they say, is a king without a soul."

responses.label: You may help King Carados win his shadow back from the piper.
You may track down the piper and take the king's shadow by force.

entries.body:
You come upon a king in the middle of the road, trying to make his horse kneel. He is an elderly man with a white beard braided with ribbons, dressed in a new doublet so tight he can barely breathe.

"Ah! A knight!" he cries. "Perfect. I am Leodegrance, King of Cameliard. You may know that my daughter is to marry the High King, and I am to send her with the finest wedding gift in Christendom: a round table where a hundred and fifty knights may sit." He lowers his voice. "Now that she is leaving, I find the hall very quiet. So I intend to marry again. There is a miller's daughter in the next village, Tegau, who is the handsomest woman in Cameliard. I want to kneel to her properly, on horseback, as they do in the romances, but the horse will not cooperate." He looks at you hopefully. "Would you carry my proposal to her first? To prepare the ground?"

responses.label: You may carry King Leodegrance's proposal to Tegau and plead his case.
You may warn Tegau privately that the old king means to have her.
* You may go to Tegau and court her on your own account.

entries.body: You bow from the saddle to the Lady of the Marsh and turn your horse's head. Her smile does not change. "They always come back," she calls after you, "in the end." You ride on through the dark marsh, and her golden lights follow you for a long way, and you do not look back.

You come upon a line of carts stopped at a bridge on the Cornish border, while a troop of soldiers pulls them apart. Bales of wool are slit open. A cask of wine is staved in. A priest's vestments lie in the mud. Overseeing it all, on a black horse, sits a thin, gaunt king in a crown too large for him, muttering.

If you have Story Token #18, turn immediately to [[1429]].

"He is here somewhere," the king says. "I know it. Every cart. Every cask." He turns red-rimmed eyes on you. "Mark. King of Cornwall. You will have heard of me, and of my wife. You will have heard what they say. There is a knight who loves her, and I will find him if I have to unpick every bale in Britain." He leans closer. "Are you he? No. He is taller. But you might know him. Every knight knows every other knight."

The carters look at you imploringly. One of them, a woman with a wool bale, has started to weep.

responses.label: You may try to talk King Mark out of his madness.
You may offer to join King Mark's search and see where it leads.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a camp spread across a whole valley, with the banners of eleven kings snapping above it. At its heart stands a pavilion of black and gold, and before it a tall, grey-eyed king is hacking at a practice post with a battle-axe.

He stops when he sees you and wipes his forehead. "A knight of Logres," he says. "Good. I am Lot of Orkney and Lothian, and I will not kneel to a boy who pulled a sword out of a stone at a fair." He spits. "Who is his father? Uther, they say. Uther, who got him on another man's wife the night her husband died. And Merlin rocked the cradle. Is that a king? I have fought for this island since before that boy was born." He holds out the axe, handle first. "Come and ride with me. You will have land, and I pay in gold, not promises. Or go back and tell Arthur that Lot of Orkney is coming."

responses.label: You may join King Lot's rebellion against Arthur.
You may slip away and warn Arthur of the size of Lot's host.
You may try to persuade King Lot to make peace with the young king.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon an alehouse at a crossroads where a big man in a plain brown cloak sits among the drovers, asking questions. What do they think of the new taxes? Is the king too young? Would they fight for him? He listens hard to every answer.

When he sees you, he grins and makes room on the bench. You realise, with a jolt, that you have seen that face before, on a coin and at the high table. It is Arthur, the High King. He puts a finger to his lips.

"They tell me the truth in here," he says quietly. "They never do at court." He leans close. "You can help me. King Nentres of Garlot rebelled against me last year and lost. He is in my prison at Carleon. My council says hang him, as an example. My heart says let him go, and he will be grateful. Which is right? I have asked eleven men and got eleven answers."

responses.label: You may counsel the king to show King Nentres mercy.
You may counsel the king to make an example of King Nentres.
You may ask the king why he goes among his people in disguise.

entries.body:
You come upon a hall hung with a great mantle of fur, trimmed all along its edge with human beards, black, red, brown and grey. Beneath it, on a carved throne, sits a big, black-bearded king eating a leg of mutton.

"Admiring my mantle?" he asks, with his mouth full. "I am Rience of North Wales. Every king I have beaten has given me his beard for the trim. Eleven so far." He points to a gap at the end. "There is room for one more. I want Arthur's. He does not have much of one yet, but it will be a curiosity." He tosses the mutton bone to a hound and leans forward. "I will pay you its weight in gold, knight. Its weight in gold. How you get it is your affair."

responses.label: You may accept King Rience's commission, and plan to bring him a beard.
You may refuse King Rience and challenge him for the insult to the High King.

entries.body:
You come upon a king sitting under an oak tree in the middle of the forest, with his crown in his lap and his boots off, soaking his feet in a stream. He is round, rosy and very cheerful.

"Hello!" he says. "Clariance, King of Northumberland. I have lost my army." He waves a hand vaguely at the trees. "Four hundred men. We were marching to join the High King against the Saxons, and I went ahead to look for a place to camp, and when I came back they had gone. Or I had. It is hard to say, in a forest." He wriggles his toes. "I am sure they are looking for me. I have the pay chest." He pats a small iron box beside him. "I should very much like to find them before the Saxons do."

responses.label: You may help King Clariance find his lost army.
You may lead King Clariance into an ambush and take the pay chest.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a crowd outside the walls of Carleon, gathered around a gallows. A king stands on the cart beneath it, with his hands tied and a rope already around his neck. He is a lean, hawk-faced man, and he is laughing at the hangman.

"Nentres of Garlot," a woman in the crowd tells you. "He rode with King Lot against the High King. The High King is away in the north and left orders. At noon, they hang him."

The king catches your eye across the crowd. "You!" he calls. "You have an honest face. Do you think a man should hang for fighting for his own country? I lost. That is my crime. If I had won, I would be the one with the rope." His men-at-arms, bound in a line behind the cart, murmur agreement. The sheriff, a fat man with a staff, looks nervous. The sun is climbing.

responses.label: You may speak for King Nentres before the sheriff and demand a delay.
You may cut King Nentres loose and help him escape.
You may hear the king's last confession before he hangs.

entries.body: "I will find her," you say. Twm's mother gives you directions to a village two days away in the mountains, where old Nest's sister keeps goats.

resolutions.label: climb to the witch's refuge and persuade her

success.body: The path is steep and the goats are hostile. You find old Nest sitting outside her sister's hut, smoking a pipe. When you tell her about Twm, she cackles. "Serves him right," she says. But you talk to her about his mother, and his sweetheart, and the barn roof, and at last she softens. "He was always a cheeky boy," she says. "But he carried my shopping once." She gives you a little bag of salt. "Tell him to eat it," she says, "and to say sorry." He does, and shrinks, and says sorry.

failure.body: The path is steep. You find old Nest outside her sister's hut, and when you tell her about Twm, she cackles, and when you ask her to lift the curse, she shakes her head. "He must come himself," she says, "and say sorry." Twm, now the size of a church, cannot fit up the path.

resolutions.label: ride the mountain roads and bring the witch down to him

success.body: You ride all night and all the next day and find old Nest outside her sister's hut, smoking a pipe. You do not argue. You tell her Twm is dying of his own size, and hold out your hand, and she looks at you and climbs up behind your saddle, grumbling. At the barn, she looks at Twm, who is now the size of a church, and bursts out laughing. Then she makes him say sorry, and pours a bag of salt down his throat, and he shrinks.

failure.body: You ride all night, but the mountain roads are steep and your horse falls lame. By the time you reach old Nest's sister, she has gone off to a fair. You never find out which one.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You put on your helm. The old fisherman nods and steers straight for the beach, into the arrows.

resolutions.label: fight your way up Dover beach

success.body: The boat grounds in the surf and you jump into water up to your chest, with arrows hissing around you. You struggle up the beach with a hundred others, and then a thousand, and Mordred's line bends, and then it breaks. By noon, the old king's banner is flying on the beach. You see him, an old grey man in battered armour, walking among the wounded. He stops by you, and grips your shoulder, and goes on. Somewhere behind you, they are carrying a great knight of Orkney up from the surf, and the king is weeping.

failure.body: The boat grounds in the surf, and you jump into the water, and an arrow takes you in the shoulder before you reach the sand. You are dragged back into the boat by the old fisherman. You watch the rest of the landing from the bottom of the boat, bleeding.

entries.body: You look up at the mountain. There is a shepherds' track, you think, over the shoulder of the hill, if you can find it in the rain.

resolutions.label: find a hidden way over the mountain

success.body: You find it: a sheep-track, faint and steep, winding up through the rocks where no wyvern would look for goats. You lead the column up it, one cart at a time, all afternoon. The wyvern watches from its rock but does not follow. At dusk, you are over the top, and the valley on the other side is green and quiet, with no smoke. The woman with the baby names her daughter after the track.

failure.body: You find a sheep-track and lead the column up it, but halfway up, it ends at a cliff. You have to turn them round and bring them down again in the dark. By morning, the wyvern has gone, but so has one of the carts, over the edge.

resolutions.label: guard the column as it passes beneath the wyvern

success.body: You form the refugees into a column with the carts on the outside and the children in the middle, and the strongest men with torches along the side facing the rock. You walk beside them with your shield raised. The wyvern hisses and lashes its tail, but it does not like fire, and it does not like order. It stays on its rock. The column passes. On the far side, the woman with the baby names her daughter for you.

failure.body: You form the column and walk beside it with your shield up, but a goat breaks loose, and the column breaks after it, and the wyvern drops from its rock into the middle of the confusion.

entries.body: You go up on deck and rouse the pilgrims, quietly, one by one: a blacksmith, two farmers, a stout nun, a Welsh archer.

resolutions.label: lead the pilgrims in seizing the ship

success.body: At dawn, when the captain comes on deck, he finds his crew tied to the mast and a knight at the wheel and a stout nun holding a belaying pin. The hooded man jumps overboard and swims for a Genoese galley. You sail the ship back to Bristol, badly, with the blacksmith navigating. The thorn goes back to Glastonbury. The pilgrims go to the Holy Land the next spring, in a different ship, and send you a letter from Jerusalem.

failure.body: At dawn, you try to seize the ship, but the crew are sailors and the pilgrims are not. The captain has you locked in the hold with the relic. You spend a very long week there before you are put ashore in Brittany.

resolutions.label: persuade the crew that their captain has sold them too

success.body: You do not rouse the pilgrims. You go to the crew instead, in the forecastle, and tell them what you heard through the planks: that the hooded man has a buyer in Tunis for the pilgrims, and has asked the price of sailors. It is not quite true. It is close enough. At dawn, the crew seize their own captain. The hooded man jumps overboard. You sail back to Bristol with the thorn.

failure.body: You go to the crew and tell them their captain has sold them too. The bosun is the captain's brother. You spend the rest of the voyage in the hold.

entries.body: "I will help you," you say. Iddawg laughs, a high, cracked laugh. The bracken parts, and the boar walks out onto the far bank. It is the size of a bull, grey and bristled, and between its ears something glints.

resolutions.label: bring down the great boar

success.body: Iddawg drives the boar out of the bracken, and you ride it down along the stream, and when it turns at bay against a rock, you both strike at once. It is a long, terrible fight. At the end, the boar lies dead in the water, and Iddawg sits beside it, weeping and laughing. He takes the comb, the razor and the shears from between its ears. The comb he keeps. The shears he gives to you. "Seven years," he says. "And now what?" He sits by the dead boar all night, and in the morning, he is gone.

failure.body: Iddawg drives the boar out of the bracken, and you ride it down along the stream. But when it turns at bay, it is faster than anything that size has any right to be. Its tusk rips your horse's belly, and you are thrown. When you get up, the boar is gone, and so is Iddawg, running after it. You find your way home alone. You dream of the boar, afterwards, every night, and wake with your hands clenched.

resolutions.label: bind the boar-king with the old words of his making

success.body: You remember the story: Twrch Trwyth was a king before he was a boar. You stand in the stream as it charges and call it by its king's name, loudly, three times. The boar stops, dripping, a spear's length from you. For a moment, in its small red eyes, you see a man. Then it turns and walks away up the valley, and Iddawg, weeping, lets it go. "It remembered," he says. "Seven years, and it remembered."

failure.body: You stand in the stream and call the boar by its king's name. It does not stop. You leap aside at the last moment and it takes a strip out of your thigh as it passes. Iddawg runs after it, shrieking with joy.

entries.body: You take off your armour and tie a rope round your waist. "If it pulls twice," you tell the captain, "haul." Then you dive.

resolutions.label: dive to the drowned village

success.body: The water is cold and clear. You swim down to the church tower and look in through the belfry. Inside, in the green light, lies a coffin, and the serpent is coiled round it, and when you touch the coffin, the serpent does not attack. It only watches. On the coffin is carved a name, *Gwenno*, and a date a hundred years old. You pull twice, and come up gasping. The captain knows the name. "The serpent's wife," he says. "It was a man once. It drowned the town the day she died." You tell the village priest. The next spring, they say a mass for Gwenno over the water, and the serpent is never seen again.

failure.body: The water is cold and clear. You swim down to the church tower, and the serpent comes out of the belfry, and looks at you, and you pull twice. You are hauled up with its breath on your heels.

entries.body: You drop your shield and run, not toward Mordred's army, but toward the pavilion, shouting, "Hold! Hold! It was an adder!"

resolutions.label: stop the two armies before they close

notes: This day on Salisbury Plain ends in parley, not battle. Tell the table

success.body: You reach the pavilion as the armies begin to move. You grab the knight who drew his sword and hold up the dead adder in your other hand, and shout until your throat bleeds, and the old king sees, and Mordred sees, and for one terrible moment, both of them hesitate. It is enough. The captains on both sides, the old ones, the ones who wanted to live, hold their men. The charge stops. The parley goes on. You do not know, afterwards, how long the peace will last. But nobody dies on Salisbury Plain that day.

failure.body: You reach the pavilion as the armies begin to move, and you shout, and nobody hears you over ten thousand men shouting. The armies meet around you like two waves. You are swept into the battle.

entries.body: You climb onto the island. It is warm under your feet, and it rises and falls, slowly, like breathing. The abbot hands you a candle.

resolutions.label: keep faith through the Mass on the living island

success.body: You kneel with the monks, and sing with them, and when the abbot raises the host, the whale lies perfectly still, as if it too were listening. The Mass ends. The abbot turns to you and smiles. "It is Jasconius," he says. "We know. He has carried us since Easter. Every year he lets us say Mass on his back. Every year, he brings us to the land of promise, a little nearer." The whale blows again, gently. You go back to your ship feeling as if you have been in a very large church.

failure.body: You kneel with the monks, but halfway through, the whale blows, and you jump to your feet and nearly overturn the altar. The abbot looks at you with great sorrow. "You did not trust him," he says. You go back to your ship alone.

entries.body: You think for a long time. The boy waits patiently, humming. Out on the river, a heron stands on one leg and watches you too.

resolutions.label: answer Taliesin's riddle

success.body: "Nothing," you say at last. "The poor man has nothing, the rich man lacks nothing, and if you eat nothing, you die." Taliesin whoops and claps his hands. "You are the first this summer!" he cries. He wakes the ferryman with a kick. As he poles you across, he sings you a song about a king who sleeps under a hill and will wake when Britain needs him, and when you reach the far bank, you find you can remember every word.

failure.body: "Bread," you say. Taliesin shakes his head sadly. "Salt," you try. "A wife." "A prayer." The boy is laughing now. At last he tells you. "Nothing," he says. "The poor man has nothing, the rich man lacks nothing..." You groan. You ride upstream to find the next ford, and it takes you all day.

resolutions.label: answer him with a riddle of your own

success.body: "I will answer," you say, "if you answer mine first. *What is it that the boy on the rope does not know?*" Taliesin opens his mouth, then closes it. He frowns. He thinks. "Everything I know, I know," he says slowly. "So what I do not know, I cannot say." He looks at you with his old eyes, and then he laughs until he falls off the rope. "A draw!" he says. "A draw! That has not happened since Merlin." He takes you across for nothing.

failure.body: "I will answer," you say, "if you answer mine first. *What has a mouth and cannot speak?*" "A river," says Taliesin, without a pause. "And a sack, and a cave, and the King of Munster. Now answer mine." You cannot. You walk upstream to the next ford.

entries.body: "The wine belongs to the monks," you say. "And so does the cellar." Dewi laughs. "Try," he says.

resolutions.label: drive the clurichaun from the cellar

success.body: You do not try holy water, or bells. You go to the monks' kitchen and come back with a loaf of bread, a pinch of salt and an iron horseshoe. You lay them on the bottom stair, and then you sit down and begin to sing a very dull hymn, very slowly, verse after verse. Dewi covers his ears. By the ninth verse, he is weeping. By the twelfth, he leaps off his barrel and out of the cellar window and away over the fields. The monks are overjoyed. The cellarer gives you a bottle of the good wine, the one the clurichaun had not found.

failure.body: You lay bread, salt and an iron horseshoe on the bottom stair. Dewi picks up the horseshoe and throws it at you. It hits you on the head. When you wake, he is still on his barrel, and he has drunk the monks' communion wine as well.

resolutions.label: trap him in an empty cask

success.body: You leave a cask with its bung out in the middle of the cellar, with a thimble of the monks' best wine at the very bottom, and hide behind the stair. At midnight, Dewi comes sniffing, and climbs in after the wine. You slam the bung in and roll the cask up the stair and down to the river, where it floats away toward Ireland, singing. The monks are overjoyed.

failure.body: You leave a cask with its bung out and a thimble of wine at the bottom, and hide. Dewi comes, and looks at the cask, and at the stair, and at you behind it. He drinks the wine from the outside, somehow, and laughs at you all night.

entries.body: You say nothing, and eat his bread, and thank him. That night, when he thinks you are asleep, you hear him slip out of the chapel. You follow.

resolutions.label: lay a trap for the outlaws in the pass

success.body: The false hermit rings his bell, and the outlaws come down from the pass with torches to rob his guest. You have already moved your horse, stuffed your blankets with straw, and cut half-through the rope bridge above the chapel. When they are all on it, you cut the rest. Twelve outlaws go into the river. The survivors flee. The hermit, you find in the morning, has fled too. You take his chapel's bell to the next church, where it is still rung every Sunday.

failure.body: The false hermit rings his bell, and the outlaws come down from the pass. You try to take them by surprise in the dark, but there are too many, and one of them has a dog. You spend the night in a thicket with the dog barking outside it.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You look down at the island. It is covered in rock and seaweed, but where it meets the sea, you see something that looks very much like an eye, the size of a barn door, closed. It opens as you watch.

resolutions.label: speak with the great sea-beast

success.body: You speak to it in the old words for the sea, which you learned from a fisherman's widow in Cornwall. The eye blinks. A voice like the tide rumbles up through the castle's foundations. "I was asleep," it says. "Someone built on me." You ask it, politely, to swim back to Gwynedd. It sighs a great sigh that sets every bell in the castle ringing, and turns, and swims. The king never learns what happened. He thinks it was your seamanship.

failure.body: You speak to it in the old words for the sea. The eye looks at you. Then the island dives. You come up among floating barrels and a very wet king, and are picked up by a Welsh fishing boat after two hours in the water.

entries.body: "A gift," you say, "from your workshops." The eldest sister smiles. "Then you must work for it," she says, "as we do." She leads you to the slipway, where the white ship is being built.

resolutions.label: labour beside the sisters of Avalon

success.body: You work with them for a day and a night that feel like a month: planing the white wood, stitching the sail of spider-silk, singing the songs they teach you to make the timbers sweet. At dawn, the ship is finished, and the eldest sister lays her hand on its prow. "It is called Prydwen," she says. "It was always meant for the young king. But you helped to build it, so it will carry you first." She gives it to you, to take to Camelot.

failure.body: You work with them, but the white wood splinters under your clumsy hands, and the silk tangles. At dawn, the eldest sister sends you home in the rowing boat with a basket of apples. "Come back," she says, "when your hands are quieter."

resolutions.label: learn the sisters' craft of binding virtue into wood

success.body: You do not plane or stitch. You sit with the eldest sister at the prow of the white ship while she sings the old words into the timber, and you learn them, line by line, until you can sing them back. By dawn, your words are in the ship too. "It is called Prydwen," she says. "It was always meant for the young king. But your song is in it now, so it will carry you first." She gives it to you, to take to Camelot.

failure.body: You sit with the eldest sister and try to learn the words, and they slide out of your head like water. At dawn she sends you home in the rowing boat with a basket of apples.

entries.body: "A thief is a thief," you say, "whatever country he comes from." Carados points you toward the green hill, where a thin tune drifts on the wind, and wrings his hands as you go.

resolutions.label: stalk the piper through the long grass and seize him

success.body: You come up the back of the hill on your belly, through grass that seems to lean aside for the piper and lean in on you. When you are close enough to hear him breathe between notes, you spring. He is light as a bundle of twigs. He shrieks and bites, and the shadow flees down the hill to its master. When you open your hands, you are holding a bundle of twigs. The king rewards you well, but you notice, riding away, that the grass on that hill bends away from your footsteps.

failure.body: You come up the back of the hill on your belly. The tune stops. When you raise your head, the hilltop is empty, and the sun is going down. You have been creeping through the grass for the whole afternoon, though it felt like minutes. When you come down, the village has its lanterns lit and nobody remembers seeing you arrive. You set off in what you hope is the right direction.

resolutions.label: ride the piper down before he can play again

success.body: You gallop up the green hill so fast that the piper has no breath to play before you are on him. You snatch the pipe from his fingers as you pass. Without its tune, the king's shadow stops dancing, looks about, and runs down the hill to its master like a dog let off a leash. The piper curses you in a voice like wind and vanishes. You keep the pipe. It is only a willow whistle now.

failure.body: You gallop up the green hill, and the piper puts his pipe to his lips and plays one note, and your horse begins to dance. It dances you right round the hilltop and down the other side and into a duckpond. By the time you have climbed out, the piper and the shadow are gone.

entries.body: You think for a long time. The snow falls. The Green Knight waits.

resolutions.label: answer what you would give up

success.body: You tell him. It is the thing you love most, and it is not a thing, and saying it aloud is the hardest thing you have ever done. The Green Knight is silent. Then he bows to you, very low, as a knight bows to a king. "That," he says, "is the first true answer." He opens the holly with his hand, and there is a path through it, going north, into a white country. "Follow it, if you like," he says. "It does not go to the vessel. But it goes a long way toward it." You walk it for a day and come out changed.

failure.body: You tell him, but it is not quite true, and you both know it. The Green Knight nods, sadly. "Another one," he says, and steps back into the holly.

resolutions.label: give up your sword to him as your answer

success.body: You do not speak. You draw your sword and lay it in the snow at his feet. The Green Knight looks at it for a long time. Then he bows to you, very low, as a knight bows to a king, and picks up the sword, and hands it back to you. "The first true answer," he says. He opens the holly with his hand, and there is a path through it, going north. "It does not go to the vessel," he says. "But it goes a long way toward it."

failure.body: You lay your sword in the snow at his feet. The Green Knight shakes his head. "That is a gesture," he says, "not an answer," and steps back into the holly.

entries.body: You take the satchel from his hands. He does not have the strength to stop you. "Please," he says. You mount your horse.

resolutions.label: carry the letters through the blizzard

success.body: You ride down the other side of the pass through the snow, and at the bottom, you read the letters. Mordred has promised the Saxon kings Kent, Sussex and Essex. You carry them to the old king's camp, where the king reads them himself, with his face like stone. "I did not believe it," he says. You are rewarded. You do not mention the messenger, and nobody asks.

failure.body: You ride down the other side of the pass through the snow and lose your way in the blizzard. When you finally reach a village, the letters are sodden and unreadable. You think, sometimes, about the man you left.

entries.body: You push your horse through the crowd to the cart. "Sheriff," you say, "he is sorry, and he has told you where the silver is. Is that not worth a life?"

resolutions.label: plead for the thief's life

success.body: The sheriff frowns. But the crowd has heard Dafydd's request, and the crowd has begun to murmur, and a woman shouts "Let him go and dig it up himself!" The sheriff looks at the crowd, and at you, and at Dafydd. "He digs it up," he says at last, "under guard. He gives it back. And then he spends seven years in the High King's galleys." Dafydd laughs aloud. "Seven years!" he says. "I thought I had seven minutes." He gives Mistress Anest her silver with his own hands.

failure.body: The sheriff frowns. "He is sorry," he says, "because he is about to be hanged. If he were not about to be hanged, he would not be sorry." He nods to the hangman. You are too late even to hear where the silver is, and you ride away with that on your conscience.

resolutions.label: offer yourself as surety for his penance

success.body: "Take the rope off him," you say, "and put it round my wrist. He will dig up the silver under guard and give it back. If he runs, hang me." The sheriff stares at you. The crowd goes quiet. At last, the sheriff nods. Dafydd digs up the silver under guard and gives it to Mistress Anest with his own hands, weeping. Then he goes to the High King's galleys for seven years, and does not run.

failure.body: "Put the rope round my wrist," you say. The sheriff considers this. "Then I will have two thieves," he says, "and I only need one." He nods to the hangman.

entries.body: "Wait here with the boy, my lady," you say. "I will bring them back to you." The queen grips your arm. "He has a hundred men," she says. "Be careful." Meliagaunt's trail is easy enough: a hundred horses and twenty prisoners leave a great deal of trampled may-blossom.

resolutions.label: attack Sir Meliagaunt's column at the river crossing

success.body: You ride ahead of the column and wait at the river crossing, where the road narrows between high banks. When Meliagaunt's men are strung out across the water, you ride out of the trees, shouting orders to an army that isn't there. The captives, hearing you, fall on their guards with their bare hands. In the confusion, half the prisoners escape, and the rest are freed within the week. Meliagaunt himself flees to Gore. The queen weeps when her ladies come home, and sends you a sleeve embroidered with may blossom.

failure.body: You ride ahead of the column and wait at the river crossing. But Meliagaunt has archers, and they have seen you. An arrow takes your horse, and before you can get to your feet you are surrounded. You spend the next week in Meliagaunt's cellars, next to the queen's knights, all of whom have opinions about your tactics.

resolutions.label: follow the column and slip the captives free at night

success.body: You follow at a distance until they camp. When the fires are low, you creep between the sleeping guards and cut the ropes of the nearest prisoners. They cut the ropes of the next, and so on, until twenty knights and ladies in green silk are slipping away through the trees. You bring them to the queen at dawn. She embraces each one, and then, to the page's astonishment, embraces you.

failure.body: You follow at a distance until they camp. When the fires are low, you creep between the sleeping guards, but one of them is only pretending to sleep. You are dragged before Meliagaunt, who laughs and adds you to his collection.

entries.body:
You rein in at the edge of the square. This is not your country, and not your law. The queen watches you turn your horse. She does not call out.

You ride out of the town at a walk. You are on the far side of the valley when the bell starts to ring, and you do not look back to see the smoke.
You sit down at the long table, in the empty place beside the drowned son's chair. The lights come out of the marsh.

resolutions.label: share the Samhain feast with the dead

success.body: They come and sit at the table, grey and quiet, and eat. You eat with them. The drowned son sits beside you. He looks at his mother across the dark, and she looks at him, and neither speaks. At dawn, they get up and go back into the marsh, and the drowned son stops and turns and lifts his hand to his mother. When you stand up, your hair has a streak of white in it. The old woman embraces you. "He is at peace," she says. "I saw."

failure.body: They come and sit at the table, grey and quiet, and you cannot bear it. You get up and run. The villagers are very angry. The dead go back into the marsh unsatisfied.

entries.body: "Let him go, my lord," you say. "But not for nothing." The king raises his eyebrows. "Go on."

resolutions.label: advise the king on terms that will bind Nentres to him

success.body: You suggest the king free Nentres, give him back his lands, and ask for nothing but his eldest son to be fostered at Camelot as a squire. "Not a hostage," you say. "A friend. In ten years he will love you like a brother, and his father will know it." Arthur stares at you, then laughs and thumps the table so hard the ale jumps. "I will do it," he says. The drovers cheer, without knowing why. Years later, Nentres's son is one of the king's most loyal knights.

failure.body: You suggest the king free Nentres and trust in his gratitude. Arthur nods slowly. The next spring, Nentres rides out of Garlot with a thousand men. When you next see Arthur, he does not blame you, which is somehow worse. "Mercy is not a plan," he says. "I should have known that." You resolve to think harder before you advise a king.

resolutions.label: speak for mercy with all your heart

success.body: You speak of the oath the king made at Pentecost: mercy to any who ask it. "Has Nentres asked?" says Arthur. "He will," you say, "if you give him the chance." Arthur is silent for a long moment. Then he nods. "Then I will go to Carleon myself and give him the chance." He pays for everyone's ale, including the drovers', and leaves at a gallop. The alewife asks who he was. You tell her he was a wool merchant.

failure.body: You speak of the oath the king made at Pentecost. "Mercy to any who ask it," says Arthur. "Nentres has not asked. He has cursed my name every day he has been in that cell." He finishes his ale. "I will think on it." You never learn what he decided, and the not knowing gnaws at you.

entries.body:
The Green Knight looks at you. "You," he says. "You owe me a blow. You did not come to my chapel on the day." He sighs, and holds out his holly branch like an axe. "But it is the Grail year, and I am tired of axes. So instead of a blow, I will take a promise. Promise me one thing, and keep it, and we are even." You promise. He does not tell you what you have promised. He only smiles, and steps back into the holly, and is gone.

For the rest of your life, you wonder what it was. You keep it anyway.

notes: Lose Story Token #14

entries.body: You strip off your armour and dive into the cold, dark pool.

resolutions.label: swim to the sleeping dragons and return

success.body: Down and down you go, through black water, until your lungs are bursting. At the bottom, in a cave of glittering stone, two dragons lie curled together, one red and one white, sleeping, with their tails intertwined. The red one opens one eye and looks at you. Then it closes it again. You swim back up, gasping. You tell the shepherd what you saw. He is silent a long time. "Curled together," he says. "Not fighting." He seems to find that hopeful.

failure.body: Down and down you go, through black water, until your lungs are bursting, and you have to turn back without seeing anything. You come up choking. The shepherd hauls you out. "Nobody ever reaches the bottom," he says.

resolutions.label: call the dragons up from the pool with the old words

success.body: You do not dive. You kneel at the edge of the pool and speak the words that Merlin, as a boy, is said to have spoken to King Vortigern. The water boils. Two heads rise out of it, one red and one white, sleepy and dripping. They look at you. They look at each other. Then, to your astonishment and the shepherd's, they curl together again, tails intertwined, and sink back down. "Not fighting," says the shepherd. He seems to find that hopeful.

failure.body: You kneel and speak the old words, and the water boils, and a red head rises, and snaps at you, and you fall backwards into the pool.

entries.body: You go and sit down by the young soldier, and say nothing.

resolutions.label: comfort the grieving soldier

success.body: You sit with him for an hour, in silence. Then you ask his brother's name. He tells you. You ask what his brother was like. He tells you, a little. Then more. Then, suddenly, he is weeping, great heaving sobs, and you hold him while he weeps. When he is done, he wipes his face and looks at the fire. "He would have laughed at me," he says. He goes and sits with the others.

failure.body: You sit with him for an hour, in silence. He never speaks. At dawn, he goes back to the war without a word.

entries.body: You ride out into the road in front of the war-band and throw down your gauntlet. "Drust," you call. "Fight me. If I win, the captives go free."

resolutions.label: fight Drust the Pict in single combat

success.body: Drust laughs and comes at you with a great axe. He is huge and fast and fearless. But he has never fought a knight in armour, and his axe glances off your helm, and you are inside his guard before he can swing again. It is a long fight. At the end of it, Drust is on his back in the heather, laughing through his blood. "Take them," he says. "Take them. You fight like a Pict." The captives walk home with you. Drust, you hear, goes back north and tells stories about you.

failure.body: Drust laughs and comes at you with a great axe. You fight well, but not well enough. He knocks you down and stands over you, and then, to your surprise, lets you live. "Brave," he says. "Stupid, but brave." The war-band goes north.

resolutions.label: ride Drust down before his axe can swing

success.body: You do not dismount. You ride at him with your lance, and he has never fought a man on a horse. He swings his great axe at your horse's legs, and you are past him before it lands, and you turn and come again, and the butt of your lance takes him in the chest and knocks him flat in the heather. He lies there laughing through his blood. "Take them," he says. "You fight like a Pict." The captives walk home.

failure.body: You ride at him with your lance, and his axe takes your horse's forelegs. You go over its head. Drust stands over you, and lets you live. "Brave," he says. "Stupid, but brave."

entries.body: You dismount and take your place beside him on the gate. He looks at you and nods.

resolutions.label: hold the causeway against Mordred's riders

success.body: The causeway is narrow. Mordred's men can only come two abreast. You and the old soldier hold it for an hour, and then another, and then Mordred's men decide the causeway is not worth it, and turn back. The old soldier sits down on the gate, very slowly. "Relieved," he says. "At last." You take him to the old king's camp, where they give him a new pair of boots and a pension.

failure.body: The causeway is narrow, but they are thirty. The old soldier falls in the first hour. You are driven back into the marsh.

resolutions.label: flood the causeway ahead of the riders

success.body: The causeway runs between two meres. You see where the old sluice is, choked with reeds, and while the old soldier holds the gate, you hack it open. The water pours across the causeway ahead of Mordred's riders, knee-deep and rising. They rein in, and look at it, and turn back. The old soldier sits down on the gate. "Relieved," he says. You take him to the old king's camp.

failure.body: You hack at the old sluice, and it gives, and the water pours across the causeway behind the riders, cutting you and the old soldier off from your own side.

entries.body: You leave your horse in the reeds and creep through the marsh to where the young men are hiding, waiting to be found.

resolutions.label: hide the young men in the fens

success.body: You know the marsh better than Mordred's men, or you learn it faster. You lead the young men deep into the fens, onto islands of floating reed where no soldier in mail would dare to follow. The soldiers search for three days and give up. When they have gone, you bring the young men home. The old woman feeds you eel pie until you cannot move.

failure.body: You lead the young men into the fens, but one of the floating islands sinks under your weight, and two of them are drowned. The others are found by the soldiers the next day.

resolutions.label: hide them under a glamour of reeds and mist

success.body: You gather the young men on an island of reeds and speak over it the old words for mist that the fen-folk use when the tax-men come. The mist comes up out of the water, thick and white. Mordred's soldiers search the marsh for three days and walk past the island a dozen times. When they have gone, you bring the young men home. The old woman feeds you eel pie until you cannot move.

failure.body: You speak the words for mist, and the mist comes, and Mordred's soldiers, who are fen-men themselves, know exactly what it means. They wait until it lifts.

entries.body: You think for a long time. Then you ask. The Lady of the Lake listens with her head on one side.

resolutions.label: bear the price of a true answer

success.body: She answers you. It is not the answer you wanted, but it is true, and you know that it is true, and it makes everything clearer. Then she lifts her hand, and you feel something slip out of you, as lightly as a fish slipping from a net. You do not know what it was. You never do. But when you ride away, you feel lighter, and you think, perhaps, it was something you did not need to keep.

failure.body: She answers you. The answer is true, and you cannot bear it. You turn away from the lake with your hands over your ears. Behind you, you feel the Lady take her price anyway. Later, you realise that what she took was the name of someone you once loved.

entries.body: You take a candle and stand with the villagers, at a respectful distance.

resolutions.label: keep the Samhain vigil with the living

success.body: You stand all night in the cold, with the candle, while the dead feast. You do not look at them directly. You only watch the old woman, whose face changes as the night goes on, from fear to grief to peace. At dawn, the lights go back into the marsh. The old woman takes your hand. "Thank you for standing with us," she says. "It is harder, standing."

failure.body: You stand all night in the cold, with the candle. Near dawn, you fall asleep on your feet, and your candle goes out. The old woman does not blame you, but you feel that something went wrong.

entries.body: You climb onto the scaffold. The headsman looks at you in confusion. The fool looks up. "Oh, good," he says. "An audience."

resolutions.label: make the angry king laugh

success.body: You do not tell a joke. You turn to the crowd and ask, very seriously, whether anyone here has ever tried to lift the new tax. A farmer shouts that he has, and it broke his back. A woman shouts that she tried too, and it vanished through her fingers. The crowd begins to laugh. You turn to the king and bow. "Sire," you say, "your fool is not guilty. He only said what everyone knows." The king stares at you. Then, slowly and unwillingly, his mouth twitches. He laughs. It is a short, bitter laugh, but it is a laugh. "Let him go," he says. "And lower the tax."

failure.body: You ask the crowd whether anyone here has ever tried to lift the new tax. Nobody answers. They are too frightened. The king says, "Very droll," and nods to the headsman, and then to his guards, who take you by the arms. You are lucky to leave that castle with your own head.

entries.body:
You sit down on the hillside beside him, among the crows. "Tell me," you say.

He tells you everything. He tells you about a queen and a knight and a fire. About a king who crosses the sea to fight his friend and comes home to find his son on his throne. About a plain in the west, in May, with a thousand ravens circling. About an adder in the heather, and a sword drawn to kill it, and two hosts that see the sword and charge. About a one-handed knight throwing a great sword into a lake, and an arm coming up to catch it. About a black barge with three queens in it, and a king who is not dead, only sleeping. "He will come back," the old monk says, weeping, "when Britain needs him most. But not for a very long time."

When he has finished, the crows rise all together and fly away west. Brother Aldhelm is asleep in the grass. You cover him with your cloak and ride on, and you cannot get the adder out of your mind.
You kneel in the courtyard at the foot of the tower and pray aloud. The ladies above you laugh, and then they stop laughing.

resolutions.label: pray for the truth to be revealed

success.body: You pray for a sign. The ladies lean further out and scream at you to stop. You do not stop. Then the bell of the castle chapel begins to ring, by itself, and at the sound, the fair lady on the tower shrieks, and her face slips, like a mask, and underneath it is something with horns. The other ladies turn to smoke. The tower is empty. The old hermit gets up very slowly. "I prayed for that for twenty years," he says. "You prayed for it for an hour."

failure.body: You pray for a sign. The ladies scream louder, and lean further out, and one of them falls. She vanishes before she hits the ground. You do not know if it was a sign or a death.

resolutions.label: bind the demons with the old words and holy water

success.body: You take the flask of holy water that every Grail knight carries and sprinkle a circle round the tower's foot, and speak the words that bind what is not what it seems. The ladies on the tower scream. Their faces slip like masks. One by one, they turn to smoke and are drawn down into the circle, and are gone. The old hermit gets up very slowly. "I prayed for that for twenty years," he says.

failure.body: You sprinkle a circle of holy water round the tower and speak the binding. The circle holds nothing. One of the ladies falls. She vanishes before she hits the ground. You do not know if it was a demon or a death.

entries.body:
The grey-bearded knight's eyes narrow. "I know your face," he says. "You fought Gaheris once. At a crossroads, over Lamorak." The Orkney knights draw their swords all at once.

You fight your way out of the camp, down the mountainside, in the dusk, with Orkney steel all round you. You escape. The Orkney knights, you hear later, have added your name to the end of their oath.
"Ride on," you say. "I will hold the lane." Jack salutes you, and Mererid blows you a kiss, and they gallop off. The dust cloud comes closer.

resolutions.label: delay the baron's men in the lane

success.body: You fell a tree across the lane, which takes longer than you expected, and when the baron's men come up, you are standing on it with your sword drawn. You tell them there is a toll. You argue about the toll. You fight three of them, one at a time, while the others cut through the tree. By the time they are through, it is past noon. At Llanfair, they find the church door open and a new-married couple sitting on the step, eating bread and honey. The baron, when he hears, sends his men home and his daughter a wedding gift.

failure.body: You fell a tree across the lane, but the baron's men simply ride round it through the field. They catch the lovers a mile from Llanfair. Jack goes to the gallows. Mererid goes to the man with gout. You go on your way, having helped nobody.

resolutions.label: lay a false trail for the pursuers

success.body: You cut a branch and drag it behind your horse down a side track, making a trail that looks like two riders in a hurry. Then you drop Mererid's silk scarf at the fork. The baron's men take the side track with a great shout and go galloping off toward the mountains. You ride to Llanfair by the other road and arrive just in time to be a witness at the wedding.

failure.body: You cut a branch and drag it down a side track to make a false trail, but the baron's huntsman is not a fool. He looks at the marks, looks at you, and sends half the men after the lovers and half after you. You spend the next two days hiding in a hayloft.

entries.body: You kneel beside the young hermit. The voices sing around you.

resolutions.label: pray until the voices' meaning becomes clear

success.body: You pray for a long time, and the voices sing, and slowly you find that you are not frightened. When you open your eyes, the young hermit is smiling. "It is not a mockery," he says. "She is only singing. She likes to sing." He stays at the temple for the rest of his life, and it becomes a place of great peace, where hunters come to pray before they hunt.

failure.body: You pray, but the voices grow louder, and harsher, and the hermit covers his ears. At last, you both flee the temple. You do not know what you heard.

resolutions.label: sing the psalms back to the voices

success.body: You do not only pray. You stand and sing, loudly, the next verse of whatever psalm the voices are singing, and they stop, and listen, and then sing the verse after. You sing to each other all afternoon, verse and answer, until the hermit is laughing through his tears. "She only wanted someone to sing with," he says. He stays at the temple the rest of his life, and it becomes a place of great peace.

failure.body: You stand and sing the next verse. The voices stop, and are silent, and do not sing again while you are there. The hermit looks at you reproachfully.

entries.body: You hold out your arms. Eirlys looks at you, and then at the door, and then, taking a breath, she lets you lift her. She weighs no more than a bundle of feathers.

resolutions.label: carry the fay girl across the church threshold

success.body: You step over the threshold. There is a moment when the air is thick as water, and Eirlys cries out, and then you are through, and she is looking round the church with eyes like stars. You set her down in the last pew. She sits through the whole Mass without moving, and when the priest lifts the bread, she weeps. Afterwards, the priest, who has been glaring at her throughout, comes over and gives her a piece of blessed bread, a little stiffly. "If you come every week," he says, "you must sit still." She comes every week.

failure.body: You step over the threshold, and the air is thick as water, and Eirlys cries out in pain. You stumble back out. She lies on the grass, shaking. "Too much," she whispers. "Too much light." She goes back into the wood, and does not come to listen at the door again.

entries.body: You look at their faces. They are tired, frightened men. "Show me your captain," you say.

resolutions.label: lead the mutiny against the cruel captain

success.body: You go to Sir Grummore's tent with them at midnight, and when he wakes up, it is to find his own men round his bed with their swords drawn, and a knight at their head. You do not kill him. You tie him to his own tent-pole and leave him for the old king's provosts. The soldiers go home. Sir Grummore, you hear, is sent to command a garrison on the Isle of Man, where there is nobody to hang.

failure.body: You go to the captain's tent at midnight, but he is awake, and he has guards. The mutiny fails. The next day, Sir Grummore hangs the sergeant. You escape into the marsh.

resolutions.label: take the captain alive by stealth instead of storm

success.body: You tell the soldiers to wait, and go alone. You crawl under the back of Sir Grummore's tent at midnight, past his sleeping guards, and when he wakes, it is to find your hand over his mouth and your knife at his throat. You tie him to his own tent-pole and leave him for the old king's provosts. The soldiers go home. Sir Grummore is sent to command a garrison on the Isle of Man.

failure.body: You crawl under the back of the captain's tent, and he is awake, sitting in the dark with a crossbow. The mutiny is over before it starts.

entries.body: "Dinabutius," you call up to him. "Do you know why your brother died?" The giant scowls. "Because your king killed him," he says.

resolutions.label: tell the grieving giant what his brother did

success.body: You tell him. You tell him of the duchess of Brittany, and the old woman on the spit, and the children. You tell him plainly and without anger. The giant listens with his great face growing grey. When you finish, he sits down on the hill, and the bell tower falls out of his hand into a haystack. "He was my little brother," he says at last. "He used to follow me everywhere." He weeps for a long time, and nobody in the town dares move. Then he gets up and walks away into the mountains, and the town rings its bell for him, crookedly, as he goes.

failure.body: You tell him of the duchess and the children. The giant listens with his face growing red, not grey. "Lies," he roars. "Arthur's lies!" He hurls the bell tower. It lands on the town hall. You realise too late that there are some things a grieving man cannot hear.

resolutions.label: pray with the giant for his brother's soul

success.body: You do not tell him what his brother did. You kneel on the hillside and ask him if his brother had a name before he was the giant of the Mount. He had: Custennin. You pray for Custennin, aloud, with all the town listening. After a while, the giant sets down the bell tower and kneels too, and puts his great hands together clumsily. When you have finished, he walks away into the mountains. The town rings its bell for him, crookedly.

failure.body: You kneel and begin to pray for his brother's soul. The giant looks down at you. "He has no soul," he says. "Your king took it." He hurls the bell tower. It lands on the town hall.

entries.body: You take off your helm and walk into the cave. At the far end, on a stone ledge, an old man lies sleeping, with a white beard that trails to the floor and his hands folded on his chest.

resolutions.label: kneel and speak to the sleeping saint

success.body: You kneel and ask him the way. For a long moment, nothing happens. Then the old man opens his eyes. They are very blue. "You are asking the wrong question," he says, in a voice like dry leaves. "Not the way. The reason." He closes his eyes again. But he has spoken, for the first time in two hundred years, and when you come out and tell the nun, she drops her basket and runs down the mountain to tell everyone. Pilgrims come for a year after. You carry the words with you: *not the way, the reason.*

partial.body: You kneel and ask him the way. The old man sighs in his sleep and turns over, like a man who has been disturbed and does not mind. You feel, as you go out, that you have been given a little of his peace.

failure.body: You kneel and ask him the way. He does not stir. The cave is cold. You come out feeling, for no reason you can name, that you have been found wanting.

entries.body: You ride into the square and throw down your gauntlet at Cadell's feet. "I will stand for the queen," you say. The crowd breaks into a roar. Cadell smiles thinly and calls for his armour.

resolutions.label: fight Prince Cadell in trial by combat

success.body: Cadell is a strong swordsman, and he fights for a crown, but you fight for a life. The combat lasts until the sun is touching the hills. Then Cadell overreaches, and you beat his sword down and put your point to his throat. "Confess," you say. He confesses, in front of the whole town, that the queen is innocent. Aeronwen is unchained. She walks to where you stand, takes your hand and kisses it. "I will not forget," she says. The men of Dyfed carry you round the square on their shoulders.

failure.body: Cadell is a strong swordsman, and he fights for a crown. The combat lasts until the sun is touching the hills. Then your foot slips on the cobbles, and his sword opens your side. You fall. The herald declares the queen guilty. As they carry you out of the square, you see the smoke begin to rise. You will carry that smoke with you for the rest of your life.

resolutions.label: charge Prince Cadell on horseback in the lists

success.body: The townsfolk clear the square, and you and Cadell ride at each other with lances across the cobbles. On the second pass, your lance takes him on the helm and lifts him out of the saddle, and he lands in the piled faggots at the queen's feet. He does not get up for some time. When he does, he confesses. Aeronwen is freed and restored to her throne, and Cadell is sent over the sea in a boat with no oars.

failure.body: The townsfolk clear the square, and you and Cadell ride at each other across the cobbles. Your horse shies at the smell of pitch from the faggots, and Cadell's lance takes you in the chest. You go down among the kindling. By the time you have been dragged clear, the herald has declared the queen guilty, and they are lighting the torches.

entries.body:
You come upon a small party on the road: two elderly nuns on mules, and between them a tall old woman in a plain grey habit who sits her horse like a queen. She has a leather case on her knees and holds it as if it were full of eggs.

"You are going toward Camelot?" she asks. "Then perhaps you will ride with us. The roads are not what they were." She studies your face. "I am Igraine. I was Queen of Cornwall, and then of all Britain, and now I am Sister Igraine of Amesbury. The High King is my son. I have not seen him since he was two hours old. Merlin took him from my arms in the night." She tightens her grip on the case. "His baby gown is in here, and a lock of his hair. He does not know I kept them. He does not know me at all. I am afraid," she says, very steadily, "that he will not want to."

responses.label: You may escort Queen Igraine to Camelot and see her safely to her son.
You may ride ahead to Camelot and prepare the High King for his mother's coming.
You may ask Queen Igraine about the night her son was born.

entries.body:
You come upon a strange procession on a moorland road: a cart hung with black cloth, drawn by two black oxen, with a lady walking beside it in mourning. In the cart, propped against a coffin, is a battered shield painted with a silver fish.

"I am the Queen of the Waste Lands," the lady says. Her voice is hoarse from weeping. "The shield is my husband's. He was the brother of King Pellam of Corbenic, and he was killed by a knight who would not give his name, in a quarrel over a hound. The knight took my husband's horse and left his shield in a ditch." She lays her hand on the painted fish. "I will not bury my lord until someone carries this shield in honour and wins back what was taken. Every knight I have asked has found a reason to ride on." She looks at you. "What is your reason?"

responses.label: You may take up the dead lord's shield and seek out the nameless knight.
You may help the queen bury her husband now, with the honours he deserves.

entries.body:
You come upon a stone well in a hollow of the hills, ringed by a hundred pilgrims waiting their turn. At the well itself sits a tall woman in a patched brown habit, with a bucket and a ladle and a thin gold circlet on her grey hair.

"Another knight," she says. "Welcome. I am Heledd. I was Queen of Powys until I gave my crown to my cousin, who wanted it, in return for this well, which he did not." She ladles water into a pilgrim's cupped hands. "It heals. Whatever ails you. But it only heals those who first tell the truth about themselves, out loud, to me." She smiles at the line of pilgrims. "Most of them turn back when they reach the front. Will you drink?"

A man near the back of the line is shouting that the well is a fraud, and that the old queen keeps the best cures for those who pay.

responses.label: You may confess the truth of yourself to Queen Heledd and drink from the well.
You may deal with the angry pilgrim before he stirs up the crowd.

entries.body:
You come upon a pavilion of green silk pitched beside a lake, with a table set before it for two. A lady in a gown the colour of a kingfisher's wing sits at the table, peeling a pear with a little silver knife. There is something of Arthur in her face, and something of the lake.

"Sit down, little knight," she says. "I have been waiting all morning, and the pear is getting brown. I am Morgan. Queen of Gore, when it suits me. The High King's sister, when it suits him." She points the knife at a bundle on the grass: a mantle of cloth of gold, set with stones that glitter like frost. "I have a gift for my brother, and no one I trust to carry it. It is the finest thing I have ever made. Will you take it to him? I will owe you a favour. A favour from me," she adds, smiling, "is worth a great deal."

responses.label: You may carry Morgan's mantle to Camelot as a gift for the High King.
You may insist that Morgan's own messenger try the mantle on first.
* You may stay and dine with Morgan and try to win her favour for yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a lady in a hooded cloak sitting on a stile in the rain, with a basket of apples on her arm and a pair of fine jewelled slippers peeping out from under a mud-stained hem. She pushes back her hood. She is handsome, past her youth, with a laugh in her eyes and a crown of red-gold braids.

"Oh, good," she says. "A knight. I am Morgause, Queen of Orkney. My husband is dead, and my sons are grown and very busy with their honour." She lowers her voice. "There is a knight called Lamorak who is waiting for me in a woodcutter's hut a mile from here, and I am late, and I have lost my way. Also, my son Gaheris has been following me since Carlisle." She looks back down the road, where a single rider is just coming into view. "He will kill Lamorak if he finds him. And me too, very likely. I would be so grateful if you would help me."

responses.label: You may take Queen Morgause to her lover by a hidden way.
You may delay Sir Gaheris on the road so that the queen can slip away.
You may tell Sir Gaheris where his mother is going.

entries.body:
You come upon a grey beach where a line of soldiers stand in the surf, flogging the waves with whips. Each time a wave comes in, they lash it, and a woman on a rock above them counts the strokes aloud. She is a big, fierce queen in blue war-paint, with a bronze torc at her throat and her hair shorn short in mourning.

"Three hundred and six," she says. "Three hundred and seven." She sees you. "You. Knight. I am Anna, Queen of the Picts. This sea drowned my husband and both my sons in a single night. So I have sentenced it to a thousand strokes, and then it will be pardoned." Her voice cracks. "Three hundred and eight. What do you want? If you have come to tell me the sea cannot feel it, I have heard that."

The soldiers look exhausted. One of them catches your eye, desperate.

responses.label: You may help Queen Anna finish punishing the sea.
You may try to comfort Queen Anna in her grief.
You may slip into the queen's undefended camp and help yourself to her treasure.

entries.body: You take the axe. It is heavier than you remember any axe being. The Green Knight kneels in the snow.

resolutions.label: strike the blow that gives the land a season

success.body: You strike. The head rolls, and does not rise. Green runs out of him into the snow, and the snow melts, and grass comes up, and far away, in the south, the rivers run faster. You kneel in the new grass for a long time. When you ride away, the wood behind you is green and full of birdsong, in the middle of winter. You do not know how long it will last. A season, he said. It is enough.

failure.body: You strike, and the axe turns in your hands, and cuts only snow. The Green Knight looks up at you, sorrowfully. "Then it is not your blow," he says. He takes back his axe.

resolutions.label: strike the blow with a prayer for the land

success.body: You kneel in the snow beside him before you lift the axe, and pray, for the land, and the old king, and the green that is going out of Britain. Then you strike. His head rolls, and does not rise. Green runs out of him into the snow, and the snow melts, and grass comes up, and far away in the south the rivers run faster. You kneel in the new grass for a long time. A season, he said. It is enough.

failure.body: You kneel and pray before you strike, and when you rise, you cannot lift the axe. The Green Knight looks up at you. "Then it is not your blow," he says.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a hunting party resting in a glade, where three queens sit on a spread cloak eating cherries. They are dressed in black, white and red, and their ladies keep a respectful distance. The queen in red spits a stone into the grass and beckons you with one finger.

"I am the Queen of Northgalis," she says. "These are the Queens of Eastland and of the Out Isles. We have a grievance, and you look like a knight who could settle it." She smiles without warmth. "There is a knight called Sir Breunor, who lives in the castle at the head of this valley. He came to our court last Candlemas, danced with each of us in turn, promised each of us his heart, and left in the night with our three best horses. We want his shield hung upside down in our hall. We will pay you in gold, or in something better."

The Queen of the Out Isles adds, "He is very handsome. Try not to spoil his face."

responses.label: You may ride to Sir Breunor's castle and take his shield for the three queens.
You may ride ahead and warn Sir Breunor that three queens want his shield.
* You may court the Queen of Northgalis and make her forget Sir Breunor.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a great crowd in the courtyard at Camelot, gathered around a knight kneeling in chains. Queen Guinevere sits on a chair beneath the cloister, with her ladies about her. She is very beautiful and very angry.

"This is Sir Gromer," a squire whispers to you. "He met a maiden in the forest and took her by force. The High King would have had him hanged, but the queen asked for his life. She has set him a riddle instead. If he answers it within a year, he lives."

The queen's clear voice rings across the courtyard. "What is it that women most desire? You have a year and a day to find out, Sir Gromer. Ask everyone. And if you cannot answer, you will hang, and deserve to." She looks up and sees you. "You. You may ride with him, if you like, and see that he asks honestly. Or you may tell me that I am being too merciful, as my husband's knights have been doing all morning."

responses.label: You may ride with Sir Gromer and help him find the answer.
You may argue before the queen that Sir Gromer should hang now.

entries.body:
You come upon a fishwife at a quayside in the west, gutting herring on an upturned boat. She has a coarse apron, a coarse shawl and a coarse voice, and the finest hands you have ever seen on a fishwife. Beneath the herring in her basket, something gleams gold.

"Don't stare," she says, without looking up. "People notice when knights stare. I am Orlaith, Queen of Leinster, and this is my crown. My husband used it as a stake in a game of dice with the King of Munster last Samhain and lost it, and I will not have it said that I was queened with a gambler's forfeit. So I took it back." She flicks a fish-head into the water. "The Munster men are searching every ship for Ireland. I need a knight to carry the basket aboard. They will not search a knight."

responses.label: You may smuggle the queen's crown aboard ship past the Munster men.
You may take the crown from Queen Orlaith and sell it to the King of Munster's men.

entries.body:
You come upon a lady sitting on a tree root in a green wood, with a garland of may blossom slipping over one eye. She is very beautiful and very muddy. Beside her stands a page of about ten, holding two horses and trying not to cry.

"Good knight," the lady says, straightening the garland. "I am Guinevere. The queen. You may not recognise me in this state." She is trying hard to sound calm. "We came a-maying this morning, ten knights and ten ladies, all in green. Sir Meliagaunt of Gore and a hundred men rode out of the trees and took them. My knights had no armour, only green silk. They fought with branches." Her voice shakes. "I told this boy to ride with me and I told the others I would bring help. Now Meliagaunt is taking them to his castle, and I do not know the way home."

responses.label: You may escort Queen Guinevere safely back to Camelot.
You may ride after Sir Meliagaunt and free the captive knights and ladies.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
"Which way do you want to go?" you ask. Cian points west, toward the mountains. "My uncle has a farm," he says.

resolutions.label: get the lovers past the Earl's men

success.body: You lead them off the road and across the plain by night, following a stream-bed, and through a wood, and past the Earl's men asleep by their fire. By dawn, you are in the hills. The young woman takes off her rich gown and puts on a shepherd's smock from Cian's pack, and laughs, and looks happier than any lady you have seen. You leave them at the uncle's farm. A year later, you hear that Lord Maelwas has a grandchild and has forgiven everyone.

failure.body: You lead them off the road and across the plain, but the Earl's men have hounds. You are caught at the edge of the wood. Cian is taken. You and the young woman are sent back to her father.

resolutions.label: carry them both out on your horse at a gallop

success.body: You put the girl in front of you and the shepherd behind, and ride straight past the Earl's watchfire before its men are on their feet, and on across the plain at a gallop, with three people on one horse and the stars wheeling. By dawn you are in the hills. You leave them at the uncle's farm. A year later, you hear that Lord Maelwas has a grandchild and has forgiven everyone.

failure.body: You put them both on your horse and gallop, and the horse, carrying three, goes lame a mile past the watchfire. The Earl's men catch up.

entries.body:
You come upon a town square in Dyfed where a stake has been driven into the ground and faggots piled around it. A queen stands chained to the stake. She is young, pale and composed, dressed in a white shift, with her dark hair unbound. A crowd stands around her, silent.

A herald reads from a scroll. "Queen Aeronwen, accused by her husband's brother Prince Cadell of killing King Rhodri by witchcraft. She has no champion. By the law of Dyfed, she burns at sunset."

Prince Cadell, a handsome man in black velvet, stands beside the herald with his hand on the hilt of his sword. When he sees you, his face tightens.

The queen raises her head. "I did not kill my husband," she says clearly. "He died of a fever. Cadell wants his throne, and there is no one left to say so." She looks straight at you. "Is there?"

responses.label: You may stand as Queen Aeronwen's champion against Prince Cadell.
You may seek out the truth of King Rhodri's death before sunset.
You may let the law of Dyfed take its course.

entries.body:
"When?" you ask. The old hermit looks at his slate for a long time.

"Not in your life," he says. "Nor mine. Nor your children's. It will come back when Britain has forgotten it was ever here, and has become something else, with other kings and other names. It will come back to someone who is not looking for it." He puts down the slate and looks at you with great kindness. "That is the secret. The stones know it. They are not sad about it. Only we are." He gives you bread and salt, and lets you sit in the circle until the sun goes down, and in the silence, very faintly, you think you hear the stones begin to sing.
Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

"I will speak for you, my lord," you say. You find Tegau at the millrace with her sleeves rolled up, arguing with a young carter about the price of oats. She hears the words "King Leodegrance" and puts her hands on her hips.

resolutions.label: plead the old king's case with courtesy

success.body: You speak of the king's kindness, his wealth and his loneliness, and you are honest about his age and his ribbons. Tegau laughs, but she listens. "He is a good man," she admits. "He paid my father's fine for him when the river flooded." She sends back an answer: she will not marry him, but she will come and dine at his hall every Sunday and argue with him about oats.
