When you bring this to Leodegrance, he claps his hands like a boy. "A courtship! A proper courtship, as in the romances!"

failure.body: You speak of the king's kindness, his wealth and his loneliness, but you get carried away and describe his beard as "silver as a lake at dawn". Tegau laughs until she has to sit down. The young carter laughs too, and so do the millhands, and by nightfall the whole village is calling the king "Old Lake-at-Dawn". Leodegrance hears of it within a day. You resolve to leave poetry to poets.

resolutions.label: win Tegau's regard by working the mill beside her

success.body: You do not make a speech. You roll up your sleeves, as she has, and carry sacks, and mend the sluice-gate, and by evening you are floury to the eyebrows. Then you tell her the king sent you, and that he is the sort of man who would have done the same. Tegau laughs. "He would not," she says. "But he might send more knights like you." She agrees to dine with the old king every Sunday. He is delighted.

failure.body: You roll up your sleeves and carry sacks, and on the fourth sack you slip on the wet stones and go into the millrace. Tegau fishes you out with a boathook. By the time you are dry, the carter has told the whole village, and nobody will hear a word about the old king.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You walk round the table to the seat with your name on it. The whole court watches.

resolutions.label: take your place among the knights of the Round Table

success.body: You sit down. The wood is warm, as if someone has just left it. All round the table, the other knights are sitting down, one by one, and when the last of them is seated, the young king raises his cup. "To the table," he says. "Where no man is higher than any other." You drink. You feel, for a moment, that you are part of something that will last forever. The young king gives each knight a gift that night. Yours is a sword, plain and good, called Clarent. "For peace," he says. "Not for war."

partial.body: You sit down, and the wood is warm, and the young king raises his cup. You drink with the others. You are a knight of the Round Table. It is enough.

failure.body: You walk to the seat, and as you touch it, your name fades. The court whispers. You are not ready. You go out of the hall with your face burning.

entries.body: You ride ahead to the hill, where the Bishop of Hereford is waiting in a tent, counting silver. He is a lean man with sharp eyes. "The giant," he says. "Yes. A very useful giant."

resolutions.label: hold the bishop to his word

success.body: You ask him, plainly, whether he means to baptise the giant. He hesitates for a moment too long. You remind him of what is written about those who make promises to the simple and do not keep them. You mention that you will be riding to Canterbury soon. The bishop goes pale. When Hu arrives, sweating, with the chapel on his back, the bishop is waiting at a pond in his best vestments. Hu is baptised with a whole bucket, and after, he picks you up and kisses you on both cheeks, which is like being kissed by a haystack.

failure.body: You ask him whether he means to baptise the giant. "Of course," he says smoothly, "once the chapel is consecrated. And the tower rebuilt. And the road." He smiles. You realise that Hu will be carrying things for this bishop for the rest of his life, and there is nothing you can say to stop it.

resolutions.label: drive a hard bargain on the giant's behalf

success.body: You point out that a giant who carries chapels is worth more than a bishop's silver, and that the Abbot of Gloucester, who has three chapels to move, would be very glad of him. The bishop's eyes narrow. You haggle for an hour. At the end, the bishop agrees to baptise Hu at once, pay him a cow a week for his labour, and give him a hut of his own on the hill. Hu, when he hears it, cannot believe his luck. "A cow a week," he keeps saying. "A cow!"

failure.body: You point out that the Abbot of Gloucester would be glad of such a giant. The bishop smiles. "Then take him to Gloucester," he says, "and the abbot will ask him to carry three chapels, and baptise him never." You have no answer.

entries.body: You wait until the Queen of the Fay has fallen asleep in her bower, with the weaver's head in her lap. Then you creep closer.

resolutions.label: unmake the King of the Fay's enchantment

success.body: You find what you are looking for tucked into Titania's crown: a sprig of a purple flower, still wet with dew. You pluck it out and crush it and rub the juice on her eyelids, then on the weaver's long ears. The queen wakes, and looks at the weaver, and screams. The weaver's head is his own again, and he is very disappointed. His wife hauls him out of the wood by the ear. The Fay Queen looks at you with cold, beautiful eyes. "My husband," she says, "will be very sorry he did that." She rewards you with a single rose that never fades.

failure.body: You find a sprig of purple flower in her crown, and pluck it, and crush it, and try to rub the juice on her eyes. She wakes before you can. She looks at you, and her eyes are full of the juice's glamour, and she falls deeply in love with you. It is a very bad week. When the spell wears off, she does not forgive you.

resolutions.label: find the flower that undoes the love-spell

success.body: Every love-spell has its antidote, the old women say, and it grows near the flower that made it. You search the wood round the bower until you find it: a small white flower, growing beside the purple one. You crush it and rub it on the Queen's eyelids as she sleeps, and on the weaver's long ears. The Queen wakes, looks at the weaver and screams. His head is his own again. His wife hauls him out of the wood by the ear.

failure.body: You search the wood for the antidote and find a small white flower, and rub it on the Queen's eyelids. It is the wrong flower. She sneezes, wakes and has you thrown out of the wood by a great many very small guards.

entries.body: "Come," you say. "Take hold of my stirrup. We will walk out together." Owain shrugs and picks up his sack. "Many have tried," he says. "Well, one. Me."

resolutions.label: break the spell of the crossroads

success.body: You do not follow the roads. You turn your back to the signpost and walk straight out across the fields, through a hedge, over a ditch and through a pond. Owain follows, cursing. You keep going straight, through a farmyard and a barn and another hedge, and after an hour, you come out on a road you do not know. Owain falls on his knees and kisses it. Then he goes into the next village and sells everything in the sack and gives the money to the church. He says it is the only way to be sure.

failure.body: You turn your back to the signpost and walk straight out across the fields. After an hour, you come to a crossroads, and there is a stone, and there is a signpost pointing to itself. Owain sits down on the stone. So do you.

resolutions.label: follow the stars, not the roads

success.body: You wait until night and look up. The roads may be bewitched, but the stars are not. You take the pole star over your left shoulder and walk straight, with Owain holding your stirrup, over hedge and ditch and field, never looking at a signpost. By dawn you are ten miles away on a road you do not know. Owain falls on his knees and kisses it. He sells everything in the sack and gives the money to the church.

failure.body: You wait for night and take the pole star over your shoulder and walk. At midnight, clouds cover the sky. At dawn, you are at the crossroads.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You know this beast. You rode after it once with a foolish old king, calling *left, always left*. You draw your sword and ride at the Saxon, who flees without loosing his arrow.

Then you kneel beside the Questing Beast and pull the arrow out of its side, and bind the wound with your own cloak. It watches you all the while. When you are done, it gets to its feet, slowly, and walks away into the trees, and at the edge of the clearing, it stops and looks back. From its belly comes the sound of hounds, and it is almost like laughing.

notes: Lose Story Token #2

entries.body: You take your place among the guard at the stake. The law is the law. The king made it. The riders come out of the woods like a storm.

resolutions.label: hold the stake against the rescuers

success.body: You fight at the stake as the riders crash into the guard. They are the best knights in the world, and there are many of them, and they are fighting for their queen. You hold them longer than anyone. But at last they break through, and cut the queen's chains, and carry her away. The king, afterwards, sends for you. "You held," he says. "Longer than anyone. I will not forget." He looks at the ashes, where Gareth and Gaheris lie. "Nobody will forget," he says.

failure.body: You fight at the stake, and the riders break through the guard in the first charge, and you are struck down. When you come to, the queen is gone, and Gareth and Gaheris are dead in the ashes, and the war has begun.

resolutions.label: form the guard into a wall round the stake

success.body: You do not fight alone. You take command of the guard, who are frightened and disordered, and form them into a ring round the stake, shields locked, as the old king taught at Badon. When the riders come out of the woods, they strike a wall. It holds longer than anything could have held. At last, they break through and carry the queen away. The king, afterwards, sends for you. "You held," he says.

failure.body: You form the guard into a ring, but the riders are the best knights in the world, and they come through the ring at its weakest place, which is where Gareth and Gaheris are standing unarmed.

entries.body: "I am the old king's," you say. "Tell me when." The goldsmith grips your hand.

resolutions.label: seize the Ludgate for the old king

success.body: When the old king's army is sighted from the walls, you lead the loyalists to the Ludgate at midnight. The sergeant of the watch has made sure his men are drunk. You overpower the rest, and throw open the gate, and the old king's vanguard pours into London with torches. By dawn, the city is his. The goldsmith weeps. The laundress kisses you on both cheeks. The old king, riding in at noon, stops his horse beside you and lifts his hand to you.

failure.body: When the old king's army is sighted, you lead the loyalists to the Ludgate, but Mordred's men are waiting. Someone talked. Half the loyalists are taken. You escape over the wall.

resolutions.label: slip over the wall and bring the king's vanguard to the gate

success.body: You do not wait inside. You go over the wall the night before, find the old king's vanguard camped at Brentford, and ride back with their captain in the dark. At midnight, the loyalists open the Ludgate from inside, and you ride through it at the head of a hundred horse. By dawn, London is the old king's. The goldsmith weeps. The laundress kisses you on both cheeks.

failure.body: You go over the wall and ride to Brentford, but the vanguard's captain does not trust you, and keeps you under guard until morning. By then, the loyalists have tried the gate alone.

entries.body: You take the sword from Bedivere's hand. It is heavier than anything you have ever carried.

resolutions.label: throw Excalibur into the lake

success.body: You walk to the edge of the water. You look at the sword for a long time. Then you throw it, with all your strength, out over the lake, and it wheels in the mist, flashing, and an arm in white samite rises out of the water and catches it by the hilt, and brandishes it three times, and draws it under. Bedivere falls to his knees. Behind you, on the shore, where the old king lies, you hear a long sigh, like a man who has put down a heavy load.

failure.body: You walk to the edge of the water, and look at the sword, and you cannot either. You give it back to Bedivere. In the end, he throws it himself, weeping, and the arm rises and catches it. You watch from the shore, ashamed.

resolutions.label: throw it far and true with your whole strength

success.body: The sword is heavier than anything you have ever carried, and your arms are shaking from the battle. You walk to the edge of the water and throw it, with everything you have left, and it wheels far out over the lake, farther than you could have thrown it, flashing. An arm in white samite rises and catches it and brandishes it three times and draws it under. Bedivere falls to his knees. From the shore, you hear a long sigh, like a man putting down a heavy load.

failure.body: You throw it with everything you have left, and it falls short, in the reeds. Bedivere wades in and throws it himself. The arm rises and takes it.

entries.body: You tie the shepherd's rope to your own, and to your horse's harness, and lower yourself into the dark.

resolutions.label: climb down and haul the flock out

success.body: The hole opens into a cavern with a sandy floor, where forty frightened sheep stand huddled round a very proud dog. You tie the sheep one by one to the rope, and the shepherd and your horse haul them up, bleating and kicking. It takes all day. Your arms are shaking by the end. The last to come up is the dog, and then you. The shepherd gives you the best of the lambs and the dog's undying devotion, which lasts about a day.

failure.body: The hole opens into a cavern. You tie the first sheep to the rope, and the shepherd hauls, and the rope snaps. You spend the night in the cavern with forty sheep and a dog, until the shepherd comes back at dawn with a longer rope and his three brothers.

entries.body: You walk down the long nave. The unicorn lifts its head and looks at you with dark, sad eyes.

resolutions.label: kneel beside the unicorn with a pure heart

success.body: You kneel beside it on the cold stone. The unicorn lays its head in your lap, as the old books say it only does for the pure. You sit with it until dawn. Then it rises, and touches your forehead with its horn, and walks out of the cathedral, and the crowd parts before it. The huntsmen do not raise a net. You feel, all that day, as though something has been washed out of you.

partial.body: You kneel beside it. It looks at you for a long time, and then lays its head back down on the altar step. It does not come to you. But it lets you stay. In the morning, it is gone, and you do not know where.

failure.body: You kneel beside it. The unicorn gets up and moves away from you to the far side of the altar. You feel every eye in the cathedral on you as you walk back down the nave.

entries.body: You row across to the white ship alone and climb aboard. The deck is warm under your feet, like a living thing.

resolutions.label: walk the deck of the ship of faith

success.body: You walk to the bed and look at the sword, and do not touch it. You kneel and pray. When you rise, you find the ship has carried you, with no wind, to the edge of a shore you do not know, where a white chapel stands on a hill. You go into the chapel. It is empty, but there is a light on the altar, and you are given, kneeling there, a peace you cannot describe to anyone afterward. When you come out, you are on the beach beside your own ship, and your sailors swear you have been gone three days.

partial.body: You walk to the bed and look at the sword. You feel the ship tilt beneath you, gently, as if deciding. Then you are back in your own boat, and the white ship is sailing away across the flat grey sea. You have been allowed to see it. That is all.

failure.body: You walk toward the bed, and the deck tilts beneath you like a tipped plate, and you slide off into the sea. When you come up, the white ship is gone.

entries.body: "The abbot is a fool," you say, "but he is not worth a curse. Curses come home." The eldest witch narrows her eyes. "What do you know about curses?"

resolutions.label: talk the witches out of their curse

success.body: You talk to them all night. You find out that the abbot burned their sister, and you promise to take it to the bishop, and you do. The bishop, who has had trouble with that abbot before, sends him to a monastery in the far north with very bad food. The witches send you a basket of eggs, very large ones, and a note that says *Thank you. Do not eat the brown ones.*

failure.body: You talk to them all night. At dawn, the eldest witch says, "You talk too much," and waves her spoon. You cannot speak for a week.

resolutions.label: lift the curse from the cauldron yourself

success.body: While the witches argue about the abbot, you lean over the cauldron and speak into it the old words for unmaking, very softly, three times. The green stuff turns grey, and then clear, and then smells of onions. The eldest witch sniffs it. "Soup," she says in disgust. "You have made it soup." She laughs until she has to sit down. They eat the soup. The abbot, somewhere in Crowland, never knows how close it was.

failure.body: You lean over the cauldron and speak the words for unmaking. The cauldron speaks back. The curse, it seems, is now on you.

entries.body: You think carefully. Then you ask her: "Whom does this feast serve?"

resolutions.label: ask the right question at the Fisher King's table

success.body: The girl smiles, a very old smile. "It serves the king," she says. "And the land. And you." She takes your hand and leads you into the hall, and you eat, and the food is everything you have ever loved. When you come out, the girl is gone, and the island is only an island, and the apple trees are in blossom, though it is autumn. Somewhere far away, you feel, a wound has stopped bleeding for a moment.

partial.body: The girl considers your question. "Nearly," she says. She lets you eat, and the food is good. But when you come out, the apple trees are bare.

failure.body: The girl shakes her head. "That is not a question," she says. "That is a greedy man's question." The hall fades, and you are standing on an empty island.

entries.body: You ride up under the rampart. "What would it take," you call up, "for you to let him go?" The brigand laughs wearily. "Take him away," he says. "That is all."

resolutions.label: negotiate the ransom of the annoying lord

success.body: You haggle, for form's sake. You get them down to fifty marks, and then to ten, and then to the brigands paying you five marks to take him. Sir Brewen is outraged at the price. You ride him home to his father, who looks at his son, and at you, and sighs, and pays you fifty marks for your trouble. "Five marks," says the father. "They paid you five marks. I would have paid them fifty."

failure.body: You haggle, but Sir Brewen hears you from inside the hut and starts shouting that he is worth a thousand marks and he will not be sold for less. The brigands, insulted on his behalf, raise the ransom again.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride at the soldiers.

resolutions.label: free the conscripts from Mordred's men

success.body: You ride through them, and they scatter, not expecting a fight. You cut the conscripts loose, and they pick up the soldiers' spears and turn on them. In minutes, the recruiting party is fleeing into the marsh. The old woman's grandsons are among the freed. She kisses your hand. The young men of the village want to ride with you. You tell them to go home and look after their grandmothers.

failure.body: You ride at the soldiers, but there are more than you counted, and they have horses. You are driven off into the marsh. The conscripts are taken away.

resolutions.label: ambush the recruiting party on the causeway

success.body: You follow them out of the village and wait where the causeway crosses a deep dyke, and when they are strung out along it with their conscripts roped between them, you come out of the reeds and cut the rope, and push the nearest soldier into the dyke. The conscripts do the rest. The old woman's grandsons are home by nightfall.

failure.body: You wait by the dyke all afternoon, up to your knees in reeds, and the recruiting party takes the drove road instead. By the time you find their tracks, they are across the river with the boys. You go back and tell the old woman, and she does not say anything.

entries.body:
The Questing Beast does not run. It walks up to you, slowly, with its serpent's head lowered, and it lays its head against your horse's neck, and it sighs.

You understand. Pellinore is dead. The Orkney brothers killed him by a ford, you learn later, and the beast has been searching for someone to chase it ever since. It knows you. You rode after it once, beside him.

You ride after it all that day, not trying to catch it, only following, the way he used to. At dusk, it stops at a pool and drinks, and looks back at you, and goes on into the dark. You find yourself weeping for a foolish old king who talked to his horse.

notes: Lose Story Token #2

entries.body: "What price?" you ask. The raven cocks its head. "An eye," it says. "Only one. You will not miss it."

resolutions.label: outbargain the raven

success.body: You laugh, and tell it that a knight with one eye is no use to ravens, since he cannot fight, and so will not die in the battle, and so will not feed them. The raven considers this. "A drop of blood, then," it says, sulkily. You give it a drop from your thumb. It tells you: in May, on a plain in the west, where two armies will meet to parley and an adder will ruin everything. You ride away knowing more than you want to.

failure.body: You try to bargain it down, but the raven only laughs, and takes its price anyway, by pecking your hand to the bone. It tells you nothing. The ravens laugh as you ride away.

entries.body: You kneel beside the bed. Evelake's fingers are cold and light. They move over your brow and your cheeks for a long time, while the monks hold their breath.

resolutions.label: bear his searching with a clean heart

success.body: At last Evelake sighs. "Not you," he says. "But you are of the company, I think. The one I wait for will ride with knights like you." He lays his hand on your head and blesses you in a language you do not know. The monks hurry to give you food, a fresh horse-blanket and a flask of water from their spring, which they say has not failed in three hundred years.

partial.body: At last Evelake sighs. "Not you," he says. "There is something unfinished in you. Go and finish it." He blesses you briefly and turns his face to the wall. The monks see you to the gate politely.

failure.body: Evelake's hand stops on your cheek. "There is blood on you," he says, "that has not been repented." The monks look at you, and you find you cannot meet their eyes. You leave the abbey without being asked to stay. At the gate, the bell rings again, all by itself, as though tolling someone out.

entries.body: You kneel on the deck of your own ship and pray. The sailors, after a while, kneel too.

resolutions.label: keep faith and wait for the ship's sign

success.body: The white ship floats beside you all night, silent. At dawn, it begins to move, very slowly, with no wind, and your own ship follows it, as though pulled by a thread. It leads you out of the grey sea into a blue one, within sight of the coast of Wales, and then it turns away west and is gone. The sailors swear they will never tell anyone. You think they will tell everyone.

failure.body: You kneel on the deck and pray, but the sailors do not, and during the night, one of them rows across to the white ship to steal the sword. There is a flash of white light, and the rowing boat drifts back empty.

entries.body: You rise from your place. "I will fight for the queen," you say. The hall goes silent. The queen looks at you with astonishment and gratitude.

resolutions.label: fight Sir Mador for the queen's honour

success.body: Sir Mador is a great knight, and he is fighting for his dead cousin, and he is very angry. You meet him in the lists at Westminster, before the whole court, and it is the longest joust of your life. At last, on the fifth course, you throw him. He yields, and swears the queen is innocent. The queen, afterwards, sends for you, and gives you her own ring, and says very quietly, "I will not forget who stood up." She does not forget.

failure.body: Sir Mador is a great knight, and he unhorses you on the third course. The queen is condemned. She is saved at the last moment by another champion, who rides in unannounced in plain armour. You watch from the side of the lists, bruised and ashamed.

resolutions.label: fight Sir Mador on foot when the lances break

success.body: Your lances shatter on the first course, and his horse is lamed, and you both come down into the sand. You fight on foot for an hour before the whole court. He is fighting for his dead cousin, and you are fighting for the queen, and at the end, you beat down his sword, and he yields, and swears the queen is innocent. She sends for you afterwards, and gives you her own ring, and says very quietly, "I will not forget who stood up."

failure.body: Your lances shatter and you fight on foot, and Sir Mador is the better swordsman. The queen is condemned, and saved at the last moment by a champion in plain armour.

entries.body: "Come with me," you say. "We will find your mother together, somewhere safe." The girl considers this for a long time, and then holds out her arms.

resolutions.label: carry the child through the war-torn country

success.body: You carry her on your saddle for five days, through a country full of Saxons and deserters, sleeping in hedges and eating what you can find. She sings the whole way. At last you reach a convent in the hills, where the nuns are taking in the children of the war. On the first evening, among the children, a woman comes running. It is her mother. You do not stay to watch. You have seen enough.

failure.body: You carry her on your saddle for five days. On the fourth, she falls ill with a fever from the cellar. You get her to the convent in time, and the nuns save her, but you have caught it too.

resolutions.label: ride her out of the war country as fast as you dare

success.body: You take her up in front of you and ride, by night, across a country full of Saxons and deserters, through fords and over downs, with her singing to her doll the whole way. In three days you reach a convent in the hills where the nuns take in the children of the war. On the first evening, among the children, a woman comes running. You do not stay to watch.

failure.body: You take her up in front of you and ride by night, and at a ford, Saxon riders see you. You outrun them, but she is thrown in the water, and takes a fever. The nuns save her. It is close.

entries.body: "I will do it," you say. Dafydd nods, and smiles. "Thank you," he says. They hang him a moment later. You ride to Ludlow.

resolutions.label: find the buried silver and bring it to the widow

success.body: The third ash tree past the mill has a patch of turned earth at its foot. You dig, and find a leather bag with forty silver marks in it. You take it to the bakehouse. Mistress Anest, a small, thin woman with flour to her elbows, stares at the bag and then at you. When you tell her how you came by it, she sits down on the bakehouse floor and weeps, for the silver and for the thief. She bakes you a loaf, the best you have ever eaten, and asks you to pray with her for Dafydd's soul.

notes: Lose 1 Treasure, if possible

failure.body: The third ash tree past the mill has no turned earth at its foot. Nor does the second, or the fourth. You dig until dark and find nothing but roots. Either Dafydd lied, or someone found it first. You go to the bakehouse and tell Mistress Anest the truth, and give her what silver you have, which is not forty marks.

resolutions.label: work out where he really buried it

success.body: The third ash past the mill has nothing under it. You sit down and think. Dafydd was a thief; he would count the ash trees from the other end, from the road he fled along. You walk to the far end of the row and count three. The earth there is turned. The bag holds forty silver marks. Mistress Anest, when you bring it, sits down on her bakehouse floor and weeps for the silver, and for the thief.

failure.body: The third ash has nothing under it. You think hard, and dig under every other ash in Ludlow, and a good many oaks. The reeve arrests you for damaging the common. You never find the silver.

entries.body: You walk into the centre of the circle and stand there, as the Shining One comes down the avenue toward you.

resolutions.label: face the Shining One with no lie in you

success.body: He stops in front of you, and looks into you, and you feel every lie you have ever told turn over in you like stones in a stream. You do not look away. At last, he smiles, and it is like the sun coming out. He puts a harp into your hands, small and plain and made of dark wood. "It plays only true songs," he says, and walks on through the circle and is gone. The islanders cheer. When you play the harp, it plays songs you did not know you knew.

partial.body: He stops in front of you, and looks into you, and you feel your lies turn over. He does not turn you to stone. But he does not smile either. He walks on.

failure.body: He stops in front of you and looks into you, and your feet go cold, and then your legs. You flee the circle before it reaches your knees. It is a month before you can walk properly.

entries.body: You push through the crowd to the edge of the pit, draw your sword and leap down into it. The crowd gasps. The mastiffs turn toward you.

resolutions.label: fight your way to the giant and break his chain

success.body: You beat the dogs off with the flat of your sword and reach the post, and strike the chain where it is weakest, again and again, until it parts. The giant rises to his full height, and the crowd goes silent. He looks at the baron on his balcony. Then he picks you up, very gently, and climbs out of the pit, and walks through the crowd, which parts for him, and out of the city gate, and does not stop until he reaches the forest. There he sets you down. "Thank you," he says. It is the only thing he ever says.

failure.body: You beat the dogs off and reach the post and strike the chain. But the baron's men are already in the pit, with spears. They drag you off. The last thing you see, before they close the door of the cell, is the giant looking at you through the crowd.

entries.body: You reach for the sack. Rhys screams and clings to it. The priest steps back, crossing himself.

resolutions.label: wrest the treasure from the mad grave-robber

success.body: It takes all your strength to prise his fingers open, one by one. When they finally let go, Rhys falls back against the church door and goes limp, and sleeps for the first time in three days. You look in the sack. There is a gold torc, a gold cup and a sword with a hilt of red enamel. You take it and ride away quickly. That night, something walks from the barrow to your inn, and stands at the door, and waits. You leave before dawn. It follows you for a long time.

failure.body: It takes all your strength to prise his fingers open. When they let go, you stagger back with the sack, and it is heavier than any sack could be, and it pulls you down onto the church steps. You cannot let go. You cannot let go. The priest has to bring a hammer.

resolutions.label: coax the sack from him with a trick

success.body: You kneel beside him and whisper that you have come from King Cunedda himself, who wants his treasure carried back by a stronger man. Rhys looks at you with desperate hope, and lets go. You shoulder the sack and walk out of the churchyard, and do not turn toward the barrow. In the sack are a gold torc, a gold cup and a sword with a hilt of red enamel. That night, something stands at the door of your inn.

failure.body: You kneel beside him and whisper that the king has sent you for his treasure. Rhys looks at you. "He did not," he says. "He told me who he would send." He clutches the sack harder, and screams, and the priest sends you away.

entries.body: "He is an enemy," you say. "The king's men will decide what to do with him." The young Saxon looks at you with despair.

resolutions.label: deliver the Saxon deserter to the king's camp

success.body: You tie his hands and lead him through the storm to the old king's camp. The captain there is a tired, grey knight called Sir Lucan. He questions the young Saxon through an interpreter, learns a great deal about the Saxon host's movements, and then, to your surprise, lets him go. "He has told us what we need," says Sir Lucan. "Why hang a boy?" You are given a purse for the information.

failure.body: You tie his hands and lead him through the storm, but in the dark, he slips his bonds and is gone into the forest. You have lost your prisoner and a night's sleep.

entries.body: You keep your head down and pour wine and listen.

resolutions.label: spy on Mordred's feast undetected

success.body: You pour wine for the Saxon kings, and they talk freely in front of a servant. By the end of the feast, you know how many men each has brought, where they will land, and what Mordred has promised them. You slip out of the hall at midnight and ride for the coast. At the old king's camp over the sea, the old king reads your account in silence. Then he calls his captains. You have given him the whole war.

failure.body: You pour wine for the Saxon kings, and one of them, a sharp-eyed old man, looks at your hands. "Those are not a servant's hands," he says. You flee, and are chased through the streets of London all night.

resolutions.label: loosen the Saxon kings' tongues with talk and wine

success.body: You pour for the oldest Saxon king and stay by him, as a good servant does, and ask him in your broken Saxon about his sons, and his ships, and his opinion of British wine. He is lonely at this feast, and he talks. By midnight, you know how many men each king has brought, where they will land, and what Mordred has promised them. You slip out and ride for the coast.

failure.body: You talk to the oldest Saxon king in your broken Saxon, and he answers you in perfect British. "Where did you learn our tongue," he asks, "serving wine?"

entries.body: You take the harp. It is lighter than you expected, and the strings are warm.

resolutions.label: play the singing stones of the Giant's Dance

success.body: You pluck a string, and the stone nearest you hums. You pluck another, and another, and slowly, clumsily, you begin to play. The stones answer, one after another, round the whole circle, until the air is thick with music and the ground is shaking under you. When you stop, Merlin is looking at you with real respect. "Nobody has played them but me," he says, "since Ireland." He does not take back the harp. He gives you his staff instead, to lean on, because your legs are trembling.

failure.body: You pluck a string, and the stone nearest you shrieks, and every stone in the circle shrieks with it. You drop the harp and cover your ears. When the noise stops, Merlin is laughing, and your ears ring for a week.

resolutions.label: dance the circle of the stones as the giants did

success.body: Merlin laughs when you give back the harp. "Then dance," he says, and plays. You dance the circle of the stones, sunwise, from stone to stone, round and round, as the giants danced at their wedding before they were turned to stone. The stones hum louder with every round. You dance until you drop. When you wake, it is dawn, and Merlin is sitting beside you. "Nobody," he says, "has danced them since Ireland." He gives you his staff to lean on.

failure.body: You dance the circle, and on the third round you trip over the altar stone and knock yourself out. Merlin plays on, regardless.

entries.body: You ask for an audience with the king. The king receives you, still red-faced. "A knight of Arthur's court," he says. "Well? Have you come to tell me to swallow my pride?"

resolutions.label: counsel the proud king against war

success.body: "No, my lord," you say. "I have come to tell you that the Earl will swallow his first, if you let him." You explain that a great king does not need three hundred marks, or a goose. He needs the Earl to say he was wrong. The king likes this. You ride to the Earl and tell him the same thing in reverse. At the end of a week, the Earl sends the king a letter of apology and a gift of barley, and the king sends the Earl a gift of a goose. Robin plays a triumphant tune on his whistle all the way through the feast.

failure.body: "No, my lord," you say. "I have come to tell you that the Earl will swallow his pride first, if you let him." The king considers this. "Or I could march on him," he says, "and he could swallow his teeth." He does march. You ride away before the first battle, with Robin's whistle playing a lament behind you.

resolutions.label: show the king that his army is too small

success.body: You ask to see the king's army. It is sixty men and a cart. You walk him round it, courteously, and then ask how many men the Earl of Buellt has. Three hundred, it turns out. The king goes quiet. "Perhaps," he says, "the goose has been punished enough." He sends the Earl a letter of stiff reproach and a gift of a goose. The Earl, who was counting his own army and found it smaller than he thought, sends back barley.

failure.body: You walk the king round his sixty men and ask how many the Earl has. "Fewer," says the king confidently. He is wrong. The army marches the next day, and you ride away before the first battle.

entries.body: The old nun sits down on a rock and passes you a piece of bread. "Collen was a soldier once," she says. "He fought for the Romans. Then he became a monk, and then an abbot, and then he got tired of being an abbot and went up into the hills. One day the King of the Fair Folk invited him to a feast on top of Glastonbury Tor. He went, with a flask of holy water. When they offered him food, he said, *I do not eat the leaves of trees.* And he threw the holy water, and the whole feast vanished, and he was sitting on the bare hilltop in the rain." She laughs. "He came here after that. He said he wanted somewhere quiet." She shakes crumbs from her lap. "Sometimes, at night, you can hear music coming from the cave. I think the Fair Folk come to visit him. I think they have forgiven him."
You sit down very slowly on the cave floor. The bear watches you. Nia watches you. You begin to hum.

resolutions.label: win the bear's trust

success.body: You hum until the bear lays its head down again. Then you take a honeycomb from the ledge beside it, very slowly, and hold it out. The bear sniffs it, and licks it, and licks your hand. You stay there until dusk, humming and feeding it honey, until it falls asleep. Then you take Nia by the hand and walk her out through the waterfall. At the edge of the wood, she turns and waves. "Goodbye, bear," she calls. You hear, from the forest, a low, contented grunt.

failure.body: You hum. The bear listens, and then it gets up, and comes over to you, and sniffs you all over, and sits on you. It is a very long afternoon. When it finally gets up, you are bruised all over, and Nia is asleep.

entries.body: "He should not follow a woman who does not want him," you say. Nimue smiles, a quick, fierce smile. "No," she says. "He should not."

resolutions.label: hold the old enchanter while Nimue speaks the spell

success.body: When Merlin comes back with the mushrooms, you take him by the arm and ask him a question about the stars. He is so pleased to be asked that he begins to answer, and while he is answering, Nimue begins to speak. The old man stops. He looks at her, and at you, and he understands. "Ah," he says. "Yes. I saw this, a long time ago." He does not struggle. The rock beside the pool opens like a door, and he walks into it, and it closes behind him. Nimue is shaking. "Thank you," she says. "The Lady of the Lake will remember you." She disappears into the pool.

failure.body: When Merlin comes back, you take him by the arm and ask him about the stars. He smiles and begins to answer, and while he is answering, Nimue begins to speak. Then Merlin looks at you, and says one word, and you find you cannot move. "You are not the first to try," he says kindly. "Nor the last." He leads Nimue away by the hand. You stand in the pool, frozen, until the sun goes down.

resolutions.label: distract Merlin while Nimue prepares

success.body: When Merlin comes back with the mushrooms, you ask him to tell you how he moved the great stones from Ireland to Salisbury Plain. His eyes light up, and he tells you, in enormous detail, for an hour. He does not notice Nimue drawing a circle round him on the grass with her toe. At the end of the story, the rock beside the pool opens, and Merlin turns, and sees, and sighs. "Oh, well done," he says to her, and walks into the stone. Nimue throws her arms round your neck. "The Lady of the Lake," she says, "owes you a great deal."

failure.body: When Merlin comes back with the mushrooms, you ask him to tell you how he moved the great stones to Salisbury Plain. He looks at you, and then at Nimue, and smiles. "Ah," he says. "Nimue, dear, your friend is a terrible liar." Nimue curses. Merlin takes her arm, and they walk off together into the trees, and you are left holding the mushrooms.

entries.body: Balin looks at you, and his face changes. "You drew it," he says. "The damsel's sword. I saw it on your belt in a dream." He takes one of his own swords from his belt. It is the twin of the one you carry. "Then it is not only me." He grips your hand. "Listen. The knight in red is my brother Balan. I know it now. The curse wanted us to kill each other. Take my sword, so there are two of them together, and the curse is split between us." You do. For a moment the air shivers. The red knight on the causeway stops, lifts his visor and cries out his brother's name. They meet in the middle of the causeway and embrace, and the ladies on the battlements begin, very slowly, to weep.

notes: Lose Story Token #19

entries.body:
As you come down to a ford, a lanky knight in battered armour hails you from the bank, where he sits eating an apple with his helmet beside him. He has a long, clever face and a nose that has been broken at least twice.

"Stop!" he calls. "Before you cross, hear me. I am Dinadan, and I am here to save your life." He points the apple across the river, where a huge knight in black armour sits a huge black horse beside a tree hung with shields. "That is Sir Tarquin. He has sworn to fight every knight of Arthur's court who crosses this ford. He has sixty-four of them in his dungeon. Their shields are on that tree." He takes another bite. "I have been sitting here for two days, thinking of reasons not to cross. I have forty. Would you like to hear them? Or I have a plan. It is not a good plan, but it is better than being shield sixty-five."

responses.label: You may cross the ford and challenge Sir Tarquin.
You may join Sir Dinadan's plan to trick Sir Tarquin.

entries.body:
You come upon a knight lying on his back in the grass outside a castle wall, staring at the sky. His horse grazes nearby, and his armour is rusted where the dew has been at it for many nights.

"Go away," he says, before you can speak. "Or stay, if you like. I am Pelleas. I love the Lady Ettarde, who lives in that castle. I won the golden circlet for her at the tournament at Carlisle, and she gave it to another lady out of spite. I have lain here every night since, in the hope that she will look out of her window." He smiles faintly. "She does, sometimes. She sends her knights out to beat me. I let them. It is something." A shutter opens high above, a pale face looks down, and the shutter slams.

responses.label: You may go into the castle and plead Sir Pelleas's case to Lady Ettarde.
You may shake Sir Pelleas out of his misery and take him away from here.
* You may go into the castle and court Lady Ettarde for yourself.

entries.body:
At a crossroads in a dark wood you come upon a knight kneeling in the road, praying aloud with his eyes squeezed shut. He is a broad, plain-faced man in grey, and he is counting on his fingers as he prays. "Seven. Eight," he mutters. "Lord, show me. Nine."

He opens his eyes as you ride up. "Thank God," he says. "I am Bors of Ganis. Look." He points down the left-hand road, where two knights are dragging a bound man along behind their horses and beating him with thorn branches. "That is my brother Lionel." He points down the right-hand road, where a knight on a grey horse is carrying off a struggling maiden, who is screaming for help. "And that is a lady who needs me. I cannot save both. I have been praying for a sign. I think you are the sign." He gets up. "Choose. I will take the other."

responses.label: You may ride to rescue Sir Lionel from his captors.
You may ride to rescue the maiden from the knight on the grey horse.

entries.body:
As you ride down a wide green ride in the forest, you hear hoofbeats behind you, very heavy and very slow. A knight overtakes you on a horse the colour of beech leaves in May. The knight is green too: green hair, green beard, green skin, and a coat of green silk embroidered with birds. He carries no shield, only a holly branch in one hand and a great axe in the other.

"Good day," he says pleasantly. His voice is deep and courteous. "I am looking for sport. Not a joust. I have no taste for jousting. A game." He holds out the axe, handle first. "Strike me one blow with this, as hard as you like, and I will not raise a hand to stop it. In return, you will let me strike you one blow in a year and a day, at my chapel in the north. That is all. Is there any knight in this country who has the courage to play?"

responses.label: You may take the axe and play the Green Knight's game.
You may refuse the game and demand to know who the Green Knight is.

entries.body:
You come upon a knight in the courtyard of an inn, pacing up and down with a scrap of parchment. He is tall, sharp-nosed and cross-looking, and you recognise him at once as Sir Kay, the High King's seneschal.

"Ah," he says. "You. You will do. You have a courtly look." He thrusts the parchment at you. "I am in love. With Nest, who does the laundry at Camelot. She has arms like a blacksmith and a laugh like a horse and she is the only person at court who does not flinch when I speak. I have written her a poem." He looks at it with disgust. "It is terrible. You will read it to her and tell her it is good. If you laugh," he adds, "I will have you put on latrine duty until Michaelmas."

The poem begins: *O Nest, thou art as white as linen, and as starch'd.*

responses.label: You may help Sir Kay win the heart of Nest the laundress.
You may play a prank on Sir Kay with his own poem.
* You may court Nest the laundress yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a knight crouched beside a stream, drinking from it with his face in the water, like a dog. He is naked but for a torn shirt, and very hairy, and when he raises his head you see his eyes are yellow.

He bares his teeth at you, then seems to remember himself. He stands up, and bows, very correctly. "Forgive me," he says hoarsely. "I am Sir Marrok. I was a knight of the Round Table, seven years ago, before my wife stole my clothes." His hands shake. "I am a werewolf, you understand. When I take off my clothes, I become a wolf, and I cannot come back until I put them on again. She knew. She hid them. She married my steward." He laughs, and it turns into a howl, and he stops it. "A priest found my clothes last week and I am a man again. Mostly. And I am going home to my wife."

responses.label: You may go with Sir Marrok to confront his faithless wife.
You may try to restrain Sir Marrok and find a cure for what is left of the wolf in him.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a knight in the colours of Orkney, sharpening his sword at a crossroads with long, angry strokes. He is lean and dark, with his family's hard grey eyes. You recognise Sir Gaheris.

If you have Story Token #18, turn immediately to [[1444]].

"Have you seen Sir Lamorak?" he asks. "Big man. Laughs too much." He tests the edge with his thumb. "He has been visiting my mother. My mother, a queen, a widow, a grandmother. He has shamed our house before all Britain. My brother Agravain has written it down on his list, and my brothers are all agreed that the thing must be ended." He stands up. "I know he rides this road. When he does, I will kill him. If you are his friend, you had best ride on."

Far down the road, you hear someone singing, very loud and very cheerful.

responses.label: You may help Sir Gaheris ambush Sir Lamorak.
You may take Sir Lamorak's side and fight Sir Gaheris.
You may try to reconcile Sir Gaheris and Sir Lamorak.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a little manor house in a valley, with an orchard where an old knight is chasing a pig. The pig is winning. The knight is stout and white-haired and red in the face, and he is laughing so hard that he has to stop and hold on to a tree.

"Ho!" he calls, when he sees you. "Help an old man. That pig is the fattest in the shire and it has eaten every windfall I own. I am Ector, by the way. I raised the High King." He wipes his eyes. "Raised him on this very farm. He was a good lad. Clumsy. Kay was always the clever one. Kay was always the one I thought would do something." He looks at the pig, which is regarding him insolently from beneath a pear tree. "I suppose you want to hear about him, as a boy. Everyone does. Or you could catch that pig."

responses.label: You may ask old Sir Ector to tell you how he raised the High King.
You may help Sir Ector catch his fugitive pig.

entries.body:
You come upon a knight sitting alone beside a small fire on a winter evening, reading a letter. He is slight and pale and handsome, with dark hair and grey eyes, and he looks up at you with a warm smile.

"Friend," he says. "Come and warm your hands. I am Mordred." He folds the letter and puts it inside his jerkin. "You have heard of me, perhaps. They say I am the High King's nephew. Some say worse." He shrugs as if it does not matter. "Everyone at court has an opinion of me, and hardly anyone has ever spoken to me." He passes you a cup of warm wine. "I wonder if you would do me a small kindness. I have a letter for my mother, Queen Morgause, in Orkney. It is private. Family matters. I cannot trust the court's messengers not to open it." He looks at you steadily. "I think I can trust you."

responses.label: You may carry Mordred's letter to Orkney, sealed and unread.
You may accept the letter and read it in secret on the road.
You may politely refuse Mordred's request.

entries.body: You shake your head at the porter and ride on. The music follows you across the plain. It is very beautiful.

resolutions.label: resist the call of the moonlit castle

success.body: You ride all night with the music in your ears, and you do not turn back, though your hands shake on the reins. At dawn, the music stops. You feel as though you have come through a great storm. You find, in your saddlebag, a white rose you did not put there. It does not fade.

failure.body: You ride on, but the music follows, and after an hour, you find yourself at the gate again, with the porter smiling. He takes your horse. You are there until the next full moon.

resolutions.label: pray to shut out the castle's music

success.body: You ride all night with the music in your ears, saying the psalms aloud, one after another, louder and louder, until you cannot hear anything else. At dawn, the music stops. You feel as though you have come through a great storm. In your saddlebag, you find a white rose you did not put there. It does not fade.

failure.body: You ride all night saying psalms, but somewhere around the ninetieth, you find you are singing them to the castle's tune. At dawn, you are at its gate again.

entries.body:
You come upon a knight sitting on his horse in the middle of a field, alone, facing a wooden post with a shield hung on it. He charges it. He misses. He goes back to the start, and charges it again. He misses again.

"Oh, good," he says when he sees you, and rides over. He is a sandy-haired knight with a freckled, honest face and a great deal of rust on his armour. "Sir Griflet. Of Camelot. Or I was." He sighs. "Three years ago, a squire unhorsed me at the ford at Tinmouth. A squire! In front of the queen's ladies! I swore not to go back to court until I had overthrown ten knights in fair joust. I have done nine." He looks at you hopefully, then at the post. "I have been practising. Would you be the tenth? I would be very much obliged. I am so tired of this field."

responses.label: You may joust with Sir Griflet fairly.
You may persuade Sir Griflet that his vow has been kept well enough.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a tower on an island in a lake, joined to the shore by a narrow causeway. A knight sits at the landward end of the causeway with two swords at his belt, staring at the tower. He looks as if he has not slept in days. A crowd of ladies stands on the tower's battlements, watching.

If you have Story Token #19, turn immediately to [[1200]].

"They tell me," the knight says without looking at you, "that the custom of this island is that any knight who comes here must fight the knight who keeps it. They have given me a new shield, since mine was too small. They took away my own, with my arms on it." He laughs, a dry, cracked laugh. "I am Balin. I am cursed. Everything I touch goes wrong. I struck a blow once, at Corbenic, that laid a whole land waste." He nods at the island, where a knight in red armour, with a plain shield, is riding down to the causeway. "I do not know who that is. But I think I am meant to kill him, or he me."

responses.label: You may take Sir Balin's place and fight the red knight of the island yourself.
You may persuade the red knight to unlace his helm before he fights.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You leave them and ride deeper into the forest, where the fighting is thickest.

resolutions.label: hunt the Saxon war-band through the forest

success.body: You find the Saxon war-leader and his hearth-guard making a stand behind a fallen oak. You lead the High King's men round behind them, through a stream-bed, and take them from the rear. It is a short, fierce fight. The war-leader surrenders to you personally. The High King gives you his sword.

failure.body: You find the Saxon war-leader making a stand behind a fallen oak, and charge, and are thrown. You spend the rest of the battle behind a tree, bleeding.

resolutions.label: lead the soldiers in a drive against the war-leader

success.body: You gather the scattered soldiers from the clearings and set them in a line, fifty paces apart, and drive the forest toward the river, like beaters driving deer. The Saxons, cut off from each other, fall back before you until they are caught against the water. Their war-leader surrenders to you personally. The High King gives you his sword.

failure.body: You set the soldiers in a line and drive the forest, but the line breaks at a thicket, and the Saxons come back through the gap and take you from behind.

entries.body: "The lady," you say. "Your brother would want you to save him." Bors nods once, hard, and spurs away to the left. You ride after the grey horse.

resolutions.label: catch the knight on the grey horse and fight him

success.body: The grey horse is carrying two, and you catch it in a quarter-mile. The knight drops the maiden in the road and turns on you, and you fight him on foot among the roots until he flees. The maiden, whose name is Elyn, is the daughter of a lord who swore allegiance to Arthur that morning. Her father embraces you both. When you meet Bors again, he has Lionel, bruised but alive, and his face is shining. "Twice," he says. "Twice today, God answered."

failure.body: The grey horse is carrying two, and you catch it quickly. But its rider is a far better swordsman than you expected. He cuts you twice before you can find your guard, and rides away with the maiden while you bind your wounds. You find Bors at nightfall, with his brother on the saddle behind him. You tell him you failed. "No," says Bors. "You tried. So did I."

resolutions.label: call on the knight to release the lady for shame

success.body: You catch up with the grey horse and ride alongside it. "Put her down," you say, "in God's name, or answer for it at the Judgement." The knight laughs, but then he looks at you, and something in your face stops the laugh. He sets the maiden on the road and rides away without a word. The maiden, whose name is Elyn, walks home with you, holding your stirrup. She tells you, later, that the knight took the cross the following spring.

failure.body: You catch up with the grey horse and ride alongside it. "Put her down, in God's name." The knight laughs and strikes you across the face with his gauntlet. Before you have your sword out, he is gone into the trees. You search until night, and do not find the lady.

entries.body: You take the axe. Lot grins like a wolf. "I knew it," he says. "There are more of us than he thinks." He sets you to work that same afternoon.

resolutions.label: lead a raid on the young king's supply wagons

success.body: You take thirty of Lot's horsemen down the old Roman road by night, fall on Arthur's wagons at a ford, and drive off the oxen before the guards have their boots on. Lot laughs aloud when he sees the plunder. "Now that," he says, "is how an Orkney man makes war." He gives you a share of it, and your name is spoken with respect around the fires. It is spoken differently at Camelot.

failure.body: You take thirty of Lot's horsemen down the old Roman road by night. But the wagon guards are awake, and Merlin, it seems, has told them you were coming. You lose half the men in the dark and ride back empty-handed with an arrow in your leg. Lot is not pleased. "The boy has a wizard," he growls. "I have you." You resolve to plan more carefully next time, if Lot gives you a next time.

resolutions.label: carry Lot's secret letters to the kings of the north

success.body: Lot gives you a sealed bundle and a password. You ride north in a pedlar's cloak, pass three of Arthur's patrols with a sack of ribbons and a foolish grin, and deliver the letters to King Urien in Gore and King Nentres in Garlot. Both send their men. When you return, Lot embraces you like a son. "The boy will learn," he says, "that the north does not forget."

failure.body: Lot gives you a sealed bundle and a password. You ride north in a pedlar's cloak, but at the second patrol a sergeant asks to see your ribbons and finds the letters instead. You fight your way free, but the letters are lost, and Arthur's captains now know exactly who is marching with Lot. You return to the camp to find yourself less welcome than before.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You go through the arch and sit down between a leper and a blind woman. The hermit hands you a piece of bread.

resolutions.label: eat of the miraculous bread with a humble heart

success.body: The bread is warm, and tastes of every good thing you have ever eaten, and you are full after one mouthful. The leper beside you is laughing. His sores are gone. The blind woman is looking round the table with wonder. You look at the hermit, and he looks back, and you both know, without saying it. When you ride away, you are not hungry for three days.

failure.body: The bread is only bread, to you. The leper beside you is weeping for joy. You finish your bread and go, with a feeling that you have missed something that was right in front of you.

entries.body: You take a cup and sit down among them. They wait.

resolutions.label: honour the dead with a true story

success.body: You tell them about someone you lost. You tell it simply, and truly, with the funny parts and the sad parts. When you finish, nobody speaks. Then the old sergeant raises his cup, and the whole wake raises theirs, and they drink to someone they never knew. The young soldier by the grave has turned round to listen. He comes over and sits down beside you, and after a while, he begins to talk about his brother.

failure.body: You try to tell them about someone you lost, but you cannot get the words out. You sit there with your cup. The sergeant pats you on the shoulder. "Next time," he says.

resolutions.label: sing the soldiers' own song for the dead

success.body: You do not tell a story. You ask the old sergeant what song they sang in his village for the dead, and he tells you, and you sing it, and the whole wake joins in, low and rough, and the young soldier by the grave turns round to listen. It is an old song, older than the Church, and there is something in it that the fires answer. When it ends, the young soldier comes and sits down beside you and begins to talk about his brother.

failure.body: You ask for their village song for the dead and sing it, and sing it wrong, and the old sergeant, very gently, takes over.

entries.body: "My lord," you say quietly, "there are men in Orkney colours at the foot of the mountain." The young king's grin vanishes.

resolutions.label: defend the disguised king from Lot's assassins

success.body: You and the young king slip away from the fire and go down the mountain in the dark, and find six men in Orkney colours creeping up. You fall on them together. The young king fights like a lion. When it is over, the assassins are fleeing, and the young king is laughing, with his shepherd's smock torn. "Back to the feast," he says. "I still have not finished my mutton." The shepherds never know.

failure.body: You and the young king go down the mountain, and find the Orkney men, and fight. The young king is wounded, only a little, but he is wounded, and the feast is over.

resolutions.label: lead the assassins astray on the dark mountain

success.body: You do not fight them. You go down alone and let them see you in the moonlight, and then you lead them off across the mountainside, over scree and through bog, farther and farther from the fire, until they are lost among the rocks. By the time they find their way down, it is dawn, and the young king is walking home with the shepherds, singing. He never knows. You tell him the next year.

failure.body: You lead the assassins off across the mountainside, and you lose your own way too. At dawn, you are all in the same bog, looking at one another.

entries.body: You wait for a moonless night, and climb the crag where it is steepest, where no guard will be looking.

resolutions.label: scale the crag and steal the children away

success.body: It takes you half the night to climb the crag, clinging to the rock with your fingers. At the top, you find the children in a pen by the kitchens, and you lead them out through a drain in the wall and down a goat-path, one by one, with their hands on each other's shoulders, not making a sound. At dawn, the village has its children back, and the Saxons are shouting on the walls. The old woman kisses your hands. You will not forget those twelve faces, one at a time, coming out of the drain.

failure.body: It takes you half the night to climb the crag, and near the top, a stone gives way, and you fall. You land on a ledge, with a broken arm, and have to climb back down in the dark. The Saxon ship comes two days later.

entries.body: "I will squire for you, Sir Nobody," you say. Pwca turns so red his hair seems pale. "*Sir Nobody thanks you,*" he says, "*from nowhere in particular.*"

resolutions.label: coach the fool through the joust

success.body: You spend the morning teaching Pwca to keep his lance up and his heels down. He is terrible. But he is brave, and he is light, and when he rides against his first opponent, a heavy knight on a heavy horse, the knight's lance goes clean over his head, and Pwca's catches the knight's shield and topples him. He wins three courses before he is thrown. When his helm comes off, and the crowd sees the fool, there is a roar of laughter. The Lady Tangwystl stands up, walks into the lists, and kisses him before the whole tournament. "Sir Nobody," she says. "I knew it was you."

failure.body: You spend the morning teaching Pwca to keep his lance up. On his first course, his horse bolts and carries him right out of the lists and into the river. The crowd laughs. The Lady Tangwystl laughs too, but kindly. You fish him out. "*Well,*" he says, dripping, "*she laughed.*"

resolutions.label: smuggle Pwca past the heralds

success.body: The heralds want to know who Sir Nobody of Nowhere is. You tell them he is a knight of great renown under a vow of secrecy, and that you, his squire, are not permitted to say more. You say it with such a straight face that they let him in. Pwca rides three courses and loses all of them, but he loses gallantly, and when he limps out of the lists, the Lady Tangwystl sends her page to ask Sir Nobody to sup with her. He goes, still wearing the helmet.

failure.body: The heralds want to know who Sir Nobody of Nowhere is. You invent a tale so elaborate that the herald laughs and lifts Pwca's visor. "It is the Earl's fool," he says. They throw Pwca out, and you with him. The Lady Tangwystl does not see.

entries.body: "The truth," you say. "But gently. And I will stand beside you when you tell it." Grugyn swallows and nods.

resolutions.label: tell the widow the hard truth with compassion

success.body: The widow, Lady Nest, receives you in her hall. Grugyn tells her. He does not soften it. When he has finished, she is silent for a long time. Then she says, "He was always afraid. Of horses, of the dark, of my father. He became a knight because I wanted him to." She takes the dwarf's hand. "Thank you for not lying to me. Everyone always lied to me about him." She takes down the song from the wall, where it is written on a board, and burns it. Then she asks Grugyn to stay on as her steward, and he does.

failure.body: The widow receives you in her hall. Grugyn tells her. When he finishes, she stands up and slaps him, hard, across the face, and then she slaps you. "How dare you," she says. "How dare you say that in his house." You are both put out of the gate.

resolutions.label: pray with the widow before the words are spoken

success.body: At the manor, before Grugyn says anything, you ask Lady Nest to pray with you for her husband's soul. She kneels. Grugyn kneels. You pray for a knight who was afraid, and asked to be brave, and failed, and was loved. You say it plainly. When you rise, Lady Nest's face is wet, but she is not surprised. "He was always afraid," she says. "I made him a knight." She keeps Grugyn as her steward.

failure.body: You ask Lady Nest to pray with you. She does, but when you pray for a knight who was afraid, she stands up and walks out of the chapel. She will not see either of you again.

entries.body: You take off your armour, climb into the ship's little boat and cast off into the storm alone.

resolutions.label: row through the storm to the foundering ship

success.body: You row until your arms are breaking, and reach the troop-ship, and take off six men, and row them back, and go again. You make four trips before the ship breaks up. Twenty-four men are alive because of you. When you climb back on board the last time, you cannot close your hands. A grey-bearded knight among the rescued, Sir Bedivere, looks at you and says, "The king will hear." You do not know if the king will live to hear it.

failure.body: You row until your arms are breaking, and reach the troop-ship, and take off three men, and on the way back, the little boat overturns. You are pulled from the sea half-drowned.

entries.body: You look at the pot, and at the castle, and at Eluned's face. "It is not honourable," you say. "But it is just." Eluned lets out a long breath. "Then will you help me?" she asks. "The steward's men will be watching."

resolutions.label: help Eluned slip the poison into the steward's cup

success.body: At the feast, you sit at the steward's table as a guest and talk loudly and cheerfully about tournaments while Eluned moves behind the benches with the wine jug. The steward drinks, and laughs, and drinks. By the time the dancing begins, he is dead in his chair, and the castle is in uproar. You and Eluned slip out in the confusion. At the edge of the wood, she gives you her mother's ring. "It is done," she says. Her face is white and cold, and very old.

failure.body: At the feast, you sit at the steward's table and talk loudly while Eluned brings the wine. But the steward has a food-taster, and the food-taster is not a fool. He sniffs the cup and shouts, and in a moment Eluned is seized. You fight your way out of the hall and escape into the night. You hear, a week later, what was done to her.

resolutions.label: steal into the kitchens and dose the wine yourself

success.body: You go in by the scullery window at dusk while the kitchen is full of steam and shouting, and find the steward's own flagon on the dresser, and empty the pot into it. Nobody sees you. By the time the dancing begins, Sir Loholt is dead in his chair and the castle is in uproar. Eluned meets you at the edge of the wood and gives you her mother's ring. Her face is cold and very old.

failure.body: You go in by the scullery window, and a scullion sees you, and screams, and the steward's guard come running. You get out the way you came in, with a knife in your arm, and the pot is still in your pouch.

entries.body: You shake your head. "No," you say. "Not you. Not like this." The Green Knight looks at you with his faded eyes.

resolutions.label: persuade the Green Knight to live

success.body: You tell him that the king would not want it. You tell him that the land will need someone green after the king is gone, someone to remember what it was like. You tell him that Britain has lost enough. He listens, and at last he nods. "Then I will wait," he says. "Under the hill. Until the green comes back." He walks into the mound and closes the door. You hear, as you ride away, the sound of a great axe being set down. It has been a thousand years, and some say he is waiting still.

failure.body: You tell him the king would not want it. He shakes his head. "The king," he says, "is not asked." He picks up the axe and strikes off his own head. The green goes into the land. You are left alone in the snow.

resolutions.label: show him the green he would leave behind

success.body: You take his hand and walk him through his own wood in the snow, and show him what he has not looked at in years: the buds already swelling on the hazel, the snowdrops under the oak, the green moss on the north side of every stone. "It is not going out," you say. "It is only sleeping. Like the king." He is quiet a long time. "Then I will wait," he says. "Under the hill." He walks into the mound and closes the door.

failure.body: You walk him through his wood looking for green, and find none. The snow is too deep. He takes his axe from your hands, gently, and strikes off his own head.

entries.body: You look across at the black seat. "Master Merlin," you ask. "Whose is that?"

resolutions.label: understand the mystery of the Siege Perilous

success.body: Merlin looks at you for a long time. "That is the seat of the knight who will see the Grail," he says. "He is not born yet. When he sits there, the table will be complete, and it will begin to end." He smiles, a little sadly. "Everything that is complete begins to end. Remember that, when you are old." He gives you his own staff to hold while he eats, and forgets to take it back. You keep it for a year before he asks for it. By then, you have learned a great deal from it.

failure.body: Merlin looks at you. "A seat," he says, "for someone who asks fewer questions than you." The court laughs, and Sir Kay laughs loudest. You take your own seat with your ears burning, and resolve that the next time you want to know something, you will watch and wait instead of asking.

resolutions.label: sense the seat's power with your own hand

success.body: You do not ask. You walk across the circle and lay your palm on the back of the black seat, not sitting, only touching. It is hot as a forge and cold as a well at once, and through your hand you feel it waiting, very patiently, for someone. You take your hand away. Merlin is looking at you with interest. "Most people ask," he says. He gives you his own staff to hold while he eats, and forgets to take it back.

failure.body: You lay your palm on the back of the black seat. It burns you. You spend the feast with your hand in a bowl of water, and Merlin laughing.

entries.body: You turn to Bran. "My lord," you say, "you want to marry the best archer in the Marches, and then stop her shooting?"

resolutions.label: persuade Lord Bran to love Rhian as she is

success.body: You talk to Bran long into the evening. By the end of it, he has realised that he fell in love with her the first time he saw her shoot. "My mother," he says weakly. "Your mother," you say, "can learn archery." He laughs, despite himself. The next morning, he goes to Rhian and tells her he does not care if she never touches a needle as long as she lives. She looks at him for a long time. "You still cannot shoot," she says. "No," says Bran. "Then you will have to watch," she says, "and learn."

failure.body: You talk to Bran long into the evening, but he is a young lord, and he does not like being told things. "You think I am a fool," he says stiffly. "I am a lord of Maelor." He rides away, and Rhian's family is fined for her shooting on his land.

entries.body: You sit down on the rock between them. "I will witness," you say, "and keep silent."

resolutions.label: keep the peace between the two young kings

success.body: It takes all day. They argue about borders, and cattle, and a castle that each says is his, and twice one of them gets up to leave. Twice you talk him down. At sunset, they clasp hands, and you swear on your sword to keep silent until Michaelmas. You do. At Michaelmas, the peace is proclaimed, and there is dancing in both kingdoms. Both kings send you gifts, and neither says why.

failure.body: It takes all day. They argue about borders, and cattle, and at last one of them calls the other's father a horse-thief, and the other throws the wine in his face. They ride away in opposite directions. The war goes on for another forty years.

resolutions.label: stand as their witness with sword drawn

success.body: You kneel between them on the rock with your sword drawn and laid across your knees, and swear, before either king speaks, to cut down the first man who breaks the peace of the meeting, whichever side he comes from. Both young kings look at the sword. They talk more carefully after that. At sunset, they clasp hands. At Michaelmas, the peace is proclaimed, and both send you gifts.

failure.body: You kneel between them with your sword across your knees. The King of North Wales takes it as a threat. He walks off the mountain. The war goes on.

entries.body: You draw your sword and strike the stone. It rings like a bell. Merlin laughs inside it.

resolutions.label: break Nimue's binding on the stone

success.body: You do not strike it again. You lay your hands on the shape of the old man's hand, and speak every word of unbinding you know, and some you did not know you knew, which come up out of you from somewhere deep. The stone grows warm. A crack runs across it. For a moment, you see Merlin's face, very close, very surprised. Then the crack closes again. "Nearly," he says, inside the stone. "Nobody has come so close. Not even her." He is very pleased. The stone gives off a warmth for days afterwards, and you are sure he is still laughing.

failure.body: You lay your hands on the stone and speak the words of unbinding, and the stone throws you back across the cave. Merlin, inside, sighs. "I did warn you," he says.

resolutions.label: ask Nimue herself to open the stone

success.body: You do not strike the stone. You go to the lake and call for Nimue, and when she comes, you talk to her for a long time: about Merlin, and fear, and freedom. At the end, she walks with you to the cave, and lays her hand on the smooth rock, and a crack opens across it. For a moment, you see Merlin's face, very close, very surprised. Then Nimue takes her hand away, and the crack closes. "Not yet," she says. "But one day." Merlin, inside, is laughing.

failure.body: You go to the lake and call for Nimue. She comes, and listens, and then she goes back into the lake without a word. The stone stays shut.

entries.body: "Owein," you say gently, "his mother will want to bury her son, not a stranger's glory." The boy bows his head.

resolutions.label: help Owein carry his master home

success.body: Sir Ifor's manor is two days' ride away, and the dead man must be carried over a saddle through the hills in the rain. You take turns leading the horse. On the second night Owein talks about his master for hours, and laughs sometimes, which surprises him. At the manor, Ifor's mother weeps over her son, and then over Owein. She asks him to stay on as her steward. "He always said you would be the better knight," she tells the boy. "He would want you to have his armour." Owein kneels and cannot speak.

failure.body: Sir Ifor's manor is two days' ride away, over hills in the rain. On the second day, the packhorse slips on a scree slope, and the dead man goes tumbling down into a gorge. You spend a whole day retrieving him. By the time you reach the manor, neither of you can look Ifor's mother in the eye.

resolutions.label: break the news to Sir Ifor's mother yourself

success.body: You leave Owein to watch the body and ride ahead to the manor. You find the old lady in her garden and tell her plainly, and kneel while she weeps. When Owein arrives the next day with the cart, she is waiting at the gate, and she goes straight past the coffin to the boy and holds him. "He always said you would be the better knight," she says. She gives him his master's armour, and you his master's spurs.

failure.body: You ride ahead to the manor and find the old lady in her garden. You mean to tell her gently, but you blurt it out in the first breath, and she faints among the roses. When she wakes, she will not see you, and she will not see Owein either. You resolve to find better words before you need them.

entries.body: "Let me go with you to your abbess," you say. "An honest knight's word may count for something." Sister Eleri looks doubtful. Sir Ector nods.

resolutions.label: defend the nun's honour before her abbess

success.body: The abbess is a hard old woman, but not a stupid one. You tell her, with your hand on your sword, that you watched them in the stone circle and they did not so much as touch hands. Sir Ector swears the same. Sister Eleri swears it. The abbess looks at the three of you for a long time. "Once a year," she says at last. "In the chapel. With me present." Sister Eleri weeps with relief. Sir Ector laughs aloud.

failure.body: The abbess is a hard old woman. When you swear to the nun's innocence, she asks you how you know, and you say you watched, and she asks you why a knight was watching nuns in the dark. It goes badly after that.
