resolutions.label: pray before the abbess for a sign of the nun's innocence

success.body: You ask the abbess only to kneel with you and Sister Eleri in the chapel and ask God for a sign. She does, grudgingly. You pray for a long time. Near midnight, the chapel bell rings, once, by itself, and every candle on the altar flares. The abbess gets up very slowly. "Once a year," she says. "In the chapel. With me present." Sir Ector laughs aloud.

failure.body: You kneel in the chapel with the abbess and pray for a sign. None comes. At dawn, the abbess gets up. "There is your sign," she says.

entries.body:
Mordred is standing beside the executioner, in black, looking at the queen with his warm grey eyes. He sees you and smiles. "Friend," he says. "Stand here by me. When they come, and they will come, stand by the stake. Hold it. My father will remember who held."

The horses are coming out of the woods. Mordred is watching you. So, you realise, is the queen.

resolutions.label: decide where you stand, under Mordred's eye

notes: Lose 2 Ranks of Divinity

success.body: You stand by Mordred. When the riders come out of the woods, you hold the stake with him, and you fight, and the rescuers cut their way through anyway and carry the queen off. In the crush, you see Gareth fall, unarmed, and you do not reach him. Afterward, Mordred embraces you in front of the king. "My friend held," he says. The king looks at you with an old man's eyes. You have Mordred's gratitude. It is worth a great deal. It will cost more.

partial.body: You stand by Mordred, and when the riders come, you are swept aside in the crush. Mordred does not thank you. He does not forget, either.

failure.body: You stand by Mordred, and then, when the riders come, you cannot do it. You step aside. Mordred sees. He says nothing. He does not have to.

entries.body: "Grainne!" you call across the water. "I will make you a wager. A contest of your choosing. If I win, you let us go. If you win, you may have the ship."

resolutions.label: win Grainne's contest

success.body: Grainne laughs with delight. "A drinking contest," she says. "Aboard my ship." You drink with her until the stars come out. The pirates cheer. At the end, Grainne is under the table, and you are sitting on it, very carefully. She wakes up at dawn and laughs until she has to hold her head. She lets your ship go, and gives you her own dagger. "Nobody has ever beaten me," she says. "Come back when you want a job."

failure.body: Grainne laughs with delight. "A drinking contest," she says. You are under the table before midnight. She takes the ship.

entries.body: You find Tegau at the millrace with her sleeves rolled up. She takes one look at you, and at your horse, and raises an eyebrow. "You have come from the old king," she says. "Or have you?"

resolutions.label: court the miller's daughter

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You tell her the truth: the king sent you, and you have come for yourself. Tegau laughs, which you take as a good sign, and then asks you to help her lift a sack. By sundown you have lifted a great many sacks, and she has decided you are worth knowing. The old king is heartbroken for an afternoon and then consoles himself by planning your wedding feast, which he insists on paying for.

failure.body: You tell her the king sent you, and that you have come for yourself. "So you would steal an old man's sweetheart before he has even asked her," Tegau says. "What would you do to me, then, when someone younger came riding by?" The carter, who has been listening from the cart, cracks his whip. You ride away with your ears burning.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride straight at the stocks. The crowd scatters. The priest's brother drops his torch and runs.

resolutions.label: break the stocks and carry the dwarf away

success.body: You smash the lock of the stocks with your pommel, haul the dwarf up behind your saddle and gallop out of the town gate with half the town running after you. Two miles out, he leans round and shouts in your ear, "My tools! My tools are still in my shop!" You go back for them that night, over the wall. He goes to Camelot, where the High King asks him to make a clock for the great hall. It is still there.

failure.body: You smash the lock of the stocks, but the crowd closes in before you can get the dwarf onto your horse. Somebody pulls you out of the saddle. You spend the night in the same stocks, with the dwarf beside you, and in the morning you are both run out of town with a great deal of shouting.

entries.body: "Let me go first," you say, "and see what it does." The young knight stares at you.

resolutions.label: lie in the tomb of the Grail knight

success.body: You lie down in the tomb. It is cold, and it fits you. The lid does not fall. You lie there a long time, looking up at the sky through the broken roof, and you feel, very clearly, that it is not you, and that it does not matter, and that you are welcome to lie there as long as you like. When you climb out, the young knight is on his knees. You tell him the truth. He does not believe you.

partial.body: You lie down in the tomb. The lid shivers, and slides a finger's width, and stops. You climb out quickly. It is not you. But it did not crush you either.

failure.body: You lie down in the tomb. The lid slides, and crashes down, and you roll out just in time, with your leg caught. The young knight pulls you free.

entries.body: You draw your sword. The beast watches you come. It does not try to rise.

resolutions.label: slay the Questing Beast

success.body: It is over very quickly. The beast does not fight. When it is dead, the baying in its belly stops, and the forest is very quiet. You take its serpent's head. It will make you famous. Every hall in Britain will want to hear how you killed the Questing Beast. You find, riding away, that you do not want to tell them.

failure.body: You raise your sword. The beast looks at you, and in its eyes you see, for a moment, an old king laughing, and you cannot do it. When you look again, it is gone, arrow and all, into the smoke.

entries.body: You see what he does not: a trail of blood leading away from the lodge, across the yard and into the trees. "Wait," you say. "Before you kill him, let me follow this."

resolutions.label: follow the blood trail into the forest

notes: Place a Hunting Skill Marker on your Accompanied Status Card

success.body: The trail leads to a thicket, where a second wolf lies wounded, the mate of whatever came into the lodge. It is dying, its flank torn open by a dog's teeth. You finish it and ride back. Llywarch is standing in the lodge doorway, holding his son. The baby is unhurt. Behind the cradle, he has found the first wolf. He looks at you with his whole heart in his face. "If you had not stopped me," he says. He cannot finish. He gives you the best pup of Cafall's next litter.

failure.body: The trail leads into a thicket and you lose it among the roots. When you ride back to the lodge, the yard is silent. Llywarch is sitting on the step with his son alive in his arms and his dead dog across his knees. He does not look up as you ride away.

entries.body: "Where did the piper go?" you ask. Carados points to a round green hill beyond the village, where a thin, merry tune drifts on the wind. "There," he says. "He sits on top of it every noon, and my shadow dances round him." Sure enough, when you climb the hill you find a thin man in green piping away, and a king's shadow capering around the hilltop without any king to cast it.

resolutions.label: bargain with the fay piper

success.body: You sit down cross-legged opposite the piper, which seems to amuse him. "A shadow is a poor thing to keep," you say, "since it only does what you do. Give it back, and I will teach you a song you have never heard." The piper cocks his head. You sing him a marching song the Carleon footmen use, full of rude words about Saxons. He laughs so hard he drops his pipe, and the shadow runs straight down the hill and back to its king. Carados weeps and gives you a ring from his own hand.

failure.body: You sit down cross-legged opposite the piper, which seems to amuse him. "A shadow is a poor thing to keep," you say. The piper grins and plays three bright notes. Your own shadow twitches, then stretches, then starts to tap its foot on the grass. You leap up and flee down the hill with it straining behind you, and do not stop until you are back in the village. The piper keeps the king's shadow. You never quite trust your own again.

resolutions.label: play the piper at his own game

success.body: You wait until the piper pauses for breath, then clap loudly. "Very fine," you say, "but anyone can make a shadow dance. I bet you cannot make one stand still." The piper, stung, plays a slow, heavy tune, and the king's shadow stops dead. You step onto it before he can play again. A shadow pinned under a knight's boot cannot follow a tune, and the piper knows it. He curses in a language like wind in reeds and vanishes, and you walk the shadow home.

failure.body: You wait until the piper pauses for breath, then clap loudly. "Very fine," you say, "but I bet you cannot make one stand still." The piper looks at you with pity. "I would not take that bet," he says, "from one who is already dancing." You look down. Your feet are moving. You dance down the hill and through the village and all the way to the next parish before you can stop, with the village children running after you and laughing. You resolve to be more careful whom you challenge.

entries.body: You leap from the stricken ship into the surf and wade ashore, sword in hand, to meet the wreckers.

resolutions.label: drive off the wreckers

success.body: The wreckers are not fighters. They are villagers with axes, expecting drowning sailors. When they see a knight coming out of the surf with a drawn sword, they drop their lanterns and flee up the cliff. You go up after them and put out the false beacon. In the morning, the ship's crew and most of its cargo are safe on the beach. The captain is still angry at himself. You go to the village church and ring the bell until the priest comes, and tell him what his parishioners have been doing.

failure.body: You wade ashore to meet the wreckers, but they have come for exactly this, and there are twenty of them. You are knocked down in the surf and left for dead.

entries.body:
You look at Gareth, standing unarmed by the stake in his plain tunic. He sees you, and smiles, the same slow smile he had in the kitchen apron, years ago, on the road with Lynette.

The horses are coming out of the woods. You know, suddenly, with terrible certainty, what is going to happen: the riders will cut their way through the guard, and in the crush, they will not see who is armed and who is not.

You run to Gareth.

resolutions.label: shield your old friend in the crush

notes: Lose Story Token #7

success.body: You reach him as the riders crash into the guard. You throw him down behind the faggots and cover him with your own body, and the horses go over you, and a sword meant for someone else opens your back. But Gareth is alive. When the riders have gone, and the queen with them, he sits up in the ashes and looks at you. "You came," he says. Gaheris is dead. Gareth will never forgive the house of Benwick for that. But he lives, and the house of Orkney's rage is less by one brother. It is not enough to stop the war. It is not nothing.

failure.body: You run for Gareth, and the riders come out of the woods, and the crush takes you both. When it clears, he is lying in the ashes, and you are kneeling beside him, and it is too late.

entries.body:
Julian looks at the river for a long time before he answers.

"I was a knight," he says. "I hunted, and loved it more than God. One day I cornered a great stag, and it turned and spoke to me. It said, *You will kill your father and your mother.* I fled to the other end of the world so I could not. I married. I prospered. And one night I came home and found two strangers in my bed, and I thought my wife was false, and I killed them both in the dark." He is quiet for a long while. "They were my father and my mother. They had come looking for me, and my wife had given them her own bed. So I came here. I carry travellers across the water. I have carried eleven thousand, three hundred and six. I do not know how many it will take." He smiles faintly. "Perhaps one more."

While you are talking, the leper has risen from his stone and gone. You did not see him go. Julian blesses you before you ride on to the ford.
"You will not kill a man from a hedge," you say, "while I am here." Gaheris's face goes hard as stone. "Then I will start," he says, "with you."

resolutions.label: fight Sir Gaheris at the crossroads

success.body: Gaheris fights like his whole family is watching. He is fast and furious, but fury is not skill. You wear him down, and when Lamorak comes singing round the bend, he finds you standing over the young Orkney knight with your sword at his chest. "Well met!" says Lamorak, delighted. "Who is this?" You let Gaheris go. He rides away without a word. Lamorak takes you to supper and insists on paying. "You have made an enemy of Orkney," he says cheerfully. "Welcome."

failure.body: Gaheris fights like his whole family is watching. He is faster than you, and angrier, and after a few minutes you are on the ground with his sword at your throat. Lamorak comes singing round the bend and stops dead. "Let the knight go," he says, "and fight me." Gaheris does. You lie in the road and watch them go at it. It ends with both of them bloody and nobody dead, and Gaheris swears to finish it another day.

resolutions.label: ride Gaheris down before he reaches his horse

success.body: His horse is tethered at the edge of the crossroads, and he is on foot with his whetstone. You spur between him and it. He runs for the tether and you cut him off, and cut him off again, until he stands in the middle of the crossroads, panting, with his sword drawn and nowhere to go. Lamorak comes singing round the corner and stops, astonished. Gaheris walks home. It is a long way to Orkney.

failure.body: You spur between Gaheris and his horse, but he is quicker than you think. He is in the saddle before you have turned, and he rides you down instead. Lamorak finds you in the ditch.

entries.body: You go aboard the wedding ship. The feast is splendid. The princess is young and fierce and red-haired, and she dances with you at once.

resolutions.label: win the princess's favour at the wedding feast

success.body: You dance with her, and talk with her, and when she tells you about the King of Man, you tell her what you know of him, which is that he is very kind and very deaf and has no children. The princess thinks about this for a long time. "Deaf," she says. "And kind. And seventy." She laughs. "I could do worse." She gives you a gold brooch. You hear, years later, that she ruled Man for fifty years, and very well.

failure.body: You dance with her, and tread on her foot, and she laughs, and dances with someone else. The feast goes on without you.

entries.body: "There is no knight," you say. "There are three thieves behind your tent, and a stack of other men's saddles." Gwennol's smile does not waver. "Prove it," she says.

resolutions.label: unmask the scheme before the gathered knights

success.body: You pay your five marks with a smile and ask to see the knight's shield, for the heraldry. Gwennol brings it. You turn it over. It is painted on the front and blank on the back, and still smells of fresh paint. By then a crowd of waiting knights has gathered. They search the pavilion and find the three dice-players and a great deal of stolen harness. Gwennol and her friends are marched to the sheriff. On the way, she turns and blows you a kiss. "It was a good scheme," she says. "You were just better."

failure.body: You pay your five marks with a smile and ask to see the knight's shield. Gwennol goes into the pavilion to fetch it and does not come out. When you go in after her, the back of the tent is cut open, and she and her friends and your five marks are gone.

resolutions.label: drive off the three thieves

success.body: You walk round the back of the pavilion. The three dice-players look up and reach for their cudgels. The fight is short, and at the end of it, the thieves are running across the field, and Gwennol is sitting on her stool looking resigned. You return the saddles and purses to the knights they were taken from. Gwennol, you let go, since she asks very prettily, and she promises to find honest work. You do not believe her.

failure.body: You walk round the back of the pavilion. The three dice-players reach for their cudgels, and there are three of them, and they are better at this than you expected. When you wake up, your saddle is on the heap with the others.

entries.body:
You come upon a pair of travellers on the road: a young woman on a white palfrey, talking without pause, and a big fair-haired young man trudging beside her in a kitchen apron with a rusty sword over his shoulder.

"Oh, splendid, a real knight," says the young woman. "I am Lynette. My sister is besieged by the Red Knight of the Red Lands, and I went to the High King for a champion, and he gave me this." She flaps a hand at the young man. "A kitchen boy! He smells of onions. Sir Kay calls him Beaumains, because his hands are so pretty. He has been following me for three days. Tell him to go home."

The young man says nothing. He only smiles, a little ruefully, and wipes his pretty hands on his apron. Ahead of you, where the road crosses a river, a knight in black armour waits on the bridge.

responses.label: You may ride with Beaumains and help him win through to the besieged lady.
You may take Lynette's part and try to send the kitchen boy home.
You may ask Beaumains quietly who he really is.

entries.body:
You come upon a young squire digging a grave under an oak tree beside the road, crying so hard he can barely see the spade. A dead knight lies on a cloak nearby, still in his armour, with his neck at an angle that tells its own story.

"Sir Ifor," says the squire, wiping his face. "My master. His horse threw him at the practice post this morning. He was going to the tournament at Winchester, the day after tomorrow. He would have won." The boy's name, he tells you, is Owein, and he is sixteen. He looks at the dead man's armour. "It would fit me," he says suddenly. "If I wore it, with the visor down, nobody would know. I could ride at Winchester in his name, and win, and bring the prize home to his mother, and she would never know he died a fool's death at a practice post. Would that be so wrong?"

responses.label: You may help Owein ride at Winchester in his dead master's armour.
You may persuade Owein to take his master home and tell the truth.

entries.body:
You come upon a crowd of villagers around a horse trough in a village square. A thin young squire is kneeling beside it, gazing into the water with shining eyes, while an old hermit in a sackcloth robe stands over him, shouting.

"Liar!" roars the hermit. "Blasphemer!"

"I saw it," says the squire quietly. His name, a villager tells you, is Iddo, and he serves a knight who is sick at the inn. "Last night. I came to water my master's horse, and I saw the holy vessel in the trough, shining, with a light in it like the dawn. I have not been hungry since." He looks up at you. "They say I am mad, or lying. The hermit says a squire in a horse trough cannot see what bishops pray for all their lives."

The villagers are divided. Some are kneeling beside the trough. Others are picking up stones.

responses.label: You may test whether Iddo's vision is true.
You may denounce the vision as a lie and stop the crowd kneeling to a horse trough.

entries.body:
You come upon Sir Kay in a meadow, on horseback, with a brace of hounds on a leash, looking unusually pleased with himself. In the grass ahead of him, a brown hare sits very still, watching.

"Ah," says Kay. "Good. You can help. That hare," he points with his whip, "is my squire. Madoc. He insulted a fay lady at a well last week. Called her a milkmaid. She turned him into a hare. The court wizards say the spell will break if he is caught by a hound, and quickly, before he forgets he was ever a boy." He shrugs. "Or it will kill him. The wizards were not sure. But either way, I shall have a squire or a supper." He unleashes one of the hounds.

The hare looks at you. You are almost sure it is pleading.

responses.label: You may try to break the spell on Madoc some other way.
You may join Sir Kay's hunt for the hare.

entries.body:
Outside a tavern, you find a young squire perched on the mounting block, with ink on his fingers, a quill behind his ear and a look of complete despair.

"I am Piran," he says, "squire to Sir Sagramore. Sir Sagramore is in love with the Lady Elidan of Caerwent. Sir Sagramore cannot write. So he asked me to write to her for him." He holds up a thick sheaf of letters. "I have been writing to her for six months. She writes back. She loves him now. She says she has never read such beautiful words. She is coming to meet him tomorrow." He puts his head in his hands. "Sir Sagramore is a good knight. But he says *I do not hold with words* and eats with his fingers. When she meets him, she will know. And the worst of it is," he whispers, "that I think I love her too."

responses.label: You may help Piran confess the truth to the Lady Elidan.
You may help Sir Sagramore play the part of the letter-writer tomorrow.
* You may go to meet the Lady Elidan yourself before either of them.

entries.body: You get back on your horse. "I will bring you something to put in those cups," you say.

resolutions.label: find food in the wasted land

success.body: You ride all day through the dust, and at dusk, you find a valley the waste has not reached, with a river full of fish and an orchard full of apples. You fill your saddlebags, and your shirt, and your helm, and ride back through the night. At dawn, you empty it all on the feast-table. The villagers stare at you. Then the reeve begins to laugh, and then everyone is laughing, and eating, and singing.

failure.body: You ride all day through the dust and find nothing. When you come back, the villagers are still singing. You sit down with them.

entries.body:
You come upon a boy of fourteen or so, in a squire's jerkin, standing in the middle of the road with a broom held like a lance and a pot on his head. "Halt!" he cries in a cracking voice. "I am Sir Cai of the Faerie Hill! No knight passes this road without jousting with me!"

A woman runs up the road behind him, out of breath. "I am sorry, sir," she gasps. "He is my son. He was a squire at the castle till midsummer, when he fell asleep on the faerie hill. He woke up convinced a fay queen had knighted him. He has challenged the miller, the priest and two cows." She lowers her voice. "The castle will not take him back. The priest says it is a madness from the hill and he must be kept on a chain. I do not know what to do."

The boy lowers his broom and levels it at your horse's chest.

responses.label: You may accept the boy's challenge and joust with him honourably.
You may take the boy to be cured of his madness.

entries.body: You rise from the table and kneel on the stone floor as the covered vessel passes. The maiden carrying it pauses beside you.

resolutions.label: kneel in the presence of the Grail

notes: You may remove 1 unwanted Status Card

success.body: She pauses beside you, and the light from under the cloth falls on your face, and for a moment, you are warm, and fed, and forgiven, and everything you have ever lost is given back. Then she walks on. The old king is weeping. "You knelt," he says. "Almost nobody kneels." In the morning, the castle is gone. But you are not hungry for three days, and your wounds are healed.

partial.body: She pauses beside you, and the light falls on your face, and you feel it for a moment, like sun through a closed eyelid. Then she walks on. In the morning, the castle is gone.

failure.body: She does not pause. She walks past you, and the light does not fall on you. In the morning, the castle is gone.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a squire sitting on a fallen tree with a sword across his knees, grinding the edge with a whetstone. He is perhaps eighteen, dark and hard-faced, with a bandage round his head.

"You are riding north," he says. "So is Sir Breuse Sans Pitie. Do you know him? He rides down knights who have been unhorsed. He kills them where they lie. He did it to my master, Sir Gwion, at a ford a week ago, while Sir Gwion was lying with a broken leg asking for quarter. Breuse laughed. I saw it from the trees." He tests the edge of the sword. "My name is Emrys ap Rhys. I have my master's sword, and I know where Breuse sleeps. Tonight I will kill him. If you will help me, it will be sooner."

responses.label: You may help Emrys take his revenge on Sir Breuse Sans Pitie.
You may try to turn Emrys from his revenge.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come to a wide river with a ferry, where the ferryman is a boy of twelve with a mop of golden hair and a very old face. He sits on the ferry-rope with his chin in his hands.

"I am Taliesin," he says. "I am squire to the ferry. The ferryman is my master, and he is asleep, and he will not wake until someone answers my riddle. Nobody has, this week." He grins. "I have been a salmon, and a grain of wheat, and a hen's egg. I have been a star. I was there when the stones were brought to Salisbury. Would you like to cross? Then answer me this. *I am older than the king and younger than the morning. I am in every hall and every hovel. The poor man has me and the rich man lacks me. If you eat me, you die.* What am I?"

responses.label: You may try to answer the boy's riddle.
You may ask Taliesin to sing you one of his songs instead.

entries.body:
You come upon a horse fair at a market town, where a lanky young squire with a winning smile is selling a very fine grey destrier. The crowd is admiring it. "Twenty marks," the squire is saying. "Its master is a knight of the Round Table. He has no more need of it."

A horse-coper, standing beside you, mutters, "That's the fourth he's sold this month."

You make enquiries. The squire's name is Hywel, and his master, Sir Brastias, has lain asleep for a month under an enchantment in a room at the inn. Nobody can wake him. His squire has been selling off his horses, his armour and his plate. When you catch up with Hywel behind the stables, he grins and puts a finger to his lips. "A knight who sleeps," he says, "does not need a warhorse. Half the money is yours if you keep quiet."

responses.label: You may expose Hywel's thievery to the town.
You may take Hywel's offer and a share of the money.
You may try to wake the sleeping knight.

entries.body: You ride out onto the causeway and raise your hand. The red knight stops. "Sir," you call, "before any blood is shed, will you show your face?"

resolutions.label: persuade the red knight to unlace his helm

success.body: "There is a knight on the shore," you say, "who does not know who you are, and has been given a shield that is not his own. Someone has taken pains that you should not know each other. Why?" The red knight says nothing for a long time. Then, slowly, he unlaces his helm. He is a young man with Balin's face. On the shore, Balin cries out. The two brothers meet on the causeway, and above them, the ladies of the tower draw back from the battlements and disappear inside.

failure.body: "Sir, there is a knight on the shore who has been given a shield that is not his own." The red knight laughs. "It is the custom of the island," he says. "Everyone has a shield that is not his own." He rides past you. You cannot stop what follows. When it is over, the two dead knights lie together on the causeway, and when their helms are unlaced, they are brothers.

resolutions.label: invoke the law of arms, that no knight fights in another's shield

success.body: "By the law of arms," you call, so that the ladies on the battlements hear it, "no knight may fight bearing another man's shield. That knight on the shore has been given a shield not his own. The custom of this island is broken." The red knight hesitates. The ladies look at each other. At last he unlaces his helm. He is a young man with Balin's face. The brothers meet on the causeway and weep.

failure.body: You call out the law of arms. The ladies on the battlements laugh. "Here," says one, "there is no law but the custom." The red knight rides past you. You cannot stop what follows.

entries.body:
You come upon a slender young squire standing on a hilltop after a battle, looking down at the field where the crows are already busy. The squire's jerkin is too big and the voice, when it speaks, is too high. "Have you come from the High King's host?" the squire asks. "I am looking for my brother. Rhys ap Idwal. He fought here yesterday, in the Earl of Chester's company."

When you look more closely, you see that the squire is a young woman, with her hair cropped short and her face smeared with dirt. She sees you see it and lifts her chin. "My name is Gwenllian," she says. "My father would not let me come. He said it was no place for a girl. But nobody else would look for Rhys, and I will not have him left to the crows." She hesitates. "There are men from my father's household in the next valley, looking for me. There is a reward."

responses.label: You may help Gwenllian search the battlefield for her brother.
You may take Gwenllian back to her father's men for the reward.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You let them part, and follow the Saxon through the forest, keeping far back.

resolutions.label: shadow the Saxon envoy to his fleet

success.body: You follow him for two days, through the forest and across the downs to the sea, where forty longships lie hidden in a creek. You count them, and mark the creek, and ride back to the old king's camp. The king's captains send fire-ships down the creek on a spring tide. By morning, the Saxon fleet is ash. The old king, grey and tired, gives you a gold ring from his own finger.

failure.body: You follow him through the forest, but on the second day, he doubles back, and you walk right into him. You get away, but he knows now that he was followed, and the fleet moves.

resolutions.label: learn the Saxon's road from the stars he steers by

success.body: You do not follow him close. You watch which way he goes, and which stars he keeps on his left, and you know the downs well enough to guess where a man walking that line will come to the sea. You ride round the long way and are waiting in a gorse bush above the creek when he arrives. Forty longships lie hidden below. You count them and ride for the old king's camp.

failure.body: You guess the Saxon's road by the stars and ride round to meet him at the sea. He does not come. He was walking to a different creek.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.

You come upon a crowd at a crossroads, where a young squire stands on a cart with a rope around his neck. An old knight in black lies on a bier at the side of the road. A lady in black, tall and handsome, stands beside it.

"That is Sir Morien's squire, Iolo," a carter tells you. "They say he poisoned his master last night at the inn. The lady is Sir Morien's widow. She found the squire standing over the body with the cup in his hand."

The squire is white as chalk. "I did not do it," he says to you. "I brought my master his wine, as I do every night. The lady handed me the cup herself." The widow's face does not change. The reeve is holding up his hand for silence. "The knight is a stranger," he says to the crowd, "and has no stake in this. Let him judge."

responses.label: You may show mercy and spare the young squire's life.
You may uphold the law and let the squire hang for his crime.
You may accuse Sir Morien's widow of the poisoning.

entries.body: "I will not answer," you say. "But I will play you for it. Any game you like." The Green Knight's face lights up.

resolutions.label: win the Green Knight's winter game

success.body: He chooses a game you have never heard of, played with holly berries on the snow. He is very good at it. So are you, it turns out. You play all afternoon, and as the sun goes down, you win, by one berry. The Green Knight laughs, the old great laugh. "Then you need not answer," he says. "But I will tell you mine, since you have earned it. I would give up the wood." He looks round at the holly, and the snow, and the stream. "I would give up all of it. And I cannot." He is gone.

failure.body: He chooses a game played with holly berries on the snow, and he beats you in an hour. "Then you must answer," he says. You cannot. He steps back into the holly.

resolutions.label: outlast him in the snow until he names his own answer

success.body: "I will not answer," you say, "until you tell me yours." You sit down in the snow. He sits down opposite. You sit there, in silence, until the snow covers you both to the shoulders. At dusk, the Green Knight laughs, the old great laugh. "I would give up the wood," he says. "All of it. And I cannot." He is gone. You find, when you stand up, that you are not cold at all.

failure.body: You sit down in the snow opposite him and wait. By noon, you cannot feel your feet. He is still sitting there, perfectly comfortable, when you give up and go.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You go back through the waterfall and mount your horse. The horn sounds again, nearer. You ride toward it.

resolutions.label: draw the Saxon search-party away from the cave

success.body: You find the Saxons in a clearing: a dozen men with axes, following a hound. You ride across the clearing in full view, shouting, and wheel away into the trees. They come after you, hallooing. You lead them for five miles through the forest, over streams and through thickets, until they are lost and exhausted and their hound has given up. Then you circle back to the waterfall by night. The wounded men cheer you, weakly. One of them dies before morning, but the rest live.

failure.body: You find the Saxons in a clearing and ride across it shouting. But only half of them follow you. The other half go on with the hound, toward the waterfall. You hear the screaming from a mile away, and you cannot get back in time.

resolutions.label: lay a false trail away from the waterfall

success.body: You take a bloody bandage from one of the wounded men and drag it on a string behind your horse, away through the forest to the east. The Saxons' hound finds the scent and bays, and the whole search party goes off after it. You lead them to a river and let the trail end in the water. By dark, they are miles away. The wounded men in the cave live to see the morning.

failure.body: You drag a bloody bandage behind your horse to the east. The hound follows it, but the Saxons' leader is no fool, and sends half his men on toward the waterfall anyway.

entries.body: You wade into the stream and snatch your helm out of her hands. "My armour," you say, "is not yours to wash."

resolutions.label: wrest your armour from the washer and break the omen

success.body: She lets you take it. She lets you take the shield, too, and the hauberk, and the greaves. When you have gathered it all up in your arms, she looks at you and laughs, a long, cold, delighted laugh. "Oh, a fighter," she says. "I will have to begin again." She vanishes into the mist. Your armour, in your arms, is gone too, and you are wearing it. But the dent is gone from your helm, and the washer, you feel sure, has lost your thread for now.

failure.body: You try to snatch the helm, but your hands pass through it as though it were mist. The washer does not even look up. She wrings the red water out, and begins on the shield. You ride away shaking.

entries.body: You spur your horse after the black knight. He hears you coming and turns, grinning, with the white hound under his arm.

resolutions.label: catch and unhorse the hound-thief

success.body: You catch him at a ford. He drops the hound to take up his lance, and you meet him in the water, and he goes in backwards with a great splash. The hound shakes itself on the bank and trots over to you as though it has always been yours. You bring it back to the lady. She kisses the hound, and then you. "The queen will hear of this," she says. "Both of these."

failure.body: You catch him at a ford. He drops the hound to take up his lance, and you meet him in the water, and you go in backwards. When you come up, he is gone, and so is the hound, which seems to have gone with him willingly.

resolutions.label: shame the hound-thief before his own companions

success.body: You follow him to a pavilion by a stream where his friends are drinking, and ask him, loudly, whether he is the knight who stole a lady's lapdog in front of the whole forest. His friends stop drinking. They look at the white hound on his knee. One of them laughs. Then another. The black knight goes scarlet, and hands you the hound without a word. You bring it back to the lady, who kisses the hound, and then you.

failure.body: You ask him loudly whether he stole a lady's lapdog. "Yes," he says proudly, and his friends cheer. You leave without the hound.

entries.body: "You will not survive the winter here," you say. "Come down with me, and finish your book by a fire." The old monk shakes his head. "I promised my brothers I would not leave." You lift him anyway.

resolutions.label: carry the monk and his book through the snow

success.body: You carry him down the mountain on your back through the snowdrifts, with the book wrapped in your cloak, and at the bottom, you find a village with a church and a fire. The old monk is angry for a day, and then he sits by the fire and finishes his copy in a month, warm, and gives it to the village church. They still have it.

failure.body: You carry him down the mountain on your back, but the snow is deep and the path is lost, and you spend a night in a drift. He dies in your arms before morning. You save the book.

resolutions.label: persuade him that his vow allows him to go

success.body: You ask him what, exactly, he promised his brothers. He tells you: that he would not leave the book. "Then bring the book," you say. The old monk opens his mouth, and closes it, and laughs, for the first time, perhaps, in sixty years. You carry them both down the mountain, and he finishes his copy by a fire in the village church. They still have it.

failure.body: You ask him what he promised. "That I would not leave," he says. "Not the book. The place." You cannot move him. You leave him bread and go.

entries.body: You spur your horse south, following the churned-up tracks across the plain.

resolutions.label: run down the horse-thieves

success.body: You ride all day and catch them at dusk, watering the mares at a stream. You come down on them at a gallop, shouting, and the mares, hearing a voice they do not know, scatter in every direction, and so do the thieves. By morning, you have rounded up thirty-eight mares and two thieves. The old breeder weeps when you bring them home. He gives you the pick of the foals.

failure.body: You ride all day and catch them at dusk. But there are a dozen of them, and they have bows. You are driven off. By the time you reach Hereford, the mares are sold.

resolutions.label: track them to their night camp and take the mares back while they sleep

success.body: You do not ride them down. You follow the churned-up tracks at a walk all day and find their camp at dusk, in a hollow by a stream. At midnight, you cut the mares' tethers one by one and lead them out, whispering, and when the last is out, you slap its rump and forty mares gallop north for home. The thieves wake to an empty hollow. The old breeder gives you the pick of the foals.

failure.body: You find their camp at dusk and creep in at midnight, and one of the mares whinnies at you like an old friend. So much for creeping.

entries.body: "There is no shame in living," you say. "There is a path down the back of the mountain. I will lead you." Sir Brian looks at you with his one eye.

resolutions.label: lead the garrison down the mountain by night

success.body: They argue, but you talk them round, and in the small hours, you lead them down the back of the mountain by a sheep-path, carrying the wounded. At dawn, the Saxons storm the fort, and find it empty, and the barrel dry, and a very rude message carved on the gate. The garrison marches away to join the old king's army. Sir Brian insists on carrying the empty barrel. "A souvenir," he says.

failure.body: You lead them down the back of the mountain, but the path is steep and dark, and two of the old men fall. The rest reach the bottom, but Sir Brian will not speak to you.

resolutions.label: persuade the old captain that his garrison is worth more alive

success.body: You sit down by Sir Brian and talk, not of shame, but of the old king. He will need forty veterans at the last battle more than he needs one mountain fort. Sir Brian listens with his one eye on the fire. "Forty," he says at last, "is a good number to bring to a king." In the small hours, you lead them down the back of the mountain. At dawn, the Saxons find the fort empty and the barrel dry.

failure.body: You talk to Sir Brian about the old king. He listens, and then pours you another cup. "The old king," he says, "would stay." In the morning, you stand with them on the wall.

entries.body: You step over the toadstools. The music takes you like a wave, and you are dancing, and it is the most wonderful thing you have ever felt.

resolutions.label: dance with the fair folk and come out again

success.body: You dance with a pale lady whose eyes are full of stars, and you dance with a tall lord in a cloak of leaves, and you dance, at last, with Huw, and as you dance with him, you tell him who you are and who he is, and that it has been a year. His face changes. He stops dancing. You both stop. The music falters. You walk out of the ring together, hand in hand, over the toadstools, and the fair folk let you go, laughing, as though it were the best joke they had heard in a century. It is a long time before your feet stop tapping.

failure.body: You dance with a pale lady whose eyes are full of stars, and you dance, and you dance. When you stop, it is morning, and there is nobody in the ring, and your beard is longer, and your horse is gone. A shepherd tells you it is a month later than it was.

entries.body: "My lord," you say, "you are the king. Dreams are only dreams." The old king smiles, a tired smile.

resolutions.label: stand with the old king as he prepares for battle

success.body: He nods. "That is what Kay would have said," he says. "Kay is dead too." He sits with you on the altar stone until dawn, and talks about the old days. At first light, he stands and looks at the plain, where Mordred's host is gathering. "Well," he says. "Let us go and see how the wheel turns." He gives you his helm to carry. You will carry it all day, and at the end of it, you will carry it to the water.

failure.body: He nods. "That is what Kay would have said," he says, and goes back to his tent. In the morning, you see him staring at the stones for a long time before he mounts.

resolutions.label: keep the king's watch yourself through the last night

success.body: You send the old king back to his bed and take the watch yourself, walking the camp all night among the stones and the fires, checking every sentry, so that he can sleep. He does sleep, for the first time in a week. At first light, he comes out of his tent and finds you still walking. "Well," he says. "Let us go and see how the wheel turns." He gives you his helm to carry.

failure.body: You take the watch yourself, and near dawn you fall asleep against a stone, and the king finds you there. He does not wake you. He only puts his cloak over you.

entries.body: You look at the purse. You look at the silver in Dicon's hand. "Give it here," you say. "I will take care of it." Dicon stares at you. "You want it?" he says.

resolutions.label: cut the fay purse free and keep it

success.body: You wrap your hand in a cloth, cut the strings with your dagger, and stuff the purse into a leather bag inside another leather bag, and tie it shut. The screaming is muffled. Dicon falls on his knees and thanks you. For a month, you are rich beyond your dreams. Then one night you wake to find three little people sitting on the end of your bed, looking at you. The next morning, the purse is gone. So is your horse, your cloak and your boots. But you still have most of the silver.

failure.body: You wrap your hand in a cloth and cut the strings. The purse leaps out of Dicon's belt and into your hand, and clamps shut on your fingers like a trap, and screams directly into your face. You drop it. It rolls away into the long grass, and when you look for it, it is gone. So are your own purse and your dagger.

resolutions.label: bind the purse's voice and keep it

success.body: You take the purse by its strings and speak the old words for silence over it, three times, very firmly, as you would to a dog. The screaming stops. The purse hangs quiet at your belt, full of silver, and when you take a penny out, there is another penny. Dicon falls on his knees and thanks you. For a month, you are rich. Then one night you wake to find three little people sitting on the end of your bed, looking at you.

failure.body: You take the purse by its strings and speak the words for silence. The purse opens its mouth and screams straight into your face, and your ears ring for a week. It rolls away into the long grass, and so does Dicon.

entries.body: "I will guide you through," you say. Hu beams, and the bell clangs. The gorge of Nant-y-Cwm is a slit in the rock, with a river at the bottom and the walls leaning in at the top.

resolutions.label: guide the giant and his chapel through the gorge

success.body: You walk ahead, finding the places where the rock bulges and the places where it falls away, and you call back to him: stoop, turn, sidestep, mind the tower. Hu edges through, sideways, holding his breath. The chapel scrapes the rock twice and loses a gargoyle. At the far end, he sets it down on the hill with a sigh that flattens the grass. The bishop, who has been watching, comes running. He baptises Hu in a pond, since there is no font big enough, and the giant weeps for joy and gives you the gargoyle.

failure.body: You walk ahead, calling back to him, but you misjudge an overhang. The chapel's little tower catches the rock and snaps off, and the bell goes bouncing down into the river with a noise like the end of the world. Hu sits down in the gorge and cries. It takes a day to fish out the bell, and the bishop charges him for it.

resolutions.label: take the weight of the chapel through the tightest place

success.body: At the narrowest bend, the chapel will not go through upright. You climb onto the rock above and brace your back against the little tower, and hold it tilted while Hu edges underneath, holding his breath. Your legs shake. Your back screams. The bell clangs in your ear. And then it is through, and Hu is laughing, and the chapel is on the hill. The bishop baptises him in a pond. He weeps for joy and gives you a gargoyle.

failure.body: You brace your back against the little tower, and hold, and hold, and then your legs give out and you and the tower go down into the gorge together. It takes a day to fish the bell out of the river. The bishop charges Hu for it.

entries.body: You stay the night on the island. In the morning, you find the men gathering by the boats, sharpening their knives.

resolutions.label: persuade the old outlaws to keep faith

success.body: You stand on the jetty in front of the boats and tell them what you saw when the Grail passed through Camelot: the light, and the silence, and how every knight was fed with what he loved best. You tell them that the Grail has not gone, only hidden, and that a chapel in the fens full of sinners who stopped sinning is exactly where it might be hiding. They are quiet a long time. Then, one by one, they put down their knives and go back into the chapel.

failure.body: You stand on the jetty and talk to them about the Grail, but the leader of the young ones shoves you into the water, and the boats go out. The merchant's barge is robbed. Father Ulf weeps.

resolutions.label: stand on the jetty and bar the boats

success.body: You stand at the end of the jetty with your sword drawn and tell them that any man who wants the merchant's barge must go through you, and that you will not go easily. The young outlaws look at you, and at each other, and at Father Ulf, who has come to stand beside you with a staff. Nobody goes through you. The merchant's barge drifts past in the morning, untouched. Father Ulf weeps with relief.

failure.body: You stand at the end of the jetty with your sword drawn. The young outlaws put their boats in further down the bank. The merchant's barge is robbed. Father Ulf weeps.

entries.body: You take your place in the High King's battle line. At dawn, the Saxons come down the hill.

resolutions.label: hold the line at the battle of Badon

success.body: The Saxons come down the hill like a flood, and the line holds. You fight all day. Three times the Saxons break against the young king's shield-wall, and three times they come again. At dusk, the young king himself rides along the line with his great sword, and the line surges forward, and the Saxons break for good. You have never been so tired. The young king, passing you in the dusk, stops his horse and salutes you with his sword.

failure.body: The Saxons come down the hill like a flood, and you are knocked down in the first charge. You are carried from the field. The line holds without you.

entries.body: You wade into the black water with your sword drawn. Something stirs in the depths.

resolutions.label: battle the afanc in the black lake

success.body: It comes at you from below, enormous, with its saw-teeth snapping. You fight it in the water, waist-deep, and it drags you under twice, and twice you come up. The third time, you drive your sword into its throat. It thrashes, and the water goes red, and then it floats. The villagers haul it out with ropes. In its den under the bank, they find the old woman's grandson, alive, very cold and very frightened. She carries him home in her arms.

failure.body: It comes at you from below and drags you under, and under, and under. You come up gasping on the far side of the lake, without your sword, and it is a long walk back.

resolutions.label: drag the beast into the shallows where it is weak

success.body: You do not fight it in the deep water. When it seizes your leg and drags you, you let it, and then you grab a willow root on the bank and hold on, and hold on, and haul it inch by inch into the shallows, where it cannot dive. On land it is slow and blind. The villagers fall on it with every spade and flail in the village. In its den, they find the old woman's grandson, alive.

failure.body: You grab a willow root and hold on, and the afanc pulls, and the root snaps. You come up on the far side of the lake without your sword.

entries.body: You take the money. Hywel claps you on the back. "I knew you were a sensible knight," he says. "There is still his armour. And his shield. And his hawks."

resolutions.label: help Hywel sell off the rest of the sleeping knight's goods

success.body: Between you, you sell the armour to a knight from Kent, the shield to a tavern-keeper who hangs it over the door, and the hawks to a lady who has always wanted hawks. Hywel is a delightful partner. At the end of the week he divides the money fairly, shakes your hand, and disappears. The next time you pass the inn, the tavern sign is Sir Brastias's shield, and he is still asleep upstairs.

failure.body: You try to sell the armour to a knight from Kent, who happens to be Sir Brastias's cousin. He recognises it at once. Hywel runs. You are the one who is caught with the armour in your hands. The reeve puts you in the stocks, and the townsfolk throw what they have.

resolutions.label: drive the knight's horses to the great fair at Chester

success.body: You take the last three destriers to Chester fair yourself, riding one and leading two, and sell them to three different lords for three very good prices. Hywel is delighted with you. At the end of the week he divides the money fairly, shakes your hand and disappears. Sir Brastias, you hear, is still asleep.

failure.body: You take the destriers to Chester fair, and the first lord who looks at them is Sir Brastias's brother. He knows the horses. He knows the brand. He does not know you, but he soon does.

entries.body: You take the priest aside. "Father," you say, "if the font is too small, it is the font that must change, not the soul."

resolutions.label: argue the giant's case from scripture

success.body: You remind the priest of the whale that swallowed Jonah and was sent by God, and of Goliath, who was a giant and a Philistine, and this is neither. You remind him of Saint Christopher, who in some tellings was a giant and carried Christ over the water. The priest listens and chews his lip. At last he nods. "The mill-pond," he says. "I will use the mill-pond." The whole village comes to watch. Ysbaddaden is baptised in the mill-pond, and the millwheel stops for an hour, and nobody minds.

failure.body: You remind the priest of Saint Christopher, who in some tellings was a giant. "That," says the priest firmly, "is a story for children." The giant, who has been listening, sighs and goes home. You pass his hut later and see him sitting in the doorway with his head in his hands.

resolutions.label: shame the priest with the giant's own humility

success.body: You bring the priest out of the church and make him look at the giant, properly: at the patched smock, the enormous hands folded together, the careful way he kneels so as not to crush the graves. "He has given up eating sheep," you say. "What have you given up?" The priest is silent a long while. Then he fetches his book and goes down to the mill-pond. The whole village comes to watch the baptism.

failure.body: You ask the priest what he has given up. "My patience," he says, "with knights." He goes back into the church. The giant sighs and goes home.

entries.body: You push the iron door very gently. It swings open without a sound. Inside, in rows as far as your lantern can reach, knights lie asleep beside their horses, in armour you have only seen in old carvings.

resolutions.label: walk among the Sleepers without waking them

success.body: You walk softly down the rows. You see faces you know from tapestries, and faces you do not know at all. At the end of the cave, on a stone throne, sits an empty chair with a crown on it. There is dust on the crown. You do not touch it. You go out as quietly as you came, and close the door behind you. The boy looks at your face and asks nothing. You ride on toward the war with a strange lightness in your chest.

failure.body: You walk softly down the rows, but at the end, your spur catches on a stirrup, and the stirrup rings. All along the rows, a thousand eyes open. "Is it time?" a voice asks. You cannot answer. They close their eyes again, one by one, and you flee.

entries.body: "Wait," you say. "Let me speak to him first. If he will give up your mother, will you let him live?" Gaheris hesitates. "He will not," he says. "But try, if you like. I have waited long enough to wait a little longer."

resolutions.label: bring Lamorak and Gaheris to terms

success.body: You ride to meet Lamorak and tell him everything. He listens, and for once he does not laugh. "I love her," he says simply. "But I do not want her sons to kill me, or me them." Between the three of you, standing in the crossroads, you work out a peace. Lamorak will go on pilgrimage for a year. Morgause will be told nothing about it. Gaheris will tell his brothers the matter is closed. It will not hold forever. It holds for now.

failure.body: You ride to meet Lamorak and tell him everything. He roars with laughter. "Let him try!" he says, and gallops past you to the crossroads, and the fight is on before you have turned your horse. You pull them apart eventually, but not before Gaheris has sworn on his father's grave to finish it. Gaheris blames you for the warning. Lamorak blames you for the delay.

resolutions.label: make them both swear peace on a relic

success.body: You take a small bone of Saint David from your purse, which you have carried since your first pilgrimage, and hold it up between the two men. "Swear," you say, "that neither of you will draw on the other while this bone is in Britain." Neither dares refuse a saint. They swear. You keep the relic very safe after that, and you never, ever take it abroad.

failure.body: You hold up the bone between them. Lamorak laughs and swears at once. Gaheris looks at it, and then at Lamorak laughing, and spits on the ground. "I will not swear on a bone," he says, "with my mother's shame still warm."

entries.body: You ride up to the barricade and draw your sword. "The bridge is the king's," you say. "Clear it."

resolutions.label: fight your way across the Severn bridge

success.body: The first of them swings a club at your horse's head. You knock it out of his hands. The second goes into the river. The rest look at each other, and at the townsfolk gathering behind you with sticks and rolling-pins, and run. Black Cadwgan comes out of the tollhouse roaring, and you meet him in the middle of the bridge, and he goes into the river too. The townsfolk tear down the barricade with their bare hands. The baker gives you a loaf the size of a shield.

failure.body: The first of them swings a club at your horse's head, and your horse shies, and you are in the river before you have struck a blow. You swim to the bank to cheers from the brigands.

resolutions.label: ride straight through the barricade

success.body: You back your horse the length of the bridge, then put your spurs in and ride at the barricade of carts. At the last moment, your horse leaps the lowest cart. The brigands scatter like pigeons. You wheel on the far side and ride back through them, and they run. Black Cadwgan comes out of the tollhouse and meets your horse's chest, and goes into the river. The townsfolk tear down the rest with their hands.

failure.body: You ride at the barricade, and your horse refuses at the last moment, and you do not. You land among the brigands, on your back. They take a toll of your purse.

entries.body: The dwarf circles you again, lash raised. This time, you are ready.

resolutions.label: catch the lash and pull the dwarf from his pony

notes: Place a Cunning Skill Marker on your Accompanied Status Card

success.body: You catch the lash as it comes down, wind it round your wrist, and pull. The dwarf comes off his pony and lands in the road, spitting. You take the whip and break it over your knee. The dwarf stares at the pieces. All the mad glee drains out of his face, and he is only a small, frightened man. "He makes me do it," he whispers, jerking his head at the knight. "If I do not, he beats me." You lift him onto your own saddle and ride away with him, and the Knight of the Sparrowhawk, strangely, does not follow.

failure.body: You grab at the lash, but it curls round your hand and cuts it, and the dwarf pulls it away laughing and cracks it across your horse's rump. Your horse bolts. You are a mile down the road before you can stop it.

entries.body: "Come," you say to the bride. "Follow me, and do not look at the oak." The groom glares up at the tree, suspicious. Puck sticks his tongue out.

resolutions.label: lead the wedding party out of the fay wood

success.body: You turn your cloak inside out, which an old woman once told you confuses the fair folk, and make everyone else do the same. Then you walk in a straight line, whatever the path seems to do. The wood twists and turns, and Puck shrieks with laughter somewhere behind you, and at last you come out into a meadow, and there is the church, with the bell ringing. The bride kisses you. The groom, to his credit, goes back to the edge of the wood and apologises to a toadstool. You hear, from the trees, a delighted giggle.

failure.body: You lead the wedding party in what you are sure is a straight line. After an hour, you come back to the oak. Puck is laughing so hard he falls out of it. You spend the night in the wood with the wedding party, and the fiddler plays all night to keep your spirits up, which does not help.

resolutions.label: persuade Puck to let them go

success.body: You sit down under the oak and talk to Puck. You agree that the groom was rude. You agree that toadstools have feelings. You point out that the bride was not rude at all, and that it is her wedding day, and that nobody will ever leave milk out for a hob again in this parish if she is kept from her church. Puck considers this seriously. "The milk," he says. "I had not thought of the milk." He jumps down, bows to the bride, and the path to the church is suddenly straight. He gives you an acorn. It is warm, and it hums.

failure.body: You sit down under the oak and talk to Puck. You agree that the groom was rude. Puck agrees that you are very sensible. Then he makes you forget which way you came, too.

entries.body: "My lord," you say, "the High King fights for Britain. The spear that healed it should be with him." The old king looks at you for a long time.

resolutions.label: persuade the Fisher King to part with the Holy Lance

success.body: "It did not heal Britain," he says. "It wounded it. The healing came after." But he looks at you, and sees something in your face. "Take it," he says at last. "Not to fight with. To remind him." You carry the spear to the High King's camp. He takes it, and weighs it in his hand, and does not use it. But on the last day, you see it in his hand as he goes out onto the plain.

failure.body: "It is not for war," says the old king. "Nor for you." He turns his face to the wall. You leave Corbenic empty-handed.

resolutions.label: swear on the spear to use it only to remind, never to strike

success.body: You kneel by his bed and put your hand on the spear's shaft and swear, before his people, that you will carry it to the High King and that it will not be used to wound anyone. The old king looks at you a long time, and nods. You carry it to the High King. He weighs it in his hand, and does not use it. But on the last day, you see it in his hand as he goes out onto the plain.

failure.body: You kneel and swear on the spear. The old king shakes his head. "Everyone swears that," he says. "Then they strike." He turns his face to the wall.

entries.body: You look at the barrels. "What does the king want with a quarter of good French wine?" you ask. Grace laughs. "A man of sense," she says.

resolutions.label: help the smugglers land their cargo

success.body: You take command of the landing as if it were a siege. You set a watch on the cliff, a boy on the headland with a lantern, and a line of men passing barrels, and by dawn the whole cargo is up the cliff and away on carts. Grace gives you two barrels and a French sword. As for the customs man, she lets him go, blindfolded, twenty miles inland. "No sense in murder," she says. "Bad for trade."

failure.body: You take command of the landing. Unfortunately, the boy on the headland falls asleep, and the sheriff's men come along the cliff at dawn. You leave in a hurry, without the wine, down the beach and round the rocks, with your boots full of sea.

entries.body: "Hold," you say. "I will bring you help." Sir Bedivere nods. "Go quickly," he says.

resolutions.label: ride to the king's army and bring back reinforcements

success.body: You ride down the back of the pass at a gallop and find the king's army in the valley, retreating in good order. You find a captain who will listen, and bring back two hundred men up the pass at dusk. They fall on the Saxons from above. The Saxons break. Sir Bedivere, bloody to the elbows, laughs when he sees you. "Just in time," he says. "As always in the songs."

failure.body: You ride down the back of the pass and find the king's army, but no captain will spare men. You ride back up alone, too late. The pass has fallen.

resolutions.label: take the short way down through the hills

success.body: You do not go down the long road the army took. You take a shepherds' track straight down the mountain's shoulder, leading your horse, and come out on the valley floor two hours ahead of any messenger by the road. You find a captain who will listen, and bring back two hundred men up the pass at dusk. The Saxons break. Sir Bedivere, bloody to the elbows, laughs. "Just in time," he says.

failure.body: You take a shepherds' track down the mountain's shoulder, and it leads you into the wrong valley. By the time you find the army, the pass has fallen.

entries.body: You look at the knights laughing at the gate. You think of the rotten apples. "Tell me about these saddles," you say. Pebin's eyes gleam.

resolutions.label: play the saddler's trick on Sir Hugh

success.body: You free Pebin from the stocks at night, and he works in the woods for a week, and then you ride into the castle yard with a gift for Sir Hugh from an admirer: the finest saddle anyone has ever seen. Sir Hugh is delighted. He rides out to show it off the next morning, and three miles from the castle, the stitching gives way all at once, and he lands in a bog with the saddle on top of him. His friends' saddles follow, one by one, over the next month. Nobody ever proves a thing. Pebin gives you the finest bridle he ever made.

failure.body: You free Pebin from the stocks at night, and he works for a week on a saddle, and you take it to Sir Hugh as a gift from an admirer. Sir Hugh looks at it, and at you, and at the dwarf's initials stitched under the pommel. You are both in the stocks by noon.

entries.body: You pay your penny and cross. Then you go looking for the sheriff's house.

resolutions.label: uncover the sheriff's dealings with the brigands

success.body: You spend a day watching the sheriff's house, and at dusk, you see one of Cadwgan's men go in by the back door with a heavy purse, and come out without it. You follow him back to the bridge, and then you go to the Earl of Gloucester with what you have seen. The Earl, who has been wondering why his sheriff has a new horse, sends his own men. The bridge is clear by morning. The sheriff is in his own cells.

failure.body: You spend a day watching the sheriff's house and see nothing but a great many cats. When you ask questions in the town, word gets back to the sheriff, and you are arrested for vagrancy.

resolutions.label: follow the toll money to where it ends up

success.body: You watch the tollhouse from the other bank at dusk and see a boy come out with a heavy bag. You follow him through the back lanes, keeping far behind, to the sheriff's own kitchen door. You go to the Earl of Gloucester, who has been wondering why his sheriff has a new horse. The Earl's men clear the bridge by morning. The sheriff is in his own cells.

failure.body: You follow the boy through the back lanes and lose him in the fish market. By the time you find his trail again, it is dark, and you are lost in Gloucester.

entries.body: "I will kill your wolf," you say. "But you are coming with me." Gwion looks as though he might faint. "Must I?" he says. "Someone must write it down," you say.

resolutions.label: hunt the great wolf of Nant

success.body: You track the wolf up the valley by moonlight, with Gwion stumbling behind you, and find it on a ledge above the sheepfold. It is enormous. You kill it with your spear as it leaps, and Gwion, who has been hiding behind a rock, is sick. In the morning, the village carries him home in triumph with the wolf's pelt round his shoulders. He looks at you over their heads, ashamed and grateful. The ten marks are waiting in your saddlebag. So, by the next spring, is the song, which is very good, and quite true, apart from the names.

failure.body: You track the wolf up the valley by moonlight. It is enormous, and it is waiting for you. It takes your spear arm in its jaws before you can strike, and you both roll down the hill. When it flees, you are bleeding, and Gwion is gone. The next morning, you hear, he left the inn before dawn with his harp and the villagers' ten marks paid in advance.

resolutions.label: rouse the village to hunt the wolf together

success.body: You go back into the inn and tell the villagers that their hero has a plan: a drive. You set the men in a long line with torches and pans, and the dogs behind them, and drive the wolf down the valley toward the sheepfold, where you wait with your spear and Gwion stands behind you, pale. The wolf breaks from the bracken straight at you. When it is over, the village carries Gwion home in triumph. He looks at you over their heads, ashamed and grateful.

failure.body: You set the villagers in a long line with torches and pans, and they drive the wolf, but the line breaks at the stream, and the wolf goes through the gap and takes a ewe on its way. Everybody blames Gwion. Gwion blames you.

entries.body:
You look at the bleeding spear on the wall, and at the old king beneath it, and you remember the question a maiden once whispered to you by a flooded river. It is not yet time for it. But you rise from the lower table, and cross the hall, and kneel before King Pellam, and ask him quietly whom his vessel serves.

The old king looks at you for a long time. The hall has gone silent. "Not yet," he says at last, softly. "It is not yet wounded. But it will be. When it is, come back, and ask me again." He lifts you up. At that moment, across the hall, Balin draws on the invisible Garlon, and you run to stop him, and you are in time. Garlon lives. Balin is sent out of the castle with his two swords. But the old king has marked your face, and so has the spear.
You go and stand beside the abbot in the gate, with your hand on your sword.

resolutions.label: hold the abbey gate against the Irish warriors

success.body: The Irish chief looks at you, and at the abbot, and at the refugees who have picked up sticks and stones and are standing behind you. He laughs. "One knight and a crowd of beggars," he says. But he does not charge. After a long while, he turns his horse. "Keep them, then," he calls back. "Feed them yourself." You help the monks plough a new field for the refugees. By harvest, they are feeding themselves.

failure.body: The Irish chief looks at you and laughs, and charges. You fight in the gate, and the refugees fight behind you, but the Irish are warriors and they are not. By nightfall, half the refugees have been driven to the shore.

resolutions.label: lead the refugees to raise a rampart round the abbey

success.body: You do not wait for the Irish to charge. You set every refugee who can lift a spade to dig, all night, beside you, deepening the abbey's old earth bank and piling thorn on top of it. At dawn, the Irish chief rides up and finds a rampart and three hundred angry Britons behind it with spades. He laughs. "Keep them, then," he calls. "Feed them yourself." By harvest, they are feeding themselves.

failure.body: You dig all night beside the refugees, but a rampart is not built in a night. The Irish come over it at dawn.

entries.body: You look at the miller. "Open the cage," you say. The miller laughs and takes up a cudgel. "Come and open it yourself," he says.

resolutions.label: break the iron cage and free the fay

success.body: You knock the cudgel out of the miller's hands and put him in his own millpond. Then you take your sword to the cage's lock. It takes a long time, and the iron screams, and the fay girl screams too, but at last the door swings open. You lift her out. She is as light as a breath. At the edge of the wood, she steps out of your arms and stands on her own, and begins to grow solid again. "The hill will remember," she says. "The hill always remembers." She kisses your forehead, and it is like being kissed by the wind.

failure.body: You knock the miller into his millpond and take your sword to the lock. It will not break. You hack at it until your sword is notched and your arms ache, and at sunset, the fay girl fades away entirely, leaving nothing in the cage but a smell of apple blossom. The miller climbs out of the pond, cursing you for his lost fortune.

resolutions.label: open the lock with a charm while she still breathes

success.body: You do not fight the miller. You lay your hand on the iron lock and speak the words for opening, and the lock clicks, and the door swings wide while the miller is still shouting. You lift her out. She is as light as a breath. At the edge of the wood, she steps out of your arms and grows solid again. "The hill will remember," she says, and kisses your forehead. The miller's flour, you hear, never rises again.

failure.body: You lay your hand on the lock and speak the words for opening. Iron does not listen to charms. At sunset, the fay girl fades away in the cage, leaving a smell of apple blossom.

entries.body: You wait until the griffin flies off to hunt, then start up the cliff with a sack over your shoulder.

resolutions.label: climb the cliff and steal the griffin's eggs

success.body: It is a terrible climb. Your fingers bleed and your arms shake. But you reach the nest while the griffin is still away, and there are two eggs in it, golden and warm, each the size of a man's head. You put one in the sack and leave one, because you are not a monster. You are halfway down when the griffin comes back, and screams, and dives, and you fall the last twenty feet into a hayrick. The Lord of Dinas pays you a fortune. The griffin circles the valley for a month.

failure.body: It is a terrible climb, and you are only halfway up when the griffin comes back. She knocks you off the cliff with one sweep of her wing. You land in a stream. The villagers pull you out and tell you, with feeling, that they did not ask you to do that.

resolutions.label: lure the griffin away with a decoy and climb

success.body: You hang a dead sheep from a tree on the far side of the valley, where the griffin can see it from her nest. She screams and dives for it. While she is tearing at it, you are up the cliff by the short way and back down with a golden egg in a sack. You leave the second egg, because you are not a monster. The Lord of Dinas pays you a fortune. The griffin circles the valley for a month.

failure.body: You hang a dead sheep across the valley. The griffin looks at it, and then at you, halfway up her cliff. She prefers you.

entries.body: "Leave it to me," you say, and dismount. The pig watches you. It has a look in its eye that you do not like.

resolutions.label: outwit the pig

success.body: You do not chase it. You sit down under the pear tree, as far from the pig as you can get, and wait. After a long while, the pig becomes curious and wanders closer. After a longer while, it decides you are not dangerous. Then you seize it by the back leg and hold on while it screams like a devil and drags you twice around the orchard. Ector laughs until he falls over. "That is how the boy did it," he gasps. "Exactly how he did it." He gives you a ham at Christmas, every Christmas, for the rest of his life.

failure.body: You do not chase it. You sit down and wait. The pig sits down too. After an hour, Ector goes indoors for his dinner. After two hours, it starts to rain. After three hours, the pig gets up and walks away into the woods, and you realise it has been waiting for you to give up. You resolve never again to underestimate a pig.

resolutions.label: tackle the pig with all your strength

success.body: You chase the pig round the orchard three times, over the wall and into the duckpond, and finally bring it down in the mud with a flying leap. You are covered head to foot. Ector is helpless with laughter. "Kay would never have done that," he wheezes. "Kay would have sent a servant." That night he feeds you roast pork, which seems hard on the pig, and tells you stories of the High King as a boy until the fire is out.

failure.body: You chase the pig round the orchard three times and into the duckpond. The pig swims better than you do. You come out covered in weed with the pig nowhere to be seen. Ector gives you a towel and a cup of cider. "It got away from Arthur too," he says. "Twice."

entries.body: You go down into the hold at night and search among the cargo.

resolutions.label: find and hide the stolen thorn

success.body: You find it in a barrel of salt fish: a small crystal box with a dark thorn inside. You take it and put a thorn from the ship's bramble-broom in its place. The hooded man sells his fake at Tunis to a Moorish merchant for a fortune, and nobody is ever the wiser. The real one goes back to Glastonbury in your pocket. You warn the pilgrims, and they get off the ship at the next port, all forty of them, and walk.

failure.body: You find the barrel of salt fish, but the hooded man finds you. You wake up in the sea, clinging to a spar, and are picked up by fishermen off the Scillies. The ship is gone.

resolutions.label: guard the relic's hiding place through the voyage

success.body: You find the thorn in a barrel of salt fish and move it to your own sea-chest, and sit on the chest for eleven days with your sword across your knees. The hooded man looks at you. The captain looks at you. Nobody tries it. At Genoa, you walk down the gangplank with the chest on your shoulder, and warn the forty pilgrims to walk down after you. The thorn goes home to Glastonbury.

failure.body: You move the thorn to your sea-chest and sit on it with your sword across your knees. On the fourth night, you fall asleep. On the fifth morning, the chest is empty.

entries.body: "Twenty men cannot beat forty," you say. "But twenty men who know the forest can tell the old king where forty Saxons are." Sir Hervi frowns. Then he nods.

resolutions.label: scout the Saxon host with the outlaws

success.body: You spend a week creeping through the forest with the outlaws, counting Saxons, marking their camps, noting their roads. At the end of the week, you ride to the old king's camp with a map drawn on a piece of bark. The old king's captains use it to ambush the whole Saxon host at the river. Sir Hervi and his outlaws are given a pardon and a place in the old king's army.

failure.body: You creep through the forest with the outlaws, counting Saxons, but one of the outlaws is a Saxon spy. On the fourth night, you are ambushed.

entries.body: "Show me," you say. The young priest leads you round to a grating in the alley behind the church, where you can look down into the cave from above.

resolutions.label: catch the shrine-keepers in their fraud

success.body: You watch through the grating for an hour. The shining monk is real enough, an old man who sits and prays and speaks to no one. But between visitors, the monks who keep the shrine are counting coins and laughing, and one of them is dabbing oil of phosphor on a cloth to make the cave shine brighter.
