You and the priest go down with the bishop's sergeant. The keepers are taken away. The old monk, it turns out, never knew about the phosphor. He goes on praying in the dark, alone, and the priest brings him bread every day.

failure.body: You watch through the grating for an hour and see nothing but an old man praying. When you go to the bishop with your suspicions, the shrine-keepers produce a letter of approval from the Archbishop. The young priest is sent to a parish in the Fens.

resolutions.label: make the shrine-keepers swear upon their own relic

success.body: You go down into the cave and ask the keepers, before the pilgrims, to swear on their own relic that the shining is a miracle and not their own work. They look at each other. Nobody in that city will swear a false oath on a relic in front of a crowd. The eldest keeper goes white and confesses about the oil of phosphor. The old monk, it turns out, never knew. The young priest brings him bread every day after that.

failure.body: You ask the keepers to swear on their relic. The eldest does, at once, with his hand on it, smiling. The pilgrims cheer. You leave feeling that you have made a lie holier.

entries.body: You put out a small boat and row across the dark water to the two ships, now lashed together.

resolutions.label: slip aboard and spy on the kings' meeting

success.body: You climb the anchor-rope in the dark and hide among the coiled ropes on deck. Below you, in the cabin, you hear it: the King of Ireland will land at Anglesey at midsummer, while King Lot comes down from the north. You slip back into your boat. At Camelot, the young king hears you out with Merlin at his shoulder. "Anglesey," says Merlin, thoughtfully. "Well, well." When the Irish ships come to Anglesey at midsummer, the young king's army is waiting on the beach.

failure.body: You climb the anchor-rope in the dark, but your foot slips, and you splash into the sea. Lanterns come on all over both ships. You swim for your life back to your own ship.

resolutions.label: call up a sea-fog to cover your approach

success.body: You kneel in the bow of the little boat and speak the words the Welsh fishermen use when the tax-cutters are out, and a fog rolls up off the dark water and wraps the two lashed ships. You row in under their sterns unseen and hear every word through the cabin window: the King of Ireland will land at Anglesey at midsummer. At Camelot, the young king hears it with Merlin at his shoulder. "Anglesey," says Merlin thoughtfully. "Well, well."

failure.body: You speak the fishermen's words, and a fog rolls up, and you row into it, and out of it, and into it, and never find the ships again.

entries.body: You ride to the fallen tree and throw a rope round it, and tie it to your saddle.

resolutions.label: drag the fallen tree clear

success.body: You haul, and your horse hauls, and the carters haul, and the tree moves, a foot, two feet, enough. The carts whip past it at a gallop, and the Saxons, who were busy with the rear, look up to see their prize escaping. You ride behind the last cart, fighting a rearguard for a mile. By nightfall, the bread is in the old king's camp.

failure.body: You haul, and your horse hauls, and the rope snaps. The tree does not move. The Saxons take the carts.

resolutions.label: form the carters into a wall round the carts

success.body: You do not try to move the tree. You pull the carts into a ring, in the old way, and put the carters behind them with their whips and their knives, and the dead escort's spears, and you stand in the gap. The Saxons expected carters. They find a fort. After three rushes, they give up and melt back into the trees. By nightfall, the bread is in the old king's camp.

failure.body: You pull the carts into a ring, but the carters do not know how to hold one. The Saxons are over the carts in the first rush.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman walking along the road with a sword belted round her waist over a plain blue gown. The sword is far too big for her. Its scabbard drags in the dust behind her like a tail.

"Do not trouble to ask," she says. "Everyone asks. My name is Morfudd. My lady, the Lady of Lisle, has sent me to find the best knight in Britain, and give him this sword. Only a knight without guile or treachery can draw it." She sighs. "I have been to Camelot. Twenty-six knights of the Round Table have tried. Nobody can draw it. Sir Kay pulled so hard he fell over." She holds out the hilt to you, a little wearily. "You may as well try. Everyone does."

As you reach for it, she adds, more quietly, "They say it will bring great good to whoever draws it, and great grief. I do not know which comes first."

responses.label: You may try to draw the damsel's sword.
You may help Morfudd carry the sword on to the next town.
You may ask Morfudd where the sword came from.

entries.body:
You come upon a small stone chapel on a hillside at dusk, where a young woman in a grey cloak is kneeling beside a new tomb. On the tomb lies a stone knight with his hands folded, and above it hangs a real shield and a gilded helm.

"His name was Sir Brangor," she says, without getting up. "We were to be married at Lammastide. His own cousin killed him in a quarrel over a hawk." Her voice is very flat. "I am Ceinwen. I have kept vigil here for forty nights. Tonight, I have heard, men are coming from the village to take the gilded helm and the armour from his body. His cousin has told them there is gold in the coffin." She looks up at you with dry eyes. "I cannot stop them. I have a knife, but there will be six of them."

responses.label: You may keep vigil beside Ceinwen and guard the tomb through the night.
You may persuade Ceinwen to end her vigil and come away.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman on the bank of a swollen river, holding a covered dish on a white cloth. The dish is very small, but she holds it with both hands, as though it were heavy. Her gown is white, and her feet are bare and cut from the stones.

"Please," she says. "I must cross. I am Anfelise. I serve the maiden who carries the holy vessel at Corbenic. My lady sent me with this, to a hermit who is dying, and I must bring it to him before dawn." She looks at the brown water. "I must not set it down. I must not look under the cloth. And I cannot swim."

The ford is deep and fast. On your side of the river, you notice, the grass is withered and brown. On hers, it is green.

responses.label: You may carry Anfelise and the covered dish across the river.
You may ask Anfelise to tell you about Corbenic and its king.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman sitting on a rock in a woodland pool, with her bare feet in the water and a large book open on her knees. She is reading very fast and muttering. An old man in a grey robe sits on the bank beside her, watching her with a look of great fondness.

"Merlin," the young woman says, without looking up. "Go and fetch me some more of those mushrooms." The old man gets up obediently and shuffles into the trees. As soon as he is gone, she shuts the book and turns to you.

"Quickly," she says. "I am Nimue, and I serve the Lady of the Lake. He has been following me for a year. He says he loves me. He teaches me everything I ask, because he hopes it will make me love him. I do not." Her eyes are very bright and hard. "I have nearly learned enough. There is a spell that will shut him in a cave of stone forever, where he cannot follow me any more. I need someone to hold him still while I say it." She looks at you. "Or you could run and tell him. I would understand. He is the High King's counsellor."

responses.label: You may help Nimue cast her spell on Merlin.
You may warn Merlin of what Nimue intends.

entries.body:
You come upon a tournament field outside a small castle, with pavilions of every colour and a crowd of townsfolk on the banks. A young lady in green, with a wreath of daisies, is sitting on a painted stand, looking as though she would rather be anywhere else.

She beckons you over. "I am Rhiannedd," she says. "My father has promised my hand to the winner of this tournament. There are three knights left. One is Sir Harry le Fitz Lake, who is rich and fat and sixty. One is Sir Brian of the Forest, who beats his squires. And one is Sir Ywain the Poor, who has one horse and one shield and has written me eleven songs." She blushes. "Sir Ywain will lose. He always loses. But if you enter," she lowers her voice, "and knock out the other two, and then let Sir Ywain knock you off your horse, nobody need ever know."

responses.label: You may enter the tournament and throw the final joust to Sir Ywain.
* You may enter the tournament and win Rhiannedd's hand for yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman sitting in a churchyard at noon, on a grave with no name on it, combing her long hair and singing to herself. She is barefoot and dressed in a shroud.

"Oh!" she says, when she sees you. "Can you see me? Most people cannot. I am dead, you see. I am Tegwen. I died at Michaelmas, of a fever." She pats the grave. "This is mine. They were not sure what to write." She smiles. "I like it here. It is very quiet."

The priest comes hurrying out of the church, wringing his hands. "She is not dead," he says. "She had the fever, and she lay three days like one dead, and her mother laid her out for burial. On the third night she woke up in her shroud, and now she says she died and came back wrong. She will not go home. She eats the bread from the altar. Her mother cannot look at her." He lowers his voice. "The village says she is a revenant. They say she should be burned."

responses.label: You may try to convince Tegwen that she is alive.
You may try to protect Tegwen from the frightened villagers.

entries.body: You kneel beside the young woman and begin pulling stones out of the rubble.

resolutions.label: dig the priest out of the ruins

success.body: You dig all day, until your hands bleed. At dusk, you find a hollow under the fallen beams, and in it, the old priest, alive, curled round the church's silver cross. He opens his eyes and says, "I knew someone would come." The young woman weeps. The survivors carry him out on a door. He lives, and the next Sunday, he says Mass in the ashes of his church, and the whole village comes.

failure.body: You dig all day, and at dusk, you find him, under the fallen beams. He is dead. He has been dead since morning. The young woman sits down in the rubble and does not move.

resolutions.label: pray to find him before you dig

success.body: You kneel in the ashes and pray, and ask the young woman to be very quiet, and listen. After a long time, very faint, from under the rubble at the east end, you hear a voice singing the Nunc Dimittis. You dig there. At dusk, you find the old priest in a hollow under the beams, curled round the church's silver cross. "I knew someone would come," he says.

failure.body: You kneel and pray and listen, and hear nothing. You dig all day in the wrong place. At dusk, you find him, at the east end. He has been dead since morning.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman on a rock above a castle, looking down at the smoke of the kitchens with an expression of great concentration. In her lap is a small clay pot, stoppered with wax. She jumps when she sees you and covers it with her skirt.

"You are a knight," she says. "Good. You can tell me whether knights will think this is honourable, or not." She is fair and freckled and very young. "My name is Eluned. My sister was taken last year by the giant Carnwen, who lives in the hills above this castle. The castle's steward, Sir Loholt, sold her to the giant for a hundred sheep and a promise that the giant would leave his lands alone." She uncovers the pot. "This is hemlock. Tonight is the steward's feast day. I am to serve the wine. I have thought it all through." She looks up at you. "Is it honourable?"

responses.label: You may help Eluned carry out her poisoning.
You may stop Eluned and challenge the steward yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a nunnery in a green valley, where a young nun with ink-stained fingers comes running out of the gate to meet you, clutching a scroll covered with circles and figures.

"You are going to Camelot?" she asks breathlessly. "Please. I am Sister Branwen. I keep the library here. I have been reckoning the stars for three years, and I have found something." She unrolls the scroll. "There is a great conjunction coming. In a certain year, in May, the High King will fight a battle on a plain, against his own blood, and neither of them will live." She is shaking. "Nobody will believe me. The abbess says a nun has no business looking at the stars. But somebody must tell the king."

responses.label: You may carry Sister Branwen's warning to the High King.
You may stay and study the stars with Sister Branwen.

entries.body:
You come upon a pavilion by a crossroads, hung with a painted board: *A Knight of Great Renown Challenges All Comers. Prize: One Hundred Marks.* Before it sits a pretty young woman on a stool, taking names on a wax tablet.

"Good day," she says, beaming. "I am Lady Gwennol, the knight's herald. The fee to enter is five marks. My knight is resting now, but he will joust with you at noon." She holds out her hand for the fee.

You glance into the pavilion. On a stand inside is a suit of fine armour, with nobody in it. Behind the pavilion, three burly men are playing dice beside a heap of saddles, harness and purses. When you look back, Gwennol is watching you, still smiling. "He is very shy," she says. "Five marks."

responses.label: You may expose Lady Gwennol's false challenge.
You may join Lady Gwennol's scheme for a share of the takings.

entries.body: You start up the mountain on foot, bent double against the hail. The higher you climb, the harder it beats.

resolutions.label: climb through the witch's storm

success.body: You climb with your shield over your head, and the hail rings on it like a smithy. Near the top, the wind tries to throw you off the mountain. You crawl. At last you reach the rock, and the witch, a small, fierce old woman, turns and stares at you. "Nobody has ever got this far," she says. You tell her about the child. She is quiet a long time. Then she lowers her arms, and the storm stops. "I will send the lord his money back," she says. "His storms, too."

failure.body: You climb with your shield over your head, but halfway up, a gust tears it out of your hands, and the hail beats you down. You crawl back to the village, bruised all over.

resolutions.label: turn her storm with a counter-charm

success.body: You stand in the village square in the hail and draw a circle round it with your sword, and speak the old charm for fair weather backwards, then forwards, then backwards again, as the old women do at harvest. The hail stops over the village. Above the next valley, where the lord's wheat stands golden, a black cloud gathers. Up on the mountain, the weather-witch lowers her arms and laughs. She sends the lord his money back.

failure.body: You draw a circle in the hail and speak the charm backwards and forwards. The hail turns to snow. It is June.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman standing in the middle of a village street, turning slowly round and round, as though she has lost something. She is dressed in a gown of a fashion you have only seen in old tapestries, and there are flowers in her hair that have not yet wilted.

"Where is my father's house?" she asks you. "It was here. There was a yew tree, and the smithy, and the church had a wooden spire." There is a stone church with a stone spire, and no yew tree. The villagers are gathering, staring. "My name is Angharad," she says. "I went to dance with the fair folk on the hill last night. I only stayed for one dance." An old woman in the crowd gasps and crosses herself. "Angharad," she says. "My great-grandmother's sister was called Angharad. She went up the hill one May Eve, and never came back."

responses.label: You may help Angharad find what remains of her family.
You may take Angharad back to the faerie hill to ask for her lost years.

entries.body:
You come upon a castle beside a sycamore wood, and you notice the trees before you notice the castle. From the branches of the sycamores hang forty knights in full armour, with their shields about their necks. A horn hangs from the tallest tree.

A maiden leans out of a high window. "Go back!" she calls. "I am Lyonesse, and I am besieged by the Red Knight of the Red Lands. He has hanged every knight who came to save me. He sleeps in that red pavilion." She points. "At noon, his strength increases until he is as strong as seven men. At dawn, he is only as strong as one." She looks at the sky. It is an hour before noon. "Please," she says. "Go back, or wait until dawn."

responses.label: You may blow the horn and challenge the Red Knight now.
You may wait until dark and steal into the castle to bring the lady out.

entries.body: You draw your sword and stand at the rail. The pirates throw their grappling hooks.

resolutions.label: repel the pirates from the deck

success.body: They come over the rail with cutlasses, and you meet them there. You fight at the rail for a long, bloody quarter-hour, and the sailors, taking heart, come with you. At last Grainne calls her men back, and cuts the grappling ropes, and her black ship draws away. She salutes you from her bow with her cutlass. "Next time," she calls. You are not sure you want a next time.

failure.body: They come over the rail with cutlasses, and there are too many. You are knocked down and tied to the mast. Grainne sells your horse, and your sword, and very nearly you, before she lets you go at Wexford for a ransom.

resolutions.label: command your crew to break the grapples

success.body: You do not wait at the rail. You set the sailors with axes at every grappling rope and the cook with his pot of boiling pitch at the stern, and when the pirates start to cross, the ropes are cut under them and the pitch comes over the side. Half the boarding party is in the sea. Grainne's black ship draws off. She salutes you from her bow with her cutlass. "Next time," she calls.

failure.body: You set the sailors at the grappling ropes, but the pirates have more ropes than you have axes. They come over the rail in a wave. Grainne sells your horse and very nearly you.

entries.body: You hold out your hand. The dwarf looks at you for a long time. Then he wraps the hilt in leather and gives you the sword. It is warm, and it hums against your palm.

resolutions.label: master the singing sword

success.body: You take the sword out onto the hillside and swing it. It sings with every stroke, and the song rises and changes. By the end of an hour, it is singing something different: *The one who carries me will be the greatest knight in Britain.* Only that. Nothing about May. The dwarf listens with his mouth open. "It likes you," he says. "It changed its mind." You are not sure that swords change their minds, but you keep it, and it never sings the second line again, at least not in your hearing.

failure.body: You take the sword out onto the hillside and swing it. It sings with every stroke, the same words, over and over, until you cannot bear to hear them. You bring it back to the forge and lay it on the anvil. The dwarf says nothing. You ride away with the song in your ears, and it follows you for days.

entries.body: You get down from your horse and go to the leper. He shrinks away from you. "You will catch it," he says. "Everyone says so." You lift him onto your back. He weighs almost nothing.

resolutions.label: carry the leper across the flood

notes: Lose all Ranks of Villainy

success.body: The water comes up to your chest, then your chin, and the current pulls at your legs. With every step, the leper seems to grow heavier, as though you are carrying a man, then a horse, then a whole church. Halfway across, you think you will drown. You do not put him down. On the far bank, you set him on the grass, and he unwraps the cloth from his face. There are no sores. His face is shining. "You carried more than you know," he says, and he is gone. On the near bank, old Julian is on his knees, weeping.

failure.body: The water comes up to your chest, then your chin, and with every step, the leper grows heavier. Halfway across, your courage fails. You turn back. You set him down on the near bank, gasping, and he looks at you with eyes full of pity. Then he gets up and walks into the river himself, and does not sink, and walks across it to the far bank. You kneel on the stones and cannot rise.

entries.body: You walk through the arch and sit down at the golden table. A fay lady pours you a cup of wine. Nobody speaks.

resolutions.label: keep faith with the fair folk at their last feast

success.body: You drink with them, and eat with them, and when the lament ends, you stand and raise your cup to them, and thank them for everything they have given Britain: the songs and the dances and the tricks and the terrors. They are silent a long time. Then the fay lady at the head of the table rises and kisses your forehead. "Remember," she says. When you walk back through the arch, it is dawn, and the arch is gone, and there is dew on the grass in the shape of a hand.

failure.body: You drink with them, but you cannot find the words to thank them. They leave at dawn, without a word to you. The arch is gone.

resolutions.label: sing the fair folk's lament with them

success.body: You do not only drink. When the lament begins again, you sing it with them, in their own tongue, which you did not know you knew until you open your mouth. They turn and look at you. At the end, the fay lady at the head of the table rises and kisses your forehead. "Now a mortal knows our song," she says. "It will not be lost." When you walk back through the arch, it is dawn, and there is dew on the grass in the shape of a hand.

failure.body: You try to sing their lament with them, and your mortal voice cracks on the high notes. They stop, and look at you, politely. They do not sing again while you are there.

entries.body:
"You!" King Mark's face changes when he sees you. "You were seen at Orkney, carrying messages for a queen who is not your own. I know your kind." He pulls his horse around. "Seize that knight!"

You do not wait to find out what happens to knights who are seized in Cornwall. You spur your horse over the bridge and away, with Mark's soldiers clattering behind you. They follow you for three days.
"I will ride with you," you say. Lamorak nods, and the two of you gallop after the beast as it springs away into the trees.

resolutions.label: run the Questing Beast to bay

success.body: You chase it all day, and at dusk you corner it against a cliff. Lamorak raises his spear. Then he lowers it. "My father would have wanted to catch it," he says slowly. "Not kill it. Only catch it." He laughs, a little brokenly. "We have caught it. That is enough." The beast leaps the cliff and is gone. Lamorak gives you his father's hunting horn. "He would have liked you," he says.

failure.body: You chase it all day, and at dusk you lose it, and Lamorak, and your way, all at once. It is two days before you find a road.

resolutions.label: let the beast lead you to water at dusk

success.body: You rein in and let Lamorak gallop on. The beast's feet are a hart's feet, and harts go to water at dusk. You call Lamorak back, and you wait by the pool in the rushes, and at sunset it comes, and drinks, and lifts its serpent's head and looks straight at you both. Lamorak lowers his spear. "My father would have wanted to catch it," he says. "Not kill it." He gives you his father's hunting horn.

failure.body: You wait by the pool all evening, and the beast does not come. When you find Lamorak again, he has lost it too, and blames you for the wait.

entries.body: You pay the fisherman to take you out past the rocks, west, where the white ship went.

resolutions.label: sail in search of the white ship

success.body: You sail for four days, west and west, until you come to an island with a chapel and a hermit, and in the chapel, a tomb with a knight's shield on it. The hermit tells you that Sir Bleheris came here a year ago, and saw what he came to see, and died of joy. He gives you the shield. You sail home and carry it up to the lady's window. She takes it, and looks at it, and then she puts out the lamp. "Then he found it," she says. "Then it was worth it."

failure.body: You sail west for four days and find nothing but grey sea, and on the fifth, a storm drives you back. When you come home, the lamp is still burning. The lady does not ask you what you found.

entries.body: You land in the cove and climb the cliff to the lighthouse. Inside, the old hermit is lying at the foot of the stair with a broken leg.

resolutions.label: keep the lighthouse burning through the night

success.body: You carry wood up the stair all night, and feed the fire, and keep it burning. The old hermit lies at the foot of the stair, directing you. At dawn, you see the Calais fleet sailing safely past the Goodwin Sands, their sails bright in the sunrise. You set the hermit's leg. He blesses you. "Every ship that passes tonight owes you a prayer," he says.

failure.body: You carry wood up the stair all night, but you fall asleep near dawn. The light goes out. At sunrise, you see a ship on the Goodwin Sands.

resolutions.label: relight the lamp by the old hermit's craft

success.body: The old hermit, with his broken leg, cannot climb, but he can teach. He tells you the words he says over the fire every night, the old words for a flame that will not go out in a gale, and you say them over the dying fire at the top of the tower. The flame steadies, and rises, and burns white. At dawn, the Calais fleet sails safely past the Goodwin Sands.

failure.body: The hermit teaches you the words for a flame that will not go out. You say them over the fire, and the fire goes out. He looks up at the dark tower and weeps.

entries.body: You take the axe. It is beautifully balanced and very sharp. The Green Knight dismounts, kneels, and lifts his green hair from his neck. "When you are ready," he says.

resolutions.label: strike the Green Knight's blow

success.body: You swing with all your strength. The axe goes clean through his neck, and his head rolls in the grass. You stand staring at it. Then the body gets up, walks over, picks up the head by its hair, and climbs back into the saddle. The head opens its eyes. "A good blow," it says. "A year and a day. The Green Chapel. Do not forget." The Green Knight rides away with his head under his arm, whistling. You notice your hands are steady, and you are proud of that.

failure.body: You swing with all your strength, but your hands are shaking. The axe bites deep, and the head rolls in the grass. Then the body gets up and picks up the head, and it opens its eyes and looks at you. You drop the axe. The head laughs. "A year and a day," it says. "Try not to shake like that at the chapel." You ride away, and for many nights you dream of green.

entries.body: "I did not come to fight you, my lord," you say. "But if you want a fight, I will not refuse." Lot laughs and bangs the table. "Wrestle my champion," he says. "Sigurd! Come here!" A man the size of a small house stands up.

resolutions.label: wrestle King Lot's champion

success.body: Sigurd throws you twice. The third time, you do not let him lift you. You hang on, and hang on, and hang on, until he is gasping, and then you trip him, and he falls like a tree, and you sit on his chest. The hall roars. The young red-haired boys are cheering you. King Lot laughs so hard he has to hold the table. "A knight who does not give up!" he cries. "I like that. I like that very much." He sends you home with a gift of Orkney silver, and a message for the young king that is almost polite.

failure.body: Sigurd throws you three times, and the third time, you do not get up. The boys are very disappointed. King Lot sends you home with a message for the young king that is not polite at all.

resolutions.label: outwit the champion with a wrestler's trick

success.body: Sigurd is the size of a small house and knows it. You let him throw you once, and pretend to be hurt, and when he comes to finish it with his arms spread wide, you duck under them, and trip him backward over a bench, and he falls like a tree. The hall roars. The young red-haired boys cheer you. King Lot laughs so hard he has to hold the table, and sends you home with Orkney silver and a message for the young king that is almost polite.

failure.body: You let Sigurd throw you and pretend to be hurt. Sigurd, who is not a fool, sits on you until you admit it.

entries.body: You look at the two signs. "What do you think the lords would say," you ask, "if they each saw the other side of your cart?" Hob's grin fades.

resolutions.label: bring the two lords face to face with the dwarf's cart

success.body: You ride to each lord in turn and invite them to meet at the salmon weir to inspect a new consignment of crossbows. They both come, with their men, and find themselves looking at the same cart from opposite sides. There is a long silence. Then the Lord of Cardigan begins to laugh, and after a moment, so does the Lord of Pembroke. They make peace over the salmon weir that same afternoon, and divide Hob's crossbows between them for their castle walls. Hob is not invited to the feast.

failure.body: You ride to each lord and invite them to meet at the weir. They both come, with their men, and see the cart, and are furious, but not with Hob. Each is sure the other hired you. The battle at the salmon weir is the worst of the war. Hob sells a great many crossbows afterwards.

resolutions.label: seize the cart before it sells more crossbows

success.body: You do not argue. You take the cart. Hob shouts, and his two drivers reach for crossbows, and find you have already taken the strings off them. You drive the cart to the salmon weir and tell both lords that there will be no more crossbows until they have talked. Without crossbows, they have to. They make peace in an afternoon and split the cart between them for their castle walls.

failure.body: You try to take the cart. Hob's drivers have strung crossbows, and they are not bad shots. You leave without the cart, and with a bolt through your cloak.

entries.body:
Gaheris stops sharpening and stares at you. "I know you," he says slowly. "You were on the road the day my mother went to meet him. You helped her." His sword comes up. "Agravain was right. Everyone knew but us."

There is no talking to him. He comes at you across the crossroads, and you fight for your life in the dust, and when you have beaten him off and ridden away, you know that the house of Orkney has another name on its list.
You put your hand on Bedivere's shoulder. "It is not the last thing of him," you say. "You are."

resolutions.label: give Sir Bedivere the strength to obey his king

success.body: You stand with him at the water's edge and pray, and he prays with you, and at last he lifts the sword in his one hand and throws it, and it wheels out over the lake, and the arm rises and catches it and brandishes it three times and draws it under. Bedivere turns to you with his face wet. "Thank you," he says. Together, you carry the old king down to the black barge that is waiting in the mist.

failure.body: You stand with him at the water's edge, but he cannot do it. At last, he sits down on the stones and weeps, and the sword lies in his lap, and you both hear the old king calling, weakly, from the shore.

resolutions.label: remind Bedivere of what the king made him swear

success.body: You put your hand on his shoulder and ask him, quietly, what he swore at Pentecost, all those years ago. He says it, word by word, with the sword across his palm: *no outrage, mercy to all who ask, never to fight in a wrongful quarrel.* "And to obey his king," you say. He weeps. Then he throws. The arm rises and catches the sword and draws it under. Together, you carry the old king down to the black barge.

failure.body: You ask him what he swore at Pentecost. "I swore to guard him," says Bedivere. "Not to throw away his sword." He sits down on the stones and weeps, and the sword lies in his lap.

entries.body: You take a slow step forward, then another. The bear raises its head.

resolutions.label: grab the child and run before the bear can stop you

success.body: You scoop Nia up under one arm and run for the waterfall. The bear roars and lumbers after you. You burst through the water, throw the girl onto your saddle and leap up behind her, and your horse, which has smelled the bear, needs no spurs. You gallop out of the forest with the bear crashing behind you, until it gives up at the edge of the trees and sits down, and watches you go, and moans. Nia waves to it. Her mother, when you bring her home, faints.

failure.body: You scoop Nia up and run, but the cave floor is slippery with spray, and you go down on your back, and the bear stands over you. It sniffs you. Then it takes Nia gently by the back of her smock, carries her back to her rock, and lies down in front of her. You back out of the cave. You will have to think of something else.

resolutions.label: wait for the bear to sleep and take her then

success.body: You sit down at the mouth of the cave, behind the curtain of water, and wait. You wait until the bear's breathing is slow and deep and its paws twitch in a dream. Then you slip in, lift Nia, put a finger to her lips and slip out again. She waves to the bear from your saddle. Her mother, when you bring her home, faints.

failure.body: You wait for the bear to sleep. So does Nia. So, after a long ride, do you. You wake with the bear's nose an inch from your face.

entries.body: "Good people," you say loudly, "that is a pig's knuckle." The crowd goes quiet. Brother Cadoc's smile does not flicker. "Blasphemy!" he says. "Who will you believe, a knight or a man of God?"

resolutions.label: prove the relic false before the crowd

success.body: You ask for the relic, and hold it up, and ask whether any of them has ever butchered a pig. Half the village has. They crowd round and look, and the murmuring turns to anger. The blacksmith's wife snatches the tray of pardons and finds they are cut from the lead of the church roof. Brother Cadoc is chased out of the village with a pitchfork behind him, and the villagers get their pennies back. The priest thanks you. His roof has been leaking for a month.

failure.body: You ask for the relic and hold it up and ask whether any of them has ever butchered a pig. But Brother Cadoc is quicker. He cries out that you have defiled the saint with your unclean hands, and falls on his knees weeping, and the villagers believe him. They drive you out of the village with stones. You resolve to be a little less certain in front of a crowd.

resolutions.label: shame the friar into confessing

success.body: You get down from your horse and kneel in the road before Brother Cadoc, and ask him, very seriously, to pray over you with the saint's relic, since you have sinned greatly. Cadoc has to. He lifts the pig's knuckle and opens his mouth to pray, and you look him in the eye, and he cannot do it. His face crumples. "I cannot," he says. "God forgive me, I cannot." He confesses to the whole village. They are so astonished that they forgive him. He goes to the nearest monastery to do penance, taking nothing but the knuckle, which he says he will keep to remind himself.

failure.body: You kneel in the road and ask Brother Cadoc to pray over you with the relic. He does, beautifully, with tears streaming down his face. The villagers are moved. You are sure he is laughing inside. When he finishes, he charges you a shilling.

entries.body: You haul Pelleas to his feet by his surcoat. "Enough," you say. "There are other windows in Britain."

resolutions.label: rouse Pelleas from his despair

success.body: You sit him down by a fire and make him eat, then you make him pray with you, for the first time in a month. Afterwards he stares into the flames. "I have been praying to a window," he says. By morning, he has scrubbed the rust from his armour. He rides away east with you as far as the crossroads, and there he grips your hand. "If I hear of you in need," he says, "I will come." You hear later that he has married a lady of the Lake, and is happy.

failure.body: You sit him down by a fire and make him eat. But as dawn breaks, the shutter opens above, and a pale face looks down, and Pelleas is on his feet and back at the wall before you can stop him. You leave him there. You cannot save a man who does not want to be saved.

resolutions.label: drag him away by main force

success.body: Pelleas will not come, so you tie him across his own saddle like a sack of flour and lead his horse away. He curses you for ten miles, weeps for another five, and falls asleep. In the morning, he is quieter. "I am hungry," he says, surprised. "I have not been hungry in a month." He leaves you at the next town with a gruff thanks and his best spurs.

failure.body: Pelleas will not come, so you try to tie him across his own saddle. He fights like a wildcat, and Ettarde's knights come out to see what the noise is. When they see you trying to carry off their lady's favourite nuisance, they beat you both impartially.

entries.body: You give the knight your water-skin, pick up his sword as well as your own, and go to the gate.

resolutions.label: defend the broken gate

success.body: The gate is narrow and the flagstones are slippery. Mordred's men can only come at you one at a time. You fight the first, and the second, and the third falls back, and the last two run. When you go back into the courtyard, the wounded knight has propped himself up against a wall and is watching you. "The king's baggage train," he says, "is safe. So is the king's knight." He laughs weakly. "Two of them."

failure.body: The gate is narrow. You fight the first, and the second, but the third gets past you, and when you turn, he is standing over the wounded knight. You are too late.

entries.body: You shake your head. "The law is the law, Tom," you say. Tom sighs and puts down the knife. "They always say that," he says. "Right up until it's them."

resolutions.label: bring the poacher before the verderer

success.body: Tom runs, of course. You chase him through the forest, and he is fast and knows every path, but you are faster, and you catch him at a stream. You bring him to the verderer, a fat man who cannot wait to take his hand. But you speak for Tom, and point out that the deer was old and lame, and in the end the verderer settles for a fine, which you pay. Tom stares at you. "You are a strange sort of knight," he says. He sends you a pheasant every Michaelmas for twenty years. You never ask where they come from.

failure.body: Tom runs, of course, and he knows every path in the forest, and you do not. You lose him in the first ten minutes. When you go back to the hollow, the venison has gone too.

resolutions.label: persuade Tom to come quietly

success.body: You sit down by his fire. "If you run," you say, "they will hunt you, and your children will be poachers' orphans. If you come with me, I will speak for you." Tom looks at you for a long time. Then he puts out his fire. The verderer wants his hand. You speak for him, and pay the fine yourself. Tom sends you a pheasant every Michaelmas for twenty years.

failure.body: You sit by his fire and speak of his children. Tom listens, nods, and hits you over the head with the spit. When you wake, the venison and the poacher are both gone.

entries.body: You sit down in the circle. "Read my dreams," you say. The seven hermits look at you, and then at each other.

resolutions.label: open your dreams to the seven hermits

success.body: You tell them your dreams, and they tell you what they mean. Some are funny. Some are not. At the end, the oldest of them says, "You will be there, on the plain. But you will not be there at the end. You will be somewhere else, doing something better." You ask what. He shrugs. "That, you will choose." You ride away lighter than you came.

failure.body: You tell them your dreams, and the seven hermits go very quiet, and one of them begins to weep. They will not tell you what they saw.

resolutions.label: keep silent vigil with the hermits instead

success.body: You do not tell them your dreams. You sit in their circle and keep silence with them all night, round the single candle. Near dawn, the oldest hermit speaks, without looking at you. "You will be there, on the plain," he says. "But not at the end. You will be somewhere else, doing something better." You ask what. He shrugs. "That, you will choose." You ride away lighter than you came.

failure.body: You sit in their circle and keep silence all night, and around midnight you fall asleep. You dream. The seven hermits, when you wake, are looking at you, and one of them is weeping.

entries.body: You spur your horse through the reeds toward the pilgrim. The lights dance in front of you, trying to lead you astray.

resolutions.label: reach the pilgrim through the treacherous marsh

success.body: You do not look at the lights. You look at the reeds, and the water, and the way the bog bubbles, and you ride where the ground is firmest. You reach the pilgrim as he is stepping into the deep water, and haul him back by his hood. He fights you. "The Grail!" he weeps. "It was the Grail!" You turn his face toward the lights, and as you watch, they wink out, one by one. "It was the bog," you say. He is silent all the way to dry ground.

failure.body: You ride toward the pilgrim, and the lights dance before you, and before you know it, your horse is up to its belly in the bog. By the time you have freed it, the pilgrim is gone, and so are the lights.

entries.body: "I will go," you say. "And I will bring help." The young captain looks at you. "Go quickly," he says.

resolutions.label: climb down the mountain and bring back help

success.body: You climb down the goat-path in the dark with three of the fittest men, and walk all night and all the next day to the old king's nearest camp. You find the old knight in command, Sir Lucan, and bring him back with fifty men. The Saxons in the valley see the dragon banner coming over the hill, and flee. The young captain in the fort weeps when he sees you. Of his dozen men, eleven are still alive.

failure.body: You climb down the goat-path in the dark, and one of the men with you falls. You go on, and reach the old king's camp, and come back with fifty men, but the Saxons have already stormed the fort.

resolutions.label: signal the king's army with fire from the summit

success.body: You do not climb down. You gather every stick of gorse and heather on the mountain top and build a beacon, and wait for night, and light it. Twenty miles away, on another hill, another beacon answers, and then another. By dawn, Sir Lucan is coming up the valley with fifty men. The Saxons see the dragon banner, and flee.

failure.body: You build a beacon of gorse and light it at nightfall. The wind is wrong. The smoke blows down the valley into the Saxon camp, and the Saxons, taking it as a sign, attack at dawn.

entries.body: "The merchant will not miss a little," you say. The young outlaws cheer. Father Ulf looks at you with sorrow.

resolutions.label: lead the raid on the merchant's barge

success.body: You lie in the reeds in the fen-boats until the barge comes drifting down the river, and then you are over its sides before the crew knows what is happening. They surrender at once. The barge is full of wine and wool and a chest of silver. The outlaws are delighted. You take your share. That night, Father Ulf's chapel is empty, and the island rings with drinking songs.

failure.body: You lie in the reeds until the barge comes down the river, but it has archers on board. The raid fails, and two of the outlaws are killed. Father Ulf buries them without a word to you.

entries.body: You draw your sword and walk into the dark. The breathing stops. Two eyes open in the blackness, as big as shields, and as yellow as the coins.

resolutions.label: slay the young dragon in its lair

success.body: It is the longest fight of your life. The dragon is young, but it is fast, and its breath scorches the cave walls. You keep behind the pillars of rock, and when it lunges, you strike at its soft throat. The third blow goes home. The dragon screams, and the whole mountain shakes, and then it is still. You come out of the cave blackened, singed and alive. The shepherd stares at you. The valley feasts you for a week, and the hoard is yours, though half of it turns out to be brass.

failure.body: It is the longest fight of your life, and you lose it. The dragon's breath catches you in the open, and you are thrown back out of the cave in a gout of flame. You roll in the snow. You have no eyebrows. The shepherd pats you on the back. "At least you came out," he says.

resolutions.label: sing the dragon back into its long sleep

success.body: You do not draw your sword. You stand at the mouth of the cave and sing the old song for sleep, the one Welsh mothers sing and dragons are said to hate and love. The yellow eyes blink. They blink again. They close. The breathing slows to a long rumble like a mill. You go in and take a single cup from the hoard, as proof, and leave the rest. The dragon of Dinas Emrys sleeps for a hundred years.

failure.body: You stand at the mouth of the cave and sing the song for sleep. The dragon listens with interest, and then it yawns, and the yawn is fire. You come out of the valley without eyebrows.

entries.body: You sit down at the desk beside him. He shows you how to cut a quill and mix the ink.

resolutions.label: copy the ancient gospel through the winter

success.body: You work beside him for a month, from dawn until the light fails, in the snow. You learn to write a fair hand, and you read, as you copy, the story of Joseph and the vessel, and where it went. On the last day, the old monk writes the final word and lays down his pen. "Two," he says. He gives you the copy. "Take it to Glastonbury," he says. He dies that night, in his sleep, with the other copy in his arms.

failure.body: You work beside him for a week, but your hand is not steady, and you spoil three pages. The old monk is patient. The winter is not. You leave before the snow closes the pass, and you do not know if he finishes.

resolutions.label: keep the old monk warm and fed through the winter

success.body: You do not copy. You keep him alive so that he can. You cut wood, snare hares, find the dry moss that burns slow, and stop up the scriptorium windows with turf. All winter, he writes by a fire you keep lit, and you read over his shoulder the story of Joseph and the vessel. At the thaw, he writes the last word. "Two," he says. He gives you the copy and dies that night in his sleep.

failure.body: You keep him warm and fed, but in the worst of the winter, the snow buries the woodpile, and the fire goes out for a night. He lives. His hands do not. He never writes again.

entries.body: "Tell me your plan," you say. Dinadan brightens. "It is very simple. Tarquin hates one knight above all others: the queen's champion of the house of Benwick, who is not here. So one of us rides up in that knight's colours, blue and white, and challenges him, and when he charges, the other one lets his horse out of the paddock. A man cannot joust without a horse."

resolutions.label: play your part in Dinadan's trick

success.body: Dinadan borrows a blue and white surcoat from somewhere and rides up to the ford, trumpeting like a herald. Tarquin roars and charges straight into the river, and you slip round behind the paddock and loose every horse he owns. Tarquin's charger, hearing its fellows, turns in midstream and bolts after them. Tarquin is left sitting in the ford up to his waist, bellowing. You and Dinadan open the dungeon while he is still catching horses. "Chivalry," says Dinadan, "is overrated."

failure.body: Dinadan borrows a blue and white surcoat and rides up to the ford, trumpeting like a herald. Tarquin looks at him for a long moment and bursts out laughing. "I know that knight," he calls, "and he is a head taller." Meanwhile, the paddock has a guard you did not see, and you are marched across the ford at spear-point. Dinadan escapes, still apologising.

resolutions.label: ride up in the champion's colours yourself

success.body: You borrow Dinadan's blue and white surcoat and ride up to the ford sitting as tall as you can. Tarquin roars and charges, and you turn your horse and gallop away up the bank, and he chases you for a mile, bellowing, while Dinadan opens his dungeon. When Tarquin finally realises, he is too far away to do anything but swear. Sixty-four knights buy you wine that night.

failure.body: You borrow the blue and white surcoat and ride up to the ford. Tarquin charges, and you turn to flee, and your horse slips on the bank. Tarquin is on you before you are up. Dinadan escapes, apologising.

entries.body: "Murder your captain," you say, "and you are all outlaws. Go home, and you are deserters. Neither will bring you peace."

resolutions.label: persuade the soldiers to take their grievance to the king

success.body: You talk to them all night. You tell them that the old king is a just man, that he does not know what Sir Grummore does, and that he would want to. In the morning, you go with the sergeant to the old king's camp, and he tells the story himself. The old king listens with his face growing grey. Sir Grummore is relieved of his command that day. The soldiers stay. They fight well, after that.

failure.body: You talk to them all night. At dawn, the sergeant says, "You are right," and they go home, all of them, without killing anyone. They are hanged as deserters a week later.

resolutions.label: go to the captain yourself and shame him

success.body: You walk into Sir Grummore's tent alone and tell him, knight to knight, what his men are planning, and why. You tell him what the oath at Pentecost says about outrage. He goes white, and then red, and then, surprisingly, silent. In the morning, he gathers his men and tells them he will hang no more of them. He keeps his word. They fight well for him after that.

failure.body: You walk into the captain's tent and tell him what his men are planning. He thanks you, and hangs the sergeant at dawn. The men look at you as you ride away.

entries.body: You sit down beside the old lord's chair. "Tell me," you say.

resolutions.label: hear the old lord's confession and forgive him

success.body: He tells you about every game, and every piece, and every name. It takes all night. When he is finished, he is weeping. "Forgive me," he says. "Not for them. They are gone. For me." You are no priest, but you put your hand on his head, and say that God forgives those who ask. The old lord closes his eyes and smiles. By dawn, he is dead in his chair. You bury him with his knights, and the white stone castle fades into the forest behind you as you ride away.

failure.body: He tells you about every game, and every name. But when he finishes and asks you to forgive him, you find you cannot. Too many names. He sees it in your face and nods. "No," he says. "I would not either." You ride away, and the castle stays where it is, waiting.

entries.body: "My lord," you say, "if the fool is lying, you will lose nothing by letting me look at your steward's accounts. If he is telling the truth, you will want to know." The lord hesitates. "Very well," he says at last. "And if you find nothing, the fool is whipped twice."

resolutions.label: find the steward's second ledger

success.body: You spend a day at the lord's manor with the steward, a smooth, smiling man, going through his accounts, which are perfect. Too perfect. That night, you search his room and find, under a loose hearthstone, a second ledger, with very different figures. The lord reads it by candlelight, his face growing darker and darker. The steward is arrested at dawn. The lord goes to the fair himself and kneels before Ninian, who pats him on the head and tells him his roan mare is about to foal.

failure.body: You spend a day at the manor going through the steward's accounts, which are perfect. You find nothing. Ninian is whipped twice. As they do it, he looks up at you and smiles. "The knight did not look under the hearth," he says. By the time you have gone back, the hearthstone has been mortared down.

resolutions.label: follow the steward by night

success.body: You wait outside the steward's house and follow him when he slips out after midnight. He goes to a moneylender's back door with a heavy bag, and comes out with a light one, and then goes to a loose stone in the church wall and puts something behind it. In the morning, you take the lord to the stone. Behind it is the second ledger. The steward flees to Ireland. The lord kneels before Ninian, who pats him on the head.

failure.body: You follow the steward by night, and he goes straight home to bed. So does everyone else. In the morning, Ninian is whipped twice.

entries.body: You ride up the hill with your sword drawn. "Gogyrfan," you say, "the lady does not want you. Go home." The giant looks at you with hurt eyes. Then his face goes red.

resolutions.label: fight the lovesick giant

success.body: He swings the boulder at you. You dodge. He swings again, and you slip inside his reach and strike him on the ankle with the flat of your sword, which hurts more than he expected. He sits down with a crash that shakes the mill. "All right," he says tearfully. "All right. I will go." He stumps off over the hill. The miller gives you a purse of silver and his thanks. Elin, you notice, looks up at the hill for a long time after he has gone.

failure.body: He swings the boulder at you. You dodge. He swings again, and you do not. When you wake up in the millyard, Elin is putting a cold cloth on your head, and the giant is sitting on the hill, crying and apologising.

resolutions.label: chase him off with horse and lance

success.body: You charge up the hill with your lance levelled, shouting, and the giant, who has never been charged by anyone, drops his boulder on his own foot and flees over the hill, howling. You chase him a mile, prodding. He does not come back. The miller gives you a purse of silver. Elin looks at the hill for a long time after he has gone.

failure.body: You charge up the hill with your lance levelled. The giant picks up your horse, with you on it, and sets you down gently in the millpond. Then he sits down on the hill and cries.

entries.body: You sit down with the islanders at the edge of the circle. The old woman looks at you with approval. "Most knights want the gift," she says. "Few want the songs."

resolutions.label: learn the songs of the Callanish stones

success.body: They teach you for a week. The songs are very old, and they tell of the stars and the moon and the long cycles of the sun, and of the people who raised the stones to mark them. By the end, you can look at the stones and tell the date, and the season, and when the moon will next stand still over the hills. The old woman gives you a bow of yew wood, very old, from her grandfather. "It never misses," she says, "if you sing while you shoot."

failure.body: They teach you for a week, but you cannot hold the tunes, and the words are in a tongue you do not know. The old woman pats your hand. "Some people are for gifts," she says. "Not songs."

resolutions.label: learn the stones' reckoning by watching the sky with them

success.body: You do not learn the songs. You lie on the hill among the stones for five nights with the islanders, watching the moon rise between them and the sun set in the notches of the hills, until you can see for yourself how the stones count the year. On the last night, the old woman nods. She gives you a bow of yew wood, very old, from her grandfather. "It never misses," she says, "if you know where the moon is."

failure.body: You lie among the stones for five nights, and it is cloudy for all five. The old woman pats your hand. "Some years," she says, "the sky does not want to be counted."

entries.body: "The game is over, Gwilym," you say, and hold out your hand. Gwilym clutches the seal to his chest. "Oh, but it was a good game," he says.

resolutions.label: get the seal back from the fool

success.body: Gwilym bolts out of the hayloft door, across the rooftops, over the church, and down into the churchyard, laughing all the way. You chase him every inch of it. At last you corner him in the bell-tower. He hands over the seal with a sigh. "Can I keep the pig decree?" he asks. When the Lord of Kidwelly returns, you give him his seal and tell him the whole story. He laughs so hard he forgets to be angry, and decrees that the pigs may keep their hats.

failure.body: Gwilym bolts out of the hayloft door and across the rooftops. You chase him, but the roof of the bakery is weaker than it looks, and you go straight through it into a tray of loaves. When you climb out, Gwilym is gone. The baker is very angry.

resolutions.label: appeal to Gwilym's pride in his craft

success.body: You sit down beside him in the hayloft. "The pig decree," you say, "was the best jest I have heard in a year. But a fool who hides behind a lord's seal is not a fool. He is a forger. A fool says it to the lord's face." Gwilym looks at you for a long time. Then he climbs down, walks into the hall and hands the seal to his lord in front of everyone, and tells him about the pigs. The lord laughs so hard he forgets to be angry.

failure.body: You tell Gwilym a fool should say it to the lord's face. "Then I will," he says, and does, and adds a great deal about the lord's nose. The lord is not amused. Gwilym goes in the stocks, and you are thrown out of the town for encouraging him.

entries.body: "Let me go before you, my lady," you say. "No king should meet his mother in front of the whole court without warning." Igraine considers this and nods. "You are right," she says. "Tell him gently."

resolutions.label: find the right words for the High King

success.body: You wait until Arthur is alone in the mews with his hawks and tell him the whole thing plainly. He listens with a hooded falcon on his fist. "I was told she did not want me," he says. "Merlin told me." He puts the falcon back on its perch very carefully. "Bring her in by the little door," he says, "and let nobody else be there." Later, a page tells you that the king and the old nun sat together in the mews until dark, and that both of them wept.

failure.body: You wait until Arthur is at table and ask for a word. He waves you to his side, and you tell him in a whisper that the whole high table hears. Sir Kay chokes on his wine. Merlin looks at the ceiling. The king goes white and then red and walks out without a word. Igraine is received with every honour, but her son is formal and cold, and she goes back to Amesbury within the week.

resolutions.label: arrange for the king to find her as if by chance

success.body: You do not tell him. You tell him only that there is an old nun in the chapel who knew his nurse, and would like to sing him a lullaby. The king goes, curious. Nobody else sees what happens in the chapel. But when the king comes out, he is holding the old woman's hand, and his face is wet, and he takes her in to dine at his own right hand.

failure.body: You tell him there is an old nun in the chapel who would like to see him. The king is busy, and sends Sir Kay instead. Kay listens to Igraine's story and then tells the whole court at supper, as a great joke. By the time the king hears it, it is not a lullaby any more.

entries.body: You turn your horse the other way, after the white hind. She is already far ahead, a flash of white between the trees.

resolutions.label: track the white hind to where she rests

success.body: You follow her for hours, through bracken and over streams, until you find her lying in a glade, exhausted, with her golden collar caught on a briar. You free the collar gently. She does not run. She lets you lead her back by it, all the way to the lady, who has found her hound again, carried back by a sheepish knight in black. The lady gives you the golden collar. "The hind," she says, "should go free." You agree.

failure.body: You follow her for hours, deeper and deeper into the forest, and at last she stops, and turns, and looks at you. Then she is gone, as though she had never been. You are a long way from anywhere you know.

entries.body: You ride to the sheriff's hall. The sheriff is a small, precise man who dresses in black and counts his money at a table. "The outlaw's wife," he says. "Yes. She hangs until he comes in."

resolutions.label: shame the sheriff into releasing her

success.body: You tell him that no knight of the High King's court would leave a woman to the crows for the crime of loving her husband. You tell him that the High King himself would be interested to hear of it. You say it loudly, in front of his clerks. The sheriff purses his lips. At last he says, "Take her," and goes back to counting. You bring her to Hob. He takes her in his arms, and then he looks at you. "I will come in," he says. "Not to him. To you. Tell me where to go and I will go there." You send him to Camelot, to serve in the kitchens.

failure.body: You tell him that no knight of the High King's court would do this. The sheriff looks at you with interest. "Are you a knight of the High King's court?" he asks. When you admit that you are not, or not quite, he smiles and has you thrown out.

resolutions.label: call on the bishop's authority over the dead

success.body: You remind the sheriff that the dead belong to the Church, not the sheriff, and that the Bishop of Hereford has excommunicated sheriffs for less. The sheriff stops counting. He does not know whether it is true. Neither, entirely, do you. But he signs an order to cut her down, and the priest of the village by the river buries her with bells. Hob Redcap stands at the back of the church with his hood up, and weeps.

failure.body: You remind the sheriff that the dead belong to the Church. "Then the Church," he says, "may come and ask me for them." He goes back to counting. Alis hangs on.

entries.body: "Forgive me, Sir Mordred," you say. "I am bound elsewhere." Mordred smiles and nods. "Of course, friend," he says. "Of course." He goes back to his fire. You feel his eyes on your back until you are out of sight. When you reach the next town, you find that you have been talked about already, and not kindly.

The laundress looks at you, and her face changes. "I have seen you," she says, "with him. In the palace. Talking to him like a friend." The room goes very quiet. The goldsmith's hand goes to his knife.

You get out of the Bell and Anchor alive, but only just, and with a gash across your arm. The loyalists scatter into the night. You do not know whether they will ever trust anyone again. You do not know whether Mordred will hear that you were there.

You hear it before you see it: a noise like thirty couple of hounds baying, coming from inside something that is running. A great beast crashes across the road in front of you. It has the head of a serpent, the body of a leopard, the haunches of a lion and the feet of a hart, and the baying comes from its belly. It is gone into the trees before your horse has finished rearing.

A moment later, an old knight gallops up on a lathered grey, with a crown tied to his helm with string. "Which way?" he gasps. "Which way did it go?" You point. He nods and pats his horse. "Hear that, Bellerus? Left. Always left. It is always left." He turns to you. "Pellinore. King of the Isles. I have been hunting the Questing Beast for eleven years. Nobody but a Pellinore can catch it, you know. Family tradition. But nobody said a Pellinore could not have help." He looks at you hopefully. "It is very fast."

responses.label: You may ride with King Pellinore after the Questing Beast.
You may ask King Pellinore why he hunts the beast at all.

entries.body:
You come upon a hunting lodge at the edge of a forest, where a huntsman is standing in the yard with a drawn sword. A great grey wolfhound crouches at his feet with blood all over its jaws and chest, wagging its tail uncertainly.

"Stand back," the man says hoarsely. "I am Llywarch, the king's huntsman. I left my son asleep in his cradle and the dog to guard him. I came home and found the cradle overturned and blood on the floor, and the dog, like this." His voice breaks. "Cafall. Best dog I ever had. He has killed my son." He raises the sword. The dog whines and licks his hand.

From inside the lodge, very faintly, you think you hear something. It could be a baby crying. It could be the wind.

responses.label: You may stay the huntsman's hand and search the lodge.
You may track the blood trail from the lodge into the forest.

entries.body:
You come upon a hunter kneeling in a forest glade with his bow on the ground beside him, weeping. He is a big, sunburnt man in green leather, with an arrow still nocked in his fingers.

"I saw it," he says. "I am Eustace, a forester of the Duke of Cornwall. I was hunting a white stag, the finest I ever saw, and I had it cornered on a rock, and I drew my bow. Then it turned and looked at me, and between its antlers there was a cross of light." He shakes his head. "I have killed a thousand deer. I have never thought twice. I cannot draw a bow now. My hands will not do it." He looks up. "The stag went that way. Into the old forest. I think it wants me to follow. I think if I do not, I will never know what it meant."

responses.label: You may follow the white stag with Eustace.
You may help Eustace find a hermit to hear his confession.

entries.body:
You are riding at dusk along a lonely track across a heath when you hear horns, and hounds, and hoofbeats in the sky. A huntsman appears on the track ahead of you. He is tall as a tree, with a great pair of antlers growing from his head and a chain of rusted iron round his neck. Behind him, in the clouds, you see riders with hollow faces.

"I am Herne," he says. His voice is like a stag bellowing. "My hunt rides tonight. Ride with us, knight, and you will run down such quarry as no mortal has hunted." He grins, and his teeth are very white. "Or stand aside. It is all one."

A man comes running along the track toward you, a thin, ragged peasant, looking back over his shoulder in terror. "Help me," he gasps. "They are after me. I cut a branch from Herne's oak for firewood. They are after me!"

responses.label: You may ride with Herne's wild hunt.
You may protect the peasant from the wild hunt.

entries.body:
You come upon a young woman in green leather sitting on a fallen oak with a longbow across her knees, feathering arrows. A dead stag lies at her feet. A few paces away stands a richly dressed young lord with a hawk on his wrist, looking at her with devotion and exasperation in equal measure.

"This is Rhian," says the lord. "She is the best archer in the Marches. I am Bran of Maelor, and I want to marry her. She says she will marry any man who can outshoot her." He throws up his hands. "I cannot outshoot her. Nobody can outshoot her. My mother says she must give up hunting and learn to sew if she marries me."

"I will not," says Rhian, without looking up. She nocks an arrow and, without seeming to aim, shoots a pinecone off a branch fifty yards away. "I will marry a man who can shoot, or I will marry no one." She glances at you. "Can you shoot, knight?"

responses.label: You may help Lord Bran win the archery contest.
You may help Rhian keep her freedom from Lord Bran.
* You may challenge Rhian to a shooting match yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a hunter crouched by a stream, staring at the far bank with bloodshot eyes. His clothes are in rags, his beard reaches his belt, and he has more scars than skin. Beside him lies a great spear with a head as long as your forearm.

"Shh," he hisses. "He comes here to drink. Twrch Trwyth. The great boar. He was a king once, and God made him a boar for his sins. Between his ears he carries a comb, a razor and a pair of shears." The hunter's eyes gleam. "I am Iddawg. I have hunted him for seven years. He killed my brothers and my father and my dogs. I will have that comb if it kills me." He grips your arm with a hand like a claw. "You are a knight. You have a horse. With a horse, I could catch him. Help me."

Across the stream, something huge moves in the bracken.

responses.label: You may join Iddawg's hunt for the great boar.
You may try to free Iddawg from his obsession.

entries.body: You ride to the castle gate and ask to see the Lady Ettarde. She receives you with a spark of interest. "You are not here for Pelleas," she says, "are you?"

resolutions.label: court Lady Ettarde

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You tell her of your deeds and your loves, and she listens, and laughs, and asks you to stay. By the third day, you are sure she loves you. On the fourth, you look out of her window and see Pelleas lying in the grass below, looking up. He sees you. He does not move. The next morning he is gone, and his circlet lies on the grass. You have won the lady, and you have done something that you will not boast of.

partial.body: You tell her of your deeds, and she listens with half an ear. "Pelleas has done more for me," she says, "and I do not want him either." She sends you away with a cup of wine and a yawn.

failure.body: You tell her of your deeds, and she laughs in your face. "Come back when you have lain in the grass for a month," she says.

entries.body:
You come upon a forester in a green hood sitting on the branch of an oak above a road, with an arrow on the string. He puts a finger to his lips as you ride underneath. "Get off the road, knight," he whispers. "Lord Fulk is coming."

You dismount, curious, and he drops down beside you. He is lean and weather-beaten, with a hard, sad face. "Cadfan," he says. "Lord Fulk hanged my brother last Martinmas for taking a deer in the famine winter. His children were starving. Fulk had a hundred deer, and a full larder, and he hanged him from that very oak." He nods up at the branch. "Every year Fulk rides this road to Chester at this time. This year, he will not arrive." In the distance, you hear horses.

responses.label: You may help Cadfan take his revenge on Lord Fulk.
You may stop Cadfan and bring Lord Fulk to justice another way.

entries.body: You look at the burning houses and the frightened faces in the windows. "The gate can wait," you say. "People cannot."

resolutions.label: get the townsfolk out through the burning streets

success.body: You lead them through back lanes the Orkney men do not know, with wet cloths over their faces against the smoke, down to the river-gate and out along the bank, a long, silent line of women and children and old men. You count them as they pass. Three hundred. At dawn, from the far bank, you watch York burn, and then, at noon, you watch the High King's banner go up on the Micklegate. The garrison held without you. You do not mind.

failure.body: You lead them through the back lanes, but you lose your way in the smoke, and walk them straight into a street full of Orkney men. You get most of them out. Not all.

resolutions.label: cut a way through the Orkney men blocking the lane

success.body: At the end of the lane to the river-gate, six Orkney men are looting a chandler's shop. You do not go round. You go through, fast, with your sword, and they scatter into the smoke. Behind you comes a long, silent line of women and children and old men, and you count them through the river-gate: three hundred. At noon, from the far bank, you watch the High King's banner go up on the Micklegate.

failure.body: You go through the Orkney men at the end of the lane, and one of them is better than the others. You hold them long enough for most of the townsfolk to get past. Not all.

entries.body:
You come upon an old woman sitting outside a turf hut at the edge of a forest, skinning a hare. Around her, on every branch and post, hang snares, traps, drying pelts and bunches of herbs. A tame crow sits on her shoulder. She squints up at you. "Going to rain," she says. "About noon. You will want to be under cover."

The sky is perfectly blue. She laughs at your face. "I am Mother Gwyar," she says. "I have trapped this forest for sixty years. I know when it will rain and when the deer will move and where the wolves are denning, and I can tell a man's business from the way he sits his horse." She points her skinning knife at you. "Yours is trouble. Sit down. I will teach you something, if you like. Or I will tell you a story. The crow prefers the story."

responses.label: You may ask Mother Gwyar to teach you the craft of the woods.
You may ask Mother Gwyar to tell you a story of the forest.

entries.body:
You come upon a man in a patched green tunic by a fire in a hollow, turning a haunch of venison on a spit. He is grinning, freckled and unrepentant. The rest of the deer is hanging from a branch behind him, with the High King's mark branded on its flank.

"Ah," he says. "Caught me. Tom Ash. Poacher, by trade." He waves the carving knife cheerfully. "The High King has ten thousand deer and I have a wife and six children. It seems fair to me." He cuts a slice and holds it out to you on the point of the knife. "Share and share alike. You take a haunch and ride on, and nobody need ever know. Or you can take me to the king's verderer, who will cut off my hand." He grins wider. "Your choice, sir knight."

responses.label: You may share the poacher's venison and let him go.
You may arrest Tom Ash and take him to the king's verderer.

entries.body: You climb the stair to the baron's balcony. "My lord," you say, "I will buy your giant." Baron Brisen raises his eyebrows. "Will you?" he says. "And what will you pay?"

resolutions.label: bargain with the baron for the giant

notes: Lose 1 Treasure, if possible

success.body: You haggle. The baron wants a fortune. You point out that a giant eats a great deal and grows weaker every week, and that the crowds will soon tire of the same show, and that the High King has been asking questions about barons who keep giants in pits. By the end of an hour, the baron has sold you the giant for a very reasonable price and a promise that you will not mention his name at Camelot. You lead the giant out of the city on his chain, and at the forest's edge, you take it off. He looks at you for a long time. Then he goes.

failure.body: You haggle, but the baron is enjoying himself too much. "No," he says at last. "I think I will keep him. He has years in him yet." He calls his guards to see you down the stair. Behind you, the crowd roars as the dogs go in.

resolutions.label: win the giant from the baron at dice

success.body: The baron is a gambler; everyone knows it. You propose a game. He stakes the giant. You stake your horse and armour. You play with the baron's own dice, which are loaded, as you guessed, and you have spent a long winter learning how to throw loaded dice so they roll the other way. You win. The baron cannot accuse you without admitting his dice are false. You lead the giant out of the city and take off his chain at the edge of the forest.

failure.body: You propose a game, and play with the baron's dice. They are loaded, and you cannot turn them. You lose your horse and your armour, and the giant stays in the pit.

entries.body:
You come upon a hunting party in a forest clearing: six huntsmen with hounds and a young lord in green, all sitting on their horses in a circle, staring at each other in bewilderment.

"Thank God," says the young lord. "Someone real. I am Owain of Rheged. We were chasing a white hart, the whitest I ever saw, since dawn. And we followed it into this wood, and now we cannot get out. We have ridden in every direction and we always come back here." He points at the trees. "The trees move. I am certain of it. And the hart keeps coming back to look at us." At the edge of the clearing, a white hart stands watching you with eyes like stars.

responses.label: You may lead the hunting party out of the enchanted wood.
You may follow the white hart deeper into the wood to learn what it wants.

entries.body: You sit down across from her. Mag grins and puts the pea under the middle shell. Her hands begin to move.

resolutions.label: find the pea

success.body: You do not watch the shells. You watch her hands, and her eyes, and on the third pass you see her palm the pea and slip it under her little finger. When she stops, you do not point at any shell. You take her wrist and turn her hand over. The pea drops onto the table. There is a long silence. Then Mag throws back her head and laughs until she weeps. "Sixty years," she says. "Sixty years!" She gives you a whole handful of silver pennies and a kiss on the cheek. "Never lost to an honest man," she says. "You are not one. I like you."

notes: Lose 1 Treasure, if possible

failure.body: You watch the shells. You watch them very carefully. When she stops, you point at the left one, confidently. She lifts it. Nothing. She lifts the middle one. Nothing. She lifts the right one. Nothing. The pea is behind her ear. You ride on without your spurs.

entries.body:
You hear a man shouting for help in the forest, and ride toward the sound. You find a clearing churned to mud, a dead horse, and a huntsman clinging to the branch of an oak with his leg bent at a terrible angle. Beneath the tree, a great black boar is pacing, grunting, tearing at the roots with its tusks.

"Don't come closer!" the huntsman shouts. "I am Rhodri. He has killed my horse and my dogs, and broken my leg. He has been waiting down there all day." He is grey with pain. "The branch is cracking. When it goes, I go. If you have a spear, for the love of God, use it. If not, run."

The boar turns and sees you. It lowers its head.

responses.label: You may fight the great boar to save the huntsman.
You may draw the boar away so the huntsman can be carried to safety.

entries.body:
Gaheris looks up, and sees you, and something wild comes into his eyes. "You," he says. "You fought me once. For him. For Lamorak." He stands up, with the bloody sword. "My brothers are coming. They will want to know who helped him."

You are on an island in the cold sea, in a hall full of Orkney men, with Orkney's blood-feud written against your name. You leave that hall very fast, and you do not stop until you are on a fishing boat halfway to Caithness, with the Orkney men watching from the shore.
You stand in the circle among the singers and open your mouth, and the note comes out of you as if it had always been there.

resolutions.label: sing with the stones to hold the moment

success.body: You sing all night, and all the next day, and the next night, with the islanders and the priests and the stones. Your throat bleeds. You do not stop. On the third dawn, the old priest touches your shoulder. "Enough," she says. "We have given him three more days. It is all we can give." You fall asleep in the circle. When you wake, the stones are silent. Somewhere in the south, you know, a battle has been fought. But three days is three days, and you will never know what they were for.
