failure.body: You sing all night, and at dawn, your voice gives out. The stones go on without you. When you leave, you still cannot speak.

resolutions.label: pray with the old priests that the king may pass in peace

success.body: You do not try to hold back what is coming. You kneel in the centre of the circle and pray, not that the king should live, but that he should die well and be carried somewhere safe. The old priest, hearing you, stops singing, and kneels beside you, and so do the others, one by one. The stones' note changes. It is still a lament. It is not a cry any more. When you leave, the old priest blesses you in a tongue you do not know.

failure.body: You kneel and pray that the king may pass in peace. The old priest looks at you with pity. "Then you have given him up," she says, "before we have." The stones sing on without you.

entries.body: "Give me your twenty," you say. The sergeant's face lights up.

resolutions.label: retake the gate from Lot's men

success.body: You do not attack the gate. You go up onto the walls on either side of it and come at the Orkney men from above, dropping stones and roof-tiles on them. They break and run out through the gate they were meant to open, and you slam it behind them. By dawn, York is the High King's again. The butchers of the Shambles carry you through the streets on their shoulders, which is an alarming experience.

failure.body: You lead the twenty at the gate, and the Orkney men are waiting with spears. Half your men fall. You are driven back. At dawn, Lot's army comes in through the Micklegate.

resolutions.label: call on the Orkney men at the gate to yield

success.body: You walk up to the Micklegate alone, with your sword sheathed, and call up to the Orkney men that the castle is holding, that Lot's army is still a day away, and that every man on that gate will hang at dawn unless he walks away tonight. You name their captain, whom you met once at a feast. A long silence. Then the gate-bar scrapes, and the Orkney men slip out into the dark. By dawn, York is the High King's again.

failure.body: You walk up to the gate and call to the Orkney men to yield. Their captain laughs and throws a spear. It misses. The gate opens at dawn, for Lot.

entries.body: "I will stay with you," you say. "We will face your abbot together." Brother Seisyll looks at you for a long moment. Then he puts the cork in his bottle.

resolutions.label: keep faith with the hermit through the night

success.body: At midnight, a figure in a black habit stands in the chapel doorway. It looks at Brother Seisyll, and then at you, and it does not speak. Seisyll's hands are shaking. "Say something," you murmur. He swallows. "Father," he says, "I am angry." The dead abbot nods, slowly, as though that is the right answer, and the first thing that the old hermit has said honestly in a year. Then he is gone. In the morning, Seisyll sweeps the moss from the altar. "It is a start," he says.

failure.body: At midnight, a figure in a black habit stands in the doorway. Brother Seisyll screams and flees into the forest. You stand there alone with the dead abbot. He looks at you for a long time, and then he turns and follows his monk into the dark. You do not sleep again that night.

resolutions.label: speak with the dead abbot on the hermit's behalf

success.body: At midnight, a figure in a black habit stands in the chapel doorway. You rise and bow to it. "Father," you say, "your monk has lost his faith, because God did not answer him. What should he do?" The dead abbot looks at you. Then, for the first time, he speaks, very softly. "He should keep asking," he says. He is gone. Brother Seisyll weeps, but in the morning, he is praying again. He says it is a kind of arguing.

failure.body: At midnight, a figure in a black habit stands in the chapel doorway. You rise and speak to it, but it does not answer. It only looks at you, and you have the feeling that you have said entirely the wrong thing. When it goes, it takes the hermit's courage with it.

entries.body: You lower your lance and ride at the brigands.

resolutions.label: scatter the brigands from the bishop's train

success.body: You ride through them like a bowling ball through skittles. Their leader turns and meets you, and goes off the back of his horse. The rest look at him, lying in the grass, and decide the bishop's gold is not worth it. The bishop is very grateful, in a pompous way. The young chaplain is simply grateful. You like him better.

failure.body: You ride at them, but there are too many, and they close round you. You are pulled from your horse and robbed along with the bishop. They leave you both standing on the plain in your shirts.

entries.body: You take the scroll. "I will see he hears it," you say. Branwen gives you a look of pure gratitude, and something else. "He will not listen," she says. "They never do. That is part of the reckoning too."

resolutions.label: bring the warning to the High King's attention

success.body: At Camelot, you are shown into the High King's presence in the evening. He reads the scroll slowly, while Merlin looks over his shoulder. Then he rolls it up. "Merlin told me this," he says, "when I was a boy. Now a nun tells me." He is quiet for a long time. "I will remember it," he says. "Thank her. And tell her," he adds, "that she may look at all the stars she likes." Sister Branwen, when you tell her, laughs and weeps together.

failure.body: At Camelot, you ask to see the High King and are passed from steward to chamberlain to Sir Kay, who reads the scroll and laughs. "A nun's stars," he says. "The king has a wizard for that." He throws it in the fire. You ride back to the nunnery and tell Sister Branwen. She only nods. "It is part of the reckoning," she says.

resolutions.label: swear to its truth upon your knighthood

success.body: At Camelot, when the High King hears you out and frowns, you draw your sword and lay it on the table before him. "I swear on this," you say, "that the nun's reckoning is honest, and I have checked it myself." The king looks at the sword a long time. "Then I will remember it," he says. He sends Sister Branwen a new astrolabe, and a letter in his own hand.

failure.body: At Camelot, you lay your sword on the table and swear. Sir Kay asks whether you have also checked the nun's arithmetic, and you have not. The court laughs. The king is kind, but he does not believe a word.

entries.body: You throw the purse back at his feet. "The High King's beard is not for sale," you say, "and neither am I." Rience stands up slowly. He is taller than you thought. "Then I will add yours," he says, "to the collection."

resolutions.label: fight King Rience in his own hall

success.body: Rience fights like a bear, all weight and fury, and his first blow splits your shield to the boss. But he is slow, and he has eaten a great deal of mutton. You wear him out round the long table, dodging, until he stops to breathe, and then you put your sword to his throat. He yields with bad grace. "Take the mantle, then," he snarls. You take it. At Camelot, the eleven beards are returned to eleven very grateful kings.

failure.body: Rience fights like a bear, all weight and fury, and his first blow splits your shield to the boss. His second knocks you under the table. When you wake up, you are in the road outside, and your chin is sore. Your hand goes to it. You have been shaved, very badly, with a dagger. You ride away sure of only one thing: you will not be the twelfth beard on that mantle.

resolutions.label: shame Rience before his own guests

success.body: You turn from the king to his hall. "Eleven kings have given their beards to that mantle," you say, loudly. "Eleven kings sit here as his guests, and dare not ask for them back." There is a long silence. Then an old king at the end of the table stands up, and then another. Rience looks round his hall and sees faces he cannot beat. He takes off the mantle and throws it on the table. You leave with your chin intact.

failure.body: You turn to his hall and speak of shame. The guests look at their plates. Nobody stands. Rience laughs and throws a mutton bone at your head. You leave with a bruise and a strong opinion of kings who eat with their mouths open.

entries.body: You sit down among the veterans and raise your cup. They cheer.

resolutions.label: feast with the garrison and stand with them at dawn

success.body: You feast with them all night, and sing their songs, and at dawn, you stand with them on the wall. The Saxons come up the mountain in the grey light. The garrison fights as if it were a feast day. By noon, the Saxons have had enough, and go back down the mountain to find easier prey. Sir Brian sits down on the wall and laughs until he cries. "We should have kept a cow," he says.

failure.body: You feast with them all night, and at dawn, you stand with them on the wall. The Saxons come. The garrison fights well, but four hundred is too many. By noon, you are one of six who escape down the far side of the mountain.

entries.body: "I will ride with you," you say. Herne laughs and blows his horn. Your horse screams and leaps into the air, and you are galloping over the clouds, among the hollow-faced riders, with the hounds baying below.

resolutions.label: keep pace with the wild hunt

success.body: You ride all night, over forests and rivers and sleeping towns, and you keep up with Herne at every leap. You do not look to see what you are hunting. At cockcrow, the hunt plunges down to earth, and you find yourself sitting on your horse on the heath where you started. There is frost on your armour. Herne leans down from his saddle and hangs a horn round your neck. "You rode well," he says. "Ride with us again." He is gone. The peasant, you find, is lying in the heather, asleep, unhurt. The hunt has taken something else.

failure.body: You ride all night, and at midnight your horse falters. You fall from the clouds and land in a bog. In the morning, you drag yourself out of the bog and find your horse's hoofprints leading away across the heath. You do not find the horse. You hear, from far away, a long, mocking blast on a horn.

entries.body:
"Lady," you say, "I would not take anything from you that costs you nothing to give. What counsel will you give me freely?" The Lady of the Lake laughs, and the whole lake shivers with light.

"That is a better question than most," she says. "Very well. Here is my counsel. Be careful of oaths. Keep them, but be careful of them. The young king's knights are all making oaths, and every oath is a door, and some doors only open one way." She sinks slowly into the lake, until only her face is above the water. "And when you are asked to hold a sword over water," she says, "and throw it in, do it the first time." Then she is gone, and the lake is only a lake.
You go to the royal stand. The High King is sitting alone, watching the melee with his chin in his hand. He looks old.

resolutions.label: comfort the lonely king

success.body: You sit with him. You do not talk about the quest. You talk about horses, and hawks, and the young knights who have never been to Camelot and want to see it. You make him laugh. At the end of the day, he grips your hand. "I needed that," he says. "I thought they had all gone." He gives you a ring from his own hand.

failure.body: You sit with him, and try to cheer him, but you talk about the quest without meaning to, and his face closes. "Go and fight," he says. "Everyone else is."

resolutions.label: bring the king's old companions to sit with him

success.body: You do not sit with him yourself. You go round the pavilions and find the old knights who are home from the quest, or never went: Kay, and Lucan, and Bedivere, and old Sir Ector, and bring them all to the royal stand, one by one, with some excuse. By the end of the afternoon, the High King is surrounded by his oldest friends, and laughing. He looks across at you, and knows exactly what you have done.

failure.body: You go to find the king's old companions. Kay is sulking, Lucan is ill, and Bedivere is on the quest. You come back with Sir Ector, who falls asleep.

entries.body: You go to the wash-house to deliver the poem. Nest looks up from her tub, blows a wisp of hair out of her eyes and grins at you. "Who are you, then?" she asks.

resolutions.label: court Nest the laundress

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You never do read her the poem. You roll up your sleeves and help her wring out the High King's shirts instead, which makes her laugh, and by the end of the afternoon you are good friends and possibly more. Kay finds out within the week. He is too proud to be angry. He only says, "Well. She always did have poor taste," and goes to bed early. You feel badly about Kay. You feel less badly about Nest.

failure.body: You never read her the poem. Instead you tell her that she is as lovely as the dawn. Nest looks at you with pity. "Sir Kay," she says, "wrote me a poem this morning. It was terrible. You are worse." She turns back to her tub.

entries.body:
The black barge comes to the shore, and one of the three queens lifts her veil. It is the Lady of the Lake. She looks at you across the dying king, and smiles.

"You helped my Nimue once," she says. "I have not forgotten." She holds out her hand. "Come with us. You may carry him on board, and sit by him on the crossing, and see where he goes. No other living knight will see it." Beside you, Sir Bedivere has thrown the sword at last, and a hand has risen out of the water to catch it, and brandished it three times, and drawn it under.

You lift the old king in your arms. He is very light. You carry him into the barge, and sit beside him, and the barge moves out into the mist. You will never be able to tell anyone what you saw. But when you wake on the shore at noon, alone, you are not afraid of anything any more.

notes: Lose Story Token #16

entries.body: "Can you carry me," you ask, "to where the Grail has gone?" The eagle laughs, a harsh cawing sound. "No," it says. "But I can carry you somewhere else. Hold on."

resolutions.label: hold on as the ancient eagle flies

success.body: It takes you in its claws and flies. You see all of Britain below you: the mountains and the rivers and the sea, and the little towns, and the smoke of Camelot. It flies until you are numb with cold, and then it sets you down on a hilltop you have never seen, beside a little chapel with a light in it. "There," it says, and flies away. The chapel is empty. But you sleep in it that night and dream a dream so clear that you remember it for the rest of your life.

failure.body: It takes you in its claws and flies. Halfway across the sky, your hands go numb and you slip. The eagle catches you, but by the leg, and upside down, and you do not enjoy the rest of the flight. It drops you in a bog.

entries.body: "The Lord was baptised in a river," you say. "So can you be." The giant's face lights up like a sunrise.

resolutions.label: perform the giant's baptism with true faith

success.body: You lead the giant down to the river, and he wades in up to his waist, and kneels, and the water rises round him. You fill your helm and pour it over his head, again and again, and say the words as well as you remember them. When you finish, he stays kneeling for a long time, with his eyes shut and water dripping from his beard. The priest has followed you down to the bank. When the giant rises, the priest is weeping. "I was wrong," he says. Ysbaddaden gives you a cup carved from a whole oak burl.

failure.body: You lead the giant down to the river and pour water over his head from your helm. But you stumble over the words, and the giant, who has been waiting his whole life for this, notices. "Is that all?" he asks sadly. "I thought I would feel different." He goes back up to the churchyard to wait for the priest.

entries.body: You sit down across the table from him. "What will you ask?" he says. You think carefully.

resolutions.label: ask Merlin the right question

success.body: You ask him not about yourself, or the king, but about him: what he wants. Merlin stares at you. Then he laughs, a real laugh, surprised. "Nobody has ever asked me that," he says. "I want to be surprised. Once. By anything." He looks at you. "You have just done it." He tells you a secret about the young king that nobody else knows, and makes you promise to keep it. You do. He also gives you his blessing, which is a strange thing, like being blessed by a thunderstorm.

failure.body: You ask him about your own future. Merlin sighs, as if you have disappointed him, and tells you. He leaves nothing out. You sit in his cave among the books and the stuffed birds with your hands over your face, and you wish, for a long time afterwards, that you had asked him anything else.

resolutions.label: ask him nothing, and keep him company instead

success.body: You sit down across the table. "I have no question," you say. "I thought you might like the company." Merlin stares at you. Then he laughs, a real laugh, surprised. "I want to be surprised," he says. "Once. By anything. You have just done it." He tells you a secret about the young king that nobody else knows, and makes you promise to keep it. He gives you his blessing, which is like being blessed by a thunderstorm.

failure.body: You sit down and say you have no question. Merlin looks at you. "Then you are wasting my afternoon," he says, and goes back to his writing.

entries.body: You catch Llywarch's wrist. "Wait," you say. "Listen." He tries to pull away. The dog whines.

resolutions.label: hold the grieving father back

success.body: Llywarch is strong with grief, and you have to wrestle him to the ground in the yard and hold him there while he sobs and curses. It takes a long time before he stops fighting you. Then you both hear it clearly: a baby crying, somewhere under the overturned cradle. Llywarch runs inside. He comes out with his son in his arms, whole and roaring. Behind the cradle lies a dead wolf, as big as a pony, with its throat torn out. The huntsman kneels in the yard and puts his arms round the dog's neck and weeps into its fur.

failure.body: Llywarch is strong with grief, and he throws you off before you can hold him. The sword comes down. It is only afterwards, when he goes inside, that he finds his son alive under the cradle and the dead wolf behind it. He comes back out into the yard and looks at the dog, and at you. He does not say anything. He does not have to.

resolutions.label: reason with the huntsman until he sees the truth

success.body: "Look at the dog," you say. "Does he look like a dog who has killed a child? Look at the blood on the doorstep. It goes out, not in." Llywarch stares at the doorstep. His sword arm drops. From inside, the crying comes again, louder. He runs in and comes out with his son, safe and bawling. The dead wolf lies behind the cradle. Llywarch drops his sword and falls on his knees beside Cafall. "Forgive me," he whispers. Then he looks up at you. "I will name the boy for you," he says.

failure.body: "Look at the dog," you say. "Look at the blood." But Llywarch is not listening. You go on talking, reasoning, arguing, and all the while he is looking at the dog, and at last he screams and brings the sword down. Later, he finds his son alive. You wish you had used your hands and not your tongue.

entries.body: "First tell me who you are," you say, "and what chapel you keep." The Green Knight tilts his head. "A reasonable question," he says, "and an unreasonable time to ask it."

resolutions.label: see through the Green Knight's enchantment

success.body: You look at him closely. The green is not paint. It runs through him the way sap runs through a tree. "You are no man," you say, "but you are no devil either. You are the old wood itself, testing whoever walks through it." The Green Knight laughs, a sound like wind in a whole forest. "Near enough," he says. "You have passed a better test than the axe." He gives you his holly branch, which never withers, and rides away.

failure.body: You look at him closely, trying to see what he is. The Green Knight looks back at you. After a moment you realise that you cannot remember why you wanted to know, or where you were riding, or which way the road runs. When you come to your senses, he is gone, and the ride has disappeared, and you are deep in a wood you do not know.

resolutions.label: refuse him with courtesy and hold your ground

success.body: "I will not play a game whose rules I do not know," you say, "but I will not run from you either. If you want a fight, you shall have one, fairly, today." The Green Knight looks at you for a long while. Then he smiles. "Courtesy and caution in one knight," he says. "I have not met that often." He bows from the saddle and rides away. That night, at the inn, you find a green silk purse in your saddlebag, full of silver.

failure.body: "I will not play a game whose rules I do not know," you say. The Green Knight sighs. "Then you are not the knight I was told of," he says, loudly enough for the woodcutters at the edge of the ride to hear. They are laughing as he goes. By the next town the story has arrived before you: the knight who would not take the axe.

entries.body: You spur your horse toward Lot's black and gold banner.

resolutions.label: cut through to King Lot's banner

success.body: You fight your way across the field, through Orkney men and Gorre men and Garlot men, and reach the banner, and cut down the man who carries it. It falls. The rebels, seeing it fall, lose heart. King Lot himself rides at you in a fury, and you cross swords, and then the melee sweeps you apart. By sunset, the rebels are fleeing. The young king's knights carry the black and gold banner to him, and they tell him who brought it down.

failure.body: You fight your way toward the banner, but Lot's hearth-guard are the best fighters in the north, and they drive you back. You are wounded, and carried from the field.

resolutions.label: strike at the rebels' hearts with the young king's name

success.body: You do not fight your way to Lot's banner. You ride along the edge of the melee where the lesser kings' men are, and shout to them that the young king offers pardon to any who lay down arms before sunset. Word spreads through the rebel host faster than any charge. By mid-afternoon, three kings' banners are down, not captured, but lowered. Lot fights on alone. By sunset, the rebels are fleeing.

failure.body: You ride along the edge of the melee shouting the young king's pardon. Nobody has told the young king. When he hears, he is not pleased.

entries.body: "Tell me my future," you say. Merlin puts down his apple and looks at you with his old, bright eyes.

resolutions.label: bear the hearing of Merlin's prophecy

success.body: He tells you. He tells you of battles and loves and a long road, and a plain at the end of it, in the rain. He tells it plainly, without riddles, which is somehow worse. At the end, he picks up his apple again. "Now you know," he says. "It will not help. It never helps. But you will be braver, I think, for knowing it. Most are." You ride away from the stones at midnight, and you are not afraid.

failure.body: He tells you, and you cannot bear it. You stop him halfway. He shrugs. "Most do," he says. You ride away from the stones not knowing the end, and wishing you had heard it.

resolutions.label: ask Merlin not your future but his

success.body: "Tell me yours instead," you say. Merlin puts down his apple. Nobody has asked him that. He tells you: a girl, a lake, a stone, a very long sleep. He tells it plainly. At the end, he laughs. "Now you know something about me that the young king does not," he says, "and I know something about you: that you asked." He blesses you, which is like being blessed by a thunderstorm.

failure.body: "Tell me yours instead," you say. Merlin smiles, and the smile is not kind. "No," he says. "Mine is my own business." And he tells you yours instead, all of it, plainly, while the stones hum. You ride away at midnight wishing you had let him keep his apple.

entries.body: You look at Gaheris, and at the sea, and at the ships that will bring his brothers. "Where is Lamorak?" you ask.

resolutions.label: get Sir Lamorak off the island

success.body: You find him hiding in a sea-cave on the far side of the island, naked and freezing and weeping for Morgause. You give him your cloak, and find a fishing boat, and row him to Caithness through the night. At dawn, he stands on the shore and grips your hand. "I loved her," he says. "I truly did." He goes south, to hide in Benwick. Orkney's brothers hunt for him for a year, and do not find him, and the story is that you saved him.

failure.body: You find him in a sea-cave on the far side of the island, but his pursuers find him too. You fight beside him on the rocks. He escapes. You are captured, and it takes a long time to get free.

resolutions.label: persuade the brothers that Lamorak has already fled south

success.body: You find the brothers' ships as they come into the harbour and tell them, with great regret, that Lamorak took a fishing boat for Caithness at dawn and will be halfway to Carlisle by now. You describe the boat. You describe his cloak. They sail south at once. Lamorak, hiding in a sea-cave on the far side of the island, takes a boat west to Ireland that night. You have saved him. The story is that you did.

failure.body: You tell the brothers Lamorak fled south. One of them, Agravain, writes it down, and then asks the fishermen, who say no boat left at dawn. They look at you.

entries.body: You take a bridle from your saddlebag, a plain iron one, and hold it up. The kelpie's eyes widen.

resolutions.label: bridle the kelpie with cold iron

success.body: You slip the iron bit into its mouth before it can move. It screams like the sea in a storm, and then stands still, trembling, bound. "Now you will carry me," you say, "and not drown me." It carries you across the sea in half a day. On the far shore, you take the bridle off. The kelpie looks at you with hatred and something else, and goes back into the waves. You keep the bridle. It is still wet.

failure.body: You try to slip the iron bit into its mouth. The kelpie seizes your arm in its teeth and drags you into the surf. The fisherman and three soldiers pull you out.

resolutions.label: trick the kelpie into giving up its own bridle

success.body: You do not reach for it. You admire it instead: its mane, its eyes, its fine white coat. Kelpies are vain. You tell it that a horse so fine should wear a bridle of its own, and that you would be honoured to carry it across the sea. It is so pleased that it shakes its head, and a bridle of seaweed and silver falls out of its mane into your hands. With it on, the kelpie is yours. It carries you across the sea in half a day.

failure.body: You admire the kelpie's mane and eyes and coat. It listens, pleased, and then it says, "And yours," and lowers its head to let you mount. You nearly do. The fisherman pulls you back by the belt.

entries.body:
You are wearing Lot's colours. You rode with him to Bedegraine, and now you sit your horse in his battle line, and across the field, the young king is fighting in golden armour.

King Lot rides up beside you. "Now," he says, "we will see what the beardless boy is made of." He looks at you. "You. Take my left wing. Break his knights, and the day is ours."

resolutions.label: lead King Lot's left wing into the charge

success.body: You lead the charge, and the young king's knights break before you, and for an hour, it looks as though the rebel kings have won. Then Merlin raises his staff on the hillock, and a great wind blows dust into the rebels' faces, and the young king rallies, and it is over. Lot's army is broken. You escape from the field with Lot himself, who is laughing, bitterly, in the dust. "Next time," he says. He gives you a gold arm-ring from his own arm.

failure.body: You lead the charge, and the young king's knights meet you, and you are unhorsed in the first clash. You are taken prisoner. The young king, when he sees you among the captives, looks at you for a long time. Then he lets you go. "Tell Lot," he says, "that I spared his knights." It is worse than a beating.

entries.body: You give your horse to the steward and walk in. The hall is golden, and the table groans, and at its head sits a lady in green, with a face you cannot quite look at directly. The three young men from the town are at the table, eating and laughing, with glazed eyes.

resolutions.label: keep your wits through the fay feast

success.body: You eat a little, and drink a little, and are courteous to the lady, and you never once ask her name, though you want to more than you have wanted anything. At midnight, she laughs. "You are the first to keep the condition," she says, "and keep your head." She lets the three young men go with you, and gives you a cup of green glass. When you walk out through the gate, you are in the market square, and it is dawn, and the castle is gone, and the fish stalls are back.

failure.body: You eat a little, and drink a little, and toward midnight, without meaning to, you say, "My lady, may I know your name?" The whole hall goes silent. The lady smiles. "Of course," she says, and tells you, and you forget everything else. You wake in the market square three days later, among the fish.

resolutions.label: ask her a better question than her name

success.body: At midnight, when the wish to ask her name is almost unbearable, you ask her something else instead: what she would like to be asked. The lady in green looks at you for a long moment. Then she laughs, delighted. "Nobody has ever asked me that," she says. She tells you. It is a very small thing, and very sad. At dawn she lets the three young men go with you, and gives you a cup of green glass.

failure.body: At midnight, you ask her what she would like to be asked. "My name," she says, smiling. And you ask it. You wake in the market square three days later, among the fish.

entries.body: You swing up onto the white horse's back. Its skin is cold and wet, and it rises beneath you and turns toward the sea.

resolutions.label: master the kelpie on the open sea

success.body: It plunges into the waves and gallops across them, and you cling to its mane. Halfway across, it tries to dive, and you haul its head up with all your strength, and speak to it the way you would speak to any horse that tries something foolish: firmly, and without fear. It does not dive again. It sets you down on the far shore, at the king's camp, a day before the boats. Then it looks at you, almost respectfully, and goes back into the sea.

failure.body: It plunges into the waves, and halfway across, it dives, and takes you with it. You fight your way free of its mane and come up, half-drowned, and are picked up by a fishing boat. You reach the camp three days after the boats.

entries.body: You stand at the foot of the causeway and call up to him everything you have heard: the Pentecost feast, the veiled vessel, the knights riding out, the castle that cannot be found by seekers. He listens in silence. When you have finished, he is quiet a long while. "Thank you," he says at last. "I will pray that one of them finds it. And that he remembers the rest of us." He rings his bell, softly, and the light in the window goes out.
"The leaves never stop," you say, "but I have a broom." The old woman laughs and hands you another.

resolutions.label: keep the temple through a day and a night

success.body: You sweep all day, and at night, the old woman shows you how to light the lamp in the centre of the temple, which has not gone out, she says, for a thousand years. You sit up with it all night. Toward dawn, the voices in the columns begin to sing, very softly, a hunting song in a tongue older than Latin. When you leave, the old woman gives you her blessing, in the goddess's name, which is not a name you know. You find, riding away, that you can hear the wind in the trees more clearly than before.

failure.body: You sweep all day, and at night, you sit with the lamp, and around midnight you fall asleep. When you wake, the lamp is out. The old woman is very angry. The voices do not sing.

resolutions.label: keep the temple lamp with the old words of tending

success.body: The old woman teaches you the words to say over the lamp at every hour, so that it does not go out, and you say them all night, at every hour, sitting in the middle of the temple. Toward dawn, the voices in the columns begin to sing, very softly, a hunting song in a tongue older than Latin. When you leave, she gives you her blessing in the goddess's name. You find you can hear the wind in the trees more clearly than before.

failure.body: She teaches you the words to say over the lamp at every hour. At the third hour, you say them wrong. The lamp goes out. The old woman is very angry.

entries.body: "If the adventure is worth having," you say, "it is worth a joust." Bagdemagus goes red with delight. "Now that," he cries, "is the first sensible thing anyone has said to me all year!" He lowers his visor and backs his horse to the far end of the road.

resolutions.label: meet the king's charge

success.body: Bagdemagus rides like a man with something to prove. His lance catches the edge of your shield and skids away, and yours takes him square on the chest. He goes over his horse's tail and lands sitting up in a puddle. For a moment he says nothing. Then he laughs until he wheezes and hands you the list. "Forty adventures," he says. "Tell them at Camelot that it was the King of Gore who gave you your start." You find three of them are real.

failure.body: Bagdemagus rides like a man with something to prove. You aim for his shield, but his horse swerves at the last moment and his lance takes you under the arm. You land in the ditch. The king leans down from the saddle, genuinely sorry. "Bad luck," he says. "Horses. You never know with horses." He rides off whistling. You resolve to watch the horse next time, not the man.

resolutions.label: yield the adventure to him with a good grace

success.body: You lower your lance before the first course and ride up to him instead. "My lord," you say, "a king who has waited three Pentecosts deserves the first adventure. I will hold your horse." Bagdemagus stares at you. Then he laughs until his circlet slips. "Nobody has ever given me anything," he says. He insists you ride with him, and when the copper tower turns out to hold a parrot, he laughs again and tells everyone at Camelot that you are the most courteous knight in Britain.

failure.body: You lower your lance before the first course and ride up to him instead. "My lord, the adventure is yours." Bagdemagus goes purple. "You think I cannot beat you?" he roars. "You pity me?" He rides off in a fury, and tells everyone at the next inn that you were afraid of him. You resolve that courtesy, like a lance, needs aiming.

entries.body: You draw your sword and kick open the cellar door. The men at the table leap up.

resolutions.label: seize the traitor steward

success.body: There are four of them, and they are more used to plotting than fighting. You disarm two, and the others flee through a tunnel at the back of the cellar. Sir Maldred is one of the two. He gets down on his knees and begs. You take him to the High King, who listens to him weep for an hour, and then sends him to the Holy Land for the rest of his life. You are given his horse.

failure.body: There are four of them, and one of them is very good with a sword. They escape through a tunnel. Sir Maldred is back in the High King's hall the next morning, looking innocent, and he looks at you across the room with pure hatred.

resolutions.label: bring the watch down upon them in force

success.body: You slip out of the tavern and fetch the town watch, and a dozen of the castle garrison, and set men at the cellar door and at the tunnel mouth by the river, which the tavern-keeper tells you about for a coin. Then you go in. The plotters have nowhere to run. Sir Maldred goes down on his knees and begs. The High King sends him to the Holy Land for the rest of his life.

failure.body: You fetch the watch, but it takes an hour to wake them, and when you go in, the cellar is empty and the tunnel door is swinging.

entries.body: You ride round the mountain into the next valley, where the sun is shining on fields of golden wheat. The lord, a jolly fat man called Sir Ebrauc, is sitting in his garden eating strawberries.

resolutions.label: shame the lord into ending the witch's storm

success.body: You tell him about the hail, and the flattened wheat, and the child with the bleeding head. You tell him that the High King will hear of a lord who buys storms against his neighbours. Sir Ebrauc stops eating strawberries. He goes rather pale. "I only wanted a good harvest," he says. "I did not think." He sends his steward up the mountain to pay the witch to stop, and sends half his harvest over the hill.

failure.body: You tell him about the hail and the child. Sir Ebrauc laughs. "The weather," he says, "is God's business, not mine. Have a strawberry." His men show you out of the valley.

resolutions.label: warn the lord that his neighbours are arming

success.body: You tell Sir Ebrauc, pleasantly, over his strawberries, that the men of the next valley have lost their harvest and are sharpening their scythes, and you describe exactly how a hundred angry farmers would come over the hill, and where his walls are weakest. He listens with a strawberry halfway to his mouth. By evening, his steward is riding up the mountain to pay the witch to stop, and half his harvest is going over the hill.

failure.body: You tell Sir Ebrauc about the scythes. He laughs, and shows you his forty men-at-arms. "Let them come," he says. You ride away, and the hail goes on.

entries.body: "I thank you for your counsel," you say, and lower your visor. Dinadan sighs. "They all say that," he says. "Shall I hold your purse? For your heirs?" You ride into the ford. On the far side, Tarquin laughs and levels his lance.

resolutions.label: joust with Sir Tarquin in the ford

success.body: Tarquin's lance is as thick as a young tree, but his horse labours in the ford, and you meet him before he has his speed. Your lance takes him on the helm. He sways, and you ride on and turn and come again, and the second time he goes into the water. He yields in a great spray of mud and curses. The sixty-four knights are released from his dungeon that evening, and every one of them insists on buying you wine. Dinadan comes over the ford at last. "I would have done that," he says, "on the forty-first reason."

failure.body: Tarquin's lance is as thick as a young tree. It takes you on the shield and throws you over your horse's tail into the river, and the current rolls you downstream. Dinadan fishes you out with a branch a quarter-mile below. "Shield sixty-five," he says sadly, and points: Tarquin is hanging it on the tree.

resolutions.label: fight Sir Tarquin on foot in the river

success.body: You dismount in midstream, and so, with a snort of contempt, does Tarquin. In the water his great weight is against him. The current drags at his legs, and every blow he swings nearly takes him off his feet. You keep him turning until he is gasping, then strike his sword from his hand. The dungeon is opened by nightfall. Dinadan wades across and shakes your hand. "Remarkable," he says. "Do not do it again."

failure.body: You dismount in midstream, and so, with a snort of contempt, does Tarquin. He is stronger than any man you have ever fought, and the first blow of his sword beats your shield down onto your own head. When you wake, you are lying on the bank beside Dinadan. "He threw you back," he says. "He says you are too small to keep."

entries.body: "This is a horse trough," you say loudly, "not a chapel." The hermit nods fiercely. Iddo looks at you with hurt, puzzled eyes.

resolutions.label: disperse the crowd before blood is spilled

success.body: You speak to the villagers kindly but firmly. Whatever the boy saw, you tell them, no good ever came of stoning a squire in a market square. The kneeling villagers get up, embarrassed, and the ones with stones put them down, and in a quarter of an hour the square is empty. Iddo goes back to his sick master. The hermit thanks you gruffly. You wonder, riding on, why the water in the trough was so very clear.

failure.body: You speak to the villagers firmly, but the ones who were kneeling take it badly, and the ones with stones take it as encouragement. A stone hits Iddo on the forehead. The crowd scatters in horror. You carry the boy to the inn, where his master nurses him, and you leave the village with the hermit's thanks, which you do not want.

resolutions.label: prove it was a trick of the light

success.body: You dip your hand in the trough and hold up the bottom of a broken lantern someone has thrown there, with a bit of polished brass still in it. "Here is the vessel," you say, "and here is the dawn." The crowd laughs with relief. Iddo stares at the brass for a long time. "Perhaps," he says. The hermit claps you on the shoulder. But that night, at the inn, you notice that the squire is not eating, and does not seem to need to.

failure.body: You dip your hand in the trough to find something to show the crowd, and come up empty. The water is cold as ice and clear as glass, and your hand tingles for hours afterwards. The hermit stares at you. The villagers stare at you. You mutter something and leave.

entries.body: You walk out into the ring, alone, without your sword. The mare stops screaming and looks at you, with her ears back.

resolutions.label: calm the maddened war-horse

success.body: You do not rush. You stand still until she stops trembling. Then you walk closer, slowly, talking to her, saying her name. She lets you touch her neck. She lets you take the bridle. She stands, shaking, while you check her wounds, and then she follows you out of the ring, with her head on your shoulder. The old groom weeps. You lead her back to the old king's camp. He is not there, but his steward takes her, and thanks you in the king's name.

failure.body: You stand still until she stops trembling, and walk closer, and she rears and strikes you with a hoof. You go down. She gallops away over the plain and is not seen again.

resolutions.label: soothe her as her old groom would

success.body: You find the old groom and ask him what she likes. Apples, he says, and her left ear scratched, and the king's old whistle, two notes, low and high. You walk out into the ring with an apple, and whistle the two notes. The mare stops screaming. Her ears come forward. She walks to you, trembling, and takes the apple, and lets you scratch her ear. The groom weeps. You lead her back to the old king's camp.

failure.body: You walk out with an apple and whistle two notes, and they are the wrong two notes. The mare rears. Her hoof catches your shoulder, and she gallops away over the plain.

entries.body: "Let them go," you say. Morgan raises an eyebrow. "Or?"

resolutions.label: break the enchantress's hold over the captive knights

success.body: You do not fight her. You speak to the chains. You know the old words for iron, and for binding, and you speak them backwards, one after another, while Morgan watches with her head on one side, amused and then not amused. The chains fall. The four knights stand up. Morgan claps her hands, slowly. "Very good," she says. "Very, very good." She lets them go, and you with them, and as you go, she tosses you a stone from her throne, green and warm. "Something to remember me by," she says.

failure.body: You speak to the chains, and they do not listen. Morgan laughs until she cries. "Oh, little knight," she says. She adds you to the collection. You are there a month before she gets bored.

resolutions.label: fight Morgan's champion for the captives' freedom

success.body: "Let them go," you say, "or name a champion." Morgan laughs, delighted, and claps her hands, and a knight in black armour steps out from behind her throne. You fight him in the hall of white marble while the four chained knights watch. It is a strange fight: the black knight never tires, and never bleeds. But he is enchanted, not skilled, and at last you beat his sword down and strike his helm, and it is empty. Morgan pouts. She lets the four knights go, and tosses you a green stone from her throne.

failure.body: You fight Morgan's black knight in the marble hall, and he never tires, and you do. Morgan adds you to her collection. It is a month before she gets bored.

entries.body:
You come upon a fat friar in a brown habit standing on an upturned bucket at a village crossroads, with a tray of little lead badges hung round his neck and a crowd of villagers around him.

"Pardons!" he cries. "Pardons from the Holy Father in Rome, sealed with his own seal! A penny for a small sin, a shilling for a large one! And here," he lifts a small glass box with great reverence, "is a knucklebone of the blessed Saint Petroc himself, which cures the ague, the gout, the murrain and the evil eye. A farthing to touch it!" The villagers are pressing forward with their pennies.

You look at the knucklebone. It is very clearly a knucklebone from a pig. The friar catches your eye over the heads of the crowd, and winks. "Brother Cadoc," he says quietly, when you ride close. "Of no fixed abbey. You look like a sensible knight. There is plenty here for two."

responses.label: You may expose Brother Cadoc's false relic to the village.
You may join Brother Cadoc's trade and share his takings.

entries.body:
You come upon a river, wide and fast, with no bridge and no boat. On the near bank stands a hut of reeds, and a lean old man with a staff comes out of it, bent almost double. "You wish to cross?" he says. "I carry travellers on my back. It is my penance. I am Julian." He looks at the water with a kind of weary love. "But today my back is broken. I cannot carry you, and I cannot carry him." He points.

On a stone by the river sits a leper in rags, with his face wrapped in a cloth, holding out a wooden bowl. "He came at dawn," says Julian. "He must reach the hospital on the far side before nightfall, or die in the open. Nobody will touch him. Every traveller today has ridden upstream to the ford instead." The old man sits down heavily. "I would ask you to carry him, but I know what I am asking."

responses.label: You may carry the leper across the river on your own back.
You may ask the hermit Julian what his penance is for.

entries.body:
You come upon a small church on a hill, with a tiny stone cell built against its north wall. There is no door to the cell, only a narrow window with a wooden shutter, and a stone ledge where passers-by leave bread. The shutter opens as you ride past.

"You have come a long way," says a woman's voice from inside. It is old and very clear. "I am Mother Elen. I was walled in here forty years ago, and I will be carried out when I die. I pray for everyone who passes." A thin white hand comes out of the window and rests on the ledge. "I pray for you already. I have been praying for you since you came over the hill. Would you like my blessing? It is not free. You must tell me honestly what you most need to be forgiven for." The hand turns palm-up. "Or you may leave me some bread. That is also a kindness."

responses.label: You may kneel at the anchoress's window and ask for her blessing.
You may ride to the village and bring the anchoress food and firewood for the winter.

entries.body:
You come upon a hermit standing in the middle of a meadow in his nightshirt, holding a candle, looking very cross. There is a square of bare earth at his feet, as though a small building has recently been lifted off it.

"It has happened again," he says. "I am Brother Fychan. I built myself a cell in this meadow. Every night I go to sleep in it, and every morning I wake up somewhere else. Last week I woke up in the middle of the river. Yesterday on top of the church tower. This morning," he points with the candle, "the cell is up that tree, and I was not in it. I am in the meadow. In my nightshirt." He glares at the tree, where a small wooden hut is wedged in the branches. "It is the fair folk. I told them their dancing kept me awake. Now they will not leave me alone."

From somewhere in the long grass, you hear a high giggle.

responses.label: You may help Brother Fychan make his peace with the fair folk.
You may help Brother Fychan play a trick on the fair folk in return.

entries.body:
You come upon a hermit sitting on the bank of a river, dropping a wooden bowl into the current. It floats away downstream, and as it goes, you see a folded parchment in the bottom of it.

He sees you watching and blushes to the roots of his tonsure. "I am Brother Hugh," he says. "That was a letter." He points across the river, where a small nunnery stands among apple trees. "To the Abbess Gwenfrewi. We were betrothed when we were young, and then her father sent her to the nuns and mine sent me to the monks. That was thirty years ago. She lives over there. I live over here. Every Sunday she floats me a letter in a bowl, and every Wednesday I float her one." He looks at you. "The bishop is coming on Saturday. He has heard something. If he finds the letters, we will both be sent away. To opposite ends of Britain."

responses.label: You may help the hermit and the abbess keep their letters from the bishop.
You may persuade the bishop to release them both from their vows.

entries.body: You take hold of the bell-chain. The boy covers his ears. You pull.

resolutions.label: call the Sleepers to Britain's aid

success.body: The bell rings once, deep and slow, and the whole mountain hums. The iron door swings open. In the dark cave beyond, a thousand men in old armour stir, and one of them, an old knight with a white beard, sits up and looks at you. "Is it time?" he asks. You tell him about the Saxons, and Mordred, and the king across the sea. He listens gravely. Then he stands, and all the others with him. "It is not the time," he says, "but it is a time." Three hundred of them ride out with you, and for a month the Saxons in that valley know no peace. Then, one morning, they are gone.

partial.body: The bell rings, and the door opens, and one old knight sits up. "Is it time?" he asks. You tell him about the war. He shakes his head sadly. "Not yet," he says, and lies down again. But before he sleeps, he gives you his sword.

failure.body: The bell rings, and the door opens, and a thousand men stir, and sit up, and look at you, and look out of the cave at the smoke. "Not yet," they say, all together, and lie down, and the door swings shut, and you know that you will never be able to open it again.

entries.body:
You come upon a ragged monk standing on a hill in a strong wind, preaching at the top of his voice to a field full of crows. The crows are listening. Every one of them faces him.

"The king will fall!" he shouts. "The son will strike the father and the father the son! The table will be split for firewood! The sword will go back into the water!" He sees you and points a bony finger. "You! You will be there! I have seen you there, on the plain, in the rain!" The crows turn their heads, all together, to look at you.

He climbs down from his hill, and up close, he is only an old man, trembling. "I am Brother Aldhelm," he says. "I was a monk at Glastonbury. Then I started to see things. They put me out. Now I tell the crows, because they are the only ones who will listen." He grips your arm. "Will you listen?"

responses.label: You may listen to Brother Aldhelm's prophecy.
You may try to bring Brother Aldhelm back to his abbey at Glastonbury.

entries.body: You roll up your sleeves. "What do you need?" you ask. The young woman looks at you with desperate gratitude. "Moss," she says. "Clean water. And someone to stand at the waterfall with a sword."

resolutions.label: tend the wounded and keep the cave hidden

success.body: You gather moss for the wounds and yarrow for the bleeding, and you cut bracken to hide the path to the waterfall. When the Saxons pass by that evening, following their hound, they walk within twenty yards of the cave, and the roar of the water hides every groan, and the bracken hides the path. They go on. In the morning, you help the woman move the wounded, one at a time, to a monastery in the hills. Her name is Tangwen. She says she will name her first son for you.

failure.body: You gather moss and cut bracken to hide the path, but you cut it too green, and the Saxons' hound smells it. They come through the waterfall at dusk. You fight at the entrance with your back to the wounded, and hold them long enough for the woman to get half the men out through a back passage. The other half do not get out.

resolutions.label: hold the waterfall with the men who can still stand

success.body: Four of the wounded can still hold a spear. You set them behind the curtain of falling water, where a man coming through is blind and soaked and off balance, and you stand in front of them. When the Saxons come through the waterfall at dusk, they come one at a time, and they do not come for long. By morning they have given up on the cave. Tangwen says she will name her first son for you.

failure.body: You set four wounded men behind the waterfall and stand before them. The Saxons do not come through the water. They come round the side, by a path you did not see.

entries.body: "Your master would not want you to become what killed him," you say. Emrys looks up at you. "What would you know about my master?" he asks.

resolutions.label: persuade the squire to take his case to the High King

success.body: You sit down on the log beside him and ask about Sir Gwion. It takes him an hour to stop being angry and start talking. By sundown, he has told you everything: how kind his master was, how badly he sang, how he taught Emrys to read. At last the boy puts the whetstone away. "I will take it to Camelot," he says. "I will tell the High King. If he will not act, then I will." The High King does act. Breuse is outlawed by Michaelmas.

failure.body: You sit down on the log beside him and ask about Sir Gwion, but Emrys will not talk. He gets up and leaves in the night. You hear, a week later, that a squire was found dead outside Sir Breuse's pavilion, and that Breuse was laughing.

resolutions.label: pray with the squire for his master's soul

success.body: You kneel with him in the road and pray for Sir Gwion. Emrys does not want to kneel, and then he does, and then he weeps for the first time since the ford. When he has finished, he looks very young. "I cannot kill a man," he says, "and then go to his grave and pray." He gives you his master's sword to carry to Camelot, and goes home to Gwion's family instead.

failure.body: You kneel with him in the road and pray. Emrys kneels beside you, but he does not pray. When you open your eyes, he has gone, with the sword. You never hear what became of him.

entries.body:
You come upon a village where the wells have all gone bad. The water comes up black and stinks of rotten eggs. The villagers are thin and sullen. In the churchyard, what was once a small chapel is a blackened ruin, and beside it, in a shelter of branches, a hermit sits in the ashes with his arms folded.

"I cursed them," he says, before you can ask. "I am Brother Cynan. They burned my chapel. I had kept it forty years. I prayed for them every day." His voice is quite calm. "The reeve said I was hiding silver under the altar. I was not. They burned it anyway, to make me tell. So I cursed their wells, and God, it seems, agreed with me." He looks at you with pale, steady eyes. "Their children are sick now. I am sorry for the children. But I will not lift the curse until they rebuild my chapel with their own hands, stone by stone, and the reeve kneels in it."

The reeve, a thick-set man with a beard, is standing in the lane with his arms folded too.

responses.label: You may try to lift the hermit's curse on the wells.
You may persuade the villagers to rebuild the chapel.

entries.body:
You come upon a beggar sitting under a thorn tree at a crossroads, wrapped in a filthy grey cloak, with a staff across his knees and a bowl at his feet. His beard is white and his eyes are very bright, and he is peeling an apple with his thumbnail in one unbroken spiral.

"Alms," he says, without looking up. "Alms for an old man who knows too much." He finishes the apple and holds up the peel, one long curl. "Do you know what this is? It is a man's life. One long piece, and you cannot tell where it will end until you get there." He looks up, and his eyes are much too bright for a beggar's. "Or can you?" He grins. "I will make you a bargain. Give me a riddle and I will give you one. The better your riddle, the better mine."

You have a very strong feeling that you have seen this old man before, at the High King's elbow.

responses.label: You may trade riddles with the old beggar.
You may give the old beggar alms and ask for nothing.

entries.body:
You come upon a hermitage in a lonely valley, with a small chapel and a garden and a white-bearded hermit sitting at the gate. He rises with a smile and holds out his hands.

"A traveller! Come in, come in. I am Father Emyr. You are welcome to my fire and my bread." He takes your horse's bridle and leads you through the gate. "The road ahead is dangerous. There are outlaws in the pass. Stay the night here, and in the morning, I will show you a safe way round."

He is very kind. But his hands, as he unbuckles your saddle, are as hard and callused as a soldier's, and there is a scar across his knuckles. While he is in the chapel fetching bread, you notice that the chapel bell is tied to a long rope that runs away up the hillside, toward the pass.

responses.label: You may confront the false hermit and expose him.
You may play along and turn the hermit's trap against the outlaws.

entries.body: You climb onto the other high chair and look down at the board. The white pieces look up at you with frightened faces.

resolutions.label: win the game of living chess

success.body: It is a long game. You lose a knight, then a bishop, and every time a piece is taken, it walks off the board and stands by the wall, weeping. But you see something that Guivret does not: he loves his queen, a pale lady in a black tabard, and will not risk her. You threaten her again and again, and he moves to save her again and again, until his king is alone. "Checkmate," you say. Guivret stares at the board. Then he laughs, and bows, and every piece on the board, black and white, is free.

failure.body: It is a long game. You lose a knight, then a bishop, then your queen. At last Guivret moves a pawn forward, and says, "Checkmate," softly. You climb down from the high chair and take your place on the board as a white knight. It is three days before another traveller comes, and wins, and sets you free.

resolutions.label: cheat the lord at his own game

success.body: You notice that the black pieces watch their lord's eyes, and move a moment before he speaks. So you watch them too, and see his every plan before he makes it. Then you let him see you glance, once, toward his queen, and while he moves to protect her, you walk a white pawn to the end of the board. He does not notice until it is a queen. "Checkmate," you say. Guivret stares. Everyone is free.

failure.body: You watch the black pieces' eyes, and one of them sees you doing it and tells Guivret. "Cheating," says the lord, delighted, "is a forfeit." You take your place on the board as a white knight.

entries.body:
You come upon a small chapel in a forest clearing, with its door hanging off its hinges and moss growing on the altar. An old hermit is sitting on the chapel steps, drinking from a leather bottle. He looks up at you with red eyes.

"Come to pray?" he says. "Do not bother. Nobody is listening." He takes another drink. "I am Brother Seisyll. I have prayed in this chapel for twenty-two years. Every day, three times a day. And last winter the plague came to the village below and took my sister's children, all four, and I prayed and prayed, and they died anyway." He laughs. "So I stopped. And last night, my old abbot came and stood at the end of my bed. He has been dead nine years. He did not say anything. He only looked at me." He shivers. "He is coming back tonight. I know he is."

In the chapel, behind the moss-covered altar, you see the glint of a silver chalice and candlesticks.

responses.label: You may keep vigil with Brother Seisyll through the night.
You may take the chapel's silver while the hermit is drinking.

entries.body: At midnight, the crack in the hillside widens into a doorway, and a warm golden light spills out, and the sound of hammering, very far below. Dwyfan grips your hand. "Stay close," he says.

resolutions.label: follow the dwarf into the hollow hill

success.body: You go down a long stair into a hall of silver, where a hundred dwarves are working at forges and none of them has aged a day. When they see Dwyfan, a very old woman at the nearest forge drops her hammer. "You have grown," she says. It is his mother. They weep together. The dwarves under the hill offer him the choice: stay with them, and never grow older, or go back and take one of them with him. He chooses to go back, and takes his mother, and she sees the sun for the first time in a hundred years. She gives you a silver ring from the forge.

failure.body: You go down a long stair into a hall of silver, where dwarves are working at forges. They do not see you. You call to them, and they do not hear. Dwyfan walks among them, calling their names, and they walk through him as though he were smoke. At dawn, you are thrown out onto the hillside, and the crack closes. Dwyfan sits on his stone and does not move.

resolutions.label: go into the hill with a blessed candle

success.body: You light a candle blessed at Easter and carry it before you down the long stair. The golden light dims around it, and the hammering stops, and the dwarves at their forges turn and see you, which Dwyfan says they never do. An old woman at the nearest forge drops her hammer. "You have grown," she says. It is his mother. The candle lets her walk out with him, into the sun she has not seen for a hundred years.

failure.body: You light a blessed candle and carry it down the stair, and the golden light hisses and goes out, and so does the doorway. You are thrown back onto the hillside, and the crack closes. Dwyfan sits on his stone and does not move.

entries.body: "It belongs to the monks," you say, gently. "Come. I will speak for you." Wat's face falls, but he nods.

resolutions.label: plead for Wat before the abbot of Saint Dyfrig's

success.body: At the abbey, you lay the box before the abbot and tell him everything: the boy, the blind woman, the baby. The abbot listens, stony-faced. Then he opens the box and looks at the finger for a long time. "In forty years in its shrine," he says slowly, "it has never healed anyone." He closes the box. He gives it back to Wat. "Take him out to the roads," he tells you, "and bring him back at Easter, and tell me what the saint has done." Wat walks out of the abbey weeping, with the lame boy running beside him.

failure.body: At the abbey, you lay the box before the abbot and tell him everything. The abbot listens, stony-faced, and then has Wat put in chains. "A thief is a thief," he says, "and a saint is not a pedlar." The finger goes back into its gold shrine. The lame boy sits outside the abbey gate for three days, waiting, and then limps away.

resolutions.label: let the saint show himself before the abbot

success.body: At the abbey, you do not argue. You ask the abbot only to watch. Then you bring in the lame boy, who has followed you, and Wat lays the finger on the boy's crutch, and prays. The boy stands up without it. The abbot sits down very suddenly. After a long silence, he gives the box back to Wat. "Take him out to the roads," he says, "and bring him back at Easter." Wat walks out of the abbey weeping.

failure.body: At the abbey, you ask the abbot to watch, and Wat lays the finger on the lame boy's crutch, and prays, and nothing happens at all. The abbot has Wat put in chains. The saint, it seems, does not perform for abbots.

entries.body:
You put your ear to the stone. "Ah," says Merlin. "The one who knew the riddle. Good. Listen."

He tells you: about the adder, and the sword, and the parley. He tells you where to stand, so that you can reach the knight who draws his blade. "It will not stop the battle," he says. "I do not think anything will. But you might. It is the one thing I cannot see. You." He is quiet a moment. "Tell Nimue I am not angry. I never was." You tell her. She weeps. The stone is silent after that.

notes: Lose Story Token #3

entries.body:
You come to a village where every door is marked with a cross in white chalk. The street is empty. From a barn at the end of it comes the sound of coughing, many voices, and a single voice praying above them.

A hermit comes out of the barn, a tall, gaunt man with his sleeves rolled up and a cloth tied over his face. "Do not come in," he says. "It is the plague. I am Father Mabon. I came down from my hermitage when it started. The priest fled. The lord fled." He pulls down the cloth. His face is grey with exhaustion. "There are thirty sick in there. Eleven dead in the churchyard, and nobody to bury them. And no physician within three days' ride." He looks at you. "I am not asking you to come in. I am only telling you, so that somebody knows."

responses.label: You may stay and nurse the sick with Father Mabon.
You may ride for a physician as fast as you can.
You may bury the dead so that the sickness spreads no further.

entries.body:
The Green Knight comes out of the mound, with his axe on his shoulder. He looks at you, and his green face breaks into a slow smile. "A year and a day," he says. "Exactly. You are the first to come on the day." He points to a stone by the stream. "Kneel."

You kneel. You feel the axe lift above you. It comes down.

resolutions.label: take the Green Knight's return blow without flinching

notes: Lose Story Token #14

success.body: It comes down, and you do not flinch, and it stops a finger's width from your neck. It comes down again, and you do not flinch, and it stops again. The third time, it nicks the skin of your neck, and a drop of blood falls on the snow. "That," says the Green Knight, "is for keeping your word. The other two are for not flinching." He laughs, and it is like a whole forest laughing. He takes the green sash from his own waist and ties it round yours. "Wear it," he says. "Remember."

notes: Lose Story Token #14

failure.body: It comes down, and you flinch. The axe stops. "You flinched," says the Green Knight, sorrowfully. He lifts it again, and this time, it cuts you, not deeply, but it cuts. "Now we are even," he says. "Go home." You ride away with a scar that never quite heals.

entries.body: You thank the king for his offer and ride out of the camp slowly, counting banners as you go. Once the camp is behind you, you turn for Camelot and put your spurs in.

resolutions.label: ride through the night to reach Arthur before Lot moves

success.body: You ride all night and half the next day, change horses twice, and come into Camelot on a lathered mount as the watch is changing. Arthur hears you out standing, with Merlin at his shoulder. "Eleven banners," he says. "Merlin said ten." Merlin shrugs. "I said ten would come," he says. "I did not say the eleventh would stay." Arthur gives you a new horse and a place at his council fire.

failure.body: You ride all night, but your horse goes lame on the Roman road, and you must walk the last ten miles leading it. By the time you reach Camelot, Arthur has already heard from his own scouts. "You meant well," says Sir Kay, eyeing your boots. "Your horse did not." You spend two days in the stables nursing it back to health.

resolutions.label: count every man and horse in the camp before you leave

success.body: You ride out slowly, stopping to water your horse and chat with the cooks. By the time you leave, you know how many men Lot has, how much bread they eat, and which two kings are quarrelling over the best pasture. Arthur hears it all in silence, then turns to his captains. "Two kings who quarrel over grass," he says, "will run when the grass is on fire." He grips your hand. "You have saved more lives than you know."

failure.body: You ride out slowly, stopping to water your horse and chat with the cooks. One of the cooks, it turns out, is Lot's cousin. By the time you are clear of the camp, there are ten horsemen following you. You shake them off in a wood, but you have learned nothing that Arthur's scouts will not tell him first.

entries.body: You sit down beside the woman. "Bring me a dozen eggs," you say, "and a pot of water, and put it on the fire where the child can see." She looks at you strangely, but she does it.

resolutions.label: trick the changeling into giving itself away

success.body: You crack the eggs, one by one, and throw away the yolks, and set the empty shells in the pot to boil, very carefully, as though you were brewing something important. The changeling watches. At last it sits up in its cradle and says, in a cracked old voice, "I have seen the acorn before the oak, and the egg before the hen, but I have never seen a fool brew in eggshells." Then it leaps out of the cradle and up the chimney with a shriek. There is a cry at the door. On the step lies a fat, rosy baby, fast asleep.

failure.body: You crack the eggs and set the shells to boil. The changeling watches, and then it laughs, and says, "That old trick? My grandmother told me about that one." It lies down again and screams. The mother looks at you, and then at the fire, and at the shovel.

entries.body: "My lord," you ask, "why does the spear bleed?" The old king closes his eyes. The hall goes quiet.

resolutions.label: ask about the spear and hear its story

success.body: "It is the spear of Longinus," the old king says, "which pierced the side of the Lord on the cross. A knight struck me with it long ago, in rage, and made this land a desert." He opens his eyes. "You asked about the spear. That is nearly the right question. Nearly." He smiles at you, sadly. "Someone will ask the right one. Perhaps he will have heard of you, and how close you came." In the morning, the castle is gone. But in the field of dust, where it stood, there is a single green shoot.

failure.body: "My lord," you ask, "why does the spear bleed?" The old king looks at you with great weariness. "That is not the question," he says. In the morning, the castle is gone.

resolutions.label: ask why the king bleeds, and not the spear

success.body: You do not ask about the spear. You kneel by the old king's litter and ask, with all courtesy, what ails him, and whether you may help. The old king closes his eyes, and tears run down his face. "That is nearer," he says. "That is much nearer." He tells you of the stroke, and the wound, and the waste, and at the end, he blesses you. In the morning, the castle is gone. But where it stood, there is a single green shoot.

failure.body: You kneel by the old king and ask what ails him. "You can see what ails me," he says wearily. In the morning, the castle is gone.

entries.body: You dismount and walk up to the giant baby, which stops crying to stare at you. You have calmed crying children before, though none of them were the size of a barn.

resolutions.label: soothe the giant baby until its mother comes

success.body: You sing to it. You sing every lullaby you know, very loudly, and when you run out, you sing marching songs, and drinking songs, and hymns. The baby listens, entranced, with its great thumb in its mouth. The villagers creep out of the church and join in. By the time the mother comes striding over the hill, the whole village is sitting round the baby in the ruins, singing, and the baby is asleep. The giantess weeps. She lifts it up without waking it, and before she goes, she rebuilds the mill in an afternoon.

failure.body: You sing to it. The baby listens for a moment, then opens its mouth and bellows along, completely out of tune, so loudly that every remaining window in the village breaks. By the time the mother arrives, you are deaf in one ear.

resolutions.label: feed it honey and milk from every farm in the valley

success.body: You send the villagers running to every farm for milk and honey, and pour them into the horse trough, and push it toward the giant baby. It stops crying and sniffs. Then it drinks the lot, and falls asleep in the ruins of the mill with honey on its face. When its mother comes striding over the hill, she finds the whole village tiptoeing round a sleeping baby. She rebuilds the mill in an afternoon.

failure.body: You pour milk and honey into the horse trough and push it toward the baby. It tips the trough over its own head, and screams, and all the remaining windows break. The mother, when she arrives, assumes you did it on purpose.

entries.body: You sit down beside her. "Then let us read it," you say, "while we can."

resolutions.label: read the Book of the Grail

success.body: You read all night, by candlelight, while the storm howls round the ruins. The Latin is old and strange, but between you, you make it out. It tells where the Grail goes when it leaves a land: not away, but inward, into the hearts of those who wait for it. At dawn, the pages crumble in your hands, one by one. Sister Hild is weeping. "We have it," she says, tapping her head. "Here."

failure.body: You read all night, but the Latin is too old and strange, and you understand very little. At dawn, the pages crumble. Sister Hild says nothing.

resolutions.label: read the book by your own endurance before it crumbles

success.body: The Latin is old and the light is bad and the storm howls through the ruins, but you do not stop. You read all night by one candle, and then by the next, and at dawn, when the pages begin to crumble one by one in your hands, you have read the last of them. It tells where the Grail goes when it leaves a land: inward, into the hearts of those who wait. Sister Hild taps her head. "We have it," she says. "Here."

failure.body: You read all night, but you fall asleep at the darkest hour, and when you wake, the pages have crumbled, and you have read only half.

entries.body: You get down from your horse and kneel on the other side of the stream. "Tell me," you say. The washer looks at you with her rain-coloured eyes.

resolutions.label: face the omen with a steady heart

success.body: "Not yet," she says. "Not for a long while. But I like to begin early. Some of them need time." She wrings out your helm and holds it out to you across the water. "The second washing will be in a place of great holiness. The third, on a plain, in the rain." You take the helm. It is dry. She smiles, which is terrible and kind at once. "You did not run," she says. "Most of them run. That is worth something." When the mist lifts, she is gone, and your armour is as clean as the day it was made.

failure.body: "Soon," she says, and goes on washing. You cannot make her say more. You ride away with the red water in your mind, and it does not leave you for many days.

resolutions.label: ask the washer the one question she must answer truly

success.body: You remember what the old stories say: the washer at the ford must answer one question truly, and only one. You do not ask when you will die. You ask whose armour she will wash next. She looks up, surprised, and tells you: a knight you know, who is riding to a joust tomorrow on a lame horse. You ride through the night to warn him. He does not joust. You never see the washer again.

failure.body: You ask her whose armour she will wash next. She holds up your own helm again. "The same," she says. "The same, and the same." You ride away with her answer in your ears.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride into the ambush.

resolutions.label: drive the Saxons from the supply train

success.body: You ride through them, and the carters, seeing a knight, take heart and come with you. The Saxons were expecting carters, not knights. They fall back into the trees. You chase them for a hundred yards, and come back, and the carters are clearing the tree. By nightfall, the bread is in the old king's camp. Men who have not eaten in three days weep over their loaves.

failure.body: You ride through them, but there are too many. You are pulled from your horse. The carters flee. The Saxons burn the bread.

entries.body: You set down your cup. "I do not drink to traitors," you say. The hall goes silent.

resolutions.label: shame the marsh-lords before their own people

success.body: You speak to them of the oath at Pentecost, which some of them swore, and of their fathers, who fought beside the old king at Badon. You speak to their servants, who are listening at the doors. At the end, two of the youngest lords stand up and leave the hall. They take their men to the old king. The marsh-lord has you thrown out. But two is two.

failure.body: You speak to them of oaths. The marsh-lord laughs and has you thrown in his cellar. You escape three days later, through a drain.

resolutions.label: challenge the marsh-lord to defend his toast with steel

success.body: You set down your cup. "I do not drink to traitors," you say, "and I will prove it on any man here who says Mordred is king." The marsh-lord, who is fat, looks round for a champion. His guests look at their cups. Nobody stands. At last, two of the youngest lords get up and leave the hall, and take their men to the old king. The marsh-lord has you thrown out. But two is two.

failure.body: You challenge any man there to fight you. The marsh-lord's nephew accepts, and he is very large and very sober. You are thrown out of the hall.

entries.body: "I accept," you say gravely. You dismount, since the boy has no horse, and take a stick from the hedge. The mother puts her hands over her face. The boy beams.

resolutions.label: fight the boy so that he learns something

success.body: You fight him with the stick, slowly and carefully, and you let him land a few blows and then you show him what he did wrong. After an hour, he is panting and sweating and learning faster than any squire you have seen. "You are not a knight," you tell him at last, "not yet. But you could be." The boy takes the pot off his head. His eyes are clear. "I know," he says quietly. "I only wanted someone to see." You take him to the castle and speak for him. They take him back.

failure.body: You fight him with the stick, gently, but the boy fights like a demon, and the broom catches you across the knuckles, and without thinking you strike back too hard. He goes down in the road with a bloody nose and bursts into tears like the child he is. His mother takes him home without a word. You resolve to be gentler with fools.

resolutions.label: give the boy a mock knighting that sets him right

success.body: You kneel in the road and ask him to kneel too. Then, very gravely, you knight him with his own broom, and make him swear the oath of the Round Table, every word: no outrage, mercy to all who ask, and never to fight in a wrongful quarrel.
