"Challenging cows," you say, "is a wrongful quarrel." The boy looks at the broom, and at you, and laughs, and the madness goes out of his face. His mother kisses your hands.

failure.body: You kneel in the road and knight him with his own broom. Unfortunately, this convinces him completely. He rides off on a donkey to challenge the Sheriff of Chester. His mother looks at you with great sorrow.

entries.body: You pull the peasant up behind your saddle. "Herne," you say, "this man is under my protection." Herne's eyes narrow. The riders in the clouds stop.

resolutions.label: ward the peasant against the hunt

success.body: You draw your sword and hold it up like a cross, and draw a circle round you and the peasant in the heather with the point. "Iron and ash," you say, remembering what an old woman once told you. Herne laughs, but his hounds will not cross the circle. They whine and circle. At last, Herne blows his horn, and the whole hunt goes up into the clouds and away. The peasant weeps with relief. "I will put the branch back," he says. "I will never cut an oak again." You believe him.

failure.body: You draw a circle round you and the peasant in the heather with the point of your sword. Herne looks at it and laughs. "That," he says, "is for boggarts." His hounds come over the circle and seize the peasant, and he is gone. The last thing you hear is Herne's horn, fading into the clouds.

resolutions.label: offer Herne a better bargain than the man

success.body: "He cut your oak," you say. "What will you do with him? He is too thin to be good sport. I will give you better." Herne tilts his antlered head, interested. You tell him of a black boar in the forest to the north, which has killed three knights and ravaged a dozen farms. Herne's eyes gleam. "A better quarry," he says. He sounds his horn, and the whole hunt goes streaming away over the trees to the north. The peasant kisses your hand. Next week, the boar is found torn to pieces, and the farmers rejoice.

failure.body: "He cut your oak," you say. "I will give you better sport." Herne tilts his head. "You are right," he says. "I will take you." He blows his horn, and you ride with the hunt all night, whether you want to or not. At dawn, you find yourself on the heath, with the peasant beside you, both of you covered in frost and shaking.

entries.body: You ride past the dwarf and bar the knight's way. "Your dwarf," you say, "has struck me. Answer for it." The knight looks at you at last, bored. "My dwarf," he says, "strikes whom he pleases. That is what he is for."

resolutions.label: joust with the Knight of the Sparrowhawk

success.body: You meet him on the road with lances. He is strong and arrogant, and on the third pass you knock him out of the saddle. He lies in the dust. You make him swear to take his lady to Camelot and beg the queen's pardon for his dwarf's insolence, which, it turns out, he has been doing to every knight on this road for a month. The lady, as he rides away, turns in her saddle and mouths *thank you*. The dwarf goes with them, silent, whipless.

failure.body: You meet him on the road with lances. On the first pass, he knocks you out of the saddle. As you lie in the dust, the dwarf rides over and lashes you across the back, cackling. The knight rides on without looking round.

entries.body: You nod to the lady and ride back into the wood, as though you are leaving. At dusk you come back on foot, keeping to the shadows under the hanged knights.

resolutions.label: creep past the Red Knight's watch into the castle

success.body: You slip past the red pavilion, where the Red Knight lies snoring as loud as seven men, and climb the ivy on the castle's north wall. Lyonesse is waiting at her window. She comes down the ivy after you, in her shift, with her skirts tied up, and together you creep back through the wood. At dawn, when the Red Knight is as weak as one man, you come back with a dozen knights from the next town. He does not put up much of a fight.

failure.body: You slip past the red pavilion and climb the ivy on the castle's north wall. Halfway up, the ivy tears away from the stones, and you fall into the moat with a tremendous splash. When you come up, the Red Knight is standing on the bank with a lantern. He is smiling.

entries.body: You ride at the Saxon with your sword up. He looses his arrow wild and runs. Then you kneel beside the beast.

resolutions.label: tend the ancient beast's wound

success.body: You draw out the arrow and pack the wound with moss and bind it. The beast watches you with eyes that seem very old and very tired. When you are done, it rises, and nuzzles your hand with its serpent's head, and walks away into the forest, and you hear, fading behind it, the baying of its hounds. You wonder who will chase it now.

failure.body: You draw out the arrow, but the wound is deep, and the beast is very old. It lays its head down on the leaves and sighs, and the baying in its belly goes quiet. You sit beside it until dark.

resolutions.label: pray over the ancient beast as it lies

success.body: You kneel beside it in the leaves and pray, not for yourself, but for it, and for the foolish old king who chased it all his life. It seems a strange thing to do, and you do it anyway. After a while, the beast gets up. The wound is still there, but it no longer bleeds. It nuzzles your hand with its serpent's head and walks away into the forest, and you hear, fading behind it, the baying of its hounds.

failure.body: You kneel beside it and pray, and it lays its head down on the leaves and sighs, and the baying in its belly goes quiet. You sit beside it until dark.

entries.body: You spur your horse after the hound. Kay whoops with delight. "That's it! Harder!" The hare runs like the wind, doubling and jinking through the long grass.

resolutions.label: run the enchanted hare down

success.body: You ride the hare down in a corner of the meadow, and the hound's teeth close on it. There is a flash, and a smell of burning grass, and the hound yelps and springs away. A naked boy is lying in the meadow, gasping and weeping and alive. Kay throws him a cloak. "Well," he says, sounding faintly disappointed. "Squire it is." He gives you his second-best hunting knife. Madoc does not look at you once, all the way home.

failure.body: You chase the hare across three meadows, over a wall and into a wood, where you lose it and your way at the same time. By the time you find the road again, Kay has given up and gone home. You never learn whether Madoc became a boy again. Sometimes, when you see a hare, you wonder.

resolutions.label: outride the hounds and catch the hare yourself

success.body: You spur past Kay and the hound, lean from the saddle, and scoop the hare up by the scruff at full gallop. There is a flash, a smell of burning grass, and you are holding a naked, sobbing boy by the collar. Kay rides up, disappointed and relieved in equal parts. "Squire it is," he says, and throws Madoc a cloak. The boy clings to your stirrup all the way home.

failure.body: You spur past Kay and lean from the saddle, and miss, and go over your horse's neck into a gorse bush. The hare looks back at you, and you are sure it is laughing. Then it is gone, and Kay is laughing too.

entries.body:
Merlin looks up from his writing, and sees you, and puts down his pen. "Ah," he says. "The one with the riddle. Have you worked it out yet?"

You tell him: *a fool*. He is silent for a long time. The owl on his shoulder stares at you.

"Yes," he says at last. "A fool. An old fool, who knows everything, and cannot stop himself." He sighs. "She is coming, you know. Nimue. I have seen it. I will teach her everything, and she will put me in a stone, and I will let her." He smiles at you, sadly. "Thank you for the answer. It is good to hear someone say it aloud." He gives you a staff of black wood from the corner. "I will not need it where I am going."
"Let us go to the hill," you say. "If they took a hundred years from you, they can give them back." Angharad looks up at the green hill above the village and shivers.

resolutions.label: bargain with the fair folk for Angharad's years

success.body: At twilight, you go up the hill together and knock on the side of it three times with the pommel of your sword. A door opens where there was no door, and a lady in silver comes out. You bargain with her all night: courtesy for courtesy, riddle for riddle. At dawn, the lady laughs and gives in. When you come down the hill, there is a yew tree in the village, and a smithy, and a church with a wooden spire. Angharad runs down the street to her father's house. Nobody but you and she remembers any of it.

failure.body: At twilight, you go up the hill and knock on the side of it three times. A door opens, and a lady in silver comes out, and looks at Angharad with delight. "You came back," she says. "Come and dance." Angharad goes. You try to follow, and the door closes on your hand. When you come down the hill, you do not know how long you were up there. Nobody in the village knows your name.

resolutions.label: shame the fair folk with perfect courtesy

success.body: At twilight you knock on the side of the hill, and when the lady in silver comes out, you bow as you would to a queen. You tell her how beautifully her people dance, and how well they keep time, and how sad it is that they keep poorly the time of others. She laughs, and then she stops laughing. "That was prettily said," she says, "and true." When you come down the hill, there is a yew tree in the village, and a smithy, and Angharad is running to her father's door.

failure.body: You knock on the side of the hill and bow to the lady in silver, and praise her people's dancing. She is delighted. "Then join it," she says. You dance until dawn, and when you come down, the village is no different and you are a month older.

entries.body: You climb the stairs of the inn and find Sir Brastias lying on his back in bed, in his clothes, with a sprig of something grey and dry under his pillow. He is breathing, very slowly.

resolutions.label: find the cause of his sleep and break it

success.body: You pull the sprig from under his pillow and sniff it. It is dried moonwort, bound with a hair. Someone meant him to sleep. You throw it on the fire, and it burns with a green flame, and Sir Brastias sits bolt upright, roaring for his squire. Hywel comes running, white-faced. You leave them to their reckoning. Sir Brastias sends you his best hawk in thanks, and the story of his squire's month of trading is told in taverns for years.

failure.body: You pull the sprig from under his pillow and sniff it. It smells of dust and moonlight, and the next thing you know, you are waking up in the chair beside him with a stiff neck and a week gone. Hywel has sold your horse.

resolutions.label: break the enchantment of sleep with the old words

success.body: You sit by the bed and speak the old words for waking, the ones mothers use on children who will not rise for Mass. On the third repetition, Sir Brastias sneezes. On the fifth, he opens his eyes and demands his breakfast. When he hears what his squire has been doing, his roar can be heard at the far end of the town. He gives you his second-best sword for your trouble.

failure.body: You sit by the bed and speak the old words for waking. Sir Brastias sleeps on. You, however, find you are yawning, and the next thing you know it is morning and Hywel is standing over you, grinning, with your purse.

entries.body: The Lady of the Lake stops, and looks at you, and smiles with real warmth. "Nimue has told me of you," she says. "You helped her, when she was only a girl running from an old man. She is my heir now. I owe you for her." She takes off a necklace of pearls, green and white, and puts it round your neck. "Wear it, and no water will ever drown you, and I will always know where you are." She shows you her whole palace, room by room, and at the end, she lets you hold Excalibur's scabbard for a moment, before she sends it to the young king.
"No, Sir Mordred," you say. "I will not." Mordred's smile does not change. "A pity," he says softly, and closes the door.

resolutions.label: warn the High King of Mordred's plotting

success.body: You go to the High King that same morning, and tell him, carefully, what you heard. The king listens with a heavy face. "Mordred," he says, "is my son." You say nothing. At last he nods. "I will watch," he says. "Thank you." Nothing changes, not yet. But the next time Agravain brings a list to the king, the king reads it, and burns it, in front of him. Mordred, watching, looks across the hall at you, and smiles.

failure.body: You go to the High King and tell him what you heard. The king's face darkens, but not at Mordred. "You spy on my son," he says, "in my own house?" You leave the hall in disgrace.

resolutions.label: find proof in Agravain's book before you speak

success.body: You say nothing that night. But you watch, and at dawn, when Agravain goes to Mass, you slip into the little room and find his book, and copy three pages of it: dates, times, the queen's name, and in the margin, in Mordred's soft hand, *not yet*. You take the copy to the High King. He reads it for a long time. The next time Agravain brings a list, the king burns it in front of him. Mordred, across the hall, smiles at you.

failure.body: You slip into the little room at dawn, and Mordred is sitting at the table with the book, waiting. "Friend," he says. "Looking for something?"

entries.body:
"Tell me about the stones," you say. The old giant opens both eyes, and smiles.

"They were a dance," he says. "Every stone was a giant, once, who danced at a wedding on the sabbath, and was turned to stone for it. We did not mind. We were very old and very tired, and it was a good wedding." He pats the stone behind him. "This is my wife. Rhonwen. She was a beautiful dancer." He tells you the name of every stone, and who they married, and what they danced. It takes all afternoon. At the end, he says, "Now somebody knows," and closes his eyes. When you ride away, you look back, and cannot tell which stone he was.
You draw your sword and run at the serpent. The lion's eyes find you over the serpent's coils.

resolutions.label: strike the serpent and free the lion

notes: Place a Sword & Shield Skill Marker on your Accompanied Status Card

success.body: You hack at the serpent's coils where they are wound round the lion, and the serpent lets go to turn on you, and the lion is free. It springs, and between you, you finish the serpent. The lion stands over it, panting, and looks at you. Then it lies down at your feet and puts its head on your boot. When you ride away, it follows you. It follows you for three days, and on the fourth, it is gone, but you hear its roar, sometimes, when you are in danger.

failure.body: You hack at the serpent's coils, and it lets go of the lion to turn on you, and wraps round you instead. You are crushed until your ribs crack. The lion saves you, which is humiliating.

entries.body:
The sword at your side, the damsel's sword, begins to shake in its scabbard. Across the table, Balin looks at it and goes white. "It is looking for someone," he whispers. Then Garlon, invisible, strikes Balin, and Balin draws and kills him at the table, and King Pellam roars and seizes a sword and comes at Balin, and Balin's sword breaks, and he runs, unarmed, through the castle, looking for a weapon.

Your own sword drags you after him. Through rooms full of treasure, up a stair, into a chamber where a bleeding spear hangs over a silver table. Balin reaches for it.

resolutions.label: stop Balin from striking the Dolorous Stroke

notes: Lose Story Token #19

success.body: You throw yourself between Balin and the spear, and the damsel's sword leaps out of its scabbard of its own accord and strikes Balin's hand aside. The spear stays on the wall. King Pellam, bursting into the room behind you, stops dead. Balin falls to his knees, weeping. The damsel's sword goes quiet in your hand, as if it has done what it was made for. Pellam, very slowly, lowers his own blade. "You have saved my kingdom," he says, "and you do not know how much." It will be many years before you understand what he meant.

failure.body: You throw yourself between Balin and the spear, but the damsel's sword twists in your hand and drags you aside, and Balin seizes the spear and strikes. The castle shakes. Walls fall. When you crawl out of the rubble three days later, the land around Corbenic is dust, and you know that the sword wanted exactly this.

entries.body: "You took a crown that was not yours," you say, "and you were struck down for it. God has already punished you. Is it not pride, to punish yourself further?" Sir Melias turns and looks at you.

resolutions.label: reason with the penitent knight

success.body: He argues. You argue back. You talk of the prodigal son, and of the thief on the cross, and of what the Grail is for, if not for mercy. By sundown, Sir Melias is silent. Then he laughs, a cracked, rusty laugh. "Pride," he says. "Even here. You are right." He lets you bind his back, and eats bread, and in the morning, he rides away with you as far as the edge of the forest, talking about horses.

failure.body: He argues. You argue back. At last he says, "You are very clever. The devil is clever too." He turns back to the rock and picks up his scourge. You leave him there.

resolutions.label: remind him of his duty to the living

success.body: "There are pilgrims on the forest road," you say, "and robbers too, and no knight to guard them, because the one who should is lying in a cave hitting himself." Sir Melias stares at you. "You are on the quest," you say. "The quest is not only for the vessel." He is silent a long time. Then he picks up his sword. In the morning, he rides out onto the forest road. The pilgrims there, you hear later, are very well guarded.

failure.body: You speak of his duty to the living. "The living," he says, "are what I sinned against." He turns back to the rock and picks up his scourge.

entries.body: "Sing to her," you say. "I will deal with the water." Tegid's face lights up. He tunes his lute.

resolutions.label: keep Sir Hector quiet while Tegid courts

success.body: You go up the stair to Sir Hector's room with a jug of wine, and admire his sword, and his horse, and his hair, and ask for his advice on a joust, and by the time he has finished telling you, Tegid has sung four songs, and the Lady Morwen has come down to the door, and taken the primroses, and asked the dwarf to come in. Sir Hector, looking out of the window at last, sees the door close. He looks at you. You shrug. "She likes his songs," you say.

failure.body: You go up the stair to Sir Hector's room with a jug of wine. He sees through you in a moment, pushes you aside, and empties the wine over the window-ledge onto the dwarf below. The Lady Morwen's shutter closes. Tegid goes home soaked through.

resolutions.label: speak up for the dwarf to the lady herself

success.body: You go to the lady's door and ask to speak with her. She comes down, a quiet young woman with ink on her fingers. You tell her that the dwarf under her window is the bravest man in town, since he comes back every night though he knows he will be drenched, and that he writes all his own songs. The Lady Morwen smiles. "I know," she says. "I wanted to see if he would keep coming." She goes out into the street, and takes Tegid's wet hand, and brings him in. Sir Hector's jug falls out of the window.

failure.body: You go to the lady's door and ask to speak with her. The door is opened by her father, who has heard all about the dwarf and does not approve, and who does not approve of knights who meddle, either. You are shown the street.

entries.body: You take the straight road to Hereford, riding through the night, and arrive at the fair a day before the thieves.

resolutions.label: set a trap for the horse-thieves at the fair

success.body: You tell the fair's marshal what is coming, and describe the old breeder's brand, and set yourself up as a buyer with deep pockets. When the thieves arrive with their forty mares, you look them over, and ask the price, and then you ask why the brand has been scratched. The marshal's men close in from every side. The thieves are taken. The mares go home. The old breeder names his best foal for you, which is a mixed compliment, since it bites.

failure.body: You tell the fair's marshal what is coming. But the thieves, hearing of it, sell the mares on the road to a dealer who drives them to Wales. They arrive at the fair with nothing but a cart of onions.

entries.body: You take off your armour and your boots and spit on your hands.

resolutions.label: climb the greasy pole

success.body: You climb, and slide, and climb, and slide, and the crowd roars with every slide. You take off your shirt and wrap it round the pole for grip. On the fifth try, you reach the top, and seize the ham, and slide all the way down with it clutched to your chest. The crowd goes wild. The Midsummer Queen kisses you on the cheek, and everyone cheers. You share the ham with the whole fair.

failure.body: You climb, and slide, and climb, and slide, and on the fifth try, you slide all the way down onto the drunk lord in the green hat. The crowd loves it. You do not get the ham.

resolutions.label: climb the pole with a sailor's knack of rope and knee

success.body: You watch the young men slide, and see what they do wrong. You borrow a rope, loop it round the pole and round your back, and walk up the pole like a man climbing a mast, one knee-hitch at a time. The crowd roars. At the top, you take the ham, and slide down with it. The Midsummer Queen kisses you on the cheek. You share the ham with the whole fair.

failure.body: You loop a rope round the pole and walk up it like a mast, and the rope, which is also greased, slides down with you. The crowd loves it.

entries.body: "The fair folk will pay more than any lord," you say. "Let me carry your terms to the hill." The miller grins. "A sensible knight," he says. "A third for you."

resolutions.label: drive the hardest bargain with the fair folk

success.body: You go to the hill at sunset, and the fair folk come out to meet you, cold and furious. You name the miller's price. They pay it: gold, a great deal of it, that does not turn to leaves in the morning. The miller releases the girl. She looks at you as she goes, with eyes like winter. You take your third and ride on. The miller, you hear, is the richest man in the valley for a year. Then his mill burns down in the night, and nobody ever finds out how.

failure.body: You go to the hill at sunset and name the miller's price. The fair folk look at you for a long time. Then their queen says, "No." When you return to the mill, the cage is empty, the miller is gone, and there are toadstools growing in a ring round the spot where he stood. They seem to be growing round you, too.

entries.body: You sit down by the old king's bed. His people make room for you.

resolutions.label: keep the Fisher King's deathwatch

success.body: You sit with him all night. He tells you, in a whisper, what the vessel looked like, uncovered, the one time he saw it. You do not repeat it to anyone. Near dawn, he takes your hand. "Tell them," he says, "that the waiting was worth it." He dies smiling. The castle bell rings by itself. His people bury him in the chapel, and the next morning, the castle is empty, and the gate is shut, and it will not open for you again. But you carry his words with you.

failure.body: You sit with him all night, but you fall asleep near dawn. When you wake, he is dead, and his people are weeping, and you did not hear what he said at the end.

resolutions.label: ease the old king's passing with herbs of rest

success.body: His people have been giving him wine. You give him willow bark for the pain and valerian for sleep, and sit by his bed and moisten his lips. He sleeps, and wakes, and tells you in a whisper what the vessel looked like, uncovered, the one time he saw it. Near dawn, he takes your hand. "Tell them," he says, "that the waiting was worth it." He dies smiling.

failure.body: You give him willow bark and valerian. He sleeps, and does not wake again to speak. You never hear what he wanted to say at the end.

entries.body: You follow Merlin into the trees and find him on his knees among the mushrooms. "She means to shut you in a cave," you tell him. Merlin sighs and gets up. "I know," he says. "I have always known."

resolutions.label: persuade Merlin to save himself

success.body: "If you know," you say, "why stay?" Merlin is silent for a long time. "Because I am old," he says at last, "and I have seen everything that will happen, and she is the only thing I cannot see." But you talk to him of Arthur, and the realm, and all that is still to be done, and at last he takes off his grey cloak and gives it to you. "Give her this," he says, "and tell her I have gone north." He walks away into the forest. Nimue, when you give her the cloak, is furious. The High King, when he hears, is not.

failure.body: "If you know," you say, "why stay?" Merlin smiles at you, very kindly. "Because it is going to happen," he says, "whatever you say." He goes back to Nimue. You watch them walk away together into the trees. Much later, you hear that the old man has vanished, and that no one in Britain will ever see him again.

resolutions.label: set a counter-ward on the old enchanter

success.body: You gather rowan and thread and salt while Merlin watches, amused, and bind a counter-ward round his wrist. "Nobody has ever warded me," he says. That night, by the pool, Nimue speaks her spell, and the rock beside the pool opens, and nothing happens. Merlin laughs until he coughs. Nimue stares at you with pure fury. Merlin goes home to Camelot. You have made an enemy of the next Lady of the Lake, and a friend of the last wizard.

failure.body: You gather rowan and salt and bind a ward round his wrist. Merlin looks at it and sighs. "Wrong way round," he says gently, and takes it off. That night, the rock opens, and he walks into it. You watch from the trees.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride into the cathedral close, shouting for the townsfolk to follow you.

resolutions.label: rally the town against the looters

success.body: The townsfolk hesitate, and then the blacksmith comes out of his forge with his hammer, and then the butcher with his cleaver, and then everyone. The brigands, who are only thirty and were expecting no resistance, drop the plate and flee. The saint's reliquary is found in the last cart, unopened. The old priest weeps over it. The town rings every bell it has, and the brigands, hearing them from the hills, do not come back.

failure.body: You shout for the townsfolk to follow you, but nobody does. You fight the brigands alone and are driven off. The carts roll away into the hills.

entries.body: You stand before the High King. "My lord," you say, "I go to seek the Grail." The High King closes his eyes.

resolutions.label: ride out on the quest with the king's blessing

success.body: He opens his eyes and looks at you for a long time. Then he stands, and draws his sword, and lays it on your shoulder, as if he were knighting you again. "Go," he says. "Find it. And come back, if you can, and tell me what you saw." You ride out of Camelot at dawn, with the queen watching from her window, and the High King on the walls. You do not find the Grail. But you feel it, sometimes, on the roads, like someone walking beside you.

failure.body: He opens his eyes. "Go, then," he says. "Everyone else has." He does not bless you. You ride out of Camelot with a heavy heart, and the quest is harder for it.

resolutions.label: ride out on the quest in the king's own company, not away from him

success.body: You do not ask his blessing to leave. You ask him to ride with you, for one day, as far as the first crossroads. He stares at you. Then he calls for his horse. You ride out of Camelot together at dawn, the king and one knight, and at the crossroads he draws his sword and lays it on your shoulder. "Find it," he says. "And come back." You do not find the Grail. But you feel it, sometimes, on the roads.

failure.body: You ask him to ride with you as far as the first crossroads. He shakes his head. "I cannot even ride out of my own gate," he says, "without them following."

entries.body:
You come upon an inn at a crossroads where a handsome young man in a peacock-blue doublet is standing on a table, singing to a harp about his own deeds. According to the song, he has slain a dragon, three giants and a wolf the size of a cart-horse.

When the song ends, the villagers do not cheer. An old farmer stands up. "Gwion Silvertongue," he says, "there is a wolf that size in the Nant valley. It has taken nine sheep and a boy. You will go and kill it tonight, as you killed the other one, and we will pay you ten marks." The whole room agrees. Gwion goes very pale.

He finds you in the stable an hour later. "I have never killed anything," he whispers. "I made it all up. It rhymes better." He clutches your arm. "Kill the wolf for me. I will give you the ten marks and put you in a song. Or they will find out. And they will hang me from that sign."

responses.label: You may kill the wolf and let Gwion take the credit.
You may expose Gwion Silvertongue to the villagers.

entries.body:
You come upon a gallows on a hilltop outside a market town, where a woman's body swings in chains in the wind. A lean, bearded man in a hood is sitting beneath it, looking up at her.

"Her name was Alis," he says. "My wife. I am Hob Redcap, an outlaw. You will have heard of me." You have not. "The sheriff could not catch me, so he took her instead, and said she had been hiding me. Which she had, God keep her." He does not weep. "She has hung here three weeks. The sheriff says she will hang until I give myself up, so that everyone can see what comes of loving an outlaw. I cannot cut her down. The gallows is watched from the gatehouse." He looks at you. "They would not stop a knight."

responses.label: You may cut Alis down and help Hob give her a Christian burial.
You may ride to the sheriff and demand that he release her body.

entries.body:
You come upon a thin, ragged man on a donkey, riding hard along a forest track, with a small box of carved bone clutched to his chest. A lame boy on crutches is limping after him, calling, "Master! Master Wat! Wait!"

The man pulls up when he sees you. "Please," he says. "I am Wat, a thief. I stole this from the monks of Saint Dyfrig's last week. It is the saint's finger." He opens the box. Inside, on red silk, lies a small brown bone. "I meant to sell it. But when I touched it, the boy's leg began to straighten." The boy has caught up, and you see that his crutch is under the wrong arm; he is barely leaning on it. "And a blind woman in Hereford saw again. And a baby that was dying lived." Wat's voice cracks. "The saint works for me. For a thief. The monks are after me with a bishop's warrant. They want it back in its gold shrine, where nobody can touch it."

responses.label: You may help Wat return the relic to the monks.
You may help Wat keep the relic and carry it to those who need it.

entries.body:
You come upon a man in the road with his hands clamped over his ears and a purse of green silk tied to his belt. The purse is screaming. It is a high, thin, furious scream, like a hare in a trap, and it does not stop.

"Take it off me!" the man shouts. "Take it off!" He is a sharp-faced fellow with a ferret's grin, or he was, before the screaming started. "I am Dicon, a cutpurse. I cut this from a lady at the Beltane fair. It is never empty. Every time you take a penny out, there is another penny." He pulls out a handful of silver to show you, and the scream goes up to a shriek. "But it screams! Every time I touch it! And there are little people following me. I see them at the edges of my eyes." He is almost weeping. "I cannot sleep. I cannot untie it. Please."

responses.label: You may help Dicon return the purse to its fay owner.
You may take the purse for yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a pair of young lovers on one horse, galloping toward you along a lane, looking back over their shoulders. The man is a handsome rogue in a torn shirt, with a grin as wide as the lane. The girl behind him has a silk gown hitched up to her knees and a sword across her lap.

"Help!" he calls cheerfully, reining in. "Jack Fairweather, highwayman. This is Mererid, the Baron of Powys's daughter. I robbed her coach, and she robbed me back, and we fell in love." He looks back down the lane, where a great cloud of dust is rising. "Her father's men are after us. And her betrothed, who is sixty-three."

"He has gout," says Mererid, "and seven dead wives." She looks at you levelly. "I came of my own will. I will not go back. There is a priest at Llanfair who will marry us if we reach him by noon."

responses.label: You may help the lovers escape to the priest at Llanfair.
You may return Mererid to her father for his reward.

entries.body: Llew smiles. "He was fat," he says. "Very fat. He could not ride a horse, so he had himself carried in a litter, and he used to lean out and talk to everyone in the road. Farmers, beggars, pigs. He knew the names of all the pigs in his kingdom." He laughs. "When the Saxons came, he had himself carried to the front of the army in his litter, and he leaned out and told them a joke. It was a very rude joke about a Saxon and a hedgehog. The Saxons laughed so hard they could not fight, and the next morning they went home." He wipes his eyes. "I wrote that joke. It is the only thing I ever did that mattered. He gave me a gold cup for it." He looks at the tomb. "I sold the cup when the plague came, to buy bread for the town. He would have laughed at that too." He tells you the joke about the hedgehog. It is very rude. You laugh all the way to the next town.

You come upon a man sitting on the steps of a church, rocking back and forth, with his arms around a sack. He is filthy, and there is earth under his fingernails and in his hair. "Cunedda," he whispers. "Cunedda, Cunedda, Cunedda."

The priest comes out and shakes his head. "Rhys the digger," he says. "A grave-robber. He broke into the old king's barrow on the hill three nights ago, the one with the standing stone. He came back like this. He will not let go of the sack, and he will not stop saying the old king's name." The priest lowers his voice. "And at night, something walks from the barrow to the church, and stands at the door, and waits."

Rhys looks up at you with wild eyes. "He wants it back," he says. "He wants it back, and I cannot let go."

responses.label: You may take the grave-goods back to the barrow and return them to the dead king.
You may take the sack from Rhys and keep the treasure for yourself.

entries.body: You ride to the king's side and bow. "Sire," you say, "a fool's jest is a fool's right. Is the king's word so weak that it must be defended with an axe?" The king's eyes narrow.

resolutions.label: persuade the king to show mercy

success.body: You speak of the High King's oath, and of fools who have been kept in every court since Solomon's, and of what will be said in every hall in Britain of a king who beheads his fool for a jest about taxes. The king listens, with his jaw tight. Then he looks at his brother, the treasurer, standing beside the scaffold with a fat purse at his belt, and a doubt comes into his face. "Take the fool down," he says. "And bring me my brother's accounts." The fool kisses your stirrup and weeps. The treasurer, you hear, leaves for Normandy the next week.

failure.body: You speak of the High King's oath, and of fools in every court since Solomon's, and the king listens with his jaw tight. Then he says, "Are you a fool too?" and the crowd laughs, and you have lost them. The axe falls. You ride away with the laughter in your ears.

resolutions.label: remind the king that wrath is a deadly sin

success.body: You speak quietly, so only he can hear. You remind him that there are seven deadly sins, and that his fool has committed none of them, while a king who kills a man for a jest has committed at least one, before witnesses. The king's jaw works. He glances at his confessor, standing nearby, who is nodding. At last he lifts his hand. "Take him down," he says. "And bring me my brother's accounts."

failure.body: You remind the king of the sin of wrath. "And the sin of pride," says the king, "in a knight who lectures his betters." The axe falls. You leave the town with the fool's last grin in your mind.

entries.body:
You come upon a band of outlaws in a wood, crouching in the bracken above a road, with bows strung and faces smeared with mud. Their leader, a grizzled woman with one eye and a man's jerkin, rises when she sees you and puts a finger to her lips.

"Maud o' the Wood," she whispers. "Do not make a sound. The Sheriff of Shrewsbury's tax cart comes this way at noon. Every penny in it was squeezed out of starving folk in the last month. We mean to take it back and give it where it belongs." She looks you up and down. "You have a horse and a sword. We have twelve bows and a grudge. Join us and take a share, or ride on and forget you saw us. But if you warn the sheriff, I will know it was you."

Down the road, you hear the creak of wheels.

responses.label: You may join Maud o' the Wood's ambush of the tax cart.
You may warn the sheriff's escort of the ambush.

entries.body: "Show me how you reckoned it," you say, getting down from your horse. Branwen stares at you, and then she smiles for the first time. "Nobody has ever asked," she says.

resolutions.label: learn the reckoning of the stars

success.body: You spend three nights on the nunnery roof with her, lying on your backs under the sky while she names the stars and shows you how they move. By the end, you can reckon a little yourself. On the last night, she shows you the conjunction. It is there. You check her figures twice. When you ride away, you carry something that you will never be able to forget, and you know a great deal more about the sky than any knight at Camelot.

failure.body: You spend three nights on the nunnery roof, lying on your back while she names the stars. On the second night it rains. On the third night you fall asleep. Branwen is very patient, but when you leave, you know no more than you did, and you have a cold.

resolutions.label: keep the long cold watches on the roof beside her

success.body: The nights are cold, and the roof is hard, and Branwen does not believe in blankets. You lie awake beside her for five nights while she names the stars and marks the hours. On the fifth, near dawn, she shows you the conjunction, rising over the hills exactly where she said. You ride away with frozen feet and a knowledge you will never be able to forget.

failure.body: The nights are cold, and on the second you fall asleep and roll off the edge of the roof into the nunnery's herb garden. The abbess is not pleased. Neither are the herbs.

entries.body:
You come upon an old woman sitting at a table outside a tavern with three walnut shells and a pea. A crowd of drovers stands round her. As you watch, a young drover puts down a penny, points at a shell, and loses. Then another. Then another.

"Mag Pennyfeather," she introduces herself, when the drovers have gone, grumbling. She is wrinkled, merry and sharp-eyed, and her fingers move like spiders. "Sixty years at the shell game. Never lost to an honest man." She pushes the shells toward you. "One game, knight? If you win, I will give you a silver penny. If you lose, you give me your spurs." She grins. "Or if you have the patience, I will teach you. It takes about thirty years."

responses.label: You may play Mag Pennyfeather's shell game.
You may ask Mag Pennyfeather to teach you her tricks.

entries.body:
You come upon a market stall under a striped awning, with a sign reading *EXCALIBUR — The Sword of the King — As Drawn from the Stone*. Behind the stall stands a red-faced man in a green hat, and on the stall lie about thirty swords, all identical, all with the same gilt hilt and paste jewels.

"Roll up!" he calls. "The true Excalibur, only ten shillings! Nobody can draw it but the rightful king of Britain!" He pulls one from its scabbard with a flourish. "Except me. And whoever buys it." The crowd is buying them by the armful. A little boy is clutching one twice his size and grinning. "Master Pym," the stallholder says, winking at you. "You look like a man who knows the value of a sword. Sell them with me in the next town. Knights sell better than pedlars."

responses.label: You may expose Master Pym's false swords to the crowd.
You may join Master Pym and sell his swords in the next town.

entries.body:
You come upon a highwayman sitting on a stone at a crossroads, with a mask pushed up on his forehead and a heavy sack at his feet. He looks exhausted.

"Do not bother to stand and deliver," he says. "I am Black Owain, and I am done robbing. I have been walking for nine days. Every road I take brings me back to this crossroads." He kicks the sack. "Nine days ago, I robbed an old man on this road. A beggar in a grey cloak. He did not fight. He only laughed and said, *Go wherever you like.* I have been trying ever since." He looks up at the signpost. All four arms point to the crossroads.

He opens the sack. It is full of strange things: a crystal ball, a silver star, a book bound in blue leather, a tiny golden harp. "I would give it back," he says, "but I cannot find him."

responses.label: You may help Black Owain return his loot to the old man.
You may try to lead the highwayman out of the enchanted crossroads.

entries.body: "I will fight you," you say. Dinabutius sets down the bell tower, very carefully, back where it was, only slightly crooked. He stands up. And up. And up.

resolutions.label: fight Dinabutius on the hillside

success.body: You do not fight him the way he expects. You run, and let him chase you, and lead him down into the marshes below the town, where he sinks to his knees, and then to his waist. Then you stand on the bank with your sword drawn. "Yield," you say. The giant, stuck in the mud, laughs, and then cries, and then yields. "My brother would have eaten you," he says. "I suppose I knew that." You and the townsfolk dig him out with ropes. He goes home to the mountains, and the town sends him a cart of apples every year.

failure.body: You run, and he chases you, and you lead him toward the marsh. But he knows the marsh better than you. He steps round it, and catches you on the far side, and picks you up. "Champion," he says, and puts you in the bell tower. You spend the night there, until the town pays him a hundred sheep to let you down.

entries.body:
You come upon a crowd around a gallows at a market town, where a young thief stands on the cart with a rope round his neck. He is laughing and joking with the hangman, but when he sees you, his face changes and he calls out.

"You! Knight! A last request!" The sheriff shrugs and lets him speak. "I am Dafydd Quickfingers. I robbed a widow in Ludlow last month. Mistress Anest, who keeps the bakehouse. I took her savings, forty silver marks, all she had." He looks down at you. "They never found it. It is buried under the third ash tree past the mill at Ludlow. She is starving. I did not know she had nothing else." He swallows. "Will you dig it up and take it back to her? It would be something to die with."

The hangman is waiting. The rope is tight.

responses.label: You may promise to return the thief's loot to the widow.
You may promise, then take the silver for yourself.
You may beg the sheriff for Dafydd's life.

entries.body: You look at the drowned knights, and at the Lady, and you cannot bear to choose among them. "Your treasury," you say. The Lady nods, a little sadly.

resolutions.label: choose wisely from the Lady's treasury

success.body: Her treasury is a cave of crystal under the lake, full of things the water has taken: crowns, and swords, and rings, and harps. You walk among them for an hour. At last you choose a skein of grey thread, which the Lady says will take you across any water once. She looks at you with new respect. "Most choose gold," she says. "You chose a road." You keep it.

failure.body: You choose a golden crown, and as you lift it, it crumbles into sand. The Lady looks at you. "The water's things," she says, "do not always like to leave."

resolutions.label: choose by the Lady's advice, with perfect courtesy

success.body: You walk among the crowns and swords and harps, and do not touch any of them. You turn to the Lady and ask her, courteously, what she would have you take. She looks at you with new respect, and puts a skein of grey thread into your hand. "It will take you across any water once," she says. "Most choose gold. You chose to ask." You keep it.

failure.body: You turn to the Lady and ask her what you should take. "Whatever you like," she says, bored. You choose a crown. It crumbles into sand.

entries.body: Ector sits down under the pear tree and pats the grass beside him. "Merlin brought him on a wet night," he says, "wrapped in a cloak. I asked whose he was, and Merlin said, *Yours, now.* So he was." He smiles. "I did not know he was Uther's son. I was not told. I raised him like my own, with Kay, and I beat them both when they needed it, which was often. When they grew, I made Kay my heir, because he was my blood, and I made Arthur his squire. Arthur never once complained." The old man's eyes are wet. "When he drew the sword, I knelt to him. He wept and begged me to get up. He said, *You are my father. You will always be.* And then he made Kay seneschal of all Britain, for my sake." He shakes his head. "Kay was always the clever one. But the boy was the kind one. I did not know, then, which would matter more." The pig trots up and lies down beside him, and he scratches its ears.
You lean down and whisper. "What share for a knight who stands in the armour?" Gwennol's eyes light up. "Half," she says. "You can joust?"

resolutions.label: play the knight of great renown

success.body: For a week, you are the Knight of Great Renown. You joust with every knight who pays the fee, and beat most of them, and those you do not beat, Gwennol's friends deal with behind the tent. The takings are enormous. At the end of the week, Gwennol splits the money fairly and packs up the pavilion. "You are wasted on chivalry," she tells you, and kisses you on the cheek, and is gone before the sheriff arrives.

failure.body: You put on the empty armour and ride out at noon against a young knight with a very determined look. He is Sir Gareth of Orkney, and he unhorses you on the first pass. When he lifts your visor and sees who you are, he is not angry. He is only disappointed, which is much worse. Gwennol has already fled.

resolutions.label: run the false tournament like a campaign

success.body: You take charge. You post Gwennol's friends at the road to turn back anyone who looks like a real champion, set a lookout for the sheriff, and arrange the lists so the sun is always in the challenger's eyes. For a week, the Knight of Great Renown is unbeaten. The takings are enormous. Gwennol splits them fairly, kisses you on the cheek, and is gone before the sheriff arrives.

failure.body: You post lookouts and arrange the lists, but your lookout on the road waves through a young knight with a very determined face. He is Sir Gareth of Orkney. The Knight of Great Renown is unhorsed in front of a large crowd.

entries.body: "Perhaps," you say, "the fair folk would like an apology." Brother Fychan splutters. "Apology? From me? They moved my cell into a river!"

resolutions.label: make peace between the hermit and the fair folk

success.body: You persuade the hermit to leave a bowl of milk and a honeycake on the square of bare earth that night, with a note that says *Sorry about the dancing*. In the morning, the cell is back in its place. The milk and the cake are gone. On the doorstep there is a small bunch of primroses, though it is autumn. Brother Fychan sleeps in his cell every night after that, and says that the dancing, when you get used to it, is really quite beautiful.

failure.body: You persuade the hermit to leave out a bowl of milk and a honeycake, with a note. In the morning, the milk has been drunk, and the cake eaten, and there is a second note in the bowl in a tiny, spiky hand. It says *Not good enough*. The cell is on the roof of the village inn. So is your horse.

resolutions.label: leave the fair folk a gift from the wild woods

success.body: You go into the wood and bring back the things the fair folk love: honey from a wild comb, a crown of meadowsweet, a hazel twig with nine nuts on it. You leave them on the square of bare earth with the hermit's apology. In the morning, the cell is back in its place, and on its doorstep there is a small bunch of primroses, though it is autumn. Brother Fychan sleeps well after that, and says the dancing is really quite beautiful.

failure.body: You go into the wood and bring back honey and meadowsweet and a hazel twig. Unfortunately, the honey is from a hive the fair folk keep themselves. In the morning, the cell is on the roof of the village inn.

entries.body: You look across the water at the Irish flagship, with its king standing at the prow. "Grapple her," you say. "We are going aboard."

resolutions.label: board the Irish flagship

success.body: You lead twenty men across the grappling ropes onto the Irish flagship. You fight your way along the deck to the prow, and the Irish king, a big red-bearded man, meets you with an axe. You fight him, and he yields. When the other Irish ships see their king's banner come down, they turn and flee. The young king sends for you, and embraces you, and the Irish king is sent home under oath.

failure.body: You lead twenty men onto the Irish flagship, but the Irish king's hearth-guard are waiting. You are driven back into the sea. Your crew fish you out.

resolutions.label: hail the Irish king and offer him terms

success.body: You stand in your bow and call across the water to the red-bearded Irish king that he has already lost three ships, and that the young king's fleet is behind you, and that a king who goes home now goes home a king. The Irish king looks at you, and at the fleet, and laughs. He calls his ships off. The young king sends for you afterwards and makes you a gift of the Irish king's own gold cup, sent in token of the truce.

failure.body: You call across the water to the Irish king that he should go home while he is still a king. He laughs, takes a bow from the man beside him, and shoots at you himself. The arrow takes your helmsman in the arm, and the Irish close on you while your ship swings.

entries.body: You look down at the cave, and at the longship, and you have an idea.

resolutions.label: burn the Saxons' longship in the cave

success.body: You wait until the tide is turning and the Saxons are asleep after their feast. Then you climb down the cliff with a torch and a bundle of oiled rags, and set fire to the dragon ship. It goes up like a haystack. The Saxons wake to find their only way home burning. They fight each other over the one small boat, and those who are left surrender to the village the next morning. You are given the dragon's head, which did not burn, and it is nailed over the door of the church for a hundred years.

failure.body: You climb down the cliff with a torch, but a sentry sees you. The Saxons pour out of the cave, and you run for the cliff-path with arrows in the rock around you. That night, they raid the village anyway.

entries.body: You stand in the arch. "Stay," you say. "The old king needs every friend he has."

resolutions.label: persuade the fair folk to aid the old king

success.body: You speak to them of the old king, and his oath, and the Round Table, and all the times their world and his touched. The fay lady at the head of the table listens. At last she rises. "We cannot stay," she says. "But we can give him one thing." She hands you a small silver horn. "When the end comes, blow it. We will send a ship." You carry it to the old king. He takes it, and turns it over in his hands, and smiles. "Avalon," he says softly.

failure.body: You speak to them of the old king, but they only shake their heads. "It is not our war," says the fay lady. "It never was." They leave at dawn.

entries.body: You take the wheel. "Cut the grappling ropes," you shout. "Archers to the stern!"

resolutions.label: command the ship in the sea battle

success.body: You cut the grappling ropes and turn your ship across the wind, and ram the nearest Irish ship amidships. It begins to sink. Your archers pour arrows into the next one. By the end of the afternoon, the Irish fleet is scattered, and your ship has taken two of theirs. The young king, when he hears, gives you command of the ship.

failure.body: You cut the grappling ropes and turn your ship, but you turn too far, and the Irish board you from the other side. It is a long, bloody fight on the deck. You win, barely.

resolutions.label: use the mist and the tide against the Irish

success.body: You see the mist lying on the water to the north and the tide running under it toward the Menai. You turn your ship into the mist, let the Irish follow, and let the tide carry you through the narrow place, which you know and they do not. The Irish ships behind you run onto the sandbanks one after another. By the end of the afternoon, their fleet is scattered. The young king gives you command of your ship.

failure.body: You turn into the mist and let the tide carry you, and you do not know the narrow place as well as you thought. You run onto the sandbank first.

entries.body: You dismount and take your place beside Sir Bedivere in the pass.

resolutions.label: hold the mountain pass until nightfall

success.body: The Saxons come up the pass in waves, and you meet them shoulder to shoulder with Bedivere in the narrow place where only four men can stand abreast. You fight until your arm is numb. By sunset, the pass is full of dead Saxons, and the survivors are falling back. At nightfall, Sir Bedivere lowers his shield. "Enough," he says. "We held." Of his forty men, eighteen are alive. He grips your hand. "The king will hear of this," he says. "If he lives."

failure.body: The Saxons come up the pass in waves. You fight until your arm is numb. An hour before dark, the line breaks. You and Bedivere and a handful of others escape up the mountain.

entries.body: "I am nobody's man," you say, "and the Baron sounds like a thief." Sir Hervi laughs and grips your hand. "Then welcome," he says.

resolutions.label: raid the Baron's rent-carts

success.body: You lie in wait with the outlaws by the forest road, and when the Baron's rent-carts come by, heavy with silver squeezed from his tenants, you spring out of the trees and take them without a blow struck. The guards run. That night, Sir Hervi divides the silver and sends most of it back, in the dark, to the families who paid it. He gives you a fair share. "We are thieves," he says, "but we are honest thieves."

failure.body: You lie in wait by the forest road, but the Baron has hired more guards, and crossbowmen. The ambush goes wrong. You flee through the forest with the Baron's men behind you, and several of the outlaws do not come back.

resolutions.label: ambush the Baron's guards in open fight

success.body: You set the outlaws in two lines on either side of a sunken lane and wait. When the Baron's rent-carts and their twelve guards are between the lines, you blow a horn, and forty ragged farmers rise out of the bracken on both sides. The guards throw down their spears. Sir Hervi sends most of the silver back, in the dark, to the families who paid it. He gives you a fair share.

failure.body: You set the outlaws in two lines and wait, but the Baron has hired crossbowmen. When the horn blows, they are ready. You flee through the forest with the Baron's men behind you.

entries.body: "I will carry it," you say. The ghost tells you what to say, word by word, and makes you repeat it until you have it right. Then he gives you a sign that only his son will understand: a verse of a lullaby that his nurse sang, which he says Arthur's nurse must also have known.

resolutions.label: deliver the message faithfully to the king

success.body: It takes you a month to be admitted to the king alone. When you are, you tell him every word, and sing the verse, badly. Arthur stares at you for a long while. "My nurse sang that," he says. "I had forgotten it." He asks you to tell it again, and then a third time. When you return to the cliff at Tintagel, there is nobody there, only a gull standing where the ghost stood. The king does not speak of it afterwards, but from then on he greets you by name.

failure.body: It takes you a month to be admitted to the king. By then you have told the story to so many stewards and chamberlains that half the court has heard it, and it has grown in the telling. Arthur hears it first from Sir Kay, as a joke. When you are finally brought before him, his face is cold. "My father's shame is mine to know," he says, "not the buttery's." You leave the hall knowing you have served the dead man poorly.

resolutions.label: find the dowager Queen Igraine's convent and deliver it to her

success.body: Queen Igraine lives now in a small convent on the Somerset levels, reached by paths that flood twice a day. You find the one dry way through the reeds and knock at the gate in the late afternoon. The old queen hears the apology with her hands folded. "He was always sorry afterwards," she says. "Tell him I know." When you ride past the cliff at Tintagel a season later, the ghost is gone, and the wind is only the wind.

failure.body: Queen Igraine lives now in a small convent on the Somerset levels, reached by paths that flood twice a day. You take a path that looks dry and spend the night up to your waist in brown water with your horse screaming. By the time you reach the convent, the queen has gone on pilgrimage to Glastonbury, and no one will say when she will return. You leave the message with the portress, who is deaf, and hope.

entries.body: You nod to Maud, and turn your horse, and ride back the way you came. When you are out of sight of the wood, you circle round and come to the road ahead of the cart.

resolutions.label: warn the escort and turn the ambush

success.body: You gallop up to the cart and tell the captain of the escort what is waiting in the wood. He turns the cart round and takes the long road, and the outlaws wait in the bracken all afternoon for a cart that never comes. The sheriff sends you a letter of thanks and a purse of silver. You wonder, later, whose silver it was.

failure.body: You gallop up to the cart and tell the captain of the escort what is waiting in the wood. He does not believe you. He thinks you are one of them, and arrests you. Meanwhile, the outlaws take the cart. Maud, you hear, is very disappointed in you.

resolutions.label: send the escort a false message to take the long road

success.body: You ride ahead, stop a pedlar on the road and pay him to tell the escort that the bridge by the wood is down. He does, with great conviction. The escort turns off by the long road through the hills, and Maud's outlaws wait in the bracken all afternoon for a cart that never comes. Nobody ever learns who sent the pedlar. You feel pleased with yourself for a week.

failure.body: You pay a pedlar to tell the escort that the bridge is down. He tells them. He also tells them who paid him. The escort captain thinks you are one of Maud's men sending them into a trap, and arrests you.

entries.body: You pay your penny and go down the steps into a cave hung with candles. At the far end, a thin monk sits on a stone, and his eyes do glow, faintly, in the dark, like a cat's.

resolutions.label: discern whether the vision is true

success.body: You kneel before him and look for a long time. He does not ask for money. He only says, "It was covered. It is always covered," and weeps. You understand then that his eyes were burned by what he saw and have been glowing ever since, and that the monks upstairs are selling his grief by the penny. You go up and throw the money-box into the street. The pilgrims fall on it. The young priest takes the old monk away to a quiet house, where he can see his light in peace.

failure.body: You kneel before him and look, but you cannot tell whether his eyes glow or whether it is only the candles. He does not speak. You come up the steps no wiser, and a penny poorer.

resolutions.label: kneel and pray beside the shining monk

success.body: You do not look at his eyes. You kneel beside him and pray, and he prays with you, very quietly. After a long time, he says, "It was covered. It is always covered." You understand then that his eyes were burned by what he saw, and that the monks upstairs are selling his grief by the penny. You go up and throw the money-box into the street. The young priest takes the old monk away to a quiet house.

failure.body: You kneel beside him and pray. He does not pray with you. When you rise, the keepers of the shrine are standing behind you with their hands out. "Two pennies," they say, "for praying."

entries.body: "This way, my lord," you say, and turn your horse toward the part of the forest where you know outlaws camp. Clariance follows, humming.

resolutions.label: lead the king into the outlaws' hands and take the chest

success.body: The outlaws are waiting in a hollow. You tell them the king is worth a ransom and the chest is yours. They agree to the split. By nightfall, Clariance is in a cage chattering happily to his captors, and you are riding away with a heavy iron box on your saddle. You never hear what became of the king. Some say he talked the outlaws into joining his army. You try not to think about it.

failure.body: The outlaws are waiting in a hollow. You tell them the king is worth a ransom and the chest is yours. The outlaw chief grins. "Why share?" he asks, and his men close in on you too. By nightfall you and Clariance are in the same cage. The king seems pleased to have company. It is three days before his army finds you both, and by then you have heard every story he knows.

resolutions.label: wait until the king sleeps and ride off with the chest

success.body: You make camp with him in a hollow, and he talks until he falls asleep in the middle of a sentence with his boots still on the wrong feet. You lift the chest onto your saddle and lead your horse away through the bracken, placing every hoof. By dawn you are three valleys away. You hear, later, that his army found him singing in the hollow and did not believe a word about any chest.

failure.body: You make camp in a hollow and wait for him to sleep. He does not sleep. He talks all night, about his army and his wife and his feet, and at dawn his army finds you both. The captain looks at the chest on your saddle and at you. You give it back.

entries.body: You bring your ship into the cove and leap into the surf with your sword drawn, with your crew behind you.

resolutions.label: storm the Saxon longship

success.body: The Saxons are loading, not fighting, and you are among them before they can form a shield-wall. It is a short, fierce fight on the beach and in the surf. When it is over, the Saxons who are left are rowing out of the cove in their empty ship, and the captives are free. Sister Wenna walks up the beach toward you, and, before she says anything, kneels and begins to bind the wounds of the nearest man, who is a Saxon.

failure.body: You leap into the surf, but the Saxons form a shield-wall on the beach, and you are driven back. The longship sails with its captives. Sister Wenna, you hear, heals the Frisians too.

entries.body:
You sit down on the gatehouse beside the old shepherd. "What did Merlin say," you ask, "about the dragons?"

"That the red dragon was Britain," says the shepherd, "and the white dragon was the Saxon, and that they would fight for a long time. The red would be beaten back and back, to the edge of the sea. And then a boar from Cornwall would come and tread the white dragon's neck." He scratches his chin. "That is the young king, they say. The boar from Cornwall. Born at Tintagel." He looks at the pool. "But Merlin also said the boar would die in the end, of a wound from his own blood, and the white dragon would come back." He shrugs. "Merlin says a great many things. Most of them come true."
Brother Seisyll is well into his bottle. The chapel door hangs open. You step inside quietly.

resolutions.label: steal the chapel silver

success.body: You wrap the chalice and the candlesticks in your cloak and walk out past the hermit, who is humming to himself. He does not look up. You are a mile away before you let yourself breathe. That night, at the inn, you dream of a figure in a black habit standing at the end of your bed, looking at you. You sell the silver in the morning, for a very good price, and you do not dream of him again. Mostly.

failure.body: You wrap the chalice in your cloak. When you turn, there is a figure in a black habit standing in the doorway. It is broad daylight. It does not speak. It only looks at you. You put the chalice back on the altar and walk out past it, and it turns its head to watch you all the way to your horse.

entries.body: "What can I do?" you ask. Morgan looks at you, surprised. Then she hands you a coil of black rope.

resolutions.label: prepare the barge for the king's last voyage

success.body: You work with her women all night: rigging the black sails, laying the cushions, lighting the lamps. Morgan works beside you, silent. At dawn, the barge is ready, and she sits down on the shore and puts her face in her hands. You sit beside her. After a while, she says, "Thank you," without looking up. When you leave, she gives you a cup of Avalon water. "For when he falls," she says. "Give it to him. It will not save him. It will help."

failure.body: You work with her women all night, but you tangle the black sails, and Morgan loses her temper and sends you away. From the far shore, you see her standing alone by the barge, weeping.

resolutions.label: sail the black barge's trial voyage yourself

success.body: The barge has no oars and no sail but its black one, and Morgan's women have never sailed it. You take it out onto the lake in the dusk with two of them, and learn how it answers the wind and the lake-current, and bring it back to the shore in the dark, exactly where it must wait. Morgan is standing on the shore. After a long while, she says, "Thank you," without looking at you. She gives you a cup of Avalon water. "For when he falls," she says.

failure.body: You take the barge out onto the lake in the dusk, and the black sail fills, and the barge takes you across the lake and does not come back for a day.

entries.body: "You are a good squire," you tell Piran. "Let us make your master worthy of his letters." You spend the evening with Sir Sagramore, a cheerful, enormous knight who holds his wine cup with both hands.

resolutions.label: teach Sir Sagramore to play the courtly lover by morning

success.body: You teach Sagramore six fine phrases, and how to bow, and how not to eat with his fingers. Piran hides behind the curtain and whispers the rest. When the Lady Elidan arrives, Sagramore kneels and says his six phrases with enormous feeling, and she is enchanted. The wedding is at midsummer. Piran is best man and writes the vows. You never learn whether she found out. You suspect she did, and decided that two men who loved her were better than one.

failure.body: You teach Sagramore six fine phrases and how to bow. When the Lady Elidan arrives, Sagramore kneels and says four of the six phrases, then forgets the rest and asks her if she likes pork. There is a terrible silence. Then Piran, behind the curtain, sneezes. The lady draws back the curtain, looks at the squire with ink on his fingers, and understands everything.

resolutions.label: teach Sir Sagramore to speak from his own heart

success.body: You do not teach him fine phrases. You ask him why he loves her, and make him say it, again and again, until it comes out plainly. It turns out he loves her because she once laughed at his dog, and he thought it the loveliest sound in the world. When the Lady Elidan arrives, he kneels and tells her exactly that. She is silent a moment. Then she laughs, the very same laugh. Piran, behind the curtain, sighs. He writes their wedding vows.

failure.body: You ask him why he loves her. He thinks for a long time and says, "She has very good teeth." You try to work with this. It is no use. When the lady arrives, he tells her about her teeth.

entries.body: You step into the firelight. "He comes with me," you say. Morgan laughs. "Does he?"

resolutions.label: wrest the wounded king from Morgan's power

success.body: Morgan lifts her hand, and the fire flares green, and the marsh around you begins to whisper. You speak the words you know against enchantment, and you take the wounded man by the arm, and you walk him out of the firelight, step by step, while Morgan watches, and the whispering grows fainter. At the edge of the island, she calls after you, almost fondly. "You cannot heal him, you know. Only the Grail can." You know. You take him to a hermit who can at least give him peace.

failure.body: Morgan lifts her hand, and the fire flares green, and you find you cannot move your feet. She takes her time. When she lets you go, it is dawn, and the wounded man is gone, and so is she.

resolutions.label: take him from her by strength of arms

success.body: You do not bandy words with Morgan. You draw, and step between her and the wounded man, and when her fire flares green, you strike at it with iron, and it breaks like glass. Morgan stares at her own hand. You lift the man and walk him out of the firelight. "You cannot heal him, you know," she calls after you. "Only the Grail can." You know. You take him to a hermit who can at least give him peace.

failure.body: You draw and strike at her green fire with iron, and the fire runs up your blade and into your arm. You drop the sword. Morgan laughs, and is gone, and so is the wounded man.

entries.body: You climb up the wall beside the old woman with the pitchfork.

resolutions.label: defend the walls of Winchester

success.body: You show them how to drop stones on the ram's roof, and pour water to put out fire-arrows, and throw grappling hooks to pull down ladders. The townsfolk learn fast. The ram comes up to the Westgate, and its roof is crushed by a millstone the bakers have hauled up the wall. Mordred's men pull back. They try again the next day, and the next, and at the end of a week, they give up and march away. The old woman with the pitchfork kisses you.

failure.body: You show them how to drop stones and pour water, but the ram reaches the Westgate, and the gate breaks. You fight in the street. Winchester falls.

resolutions.label: soften the ground before the gate so the ram founders

success.body: The ground before the Westgate is clay. You get the townsfolk to carry every bucket of water they have to the wall and pour it over, all night, and at dawn the road before the gate is a bog. Mordred's ram comes up to it, sinks to its axles, and stops. The men pushing it are in easy range of the bakers' millstones. Mordred's army marches away after a week of sulking.

failure.body: You pour water over the clay all night, and a hard frost comes at dawn. The road is like iron. The ram comes up to the gate at a trot.

entries.body: You spur your horse into the flood. It swims, snorting, with the current dragging at it.

resolutions.label: rescue the family through the flood

success.body: You reach the cottage and take the children first, two at a time, across your saddle, and swim them to the bank, and go back, and back again. On the last trip, you take the woman, and the man swims beside you holding the cow's rope. The cow, to everyone's surprise, swims beautifully. When they are all on the bank, the woman sits down in the mud and laughs and laughs, because the cow is safe. You laugh too.

failure.body: You reach the cottage and take two of the children, but on the way back, a floating tree strikes your horse, and you are all in the water. You get the children to the bank. By the time you swim back, the cottage roof is gone, and the family with it, all but the cow.

entries.body: "Tell me about this pig," you say. The witch grins. "Fat, spotted, fond of apples," she says. "And it was stolen from a sty with a locked gate."

resolutions.label: track down the real pig-thief

success.body: You go back to the village and look at the sty. The lock is not broken. It has been opened with a key. There is only one key, and it belongs to the reeve's nephew, who has a new spotted pig in his own sty two villages over. You bring the nephew and the pig to the reeve an hour before sunset. The torches are put out. Mother Mallt sends you a jar of salve that heals any cut overnight.

failure.body: You go to the village and look at the sty, and follow a trail of hoofprints out into the bog, and find a spotted pig, which is the wrong pig. By the time you get back, the torches are crossing the causeway.

resolutions.label: question the villagers until the lie shows

success.body: You go from house to house in the village, asking about the pig. Everyone saw it. Everyone heard it. But the reeve's nephew heard it squeal at midnight, and the pig, according to the reeve, was taken at dawn. You ask the nephew how he heard a pig that was still in its sty. He goes white. The pig is found in his cousin's sty two villages over. The torches are put out.

failure.body: You go from house to house asking questions, and by the end, everyone is sure you are the witch's friend, and some of them are sure you are the witch.

entries.body: "It would not be wrong," you say, "if you ride well." Owein wipes his eyes and begins, with your help, to take the armour off the dead knight. It takes a long time, and he weeps the whole while.

resolutions.label: coach Owein for the lists at Winchester

success.body: You spend two days teaching him everything you know about a lance, and he learns fast, because he has been watching his master for years. At Winchester, the knight in Sir Ifor's colours rides five courses and wins four. When Owein kneels to take the prize, a little silver horse, he keeps his visor down. You take him and the dead man home to Ifor's mother. She sees the silver horse, and her son's body, and the boy in her son's armour, and she understands everything. She embraces Owein. "He would have liked that," she says.

failure.body: You spend two days teaching him everything you know about a lance. At Winchester, on the first course, he is thrown, and the helm comes off, and the whole tournament sees a weeping boy in a dead man's armour. The heralds are furious. The story reaches Ifor's mother before you do. She will not let either of you through her door.

resolutions.label: keep Owein's secret from the heralds at Winchester

success.body: The heralds at Winchester want to know why Sir Ifor will not raise his visor. You tell them he has sworn a vow, and invent the details: a lady, a pilgrimage, a very large dragon. They are satisfied. Owein rides well enough not to disgrace the name, wins two courses and loses three, and comes home with his head high. Ifor's mother never learns the truth. Owein, you think, will carry it all his life, and be a better knight for it.

failure.body: The heralds at Winchester want to know why Sir Ifor will not raise his visor. You tell them he has sworn a vow, and invent a lady, a pilgrimage and a dragon. One of the heralds knew Ifor, and knew he could not abide dragons. He asks Owein to raise his visor, and the game is up.

entries.body: You mount your horse and ride to the top of the rise, between the family and the Saxons.

resolutions.label: hold the rise against the Saxon horsemen

success.body: There are eight of them, and one of you, but you have the high ground and the sun behind you, and you ride at them as though there were forty more knights behind the hill. They hesitate. You strike down the leader, and the rest wheel away, shouting, to find easier prey. When you ride back to the hollow, the family is gone, down into the dark. You hear a child's voice, very faint, calling thank you from under the ground.

failure.body: There are eight of them, and one of you. You hold them for a few minutes, long enough, you hope, and then a spear takes your horse, and you are running across the plain with Saxons behind you. You do not know if the family got down in time.

resolutions.label: make the riders think an army waits behind the hill

success.body: You ride along the top of the rise, back and forth, shouting orders to men who are not there, and then you raise your horn and blow the signal for a charge. The Saxon riders look at the rise, and at the smoke of the village behind it, and at the horn, and decide not to find out. They wheel away. When you ride back to the hollow, the family is gone, down into the dark. A child calls thank you from under the ground.

failure.body: You ride back and forth along the rise shouting orders, and the Saxons watch you for a while, and then one of them laughs and points. You are the only one there. They charge.

entries.body:
Before the adder, before anything, a page in red and black comes running through the heather to where you stand, and tugs your sleeve. "Sir," he says. "King Mordred remembers his friends. He asks you to come to his side of the field. He says there is a place for you there, and land, and he will not forget." The page looks at you. "He says, friend."

Across the plain, you see Mordred, at the pavilion, turn his head and look directly at you.

responses.label: You may go over to Mordred's side of the field.
You may send the page back and stand with the old king.

entries.body: You take your sword and sit in the doorway of the church, in the dark.

resolutions.label: catch the relic-thief in the night

success.body: Near midnight, a shadow comes over the abbey bank. You let it come, and let it creep to the church door, and when it reaches for the latch, you take it by the wrist. It is a thin, sharp-faced man with a knife and a bag. He struggles, and then gives up. In the bag, you find three other pages he has stolen from other abbeys. You give him to the abbot, who makes him copy out the whole Gospel of John as penance. It takes him three years. By the end, he has decided to become a monk.

failure.body: Near midnight, you fall asleep in the doorway. In the morning, the page is gone, cut neatly from the book with a knife. The abbot does not reproach you. That is worse.

resolutions.label: set a trap for the thief with the abbey's bells

success.body: You do not sit in the doorway. You tie a cord from the church door to the bell-rope, and set a monk at every gap in the earth bank, and wait. At midnight, the door opens a crack, and the bell booms out over the whole of Meath. The relic-thief runs straight into the arms of three large monks. In his bag are three pages stolen from other abbeys. He copies the Gospel of John as penance, and by the end he wants to be a monk.
