failure.body: You tie a cord from the door to the bell-rope. At midnight, the abbot comes to pray, opens the door, and rings every bell in Meath. The thief, hearing it, does not come. He comes the next night instead.

entries.body: "There is a hermit at the Holy Well of Saint Eluned," you say, "who heals the wits. I will take him there." The mother looks at you with desperate hope. The boy lowers his broom, suspicious.

resolutions.label: coax the boy to the holy well

success.body: You tell the boy that a knight must keep vigil before his first quest, and that the holy well is the place for it. That appeals to him. He kneels at the well all night with his broom across his knees, and the hermit prays over him, and in the morning he is very quiet. "I dreamed," he says, "that the fay queen came and took back her sword, and told me I must earn it." He goes home with his mother, and the next spring, the castle takes him back.

failure.body: You tell the boy he must keep vigil at the holy well. He kneels there all night, but at dawn he jumps up and challenges the hermit to a joust. The hermit, who was once a knight, is not amused. You take the boy home to his mother no better than before.

resolutions.label: go back to the faerie hill and undo what was done

success.body: You take the boy back to the faerie hill at midsummer twilight and make him lie down where he slept before. You sit beside him and speak to the hill, politely, and ask the fay queen to take back her gift. At midnight, a cold wind blows over the grass, and the boy wakes, and sits up, and asks why he is lying in the dark on a hill with a knight. He remembers nothing of the last month. He is a little disappointed to hear about the cows.

failure.body: You take the boy back to the faerie hill at twilight and speak to the hill, politely. At midnight, the fay queen answers you. She says the boy is her knight, and you have no right to him. When you wake in the morning, you are wearing a pot on your head, and it is very hard to take off.

entries.body: You cross the bridge with your sword sheathed, and ask the brothers politely if you may speak to the maidens. The brothers are so surprised that they let you in.

resolutions.label: broker a peace between the brothers and the maidens

success.body: The maidens, led by a woman called Lady Eleri, do not want to leave. They want food, and the right to come and go, and new books. The brothers want not to be laughed at in Wales. You spend a day going back and forth. By the end, the castle is renamed the College of Maidens, the brothers are its porters, and there is a market every Tuesday at the bridge-end. Lady Eleri gives you a book of your own.

failure.body: You spend a day going back and forth between the brothers and the maidens, and by the end, they are all agreed on one thing: that you are a busybody. They put you out over the bridge.

resolutions.label: find in the castle library the old charter of the college

success.body: While the brothers and the maidens argue, you go into the famous library, and after an hour among the shelves, you find it: the old duke's charter, which founds the castle as a house of learning for maidens, with seven brothers as its guardians. Nobody has read it in thirty years. You read it aloud in the hall. The brothers are astonished to find they are porters. The maidens are delighted. Lady Eleri gives you a book of your own.

failure.body: You search the library for an hour and find a great many sermons and a cookery book. By the time you come out, the brothers and the maidens have agreed on one thing: that you are a busybody.

entries.body: "Bring us alongside that boat," you say. Your captain swings the wheel.

resolutions.label: seize Mordred's gold before it reaches the Saxons

success.body: You bring your ship down on the rowing boat before it can reach the Saxon, and leap down into it, and the man in the fine cloak throws up his hands. The chest is full of gold. The Saxon longship comes about to fight, but your captain has the wind, and you are away up the coast before they can catch you. You bring the gold to the old king. He uses it to pay his own army, which has not been paid in three months. You have never seen soldiers so happy.

failure.body: You bring your ship down on the rowing boat, but the Saxon longship is faster than you thought. It comes between you, and its archers drive you off. The gold goes to the Saxon king.

resolutions.label: cut the rowing boat off by reading the tide

success.body: You do not chase the rowing boat. You watch which way the ebb is running and put your ship across the tide where the boat must pass to reach the longship. The man in the fine cloak is rowing against the current, and you are waiting with the current behind you. He throws up his hands. The chest is full of gold. You bring it to the old king, who pays his army with it.

failure.body: You put your ship across the tide to cut the boat off, and misjudge the ebb. The boat passes behind you, and the longship takes the gold aboard.

entries.body: You dismount and step onto the first plank. It sags. The lady watches you, smiling.

resolutions.label: cross the causeway to the Lady of the Marsh

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You do not step where the planks look strongest. You step where the reeds grow thickest beneath them, because reeds grow on firmer ground. Plank by plank, you cross. At the door, the Lady of the Marsh takes your hand, and her fingers are cool as water. "You are the first," she says, "to look down instead of forward." She does not make you marry her. She says she has changed her mind about husbands. But she gives you a ring of marsh-gold and says you may visit whenever you like.

failure.body: You step on the fifth plank, and it breaks, and you go into the bog up to your chest. The lady watches, smiling. It takes you all night to struggle free, and when you do, the castle is gone.

entries.body: You say nothing. The procession passes. You eat. It would be discourteous, you think, to ask a king about his troubles at his own table.

resolutions.label: keep a knight's perfect courtesy

success.body: You keep your silence, and the old king watches you all evening, and at the end of the feast, he thanks you for your courtesy with great sorrow. In the morning, you wake in a field of dust, and the castle is gone. You understand, too late, what you should have done. But the old king has left you a gift beside your pillow: a silver dish, very plain, with a drop of red wine in the bottom that never dries.

failure.body: You keep your silence. In the morning, you wake in a field of dust, and the castle is gone, and a hermit on the road tells you that you have failed the greatest test of your life, and that you will not be given it again.

resolutions.label: keep silence, but watch the vessel with your whole heart

success.body: You do not speak. But you do not eat, either. You watch the covered vessel pass with your whole heart, praying, and when it has gone, you rise and bow, very low, to the old king on his litter, as you would to the altar. He looks at you for a long time. In the morning, you wake in a field of dust, and the castle is gone. Beside your pillow is a silver dish with a drop of red wine in the bottom that never dries.

failure.body: You watch the vessel pass and pray. In the morning, you wake in a field of dust. A hermit on the road tells you that you have failed the greatest test of your life. You did not know it was a test.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride out of the dark, into the lanterns, shouting.

resolutions.label: fall upon Mordred's men in the storm

success.body: The storm is on your side. They cannot see how many you are, and you shout as though you were fifty. The officer turns and you cut him down, and the soldiers break and run into the dark. You cut the prisoners loose. Three are already dead in the pool. Twelve are alive. They gather round you, shivering, and one of them, a young knight with a bloody face, grips your hand. "We will not forget," he says.

failure.body: You ride out of the dark into the lanterns, and the soldiers turn, and there are ten of them, and they are not frightened. You are driven back into the marsh. Behind you, the screaming goes on.

entries.body: "We will plant a new thorn," you say. "Where the old one stood." The farmer looks at you doubtfully. "Will that be enough?"

resolutions.label: plant and tend a new fairy thorn

success.body: You find a young hawthorn in the hedge at the edge of the wood and dig it up with its roots whole, and carry it to the stump, and plant it in the old tree's place. You water it from the holy well, and tie a red ribbon on it, and leave milk and bread at its foot. You stay three nights to see it take. On the third night, you see a tall man in a cloak of leaves standing beside it, touching its leaves. He looks at you, and nods, once. The next morning, the farmer's last cow gets up and begins to graze.

failure.body: You find a young hawthorn and plant it in the old tree's place, but you damage the roots digging it up, and by the third day it is dead. That night, you see a tall man in a cloak of leaves looking at it, and then at you. You leave the farm in the morning, and your luck leaves with you.

entries.body: "What lies ahead for Britain?" you ask. The old giant is silent so long that you think he has fallen asleep. Then he says, "Put your hand on the stone."

resolutions.label: open your mind to the stone's vision

success.body: You lay your hand on the stone, and it is warm. You see the young king, and the table, and the light in the hall. You see a queen and a fire. You see a plain in the west, and the ravens. You see a barge on a lake. And then, a long way off, you see the stones still standing, and small people walking among them in strange clothes, touching them, as you are. When you take your hand away, the old giant is watching you. "It all goes on," he says. "That is the thing to know. It all goes on."

failure.body: You lay your hand on the stone, and see too much, too fast: fire and ravens and a king's face in the rain. You pull your hand away with a cry. The old giant looks at you with pity. "Small ones," he says. "Always in such a hurry."

entries.body: "The squire was found with the cup in his hand," you say. "The law is clear." Iolo's knees give way. The widow bows her head.

resolutions.label: pronounce the sentence as a knight should

success.body: You do not make a speech. You ask the squire if he wishes to confess, and he says again that he did not do it. You ask the widow if she has anything to add, and she says no. You give the sentence, as calmly as you can. The squire hangs. The widow thanks you and gives you a purse of gold "for your trouble". It is only later, at the next inn, that you hear she has married Sir Morien's steward, three days after the funeral.

failure.body: You give the sentence. The squire hangs. As they cut him down, a tavern-girl runs up the road, screaming that she saw the widow in the kitchen last night with a little bottle. The widow's litter is already a mile away. The crowd looks at you. You will not forget their faces.

entries.body: You leave the hermit praying and wade out into the bog, following the flow of the water. It is running into the island from somewhere.

resolutions.label: find the blocked outflow and drain the flood

success.body: A mile across the bog, you find it: an old stone sluice, built by the monks who drained the bog a hundred years ago, blocked by a dead ox and a year of reeds. You spend the afternoon dragging the ox free. When it moves, the water rushes through with a roar. By the time you get back to the island, the water in the cave is down to the hermit's knees, and he is weeping and thanking God. You do not mention the ox. He would be disappointed.

failure.body: You wade out into the bog following the flow of the water, and lose your footing, and go under. You come up covered in weed and leeches, far from the island. By the time you find your way back, it is dark, and the hermit is up to his neck.

entries.body: You stand in the cathedral door with your sword drawn. The Earl's huntsmen, a dozen hard men with nets and spears, stop on the steps.

resolutions.label: stand guard over the unicorn through the night

success.body: You close the great doors and bar them, and set the canons to guard the side-doors with candlesticks, and stand at the main door yourself all night. The huntsmen try twice to break in and are driven back. At dawn, the unicorn rises, walks past you out into the square and through the silent crowd, and away toward the hills. Nobody moves to stop it. Where it lay, on the altar step, there is a single white flower. The bishop puts it in a reliquary.

failure.body: You close the great doors and bar them, but the huntsmen come in through the crypt. By the time you reach the altar, they have their nets over the unicorn. It screams. You fight them, and it breaks free and runs, bleeding, into the night. You do not know if it lives.

resolutions.label: claim the cathedral's sanctuary for the beast

success.body: You stand in the great doorway and speak to the huntsmen in the old words of sanctuary: that whatever creature takes refuge at the altar is under the Church's peace for forty days, and that any man who lays hands on it lays them on the bishop. The bishop, behind you, says "Yes. Quite," a little faintly. The huntsmen hesitate, and then go away. At dawn, the unicorn rises and walks out, and leaves a single white flower on the altar step.

failure.body: You claim sanctuary for the beast. The huntsmen's leader laughs. "Sanctuary," he says, "is for Christians." They come in through the crypt that night.

entries.body: You sit down by the fire. The old nurse waits.

resolutions.label: comfort the old nurse with memories of her boys

success.body: You tell her what you know: stories of the Orkney brothers at court, at tournaments, at feasts. You tell her the good things and leave out the bad. You tell her about Gareth's kindness, and Gaheris's courage, and even about Agravain's terrible handwriting. She listens, rocking, smiling through her tears. At the end, she takes your hand. "They were good boys," she says. "Whatever anyone says. They were good boys." She gives you a brooch that belonged to Queen Morgause. "She would want a knight to have it," she says.

failure.body: You try to tell her about them, but everything you know ends in blood. She hears it in your voice. "Go," she says gently. "It is all right. Go."

resolutions.label: sit with her and spin, and listen instead of telling

success.body: You do not tell her stories. You sit down by her fire and take up the spare spindle, badly, and let her correct you, and let her talk. She talks for three days, about four wild red-haired boys and a queen who laughed too much, and you listen to every word. On the third night, she stops spinning. "Nobody has listened to me in years," she says. She gives you a brooch that belonged to Queen Morgause.

failure.body: You sit and spin with her, and break the thread three times, and she sends you away. "My boys were clumsy too," she says, "but they did not sit still to prove it."

entries.body: You raise your cup. "To King Mordred," you say. The marsh-lord beams.

resolutions.label: play the traitor to learn the lords' plans

success.body: You drink all night with them, and laugh at their jokes, and by midnight, they are telling you everything: which lord is bringing how many men to Salisbury Plain, and where they will stand. You slip away before dawn and ride for the old king's camp. You carry the list in your head. The old king's captains use it well.

failure.body: You drink all night, and by midnight, you are too drunk to remember anything. You wake up in the marsh-lord's stable, with a headache and a very bad feeling.

resolutions.label: steal the marsh-lords' letters while they drink

success.body: You drink the toast, and then you drink very little. When the marsh-lord and his guests are singing, you slip up to his solar and find the letters from Mordred in a chest under the bed, with the list of every lord's men and where each will stand. You copy it by one candle and put it back. By dawn, you are riding for the old king's camp.

failure.body: You slip up to the marsh-lord's solar and find the chest under the bed. So does his hound, which is sleeping on it.

entries.body: You walk to the foot of Sir Hector's window. "Sir Hector the Tall," you call. "Come down and I will see how tall you are on the ground."

resolutions.label: fight Sir Hector in the street

success.body: Sir Hector comes down, laughing, and draws, and stops laughing very soon. You fight him up and down the street, with the whole town hanging out of its windows, until you knock him flat on his back in the horse-trough. Tegid stands over him, dripping, and offers him a hand up. Sir Hector takes it, red-faced. The Lady Morwen, watching from her window, laughs for the first time. It is not at the dwarf.

failure.body: Sir Hector comes down, laughing, and he goes on laughing, because he is very good with a sword. When he is done, you are sitting in the horse-trough, and the whole town is laughing, and the dwarf is helping you out.

entries.body:
You come upon a small man in motley walking fast along the road with a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, bells jingling on every step. He has a round, sad, clever face, and there is a bruise on his cheek.

"Dagonet," he says, before you can ask. "The High King's fool. Formerly." He walks on, and you ride beside him. "*Sir Kay has kicked me down the stair, and put a frog into my chair, and sworn to shave my head of hair, and so I leave for anywhere.*" He sighs. "I rhyme when I am frightened. It is a very bad habit in a fool. There is a troupe of players at Sarum. They need a fool. They will not kick me." He glances up at you. "The High King will miss me, I think. He likes my riddles. But Kay says the High King needs a fool like a fish needs a saddle."

responses.label: You may help Dagonet join the travelling players at Sarum.
You may persuade Dagonet to return to Camelot, and deal with Sir Kay.

entries.body:
You come upon a small churchyard in a hill town, where a fool in faded motley sits on a tomb, telling jokes. There is nobody there to hear them. He tells one about a bishop and a goat, and then waits, and then laughs as though someone else has laughed.

"He liked that one," the fool says, when he sees you. "King Morgan Mwynfawr. He was my king for thirty years. I am Llew. He died at Candlemas." He pats the tomb. "His son, the new king, has banished laughter from the court. Anyone who laughs is fined a shilling. So I come here. The old king always laughed at my jokes. He still does, I think. I just cannot hear him." He looks at you sadly. "The new king is very unhappy. He has not laughed since his father died. I think he is afraid that if he laughs, he will cry."

responses.label: You may help Llew make the grieving new king laugh.
You may ask Llew to tell you about the old king.

entries.body:
You come upon a fair in a meadow, with stalls and jugglers and a crowd around a wooden platform. On the platform, a thin fool in a patched coat is standing on one leg with his eyes closed, speaking in a high, clear voice.

"The miller's wheel will stop at Michaelmas," he says. "The lord's roan mare will foal twins. The bridge will fall, and nobody on it." The crowd laughs. "Ninian the Simple," a woman beside you explains. "He says things. Sometimes they happen." At that moment, a lord in a fur-trimmed cloak pushes to the front with two men-at-arms. "That fool," he says, "told the whole fair last week that my steward was stealing from me. My steward is a good man. I want the fool whipped."

Ninian opens his eyes and looks straight at you. "The knight will stand between," he says. "The knight will see the ledger."

responses.label: You may protect Ninian from the lord's men.
You may test the truth of Ninian's prophecy about the steward.

entries.body:
You come upon a jester lying in a ditch, laughing. He has been laughing, you gather, for some time. His face is purple, his ribs are heaving, tears are streaming down his cheeks, and between gasps he is trying to say something.

A woman in a travelling cloak stands beside him, wringing her hands. "He is Pedr, my husband," she says. "He is a jester to the Lord of Gwent. Three days ago he made a jest about an old woman at a well. She was a witch. She said, *Since you think it so funny, laugh.* And he has not stopped." She kneels beside him. "He cannot eat. He cannot sleep. He is dying of it." Pedr looks at you desperately, and laughs, and laughs.

responses.label: You may try to break the witch's curse on Pedr.
You may seek out the witch and persuade her to lift it.

entries.body:
You come upon a small, red-haired fool in green motley sitting on a fence outside a tournament field, polishing a very old and very dented helmet. "Pwca," he says, with a bow that nearly topples him off the fence. "Fool to the Earl of Hereford. I have entered the tournament."

He points to the stand, where the Earl's daughter, the Lady Tangwystl, sits under a canopy with her ladies, looking bored. "The prize is a kiss from her," he says. "I have loved her for six years. I make her laugh, and she is kind to me, and she does not know. Nobody lets a fool into the lists. But I have borrowed a horse and a helmet and a name." He shows you a painted shield: *Sir Nobody of Nowhere*. "Will you be my squire? Nobody lets a fool into the lists, but nobody stops a knight's squire either."

responses.label: You may squire for Pwca in the tournament.
* You may enter the tournament and court the Lady Tangwystl yourself.

entries.body:
You come upon a small castle where the courtyard is in uproar. A man in a crown and ermine robe is sitting on the well-head, telling jokes to the kitchen maids. A man in motley, with bells on his hat, is standing on the steps of the hall, shouting orders at the soldiers, who are obeying him.

The steward runs up to you, sweating. "Thank God," he says. "Three days ago, the king and his fool drank from the same flask at a fair. When they woke, the king thought he was the fool, and the fool thought he was the king. They have each put on the other's clothes. The king is telling the worst jokes you have ever heard." He lowers his voice. "The fool, on the other hand, is a much better king. He has lowered the taxes and pardoned the poachers and ended a feud with the Earl next door. The people love him." He wrings his hands. "What do we do?"

responses.label: You may restore the king and the fool to their right minds.
You may help the fool stay on the throne.

entries.body: You stand in the bow with a spear. The serpent rises again beside the boat, its jaws wide.

resolutions.label: drive your spear into the sea serpent

success.body: You take the captain's harpoon and the ship's rope and wait until the serpent rises, and throw. The harpoon goes deep behind its eye. The serpent screams and dives, and the rope runs out so fast it smokes, and the whole boat is dragged across the bay. You hold on. At last the rope goes slack, and the serpent floats up, dead. The sailors cheer until they are hoarse. When you sail home, the drowned village is still there under the water, and its church bell, very faintly, is ringing.

failure.body: You throw the harpoon, and it glances off the serpent's scales. The serpent's tail sweeps the deck, and you are in the sea. The sailors haul you out. The boat limps home.

resolutions.label: learn the serpent's tide and slip past when it sleeps

success.body: You ask the old captain when the serpent rises, and when it does not. He does not know. But you watch the gulls and the water for a day, and see that the serpent comes up only on the flood tide, to feed, and lies still on the ebb. On the ebb, at dawn, you row the ship across the drowned village in silence, with the oars muffled in rags. The serpent does not stir. Far below, very faintly, a church bell is ringing.

failure.body: You watch the gulls and the water and choose the ebb tide. The serpent, it turns out, is hungry on the ebb as well.

entries.body:
You come upon a fool in black and white motley in the kitchens of Camelot, stirring something in a bucket with a gleeful look. The kitchen is empty. It is an hour before the Whitsun feast.

"Shhh," he says. "I am Crach. I was Sir Kay's fool until he gave me away to the Bishop of Winchester for a pair of boots. The bishop is very dull. Now I am back for the feast, and I have a surprise for Sir Kay." He lifts the stirring stick. It drips with goose fat. "He always stands on the same flagstone when he carves the swan. Right in front of the high table. In front of the High King. And the queen. And all the ambassadors from Rome." He grins. "I have been waiting a year."

responses.label: You may help Crach grease Sir Kay's flagstone.
You may warn Sir Kay of Crach's plan.

entries.body:
You come upon a small, dusty court in the hills, where a king in a dented crown is shouting at his council about a goose. A fool in faded blue sits on the steps of the throne, playing a tin whistle, very quietly.

"The Earl of Buellt's goose," the king roars, "came onto my land and ate my barley! I demand reparation! Three hundred marks and the goose!" His councillors nod. "If he will not pay, we march!" The fool plays a mournful little tune on his whistle.

After the council, the fool finds you in the courtyard. "I am Robin Goodfellow," he says. "No relation. I have been this king's fool for twenty years. He is not a bad king. He is only proud, and the Earl is proud too, and they have both been drinking. If there is a war, three hundred men will die for a goose." He looks at you with sad, shrewd eyes. "Help me stop it. I have an idea. It is a fool's idea."

responses.label: You may help Robin Goodfellow with his fool's plan.
You may counsel the king directly against the war.

entries.body:
You come upon a fool dressed in motley sitting in a hayloft above a market square, with a stolen seal and a pot of wax, writing on parchment with great concentration. Every so often, he drops a sealed parchment out of the hayloft door, and a small boy runs off with it.

He sees you and grins. "Hush. I am Gwilym. I stole the Lord of Kidwelly's seal. Every decree I write, the heralds read out in the market as if my lord had sent it." He holds up his latest. "*By order of the Lord of Kidwelly, every pig in the town shall wear a hat on Sundays.*" He giggles. "They obeyed! Every pig!" He writes another. "And this one: *The Lord's steward shall stand in the pillory for an hour every Friday, for the good of his soul.* Nobody likes the steward." He looks at you. "The lord will be back from his hunting next week. What shall I write before he comes?"

responses.label: You may take the seal from Gwilym and return it to the lord.
You may help Gwilym write one last decree that will do some good.

entries.body:
You come upon a man in plain grey sitting on a milestone, weeping. He is small and round-faced, with a shaved head and a nose that is plainly meant for a red cap and bells. "I have lost my motley," he says, before you ask. "I am Hwfa, the fool of Caerleon. Or I was. I diced with a knight last night at the inn, and I lost my coat, my cap, my bells and my bauble. Without them, I am not a fool. I am only a vagabond." He sniffs. "The sheriff hangs vagabonds."

He points down the road, where a knight in black is riding away at a walk, with a motley coat tied across his saddle and a jingling cap hung on his lance like a trophy. "Sir Brun," Hwfa says. "He won it fairly. Mostly. He says he will hang it in his hall and tell people he defeated a fool in single combat."

responses.label: You may challenge Sir Brun for the fool's motley.
You may win back the motley at dice.

entries.body:
You come upon a crowd outside a castle, gathered round a scaffold where a fool in tattered motley is kneeling at the block. The headsman leans on his axe, waiting. A king sits on a horse nearby, tapping his fingers, with a face like thunder.

"What has he done?" you ask a woman in the crowd. "Made a jest," she says. "At the Easter feast, the king asked him what he thought of the new tax. And the fool said, *Sire, it is so heavy that the poor cannot lift it, and so light that it slips through your treasurer's fingers.*" She lowers her voice. "The treasurer is the king's brother."

The fool raises his head and sees you. He is quite young, with a face made for laughing. "Sir knight!" he calls. "Do you know any good last words? I have used all mine up."

responses.label: You may plead with the king for the fool's life.
You may help the fool escape from the scaffold.
You may make the king laugh, and change his mind.

entries.body: You leave the huntsmen in their clearing and walk toward the white hart. It does not run. It turns and walks into the trees, and looks back, and waits for you.

resolutions.label: follow the white hart to its secret

success.body: It leads you to a pool in the heart of the wood, where a lady in white sits on a stone. "You did not try to shoot it," she says. "That is the first time in a hundred years." She tells you that the hart is her brother, turned into a beast by a jealous witch, and that the wood holds any hunter who chases him. "But you only followed," she says. She touches the hart's head, and for an instant you see a young man standing there, laughing. Then he is a hart again. "Not yet," she says. "But one day." She releases the hunting party for your sake.

failure.body: It leads you deeper and deeper into the wood, and you follow it for what seems like an hour. When you come out, the hunting party is gone, and so is the autumn. It is spring. You do not know where the months went.

resolutions.label: follow the white hart with a prayer on your lips

success.body: You follow it praying, as the old hunters say you must, and the wood that has twisted round the huntsmen all day lets you pass straight. The hart leads you to a pool where a lady in white sits on a stone. "You prayed," she says. "Nobody prays for a hart." She releases the hunting party for your sake, and touches your forehead, and you feel it for days afterward, cool as water.

failure.body: You follow it praying, but the wood twists round you all the same, and when you come out, it is spring, and you do not know where the months went.

entries.body: You look up at the ladies on the tower. You cannot let them die. "Come down," you call. "I will love you."

resolutions.label: go to the lady on the tower

success.body: The fair lady laughs, and comes down the stair, and takes your hand. She is warm and soft and very beautiful. She leads you into a chamber hung with silk. Then, as the door closes, you see her shadow on the wall, and it has horns. You break away and run. Behind you, the castle fills with laughter. The old hermit is waiting at the gate. He does not reproach you. "Now you know," he says, "what they wanted." You are shaken for a long time. But you are not lost.

partial.body: The fair lady comes down the stair and takes your hand, and as she does, you feel how cold her fingers are, and you let go. She laughs and vanishes.

failure.body: The fair lady comes down the stair, and takes your hand, and you go with her, and you do not remember what happens next. You wake outside the castle, three days later, with your soul feeling bruised.

entries.body: You dismount and kneel in the road. The dwarf looks at you gravely, then lifts the little bell and rings it over your head.

resolutions.label: receive the blessing of Saint Teilo's bell

success.body: The sound goes through you like light through water. For a moment you are aware of every fault in you, and then, just as clearly, of every one forgiven. When you rise, Brother Ifan is smiling. "The saint likes you," he says. You ride with him over the pass after all, and the robbers at the top, hearing the bell, let you both through without a word.

failure.body: The bell rings, but for you it sounds flat and cracked. Brother Ifan frowns and rings it again. It is no better. "It does that," he says gently, "when a man's heart is not quiet. Come back when it is." You ride on troubled.

entries.body: You cross the swaying bridge with your sword drawn. At the gate, the seven brothers come out to meet you, one after another, each older and fatter than the last.

resolutions.label: defeat the seven brothers

success.body: You defeat them one after another. The eldest is sixty and wheezes. When the last yields, the gate opens, and the maidens come out, sixty of them, with books under their arms and very cross faces. "We did not ask to be rescued," says their leader, a woman in spectacles called Lady Eleri. "But since you have, you may carry the library down the bridge." You spend a week doing it. They found a school in the valley, and you are its first benefactor.

failure.body: You defeat four brothers. The fifth pushes you off the bridge. You are fished out of the moat by the maidens, who are very kind and lend you a book while you dry.

entries.body: You ride out on the Caerwent road and meet the Lady Elidan's party at dawn. She is very lovely, with a sheaf of letters tucked into her sleeve and a look of great expectation on her face.

resolutions.label: court the Lady Elidan

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You ride beside her all morning and tell her tales of your own deeds and loves, and she laughs and blushes and forgets to look at her letters. By noon, she has forgotten Sir Sagramore entirely. "Words on a page are one thing," she says. "A knight at my side is another." Piran, when he hears, is heartbroken. Sagramore is relieved. You are not sure what you are.

partial.body: You ride beside her all morning. She is courteous and kind, but her eyes keep going to the road ahead. "Forgive me," she says. "I have been promised something beautiful." She rides on. You arrive at the tavern in time to watch Sagramore disappoint her.

failure.body: You ride beside her all morning and do your best, but next to Piran's letters your conversation is very thin. "Sir Sagramore writes," she says pointedly, "far better than you speak."

entries.body: You lift the wounded knight across your saddle and lead your horse out through a gap in the back wall.

resolutions.label: escape through the forest with the wounded knight

success.body: You lead your horse down a streambed where the hoofprints will not show, and up through a stand of holly, and lie still in a hollow while Mordred's men crash past twenty yards away. By nightfall, you have found the old king's camp. The wounded knight is carried to the surgeons. He grips your hand as they take him. "Sir Lucan will hear of this," he says. "I will tell him myself."

failure.body: You lead your horse down a streambed, but the horse stumbles on the stones, and the wounded knight cries out. Mordred's men hear it. You run. You get away, but the knight does not.

resolutions.label: ride hard for the king's camp with him across your saddle

success.body: You tie the wounded knight across your saddle and ride, not away from Mordred's men, but past them, at a gallop, before they have finished coming through the gate. They shout and turn, but you are already gone. By nightfall you are in the old king's camp, and the surgeons are taking the knight. "Sir Lucan will hear of this," he says as they carry him off.

failure.body: You ride hard past Mordred's men, and one of them has a spear. It takes your horse. You and the wounded knight go down together in the road.

entries.body: Pellinore looks at you as though no one has ever asked him that before. "Why?" he says. "Well. My father hunted it. And his father. It came out of a king's daughter, you know, who loved her own brother and was refused, and gave herself to a devil, and the devil got the Beast on her. So the Beast is a kind of sin, running round Britain with hounds in its belly, barking." He scratches his beard. "Merlin says only a knight of my blood can catch it. Merlin says a lot of things. He also said a son of mine will see the Grail. I would like that. I have a lot of sons." He brightens. "Anyway, it gives a man something to do." He gallops off to the left, calling to his horse. You find his spare gauntlet on the road, and keep it.
You ride out of the dark with your sword drawn. Both men leap to their feet.

resolutions.label: take the map from Mordred's envoy and the Saxon

success.body: Mordred's man runs. The Saxon does not. He draws a long knife and comes at you, and fights like a wolf. But you are mounted and he is not, and at last he goes down under your horse's hooves. You take the map and the gold to the old king's camp. The king's captains read the map and change their plans. When the Saxon fleet comes to the Medway at midsummer, the old king's ships are waiting for it.

failure.body: Mordred's man runs, and the Saxon comes at you with a long knife, and gets under your guard. When you have fought him off, both men are gone, and the map with them.

resolutions.label: turn the envoys on each other with a word

success.body: You step into the firelight with your hands empty. "Friend," you say to Mordred's man, "the king says the Saxon is to have Kent only. Not Sussex." The Saxon's hand goes to his knife. Mordred's man protests. In the argument that follows, neither of them sees you pick up the map. When they have finished shouting, they are both gone, in opposite directions, and so is the map, with you.

failure.body: You step into the firelight and tell Mordred's man the king has changed his mind. Mordred's man does not know you. Neither does the Saxon. They agree about that, at least.

entries.body: You fall into step beside the young man while Lynette rides ahead, still talking. "Who are you?" you ask quietly. Beaumains glances at you. "Can you keep a secret?" he says. "My name is Gareth. My mother is the Queen of Orkney, and my brothers are knights of the Round Table. I came to court in disguise because I wanted to be judged for what I did, not whose son I was. Sir Kay put me in the kitchen for a year." He grins. "It was a good year. I learned to make pastry." He nods at Lynette's back. "She will find out in the end. I hope she will be sorry. I think I will marry her sister." You promise to keep his secret, and you do.
You look at the ramparts. They are old and crumbling, and the brigands are few.

resolutions.label: storm the brigands' hill-fort

success.body: You find a place where the ramparts have slumped, and climb it at dawn, and are among the brigands before they are awake. It is not much of a fight. They seem almost relieved. Sir Brewen of Dinas is sitting in a hut, tied to a chair. He does not thank you. He complains about the food, and the chair, and the smell, all the way down the mountain. His father pays you a hundred marks, and says, gloomily, that you may keep him if you like.

failure.body: You find a place where the ramparts have slumped and climb it at dawn, and the brigands are awake and waiting. You are tied to the chair next to Sir Brewen, who talks to you for two days.

resolutions.label: climb in by the old ditch and free him unseen

success.body: You go round the back of the hill-fort, where an old ditch runs under the rampart, and crawl up it at dusk. The brigands are at their supper, arguing. You find Sir Brewen tied to a chair in a hut, and put your hand over his mouth, and he bites it. You carry him out anyway. His father pays you a hundred marks, and says, gloomily, that you may keep him if you like.

failure.body: You crawl up the old ditch, find Sir Brewen, and put your hand over his mouth. He bites it, and screams, and complains. The brigands tie you to the chair beside him.

entries.body: You kneel beside Pedr in the ditch. His eyes are desperate, but his mouth will not stop laughing.

resolutions.label: unravel the laughing curse

success.body: You remember an old saying: a curse of the tongue is broken by silence. You tell Pedr's wife to hold her hand over his mouth, and you do the same, and you both hold him still while he laughs into your palms. It takes an hour. Then, slowly, the laughter becomes breathing, and the breathing becomes weeping, and then he is silent. He lies in the ditch for a long time. At last he croaks, "That was not funny." His wife laughs, then, and he does not.

failure.body: You try every charm you know. You say the Paternoster backwards. You sprinkle him with salt. Pedr laughs harder. At last, you say something that you think will work, and it makes him laugh so hard he falls back into the ditch, and you catch it too. You laugh all the way to the next village, and for most of the next day.

resolutions.label: keep Pedr alive until the curse wears itself out

success.body: You do not try to break the curse. You make a litter and carry Pedr to a woodcutter's hut, and feed him broth through a reed between laughs, and give him poppy to make him sleep, laughing, and dose him with every herb you know that calms the breath. On the seventh day, the curse, having nothing more to feed on, wears thin. On the eighth, he stops. He is very weak, and very thin, and he will not tell a joke for a year. But he lives.

failure.body: You carry Pedr to a woodcutter's hut and try to feed him broth, but he chokes on it, laughing, and you cannot get him to sleep. On the fourth day, you ride for help. When you come back, the hut is quiet. His wife is sitting at the door.

entries.body: You walk along the rows of the drowned knights for a long time. The Lady waits.

resolutions.label: choose which drowned knight shall live again

success.body: You do not choose the greatest knight, or the handsomest, or the one you knew best. You choose a young knight with a plain shield and a wedding ring, whom nobody would have missed but his wife. The Lady looks at you, and smiles. "That is how I would have chosen," she says. The young knight wakes, and weeps, and you lead him up out of the lake. His wife, in a village in Somerset, will not believe it until she sees him. Then she will not let go of him for a week.

failure.body: You walk along the rows, and cannot choose. Every face is someone's son. At last, the Lady takes your hand. "It is all right," she says. "Nobody can." She sends you home with nothing.

resolutions.label: ask the drowned knights themselves who should go

success.body: You do not choose. You kneel among the biers and pray, and ask, aloud, which of them most needs to go back. The Lady watches, surprised. One by one, the drowned faces are still. Then one of them, a young knight with a plain shield and a wedding ring, stirs, and sighs. "That is how I would have chosen," says the Lady. He wakes and weeps, and you lead him up out of the lake. His wife, in Somerset, will not let go of him for a week.

failure.body: You kneel among the biers and ask them. None of them stirs. The Lady takes your hand. "It is all right," she says. "Nobody can." She sends you home with nothing.

entries.body: You ask for leave to speak before the King of Meath. He is a stern, grey man, and he looks at you with suspicion. "A stranger," he says. "Speak."

resolutions.label: persuade the King of Meath to a wiser judgement

success.body: You do not argue the law. You ask the king how many men will die for one book. You ask the old abbot whether his psalter is worth more for having a twin, or less. You ask the young monk whether God wants his words fought over. By the end, the hall is quiet. The king strokes his beard. "Let the copy stay at Kells," he says at last, "and let the monk who made it make a third copy, for the old abbot, as penance. And let nobody lift a spear." The young monk groans at the thought of copying it again. His kinsmen go home. The abbot of Kells gives you a page of the copy, beautifully illuminated, to keep.

failure.body: You ask the king how many men will die for one book. "As many as need to," he says, "for the law." The young monk's kinsmen march. You leave Ireland on the morning of the battle.

resolutions.label: stand as the young monk's champion if it comes to war

success.body: You do not argue the law. You offer to settle the matter by combat, you for the young monk and any warrior for the old abbot, so that one man bleeds instead of a thousand. The King of Meath is astonished. The old abbot's kinsmen put forward a champion. You fight him in the churchyard at Kells before both families. When he yields, the king rules that the copy stays at Kells. Nobody lifts a spear.

failure.body: You fight the old abbot's champion in the churchyard. He is an Irish champion, and you lose. The young monk's kinsmen march anyway.

entries.body: You look at the smoke over the walls, and at the herald, and at the land Claudas is offering. "I will stand aside," you say.

resolutions.label: take King Claudas's bargain

success.body: Claudas takes Benwick a month later. Old King Ban dies of grief on a hill overlooking his burning castle, with his queen beside him. Claudas is as good as his word. He gives you a manor on the river, with vineyards, and a purse of gold. When the young British king hears of it, he says nothing. He does not need to.

partial.body: Claudas takes Benwick. He gives you a small manor on a marshy stretch of the river, with a leaking roof and a steward who steals, and then he forgets you, and so does everyone else. The wine from its vineyard is very sour.

failure.body: Claudas takes Benwick, and then decides that a knight who can be bought once can be bought again, by someone else. He sends you home with nothing.

entries.body: You walk into the ring of torches. Morgan pats the stone beside her. "Sit," she says. "Have you ever been to Camelot's treasury?"

resolutions.label: help the queens steal the scabbard

success.body: You help them plan it. You tell them which guards drink and which do not, and which door of the treasury sticks. Two weeks later, the scabbard is gone from Camelot, and nobody knows how. Morgan sends you a gift: a cloak that keeps you warm in any weather, and a note that says, *My brother will bleed now. Thank you.* You wear the cloak. It is very warm. You try not to think about the note.

failure.body: You help them plan it, but on the night, the treasury guard is Sir Kay, who is not drinking, and who knows your face. You flee Camelot, and the queens do not help you. Morgan, you hear, laughs.

resolutions.label: steal the scabbard from Camelot yourself

success.body: You do not wait for the queens' plan. You go to Camelot on a moonless night and climb to the treasury window by the ivy, and the scabbard is there on its hook, embroidered, humming faintly. You take it. The next morning, it is in Morgan's hands. She sends you a cloak that keeps you warm in any weather, and a note: *My brother will bleed now. Thank you.* You wear the cloak. You try not to think about the note.

failure.body: You climb to the treasury window by the ivy, and Sir Kay is inside, eating a pie he has hidden there. He knows your face. You flee Camelot, and the queens do not help you.

entries.body: You kneel and put your ear against the cold stone. From inside, very faint, you hear an old man's voice.

resolutions.label: understand Merlin's last message

success.body: He speaks slowly, so that you will not miss it. He tells you that the king will die, but not all the way. That there is a barge, and an island, and a sleep. That Britain will forget him, and then remember him, again and again, for a thousand years. "Tell him," Merlin says, "that it was worth it. The table. All of it. Tell him I said so." You carry the words to the king on the eve of the battle. He weeps, and laughs, and says that Merlin never told him anything so kind in his life.

failure.body: He speaks, but his voice is so faint, and the wind is so loud, that you catch only a few words. *Worth it*, you think he says. Or *worse than it*. You never know which.

resolutions.label: carry his last words to the king with perfect faithfulness

success.body: You put your ear to the stone and hear only a few words: *worth it*. You do not guess the rest. You carry exactly those words to the old king on the eve of the battle, and tell him honestly that you heard no more. He sits with them for a long time. "Worth it," he says. "The table. All of it." He weeps, and laughs, and says that Merlin never told him anything so kind in his life.

failure.body: You carry Merlin's words to the old king, but by the time you reach his camp, you are not sure any more whether he said *worth it* or *worse than it*. You tell the king the first. You never know if you lied.

entries.body: "Fight," you say. "If the old king wins, he will remember who stood with him." The young men cheer. Father Idris looks at you sadly. "And if he loses?" he asks.

resolutions.label: lead the village men into battle for the old king

success.body: You lead forty men with bill-hooks and bows out of the marsh and onto the flank of Mordred's army, at the moment it is pressing the old king's line hardest. They do not expect peasants. They break. That night, an old knight with a white beard rides into the marsh to thank the people of four villages by name, and swears that the old king will know of it. Six of your men are dead. The village mourns them with pride.

failure.body: You lead forty men with bill-hooks and bows onto the flank of Mordred's army. They are brave, and they are not soldiers. Mordred's horsemen ride them down. You bring nineteen of them back to the marsh. Father Idris does not reproach you. He does not need to.

entries.body: You thank the herald and ride on, past the camp, round the walls, to where the river runs under them.

resolutions.label: break through the siege lines into Benwick

success.body: You wait for night and swim your horse up the river under the walls, where the siege lines are thinnest, and come up at a water-gate, and shout King Ban's name until they let you in. The old king, grey and gaunt, embraces you. You spend a month on the walls. You show them tricks you learned from the young British king's engineers. When the young king's army lands on the coast at last, Claudas breaks his siege and flees. King Ban gives you a white horse from his own stable, the fastest in Gaul.

failure.body: You swim your horse up the river under the walls, but Claudas's men have laid a boom across it. You are caught, and taken to Claudas, who laughs and sends you home without your horse.

resolutions.label: find the river-way under the walls

success.body: You do not fight through the siege lines. You walk the riverbank at dusk, as a fisherman would, and find where the old eel-weirs run under the water-gate, below the besiegers' boom. At midnight, you swim your horse along the weirs, in the dark, under the walls, and come up at the water-gate shouting King Ban's name. You spend a month on the walls. When the young king's army lands, Claudas flees. King Ban gives you a white horse from his own stable.

failure.body: You find the old eel-weirs and swim your horse along them at midnight. The besiegers have found them too.

entries.body: You kneel before the Queen of Northgalis. "My lady," you say, "a knight who would leave you in the night is not worth a shield. Surely there are others." The queen looks you up and down. Her companions giggle.

resolutions.label: woo the Queen of Northgalis

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You spend the afternoon with the three queens, and by evening the Queen of Northgalis has entirely forgotten Breunor. "You dance better," she decides, "and you have not stolen anything yet." She gives you a green sleeve to wear at the next tournament and invites you to her court at Candlemas. The other two queens are jealous, which pleases her more than anything.

failure.body: You spend the afternoon with the three queens, but your dancing is worse than Breunor's and your compliments are worse still. "I am not a pear tree," says the Queen of Northgalis, "to be praised for my shape." The queens ride off without you, and you sit alone in the glade among the cherry stones.

entries.body: Every soldier the queen has is on the beach, and the camp above the dunes is guarded by one old man asleep against a tent-pole.

resolutions.label: steal from the queen's tent

success.body: The queen's tent is full of bronze, amber and gold, the treasure of a whole kingdom packed for a journey that will never happen now. You fill a saddlebag and walk out past the old man, who snores. Down on the beach, the counting goes on, "Six hundred and one. Six hundred and two," and nobody looks up. You ride away rich and do not look back.

failure.body: The queen's tent is full of bronze and amber. You are filling your saddlebag when the old man, who was not asleep, puts a spear to your back. They take you down to the beach and make you stand in the surf beside the soldiers. "You will take the thief's share," the queen says. "The sea's strokes are yours now." You are there until nightfall, and the soldiers do not let you forget it.

resolutions.label: overpower the old guard and take what you want

success.body: The old man is not asleep, but he is old. You knock the spear out of his hands and tie him to his own tent-pole, and fill your saddlebags with bronze and amber. He curses you the whole time. Down on the beach, the counting goes on. You ride away rich.

failure.body: The old man is not asleep, and he is not as old as he looks. He knocks you flat with the butt of his spear and shouts, and a dozen soldiers come running up from the beach. They make you stand in the surf with a whip until nightfall.

entries.body: You kneel beside Rhys and put your hand on the sack. "Let me carry it back for you," you say. For a long moment, his fingers stay clenched. Then, slowly, they open.

resolutions.label: return the treasure to the barrow and appease the dead king

success.body: You carry the sack up the hill at dusk. The barrow is open, a black mouth in the turf. Inside, in the dark, a tall figure sits on a stone throne, with a crown on its skull. You lay the gold before it: a torc, a cup, a sword with a hilt of red enamel. You pray for the old king's soul, and ask pardon for the thief. The skull does not move. But when you come out, the barrow closes behind you with a long sigh of earth. In the morning, Rhys is sane, and weeping, and swears he will dig nothing but turnips.

failure.body: You carry the sack up the hill at dusk and into the black mouth of the barrow. Inside, a tall figure sits on a stone throne. You lay the gold before it and begin to pray, but the figure lifts one bony hand and points at you. You flee. The gold is back where it belongs. But you hear, all the way down the hill, a dry voice saying *Cunedda, Cunedda*, and it is saying it in your head.

resolutions.label: seal the barrow with the old words against the dead

success.body: You do not go into the barrow. You walk three times round it at dusk, sunwise, with the sack on your shoulder, and lay the gold on the capstone, and speak the old words that close a grave. The standing stone hums. When you look again, the gold is gone, and the entrance to the barrow is grass. In the morning, Rhys is sane and weeping, and nothing walks from the barrow to the church again.

failure.body: You walk three times round the barrow and speak the old words, and get them the wrong way round. The barrow opens wider. That night, something walks from the barrow to your inn instead of the church.

entries.body: "He cannot outshoot you," you say to Rhian. "But perhaps he can do something else as well." Bran looks at you with desperate hope.

resolutions.label: teach Lord Bran to track as well as Rhian shoots

success.body: You take Bran into the forest for a week, and teach him everything you know about tracking: how to read a bent blade of grass, a turned leaf, a smell on the wind. At the end of it, you set a match: Rhian to shoot a deer, Bran to find it first. Bran finds three deer before Rhian finds one. She is astonished, and then delighted. "He can find them," she says, "and I can shoot them. That will do." They are married at midsummer, and his mother is given a pair of very fine gloves.

failure.body: You take Bran into the forest for a week and teach him to track. He is a poor pupil, and on the fourth day, he tracks a wild boar straight to its lair, and it chases you both up a tree. Rhian finds you there two hours later and shoots it. She laughs until she cries. Bran does not propose again.

resolutions.label: teach Lord Bran to shoot from the saddle

success.body: Bran cannot outshoot Rhian standing. But Bran was born on a horse, and Rhian was not. You spend a week teaching him to loose an arrow at full gallop, and at the end of it you set the match again: from horseback. Bran hits the mark at a gallop four times out of six. Rhian cannot hit it once. She stares at him. Then she laughs. "Teach me," she says. They are married by midsummer.

failure.body: You spend a week teaching Bran to shoot from horseback. On the last day, he shoots his own horse in the ear. Rhian laughs until she cries. Bran does not propose again.

entries.body: You kneel and lift the old king in your arms. Sir Bedivere takes his feet. Together, you carry him down to the water.

resolutions.label: carry the dying king to the barge

success.body: The water is cold, and the king is heavier than he looks, and your legs are shaking from the battle. But you carry him out, waist-deep, to the barge, and the three queens reach down and take him, and lay his head in the lap of the one in the middle. She is weeping. The old king looks up at you. "Carnwennan," he says, and presses his dagger into your hand. "Keep it. For the next time." The barge goes out into the mist, and you stand in the water until you cannot see it any more.

failure.body: You carry him out into the water, but your legs give way, and you both fall. The three queens reach down and lift him out of the lake themselves, and the barge goes out into the mist. You are left kneeling in the water, with nothing.

resolutions.label: command the barge-queens by the old king's own right

success.body: You do not carry him yet. You stand in the water and call to the three queens, in the old king's name, that he will go to his barge borne by his knights, as a king goes, and not lifted like a sack. The queen in the middle lowers her veil and nods. You and Bedivere carry him out between you, and lay his head in her lap. He looks up at you. "Carnwennan," he says, and presses his dagger into your hand. "For the next time."

failure.body: You call to the three queens in the old king's name. They do not answer. They reach out of the barge and take him from the shore themselves, and it goes out into the mist.

entries.body: You stand at the foot of the Tor and call out to the pilgrims. "Do not go with them! I will guide you, and charge you nothing."

resolutions.label: lead the pilgrims safely up the holy hill

success.body: The false monks glare at you. But the pilgrims come to you, and you lead them up the Tor in a long line, with the strongest men at the back and the women and children in the middle, and the false monks follow for a while, and then give up. At the top, the pilgrims pray. On the way down, they sing. The false monks have gone by nightfall, looking for easier pickings.

failure.body: You call out to the pilgrims, but the false monks call louder, and the pilgrims prefer men in habits to a stranger in armour. That evening, three more are robbed.

entries.body: You wait until night, and swim to the longship with a knife and a bag of tools.

resolutions.label: sabotage the Saxon ship in the dark

success.body: You swim under the longship's hull and cut through the lashings of three of its planks, so that they will hold on the beach but not in the open sea. Then you swim away. At dawn, the Saxons sail. A mile out, their ship begins to sink. They row desperately back to shore, straight into the arms of the local lord's men, whom you have warned. The captives are freed. Sister Wenna thanks you, and asks you, gently, not to do anything like that again, because the Saxons might have drowned.

failure.body: You swim under the longship's hull, but the Saxons have a watchman. He sees you. You barely escape back to your ship, and the longship sails at dawn.

entries.body: You sit down on the grass beside her. "Tegwen," you say, "the dead do not eat bread. Tell me what it was like, when you woke up."

resolutions.label: coax Tegwen back to the living

success.body: She tells you about the fever, and the dark, and waking in the shroud with the candles burning low and her mother asleep in the chair. She thought she was dead, because she could not believe anyone would have laid her out otherwise. As she talks, you ask her small things. Is she cold? Is she hungry? Does her foot hurt where she stubbed it on the gravestone? Yes, she says, and yes, and yes. Slowly, a new look comes into her face. "Oh," she says. That evening, her mother comes into the churchyard and holds her, and the two of them walk home together.

failure.body: She tells you about the fever and the dark. You ask whether she is cold, and she says no. You ask whether she is hungry, and she says no. You ask whether her foot hurts, and she says she cannot feel it. You leave her singing in the churchyard, and you do not know, any longer, which of you is right.

resolutions.label: bring her to take the sacrament with the living

success.body: You ask the priest to say Mass for her in the churchyard, and you kneel beside her, and when the priest offers her the bread, she takes it. "The dead do not take communion," the priest says gently. Tegwen looks at the bread in her hand for a long time. Then she eats it, and weeps, and asks for her mother. By evening she is home, in her own bed, asking for soup.

failure.body: You ask the priest to say Mass for her. Tegwen watches, but when he offers her the bread, she shakes her head. "Not for me," she says. "I am past all that." She goes back to her grave and sings.

entries.body: You draw your sword and step in front of her. "The first man who lays a hand on her," you say, "goes over the side himself."

resolutions.label: hold off the crew until the storm passes

success.body: The crew hesitates. The storm roars. You stand there with your sword in the pitching stern for an hour, and nobody comes at you, and at last the storm eases, and the sun comes out, and the sailors look at each other in shame. Elaine thanks you with great dignity. At Waterford, she walks down the gangplank, and turns, and says, "If my father asks, tell him you never saw me." You never do.

failure.body: You stand in front of her with your sword drawn, but a wave knocks you off your feet, and while you are down, the crew seizes her. She goes over the side. The storm stops at once. The sailors look at each other, pale. You do not know what to believe.

resolutions.label: read the storm and show them it will pass

success.body: You shout above the wind to the captain: look at the clouds, low and fast and ragged in the west; look at the swell, lengthening. It is a squall, not a gale, and it will blow out by dawn. The old sailors look, and nod, and the young ones listen to the old ones. By the time the stars come out, nobody is talking about witches. At Waterford, the young woman thanks you with great dignity.

failure.body: You shout to the captain that it is only a squall. Then the mast cracks. Nobody listens to you after that, and it takes your sword to keep her on board.

entries.body: "Teach me," you say. Mag looks at you shrewdly. "It is not a knight's game," she says. "It is a game for people who have to eat." "Then teach me to see it," you say, "so I can keep the drovers from losing their pennies."

resolutions.label: learn the con-woman's craft

success.body: Mag spends an afternoon with you, and she shows you everything: the palm, the pass, the shill in the crowd who wins to encourage the others. She shows you how to tell a loaded die by its sound on the table, and how a card is marked with a fingernail. "Now you know," she says at the end. "Nobody will ever cheat you again. That is worth more than a silver penny." She is right. You never lose at dice after that, and you never play.

failure.body: Mag spends an afternoon with you, and at the end of it, you know how the trick is done and still cannot see it. "You have honest eyes," she says, not kindly. "They want to see what is there." She charges you a silver penny for the lesson.

entries.body: You take the warning, written on a scrap of vellum in seven hands. It is a long ride to Camelot.

resolutions.label: bring the hermits' warning to the king

success.body: The High King reads it in his solar, alone. He is silent a long time. "Merlin told me this," he says at last, "when I was a boy. Seven hermits tell me now." He puts the vellum in the fire. "I have always known," he says. "It does not help, knowing. But thank them for me." You ride away from Camelot knowing that you have given an old man a heavy thing to carry, and that he thanked you for it.

failure.body: The High King's chamberlain takes the vellum and promises to give it to the king. You learn later that it was given to Mordred instead.

resolutions.label: ride to Camelot faster than any other word

success.body: You ride as though the plain were already on fire. You change horses at every abbey, and reach Camelot in four days, and are brought to the High King's solar before the chamberlain can stop you. The king reads the vellum alone. "Merlin told me this," he says, "when I was a boy." He puts it in the fire. "Thank them for me." You ride away knowing that you have given an old man a heavy thing to carry.

failure.body: You ride as fast as you can, and your horse falls on the mountain road. By the time you reach Camelot on foot, the chamberlain takes the vellum, and it goes to Mordred instead.

entries.body: Sir Bedivere holds out the sword to you, weeping. "You do it," he says. "I cannot." You take it. The old king has closed his eyes.

resolutions.label: keep Excalibur and slip away

notes: Lose all Ranks of Divinity

success.body: You do not go to the water. You walk away along the shore with the sword under your cloak, while Bedivere kneels by the king. Nobody stops you. When you are a mile away, you look back. The black barge is going out into the mist, and on the shore, Bedivere is shouting after you. You do not turn round. The sword is yours now. It does not feel as you thought it would. It feels as though it is waiting.

partial.body: You walk away along the shore with the sword under your cloak. After a mile, it is so heavy you can hardly carry it. After two, you cannot. You drop it in a stream, and it sinks, and you run.

failure.body: You take the sword and turn to go, and Sir Bedivere sees your face, and knows. He takes it back from you with his one good hand, and throws it into the lake himself, and the hand rises to catch it. He does not speak to you again.

entries.body: You stay aboard, and help the captain get his crew into the boat, and off the rocks, away from the shore.

resolutions.label: bring the crew safely off the rocks

success.body: You row the boat away from the rocks, and away from the wreckers' shore, along the coast in the dark, with the crew bailing, until you find a cove with no lights. By dawn, everyone is safe. The ship is lost, but the crew are alive, and the captain, weeping, says he owes you his life. You find the village priest the next day, and he rings his bell, and the wreckers are ashamed. Some of them.

failure.body: You row the boat away from the rocks, but a wave overturns it, and you swim for the shore. The wreckers are waiting. You are robbed, but alive.

resolutions.label: read the rocks and find the way off them

success.body: You do not go ashore toward the wreckers' lanterns. You watch the breakers and see where the tide is running out between the rocks, and you get the crew into the boat and let the ebb carry you through a gap you could not see by day. By dawn you are in a cove with no lights and no wreckers. The ship is lost, but the crew are alive.

failure.body: You watch the breakers and choose a gap, and the ebb carries the boat straight onto the wreckers' beach. You are robbed, but alive.

entries.body: You take hold of the hilt. It is cold, and it seems to shift slightly under your hand, as if it is deciding something.

resolutions.label: draw the sword from its scabbard

success.body: The sword slides out as easily as if it had been greased. It is a beautiful blade, grey as a winter river. Morfudd stares at you. "Oh," she says. "Oh, no. I mean, well done." She holds out her hands for it. "Now give it back, please. My lady only meant it to be drawn, not kept." But the sword does not want to go back in the scabbard, and you do not want to give it. "Then keep it," Morfudd says, very quietly, "and God help you." She walks away down the road without it.

failure.body: You pull. Nothing happens. You pull harder, and the scabbard comes up off the ground and drags Morfudd forward with it, and she falls into a ditch. "Twenty-seven," she says, from the ditch.

entries.body: "I will come with you," you say, "and see that justice is done, and nothing more." Marrok looks at you with his yellow eyes. "Justice," he says. "Yes." His manor is a day's walk away, and he will not ride, because horses will not carry him.

resolutions.label: see that Marrok's wife faces justice before the lord of the manor

success.body: At the manor, the steward goes white as milk, and the lady drops her cup. You make Marrok wait outside while you go to the lord of the shire and lay out the whole thing before him, slowly and plainly. The lady is stripped of the manor and sent to a convent; the steward is exiled. Marrok walks in through his own front door for the first time in seven years. He sits by his own fire and weeps. Then he bows to you, very correctly. "You kept me a man," he says.

failure.body: At the manor, the steward goes white as milk, and the lady drops her cup. Before you can speak, Marrok is across the room. You pull him off the steward, but not before the man's arm is broken, and the lady has fled screaming into the night. The shire reeve arrives in the morning and takes Marrok away in chains. He goes quietly.

resolutions.label: stand between Marrok and his wife when the wolf rises

success.body: At the manor, the lady screams, and Marrok's lips pull back from his teeth. You step between them, sword drawn. "Marrok," you say. "You are a knight." He stops. He shakes. After a long moment, he straightens. "I am a knight," he says. He turns his back on his wife and her steward and asks for his old sword and his old horse. When he rides away, the horse carries him, for the first time in seven years. He takes you with him as far as Camelot, and there he tells the High King you saved his soul.

failure.body: At the manor, the lady screams, and Marrok leaps. You step between them. Marrok's teeth close on your forearm, and there is a long moment when he does not let go. Then he does, and flees howling into the dark. You bind your arm. It aches at every full moon, afterwards.

entries.body: You walk over to the chess table in the corner. Mordred looks up with his warm smile. Agravain does not look up at all. "Friend," says Mordred. "Do you play?"

resolutions.label: beat Mordred at his own game

success.body: You sit down and play him. He is very good. But he is watching you more than the board, and you see it, and you let him think you are watching the queen's window, and then you take his queen. Agravain stops writing. Mordred stares at the board. Then he laughs, a real laugh, surprised. "I did not see that," he says. "I always see everything." He tips over his king. From then on, he watches you very carefully. It is a kind of victory.

failure.body: You sit down and play him. He beats you in eleven moves, gently, as if he were teaching a child. Then he looks up at you with his warm grey eyes. "Everyone has a weakness, friend," he says. "Now I know yours."

resolutions.label: confront Mordred and Agravain openly before the court

success.body: You do not sit down to their game. You ask them, loudly enough for the hall to hear, what is written in Agravain's book, and why it has the queen's name in it. The hall goes quiet. Agravain closes the book. Mordred smiles. "Friend," he says, "you are very interested in our affairs." But the High King has heard, and looks at his son for a long time, and Agravain's book is not seen in the hall again.

failure.body: You ask them loudly what is in Agravain's book. Mordred opens it and reads out a page of household accounts. The hall laughs. At you.

entries.body: "A thousand strokes is a heavy sentence, my lady," you say. "Your men are tired. Let me lay on the rest." The queen looks at you with sudden, desperate gratitude. She holds out her own whip.

resolutions.label: lash the waves until the sentence is done

success.body: You wade into the cold sea and lash the waves as the queen counts. Your arm aches by five hundred and burns by eight hundred. At nine hundred and ninety, a wave comes in that is taller than the rest, and you strike it, and it falls at your feet like a dog lying down. At one thousand, the queen rises from her rock. "It is pardoned," she says. Then she sits down on the sand and weeps at last, properly, like a woman and not a queen. Her soldiers bring you dry clothes and a torc of bronze.

failure.body: You wade into the cold sea and lash the waves as the queen counts. At six hundred, a wave knocks you off your feet, and you swallow half the sea. The soldiers drag you out, choking. The queen looks down at you from her rock. "You see," she says. "It fights back." She orders the flogging to go on.

resolutions.label: bless the waters so that the sentence may be ended

success.body: You wade into the surf, not with a whip, but with your hands raised, and ask God to take back the sea's guilt and give the queen her peace. The soldiers stop. The queen stops counting. You pray aloud, for the drowned king and his sons by name, until the tide turns. Then Anna comes down from her rock and kneels in the water beside you, and weeps at last. Her men carry you both out.

failure.body: You wade into the surf and raise your hands and pray. The queen watches you for a long time. "You pray for the sea," she says coldly. "I asked you to punish it." Her soldiers put you back on your horse.

entries.body:
You feel the ground shake before you see him. Over the brow of the hill comes a giant as tall as an oak, walking slowly and carefully, with a whole stone chapel strapped to his back with ropes as thick as your arm. The bell in the little tower clangs at every step.

He stops when he sees you and bends down, very gently, so as not to spill the chapel. "Good day, small knight," he says. His voice is like a cart going over a bridge. "I am Hu. I am carrying this chapel for the Bishop of Hereford, from the valley where nobody goes to church, to the hill where everybody will. When it is done, the bishop has promised to baptise me." He smiles shyly. "Nobody has ever baptised a giant. I have carried it forty miles. There is only the gorge of Nant-y-Cwm left, and the gorge is very narrow." He looks worried. "And the bishop, I think, has not finished counting what the chapel is worth."

responses.label: You may help Hu carry the chapel through the narrow gorge.
You may ride ahead to the bishop and make sure he keeps his promise to the giant.

entries.body:
You come upon a giantess sitting on a hillside, piling stones on a great cairn. She is weeping, and each tear hits the ground like a bucket of water. The cairn is already as high as a house.

"Go away, knight," she says, without looking at you. "Your kind did this." She lays another boulder on the pile. "I am Morfran. That is my husband under there. Cawr. He was a shepherd. He kept goats. He never hurt anyone. Three knights came through the valley last week, looking for a giant to kill, for the glory of it, and they found him asleep in the sun." She wipes her face with a hand the size of a door. "They are coming back tomorrow for me. They said so. They said a giantess would make a better story."

responses.label: You may stand with Morfran against the three knights.
You may ride to meet the three knights and turn them from their purpose.

entries.body:
You come upon a small church in a village where the priest is standing in the doorway with his arms spread wide, and a giant is kneeling in the churchyard, looking in through the door with enormous, hopeful eyes. The giant's head is as big as the doorway.

"I want to be baptised," the giant says to you, very politely. "I am Ysbaddaden the Younger. My father was a very bad giant, and I am trying to be a good one. I have given up eating sheep. I help with the harvest. But the priest says the font is too small, and the church door is too small, and I am too big to be a Christian." He looks at his great hands. "Is that true?"

"The canon law," says the priest, a little desperately, "says nothing about giants."

responses.label: You may baptise the giant yourself in the river.
You may persuade the priest that a giant may be baptised.

entries.body:
You come upon a young man sitting in a barn with his head poking out through a hole in the roof. The rest of him fills the barn completely. He is not a giant. He is a very ordinary young man, only grown to three times his proper size, with his shirt split at the seams and a patched blanket round his middle.

"Twm," he says miserably. "The miller's son. Or I was. I laughed at old Nest Morgan when she fell in the millrace, and she said, *Since you think yourself so big, grow.* And I did. I grow a hand's width every night." He looks down at his feet, which are sticking out of the barn door. "I will be as big as a church by midsummer. My mother cannot feed me. My sweetheart will not come near me." His lip trembles. "Old Nest has gone to her sister's in the mountains. Nobody knows where."

responses.label: You may find a cure for Twm's growing.
You may seek out old Nest in the mountains.

entries.body:
You come upon a giant sitting on a hillside above a mill, with a boulder in his lap, gazing down at the millyard. He is young, as giants go, with a shock of red hair and a face like a sad potato. A woman is hanging out washing in the millyard. Every so often, the giant sighs, and the washing blows off the line.

"That is Elin," he tells you. "The miller's wife. I love her. I am Gogyrfan." He looks at the boulder in his lap. "Every morning I leave her a present. A boulder. Or a tree. Yesterday I left her a cow. She does not seem pleased." Below, the miller is shouting and shaking his fist at the hill. "Her husband says he will fetch knights to kill me. I would not mind so much, if she would only look at me first."

responses.label: You may help Gogyrfan find a love better suited to him.
You may drive the lovesick giant away from the mill.

entries.body:
You come upon a fire on a rocky island in a bay, cut off at high tide. Beside the fire an old woman sits weeping, turning a spit on which something is roasting that you do not look at too closely. From a cave above her comes the sound of snoring, like a storm in a chimney.
