"Go back, knight, before the tide turns," she whispers. "He will wake. He is the giant of the Mount. He has eaten every knight who came here for twenty years. I am his cook. He took me from Brittany with my lady, the duchess, and he killed her, and he keeps me to turn his spit." She pulls up her sleeve. There is a chain round her ankle, fixed to a ring in the rock. "He is mad, knight. He talks to the duchess's body. He says she will wake up and love him." The snoring stops, and then starts again.

responses.label: You may free the old woman while the giant sleeps.
You may wake the giant of the Mount and fight him.

entries.body: You put the horn to your lips and blow a long, hard blast. The red pavilion shakes. The Red Knight comes out, fastening his helm. He is enormous, and he is laughing.

resolutions.label: fight the Red Knight as his strength grows toward noon

success.body: You fight until the sun is overhead, and you feel every blow he strikes grow heavier. You fight on past noon, when the Red Knight is as strong as seven men, and you are sure you will die. But he has not fought a real opponent in a year, only boys who came to die, and he tires. At the second hour after noon, he stumbles, and you are on him. He yields. Lyonesse comes down from her tower and opens the gate with her own hands. The forty knights are cut down and buried, and the Red Knight is sent to Camelot in chains.

failure.body: You fight until the sun is overhead, and every blow he strikes is heavier than the last. At noon, he beats your shield down onto your helm and you fall. He does not hang you. He looks down at you, and at the lady in the window. "Go and tell them at Camelot," he says, "that the Red Knight still waits." You go, bleeding.

resolutions.label: charge him at once, before his strength can grow

success.body: You do not wait for him to finish fastening his helm. You ride at him across the meadow as he runs for his horse, and he has to meet you on foot, half-armed, an hour before noon, with only the strength of three men. It is enough to make it a fight, and not enough to win it. He yields with his helm in his hand. Lyonesse comes down from her tower. The forty knights are cut down and buried.

failure.body: You ride at him across the meadow, but he is quicker than a man that size should be. He catches your lance under his arm and pulls you out of the saddle. He does not hang you. "Go back to Camelot," he says, "and tell them to send me someone who can wait."

entries.body:
You come upon a giant sitting on a hill above a town, with the town's bell tower in his fist like a stick of celery. The townsfolk are huddled in the square below, looking up.

"I am Dinabutius," he booms. "My brother was the giant of the Mount, whom the High King killed. I want a champion of Arthur's court to fight me, here and now. If none comes, I will squash this town." He shakes the bell tower. The bell clangs. "One champion. That is all I ask."

The mayor of the town comes running up to you. "Please," he gasps. "The giant's brother ate children. Everyone knows it. But this one has never hurt anyone. He is only grieving. And very, very angry."

responses.label: You may accept the giant's challenge and fight him as Arthur's champion.
You may tell the giant the truth about his brother.

entries.body:
The old woman looks at you, and her face hardens. "I know your name," she says. "My Gaheris wrote it on his list. You fought him once." She points at the door with her spindle. "Get out of this hall."

You go. On the shore, the Orkney fishermen watch you as you wait for a boat, and none of them will speak to you, and the wind is very cold.

You come upon an old, old giant sitting on Salisbury Plain with his back against a standing stone. He is grey as the stone itself, with lichen growing in his beard, and he is so still that at first you think he is a stone too. Then he opens one eye.

"Ah," he says slowly. "A small one. I am Gwrgi. I am the last of the giants who built this." He waves a hand at the great ring of stones. "Not here. In Ireland, on the Hill of Killaraus. We carried the stones from Africa on our backs, because they heal. Then a small one called Merlin came and took them, and brought them here, to mark the graves of his king's men." He chuckles, a sound like rocks sliding. "I followed them. I have been sitting here ever since, making sure he put them back right. He did not. That one is upside down." He closes his eye. "Ask me something. I have not been asked anything for four hundred years."

responses.label: You may ask the old giant to tell you the history of the stones.
You may ask the old giant for his counsel on what lies ahead for Britain.

entries.body:
You come to a stone bridge over a deep river, where a fat giant in a leather apron sits on the parapet with his feet dangling in the water. A board beside him reads *TOLL: ONE CHEESE*.

"Good morning," he says, holding out a hand. "I am Cormoran. One cheese, please." You explain that you have no cheese. He looks shocked. "No cheese? Then you cannot cross. That is the rule." He leans closer. "Of course, if you cannot pay, you may play. If you can make me say *yes* three times, you may cross for free. If you cannot," he grins, showing teeth like gravestones, "then you are the cheese."

Behind him, you see a pile of bones under the bridge, and a very large number of cheese rinds.

responses.label: You may try to trick Cormoran into saying yes three times.
You may fight the giant for the right to cross.

entries.body:
You hear the crying from a mile away: a sound like a whole herd of cows bellowing at once. You follow it to a valley where a village lies half flattened, and in the middle of the ruins sits a giant baby, the size of a barn, wearing a nightshirt made of a whole sail and wailing at the top of its lungs.

The villagers are hiding in the church. The priest leans out of the window. "It came over the hill at dawn," he calls. "It is lost. It sat on the mill. It ate the blacksmith's apple tree. When it cries, the windows break." He points up at the mountains, where, very far off, you hear a sound like thunder, but rhythmic, like a voice calling. "Its mother is looking for it," says the priest. "I would much rather she did not find it here."

responses.label: You may carry the giant baby home to its mother in the mountains.
You may calm the giant baby until its mother finds it.

entries.body: You throw ropes into the sea, and haul the drowning monks aboard your ship, one by one.

resolutions.label: rescue the drowning monks from the sea

success.body: You haul out eleven monks, half-drowned, and your crew wraps them in blankets. The pirates, seeing your ship full of rescued monks and a knight in the bow, decide there are easier prizes and sail away. The rescued monks sing a psalm on your deck, soaking wet. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard.

failure.body: You haul out three monks, but the sea is rough and the rope keeps slipping through your cold hands, and the rest are lost. The pirates take the monks' ship and sail away laughing. The three you saved sing a psalm for their brothers on your deck, and you cannot join in.

resolutions.label: pray the monks up out of the sea

success.body: You throw every rope you have over the side and kneel in the bow and pray aloud, and the drowning monks, hearing a prayer they know, swim toward it. You haul out eleven of them, half-drowned, singing. The pirates, seeing a ship full of rescued monks and a knight in the bow, decide there are easier prizes. The monks sing a psalm on your deck, soaking wet. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard.

failure.body: You kneel in the bow and pray aloud. The monks hear you, but the sea is rough. You haul out three. The rest are lost.

entries.body:
You come upon a crowd in a city square, gathered around a great pit. In the pit, chained by the neck to a post, a giant crouches, covered in bites and scratches. A dozen mastiffs are being led down into the pit by their handlers. The crowd is laying bets.

On a balcony above, a baron in red velvet is watching with a cup of wine in his hand. "Baron Brisen," a man beside you says. "He caught the giant in the forest last year. Every Sunday he baits it with dogs. It is very popular." The giant looks up. His eyes are gentle, bewildered and exhausted. He catches sight of you, and something in your face makes him raise one chained hand, very slightly, as if to ask for help.

responses.label: You may free the giant from the pit by force.
You may buy the giant's freedom from the baron.

entries.body: "Your lord has waited long enough, my lady," you say gently. "Let him rest." The queen looks at you for a long time. Then she nods.

resolutions.label: give the dead lord a burial fit for a king's brother

success.body: There is no churchyard for ten miles, so you dig the grave yourself on the hillside above the road, in stony ground, while the queen sings. It takes until nightfall. When it is done, you set the shield at the head of the grave. The queen kneels, and when she stands again, something in her face has eased. "I thought I needed vengeance," she says. "I needed to stop walking." She gives you a silver brooch shaped like a fish.

failure.body: There is no churchyard for ten miles, so you begin to dig the grave yourself in the stony hillside. By nightfall your hands are bleeding and you have barely broken the ground. The queen watches you in silence, then turns the oxen and goes on down the road. "Another knight with a reason," she says. You resolve to learn the use of a spade.

resolutions.label: pray over the dead lord and give his widow comfort

success.body: You kneel beside the cart and pray for the dead man's soul, and for his widow, and for the knight who killed him. At the last, the queen gasps. "You pray for him? For that one?" "For him most of all," you say. She is silent a long while, and then she laughs through her tears. "My husband would have liked you," she says. The next village has a priest, and the lord is buried with bells.

failure.body: You kneel beside the cart and pray. But when you pray for the knight who killed her husband, the queen rounds on you. "You would forgive him? You?" She drives the oxen on, and the black cart rumbles off toward the next knight who might ride by.

entries.body: You ride into the crowd and pull the old woman up onto your saddle. "Enough," you say.

resolutions.label: face down the frightened villagers

success.body: You speak to them from the saddle, with the old woman clinging to your back. You ask which of them has not lost a harvest to hail before, when there was no witch. You ask which of them has prayed on the heath. You ask them what the Grail would say. At last, the rope drops. They go home, sullen and ashamed. The old woman gives you a loaf of bread and a blessing, and goes on praying on the heath, every night, until she dies.

failure.body: You speak to them from the saddle, but they have lost everything, and they want someone to blame. They drag you both down. You are beaten, and the old woman is ducked in the millpond, and lives, but only just.

resolutions.label: hold the mob back with the flat of your sword

success.body: You set the old woman behind you in her own doorway and face the crowd with your sword drawn and turned flat. The first man with a rope comes at you and goes down with a bruise on his arm. The second thinks better of it. The rope drops. You stand in the doorway until the crowd has gone home, sullen and ashamed. The old woman gives you a loaf and a blessing, and goes on praying on the heath.

failure.body: You face the crowd in the doorway with your sword flat, but a stone takes you on the temple. When you wake, the old woman has been ducked in the millpond. She lives, but only just.

entries.body: You bow deeply. "Lady," you say, "I am honoured beyond words. But I cannot love where I cannot speak." Tryamour's face goes very still.

resolutions.label: refuse her without giving offence

success.body: You speak of honour, and of the High King's court, where a knight's life is lived in the open, and of how any love you gave her would be a poor, half-hidden thing. You speak with such care that, at the end, the fay lady laughs softly. "You are the first," she says, "to say no to me kindly." She touches your forehead with one cool finger. "Go, then. And when the day comes that you need something from under the hill, say my name once. Only once." She and her pavilion fade like mist on the water.

failure.body: You speak of honour, and the High King's court. Tryamour's face goes colder with every word. "So," she says, "a mortal refuses me." She lifts her hand. When you come to your senses, you are lying in the river, and your horse is gone, and it is winter.

entries.body: "I will do it," you say. Dafydd smiles at you with pure relief. "Thank you," he says. They hang him. You ride to Ludlow, and find the third ash tree past the mill, and dig.

resolutions.label: dig up the silver unseen

success.body: It is there: a leather bag with forty silver marks, heavy in your hands. You ride away without going near the bakehouse. The silver buys you a new horse, new harness and a great deal of wine. You do not go back to Ludlow. Sometimes, when you eat bread, you think of a thin woman with flour on her hands.

failure.body: It is there: a leather bag of silver. As you lift it out, a small, thin woman with flour to her elbows steps out from behind the mill. "Dafydd's brother told me he had buried it," she says. "I have been watching these trees for a week." She takes the bag out of your hands. She does not say anything else. She does not have to.

entries.body: You wait until the monks file out to sing their office. The crown is black with age, but where your thumb rubs it, it shines red gold, and there are stones in it the size of hazelnuts. Evelake has not stirred.

resolutions.label: lift the crown and slip out unseen

success.body: You slide the crown under your cloak and walk out past the chanting monks, bowing your head as you go. Nobody looks up. You are a league away before the bell starts ringing behind you, fast and furious, and it keeps ringing until you are out of earshot. The crown fetches a very good price from a goldsmith in Winchester who asks no questions. You do not sleep well for a week.

failure.body: You slide the crown under your cloak. "Put it back," says Evelake, quite clearly, from the bed. He has not moved. "It was taken from me once before. It did not go well for the man who took it." You put it back. When you turn, the abbot is standing in the doorway, and his face tells you that the old man was not the only one watching. The monks do not raise a hand to you, but they walk you to the gate in silence, and the bell tolls all the while.

resolutions.label: climb in by the bell-tower at night and take it

success.body: You wait until the abbey is dark and climb the bell-tower by the ivy, and come down the ladder inside the church without a sound. The crown is on the altar where it always is, beside the sleeping old king. You take it and go out the way you came. The bell rings as you reach the ground, but you are already running. The crown fetches a fortune in Winchester. You try not to wonder whether the bell rang by itself.

failure.body: You wait until dark and climb the bell-tower by the ivy, and put your foot on the bell-rope by mistake. The bell booms out over the whole valley. Every monk in the abbey is in the church with a candle before you reach the altar. They do not raise a hand to you. They simply watch you climb back down.

entries.body: You spur your horse through the rain and smoke toward the burning stand.

resolutions.label: pull the ladies from the burning stand

success.body: You ride your horse straight at the railing and break it down, and the ladies stream out through the gap, coughing and screaming. You go back twice for those who have fallen. When the last is out, the stand collapses behind you in a roar of sparks. A lady in a scorched blue gown throws her arms round your neck and kisses you in front of the whole tournament. She is, you learn later, the Countess of Cornwall. Her husband sends you a gold cup, and a slightly stiff letter.

failure.body: You ride your horse at the railing, but your horse, maddened by the fire, refuses and throws you. You get up and break the railing with your hands, burning them. The ladies get out. You are the last to leave the stand, and your surcoat is on fire.

resolutions.label: go into the fire on foot and break the railing

success.body: Your horse will not go near the flames, so you leave it and run into the stand on foot, with your cloak soaked in a horse-trough over your head. You tear down the railing with your hands. The ladies stream out through the gap. You go back twice for those who have fallen. When the last is out, the stand collapses behind you. A lady in a scorched blue gown throws her arms round your neck.

failure.body: You run into the stand with your wet cloak over your head, and the smoke is too thick to see through. You get two ladies out before your cloak catches fire and you are dragged clear yourself.

entries.body: You leave your horse and wade into the reeds, following the sound of fighting.

resolutions.label: find the lost knight in the fog-bound marsh

success.body: You follow the shouting, and the splashing, and at last you find Sir Griflet, up to his waist in water, fighting three Picts with his back to a willow. You come at them from behind. They flee into the fog. Griflet embraces you. "Tenth time I have been rescued this year," he says. "I am keeping count." You lead him back to his squire, who weeps.

failure.body: You follow the shouting into the fog, and lose your way, and wander for hours among the reeds. When the fog lifts, the battle is over, and you are a mile from anywhere.

resolutions.label: call the lost knight through the fog with his own horn-call

success.body: You ask the squire what his master's horn-call is, and he tells you: three short, one long. You blow it, again and again, into the fog, as a knight's own call to his own men. At last, faintly, from far out in the reeds, it is answered. You follow it, and find Sir Griflet up to his waist in water with his back to a willow and three Picts round him. They flee at your coming. "Tenth time I have been rescued this year," says Griflet.

failure.body: You blow Sir Griflet's horn-call into the fog, three short and one long. The Picts have heard it too, and they know what it means: a knight, alone, calling. They come to it out of the reeds from three sides, and you fight them knee-deep in water until your own men find you.

entries.body: "Teach me," you say. Mother Gwyar grins toothlessly. "Put your boots by the fire," she says. "You will be here a while."

resolutions.label: learn the old trapper's lore

success.body: You stay with her for three days. She shows you how to read the clouds, and the ants, and the way a spider spins its web before a storm. She shows you how to set a snare that will not break a hare's neck, and how to find water on a hillside by looking at the ferns. On the first day, it rains at noon. On the third day, you tell her it will rain at dusk, and it does. She cackles. "Now you know one thing," she says. "Only another thousand to go."

failure.body: You stay with her for three days, and at the end of it you can tell a raven from a crow, and not much else. She shakes her head. "You listen with your ears," she says. "You have to listen with your feet." It rains at noon on the first day, as she said it would, and you are caught in it.

resolutions.label: prove your hardiness to the old woman

success.body: "First," she says, "you sleep out. No fire. No cloak." You spend the night in the forest in the rain, with nothing but your shirt, and in the morning, she finds you shivering under a holly bush and looks satisfied. "Good," she says. "Now you know what a deer knows." She teaches you for the rest of the day, and you learn more than you thought possible.

failure.body: "First," she says, "you sleep out. No fire. No cloak." You last until midnight, and then you creep back to her hut and knock on the door. She lets you in without a word, and gives you broth, and does not teach you anything at all.

entries.body: You take the letter with thanks. Two nights later, alone in an inn, you hold it over a candle and ease the seal loose with a hot knife.

resolutions.label: read the letter and reseal it without trace

notes: Gain 1 Rank of Divinity if you warn the High King of this letter at the next City you visit

success.body: The letter is short. *Mother, it is as you said. My father knows what I am. He has not yet decided what to do about it. I have begun to make friends. Burn this. M.* You reseal it perfectly and carry it to Orkney, and nobody is any the wiser. But from then on you watch Mordred at court, and you notice how many friends he has begun to make.

failure.body: The seal cracks in two. You try to mend it with candle wax, and it looks exactly like a seal that has been mended with candle wax. When you give it to Queen Morgause, she looks at it for a long moment and then at you. "My son will be interested to hear of this," she says. You never learn what the letter said. Mordred, when you next see him, is as warm as ever. That is what frightens you.

entries.body: You dismount and give the porter the bread from your saddlebag. He looks at it for a long time, as though he has forgotten what it is.

resolutions.label: bless the porter and the dead castle

success.body: He eats. As he eats, he begins to weep, and as he weeps, you pray: for him, for the castle, for the wasted land. When he has finished the bread, a little green shoot has come up through the cracked flagstone at his feet. "I had forgotten," he says, "what it was to be hungry." He gets up, takes off his rusted armour and walks out of the castle without looking back. You never know where he goes.

failure.body: He eats, but the bread turns to dust in his mouth. He looks at you with his empty eyes. "Nothing here eats," he says again. You ride away over the dead fields.

entries.body:
Taliesin looks pleased. He stands up on the ferry-rope, balancing like a bird, and sings.

He sings of Ceridwen's cauldron, and the three drops that fell on a boy's thumb and made him wise. He sings of the flight across the world as hare and fish and bird, and the witch who followed as hound and otter and hawk. He sings of the grain of wheat and the black hen, and the leather bag on the sea, and the prince who opened it and said *What a radiant brow*. His voice is high and clear and very old. When he stops, the ferryman is awake, and the heron has gone, and it is evening. He takes you across in silence, and at the far side, he touches your forehead with one finger. "Remember," he says.
You walk the avenue with the hermit, touching each stone. They are cold as ice. At the centre of the circle, you find it.

resolutions.label: restore the silent stones

success.body: A black stone has been set in the centre of the circle, where no stone should be. It is warm, and it hums with a low, ugly note that drowns out the others. You dig round it with your hands, and heave, and topple it, and roll it down the hill into the frozen loch, where it breaks the ice and sinks. At once, the frost melts. The stones begin to sing, a high, clear note, all together. The hermit weeps. He gives you a small grey stone from the circle, warm as a hand. "It will always know where the Grail is," he says. "It will not always tell you."

failure.body: You find a black stone in the centre of the circle and try to move it, and it burns your hands like ice. You cannot shift it. The stones stay silent.

resolutions.label: heave the black stone out of the circle

success.body: It is a black stone in the centre of the circle, where no stone should be, humming a low, ugly note. You wrap your hands in your cloak against the cold that burns, and dig round it, and heave, and heave again, until it topples and rolls down the hill into the frozen loch. At once the frost melts. The stones begin to sing. The hermit gives you a small grey stone from the circle, warm as a hand. "It will always know where the Grail is," he says.

failure.body: You wrap your hands and heave at the black stone. It does not move. Your hands are frostbitten for a month.

entries.body: You wrap the book in your cloak and carry it down to your boat as the first drops of rain begin to fall.

resolutions.label: bring the rotting book through the storm

success.body: The storm catches you halfway to the mainland. You lie on the book in the bottom of the boat while the waves break over you, and let your own back take the rain. At dawn, you reach the shore, soaked to the bone, and the book is dry. Sister Hild takes it to a convent where the nuns know how to mend old books. They copy it. You are allowed to read one page, and you do not tell anyone what it says.

failure.body: The storm catches you halfway to the mainland, and a wave washes the book out of your arms. You dive for it, and catch it, but half its pages are gone to the sea.

resolutions.label: keep the book dry with a charm against water

success.body: You do not trust the boat. You lay the book on the altar-stone of the ruined church and speak over it the old words that keep a thing dry, the ones the monks of the islands used for their books, and wrap it in your cloak. The storm catches you halfway to the mainland, and the waves break over the boat, and the book is dry when you land. The nuns of the mainland copy it. You are allowed to read one page.

failure.body: You speak the old words over the book, and wrap it, and set out. The storm catches you, and the charm, it turns out, keeps water out and not in. The cloak fills like a bucket.

entries.body: "You have waited long enough," you say, and kneel on the wet rock. The ghost looks down at you with something between hope and scorn. "Priests have tried," he says.

resolutions.label: pray for the soul of King Uther

success.body: You pray until your knees are numb and the rain has stopped. Somewhere in the middle of it, the ghost kneels beside you. You hear him say the words he wanted to say, not to Arthur or to Igraine, but to Heaven. When you open your eyes the cliff is empty. A little way off, a fisherman's wife is staring at you. "The crying's stopped," she says. "Twenty years he's cried on that cliff, and it's stopped." The village sends you away with bread, cheese and a great deal of gratitude.

failure.body: You pray until your knees are numb, but the words keep sticking. The ghost watches you with his son's eyes, and you cannot stop thinking about what he did. At last he turns away. "You judge me," he says. "They all do." He walks back to the edge of the cliff and resumes his watch. You ride away with his grief heavy on you, and it does not lift for many days.

resolutions.label: speak the old words that release a bound spirit

success.body: You draw a circle on the rock with the point of your sword and speak the words an old wise woman once taught you, for those who cannot leave a place. The wind drops. The ghost looks down at the circle, and then at you. "It was only a knot," he says, wonderingly, "and I could not untie it." He steps across the circle and is gone. The fisherfolk of the village give you a basket of smoked mackerel and their prayers.

failure.body: You draw a circle on the rock and speak the old words, but you stumble over the third line, and the wind snatches it away. The ghost looks at you with his son's eyes. "Even the witches cannot help me," he says, and turns back to the sea. You ride away with the knot still tied.

entries.body: You watch the fool in the crown, pardoning a poacher and paying a widow's debts from the treasury. You watch the king at the well, telling a joke about a dog that is not funny. "The people love him," you say. "Let us leave well alone."

resolutions.label: keep the fool on the throne

success.body: You and the steward spread it about that the king had a vision at the fair and has become a new man. Nobody who has seen the new king at work is surprised. The real king is quite happy in motley, and falls in love with a kitchen maid, and nobody minds. The fool reigns for twelve years and is remembered as the best king that castle ever had. You are given a manor, which the fool says is only fair, since you gave him a kingdom.

failure.body: You and the steward spread it about that the king has become a new man. Unfortunately, the king's brother does not believe it, and marches on the castle with a hundred men. The fool, being a fool, surrenders at once. The king, being a fool, does too. You flee over the wall.

resolutions.label: secure the castle for the new king

success.body: You go to the captain of the guard, who has liked the new king better from the first day, and together you change the watchwords, move the old king's loyal men to the far towers, and set a guard on the gate against the king's brother. When the brother comes with a hundred men, he finds the gate shut and the walls manned. He goes home. The fool reigns for twelve years and is remembered as the best king that castle ever had.

failure.body: You change the watchwords and set a guard on the gate. The king's brother comes with a hundred men, and the captain of the guard, after a night's thought, opens the gate for him. You flee over the wall.

entries.body: "We will find him," you say. Gwenllian gives you a brief, fierce nod and starts down the hill. The field is wide, and the light is going.

resolutions.label: search the battlefield among the dead and wounded

success.body: You search until long after dark, by torchlight, turning over the dead and listening for the living. It is grim work, and Gwenllian does not flinch from any of it. At last, in a ditch at the far edge of the field, you find a young man with a broken leg and a head wound, alive, who opens his eyes and says, "Gwen? You're not supposed to be here." She weeps and laughs at once. You carry Rhys home between you. Their father, when he sees them, does not say a word about what is proper for girls.

failure.body: You search until long after dark, turning over the dead. The work is grim, and the smell is worse, and by midnight you are sick and shaking. You do not find Rhys. In the morning, Gwenllian goes on alone. You leave the field with a fever and the faces of the dead in your dreams.

resolutions.label: track the wounded who crawled from the field

success.body: You see what she has not: a trail of blood and flattened grass leading away from the field to a stream, where the wounded have crawled to drink. You follow it into a hazel wood, and there, lying by the water with a broken leg, is a young man who looks just like her. "Gwen?" he says. "You're not supposed to be here." She throws her arms around him. Their father, when he hears the story, sends you a good sword.

failure.body: You follow a trail of blood away from the field into a hazel wood, and find a camp of wounded men there, and none of them is Rhys. By the time you have questioned them all, it is dark, and Gwenllian has gone back to the field alone. You never learn whether she found him.

entries.body: You tie your horse and start up the mountainside toward the ledge, through the falling stones.

resolutions.label: lead the pilgrims down the storm-swept mountain

success.body: You find a way that the water has not found yet, across the scree and down a gully, and you rope the pilgrims together and lead them down it, one careful step at a time. It takes all night. At dawn, you are at the bottom, and the old abbess counts them, twice, and all twenty are there. She embraces you, and blesses you, and says that she will pray for you at Saint David's every day she lives.

failure.body: You find a way down the scree, and rope the pilgrims together, but halfway down, the scree moves. Three of them are swept away. The rest reach the bottom, weeping. The abbess does not blame you. She blames the mountain.

resolutions.label: rope them together and command the descent

success.body: You climb up to the ledge and take charge as if the pilgrims were a company of foot. You rope them together, the strong between the weak, and give each a place and a task, and bring them down the gully in good order, one careful step at a time, calling the steps aloud. At dawn, the abbess counts them, twice. All twenty are there.

failure.body: You rope them together and call the steps aloud, but the wind takes your voice, and the pilgrims stop and start at different times, and the rope jerks, and one of them falls, and takes three with him.

entries.body: "The lady is right," you say to Beaumains. "This is no work for a kitchen boy. Go home before you are hurt." Beaumains shakes his head, still smiling. "I was sent," he says. "I will go on."

resolutions.label: persuade Beaumains to turn back

success.body: You talk to him long and earnestly about the dangers of the road. He listens with great courtesy. Then he says, "Thank you," and goes on. Lynette looks at you with new respect. "At least you tried," she says. "You may ride with us, if you like, to see him killed." You do ride with them, and he is not killed. By the end of the week you are both very glad you came.

failure.body: You talk to him long and earnestly about the dangers of the road. Beaumains listens with great courtesy, then picks you up by your belt, sets you on your horse, and turns its head the other way. "Thank you," he says, and goes on. Lynette laughs so hard she nearly falls off her palfrey.

resolutions.label: prove the kitchen boy unfit by fighting him

success.body: You draw and challenge him, meaning to disarm him gently. You never manage it. He fights like no kitchen boy you have ever seen, and after a long, hard bout he stops, lowers his rusty sword, and says, "You are good. Very good. I am glad we are not enemies." Lynette is staring at him with her mouth open. You shake his hand. He is the best swordsman you have ever faced, and you tell him so.

failure.body: You draw and challenge him, meaning to disarm him gently. Instead he disarms you, not gently at all, and your sword lands in a bramble bush. "I am sorry," he says, and he truly is. Lynette laughs until she weeps. You resolve not to judge a knight by his apron.

entries.body: You spur your horse toward the golden armour.

resolutions.label: fight your way to the young king's side

success.body: You cut your way through the melee and reach the young king just as his horse is killed under him. You pull him up onto your saddle, and ride him back to his own lines, and he takes a fresh horse and goes straight back into the fight. At the end of the day, the rebel kings are broken, and the young king comes to find you. "You carried me," he says. "I will not forget." You are made a knight of his household.

failure.body: You cut your way toward the young king, but you are knocked from your horse halfway there. You spend the rest of the battle fighting on foot, in the mud, with no idea who is winning.

resolutions.label: rally the young king's scattered knights to him

success.body: You do not cut your way to the young king. You ride along the back of his line, where his knights are being pushed back, shouting his name and pointing at the golden armour, and they see it and rally, and you lead them back into the melee in a wedge. You reach him just as his horse is killed. His knights close round him. At the end of the day, the rebel kings are broken, and he comes to find you.

failure.body: You ride along the back of the line shouting his name, and nobody can hear you over the battle. You are knocked from your horse and spend the rest of the day on foot, in the mud.

entries.body: You wade to the abbey door and stand on the threshold. "Brother Anselm," you call. A grey figure rises out of the water in the nave.

resolutions.label: lay the drowned abbot's spirit to rest

success.body: He is an old man, dripping, with a gold chalice in his hands. "I could not save it," he says. "I could not save any of it." You tell him that he tried, and that God knows it, and you pray with him until the tide begins to turn. At the last moment, he holds out the chalice. "Take it," he says. "Give it to a church that is not under the sea." You take it, and run. When you look back, the abbey is under the water, and the ghost is gone.

failure.body: He is an old man, dripping, with a gold chalice in his hands. You begin to pray, but the tide turns, and you have to run. He is still in the nave when the sea comes in.

resolutions.label: read the abbot's name from the drowned stones and speak it

success.body: You find the abbey's foundation stone in the mud by the door, and scrape it clean, and read the names on it, and among them is his: Anselm, abbot, the year of the flood. You speak it aloud into the nave. A grey figure rises out of the water, holding a chalice. "Someone remembers," it says. You pray with it until the tide begins to turn. At the last moment, it holds out the chalice. When you look back, the abbey is under the water, and the ghost is gone.

failure.body: You scrape the foundation stone clean, and the names are worn away. You speak the wrong name into the nave. The water rises faster than it should.

entries.body: You ride with the girl to the village and gather everyone left: old men, women, children, a priest. "They will come tonight," you say. "We will be ready."

resolutions.label: rally the village to hold against the Saxon raid

success.body: You spend the day teaching grandmothers to throw nets, boys to sling stones and the priest to ring the bell when he sees torches. You block the lane with upturned boats and pile seaweed on the thatch so it will not burn. When the Saxons come up from the beach at midnight, they walk into a village that fights back from every doorway. They lose five men in the lane and go back to their ship in disgust. At dawn, the village cheers you until your ears ring. The girl, whose name is Morwenna, ties a fishing charm to your bridle.

failure.body: You spend the day teaching grandmothers to throw nets and boys to sling stones. When the Saxons come at midnight, the barricade of boats holds for a while, but then the thatch catches, and the villagers break and run for the church. You hold the church door until dawn, when the Saxons, laden with plunder, go back to the sea.

entries.body: "I think he should come," you say. Lynette rolls her eyes. "Two fools, then," she says. Beaumains gives you a look of such plain gratitude that you feel embarrassed. The black knight on the bridge lowers his lance.

resolutions.label: stand beside Beaumains against the knight on the bridge

success.body: The black knight comes at Beaumains first, sneering, and Beaumains, to your astonishment, beats him off the bridge in four strokes. A second knight comes out of the trees, and you take him. When both are sitting in the river, Lynette looks at the kitchen boy for a long moment. "You were lucky," she says. "You both were." But she rides a little closer to him after that. At the next crossroads Beaumains grips your hand. "I will not forget you," he says. You have the feeling that he means it.

failure.body: The black knight comes at Beaumains first, and Beaumains beats him off the bridge in four strokes. A second knight comes out of the trees, and he beats you. You lie in the river while the kitchen boy chases him off with his rusty sword. "Two fools," says Lynette, "and one of them wet." Beaumains helps you out without a word and lends you his apron to dry your face.

resolutions.label: scout the road ahead so Beaumains is not ambushed

success.body: You ride ahead and find what Lynette did not know: the Red Knight's men have set three ambushes along the road, at the bridge, the ford and the wood. You bring Beaumains round them by sheep-paths, so that he meets each knight alone and on his own terms. He beats them all. By the end, Lynette has stopped calling him a kitchen boy and has started calling him "sir", in a very small voice. Beaumains thanks you, and rides on to his sister's castle to face the Red Knight alone.

failure.body: You ride ahead to scout, and ride straight into the Red Knight's men waiting in the wood. They take your horse and your sword and tie you to a tree. You are rescued two days later by a big fair-haired young man in an apron, who says nothing about it and does not have to.

entries.body: You draw your sword and step between the mare and the soldiers in red and black. "She is the king's," you say.

resolutions.label: drive off Mordred's men from the king's mare

success.body: You call to the old king's men among the ring, and they come to your side, and together you drive Mordred's soldiers back across the plain. The Saxons, who have no quarrel with a horse, wander away. When the plain is clear, the old mare comes of her own accord and stands beside you, and the groom leads her home.

failure.body: You call to the old king's men, but there are not enough of them. Mordred's soldiers throw a rope over the mare, and drag her away screaming, and there is nothing you can do.

entries.body: "Grapple her!" you shout. "We are going aboard!"

resolutions.label: storm Mordred's flagship

success.body: You lead your crew across the grappling ropes onto Mordred's flagship, and fight your way to its helm, and turn it aside, so that its ram strikes nothing but water. Mordred is not aboard. His captain surrenders. When you bring the red and black sails down, the Saxon ships see it, and flee. The old king watches from his own deck, and lifts his sword to you.

failure.body: You lead your crew across the grappling ropes, but Mordred's men are the best in his fleet. You are driven back. The ram strikes the old king's ship, and it is holed, but it does not sink.

resolutions.label: call on Mordred's rowers to rise against their masters

success.body: You leap onto the flagship's rowing deck, not its quarterdeck, and shout to the rowers chained at the oars that the old king frees every slave who turns against Mordred today. They stop rowing. The flagship slews round, dead in the water, a length from the old king's ship. Its captain surrenders. When the red and black sails come down, the Saxon ships flee.

failure.body: You leap onto the rowing deck and shout to the rowers that the old king will free them. They are Frisians, and do not understand a word of British. The overseer does. He brings his whip down across your face, and you are driven back over the side before the ram strikes.

entries.body: You leave your sword with the monk and walk into the chapel with your hands open. "Good evening," you say. "I hear you have something to sell."

resolutions.label: trick the brigands out of the relic

success.body: You tell them you are a merchant, and that the casket is worth nothing, because everyone knows gold on a relic is only gilt, but that you will buy it off them for a silver penny as a curiosity. You show them the silver penny. They look at the casket, and at the penny, and at each other. One of them bites the casket. "Gilt," he says, disgusted. It is not gilt. It is solid gold. But you have made them doubt, and they sell it to you for three pennies. You carry it back to the monk, who faints.

failure.body: You tell them you are a merchant and the casket is worthless gilt. One of them bites it. "Gold," he says. "Solid gold." They look at you with new interest, and at your purse. You leave without the casket, or your purse.

entries.body: You climb down the rocks and wade into the cave. The water is cold and green, and the bells are very loud, and under them, you hear the singing.

resolutions.label: resist the sea-singer's enchantment

success.body: At the back of the cave, on a rock above the water, sits a woman with seaweed in her hair, singing, and at her feet sits a young fisherman, staring at her with empty eyes. The song pulls at you too. You stuff your ears with wax from a candle stub and walk straight to the boy, and lift him, and carry him out. The singer stops singing. As you go, she calls after you, very sadly, "They never stay." The boy wakes up on the beach in his father's arms and remembers nothing.

failure.body: At the back of the cave sits a woman with seaweed in her hair, singing, and you forget, for a while, why you came. When you come to your senses, the tide has turned, and you are sitting on the rock at her feet beside the boy. You have to swim for it, and you drag him out, but you are half-drowned by the time you reach the beach.

resolutions.label: swim in with your ears stopped with wax

success.body: You stuff your ears with wax from a candle stub until you can hear nothing but your own heart. Then you swim into the cold green cave and do not look at the woman on the rock. You find the fisherman's son by feel, sitting at her feet, and haul him into the water and out through the cave mouth, with her mouth moving silently behind you. He wakes on the beach in his father's arms and remembers nothing.

failure.body: You stuff your ears with wax and swim into the cave. The water is colder than any water should be. Halfway in, your limbs go numb, and you have to turn back. The bells ring on.

entries.body: "Do not," you say. "Not on a dare. Not like this." The young knight looks at you, and at the tomb, and back.

resolutions.label: talk the young knight out of his folly

success.body: You tell him that the knight who sees the Grail will not need to be dared into anything, and that pride is the surest way to lose the quest. You tell him what the hermits say: that the humble will see it, not the brave. He listens, and at last he laughs, shakily. "My friend will call me a coward," he says. "Your friend," you say, "is not here." He rides away with you. That night, you hear, the lid of the tomb moved of its own accord and closed.

failure.body: You tell him that pride is the surest way to lose the quest. He flushes. "You think I am not worthy," he says, and climbs into the tomb. The lid falls. You pull him out with a broken arm.

resolutions.label: take his dare yourself, and win it without the tomb

success.body: "Your friend dared you to lie in it," you say. "Very well. I dare your friend to watch you not do it, and then tell everyone you did." The young knight stares at you. Then he laughs. When his friend comes back, the young knight tells him he lay in the tomb and saw a vision of angels. The friend is terribly impressed. That night, the lid of the tomb moves of its own accord and closes.

failure.body: You suggest he simply tell his friend he did it. He is shocked. "Lie?" he says. "On the Grail quest?" He climbs into the tomb to prove his honesty, and the lid falls, and you pull him out with a broken arm.

entries.body: You climb up to the ledge and kneel with the pilgrims in the rain. The abbess smiles at you and begins the psalm again.

resolutions.label: pray with the pilgrims through the storm

success.body: You pray and sing with them all night. The storm roars. Stones fall on either side of the ledge, but none on it. At dawn, the rain stops as if a door had closed, and the sun comes out, and the water drains away from the path below. The pilgrims walk down singing. The abbess says it is a miracle. You are not sure. You are sure that you have never been so cold, or so happy.

failure.body: You pray and sing with them all night. At dawn, a stone falls on the ledge and breaks your leg. The storm passes. The pilgrims carry you down.

entries.body: "Then we will follow it together," you say. Eustace picks up his bow, looks at it, and leaves it lying in the grass. "I will not need it," he says. You go into the old forest on foot.

resolutions.label: follow the white stag into the old forest

success.body: The stag leads you through the forest all day, always just ahead, never quite out of sight. At dusk, you come to a ruined chapel with a spring in its floor. The stag drinks from the spring and vanishes. Inside the chapel, an old priest is waiting for you. "He sent you," he says. "He always does." He baptises Eustace in the spring. Eustace stays, and becomes the priest's helper. When you leave, he blesses you, and you feel the blessing like warm water.

failure.body: The stag leads you through the forest all day. At dusk, you lose it. You and Eustace sit down on a log, exhausted and lost. "Perhaps," says the forester at last, "it was not meant for you." In the morning he goes on alone. You find your way out of the forest a day later.

resolutions.label: keep faith with the stag through a night of trial

success.body: The stag leads you to a rock in the middle of the forest and stops there. When you come near, it vanishes. Night falls. You and Eustace kneel on the rock, and all night long you hear things moving in the forest around you: wolves, and worse. Neither of you moves. At dawn, the stag is back, standing on the rock beside you, with the cross of light between its antlers. It bows its head to Eustace, then to you, and walks away. Eustace laughs aloud. "It is enough," he says. "It is enough."

failure.body: The stag leads you to a rock and vanishes. Night falls. All night long you hear things moving in the forest. Toward midnight, your courage fails, and you draw your sword and rush into the dark. When you come back, shamefaced, Eustace is still kneeling. You do not see the stag again. He does.

entries.body: "Wait," you say. "Look at the sky. Look at the hills." You point to the west, where another black cloud is gathering over the heath.

resolutions.label: read the weather and prove it no witch's doing

success.body: You show them how the storms come over the hills from the sea, and gather on the heath where the air is cold, and break over the village. You tell them it has happened for a hundred years and will happen for a hundred more. Then you show them where to plant a windbreak of hawthorn and hazel along the edge of the heath, to break the hail. They listen. They let the old woman go. The next spring, they plant the hedge. It is still there.

failure.body: You show them the clouds gathering over the heath, and at that very moment, the old woman looks up at them and mutters something, and the hail begins again. Nobody listens to you after that.

entries.body: You walk out across the plain, looking at the ground, listening. The plain is chalk, and chalk, you know, is full of holes.

resolutions.label: find the cave's other entrance

success.body: Half a mile away, you find a clump of hawthorn where the ground dips and the grass is greener. Pushing through, you find a narrow crack in the chalk, with a breath of cool air coming out of it and, faintly, the sound of bleating. You squeeze in and follow the passage down to a cavern where forty sheep are milling round a dog. You lead them out through the crack, one at a time, all afternoon. The shepherd weeps and dances. He tells everyone in the village that you have the gift of finding.

failure.body: You walk out across the plain looking for another way in, and walk until dark, and find nothing but a very large number of rabbit holes. When you come back, the shepherd and his brothers are lowering a ladder.

entries.body: You dismount and string your own bow. Rhian grins and stands up. Bran looks aghast.

resolutions.label: outshoot the huntress

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: She shoots first, and hits a knot on a tree at a hundred paces. You shoot second and split her arrow down the middle. The forest goes silent. Rhian stares at the tree. Then she turns to you with a look you have never seen on anyone's face before. "Nobody has ever done that," she says. Bran, very quietly, rides away. That night, by her fire, Rhian tells you she did not mean it about marrying the man who could outshoot her. "But I might," she says, "if you asked."

failure.body: She shoots first and hits a knot on a tree at a hundred paces. You shoot second and hit the tree. The wrong tree. Rhian laughs so hard she has to sit down. "Better than Bran," she says generously. "Just."

entries.body:
"Tell me," you say, "the oldest thing you know." The eagle is quiet a long time. Then it speaks.

"Before the kings, there was a salmon in the Llyn Llyw that knew everything, because it had swum there since the first water fell. Before the salmon, there was the Stag of Rhedynfre, who saw an acorn become an oak and the oak become a stump. Before the stag, there was nothing but the sea and the stones and a voice over the water." It ruffles its white feathers. "The voice is the oldest thing I know. I heard it once, when I was young. I think the vessel you are all chasing is only a cup that it drank from." It closes its eyes. "Go down now. I am tired." You go down the mountain with the wind at your back, feeling very young.
You look at the dust cloud, and at the girl, and you make up your mind. "Your father will pay well for you," you say. Mererid's hand tightens on the sword.

resolutions.label: take the baron's daughter from the highwayman

success.body: Jack fights you, and he is good, but he is fighting with one arm round Mererid. You disarm him and pull her off the horse. She screams, and kicks, and bites your hand. Jack flees. The baron's men arrive and take her from you, and the baron pays you a fat purse of silver and a fine sword. Mererid does not look at you once. You hear, the following year, that she is widowed already, and very rich, and has put a price on your head.

failure.body: Jack fights you, and Mererid fights you too, and she is better with a sword than he is. When you wake up in the lane, they are gone, and the baron's men are standing over you, asking what happened. You tell them. They laugh.

resolutions.label: ride them down before they reach the church

success.body: You wheel your horse and gallop after them. They are two on one horse, and you are one, and you catch them a mile short of Llanfair. You seize the girl's bridle-arm and drag her across to your own saddle while Jack shouts and curses. When the baron's men come up, you hand her over. The baron pays you a fat purse and a fine sword. Mererid does not look at you once.

failure.body: You gallop after them, but Mererid is a better rider than Jack, and she takes the reins and leads you through a ford and a bog and a gorse thicket. You come out of the gorse torn and alone, and hear the church bell ringing at Llanfair.

entries.body: You stand very still in the middle of the ring of columns and listen.

resolutions.label: discern the nature of the singing voices

success.body: You listen until you can hear each voice. They are not one goddess. They are hundreds of people, all the people who ever prayed in this place, to whatever god they had, and the wind has kept their voices. You tell the hermit. He is quiet a long time. "Then I will add mine," he says, and begins to sing, and the voices sing with him.

failure.body: You listen until the voices fill your head, and then you cannot stop hearing them, even when you have ridden away. It is a week before they fade.

resolutions.label: listen with a hermit's patience, day and night

success.body: You sit in the middle of the temple for a day and a night without food, and listen, until you can hear each voice apart. They are not one goddess. They are all the people who ever prayed in this place, to whatever god they had, and the wind has kept their voices. You tell the hermit. "Then I will add mine," he says, and begins to sing, and the voices sing with him.

failure.body: You sit and listen for a day and a night, and the voices fill your head until you cannot stop hearing them. It is a week before they fade.

entries.body: "I will joust with you," you say, "but I will not let you win." Griflet looks shocked. "I should hope not," he says. "What would be the good of that?"

resolutions.label: joust with Sir Griflet

success.body: Griflet has practised well. His lance takes your shield squarely, and yours takes his, and both shatter, and you both stay in the saddle. You try again. On the third pass, your lance catches him just below the gorget, and he goes over his horse's tail into the grass. He lies there looking at the sky. "Well," he says eventually, "that is nine, then, still." But he is laughing. You ride with him to the next town and stand him a supper. The next week you hear that he beat a knight at Carlisle, and has gone home.

failure.body: Griflet has practised well. His lance takes you squarely, and you go over your horse's tail into the grass. He is so delighted he gets down and helps you up and embraces you. "Ten!" he says. "Ten!" He rides off toward Camelot singing. You are left in the field with a bruised back and the wooden post, which seems to be looking at you.

resolutions.label: fight him on foot instead, sword to sword

success.body: "A joust is ten courses of luck," you say. "Let us fight on foot, and see who is better." Griflet is delighted. You fight in the field for an hour, and he is better than any knight of nine victories has a right to be. At last you beat his sword down and he yields, laughing. "Nine," he says. "Still nine. But it was a good fight." He rides home the next week anyway. He says he has learned enough.

failure.body: "Let us fight on foot," you say. Griflet is delighted, and fights like a man who has practised on a post for three years, which he has. He beats you soundly. "Ten!" he cries. He rides home singing.

entries.body: You wait until dark, and draw your sword.

resolutions.label: rescue the captives from the Saxon shrine

success.body: At midnight, the Saxons are asleep round their fires. You go into the temple on foot, cut the captives free, and give them the Saxons' own spears. The four of you are out of the clearing before anyone wakes. At dawn, you hear the drums start, and stop, and a great roar of Saxon anger. The captives laugh and weep. One of them is a priest, and he blesses you all the way home.

failure.body: At midnight, you go into the temple, but the priest in the wolfskin is not asleep. He howls, and the Saxons wake. You fight your way out, alone.

resolutions.label: break the Saxons' feast with a sudden charge

success.body: You do not wait for dark. You wait for the feast, when the Saxons are drunk and singing round the idol, and then you ride straight into the temple clearing at a gallop, shouting, scattering fires and men and wolfskins. In the confusion, you cut the three captives free and pull one up behind you, and the other two run beside your stirrups into the forest. At dawn, you hear the drums start, and stop.

failure.body: You ride into the clearing at a gallop, and your horse shies at the fire, and throws you at the foot of the idol. You spend the night tied to the stake beside the captives until the old king's men find you.

entries.body: You look at the queen at the stake, and at the executioner's torch, and at the king who cannot watch. You draw your sword and run toward the queen.

resolutions.label: cut the queen free from the stake

success.body: You reach her as the riders come out of the woods, and cut her chains with one blow, and lift her onto your horse, and ride for the trees. The riders of Benwick close round you, and carry you both away. Behind you, in the crush at the stake, the killing has begun. You will learn later who died. The queen, on your saddle, is holding onto you very tightly. "Thank you," she whispers. "God forgive us all." She gives you a necklace of pearls from the lake, which she has worn since her wedding.

failure.body: You run toward the queen, and the guard catches you before you reach the stake. You are held down in the grass while the riders come. They free her anyway. You are arrested by the king's men for treason.

resolutions.label: loose the queen's chains with a word before the torch falls

success.body: You do not run. You stand at the edge of the crowd and look at the chains, and speak the old words for opening, which work on locks and gates and sometimes on the iron of a stake. The chains fall from the queen's wrists into the faggots. She looks down at them, astonished, and in that moment the riders come out of the woods and reach her, and she is gone. Nobody saw you. She sends you, a month later, a necklace of pearls from the lake.

failure.body: You speak the old words for opening, and the chains do not fall. The riders come anyway, and cut them.

entries.body: You let them pass, and follow at a distance, keeping to the high ground.

resolutions.label: creep into the Pictish camp and free the captives

success.body: At midnight, the Picts are asleep round their fire, and the captives are tied to a stake at the edge of the camp. You crawl through the heather, cut their ropes one by one, and lead them away in a long, silent line. By dawn, you are ten miles south. The Picts, you hear, spend two days looking for them and then give up, blaming the fairies.

failure.body: At midnight, you crawl into the camp, but a dog barks. You flee into the heather. The captives go north.

resolutions.label: sing the war-band to sleep with a Pictish lullaby

success.body: You learned it from a nurse in the north: an old Pictish song for sleep, with words older than the Picts. You creep to the edge of the camp at midnight and sing it softly into the dark, over and over. The guards' heads nod. The fire burns low. When every man is snoring, you walk in and cut the captives free and lead them out in a long silent line. The Picts spend two days looking for them, and blame the fairies.

failure.body: You creep to the edge of the camp and sing the old lullaby. The Picts know it too. They sing the second verse back at you, and then come looking.

entries.body: Mother Gwyar puts down the hare and wipes her knife. "When I was a girl," she says, "there was a knight who came to this forest to hunt a white hart. He was very young and very beautiful. My mother said I should keep away from him. I did not." She laughs. "He chased the hart for a year and a day, and he never caught it, and one morning he came to our hut and said he was tired, and asked for water. My mother gave it to him. He drank it and lay down under that oak, there, and went to sleep. He is still there." She points. There is a long mound under the oak, grown over with moss and violets. "He was a king's son, they say. Nobody ever came to look for him. The hart comes and stands by him sometimes, at dusk. I think it is sorry." The crow croaks. She feeds it a scrap of hare. "That is the story," she tells you. "It is going to rain." At noon, it does, and you are glad of her roof.

Years have passed. Arthur's beard is thick and there is grey in it. The Round Table is full but for one seat, which has stood empty since the day it was made. Gold letters on its back read *the Siege Perilous*, and no one who has sat in it has lived to stand up again.

It is Pentecost once more. The hall at Camelot is full, and the talk is of tournaments and marriages, when every door and shutter in the castle slams at once. A thunderclap shakes the roof. Then a light comes in, brighter than the sun on water, and every face in the hall looks younger in it. Something covered in white samite passes down the length of the tables. No one carries it. Wherever it goes, each knight finds before them the meat and drink they love best. Then it is gone, and the doors creak open on an ordinary evening.

For a long moment nobody speaks. Then Sir Bors stands up so fast that his bench goes over. "I saw it covered," he says, "and I will not rest until I see it bare. I swear to seek it for a year and a day, and longer if God wills." One by one, the knights of the Round Table rise and swear with him.

Arthur does not rise. "You have broken my fellowship," he says quietly, "and I will never see all of you at this table again."

By morning, the rivers in the west have begun to run low, and word comes that the fields around Corbenic have turned to dust.

Each Knight chooses how to answer the Grail's call:

Those who swear to seek the Grail and its mysteries, whatever it costs them, gain 1 Rank of Divinity.

Those who stay to protect the people and the ladies they love while the fellowship scatters, gain 1 Rank of Romance.

Those who say aloud what several at the table are thinking, that a court without its best knights is a court for the taking, gain 1 Rank of Villainy.

notes: Every Knight gains Destiny equal to their highest Rank of Renown
Every Knight who is Betrothed and has 0 Ranks of Villainy gains 1 Rank of Romance

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf on a tall white mule, dressed in a herald's tabard so long it trails in the dust, blowing a silver trumpet at a crossroads where there is nobody to hear it. He lowers the trumpet when he sees you and bows from the saddle.

"Tudwal," he says. "Herald to King Ryons of the Out Isles. I bear a challenge to the High King Arthur." He unrolls a parchment with great care. "*King Ryons, having defeated eleven kings, demands that Arthur send him his beard and his fealty, or be defeated as the twelfth.*" He rolls it up again and looks unhappy. "It is very rude. I told the king it was rude. He said a herald's job is to carry words, not to taste them." He sighs. "By the law of heralds, I must have a knight to escort me into Camelot. And his champion is two days behind me, to fight any knight who answers. I have been refused by six knights already. They all say they do not want to be seen with the message."

responses.label: You may escort Tudwal the herald to Camelot.
You may answer King Ryons's challenge yourself, against his champion.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf walking along the road leading a riderless horse. A knight's shield is strapped to the saddle, dented and scraped, with a broken lance-head still stuck in it. The dwarf is walking slowly, as if he does not want to arrive.

"Grugyn," he says, when you draw level. "Squire to Sir Madoc of the Vale. Sir Madoc is dead." He pats the shield. "I am taking this home to his widow. She will ask how he died." He is quiet for a while. "He died running. There were five outlaws on the road, and he turned his horse and ran, and they caught him at a ford. I hid in a ditch." He looks up at you, and his eyes are wet. "She thinks he was the bravest knight in Wales. She has a song about him. What do I tell her?"

responses.label: You may go with Grugyn and help him tell the widow the truth.
You may help Grugyn find a kinder story for the widow.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf in a pilgrim's grey habit, sitting by the road at the foot of a mountain pass, with a small bronze bell wrapped in a cloth on his knees. He rings it gently as you pass, and the sound is so clear and sweet that your horse stops of its own accord.

"Brother Ifan," he says. "From the Abbey of Saint Teilo. This is the saint's own bell. It rang by itself when he died. I am carrying it to Rome for the Holy Father to bless." He looks up at the pass. "There are robbers in the pass. They took everything from the last pilgrims. They would take the bell for its bronze and melt it." He smiles. "I am not afraid for myself. I am a small target. But I would like the bell to reach Rome."

responses.label: You may escort Brother Ifan and his bell over the pass.
You may kneel and ask Brother Ifan to bless you with the saint's bell.

entries.body:
You come upon a forge in a hillside, where a dwarf in a leather apron is hammering at a sword on an anvil. Each time the hammer falls, the sword sings: a high, sweet note that hangs in the air. The dwarf stops when he sees you, and the note fades.

"Gofannon," he says. "Smith. Listen." He strikes the blade once more. This time, you hear words in the note. *The one who carries me will be the greatest knight in Britain,* it sings, *and will die by me on a plain in May.* The dwarf wipes his forehead. "I did not mean it to do that," he says. "I only meant it to be sharp. It has been singing that for a week. I cannot sell it. Nobody will buy it." He looks at you sideways. "Unless you want it?"

responses.label: You may take the singing sword, whatever it foretells.
You may help Gofannon silence the sword's prophecy.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf standing beneath a lady's window in a small town, holding a lute and a bunch of primroses. He is dressed in his best: a red doublet, a feathered cap, and a sword that nearly touches the ground. He is also soaking wet.

"Tegid," he says, bowing. "They have been throwing water. Not the lady. Her suitor." He points to the next window, where a very tall, handsome knight is leaning out with a jug, grinning. "Sir Hector the Tall. He says a dwarf courting a lady is the funniest thing he has ever seen." Tegid looks up at the lady's window, where a shutter is half-open. "The Lady Morwen has never laughed at me," he says quietly. "Not once. I think, perhaps, she likes my songs. But she will not come to the window while he is there."

The tall knight tips his jug. You step back just in time.

responses.label: You may help Tegid win the Lady Morwen's heart.
You may challenge Sir Hector the Tall for his insults.

entries.body: You push through the crowd to the church steps. The preacher turns on you, pointing. "A knight!" he cries. "Proud and sinful! Lay down your sword!"

resolutions.label: unmask the false prophet

success.body: You lay down your sword on the pile of gold. Then you pick up the preacher's own leather satchel, which is lying behind the pillar where he thought nobody could see it, and turn it upside down. Out fall the gold rings from the last three towns, each with its owner's mark, and a map of the next three, and a very fine pair of boots. The crowd goes silent. Then it goes for the preacher. You get him to the gaol before they can hang him, which he does not thank you for.

failure.body: You lay down your sword on the pile of gold, meaning to turn the tables on him. The preacher snatches it up and cries that the knight has made his sacrifice! The crowd cheers you. He is gone in the night with the gold, and your sword.

resolutions.label: answer him scripture for scripture

success.body: Every time he cries out a verse about judgement, you answer him with the next verse, which is about mercy. He does not know the next verses. You do. The crowd, which knows its psalms, begins to smile, and then to laugh, and then to pick its rings back up. The preacher is gone by morning, and so is his satchel, but not the town's gold.

failure.body: You answer him verse for verse, and he answers you back, in Latin, and the crowd, who have no Latin, decide he is the holier man. They throw more gold on the pile.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf on a black pony in the middle of a road, with a long whip in his hand. As you approach, he spurs toward you and cracks the whip across your horse's face, then yours. "Make way!" he shrieks. "Make way for the Knight of the Sparrowhawk!"

Behind him, at a walk, rides a big knight in armour painted with sparrowhawks, and beside him a lady, very pale. The knight does not look at you. The dwarf rides round you in a circle, cracking his whip at your ears. "Nobody passes my master!" he cries. "Nobody!" There is a mad glee in his face. The lady behind them catches your eye and very slightly shakes her head.

Your cheek is bleeding where the lash caught it.

responses.label: You may challenge the Knight of the Sparrowhawk for his dwarf's insult.
You may seize the whip from the mad dwarf.

entries.body: "Make sail," you say. "Every scrap of canvas you have. We are going to Camelot."

resolutions.label: outrun the enemy ships to the coast

success.body: You crowd on sail and run before the wind, and at dawn, you are in the Severn estuary, and by noon, you are riding for Camelot. The young king hears your news and sends riders to every lord in the west. By the time the Irish and Orkney ships make their landing, the coast is watched. They turn back. The young king gives you a ring and his thanks.

failure.body: You crowd on sail, but the wind drops, and you are becalmed for two days. By the time you reach Camelot, the young king has already heard from his own spies.

resolutions.label: steer by the coast in the dark to the Severn

success.body: You know this coast. You take the helm yourself and hug the shore, running inside the islands where the big ships cannot follow, reading the rocks by the white of the surf. At dawn, you are in the Severn estuary, and by noon you are riding for Camelot. The young king sends riders to every lord in the west. When the Irish and Orkney ships come, the coast is watched. They turn back.

failure.body: You take the helm and hug the shore, and at midnight you hug it too closely. The ship grounds on a sandbar and you wait for the tide. By the time you reach Camelot, the young king has already heard.

entries.body: You put your hand on the sword with theirs. "I was there," you say. "I saw Gareth fall." The grey-bearded knight nods slowly.

resolutions.label: swear the oath of vengeance and ride with Orkney

success.body: You ride with them for a month, across the sea, to the siege of Benwick, and you fight beside them in the trenches before the castle walls. They are brave and bitter, and they trust you like a brother. When they go home, the grey-bearded knight gives you an Orkney brooch. "You are one of us now," he says. You are not sure that is a good thing.

failure.body: You ride with them to the siege of Benwick. In the first assault, the Orkney knights charge too early, in their rage, and are cut down under the walls. You are carried from the field.

resolutions.label: join their oath by the old Orkney rite of blood

success.body: They do not only swear. They cut their palms and grip the sword-blade. You cut yours and grip it too, and hold it longest, while the grey-bearded knight counts. The Orkney men nod. You ride with them to the siege of Benwick and fight beside them in the trenches, and they trust you like a brother. When they go home, the grey-bearded knight gives you an Orkney brooch.

failure.body: You cut your palm and grip the sword, and let go before the count ends. The grey-bearded knight looks at you coldly. "Not one of us," he says. They ride without you.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf sitting in the stocks outside a castle gate, with a placard round his neck that reads THIEF. He is dignified and furious. Rotten apples lie all around him.

"Pebin," he says. "Master saddler. I made a saddle for Sir Hugh of the castle. He said it was too small for a real man's backside and would not pay. When I went to ask for my money, his knights said I had stolen a silver cup, and put me here." He looks up at the gate, where two knights are lounging, laughing at him. "I did not steal a cup. I would not know what to do with a cup. I have one cup, and it is wood." He clenches his small fists. "When I get out of here, I am going to make Sir Hugh a saddle with a burr in it that he will never forget. And one for each of his friends."

responses.label: You may help Pebin prove his innocence.
You may help Pebin take his revenge on Sir Hugh.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf in a black gown and a scholar's cap, kneeling beside a wounded knight at the side of the road, with a leather bag of instruments open beside him. The knight is grey-faced and breathing badly. There is a bloody bandage round his thigh.

"Meddyg," says the dwarf, without looking up. "Physician, of Salerno. He was gored by a boar. The wound is poisoned." He peers into his bag and curses. "I need comfrey and yarrow and the root of the water-avens, fresh. I have none. And I need someone to hold him still while I clean it, and he is a very big knight." He glances at you. "You will do. Or you can go and find me the herbs. Either way, be quick."

responses.label: You may hold the wounded knight while the dwarf physician works.
You may search the countryside for the herbs the physician needs.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf sitting on a cart piled high with crossbows at a crossroads, smoking a clay pipe. The cart has two painted signs: one on the left side, reading *ARMS FOR THE LORD OF CARDIGAN*, and one on the right, reading *ARMS FOR THE LORD OF PEMBROKE*.

"Hob Crookback," he says, grinning. "Merchant of war. Cardigan and Pembroke are fighting over a salmon weir. I sell to both. Whichever side of the cart faces the customer." He taps the signs. "The more crossbows they buy, the longer the war. The longer the war, the more crossbows they need. It is a beautiful trade." He winks at you. "I need a knight to ride with me. Knights are respectable. A third of the takings, and you need do nothing but look stern."

responses.label: You may expose Hob's trade to both lords.
You may ride with Hob and take a third of the takings.

entries.body: You put your hand on Cadfan's bow. "Let me go to him first," you say. "If he will not hear me, then do as you will." The forester stares at you. "He will not hear you," he says. "But go."

resolutions.label: confront Lord Fulk on the road

success.body: You ride out into the road and bar Fulk's way, and before his men, you tell him what he did. You do not raise your voice. When you finish, Fulk is white with anger. "You dare?" he says. But his own men are looking at him, and one of them, you see, is weeping. "I had a brother too," the man says. Fulk looks at them all. At last he takes off his rich cloak and throws it on the road. "Give it to the widow," he says, and rides on. Cadfan comes down from the tree and picks it up, and stands there holding it, and does not know what to do with his anger.

failure.body: You ride out into the road and bar Fulk's way. Fulk laughs in your face. "A knight-errant," he says, "defending poachers." His men ride you down, and he goes on toward Chester. You lie in the road. From the oak above, you hear a bowstring sing.

resolutions.label: take Cadfan's case to the Earl of Chester

success.body: You and Cadfan ride to Chester by the back roads and reach the Earl's court the day before Fulk does. You tell the Earl the whole story, with Cadfan standing beside you in his green hood, and the Earl, who has little love for Fulk, listens. When Fulk arrives, he finds himself answering charges. He is made to pay the widow a hundred marks, and every deer in his forest is declared free to the poor in a famine year. Cadfan does not smile, but he shakes your hand.

failure.body: You and Cadfan ride to Chester by the back roads and reach the Earl's court. But the Earl is Fulk's cousin, and he listens to your tale with a bored look. "The poacher was hanged according to law," he says. Cadfan leaves the court without a word. You hear, a week later, that Fulk has been found dead on the Chester road with an arrow in his throat.

entries.body:
You come upon a dwarf sitting on a stone at the foot of a green hill, with his chin in his hands. He is old and white-bearded, with a pick on his shoulder, and he is staring at a crack in the hillside no wider than a man's hand.

"Dwyfan," he says. "Miner. My people went into this hill a hundred years ago to dig for silver. They found a door. They went through it." He points at the crack. "The door closed. I was a child, too small to go with them. I have come back every year since, on midsummer night, when it opens again. Tonight is midsummer." He looks at you. "I am too old to go in alone. The last three knights I asked said I was mad. Perhaps I am."

responses.label: You may go into the hill with Dwyfan to find his lost kin.
