You may persuade Dwyfan to let his kin go.

entries.body: You climb the church steps beside the preacher and turn to face the crowd. "Good people," you say, "the Grail was not taken from you for your rings."

resolutions.label: speak to the crowd of true repentance

success.body: You speak of the Grail, and of what the hermits say: that it asks for clean hearts, not gold. You tell them to take their rings home and give bread to the poor instead. The rain eases as you speak, and the thunder rolls away east. The crowd takes back its gold, a little shamefaced, and the preacher, seeing no profit in the town, is gone by morning. The priest of the town, who has been hiding in his church, comes out and blesses you.

failure.body: You speak of the Grail and of clean hearts, but the lightning strikes again as you speak, and the preacher cries, "You see? God does not hear him!" The crowd drags you off the steps.

entries.body:
You come upon a crowd in a market town, gathered around a dwarf in the stocks. Someone has piled faggots around the post of the stocks. A priest in black is reading from a scroll, and the crowd is shouting "Witch! Witch!"

"Idwal the clockmaker," a woman tells you. "He made a clock for the church, with little figures that come out and strike the bells. The priest says it is sorcery, that the little figures are devils. The priest's brother makes church bells." She lowers her voice. "The clock was very good."

The dwarf sees you. "Sir knight!" he calls. "Tell them! A clock is only wheels. It is only wheels and weights! I can show you!" The priest's brother is lighting a torch.

responses.label: You may prove that the dwarf's clock is honest craft and not sorcery.
You may free the dwarf by force before the fire is lit.

entries.body: You ride your horse up the warehouse steps, through the flood, to the merchant's door. His servants lower their spears.

resolutions.label: break open the hoarder's warehouse

success.body: You do not fight the servants. You shout to the men on the rooftops, and they come swimming and wading from every side, forty of them, and the servants look at the forty and at their master and put down their spears. You break the door. The grain is handed out in sacks, by boat, from roof to roof, all night. The merchant stands on his steps in the rain, shouting that he will go to the king. You tell him that you hope he does. The king, when he hears, makes him pay for the new bridge.

failure.body: You shout to the men on the rooftops, but they are frightened and cold, and they do not come. The servants drive you back down the steps with their spears. The grain stays behind its door.

resolutions.label: prove the merchant broke the guild's own law

success.body: You wade to the guildhall, find the charter on its wall, and read it aloud from the steps to every roof within earshot: no merchant of Winchester may hold back grain in a time of flood, on pain of losing his freedom of the city. The merchant goes pale. His own servants look at him and step away from the doors. By nightfall the grain is going out by boat, and the merchant is sitting in the guildhall explaining himself.

failure.body: You wade to the guildhall and read the charter aloud, and a clerk shouts back that the clause was repealed at Candlemas, at the merchant's own request. You wade back, wiser in the ways of guilds.

entries.body: "We fight, my lord," you say, "and end it." The old king nods wearily.

resolutions.label: lead the assault on the walls of Benwick

success.body: You lead the assault on the north wall, where the ditch is shallowest. It is a terrible fight on the ladders. You reach the top, and hold it, and the defenders fall back. But then a trumpet sounds from the keep, and the gates open, and the queen's champion rides out alone, unarmed, and kneels in the mud before the old king's pavilion. "I will not fight my king," he says. The old king weeps. The assault is called off. You are praised for taking the wall. You are not sure what you have won.

failure.body: You lead the assault on the north wall, and it fails. You are carried from the ditch with an arrow in your leg. The siege goes on.

resolutions.label: break the walls with a mine under the north tower

success.body: You do not climb ladders. You take thirty men and dig, for a month, under the north tower, in the wet and the dark, propping the tunnel with timber. On the last night, you fire the props. The tower groans and falls. But before the army can pour through the breach, the gates open, and the queen's champion rides out alone, unarmed, and kneels in the mud before the old king's pavilion. The old king weeps. The assault is called off.

failure.body: You dig for a month under the north tower, and the defenders dig a counter-mine, and the two tunnels meet in the dark. You are dragged out, half-buried.

entries.body: "I will help you," you say. Gaheris grins without humour. "Good. He is strong. It will take two." You hide in the hedge on either side of the road, and the singing comes closer.

resolutions.label: spring the ambush on Lamorak

success.body: Lamorak rides into the crossroads with his helmet off and his head thrown back in song. You and Gaheris burst out of the hedge on either side. Lamorak fights like a bear, and laughs while he fights, but two is too many. He goes down under Gaheris's sword. For a long moment Gaheris stands over him, breathing hard. Then he cleans his blade on the grass. "It is done," he says. "Orkney thanks you." He gives you Lamorak's horse. It is a fine horse. You find it hard to look at.

failure.body: Lamorak rides into the crossroads singing. You and Gaheris burst out of the hedge on either side, but Lamorak hears you coming. He knocks Gaheris out of the saddle with one blow and rides you down with the next. When you wake, he is sitting on a milestone, bandaging Gaheris's head. "Tell your mother," he says to the groaning Gaheris, "I am sorry I will be late."

resolutions.label: stalk Lamorak and take him at the stream

success.body: You leave Gaheris in the hedge and go ahead alone, and find Lamorak watering his horse at a stream with his helmet off, singing. You come out of the reeds behind him. He turns, and sees your sword, and stops singing. You bring him back to the crossroads with his hands tied. Gaheris draws, and then looks at the big man standing quietly in the road, and cannot do it. He sends Lamorak across the sea instead. It is not what either of you meant.

failure.body: You go ahead alone through the reeds, and a heron gets up in front of you with a great clatter. Lamorak looks round, laughs, and rides off at a gallop. Gaheris blames you. So does the heron.

entries.body: You kneel and take the wounded knight by the shoulders. The dwarf nods. "He will fight," he says. "Hold him anyway."

resolutions.label: hold the knight still through the physician's work

success.body: The knight fights like a bull. You hold him. It takes an hour, and at the end you are bruised all over, but the dwarf has cleaned the wound and packed it with moss and wine and stitched it with silk, and the knight is sleeping. "He will live," says Meddyg. "You have strong arms." While you rest, he tells you what he did and why, and by the end of the afternoon, you know more about wounds than any knight you have met.

failure.body: The knight fights like a bull. In his fever, he throws you off and knocks the dwarf into the ditch. By the time you have pinned him down again, the wound has torn open further. He lives, but he will limp for the rest of his life, and the dwarf does not thank you.

entries.body: "What did the king feed them?" you ask. The boy stares. "Mutton," he says. "And he sang to them. The same song. It is a drinking song. It is very rude."

resolutions.label: lead the lions home with the king's song

success.body: You carry a leg of mutton through the burning streets, singing the old king's drinking song at the top of your voice, with the boy beside you, until the lioness comes out of an alley and stops and stares at you. Then the lion. They follow you, growling low, all the way to the castle stables, and walk in, and lie down. The boy shuts the door on them and bursts into tears. The garrison on the walls, who have heard every word of the song, are laughing too hard to shoot.

failure.body: You carry a leg of mutton through the streets, singing. The lioness comes out of an alley, and stops, and stares at you. Then she takes the mutton, and then she takes a swipe at you, and then she is gone into the smoke.

resolutions.label: herd the lions home from the saddle like cattle

success.body: You ride through the burning streets with the menagerie boy up behind you, and when you find the lioness, you do not go near her. You ride round her, wide, the way a drover works a bull, and turn her gently with the horse's shoulder, and turn her again, toward the castle. The lion follows the lioness. They walk into the castle stables side by side, and the boy slams the door. The garrison cheers.

failure.body: You ride round the lioness to turn her, and she turns on your horse instead. You are thrown into a burning doorway. The lions are gone into the smoke.

entries.body: You look at the mantle, then at Morgan. "My lady," you say, "a gift for a king should be tried before it is given. Let your page put it on." Morgan's smile does not move. Her page, a pale boy of twelve, goes whiter still.

resolutions.label: see through Morgan's gift

success.body: You watch Morgan's face and the boy's face, and you know. "Never mind the boy," you say. "Put it on the table." Morgan shrugs and drapes the mantle over the table, and the table bursts into flame and burns to a heap of ash in a moment. Morgan sighs. "You are no fun at all," she says, and she and her pavilion and her page are gone, leaving only a scorched circle on the grass and a pear with one bite out of it. At Camelot, Arthur hears the tale and gives you a horse from his own stable.

failure.body: You insist on the trial. Morgan sighs and nods, and the boy puts on the mantle. Nothing happens. He walks up and down, and it fits him very well. "Satisfied?" asks Morgan. She wraps it up and sends him off to Camelot with it, and you ride away feeling foolish. That night you hear that the page burned to death on the road at dusk. You should have trusted what you knew.

resolutions.label: unmake the enchantment in the mantle

success.body: You lay your hand on the mantle and feel it shiver, like an animal. There are words woven into its hem, fire-words in gold thread. You find the end of the thread and pull. The mantle comes apart in your hands in a long, hissing unravelling, and the gold falls on the grass as ash. Morgan watches with interest. "Where did you learn that?" she says. "I must be more careful." She vanishes with her pavilion, but she leaves the silver knife behind, and you keep it.

failure.body: You lay your hand on the mantle and feel it shiver, like an animal. You look for the end of the spell and cannot find it. The mantle, it seems, has found you. Your hand is stuck to the cloth, and it is getting hotter. You tear yourself free, leaving skin behind. Morgan laughs until she cries. "Oh, little knight," she says. "Leave the weaving to the weavers."

entries.body: "The dead must be buried," you say, "or there will be more." Father Mabon closes his eyes. "Thank you," he says. "I have not had the strength."

resolutions.label: dig graves for the plague dead

success.body: You dig for two days, from dawn until dark. You bury eleven people, and then three more who die while you are digging. You say what prayers you know over each of them. At the end, you are black with earth to your elbows, and too tired to stand. Father Mabon brings you water. "They will be remembered," he says. The sickness, whether by God's mercy or because the dead are in the ground, begins to ebb.

failure.body: You dig for a day. On the second morning, you wake with a fever. You dig on anyway, because there is nobody else, until you fall into the grave you are digging and cannot climb out. Father Mabon finds you there and drags you into the barn with the others.

entries.body: "Let him out," you say. "Let him see the end. He has earned that." Nimue looks at you with red eyes.

resolutions.label: persuade the Lady of the Lake to free Merlin

success.body: You talk to her for a long time. About what she was afraid of, and what she is afraid of now. About how he taught her everything, and she has never had anyone to teach. At last, she stands up, and lays her hand on the stone, and speaks a single word. The stone opens like a door. Merlin walks out, very old and very thin, blinking in the daylight. He looks at Nimue. She looks at him. Then he laughs, and holds out his arm, and she takes it, and they walk down the hill together, toward the plain, to see the end. He looks back once, and winks at you.

failure.body: You talk to her for a long time, but she only shakes her head. "If I let him out," she says, "he will be kind to me. I could not bear it." She stays on the rock. You ride to the war.

resolutions.label: break the stone for her, with her leave

success.body: "I cannot open it," Nimue says. "I have tried. My hand will not do it." "Then lend me your words," you say, "and let my hand do it." She looks at you a long time, and then whispers the word in your ear. You lay your hand on the stone and speak it. The stone opens like a door. Merlin walks out, very old and very thin, blinking in the daylight. He looks at Nimue. Then he laughs, and holds out his arm, and she takes it.

failure.body: Nimue whispers the word in your ear, and you speak it over the stone, and the stone does not know your voice. It stays shut. Nimue stays on her rock.

entries.body: You ride past the porter into the dead courtyard. The laughing stops. A king in black comes out onto the steps of the keep, holding a spear with a black point.

resolutions.label: stand against the lord of the Castle Mortal

success.body: He is strong with a dark strength, and his spear is cold as winter. But he has not fought a knight in a very long time, and he is afraid of you, and you see it. You beat down his spear and press him back into his keep, and he flees down a stair into the dark, and a door slams, and somewhere deep underground, a bolt is shot. Outside, it begins to rain for the first time in a year. The porter is standing in the courtyard with his face turned up, weeping.

failure.body: He is strong with a dark strength, and his spear is cold as winter. It touches your side, only touches it, and the cold goes into you and stays. You flee the Castle Mortal, and it is a long time before you are warm again.

entries.body: You take the spade. The ground is frozen hard as iron.

resolutions.label: dig through the frozen ground of Avalon

success.body: You dig all day, and at dusk, your spade strikes stone. It is a slab, carved with a cross, and under it, in the dark, an old man lies with his arms crossed, as if asleep, with two small crystal vessels at his feet. He is not decayed. The monk falls to his knees. Neither of you touches anything. You put the slab back, and fill in the earth, and when you stand up, the apple trees around you are in blossom.

failure.body: You dig all day, and at dusk, you are waist-deep in a hole with nothing in it but stones. The monk thanks you, and goes on digging alone. You leave with blistered hands.

resolutions.label: find the grave by the old signs of the island

success.body: You do not dig where the monk has been digging. You walk the island and look at the ground, and at the moss, and at where the snow does not lie. At the foot of the hill, there is a place where the frost never forms, and a wild rose grows through it in winter. You dig there. Your spade strikes a slab carved with a cross, and under it an old man sleeps with two crystal vessels at his feet. You put the slab back. When you stand up, the apple trees are in blossom.

failure.body: You walk the island looking for signs, and find a place where the frost never forms, and dig. It is a hot spring. The monk thanks you. His feet, at least, are warm.

entries.body: You go into the church and speak to the priest, a stern old man called Father Rhodri. "There is a girl at your door who wants to hear Mass," you say. "She cannot come in. You could come out." Father Rhodri's eyebrows go up.

resolutions.label: persuade the priest to say Mass under the sky

success.body: You remind him that the Lord preached on hillsides and by lakes, and that Saint Columba said Mass on a rock in the sea. You remind him that the girl has been listening at his door every Sunday for a year, and that she likes his singing. That last one does it. He harrumphs. The following Sunday, and every Sunday after, Father Rhodri says Mass in the churchyard, under a yew tree, whatever the weather, and the congregation stands on one side, and on the other side stand Eirlys and, by the end of the summer, several of her cousins.

failure.body: You remind him that the Lord preached on hillsides. Father Rhodri reminds you that the Lord also cast out devils, and closes the church door.

resolutions.label: give her leave by the old rite of the threshold

success.body: You remember that the fair folk may cross any threshold where they are invited three times, with bread and salt. You fetch bread and salt from the priest's own kitchen, and stand in the doorway and invite Eirlys in, three times, by name. On the third, she steps over the threshold as lightly as a leaf. She sits in the last pew through the whole Mass. The priest glares, and then, at the end, gives her a piece of blessed bread.

failure.body: You stand in the doorway and invite her in three times with bread and salt. On the third, she steps forward, and screams, and falls back onto the path. The salt was the priest's holy salt. She goes back to the wood and does not come to listen again.

entries.body: You grin up at the little man. "What did you have in mind?" Puck's eyes shine.

resolutions.label: play a fay prank on the rude bridegroom

success.body: You and Puck spend the evening leading the groom, and only the groom, round and round the oak, while the rest of the party goes on to the church with the priest. When he finally stumbles into the churchyard at midnight, muddy and wild-eyed, the bride is waiting at the door with her arms folded. "And what," she says, "is your excuse?" He tells her it was a toadstool. It is the best wedding story in that parish for a hundred years. Puck gives you a mushroom. You do not eat it.

failure.body: You and Puck spend the evening leading the groom round the oak. But Puck, it turns out, cannot tell the difference between one rude mortal and another, and around midnight, you realise you are going round the oak too. By dawn, you and the groom are the best of friends, which is the only good thing to come of it.

entries.body: You sit at the high table. "My lord," you say, "the young king does not want your crown. He wants your friendship."

resolutions.label: persuade King Lot to make peace

success.body: You talk long into the night. You speak of the Saxons, and of his sons, who will have to choose sides one day. You tell him the young king has asked about them, by name, and would like to foster them at his court. At that, Lot goes quiet, and looks at his boys wrestling on the floor. Morgause puts her hand on his arm. At last he says, "One son. The youngest. Gareth. He is too gentle for Orkney. Let him go to Camelot." It is not peace. But it is the beginning of one.

failure.body: You talk long into the night, but Lot drinks more and more, and at last he throws a bone at you and roars that the beardless boy can come and fight him if he wants Orkney. You leave in the morning, with the wind in your face.

resolutions.label: win Lot's respect with a feat of Orkney seamanship

success.body: You do not argue with Lot. You accept his challenge to ride the Orkney way: along the beach at low tide, through the surf, round the skerries, racing his own sons. You come in second, behind the youngest, Gareth, and ahead of Lot. Lot roars with laughter and slaps your back. That night, over the mead, he listens to you. "One son," he says at last. "The youngest. He is too gentle for Orkney. Let him go to Camelot."

failure.body: You race Lot's sons along the beach through the surf, and your horse is not an Orkney horse. It falls in the surf. Lot laughs, and does not listen to anything you say after that.

entries.body: "Abbot!" you shout. "That is a whale!" The abbot waves cheerfully. "We know," he calls. "He is very comfortable."

resolutions.label: bring the monks safely off the whale

success.body: You bring your ship alongside and throw them ropes. The abbot does not want to go, but the younger monks do, and while you argue, the whale decides the matter for you by beginning, slowly, to sink. The monks scramble aboard with their chalice and their candles, and the abbot comes last, dripping. The whale sinks, and rises again a hundred yards away, and blows, and swims away west. "He will come back for us," says the abbot, rather crossly. "Next Easter." You are sure he will.

failure.body: You bring your ship alongside and throw them ropes, and the whale, disturbed, dives. The monks, the chapel and very nearly your ship go down in a great swirl. You fish out six of them. The rest you never find.

entries.body: "You are safe now, my lady," you say. "We will get you home." The queen does not look safe. She looks at the trees on every side as though Meliagaunt's men might come out of them. The page, whose name is Aled, holds her bridle.

resolutions.label: find the way back to Camelot through the woods

success.body: You find a stream and follow it downhill, knowing it must reach the river, and the river must reach Camelot. By dusk you can see the towers. The queen's knights are brought home within the week, when the High King marches on Gore. Guinevere does not forget. She sends for you on the next feast day and seats you among her own household. "You kept your head," she says, "when I had lost mine."

failure.body: You find a stream and follow it downhill, but it runs into a marsh, and you spend the night in it with the queen, the page and two very unhappy horses. You bring her home at noon the next day, wet and furious. The High King thanks you. The queen does not.

resolutions.label: ride hard for Camelot with the queen behind you

success.body: You take the queen up behind your saddle and the page on the second horse, and you ride. Branches whip your face. The queen holds on and says nothing. By noon you are clattering over the drawbridge at Camelot, and the High King is running down the steps. By nightfall his army is marching on Gore. The queen does not forget who carried her home.

failure.body: You take the queen up behind your saddle and ride, but a low branch sweeps you both off in a tangle of green silk and armour. The queen is unhurt. Her temper is not. You walk the rest of the way.

entries.body: You tie a rope round your waist, and the pilgrims lower you down into the red dark.

resolutions.label: explore the holy cave beneath the well

success.body: At the bottom, the well opens into a cave, and the water runs through it from a crack in the chalk. You follow the stream on hands and knees until you find what has happened: a rockfall has half-blocked the spring. You shift the stones one by one, with your hands bleeding, and as the last one moves, the water gushes out red as rubies, and the whole cave fills with a scent of roses. When they haul you up, the pilgrims are shouting. The water in the bucket is as red as blood.

failure.body: At the bottom, the well opens into a cave, and you follow the stream on hands and knees until the passage is too narrow to go on. You come up empty-handed, soaked red to the skin, and it does not wash off for a week.

entries.body: You go out to the edge of the island as the torches come across the bog. There are twenty villagers, led by the reeve.

resolutions.label: turn the mob back without bloodshed

success.body: You stand on the causeway and ask them what they will do if they are wrong. You ask the reeve's wife who cured her son's fever last winter, and she looks at her feet. You ask the blacksmith who set his broken arm. By the end, half the torches are going back across the bog. The reeve goes on shouting for a while, but nobody follows him. Mother Mallt watches from the cave mouth and gives you a charm on a string. "Against drowning," she says. "You never know."

failure.body: You stand on the causeway and ask them what they will do if they are wrong. The reeve says they will say sorry. They push past you. By the time you have fought your way back to the cave, it is burning, and Mother Mallt is gone. Somewhere in the bog, a great many frogs are croaking.

resolutions.label: hold the causeway with the flat of your sword

success.body: The causeway to the island is a single plank wide. You stand on it with your sword drawn, and the first villager who comes at you goes into the bog, and so does the second, and the third decides the witch can keep the reeve's pig. By midnight the torches have gone home. Mother Mallt watches from the cave mouth and gives you a charm on a string. "Against drowning," she says.

failure.body: You stand on the causeway, but the villagers come round through the reeds instead. By the time you have fought your way back to the cave, it is burning.

entries.body: You ride up to the castle gate under a branch of green leaves. After a long wait, a tall young Saxon with fair hair comes out onto the wall. "Cynric," he says. "Speak."

resolutions.label: bargain with the Saxon prince

success.body: You do not plead. You tell him, coldly, of the villages you have burned and the kings you have cheated, and you tell him you are a man who could be useful to Mordred, and to him, if he were generous. Cynric listens, and smiles. "A knight after my own heart," he says. He sells you the children for a promise and a purse, and you walk them back down the hill to their mothers. You are not sure whether the promise you gave him was a lie. Neither is he.

partial.body: You tell him of your wicked deeds. Cynric laughs. "I have done worse before breakfast," he says. But he lets you take three of the children, the smallest, for your purse.

failure.body: You tell him of your wicked deeds, and he laughs at you. "A choirboy," he says. "Go home, choirboy." The gate stays shut.

entries.body: You look at the Green Knight's lady, who has come out of the mound behind him. She is very beautiful, with green eyes and a smile that says she has already decided about you.

resolutions.label: win the favour of the Green Knight's lady

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You stay three days. She comes to you each morning, while her husband is hunting, and you talk, and laugh, and kiss. On the third day, she gives you a green sash. In the evening, the Green Knight looks at you across the table and laughs. "She likes you," he says. "She has not liked anyone in a hundred years." He does not seem to mind. You do not ask why. You keep the sash.

partial.body: You stay three days, and she is charming, and kind, and laughs at you a little. On the third day, she says, "You are very sweet," and goes hunting with her husband instead.

failure.body: You stay three days. On the third evening, the Green Knight looks at you across the table, not laughing. "I know," he says. You leave before dawn.

entries.body: You climb the broken stair of the tower. At the top, in a room full of books and smoke, an old man with a white beard is staring into a bowl of water.

resolutions.label: break the old scholar's obsession

success.body: He shows you what he sees in the bowl: a cup, very far away, that recedes whenever he reaches for it. You look at it, and at him, and you understand. "You are looking for it," you say, "so it runs from you. The hermits say it comes to those who are not looking." The old man is silent a long time. Then he laughs, and tips the bowl out of the window, and comes down the stair with you. His pupil weeps with joy.

failure.body: He shows you what he sees in the bowl, and you look, and you cannot stop looking. It is a week before his pupil drags you out of the tower.

resolutions.label: smash the scrying-bowl before it takes you too

success.body: You do not look into the bowl. You walk straight up to the old man's table and knock the bowl onto the floor with the flat of your sword. The water runs away between the boards. The old scholar stares at the wet floor for a long time. Then he laughs, a cracked, astonished laugh, and comes down the stair with you. His pupil weeps with joy.

failure.body: You walk up to the table and knock the bowl to the floor. It does not break. It does not even spill. The old man looks up at you. "It is not that sort of bowl," he says.

entries.body: You do not go in. You walk slowly round the castle walls, looking for the seam in the spell.

resolutions.label: find the flaw in the fay glamour

success.body: On the north side, where the castle should cast a shadow in the morning sun, it casts none. You kneel where the shadow should be and find a single green thread lying on the cobbles. You pick it up and pull. The castle ripples like a reflection in a pond. You keep pulling. With a sound like a sigh, the whole thing unravels into a skein of green silk, and three dazed young men are sitting on the cobbles, holding goblets that turn to acorns in their hands. You keep the skein. It never tangles.

failure.body: You walk round the castle looking for the seam in the spell, and on the third circuit you realise the castle is walking round you. You are dizzy and sick by the time you find the gate again, and the steward bows you in anyway.

entries.body: You look at the tracks of many horses leading away from the village. "Which way did they go?" The old man points north.

resolutions.label: hunt down the village-burners

success.body: You follow the tracks for two days and find them camped by a river: twenty men in Mordred's colours, drinking and dividing the lord's silver. You do not attack them. You ride to the nearest of the old king's captains, and lead his men back to the river by night. By dawn, the raiders are prisoners. The silver goes back to the village. It is not enough to rebuild the church. It is enough to start.

failure.body: You follow the tracks for two days and find them camped by a river, but they have set a watch, and they see you. You are chased for a day.

resolutions.label: bring the raiders to the old king's captains to judge

success.body: You follow the tracks only as far as you need to, then ride to the nearest of the old king's captains and bring him back with thirty men. You set them in a ring round the raiders' camp by the river in the dark, and at dawn, you call on the raiders to surrender. They look at the ring of spears, and do. The lord's silver goes back to the village. It is enough to start the church again.

failure.body: You bring thirty of the old king's men to the raiders' camp, but the captain wants the silver more than justice. The village never sees it.

entries.body: Bagdemagus sighs and pats his horse's neck. "They say I lose my temper. Once, at a tournament, I lost it at a man who had lost his first, and I was the one they remembered. And once I said the queen's hounds were fat, which they were." He rolls up the list slowly. "A king cannot be a knight of the Round Table on the strength of being a king, you see. He has to be a knight first. Arthur says so. It is a fine rule, and I hate it." He mounts, shakes your hand and rides off to find the copper tower. You think, as he goes, that he may be the most honest king in Britain.
You draw your sword and step into the firelight. "The High King will hear of this," you say. The Queen of Northgalis shrieks. Morgan only smiles.

resolutions.label: break the queens' spell and escape

success.body: Morgan raises her hand, and the torches flare up green, and the air thickens like honey. You speak the only prayer you know against sorcery, loudly, and hold your sword-hilt up like a cross. The green fire gutters. The four queens are gone, in four directions, like smoke. You ride to Camelot through the night. The High King moves his scabbard to a new vault. Morgan, you hear, is very annoyed.

failure.body: Morgan raises her hand, and the torches flare green, and you forget what you were saying. You wake at dawn under the oak, alone, with no memory of what you heard, only a feeling that it mattered.

resolutions.label: ride for Camelot before the queens can stop you

success.body: You do not stay to argue with four queens. You turn your horse and ride. Behind you, the torches flare green and something shrieks through the trees after you, and you do not look back. By dawn you are at Camelot's gate. The High King moves his scabbard to a new vault, and sets his own knights to guard it. Morgan, you hear, is very annoyed.

failure.body: You turn your horse and ride, and something green comes through the trees after you and takes your horse's legs from under it. You walk to Camelot, too late.

entries.body: You dismount and set your spear. The boar charges.

resolutions.label: kill the boar with your spear

success.body: It comes at you like a thunderbolt, and you set the butt of your spear against a root and let it run onto the point. The shock throws you backward, but the spear holds. The boar screams and thrashes and drives itself up the shaft toward you, and then it is still. Rhodri lets go of the branch and falls into your arms. "I have hunted boar for twenty years," he gasps, "and never seen that done." You carry him home to his lodge, and his wife feeds you for a week.

failure.body: It comes at you like a thunderbolt. You set the spear, but the ground is soft, and the butt slips, and the boar's tusk opens your leg from knee to hip. You drag yourself up beside Rhodri in the tree. The two of you wait there until dawn, when the boar at last loses interest and trots away.

resolutions.label: hold the boar at bay until nightfall

success.body: You have no spear. You put your back to the oak and your shield in front of you and keep the boar off with your sword for hour after hour, as it charges and charges again. Your arm goes numb. Your shield splits. At dusk, the boar gives a grunt of disgust and trots off into the forest. You help Rhodri down from the tree and carry him home on your back. His family give you their best cloak and more thanks than you can bear.

failure.body: You put your back to the oak and your shield in front of you. The boar charges again and again, and after an hour, your arm gives out, and you drop the shield, and you have to scramble up the tree beside Rhodri. The branch cracks under your weight. You both fall.

entries.body: You step between the bishop's men and the beggars. "If Joseph rested here," you say, "he rested among the poor."

resolutions.label: shame the bishop's men into leaving the family be

success.body: You remind the steward that the holy vessel was used at a meal for poor men, and that Joseph gave his own tomb away. You ask him what the Grail would think of a shrine built by throwing children into the street. The crowd murmurs. The steward goes red. When the bishop hears of it, he is annoyed, but he builds the shrine round the family instead, and gives the beggar woman the keeping of it. She does it very well, and charges the pilgrims nothing.

notes: Lose 1 Treasure, if possible

failure.body: You remind the steward that the vessel was used at a meal for poor men. The steward reminds you that the bishop owns the land. The family is thrown out. You find them lodging in an inn, at your own cost.

resolutions.label: make the family's claim good by the old law of dwelling

success.body: You remind the bishop's steward of the law, older than any bishop, that whoever has lived seven winters under a roof, unchallenged, may not be put out of it. The beggar woman has lived there seven years and a month. The steward goes to find his master. The bishop, who does not want to be the man who threw a family out of Joseph's resting place, builds his shrine round them, and makes the beggar woman its keeper.

failure.body: You remind the steward of the law of seven winters. He produces a lease, signed by the bishop's grandfather, that says otherwise. The family is thrown out.

entries.body: You ride into the circle. "No blood," you say. "Not in the young king's name."

resolutions.label: persuade the old priests to spare the bull

success.body: You tell them that the young king swore at Pentecost to give mercy to any who ask it. "The bull cannot ask," you say, "so I ask for it." The old woman looks at you for a long time. Then she laughs. "Then the bull goes free," she says, "in the king's name. The old gods will understand. They were always fond of a clever answer." She puts the golden bough in your hand. The riders never come.

failure.body: You tell them about the young king's oath. The old woman shakes her head. "Your king's oath," she says, "is not our gods' oath." They send you out of the circle. You hear the chant end behind you, and then silence.

resolutions.label: offer yourself in the bull's place

success.body: "Take my blood instead," you say, and hold out your arm. The old woman looks at you for a long moment. Then she nods, and draws a single line across your palm with her bronze knife, and lets three drops fall on the stone. The chant rises and ends. "The old gods like a brave gift," she says, "better than a big one." The bull goes free. She puts the golden bough in your bleeding hand.

failure.body: "Take my blood instead," you say. The old woman looks at you with pity. "The gods asked for a bull," she says. They send you out of the circle, and the chant ends behind you.

entries.body: You look at the nun. "Do you want to be walled up?" you ask. She hesitates. "No," she whispers.

resolutions.label: spirit the nun away before the walling-up

success.body: You take her up behind your saddle and ride through the night to a convent in the next county, where the abbess is a sensible woman who has no patience with walling-up. Sister Eleri is taken in. Sir Ector de Maris, riding beside you, grips your hand at the gate. "We will meet again next year," he tells her. She laughs. "Somewhere else," she says.

failure.body: You take her up behind your saddle and ride through the night, but the abbess's men are on the road. They take her back. The next day, the last stone is set in her wall.

resolutions.label: hide her among the travelling nuns on the road

success.body: You find a band of Poor Clares walking to Canterbury and ask them, quietly, to take one more. Sister Eleri walks away in their midst with her face down, and the abbess's men search every road but that one, because who would look for a runaway nun among nuns? She reaches a convent in Kent where nobody walls anyone up. Sir Ector de Maris writes to her there, once a year.

failure.body: You ask the Poor Clares to hide her. Their prioress is the abbess's sister. Sister Eleri is back in her own convent by nightfall.

entries.body: You look at the outlaws, ragged and hungry and fierce. "Show me the ford," you say.

resolutions.label: plan and lead the attack at the ford

success.body: You study the ford all day. That night, you send half the outlaws upstream to make noise and light fires, and when the Saxons go to see, you fall on their camp with the other half. It is over in minutes. The Saxons flee into the river, and many drown. The outlaws take their weapons, their horses and their food. Sir Hervi embraces you. "The best night's work I have done since I lost my land," he says.

failure.body: You send half the outlaws upstream to make noise, but the Saxons are not fooled. They wait for the other half and cut them down in the river. You and Sir Hervi escape with six men.

resolutions.label: use the ford itself against them

success.body: You spend the day walking the river and find what you need: a mill-dam a mile upstream. At midnight, when the Saxons are asleep by the ford, you open the sluice. The river rises three feet in a quarter of an hour, and the Saxon camp is under water, and the outlaws are waiting on the bank. The Saxons who reach dry ground do not reach it with their weapons. Sir Hervi embraces you.

failure.body: You open the mill-sluice at midnight, and the river rises, and floods the outlaws' camp, which is lower than the Saxons'. It is a long, wet night of recriminations.

entries.body: You kneel on the rocks beside the fisherman. The bells ring out beneath the waves.

resolutions.label: pray for the souls of the drowned town

success.body: You pray for the people of Llys Helig, for their sins and their long drowning, and ask that they be allowed to rest. The fisherman prays with you. Near midnight, the bells ring one last time, very slowly, and stop. In the silence, you hear the singing in the cave stop too. A moment later, a young man comes stumbling out of the cave, soaking and confused, and his father runs to him across the rocks. Neither of them hears the bells again.

failure.body: You pray for the drowned town until midnight. The bells go on ringing. The fisherman goes home alone. You ride on, and the bells ring in your dreams for a week.

entries.body: "Show me the abbot's soldiers," you say. Aelfgifu grins. "Tomorrow," she says. "Sleep with us tonight."

resolutions.label: fight the abbot's soldiers in the fens

success.body: The abbot's soldiers march into the fens the next day in their heavy mail, expecting fish-folk. They find the causeway gone and the water rising, and the fen-outlaws on their stilts all round them, and a knight on the only dry ground, waiting. By noon, they are wading back to Ely, soaked and humiliated. Aelfgifu gives you a fish-spear with a silver head. The abbot, you hear, decides the fens are God's business after all.

failure.body: The abbot's soldiers march into the fens, and you lead the fen-outlaws against them, but the soldiers have crossbows. The outlaws scatter into the reeds. You are taken to Ely.

resolutions.label: draw the soldiers into the deep fen

success.body: You tell Aelfgifu your plan, and she grins. The next day, you ride out alone in front of the abbot's soldiers and let them chase you, along a path that only you and the fen-folk know is firm, until it isn't. They go into the mud to their waists in their heavy mail. The fen-folk rise around them on their stilts. The soldiers wade back to Ely, soaked and humiliated, and the abbot decides the fens are God's business after all.

failure.body: You let the abbot's soldiers chase you along the hidden path. You take a wrong turn yourself. You and the soldiers spend a companionable afternoon waist-deep in the same bog.

entries.body: "I will carry your herring, my lady," you say. The queen grins, which makes her look ten years younger. "Carry it like a man who hates fish," she says. "Nobody searches a man who hates fish."

resolutions.label: bluff your way past the Munster searchers

success.body: At the gangplank, a Munster sergeant asks what is in the basket. "Herring," you say, "for my lord's table, God help him," and you hold it out so that the smell hits him full in the face. He waves you through, coughing. Orlaith follows you aboard with her shawl over her head. When the ship is out of the harbour, she takes the crown out of the fish and puts it on, scales and all, and laughs at the Munster shore. She gives you a gold ring she was saving for a bribe.

failure.body: At the gangplank, a Munster sergeant asks what is in the basket. "Herring," you say, and hold it out. The sergeant is a fisherman's son, and he knows that herring does not clink. They seize the crown, and the queen, and you. Orlaith spends the voyage to Munster in the hold beside you, telling you exactly what you did wrong.

resolutions.label: get the basket aboard by main strength

success.body: The quay is too crowded for a knight to walk through, so you join the dock porters and carry the basket aboard on your back, with ten others, in a long sweating line. Nobody searches a porter. By the time you set it down in the hold, your back will never be the same, but the crown is safe. Orlaith presses a kiss on your forehead. "A knight who carries," she says. "There's a thing you don't see."

failure.body: The quay is too crowded for a knight to walk through, so you join the dock porters and carry the basket on your back. Halfway up the gangplank, your foot slips on a fish-scale, and you and the basket go into the harbour together. The crown sinks. The queen stands on the quay, silent as stone, and then turns and walks away into the town.

entries.body: You wait until the ghost has marched to the far end of the colonnade, and then you slip into the ruins behind him.

resolutions.label: creep past the ghost and find the treasury

success.body: You find the treasury under a fallen arch, and in it a strong-box, rusted through, full of silver coins with a Roman emperor's face on them. You fill your helmet and slip out again. Behind you, the ghost is still marching, still calling the watchword. You wonder, riding away, how long he will go on guarding an empty box.

failure.body: You find the treasury under a fallen arch, and reach for the box, and a cold hand closes on your shoulder. You flee. You are not sure how you got out, only that you did, and that you will not go back.

resolutions.label: find the treasury from the old Roman plan

success.body: You do not creep about in the dark. You find a Roman stone in the church wall with an inscription on it, and read it, and learn that the treasury lay under the shrine of Sulis. You go straight there by daylight, while the ghost sleeps, and find the strong-box under the fallen altar, full of silver with an emperor's face on it. You wonder, riding away, how long he will go on guarding an empty box.

failure.body: You read the Roman inscription and go to the shrine of Sulis, and dig, and find the ghost there instead, guarding it by day as well. You flee.

entries.body: You sit down on the stone beside the old dwarf. "A hundred years," you say. "What would you say to them?"

resolutions.label: help the old dwarf make his peace

success.body: Dwyfan thinks for a long time. "I would tell them," he says at last, "that I lived. That I married. That I had children and grandchildren, and taught them all to dig." He looks at the crack in the hill. At midnight, when it opens, and the golden light spills out, he does not go in. He only stands at the door and says it, all of it, loudly, into the light. Far below, the hammering stops. Then, very faintly, someone calls his name, and laughs. When the door closes, the old dwarf is smiling.

failure.body: Dwyfan thinks for a long time, but he cannot find the words. At midnight, when the crack opens, he goes in without a word to you, and it closes behind him. You wait until dawn, but he does not come out.

entries.body:
You come upon a wedding party wandering in circles in a wood at dusk: a bride in a wreath, a groom in his best, a priest, a fiddler and a dozen guests, all looking very tired and very cross. The bride is in tears. "We have been walking since noon," she says. "The church is only a mile away. We keep coming back to this same oak."

Up in the oak, sitting on a branch, is a small brown man with pointed ears and a grin, swinging his legs. He waves at you. "Puck," he says. "Robin Goodfellow, some call me. Do not tell them I am here. This is the best fun I have had all year." He giggles. "The groom kicked a toadstool this morning. On purpose. I am teaching him manners." He leans down. "You can help me, if you like. Or you can spoil it. Everybody always spoils it."

responses.label: You may lead the wedding party out of the wood to their church.
You may join Puck's prank on the wedding party.

entries.body:
You come to a ford at dawn, where the mist lies on the water, and there is a woman kneeling at the stream's edge, washing armour. She is thin and grey and very old, and her long hair trails in the water. She is weeping as she scrubs, and the water that runs from the armour is red.

As you ride closer, you see that the armour is yours. Your own shield, with your own device, lies beside her on the bank. The helm she is washing has the dent in it from your last fight. You look down. You are wearing your armour. You are also watching her wash it.

The washer looks up. Her eyes are like pools of rain. "I wash the armour of those who will die," she says. "I wash it three times before the end. This is the first."

responses.label: You may ask the washer at the ford when and how your death will come.
You may take your armour from the washer by force.

entries.body:
You come upon a small church in a valley on a Sunday morning, with the bell ringing for Mass. Outside the church door, on the path, stands a girl with hair like thistledown and a gown like cobwebs, with bare, green-stained feet. She is looking in at the open door with longing.

"I cannot go in," she says to you. "I am of the fair folk. My name is Eirlys. Every Sunday I come and listen at the door. I like the singing. I would like to see the candles, and the painted saint, and the bread." She puts out her hand toward the doorway, and snatches it back as though the air had burned her. "But we cannot cross a church threshold. Unless," she looks at you shyly, "someone carries us."

The priest, inside, has seen her. He is frowning.

responses.label: You may carry Eirlys across the threshold into the church.
You may persuade the priest to say Mass in the churchyard.

entries.body:
You come upon a bower in a wood, hung with honeysuckle and roses, where a lady of unearthly beauty lies on a bed of moss, stroking the long grey ears of a man with the head of a donkey. She is crowned with starlight. He is wearing a weaver's apron and looks bewildered.

A plump woman in a shawl is hiding behind a tree nearby. She grabs your sleeve. "That is my husband," she whispers. "Nick. The weaver. He went into the wood to rehearse a play, and he came out like that, and now she will not let him go." She points at the lady. "That is Titania. The Queen of the Fay. She has been bewitched to love him. By her own husband, the King, for a joke." She wrings her hands. "Nick does not mind. He thinks it is wonderful. But I want him home. He has looms to mend."

responses.label: You may break the spell on Titania and the weaver.
You may trick the Fay Queen into giving the weaver up.

entries.body:
You come upon a pavilion of white silk pitched by a river, so fine that the sunlight shines through it. A lady steps out to meet you. She is the most beautiful woman you have ever seen, and she seems to have been expecting you.

"At last," she says. Her voice is like water over stones. "I have watched you for a long time, knight. I am Tryamour. My father is a king under the hill. I have come to offer you my love." She smiles. "I will give you a purse that never empties and a horse that never tires, and I will come to you whenever you are alone and call my name. There is only one condition." Her smile does not change, but something behind it does. "You must never speak of me to any mortal. Not one word. Not ever. If you do, I will be gone."

responses.label: * You may accept the fay lady's love and her condition.
You may courteously refuse the fay lady's offer.

entries.body:
You hear music in a wood at midnight: a fiddle, a pipe and a drum, playing faster than any mortal musicians could play. You follow it to a clearing where a ring of toadstools circles a patch of bright green grass. Inside the ring, a crowd of tall, pale, laughing people are dancing, and in the middle of them, dancing wildest of all, is a young man in a miller's smock with a face white as flour and blood on his feet.

Outside the ring, a girl is sitting on the ground, weeping. "That is Huw," she says. "My brother. He went into the ring a year ago tonight. He thinks it has been an hour. He will dance until he dies. They always do." She looks at you. "If someone reaches into the ring and pulls him out, without setting foot inside, he will be free. But if they step inside, they will dance too."

The music calls to you. Your feet are already tapping.

responses.label: You may reach into the fay ring and pull Huw out.
You may step into the ring and join the fay revel.

entries.body: You look at the giant baby, and the giant baby looks at you, and stops crying for a moment in surprise. You have no idea how you will carry it anywhere.

resolutions.label: lead the giant child home through the mountains

success.body: You do not carry it. You coax it. You find a cow, which the baby likes, and you walk ahead of it with the cow on a rope, and the baby crawls after, laughing. You follow the sound of the mother's voice up the mountains all day. At dusk, a giantess as tall as a church comes striding down the slope, weeping with relief, and scoops the baby up. She looks at you. Then she puts something in your hand. It is a ring. On her finger, it was a ring. In your hand, it is a bracelet. "Thank you, little one," she says.

failure.body: You coax it with a cow, and it crawls after you, laughing, up the mountain. Then it loses interest in the cow and sits on it. You are halfway up a mountain with a crying giant baby and a flat cow when the mother comes down the slope, sees you, and assumes the worst.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride at her. She laughs, and the mud rises round your horse's legs.

resolutions.label: banish the bog-hag with faith and steel

success.body: You leave your horse stuck in the mud and wade on toward her on foot, speaking the Paternoster aloud with every step. She screams and stirs harder, and the rain lashes you, but you keep coming. When you reach the tussock, you touch the cross of your sword-hilt to her forehead. She shrieks and sinks, down and down, into the black water, and the storm stops as if a door had closed. The villages are saved. Your horse, when you dig it out, is very sulky.

failure.body: You wade toward her, praying, but halfway there, the mud takes you to the waist. She laughs and dances on her tussock, and the storm rages until dawn, when she simply gets bored and sinks away. The villages are flooded.

resolutions.label: bind her with the old words of the bog

success.body: You do not ride at her. You stand at the edge of the black water and call her by the names the marsh-folk use, one after another, until you find the one that makes her stop stirring. Then you bind her with it: back into the bog, until the Grail returns. She shrieks and sinks, and the storm stops as though a door had closed. Your horse, when you dig it out of the mud, is very sulky.

failure.body: You call her by the names the marsh-folk use, and one of them is not hers. It is her mother's. Something much bigger stirs under the bog. You flee, and the storm follows you for three days.

entries.body:
You come upon a farmer in a field of dead cattle, sitting on a stone with his head in his hands. Every cow in the field is lying on its side, stiff. In the middle of the field is the stump of an old hawthorn tree, freshly cut.

"I cut it down for firewood," the farmer says. "Last Candlemas. Everyone said not to. Everyone said it was a fairy thorn. I said I was a Christian and did not believe in that." He laughs bitterly. "The next morning, the first cow died. One a week since. Now it is the children who are coughing." He looks at you. "Last night I saw a tall man in a cloak of hawthorn leaves standing in the field, with a crown of thorns on his head. He looked at my house. He did not say anything."

responses.label: You may go to the King of the Fay and plead for the farmer.
You may help the farmer make amends to the fay by replanting the thorn.

entries.body:
You come upon a lake in a hollow of the hills, so still that it reflects the sky perfectly. In the middle of the lake, standing on the water, is a lady in white samite, with her long dark hair unbound.

"Come to the edge," she says, and her voice carries across the water as though she were beside you. "I am the Lady of the Lake. I gave the young king his sword. I will give you something too, if you like. One true answer, to one question, about yourself or about what is to come." She smiles. "But a true answer has a price. I will take one memory from you in exchange. You will not know which one until it is gone."

responses.label: You may ask the Lady of the Lake your question and pay her price.
You may ask the Lady of the Lake for her counsel instead, freely given.

entries.body:
You come upon a little man in a red cap and a green coat sitting on top of a wine barrel in a monastery cellar, drinking from a thimble. The cellarer, a round monk, is standing at the bottom of the stair, wringing his hands. "The clurichaun," he whispers to you. "He has been in our cellar a month. He drinks a barrel a week. We cannot get him out."

The little man lifts his thimble. "I am Dewi," he says, "and I will grant three wishes to any mortal who can beat me at a bargain. Or I will leave, and take the wine with me, if you can make me." He grins. "Nobody ever does either. The monks have tried holy water, and bells, and a cat. I drank the holy water and made friends with the cat."

responses.label: You may bargain with the clurichaun for his three wishes.
You may drive the clurichaun out of the monastery cellar.

entries.body:
You come upon a woman sitting on the step of a cottage with a baby in her arms. The baby is thin and wizened and has a face like an old man. It is screaming. The woman is staring at it with dry, hollow eyes.

"It is not mine," she says. "It is a changeling. They took my Gwion in the night and left this in his cradle. It eats and eats and never grows. It bites. It looks at me like an old man." She shudders. "The wise woman says I must put it on a shovel over the fire, and when it flies up the chimney, they will bring my Gwion back." She looks down at it. "But what if it is only a sick child? What if it is mine?"

The baby stops screaming and looks at you. It winks.

responses.label: You may go to the fay fort on the hill to bring back the stolen child.
You may trick the changeling into revealing itself.

entries.body: "Thirty years is long enough," you say. "Let me speak to the bishop." Brother Hugh goes white. "You would tell him?" "I would ask him," you say.

resolutions.label: plead for the old lovers before the bishop

success.body: The bishop is a brisk, hard-faced man who does not like knights. You meet him on the road and ride beside him for two days, talking. You talk about vows, and about what was done to two young people thirty years ago against their will. You talk about mercy. On the second evening, the bishop sighs and rubs his eyes. "I was betrothed once too," he says. "She died." On Saturday, he releases Brother Hugh and the Abbess Gwenfrewi from their vows. They are married by the river on Sunday, and they float a bowl downstream with a letter in it for you.

failure.body: The bishop is a brisk, hard-faced man who does not like knights. You meet him on the road and try to talk to him about mercy. He listens for a quarter of an hour and then says, "So it is true." On Saturday, Brother Hugh is sent north, and the abbess is sent south. You do not see the wooden bowl again.

resolutions.label: remind the bishop that God is merciful to old lovers

success.body: You ride beside the bishop for two days and speak of vows made by children, against their will, and of what the Lord said about the Sabbath being made for man. On the second evening, the bishop sighs. "I was betrothed once," he says. On Saturday he releases Brother Hugh and the Abbess Gwenfrewi from their vows, and on Sunday he marries them himself, by the river.

failure.body: You speak to the bishop of mercy and the Sabbath. He quotes Saint Paul back at you for an hour, and knows more of him than you do. On Saturday, Brother Hugh is sent north.

entries.body: "Singing will not save him," you say. "Swords might." The old priest looks at you sadly, but she does not stop you.

resolutions.label: bring a band of islanders across the sea to the war

success.body: You gather thirty of the refugees' young men and the islanders' fishing boats, and sail south through the Minch in a gale. You land in Galloway, and march south, and join the old king's army a week before the last battle. The islanders fight like demons. Most of them are dead by the end. The ones who live go home to Lewis and tell their children that they stood with Arthur. You are the one who led them. The old priest sends you the bow of the island's greatest archer, who did not come back.

failure.body: You gather thirty young men and sail south, but a storm scatters the boats in the Minch. You land in Galloway with six men, too late for anything.

resolutions.label: steer the island boats through the Minch in a gale

success.body: You gather thirty young men and the islanders' boats, and you do not wait for fair weather. You read the gale and the tide-races of the Minch as the island fishermen taught you, and bring every boat through to Galloway, and march south. You join the old king's army a week before the last battle. The islanders fight like demons. The ones who live go home to Lewis and tell their children that they stood with Arthur.

failure.body: You read the gale and the tide-races, and read them wrong. The boats are scattered. You land in Galloway with six men, too late for anything.

entries.body: "I will take the summit," you say. The young king grips your hand. "Take thirty men," he says. "The best climbers."

resolutions.label: storm the summit of Badon by night

success.body: You lead thirty men up the back of the hill in the dark, over rocks and through gorse. At the top, the Saxon archers are asleep. You take them by surprise. By dawn, the young king's banner is flying on the summit, and the Saxon host below looks up and sees it and loses heart. The battle of Badon is the greatest victory of the young king's reign. He sends for you afterwards and gives you a golden spur.

failure.body: You lead thirty men up the back of the hill in the dark, but a dog barks in the Saxon camp. The archers are awake. You are driven back down the hill with half your men. The battle is won anyway, at dawn, but at a terrible cost.

resolutions.label: find the goat-path the Saxons do not guard

success.body: You go up the back of the hill alone first, in the dusk, and find it: a goat-path through the gorse, hidden by a fold of the hill, where the Saxons have set no watch because no army could climb it. It is steep. Thirty men can climb it. At midnight, you lead them up in single file. By dawn, the young king's banner is flying on the summit of Badon, and the Saxon host below loses heart.

failure.body: You find a goat-path through the gorse and lead thirty men up it at midnight. It ends at a cliff. You come down again at dawn, and the battle is won anyway, at a terrible cost.

entries.body:
You come upon a mill beside a stream, where a big, sweating miller is standing guard over an iron cage in his yard. Inside the cage, a fay girl is huddled against the bars. Where she touches the iron, her skin is burned black. She is fading, growing more transparent every hour, like frost in the sun.

"Caught her myself," the miller says proudly. "She was stealing milk. The fair folk will pay any price to get her back. I have sent word to the hill. They have until sunset." He looks at the fading girl without pity. "If they do not pay, I will sell her to a lord who collects curiosities. Iron does not kill them, you know. Not quickly."

The fay girl lifts her head and looks at you. She does not beg. She only looks.

responses.label: You may free the fay girl from the miller's cage.
You may help the miller sell the fay girl to the highest bidder.

entries.body: You look at the crystal ball, and the silver star, and the book of blue leather. "I think I know whom you robbed," you say. "And I think he is waiting for you to find him."

resolutions.label: find the old enchanter to return his things

success.body: You sit down at the crossroads and think. An old man who laughs when he is robbed. A curse that brings you back to where you started. "He is here," you say. "He always was." You stand up and bow to the signpost. "Master Merlin," you say, "the thief would like to return your things." The signpost laughs, and is an old man in a grey cloak, leaning on a staff. "Took you long enough," he says to Owain. He takes his sack. To you, he gives the tiny golden harp. "It plays by itself," he says. "Mostly lullabies." Owain walks away down the road, and does not come back.

failure.body: You search the roads around the crossroads all day for an old man in a grey cloak. At sunset, you come back to the crossroads, having gone round in a circle. You try again, and again. Owain watches you with sympathy. You spend the night beside him on the stone.

entries.body: You go to Saint Martin's after dark. Two of Mordred's soldiers are dicing by a door in the crypt, beside a lantern.

resolutions.label: overpower the guards and lead the prisoners out

success.body: You come on the guards before they can reach for their spears and put them both down on the crypt floor. Beyond the door, in the caves, thirty men lie in the dark, weak with thirst. You bring them out a few at a time, through the crypt and the churchyard and down to the river, where a fisherman who remembers the old king ferries them across. The last of them, an old knight with a white beard, grips your hand. "The king will hear of this," he says, "if he lives." You hope he does.

failure.body: You come on the guards, but one of them gets to the bell-rope before you can stop him. The crypt fills with soldiers. You flee through the churchyard. Behind you, the prisoners are knocking, three knocks and a pause, and you cannot go back.

entries.body: You go to the nearest well and look down into the black water. Behind you, Brother Cynan laughs. "You think you can undo what God has done?" he says.

resolutions.label: cleanse the village wells

notes: Lose 1 unwanted Status Card, if you have one

success.body: You kneel at the well and pray. You pray for the village, and for the children, and for the reeve, and for the hermit, who has been wronged. You pray for a long time. Toward evening, the hermit comes and kneels on the other side of the well. He does not say anything. He only prays too. At dusk, the water in the well goes clear. Brother Cynan weeps. "I did not want to hate them," he says. The next day, without being asked, the villagers begin to clear the ruins of the chapel.

failure.body: You kneel at the well and pray, and chant the words for cleansing water. The well stays black. Behind you, Brother Cynan shakes his head. "It is not the water," he says. "It is them." The children are still coughing when you leave.

entries.body: "I will ride with you," you say. Maud grins with half her teeth. "Then take the front," she says. "When I whistle, you stop the horses."

resolutions.label: lead the attack on the tax cart

success.body: When the cart rounds the bend, you ride out in front of it and seize the lead horse's bridle, and Maud's archers stand up in the bracken with their bows drawn. The escort takes one look and throws down its weapons. The cart holds nine hundred silver pennies. Maud gives you a hundred, and the rest goes back to the villages in sacks, left on doorsteps in the night. For years afterwards, in that country, people speak of the knight who robbed the sheriff.

failure.body: When the cart rounds the bend, you ride out in front of it, but the escort is twice as large as Maud said, and they have crossbows. The outlaws flee. You are dragged off your horse and taken to Shrewsbury in the tax cart, sitting on the sheriff's money.

resolutions.label: shoot the escort's horses from the bracken

success.body: You take a bow from one of Maud's men and lie in the bracken, and when the cart rounds the bend, you shoot the lead horse of the escort, and then the second. The cart stops. The escort, on foot and surrounded by bows, throws down its weapons. Nine hundred silver pennies go back to the villages in sacks, left on doorsteps in the night. Maud gives you a hundred of them.

failure.body: You lie in the bracken with a borrowed bow, and your first arrow goes into a tree, and the escort sees where it came from. They charge the bracken. The outlaws scatter, and you are left in the ditch with a sergeant sitting on you.

entries.body: You look at the children on the roof, and the water still rising. The grain can wait. You ride into the flood.

resolutions.label: carry the stranded families to high ground

success.body: You ride back and forth through the flood all day and half the night, with children on your saddle and old men clinging to your stirrups, and your horse swimming in the deep places. By dawn, everyone in the lower town is on the hill by the cathedral, cold and wet and alive. You fall asleep on the cathedral steps. When you wake, the bishop has opened the cathedral's own granary, and is shaming the merchant into opening his.

failure.body: You ride into the flood, and your horse loses its footing in a sunken street, and you are both swept away. You fetch up against a church wall a mile downstream. By the time you get back, others have done the rescuing.

resolutions.label: gather the boats and command the rescue

success.body: You ride to the upper town and turn out every man with a boat, a door or a barrel. You set them in pairs, give each a street, and send the strongest swimmers to the farthest roofs. By midnight, the lower town is empty and the cathedral hill is full of wet, living people. The bishop, shamed, opens his granary, and then shames the merchant into opening his.

failure.body: You gather the boats, but in the dark and the rain nobody can hear your orders, and two boats go to the same roof while a third roof goes under. You save most of them. You count the rest for a long time.

entries.body: You look at the great wooden idol, and at the Saxons, and you remember what an old soldier once told you: take away a man's god, and you take away his courage.

resolutions.label: set fire to the idol of Woden

success.body: You creep into the temple at midnight and pour oil on the idol's feet, and set it alight. The Saxons wake to see their god burning. They cry out in terror. They think it is a sign. By the time the idol falls, they have fled into the forest, leaving their captives, their feast and their weapons. The captives walk out of the temple at dawn, blinking at the smoke.

failure.body: You creep into the temple and pour oil on the idol's feet, but a guard sees you. The Saxons drag you before the idol. You spend a very long night tied to the stake beside the captives, and are rescued at dawn by a band of the old king's men.

resolutions.label: preach the true God to the Saxons' own priest

success.body: You walk into the clearing unarmed, in the full light of their fires, and stand before the priest in the wolfskin and tell him about a God who wanted no man's blood. The Saxons are so astonished that nobody moves. The priest argues, in broken British. You argue back. At the end, he looks at the three captives, and at the idol, and at you, and cuts the captives loose himself. "Your god is brave," he says. "Or you are mad."

failure.body: You walk into the clearing and preach. The Saxons listen politely, and then tie you to the stake beside the captives. The old king's men find you all at dawn.

entries.body: You kneel beside the hermit and pray, for the lion and for the serpent and for yourself.

resolutions.label: pray until the struggle is ended

success.body: You pray until your knees ache. Toward evening, the lion gives one great heave and throws off the serpent, which slithers away into the grass. The lion lies down, bloody and panting. The hermit looks at you. "It has never won before," he says. "Never. Not in thirty years." He looks at you very strangely all evening.

failure.body: You pray until your knees ache, and the lion's roars grow weaker and weaker. At dusk, the serpent unwinds itself and slithers away, and the lion does not rise. The hermit tells his beads. "Tomorrow," he says, "there will be another."

entries.body: You kneel beside him. The hermit kneels on the other side. "Tell it all," you say. "Every word."

resolutions.label: bring the dying knight to true repentance

success.body: He tells it all. The crossroads, and the bog, and the screaming, and the year since. At the end, he weeps like a child. The hermit absolves him. Near dawn, the storm stops, and the knight asks you to open the door so he can see the sky. He dies looking at it. You bury him under an oak, and carve on it, at the hermit's suggestion, *He went back in the end.*

failure.body: He tells some of it, and then stops, and says, "No. He was a fool. He would have told me wrong too." He turns his face to the wall. He dies before dawn, and the hermit looks at you and says nothing.

entries.body: "Come," you say. "Glastonbury is not far. They will take you back if I speak for you." Brother Aldhelm shakes his head. "They will not," he says. "They are afraid of what I see." But he lets you help him onto your horse.

resolutions.label: persuade the abbot to take him back

success.body: The Abbot of Glastonbury is a stern man, but you speak honestly to him. The old monk is not mad, you say. He is only frightened, and he has nowhere else to go. You offer to pay for his keep for a year. The abbot looks at Brother Aldhelm for a long time. Then he sighs. "He may keep bees," he says, "and he may talk to them. But not in chapel." Brother Aldhelm is happier with bees than with crows, and his prophecies, the brothers say, have become much more cheerful.

failure.body: The Abbot of Glastonbury will not see you. His porter says the old monk is a shame to the house. When you leave, Brother Aldhelm gets down from your horse and walks away up the hill, toward a field of crows.

resolutions.label: calm the old man's visions with prayer

success.body: At Glastonbury, you do not go to the abbot. You go to the chapel and kneel beside Brother Aldhelm all night. Toward dawn, he stops trembling. "It is quieter," he says, surprised. "They have stopped shouting." When the brothers come in for Matins, they find him kneeling in his old place, singing the psalm with them. Nobody says a word. The abbot, when he hears, lets him stay.

failure.body: You kneel beside Brother Aldhelm all night, praying. Toward dawn, he grips your arm and whispers, "I see you there. On the plain. In the rain." And for a moment, so do you. You leave Glastonbury in a hurry, and the vision goes with you.

entries.body: You step between Ninian and the lord's men. "He is a simple man," you say. "Let him be." The lord's face darkens. "He is a slanderer," he says, "and my men will have him."

resolutions.label: hold off the lord's men

success.body: The two men-at-arms come at you, but their hearts are not in it, and after a few blows they back off. The crowd cheers. The lord, red with rage, rides away. That evening, Ninian comes to you as you eat. "The ledger," he says. "The steward keeps two." He goes away again, humming. The next week, you hear that the lord found the second ledger, and that the steward has fled to Ireland with a great deal of money. The lord sends you a gift of wine, and an apology to Ninian, which Ninian ignores.

failure.body: The two men-at-arms come at you, and they are better than you expected, and the crowd does not help. When you get up, Ninian has been whipped, and the lord is gone. The fool is sitting in the grass, bleeding, humming. "The knight will see the ledger," he says to you, "later."

resolutions.label: vouch for the fool on your own honour

success.body: You put your hand on your sword-hilt. "I will stand surety for him," you say to the lord. "If his words are slander, I will answer for them myself, in the lists, against any man you name." The lord looks at you, and at your sword, and at the fair watching. He does not want a joust. He wants his steward to be honest. "A week," he says. By the end of the week, he has found the second ledger himself.

failure.body: You offer to answer for the fool's words in the lists. The lord names his steward's nephew, who is very large. It goes badly. The fool is whipped anyway.

entries.body: "We will find them, my lord," you say. Clariance puts his boots on the wrong feet and cheerfully climbs onto his horse. "Splendid! Which way?"

resolutions.label: read the forest and follow the army's trail

success.body: Four hundred men leave a great many signs. You find trampled bracken, broken branches and the remains of a very large breakfast. By noon you can hear them: four hundred Northumbrians, all shouting "Clariance!" in different directions. The king rides into the middle of them beaming. "There you all are," he says. "I have been looking everywhere." His captain looks at you with heartfelt gratitude and gives you a fine hunting horn.

failure.body: Four hundred men should leave a great many signs, but the forest floor has been churned by wild pigs, and you follow the wrong trail for a day. You come out on a hillside just in time to see the Northumbrians marching away on the far side of the valley. Clariance waves happily at them. They do not see him. You spend another two days catching them up, and the king talks the whole way.

resolutions.label: take command of the search as the army's captain would

success.body: You climb the tallest oak and look for smoke. When you see it, you blow three long blasts on your horn, the signal every army in Britain uses to rally. Within the hour, a troop of Northumbrian horsemen comes crashing through the undergrowth, swords drawn. Clariance is so pleased he makes you an honorary captain of his army, and his men give you a cheer that sends every bird in the forest into the air.

failure.body: You climb the tallest oak and look for smoke. You see it, and blow three long blasts on your horn. Within the hour, horsemen come crashing through the undergrowth, swords drawn. Unfortunately, they are Saxons. You and the king escape by hiding in the stream, up to your necks, while they search the bank. By the time they leave, you are both very cold and very quiet.

entries.body: "How much?" you ask. The fen-man names a price. It is everything you have.

resolutions.label: lead the old king's men by the hidden way

notes: Lose 1 Treasure, if possible

success.body: You pay. The fen-man leads you and fifty of the old king's men by night, through the reeds and along paths under the water that only he can see. At dawn, you come out behind Mordred's men on the causeway. They break. The causeway is the old king's. The fen-man, you notice, is looting the dead before the fighting is over.

failure.body: You pay. The fen-man leads you by night through the reeds, and then he vanishes, and you are left in the marsh with fifty men and no path. It is a long night.

resolutions.label: haggle the fen-man down to a fair price

success.body: You do not pay everything. You sit down in his boat and haggle, as a fen-man haggles, over eels and ale and his grandmother's health, for an hour, until he is laughing and the price is a quarter of what he asked.
