Then he leads you and fifty of the old king's men by night through the reeds. At dawn, you come out behind Mordred's men on the causeway. They break.

failure.body: You haggle with him for an hour, and at the end of it, he paddles off to Mordred's side instead. They pay more.

entries.body: You take a lantern and ride out into the storm. The hermit calls after you that you are mad.

resolutions.label: search the drowned bog in the storm

success.body: You find the bog by the crossroads, a mile away, and in it, clinging to a dead tree, up to his chest in the water, a knight. He has been there, he says, for a day, not a year. The wounded man was feverish. You haul him out and bring him back to the hut, and the wounded knight sees him, and weeps, and grips his hand, and asks his pardon, and gets it. Both of them live.

failure.body: You ride out into the storm and search the bog by the crossroads all night, and find nothing but a shield, sinking. When you get back to the hut, the wounded knight is dead.

resolutions.label: ride the edge of the bog by the lightning

success.body: You do not wade in. You ride the firm edge of the bog at a gallop, and every time the lightning flashes, you look. On the fourth flash, you see him: a knight up to his chest, clinging to a dead tree. You throw him a rope from the saddle and haul him out with your horse. He has been there a day, not a year. The wounded man in the hut grips his hand and asks his pardon. Both of them live.

failure.body: You ride the edge of the bog by the lightning, and the lightning strikes a tree beside you. Your horse bolts into the bog. By the time you are out, the wounded knight in the hut is dead.

entries.body: You wade through the mud to where the king's banner lies, torn and filthy, and lift it.

resolutions.label: raise the king's banner and rally the host

success.body: You plant it on the highest ground in the camp, in the lightning, and stand beside it with your sword drawn, and call out to the men that you are staying, and so is the dragon. Men come. First a few, then dozens. By midnight, the storm has blown over, and there are more men round the banner than were there at sunset. The old king comes out of his tent and sees it, and stands for a long time, and then he walks over and puts his hand on your shoulder, and says nothing at all.

partial.body: You plant the banner on the highest ground and stand beside it. Some men come. Some do not. In the morning, the army is smaller, but it is still an army.

failure.body: You plant the banner and stand beside it in the rain. Nobody comes. In the morning, you are still standing there, and half the camp is gone.

entries.body: You take the young monk aside. "Is the book worth a war?" you ask. He looks at it for a long time. "No," he says. "But it is beautiful."

resolutions.label: hide the disputed book and cool the quarrel

success.body: You wrap the book in oilcloth and hide it in the abbey's bread oven, which has not been lit in a week. Then you go to the old abbot and tell him that the copy has been lost in a fire, and to the young monk's kinsmen that there is nothing left to fight for. By the time the book is taken out of the oven, a year later, everyone has calmed down. The young monk leaves Ireland in shame, and founds a monastery on an island in the north called Iona. You are not sure you did the right thing. You are sure nobody died.

failure.body: You hide the book in the bread oven, and the baker, not knowing, lights it the next morning. The young monk weeps. The kinsmen march anyway.

resolutions.label: mediate between the two abbots in the church

success.body: You bring the two abbots into the stone church together and sit between them, with both books on the altar. You ask the old abbot what he truly wants. It is not the book. It is to be asked. You make the young monk ask him, on his knees, for leave to keep the copy. The old abbot, astonished and moved, gives it. The kinsmen go home. The young monk still leaves Ireland, of his own choice, and founds a monastery on an island called Iona.

failure.body: You bring the two abbots together in the church and ask the young monk to kneel and ask the old abbot's leave. He will not. "God's words need no man's leave," he says. The old abbot walks out, white with anger, and by nightfall the kinsmen are marching.

entries.body: You do not sit. You take off your sword and roll up your sleeves, and carry the bread and fish up and down the table.

resolutions.label: serve at the hermit's table until all are fed

success.body: You serve all day. The line of the hungry never ends: beggars, pilgrims, soldiers, children. As the sun goes down, the last of them is fed, and the hermit sits down and gives you a piece of bread, and you realise you have not eaten all day. It is the best bread you have ever tasted. "The ones who serve," says the hermit, "always get the last piece. It is the best one."

failure.body: You serve all day, and by evening, you are so tired you drop a basket of fish in the mud. The hermit only laughs and picks them up. But you go away feeling you have been clumsy with something holy.

resolutions.label: keep the long line of the hungry in good order

success.body: The line of the hungry is pushing and shoving and near a riot, because every one of them is sure the bread will run out. You walk up and down it and talk to each of them, calmly, and put the children and the lepers at the front, and the strong men at the back, and tell them there is enough. There is. By sunset, the last of them is fed. The hermit gives you a piece of bread, and it is the best bread you have ever tasted.

failure.body: You try to put the line in order, and the strong men at the back do not want to be at the back. There is a fight. The hermit breaks it up, not you.

entries.body: You draw your sword. Cormoran sighs, and stands up, and picks up a club made from an entire millstone on a pole. "Nobody ever wants to play any more," he says sadly.

resolutions.label: fight Cormoran on the bridge

success.body: The bridge is narrow, and the giant is wide, and his club is slow. He swings at you and misses and takes out a chunk of the parapet. You duck under the next swing and drive your sword into his foot. He howls and hops, and hops right off the bridge into the river. He comes up spluttering. "All right!" he says. "All right! Cross! Cross!" You cross. On the other side, you leave him a cheese, which you buy at the next village and send back by a boy, out of pity.

failure.body: The bridge is narrow, and the giant is wide. His club catches you on the shield and knocks you right off the bridge into the river. You come up gasping on the far bank, which is at least the right side. The giant is laughing too hard to follow you. Your horse is still on the other side.

entries.body: You turn your horse and ride hard for the nearest village on the high ground.

resolutions.label: rouse the villages and lead the boats out into the flood

success.body: You burst into the village alehouse and shout that the marsh is flooding, and in ten minutes every man with a boat is on the shore. You organise them: two boats to each roof, the fastest rowers to the farthest houses. By morning, every family in the marsh has been brought off, and most of their cows. The marsh-folk remember you in their songs for a long time, as the knight who rang the bell.

failure.body: You burst into the village alehouse and shout that the marsh is flooding, but it is late and they are drunk, and it takes an hour to get them moving. By the time the boats reach the marsh, three roofs are empty.

resolutions.label: guide the boats through the drowned fields

success.body: You know how water lies. You stand in the bow of the first boat and read the flood: where the hedges run under it, where the ditches will snag an oar, where the old lane lies straight beneath the surface. The boats follow your hand. By dawn, every roof in the marsh is empty, and nobody has capsized. The marsh-folk remember you in their songs.

failure.body: You stand in the bow and read the flood, and read it wrong, and your boat runs onto a drowned hedge. It takes an hour to get free. Three roofs are empty when you reach them.

entries.body: You look at the widow. "The squire says you handed him the cup," you say. "Did you?" The widow's face does not change. "What are you suggesting?" she asks, very coldly.

resolutions.label: uncover the widow's guilt

notes: Place a Wisdom Skill Marker on your Accompanied Status Card

success.body: You ask for the cup. The widow says it has been washed. You ask the tavern-keeper who washed it, and he says nobody did, because it was taken away by the widow's maid. You find the maid. She is terrified. She tells you about the little bottle, and the steward, and the promise of a manor. When you bring her before the crowd, the widow's face finally changes. The squire is freed. The widow is taken away in chains. Iolo swears himself to your service, and rides with you as far as Camelot.

failure.body: You ask for the cup. The widow says it has been washed. You ask who washed it, and nobody knows. You ask the widow's maid, and she says nothing. The widow smiles at you at last. "You have accused a grieving woman," she says, "before a whole crossroads, of murdering her husband." The crowd turns on you, and the squire hangs anyway.

resolutions.label: trap the widow into betraying herself

success.body: You bow, and apologise, and say that of course the squire is guilty. Then you mention, as if in passing, that the physician found no poison in the cup at all, only in the jug, which the steward carried. The widow's face flickers. "The steward?" she says, too quickly. "He would never." In the silence that follows, the crowd turns its head, slowly, toward the steward, who is already running. The squire is freed.

failure.body: You bow and say the squire is guilty, and mention the jug. The widow smiles. "How interesting," she says, "since there was no jug." You have told a lie in front of a whole crossroads, and been caught in it.

entries.body: Morfudd walks beside you for a while before she answers. "My lady had a brother," she says, "who was killed by a knight with two swords. My lady had a smith forge this sword from the dead brother's sword, and a witch put a charm on it. It will only come out of the scabbard for a knight with no guile in him, and when it does, it will look for the knight who killed her brother. It will not rest until it finds him." She looks at the ground. "My lady says that is justice. I think it is a trap. Whoever draws it will be drawn after it." She stops. "I do not want to give it to anyone, now. But my lady will beat me if I come home with it." You walk together to the next crossroads and she thanks you for listening.
"Then the saint has chosen you," you say. "Let us go on, and see where he sends you." Wat laughs, and the boy laughs, and behind you, in the forest, you hear the monks' horses.

resolutions.label: keep Wat ahead of the monks

success.body: You lead him off the track and through a stream and up over a ridge, and the monks go on down the valley, calling for a man on a donkey. For a month, you travel with Wat along the back roads of the Marches, and wherever he goes, something happens. A fever breaks. A well runs sweet. A mad woman is calm. At the end of the month, Wat takes the finger back to the abbey himself, and lays it on the altar, and walks away. "It was never mine," he says. "I only carried it."

failure.body: You lead him off the track and through a stream, but the monks have a hound. They catch you on the ridge, and take the finger, and take Wat, and take you too, for good measure, to be tried by the bishop for sacrilege.

resolutions.label: ride ahead of the monks with Wat up behind you

success.body: You pull Wat up behind your saddle, put the lame boy on the donkey, and ride. The monks' horses are old and fat. By nightfall you are two valleys ahead, and by the end of the week you are in the Marches, where nobody has heard of Saint Dyfrig. Wherever Wat goes, something happens: a fever breaks, a well runs sweet. At the end of a month, he takes the finger back to the abbey himself.

failure.body: You pull Wat up behind your saddle and ride, and your horse, carrying two, goes lame at the first ford. The monks come up with a bishop's warrant. Wat goes in chains, and you go with him.

entries.body: You wade across the mud to the abbey door. Inside, the nave is knee-deep in black water, and the gold is further in than you thought.

resolutions.label: find the treasure and escape the tide

success.body: You watch the water, and the gulls, and you know when the tide is about to turn. You find the gold, a chalice and two candlesticks, in the sanctuary, and you are out of the door and across the mud with the water chasing at your heels. The fisherman stares at you. You take the chalice to the nearest church. The candlesticks, you keep.

failure.body: You find the chalice in the sanctuary, and turn, and the tide is already at the door. You swim out through a window. You lose the chalice.

resolutions.label: ask the drowned abbot for leave to take it

success.body: You stand in the drowned nave and bow, and say aloud that you have come for the abbey's gold, not to keep, but to give to a church that is not under the sea. The water in the nave ripples. A grey figure rises out of it, with a chalice in its hands. It looks at you a long time, and then holds the chalice out. You take it, and run, as the tide turns. You give it to the nearest church. It is still there.

failure.body: You stand in the nave and ask for leave. Nothing answers. You reach for the chalice anyway, and the water closes over your feet like a hand, and it is a long, cold struggle to the door.

entries.body: You wait by the colonnade as night falls. The soldier appears, grey and translucent, with a short sword at his hip. He stops in front of you and says something in Latin.

resolutions.label: answer the ghost's watchword and release him

success.body: You know a little Latin from the priests. He is asking for the watchword. You think about it for a long time. Then you say the only thing you can think of that a Roman soldier would want to hear: "The legion has gone home. You may go home too." The ghost stares at you. Then he takes off his helmet, and he is only a boy of eighteen, with a tired face. He salutes you, and walks into the green water, and is gone. The townsfolk never hear him again.

failure.body: You try to answer him in your little Latin, and get it wrong. The ghost draws his short sword. You wake face-down at the edge of the water, choking, with the reeve pulling you out.

resolutions.label: stand guard beside him until his watch is relieved

success.body: You draw your sword and fall in beside the ghost, and march with him up and down the colonnade, in step, all night. At dawn, you halt, and turn to him, and salute, and say in your little Latin: "Relieved." He stops. He takes off his helmet, and he is only a boy of eighteen, with a tired face. He salutes you back, and walks into the green water, and is gone.

failure.body: You fall in beside the ghost and march with him, but you fall out of step, and he turns on you with his short sword. You wake face-down at the edge of the water.

entries.body: You step into the middle of the circle, between the young men and the cracked stone. "This is a king's grave," you say. "Leave it be."

resolutions.label: guard the king's grave through the night

success.body: The young men argue, but you stand your ground, and at last they go back to their fires. You keep watch all night by the cracked stone. Near dawn, the light from the crack grows brighter, and brighter, until the whole circle is lit as if by the sun. Then it fades, and the crack is closed, and the stone is whole again. The pilgrims fall on their knees. The old pilgrim woman kisses your hands. "It has gone to meet the vessel," she says. "You let it go in peace."

failure.body: The young men do not argue. They push past you, and you fight them, and in the struggle, somebody knocks over a torch, and the grass in the circle catches fire. When it is out, the light is gone, and the stone is black.

resolutions.label: calm the pilgrims with a vigil of your own

success.body: You do not bar the young men with your sword. You kneel beside the cracked stone and begin to pray aloud, and ask everyone who wants to see the old king to kneel with you instead. The pilgrims come, and kneel, and so, grumbling, do the young men. All night, the circle prays. Near dawn, the light from the crack grows brighter, and brighter, and fades, and the stone is whole again. The pilgrims weep.

failure.body: You kneel and pray aloud, and ask them to kneel with you. The young men do not. They lift the stone while everyone else is praying, and the light goes out.

entries.body:
You remember the maiden by the flooded river, and what she whispered in your ear. It is so simple that you laugh aloud, and the whole hall turns to look at you.

You rise, and go to the old king on his litter, and kneel, and ask him: "Whom does the Grail serve?"

The old king looks at you. His eyes fill with tears. "Nobody has asked," he says. "In twenty years, nobody has asked." He tells you the answer, and it is the simplest thing in the world. As he speaks, the blood stops running down the spear. The wound in his thighs closes. Outside, you hear rain, for the first time in years, falling on the dust.

The maiden comes back into the hall, and uncovers the vessel, and you see it, just for a moment, before the light is too bright. When you can see again, the old king is standing, for the first time in twenty years, and weeping, and embracing you.

notes: Lose Story Token #15
Every other Knight gains 1 Rank of Divinity, for the land is healed

entries.body: "My lord," you say, "the dead do not come back for nothing. Make the treaty."

resolutions.label: persuade the old king to seek terms with Mordred

success.body: The old king listens. He looks at the stones, and at the sky, and at you. At last, he nods. "A treaty," he says. "A parley. A month." He sends heralds at dawn. Mordred agrees to meet. You do not know, going to bed that night, whether it will save anything. But the old king sleeps, for the first time in a week, and in the morning, he gives you his spear. "Hold it for me," he says, "while I talk." You will hold it, later, on the plain, when everything goes wrong.

failure.body: The old king listens, and then shakes his head. "I have made too many treaties," he says. "Mordred breaks them all." He goes back to his tent. In the morning, he goes out to fight. You hold his stirrup as he mounts.

resolutions.label: read the king's dream as the old wise men would

success.body: You ask him to tell you the dream again, every detail, and you read it as the old dream-readers read, not as a fear but as a message. The wheel is Fortune. The water is war. The nephew with the crowd of ladies is a gift: he has been sent to buy the king a month. "Take the month," you say. The old king is silent a long while. Then he sends heralds at dawn. He gives you his spear. "Hold it for me," he says, "while I talk."

failure.body: You ask him to tell you the dream again, and you read it as the old dream-readers read, and you read it wrong. The old king listens, and nods, and goes out to fight.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride into the marsh with the lord's men.

resolutions.label: break the fanatics' line

success.body: You find the place in their line where the marsh is firmest and lead the charge through it. The white-robed men break, and the boys throw down their spears and run. You shout for the lord's men to let them go. Some of them listen. At the end of the day, the monastery is taken, and the false prophet is in chains. You do not feel like a hero.

failure.body: You lead the charge, but the fanatics do not break. They fight to the last, singing. You are wounded. The lord's men win, at a terrible cost.

resolutions.label: call on the boys to lay down their spears

success.body: You ride out between the lines with your helm off and your hands empty, and call out to the white-robed boys, not in anger, but as a priest calls to children, that God does not want them to die for a man in a tower. You tell them the Grail feeds; it does not starve. The singing falters. A boy of fourteen lowers his spear, and then another. By nightfall, half of them have walked out of the marsh to their mothers.

failure.body: You ride out between the lines with your hands empty and call to the boys. They sing louder, and charge.

entries.body: You catch the fool's eye and glance at your horse. He understands at once. He grins, and when the headsman lifts his axe, the fool rolls sideways off the block and runs.

resolutions.label: snatch the fool from the scaffold

success.body: You ride through the crowd, reach down, and haul the fool up behind your saddle by his motley, and you are away before the king's men can move. You ride hard for the border with arrows singing past. That night, in a barn, the fool laughs until he cries. "The king will be so angry," he says. "It was worth being beheaded for, almost." He goes to Ireland, where the kings like jests, and you are not welcome in that castle again.

failure.body: You ride through the crowd and reach for the fool, but your hand closes on his cap, and it comes off with a jingle, and he falls back onto the scaffold. You are dragged from your horse by the king's men. They make you watch.

entries.body: You ride to the edge of the marsh and blow your horn, three long blasts.

resolutions.label: rally the scattered soldiers in the fog

success.body: The men come to your horn, one by one, out of the fog, soaked and lost. You form them up on a hummock of dry ground, and send out parties to bring in the others, and by noon, you have a hundred men in a solid shield-wall. The Picts, finding no more stragglers to pick off, go back to their boats. Sir Griflet is brought in by his squire, half-drowned and cheerful.

failure.body: You blow your horn, and the men come to it, and so do the Picts. You fight on the hummock of dry ground until the fog lifts.

resolutions.label: lift the fog with the fen-men's words

success.body: An old fen-man with the army tells you the words his grandmother used to thin a fog for the eel-boats. You say them from the hummock, loudly, three times. The fog does not lift. It thins, just enough to see a spear's length. It is enough. Your men find each other, and the Picts, who were counting on the fog, find themselves in the open. They go back to their boats.

failure.body: You say the fen-man's words from the hummock, and the fog thickens instead. The old fen-man shrugs. "She was not a very good grandmother," he says.

entries.body: Arthur leans back against the wall. "Because I was a nobody until I was fifteen," he says. "Sir Ector's foster-son. I mucked out stables. I fetched Kay's sword. I was sent back for it once and could not find it, and I took the first sword I saw, and that was the one in the stone." He grins. "Everyone kneels now. Nobody tells me anything. So once a month I put on this cloak and come here, and a man called Hob tells me his taxes are a disgrace, and I go home and lower them." He points across the room. "That is Hob. Buy him an ale. He has earned it." You do, and spend a merry evening learning more about the cattle trade than you ever wanted to know.
You wade into the water and take the hermit by the arm. He struggles. "My vow," he says. "My vow!"

resolutions.label: convince the hermit that his vow is kept

success.body: "God took your vow," you say, "and sent me." The hermit stares at you. Then, slowly, his face crumples, and he lets you lead him out of the water. You build a fire and wrap him in your cloak. By morning, he is warm and weeping. "I think," he says, "I wanted to die, and called it prayer." Two days later, you hear, the bog begins to fall.

failure.body: "God sent me," you say. The hermit looks at you with contempt. "The devil also sends people," he says, and pulls away from you, and stands in the water with his arms raised. You cannot drag an old man from his prayers by force. You leave him there.

resolutions.label: carry the hermit out bodily, vow or no vow

success.body: You do not argue. You pick the old man up, dripping, and carry him out of the cave while he beats your shoulders with his fists and prays at you. You build a fire and wrap him in your cloak. By morning, he is warm and weeping. "I wanted to die," he says, "and called it prayer." Two days later, the bog begins to fall.

failure.body: You pick him up, and he fights like a cat, and you both go under in the cold water. You come up choking, and he is still in the cave, standing, praying. You leave him there.

entries.body:
The Green Knight looks at you, and the grey in his face turns, a little, to green. "You," he says. "You kept your word, once. You came to my chapel. You took my blow." He holds out the axe, handle first. "Then you are the only one I will let do this."

He kneels in the snow, and lifts his faded hair from his neck. "Strike," he says. "For the land. For your king. I have been green long enough."

resolutions.label: strike the Green Knight's last blow

notes: Lose Story Token #14
Every Knight may remove 1 unwanted Status Card

success.body: You strike. His head rolls in the snow, and it does not rise, and the body does not get up. But green runs out of him into the ground like water, and spreads, and where it spreads, the snow melts, and grass comes up, and the stream runs faster. You stand in the middle of a green circle in the white wood, weeping. Far to the south, men will say later that the spring came early that year, the last year of the old king. It did.

notes: Lose Story Token #14

failure.body: You lift the axe, and you cannot bring it down. The Green Knight waits. At last he gets up, and takes the axe from you, gently. "It was never your blow," he says. "I should have known." He walks into the wood and is gone.

entries.body: "My lady," you say, "a year is a long time. Tanwen must live with what he did every day of it." Tanwen looks up at you for the first time. The queen's eyes narrow.

resolutions.label: argue for the maiden's justice before the court

success.body: You speak plainly. The law of the realm is that such a man hangs. The queen's mercy is a fine thing, but it was not the queen he wronged. When you have finished, the queen turns to Tanwen. "What do you want?" she asks. The miller's daughter stares at her, astonished. "His lands," she says at last. "For my family. And for him to go on a pilgrimage and never come back." The queen smiles, very slightly. "That," she says, "is the answer to my riddle." Gromer leaves for Jerusalem the next morning.

failure.body: You speak plainly. The law of the realm is that such a man hangs. The queen hears you out with a stony face. "The law of the realm," she says, "is my husband's. The mercy is mine. Do not tell me which to prefer." She dismisses you from her presence, and the court is cool toward you for a season.

resolutions.label: cite the old law of the realm before the court

success.body: You recite, word for word, the law Uther made and his son kept: that a man who forces a maiden forfeits his life, or his lands, at the maiden's choice. You turn to Tanwen. "The choice is hers," you say. The whole court looks at the miller's daughter. "His lands," she says. The queen raises an eyebrow, and then she nods. Gromer leaves court that day without a penny, and Tanwen's family have a farm.

failure.body: You recite the old law, and get a word wrong, and a clerk corrects you, and then the queen corrects the clerk. By the end, the court is arguing about grammar and nobody is thinking about Tanwen at all.

entries.body: You take hold of one half of the cracked altar stone. Three young pilgrims take the other. You heave.

resolutions.label: lift the stone and look upon the buried king

success.body: The stone lifts. Beneath it lies an old king in bronze armour, with his hands folded on a sword, and his face as fresh as if he had just died. The light comes from his chest. As you look, he opens his eyes, and looks at you, and smiles. "Not yet," he says, in a voice like wind in the grass. "But soon. Tell my nephew's son to be ready." He closes his eyes. You lower the stone very gently. The light goes on shining through the crack.

partial.body: The stone lifts. Beneath it lies an old king in bronze armour, sleeping. The light comes from his chest. You lower the stone, gently, without waking him.

failure.body: The stone lifts, and the light goes out, and beneath it there is only dust. The pilgrims groan. You have woken nothing, and put something out.

entries.body: "I will carry it," you say. Mordred's face lights up. He grips your hand. "Thank you, friend," he says. "I will not forget it. I never forget anything."

resolutions.label: ride north to Orkney through the winter

success.body: It is a hard road north in winter, over the high moors and across the sea from Caithness in an open boat. Queen Morgause receives the letter in her hall and reads it with an unreadable face. Then she burns it. "Tell my son," she says, "that I understand." When you return, Mordred thanks you warmly and gives you a fine grey horse. You never learn what was in the letter. But from then on, Mordred greets you at court as a friend, and others notice it.

failure.body: It is a hard road north in winter. On the high moors, a blizzard catches you, and you spend two nights in a shepherd's hut with your fingers turning black. By the time you reach Orkney, Morgause has already gone south. You leave the letter with her steward. Mordred thanks you anyway, warmly. "It is the thought," he says.

resolutions.label: ride hard by the coast road before the snows

success.body: You take the coast road north, changing horses at every abbey, and reach Caithness before the first snow. The ferrymen say you are mad. Queen Morgause receives the letter, reads it and burns it. "Tell my son I understand," she says. When you return, Mordred embraces you. From then on, he greets you at court as a friend, and others notice it.

failure.body: You take the coast road north and ride your horse lame at Berwick. The snows come while you are waiting for another. You reach Orkney a month late. Mordred thanks you warmly anyway. It is the warmth that makes you uneasy.

entries.body: You catch Nentres's eye and nod toward your saddle. He understands at once. When the sheriff turns to read the sentence, you spur your horse at the cart.

resolutions.label: cut him down and ride for the forest with him

success.body: Your sword severs the rope as you pass. Nentres drops onto your horse's rump like a sack of meal, and you are through the crowd and away before the sheriff has finished his sentence. You ride hard for the forest with arrows humming after you. That night, by a small fire, Nentres gives you a gold ring from his own hand. "Garlot remembers its friends," he says. "And its enemies. Arthur will not forget this." He rides north at dawn.

failure.body: Your sword severs the rope as you pass, but Nentres, with his hands tied, cannot grab hold. He falls between your horse's hooves, and the sheriff's men are on you both before you can turn. You spend the night in the gaol at Carleon. Nentres hangs at noon the next day, and they make you watch.

resolutions.label: slip the hangman a purse and cut the rope in the crush

success.body: You press close to the cart and let the hangman see the weight of your purse. He sees it. When the sheriff turns to read the sentence, the hangman fumbles the knot, and in the moment of confusion you cut Nentres's bonds and he is off the cart and into the crowd. By the time the sheriff looks up, there is nobody on the cart but a hangman with a heavier belt. Nentres sends you a gold ring from Garlot a month later.

failure.body: You let the hangman see the weight of your purse. He sees it, and so does the sheriff. You spend the night in the gaol at Carleon, lighter by one purse.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride into the marsh, shouting. The ravens rise in a black cloud.

resolutions.label: scatter the ravens and their master

success.body: You shout the old words against carrion birds and swing your sword, and the ravens scatter, cawing. The great raven stands its ground until the last, glaring at you, and then it too flaps heavily into the air. "We will be back," it croaks. "In May." It flies east. But the marsh is quiet after that, and the people of the village nearby say that for the first time in a year, they can sleep.

failure.body: You shout and swing your sword, and the ravens rise, and they come at you, all of them, in a black storm of beaks and claws. You flee the marsh with your face bleeding.

entries.body:
As you walk your horse through the back lanes of Carleon, a boy in a torn smock grabs your stirrup. "Sir! Sir! They took my sister down the old well behind the tanner's yard." He drags you to a dry well in a courtyard, where a rope ladder hangs down into darkness. From below you hear voices, the chink of metal and a girl crying.

"The Rat King's men," the boy whispers. "They have tunnels under the whole town. They steal from the churches and melt it down there. My sister saw them with the bishop's candlesticks, so they took her." He looks at you. "The sheriff will not go down. He says there are a hundred of them."

responses.label: You may climb down the well and rescue the girl from the thieves' tunnels.
You may fetch the town watch and lead them against the thieves.

entries.body:
You ride into Winchester on market day and find the whole town standing in the square with their mouths open. In the middle of the market, where yesterday there were fish stalls, there is a castle. It is small and perfect, with blue slate roofs and gold weathercocks, and its gate stands open. A steward in green livery stands at the gate, bowing.

"Welcome, welcome," he calls to you. "My lady invites every knight in Winchester to dine. Only one condition. You must not ask her name." The townsfolk mutter. A fishwife tells you that three young men went in at dawn and have not come out, though she can hear them laughing.

responses.label: You may accept the invitation and dine in the castle.
You may find a way to break the enchantment on the castle.

entries.body:
You ride into Chester and find the market square empty and silent. Every door is barred. In the middle of the square, beside the town well, three men lie on the cobbles, turned to grey stone, with looks of surprise on their faces.

A voice hisses at you from a shuttered window. "Do not look at the well! There is a basilisk in it. A cockerel's egg, hatched by a toad, that is what the priest says. It looks out at noon, and whoever it looks at is stone." A frightened face appears at the crack. "The mayor has offered a hundred marks to anyone who kills it. Nobody can get near it without looking."

The sun is climbing toward noon.

responses.label: You may kill the basilisk in the well.
You may trap the basilisk so it can be taken away.

entries.body:
You ride into Winchester in a storm so fierce that the river has burst its banks. The lower town is under water to the height of a man's waist. People are standing on the roofs. On the steps of a great stone warehouse, above the flood, a fat merchant in a fur cloak is standing with six armed servants, guarding his doors.

"Grain," a woman on a roof shouts to you. "He has a year's grain in there. He bought up the whole harvest in the spring. Our stores are all under water, and he will not sell but at ten times the price." Her children are huddled against her. "They will starve before the water goes down."

The merchant looks at you coolly. "My grain," he says, "and my price."

responses.label: You may force the merchant to open his warehouse.
You may rescue the stranded families from the rooftops.

entries.body:
You ride into Gloucester and find the great bridge over the Severn blocked by a barricade of carts. A dozen hard-faced men with clubs stand at it, taking a toll from everyone who crosses. A woman with a basket of eggs pays two eggs. A friar pays a penny. A farmer who cannot pay is thrown in the river.

"Black Cadwgan's men," a baker tells you. "They took the bridge a month ago. The sheriff is paid to look the other way. Half the town cannot get to the market on the far side." He looks at your sword. "Cadwgan himself sits in the tollhouse. He is a big man. They say he has killed six."

responses.label: You may break the brigands' hold on the bridge by force.
You may pay the toll and cross, then find proof of the sheriff's bribes.

entries.body:
You are drinking in a tavern in Carleon when a hooded man slips past your table and down the cellar stairs. A moment later, another follows, and you glimpse under his hood the face of Sir Maldred, one of the High King's own stewards. The tavern-keeper sees you looking and goes pale.

"Do not go down there," he whispers. "They meet every Friday. Men from the north. Orkney men, King Lot's men. And our own steward, God help us." He wipes the counter nervously. "They pay me well not to hear anything."

Through the floorboards, you hear voices, and the chink of coins.

responses.label: You may creep down and listen to the traitors' meeting.
You may burst in and arrest the traitors.

entries.body:
You ride into Bath and find the townsfolk gathered at the edge of the old Roman baths, which lie in ruins at the heart of the town, full of green water and broken columns. Every night, they say, a soldier in Roman armour marches up and down the colonnade, calling out a watchword nobody understands, and every morning, somebody who went too close is found face-down in the water.

"He guards the old treasury," the reeve tells you. "There is gold down there, from the Romans. Everyone knows. But nobody can get past him." He looks at the ruins nervously. "And now children have started daring each other to go in."

At dusk, you hear it: the tramp of hobnailed sandals on stone.

responses.label: You may face the Roman ghost and lay him to rest.
You may slip past the ghost and search for the Roman gold.

entries.body: You kneel before the altar. The monks withdraw. You look at the page for a long time.

resolutions.label: read the living page of the book

success.body: The ink moves, and you watch it, and after many hours, you begin to see: not letters, but a road, and a sea, and a ship with no sails, and an island in the east where a city of white stone stands. *Sarras*, you think, though you do not know how you know the name. The ink goes still. The cup stops glowing. In the morning, the page is only a painting again. But you have seen where the vessel is going, and you tell the abbot, and he writes it in the margin, and it is there still.

failure.body: The ink moves, and you watch it all night, and it makes no sense at all. At dawn, the page is still, and you have a headache that lasts a week.

resolutions.label: follow the moving ink with a seer's eye

success.body: You do not read it as writing. You let your eyes go soft, as the seers do, and watch the ink as you would watch smoke. After many hours, you see: a road, a sea, a ship with no sails, a city of white stone in the east. *Sarras*, you think. The ink goes still. In the morning, the page is only a painting again. But you tell the abbot, and he writes it in the margin, and it is there still.

failure.body: You let your eyes go soft and watch the ink, and see nothing but ink. At dawn, you have a headache that lasts a week.

entries.body:
You ride into York and find it at war with itself. King Lot's men have come over the walls in the night, and the High King's small garrison is fighting them street by street. Houses are burning. In the Shambles, the butchers are fighting Orkney men with cleavers.

A sergeant of the garrison, bloody and hatless, grabs your bridle. "Sir! The castle is holding, but the Orkney men have the Micklegate, and if they open it, Lot's whole army comes in. We have twenty men to take it back." He looks at you. "Or you could get the women and children out through the river-gate, before the whole city burns."

responses.label: You may lead the assault on the Micklegate.
You may lead the townsfolk to safety through the river-gate.

entries.body:
You arrive at Camelot on the feast of Pentecost and find the great hall full, the tables laden and nobody eating. The young High King is sitting at the high table with his hands folded, looking at the door. "It is the custom," Sir Kay mutters to you, with his stomach growling. "He will not eat at a high feast until he has seen a marvel or heard of an adventure. Usually one turns up. Today, nothing." He glares at the door. "The swans are going cold."

The king catches your eye. "You," he says. "You have ridden far. Have you brought me a marvel?" The whole hall turns to look at you.

responses.label: You may tell the king a marvellous tale of your adventures.
You may go out and find the king a marvel before the swans go cold.

entries.body:
As you ride through the forest in golden sunlight, you hear a child crying behind a waterfall. You dismount and push through the curtain of water, and find yourself in a cave, where a little girl of four sits on a rock with her knees drawn up. Beside her, curled asleep on a heap of bones and bracken, is a brown bear the size of a haycart.

The girl sees you and puts her finger to her lips. "Shh," she whispers. "You will wake him. I am Nia. I got lost and he found me and he brought me here. He gives me honey." She looks at the bear with great affection. "But I want to go home now. My mother will be cross."

The bear's nose twitches. It opens one small, dark eye.

responses.label: You may snatch Nia away from the bear.
You may coax the bear to let Nia go.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in golden sunlight, you come upon a castle of white stone where there was no castle marked on any map. The gate is open. In the courtyard, the flagstones are laid out in black and white squares, and on them stand thirty-two people in painted tabards, stock still: kings, queens, knights, bishops and a great many servants as pawns.

A lord in a black tabard sits on a high chair at one end. "Welcome, knight!" he calls. "I am Lord Guivret. My opponent has fled. Will you take the white? If you win, I will release all these people. They are travellers, like you, who lost to me. If you lose, you will join them." He smiles. "White moves first."

responses.label: You may play Lord Guivret's game of living chess.
You may refuse the game and free the captives by force.

entries.body: You look at the chained knights, and at Morgan. "Let them go," you say, "and I will stay."

resolutions.label: win Morgan le Fay's favour

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: Morgan looks at you with delight. "Now that," she says, "is not dull." She frees the four knights with a wave of her hand. You stay with her for a week. It is a strange, wonderful, frightening week, and at the end of it, she lets you go, with a kiss and a ring. "Come back when you are bored of my brother," she says. You find that you think of her more often than you should.

partial.body: Morgan looks at you, and sighs. "Kind," she says, "but not interesting enough." She frees one of the four knights anyway, for your trouble.

failure.body: Morgan laughs. "You?" she says, and looks you up and down as though you were a horse she had no intention of buying. She keeps the four knights, and sends you away across the warm lake in a boat rowed by a black swan, which bites you twice on the way.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in golden sunlight, a pure white hind breaks from the trees ahead of you, with a golden collar round her neck. A white hound runs at her heels, and behind them both, a lady on a white palfrey, shrieking. "My hound! Somebody catch my hound!" Behind her again, a knight in black gallops out of the trees, snatches up the hound as it passes, and rides away laughing.

The lady reins in beside you, flushed and furious. "That was my brachet," she says. "A wedding gift for the queen. The white hind was a gift too. Now they are both gone." She points in two directions at once. "The hind that way. The thief that way. I cannot follow both."

responses.label: You may ride after the knight who stole the hound.
You may hunt down the white hind with the golden collar.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in golden sunlight, the sky turns black in a moment and a storm breaks over the trees. You find shelter in a woodcutter's hut, where two strangers are already sitting by the fire: a young man in a fine cloak who says he is a merchant and keeps one hand on a leather satchel, and a lean, sharp-eyed woman who says she is a pedlar and has no pack.

The storm roars all night. Near midnight, you wake to see the woman's hand in the young man's satchel. She freezes when she sees you watching. Then she puts a finger to her lips, and draws out a letter sealed with the arms of King Lot of Orkney.

responses.label: You may seize the letter and learn what the "merchant" is carrying.
You may stop the thief and protect the young man's satchel.

entries.body: As you ride through a forest in golden sunlight, you come to a great oak with a clearing beneath it, where forty outlaws are sitting round a fire. They are thin, ragged farm folk, men and women both, and their leader is a tall man in a patched surcoat with a knight's belt. "Sir Hervi de Rivel," he says, rising. "Once of Arden Manor. The Baron of Arden took my land for debts I never owed, and turned my tenants off theirs. So we took to the forest." He looks at you steadily. "We rob the Baron's carts. Only the Baron's. Will you join us, or are you the Baron's man?"

responses.label: You may join Sir Hervi's outlaws against the greedy Baron.
You may take Sir Hervi's case before the High King's justice.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest at midnight under a full moon, you see a ring of torches under a hollow oak. Twelve figures in hooded robes of green and white are standing in a circle, chanting in an old tongue, around a stone on which lies a sword, a golden bough and a very frightened white bull.

One of them turns, and lowers her hood. She is an old woman with bright eyes. "A knight," she says. "Welcome. We are the last of the old priests of this land. We are praying for the young king, that his reign may be long." She smiles. "The bull is for the old gods. They like the young king too. But King Lot has sent men to stop us. They are coming through the wood now."

You hear horses.

responses.label: You may defend the old priests' rite from King Lot's men.
You may stop the sacrifice of the white bull.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in golden sunlight, you come upon a ruined temple in a clearing, with a ring of broken columns and no roof. When the wind blows through the columns, it makes a sound like voices. You stop to listen, and realise the voices are saying something.

An old woman is sweeping the temple floor. "The Temple of the Voices," she says. "It was built by the Romans to their goddess of the hunt. The wind speaks true, if you ask it the right question. Most people do not like the answers." She leans on her broom. "Ask it something. Or help me sweep. The leaves never stop."

responses.label: You may ask the wind in the ruined temple a question.
You may help the old woman keep the temple.

entries.body:
You come upon a battle in the Forest of Celidon, where the High King's men are hunting a Saxon war-band through the trees. It is a strange, broken fight, with men in twos and threes fighting among the oaks. In a clearing, you find a Saxon boy of fifteen, with a broken spear, backed against a tree by three British soldiers. He is crying.

"Kill him," says one of the soldiers. "They killed my brother." The boy looks at you, and says something in his own tongue.

responses.label: You may spare the Saxon boy.
You may leave the soldiers to their vengeance and join the hunt.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in golden sunlight, you come to a stone arch standing alone in a clearing, with nothing on either side of it. But through the arch, you see a great feast: tables of gold, and tall fair people dancing, and music you can almost hear.

A small man with pointed ears is standing by the arch. "Come in," he says, grinning. "The fair folk are feasting. Every mortal who comes through is welcome. You may eat and drink as much as you like." He winks. "Only, if you eat, you may find it hard to leave. And if you do not eat, they may be offended."

responses.label: You may go through the arch and join the fay feast.
You may go through the arch but refuse to eat.

entries.body:
You come to a cave high on a mountainside, where the rocks around the entrance are scorched black and the air smells of hot metal. A trail of gold coins leads into the dark. From inside, you hear something breathing: a long, slow sound like a blacksmith's bellows.

A shepherd hiding behind a rock hisses at you. "The dragon of Dinas Emrys," he says. "Only a young one. Only the size of a church. It has taken twenty sheep this month. The last knight who went in came out without his eyebrows, and the one before him did not come out at all." He points at the coins. "It has a hoard. They always have a hoard."

responses.label: You may enter the cave and fight the dragon.
You may sneak into the cave and take some of the dragon's hoard.

entries.body:
You come upon a castle on a crag, with seven towers and seven banners, and a rope bridge swaying across the chasm to its gate. A herald stands at the bridge-end. "The Castle of Maidens," he announces. "Held by the seven sons of Duke Lianor. They have imprisoned every maiden who passed this road for seven years. Many knights have tried to free them. Most are in the moat."

A knight is sitting on a rock nearby, eating bread. "Do not believe him," he says. "I went in last week. The maidens do not want to be freed. The seven brothers are dreadful, but the castle has the best library in Wales, and nobody makes them marry." He shrugs. "They asked me to tell any knight who comes to leave them in peace. Only the brothers are getting old, and the maidens are running out of food."

responses.label: You may storm the Castle of Maidens and overthrow the seven brothers.
You may go to the maidens and learn what they truly want.

entries.body: When Father Emyr comes back with the bread, you are standing in the doorway with your sword drawn. "Ring your bell, father," you say, "and I will cut the rope before it sounds." The hermit's face changes. He is not old at all.

resolutions.label: overpower the false hermit before he can warn his friends

success.body: He goes for a knife hidden in the bread. You are faster. After a brief, ugly struggle on the chapel floor, he is tied to his own altar rail with his own bell-rope, cursing. You ride on up the pass at dawn, and when the outlaws come down to meet you, expecting a sleepy traveller, they find a wide-awake knight instead. They scatter. In the next town, the reeve pays you a bounty for the false hermit, whose name is Emyr the Knife.

failure.body: He goes for a knife hidden in the bread. You are faster, but he is stronger, and in the struggle he gets a hand on the bell-rope and gives it one long pull. You hear the bell ring up on the hillside. You flee through the back of the chapel just as twenty men come down from the pass with torches. They keep your horse.

resolutions.label: trap him with questions about his own hermitage

success.body: When he comes back with the bread, you ask him, pleasantly, which saint his chapel is dedicated to, and when its feast day falls, and which psalms he sings at Terce. He does not know. He is still thinking of an answer when you take the bread-knife out of his loaf. By then he knows that you know. He sits down on his own doorstep and laughs. You take him to the reeve in the next town, who pays a bounty for Emyr the Knife.

failure.body: You ask him which saint his chapel is dedicated to. "Saint Emyr," he says at once, without blinking, and tells you all about him. You are almost convinced. That night, the bell rings, and you only just get away.

entries.body: "There is always a cure," you say, with more confidence than you feel. You climb up onto the barn roof and sit beside Twm's head to think.

resolutions.label: find the herb that will shrink him again

success.body: You remember an old wives' saying: what swells in spite shrinks in dew. You spend three nights gathering dew from the leaves of lady's mantle at dawn, a thimble at a time, until you have a bucket. Twm drinks it all in one gulp. The next morning, he is a hand's width shorter. The morning after, two. By the end of the week, he is his own size again, and wearing his father's shirt. His sweetheart comes back. You tell him to go and apologise to old Nest, and to his credit, he does.

failure.body: You try every herb you know. Dandelion. Tansy. Rue. Twm drinks them all and grows another hand's width. On the fourth night, the barn roof gives way. You leave him sitting in the ruins, the size of a haystack, weeping.

resolutions.label: unmake the witch's curse

success.body: You write old Nest's words on a strip of bark, *Since you think yourself so big, grow*, and then you write them again underneath, backwards. You bind the bark round Twm's wrist with a red thread and make him say, every hour, *I am small, I am small.* It takes a week. On the seventh day, he wakes up in the barn with room to spare. His mother cries. He goes to find old Nest and apologise, and she gives him a piece of her mind and a honey-cake.

failure.body: You write the witch's words backwards on a strip of bark and bind it round Twm's wrist. Then you realise that you have spelt one of the words wrong. In the morning, Twm is the same size. You are not. Your boots no longer fit.

entries.body:
You come upon a village at the foot of a mountain where the people are nailing their chickens into their henhouses. High above them, on a ledge, is a nest the size of a haystack, woven from whole trees, and on its rim sits a griffin, with an eagle's head and a lion's body, glaring down.

"The Lord of Dinas has offered a fortune for its eggs," says the headman. "Griffin eggs are worth their weight in gold. His huntsmen went up yesterday. The griffin threw them off the mountain." He looks up at the nest. "Now she is angry, and she takes our sheep. We just want her to calm down."

responses.label: You may climb to the nest and take the griffin's eggs.
You may climb to the nest and make peace with the griffin.

entries.body:
You come upon a village on a mountainside being hammered by hailstones as big as eggs. The sky above the village is black, but above the next valley, it is clear and blue. On the mountaintop above, you see a figure standing on a rock with her arms raised.

"The weather-witch of Moel Famau," a villager shouts to you through the hail. "The lord of the next valley pays her to keep the storms on us. His harvest thrives. Ours is flattened." A child has been hit by a hailstone and is bleeding. "Nobody can climb to her. The storm beats them back."

responses.label: You may climb the mountain and confront the weather-witch.
You may go to the lord who hired the witch.

entries.body:
You come to a hill-fort on a mountain, where a band of brigands has barricaded itself behind the old ramparts. From inside comes the sound of a man shouting. "Do you know who I am? I am Sir Brewen of Dinas! My father will hang every one of you!"

A brigand on the rampart calls down to you. "Ransom for the young lord," he says. "A thousand marks. His father will not pay. The young lord is very annoying." Another voice, the young lord's, shouts, "I heard that!" The brigand sighs. "We would let him go for five hundred. For a hundred. For some peace."

responses.label: You may storm the hill-fort and rescue the young lord.
You may negotiate the young lord's release.

entries.body:
You come upon two pavilions pitched on a high mountain meadow, one flying the banner of the King of North Wales and the other the banner of the King of South Wales. Their fathers have been at war for forty years. Between the pavilions, on a flat rock, sit the two young kings, alone, with a flask of wine, trying very hard not to look at each other.

One of them sees you and waves you over urgently. "We need a witness," he says. "We have come to make peace, secretly, without our councils. But there must be a witness who is neither North nor South." The other king looks at you suspiciously. "And he must swear," he says, "to keep it secret until the peace is proclaimed."

responses.label: You may witness the kings' secret peace.
You may take word of the meeting to the High King.

entries.body:
You come upon the ruins of a fortress on a hill in Snowdonia, where the walls have fallen into a pool at its heart. An old shepherd is sitting on the broken gatehouse. "Dinas Emrys," he says. "King Vortigern built a tower here, and every night it fell down. Merlin, when he was a boy, told him why: two dragons were fighting in the pool beneath, a red and a white." He points at the pool. "They say the dragons are still down there, asleep."

As he speaks, the pool bubbles. Something red stirs under the water.

responses.label: You may dive into the pool to see the sleeping dragons.
You may ask the shepherd to tell you more of Merlin's prophecy.

entries.body:
You come upon the High King's army drawn up on the slopes of a great hill in the Golden Age, facing a Saxon host three times its size. It is the eve of the battle of Mount Badon. Fires burn all across the hill. The young king is walking among his men, clasping hands.

He sees you and stops. "You," he says. "Good. I need a knight who is not frightened of heights." He points up at the summit of the hill, where the Saxons have a camp of archers. "They command the whole slope. If someone could take the summit before dawn, we would win. If not…" He shrugs. "We will fight anyway."

responses.label: You may lead a night assault on the Saxon archers on the summit.
You may stand in the High King's battle line at dawn.

entries.body:
You climb to the top of a mountain at midnight, following a sound of music, and find a feast on the summit, round a great bonfire: shepherds and shepherdesses, drovers, a miller, a smith, dancing and eating mutton and drinking from a barrel. It is Midsummer Eve. They welcome you with a shout.

Among them, sitting on a rock with a leg of mutton, is a big, cheerful man in a shepherd's smock, with a very good sword at his hip and a face you have seen on a coin. He sees you recognise him and puts a finger to his lips. It is the young High King.

"Do not tell them," he says quietly, when you sit down beside him. "They do not know. They think I am Artie from over the hill." He grins. "I have not had so much fun in a year."

responses.label: You may keep the king's secret and join the shepherds' feast.
You may warn the king that he has been followed by King Lot's men.

entries.body:
You come upon a shepherd standing on a wide plain beside a hole in the turf, weeping. The hole is as wide as a cart and goes straight down into darkness. From the bottom, very faintly, you hear sheep bleating.

"The ground opened last night," he says. "Swallowed the whole flock. Forty sheep. And my dog went down after them." He wipes his face. "I have been calling all morning. The dog barks back. The sheep bleat. There must be a cave down there." He looks at you. "I have a rope. It is not long enough. It is never long enough."

responses.label: You may climb down into the sinkhole and bring up the flock.
You may search the plain for another way into the cave below.

entries.body:
You come upon a castle on a wide plain under a full moon, with torches burning on its walls and music playing inside. There was no castle here when you passed by in daylight. The gate is open, and a porter with a lantern beckons you in. "Welcome to Castle Perilous," he says. "My lord holds a tournament every full moon, and every knight who rides in the lists wins a prize." He smiles. "Every knight who loses stays until the next full moon."

In the lists inside, knights are jousting by torchlight, and their horses do not seem to touch the ground.

responses.label: You may ride in the moonlit tournament.
You may ride on past the castle without entering.

entries.body: "I will do what I can," you say. Kay looks at you suspiciously, as he looks at everything. "Nothing clever," he says. "She hates clever."

resolutions.label: read the poem to Nest, and speak well of Sir Kay

success.body: You find Nest at the wash-house with her sleeves rolled up. You read the poem with a straight face, which takes every ounce of your courage. Then you tell her what you have seen of Kay: that he is sharp because he is afraid of looking foolish, that he has never missed a day's duty in twenty years, and that he rewrote this poem eleven times. Nest laughs her horse's laugh until she has to sit on the mangle. "Tell him," she says, "he may take me to the Lammas fair. And he may leave the poem at home." Kay, told this, turns bright red and says nothing at all for an hour.

failure.body: You find Nest at the wash-house and read her the poem. At *starch'd*, your voice cracks, and you have to stop, and she sees your face. "Is this a joke?" she asks. You swear it is not, but she has seen the laugh in your eyes. When Kay hears that Nest threw the poem in the copper, he is quite sure whose fault it is. You spend a fortnight on latrine duty.

resolutions.label: bring Nest flowers from the meadow in Kay's name

success.body: You go out to the water-meadows and pick an armful of meadowsweet and marigolds, the flowers laundresses use to scent the linen, and take them to the wash-house. "From Sir Kay," you say. Nest looks at the flowers, and at you, and smells them, and laughs. "He knows what I use?" she asks. "He noticed," you say. She is quiet a moment. "Tell him he may walk me to the Lammas fair." Kay turns red for a whole day.

failure.body: You go out to the water-meadows and pick an armful of flowers. Unfortunately, half of them are cowbane. Nest takes one look and drops them in the copper. "Is he trying to poison me?" she asks. Kay hears of it within the hour.

entries.body:
You come upon a herd of cattle lying dead on a wide plain, all facing the same way. A little further on, grazing beside a stream, is a beast like a black buffalo, with a head so huge and heavy that it droops to the ground. Its eyes are hidden under a mane of matted hair.

A cowherd is hiding behind a gorse bush. "The catoblepas," he whispers. "Do not let it look at you. Its eyes kill. It can hardly lift its head, praise God, but when it does…" He points at the cattle. "It lifted its head yesterday. I was behind the bush. The Earl says it must be killed before it wanders into the village."

responses.label: You may kill the catoblepas without meeting its eyes.
You may drive the catoblepas away across the plain.

entries.body:
You come upon a tournament on a wide plain as a thunderstorm breaks over it. Pavilions are blowing away. Horses are bolting. Knights in half-buckled armour are running for cover. And in the middle of the lists, a lightning bolt has struck a stand full of ladies, and set it on fire.

The ladies are trapped behind the wooden railings. The fire is spreading. Nobody seems to be doing anything about it.

responses.label: You may ride into the burning stand and bring the ladies out.
You may rally the scattered knights to fight the fire.

entries.body:
You come upon a horse-breeder's farm on a wide plain, where the paddocks are empty and the gates are broken. The breeder, an old man with a white beard, is sitting on the fence with his head in his hands. "Horse-thieves," he says. "Forty mares, last night. They came from the south, from the Marches. They will sell them at the Hereford fair in three days." He looks up. "The finest mares in Britain. The High King's own destriers came from my stud."

In the mud, you can see the tracks: forty mares and a dozen riders, heading south at a gallop.

responses.label: You may ride after the horse-thieves and take back the mares.
You may ride ahead to the Hereford fair and catch the thieves there.

entries.body:
You come upon a ring of standing stones on a wide plain at dusk, where a young man and a young woman are standing in the middle, holding hands and whispering. They spring apart when they see you. The young woman is dressed richly; the young man is a shepherd.

"Please," she says. "Do not tell. I am Gwenhwyfach, daughter of Lord Maelwas. This is Cian. We meet here every full moon. My father wants me to marry the Earl of Hereford, who is fifty. If he finds out about Cian, he will hang him." She takes Cian's hand again. "We mean to run away tonight. But the Earl's men are watching the roads."

responses.label: You may help the young lovers escape the Earl's men.
You may persuade the young lovers to go to her father with the truth.

entries.body:
You come upon an old Roman road running straight across a wide plain, where a milestone stands beside the ruins of a marching camp. As the sun sets, you hear the tramp of feet, and along the road comes a column of Roman soldiers, ghostly, in rank upon rank, with their eagle held high. They march straight toward you.

An old drover sitting by the milestone calls out, "Get off the road! The Ninth Legion. They march every Midsummer Eve. Anyone who stands on the road is taken with them." He is already dragging his cattle into the ditch.

responses.label: You may stand your ground on the road and challenge the ghostly legion.
You may step aside and follow the legion to see where it goes.

entries.body: You look at the youngest of the nine. She has dark hair and grey eyes, and she is laughing at you. "Me?" she says. "Why me?" "Because you laughed," you say.

resolutions.label: walk in the orchards of Avalon with the youngest sister

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You walk with her all day among the apple trees, and she shows you the secret places of the island: the pool where the swans nest, the hill where you can see every shore of Britain at once, the grave of a king who has not died yet. At sunset, she gives you a ring of plaited apple-bark and kisses you. "When you are old," she says, "come back. I will still be here." She will. You will not forget.

partial.body: You walk with her in the orchard, and she is kind, and funny, and a little sad. At sunset, she sends you home. "Another time," she says. "Another life."

failure.body: You walk with her in the orchard, and she yawns. "You are very mortal," she says, not unkindly, and sends you home.

entries.body:
You come upon a great battle on a wide plain at Bedegraine, where the eleven rebel kings under King Lot of Orkney are fighting the young High King's army. It is a vast, confused melee, horsemen and footmen, banners everywhere. Merlin sits on a black horse on a hillock above the field, watching.

If you have Story Token #1, turn immediately to [[1575]].

The young king is in the thick of the fight, in golden armour, laying about him with his great sword. Around him, his knights are being pushed back. On the other side of the field, you see King Lot's black and gold banner.

responses.label: You may ride to the young king's side.
You may ride for King Lot's banner and strike at the heart of the rebels.

entries.body:
You come upon a great fair on a wide plain on Midsummer Day, with a feast laid out on trestles under the sky, and jugglers and wrestlers and a maypole, and a hundred villages gathered. In the middle of it, on a platform, is a greasy pole with a ham on top, and a ring of young men trying and failing to climb it.

A very drunk lord in a green hat calls to you from the feast-table. "A knight! The best climber gets the ham, and a kiss from the Midsummer Queen!" He points at a pretty girl in a crown of daisies, who blushes. "Nobody has managed it in six years."

responses.label: You may climb the greasy pole for the ham.
You may take on the champion wrestler of the fair instead.

entries.body:
You come to an island of firm ground in a wide bog, where a cave opens under a hump of rock. Smoke curls out of it. Hanging round the entrance are strings of dried frogs, bundles of herbs and a great many small bones. A woman's voice calls out from inside. "Come in, knight. Mind the cauldron."

Inside, by the fire, sits a crone with a face like a walnut, stirring a pot. "I am Mother Mallt," she says. "The village says I am a witch. They are right. They also say I stole the reeve's pig. They are wrong. They are coming tonight to burn me out." She taps her spoon on the rim of the pot. "I could turn them all into frogs. But I am old, and it is tiring, and there are so many frogs already."

responses.label: You may defend Mother Mallt from the villagers.
You may find the reeve's real pig-thief.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a bog at dusk, you see golden light shining across the water. It comes from the windows of a castle built on great wooden stilts over the marsh, with lanterns hung all along its walkways. A causeway of planks leads to its door, where a lady in a gown of silver-green is standing, as though waiting.

"You are welcome, knight," she says. "I am the Lady of the Marsh. I have been waiting for a husband for a hundred years. The knight who can cross my causeway without falling in the bog may have my hand, and my castle, and all the marsh." She smiles. "Many have fallen in. The bog keeps them."

The planks of the causeway are thin and old. Under them, the black water bubbles.

responses.label: * You may attempt the Lady of the Marsh's causeway.
You may ride on, and leave the lady to her waiting.

entries.body:
You come upon a lake at the edge of a marsh, still and black, where a village of reed huts stands on the shore. The villagers are standing in the water up to their knees, holding hands in a long line, as if to stop something coming out.

"The afanc," says an old woman. "It lives in the lake. It is like a beaver as big as an ox, with teeth like a saw. It comes out at night and drags people into the water. It took my grandson." She tightens her grip on her neighbour's hand. "They say it can only be taken by a maiden it falls asleep on, and then dragged out with chains by oxen. We have no maiden brave enough. We have no oxen."

responses.label: You may fight the afanc in its lake.
You may lure the afanc out and trap it.

entries.body:
You come upon a family on the roof of their cottage in the middle of a marsh, in a storm, with the water rising round them. There is a man, a woman, four children and a cow, somehow, on the roof. The water is already at the eaves. "Help us!" the woman cries. "The dykes have gone! The whole marsh is flooding!"

The water between you and the cottage is deep and fast, full of floating branches. Further out in the marsh, you see other roofs, and other people on them.

responses.label: You may swim your horse out to the cottage and rescue the family.
You may ride for help to save everyone in the flooding marsh.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through the fens at dusk, you hear a whistle, and suddenly there are men all round you, rising out of the reeds on stilts, with fish-spears. They are the fen-outlaws: marsh folk who live in the reeds and rob anyone foolish enough to cross the fens without a guide.

Their leader, a lean woman with a face tattooed with blue dots, points her fish-spear at your throat. "Wulfric's daughter," she says. "Aelfgifu. You are in our fens. You pay the fen-toll, or you go in the bog." She looks you up and down. "Or you do us a service. The abbot of Ely has hired soldiers to drive us out. We need someone who can fight on land."

responses.label: You may help the fen-outlaws against the abbot's soldiers.
You may bargain your way through the fens.

entries.body:
You come upon a fire on an island in a marsh at midnight, where three old women are sitting round a cauldron, cackling. They are witches, plainly: the eldest has a beard, the middle one has one eye, and the youngest has a raven on her shoulder. "Company!" cries the eldest. "Sit, sit. We are cooking a curse for the Abbot of Crowland. He called us hags."

"You are hags," says the one-eyed one. "That is not the point," says the eldest. The raven laughs. They offer you a bowl of something green. "Help us with the curse," says the youngest, "and we will give you a gift. Or eat the soup. Most people do not survive the soup."

responses.label: You may help the witches curse the Abbot of Crowland.
You may persuade the witches to let the abbot be.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a marsh at low tide, you see, rising out of the mud, the roofs and towers of a drowned abbey. The sea took it a hundred years ago. At low tide, you can walk to it across the mud, and its door is open.

A fisherman calls out to you. "Do not go in! Brother Anselm's ghost is in there! He was the abbot. He drowned trying to save the abbey's treasure, and he still guards it." He shivers. "The tide comes in fast. Anyone who is inside when it turns is drowned."

Through the open door, you see something gold glittering in the mud.

responses.label: You may search the drowned abbey for its treasure before the tide turns.
You may speak with the drowned abbot's ghost.

entries.body:
You come upon a battle in the marshes of the Fens, where the young High King's men are fighting a war-band of Pictish raiders who have come down the coast in boats. The fighting is waist-deep in water, among the reeds. Nobody can see anybody. Men are shouting and splashing in the fog.

A young squire comes stumbling out of the reeds toward you, soaked and terrified. "My master!" he cries. "Sir Griflet! He is out there, in the fog, with the Picts all round him! I lost him!"

responses.label: You may plunge into the marsh to find the lost knight.
You may take command of the scattered men in the fog.

entries.body:
You come upon a marsh village on Samhain night, where the villagers are laying a feast on long tables outside their houses: bread, pork, apples, ale. But nobody is sitting down. They are standing back, in silence, with candles in their hands.

"The feast is for the dead," an old woman tells you. "On Samhain, they come back from the marsh to eat with us. We lay a place for everyone who died this year." She points to the end of the table. "That place is for my son. He drowned at Easter." She looks at you. "Sometimes, a living guest must sit at the table too, to show them the way. Will you?"

Out on the marsh, you see lights, coming closer.

responses.label: You may sit at the table of the dead.
You may stand guard with the living.

entries.body:
As you ride along a cliff-top at low tide, you see a line of lanterns moving along the beach below, into a sea-cave at the foot of the cliff. Men are rolling barrels in from a boat. When you climb down to see, a grizzled woman with a cutlass steps out of the shadows. "Evening, sir knight," she says. "Grace Penhale. Honest trader." She jerks her head at the barrels. "French wine. The king's customs man wants a quarter of every barrel. We think that is too much."

From further back in the cave, you hear another sound: a man crying out. Grace's face tightens. "That," she says, "is the customs man. He came poking about. We have not decided what to do with him."

responses.label: You may free the customs man from the smugglers.
You may help the smugglers and share their wine.

entries.body:
As you sail along a rocky coast in bright sunshine, you see a castle on an island that was not on the sailor's chart. As you watch, it moves. The whole island is drifting slowly across the bay against the wind, castle and all. On the battlements, a man in a gold crown is waving at you frantically.

"Help!" he shouts across the water. "I am King Maelgwn of Gwynedd! I bought this castle from a man in a green hat for a very good price. He said it had the finest sea-views in Britain. He did not say the views changed!" He waves at the sea. "We have been drifting for a month. We are nearly in Ireland. I am out of wine."

responses.label: You may board the drifting island and steer it back to shore.
You may bargain with the island itself, which you suspect is alive.

entries.body: You sit down on a barrel opposite him. "Let us bargain," you say. Dewi's eyes glitter.

resolutions.label: outbargain the clurichaun

success.body: He offers you three wishes for your horse. You offer him your horse for four wishes. He says three, and your horse, and your sword. You say four, and the horse, and the cellarer's best barrel. He says three. You get up to leave. "Wait!" he cries. You bargain all night. By dawn, you have three wishes, and he has your horse, which comes back to you the next day of its own accord, having kicked him. You use the first wish to get him out of the cellar. The other two, you keep.

failure.body: He offers you three wishes for your horse. You agree too quickly. He grants them, too literally. You wish for gold, and it rains gold coins on your head until you are bruised. You wish for it to stop, and it does, and all the gold vanishes with it. You wish you had never met him, and you wake up on the road outside the monastery with no idea why you are so sore.

resolutions.label: outdrink the clurichaun

success.body: "A drinking match," you say. "If I am standing at dawn, you leave." Dewi hoots with delight. You drink from thimbles, which is not as easy as it sounds, because he keeps refilling them. At dawn, you are standing, just, holding onto a barrel. Dewi is asleep inside another one, snoring. You roll the barrel out of the cellar and down the hill into the river. The monks give you a bottle of the good wine.

failure.body: You drink with him from thimbles all night. At midnight, you are under the table. At dawn, the monks find you asleep in their communion wine. Dewi is sitting on your chest, singing.

entries.body:
As you sail along a rocky coast, the sea ahead of you begins to boil. A huge head rises out of the water, green and scaled, with a mane of seaweed, and it looks at your boat. The sailors scream. The head sinks again, and a moment later, you see, under the clear water, the drowned roofs of a village, with a church tower, and the serpent coiled round it.

"Porth Llys," says the old captain, shaking. "Drowned a hundred years ago. The serpent guards it. It sinks every boat that passes over." He looks at you. "Unless it is fed. We used to throw it a sheep. We have no sheep today."

responses.label: You may fight the sea serpent.
You may dive to the drowned village to learn why the serpent guards it.

entries.body:
You are at sea in a small ship when a storm blows up out of a clear sky. The waves grow high as houses. The sailors are praying and weeping. Then the captain points at a young woman sitting in the stern, wrapped in a grey cloak. "It is her," he shouts. "She came aboard at Bristol and would not give her name. She is a witch, or she has done some great sin. The sea wants her!" The crew surges toward her.
