The young woman stands up and faces them. "I am Elaine," she says. "I have fled my father because he would marry me to a man I hate. That is my only sin." She looks at you. "Will you let them throw me in?"

responses.label: You may defend the young woman from the frightened crew.
You may take the helm and save the ship from the storm.

entries.body:
You are sailing across the Irish Sea when a black ship with a red sail comes over the horizon, fast. It flies no banner. "Pirates," says your captain, going white. "Grainne of the Isles. She takes every ship she catches, and sells the crews in Dublin."

The black ship draws alongside. A woman in a man's coat, with a cutlass and a laugh like a gull, stands in its bow. "Heave to!" she calls. "Or I will board you!" She sees you, and grins. "A knight! I have never taken a knight. Surrender, and I will only sell your horse."

responses.label: You may fight off the pirates when they board.
You may challenge Grainne of the Isles to a contest instead of a fight.

entries.body:
You are sailing off the coast of Wales at night when your ship passes another, sailing without lanterns. As it slides past in the moonlight, you see its banner: the arms of the King of Ireland. And beyond it, waiting, another ship, flying the double-headed eagle of King Lot of Orkney.

"A secret meeting," your captain mutters. "Irish and Orkney. That means war for the young king." He looks at you. "We could follow and see what they say. Or we could go on our way and pretend we saw nothing. Nobody likes the ones who see things."

responses.label: You may board the ships and learn what they are plotting.
You may race to Camelot to warn the young king.

entries.body:
As you sail past Dover, you see the old Roman lighthouse on the cliff, half-ruined, with a light burning at the top of it. The fishermen say an old hermit lives there, keeping the light, so that ships will not wreck on the Goodwin Sands. But tonight, the light is flickering, and going out.

"If it goes out," your captain says, "the whole Calais fleet will be on the Sands before morning."

responses.label: You may climb up to the lighthouse and help the hermit keep the light.
You may warn the ships at sea yourself.

entries.body:
You are at sea with the young High King's fleet when Irish ships come out of the mist off Anglesey: twenty long ships with painted sails, bearing down on the king's fleet. Your ship is in the front line. The Irish are already throwing grappling hooks.

The captain of your ship is dead, struck by an arrow. The crew look at you. "What do we do?" asks the helmsman.

responses.label: You may take command of the ship and fight the Irish.
You may lead a boarding party onto the Irish flagship.

entries.body:
You are sailing across the Irish Sea when you come upon a great ship decked with flowers and banners, and hear music and laughter across the water. It is a wedding feast. The King of Ireland's daughter, the sailors tell you, is called Ethne, and she is sailing to marry the King of Man.

A boat puts out from the wedding ship and rows over. A herald calls up. "The princess invites any knight at sea to her wedding feast! It is the custom of Ireland!" He lowers his voice. "Also, the princess does not want to marry the King of Man. He is seventy. She wants to know if you can sail."

responses.label: You may join the wedding feast and dance with the princess.
You may help the princess escape her wedding.

entries.body: "Let me see her," you say. "There may be another way." The black knight hesitates, then stands aside.

resolutions.label: find a true cure for the lady's sickness

success.body: The lady lies in a dark room with her face veiled. You ask to see her hands. It is not leprosy. It is a scaling of the skin you have seen before, among the salt-workers of Droitwich, and it is cured with oatmeal baths and goose fat and sunlight. The lady laughs, bitterly, and then weeps. You open her shutters. You stay a month. At the end of it, her skin is clear, and the custom is ended, and she founds a hospital in the castle for the maidens who were bled.

failure.body: The lady lies in a dark room with her face veiled. You try every remedy you know, and none of them works. On the tenth day, the black knight comes to tell you that there is a new maiden in the courtyard. You leave that castle with a heavy heart.

entries.body: You ride to the watch-house and hammer on the door. The captain of the watch, a fat man in a leather jerkin, does not want to go down any well.

resolutions.label: rouse the watch and lead the raid on the tunnels

success.body: You shame the captain, cajole his men and recruit three butchers and a smith from the tavern next door. You send men down the well, down the grating in the fish market and down the old cellar under the church, all at once. The thieves, caught from three sides, surrender without a fight. The girl is found safe. The Rat King, a small man in a velvet hat, is caught trying to leave in a barrel of eels. The town gives you a feast.

failure.body: You rouse the watch and lead them down the well, but the thieves hear you coming a long way off. By the time you reach the vault, it is empty, and the tunnels beyond it go on for miles. The girl is let go the next day. The watch captain tells everyone it was a waste of a good evening.

resolutions.label: find the tunnels' other mouths and block them

success.body: You do not go down the well. You walk the town with the tanner's boy and look for the other ways in: a grating in the fish market, a loose stone behind the church, a cellar door that smells of damp. You put a watchman on each, and then you drop a lit bundle of wet straw down the well. The thieves come coughing up out of every hole at once, into waiting arms. The girl comes up last, blinking. The bishop gets his candlesticks back.

failure.body: You find three of the tunnels' mouths and set a watch on each, but you miss the fourth, under the river wall. When you smoke the well, the thieves are gone by the river. The girl is let go the next morning, frightened into silence.

entries.body: You rein in on the road and raise your hand. "Halt!" you call. The ghostly column comes on.

resolutions.label: stand before the ghost legion

success.body: The column stops, an arm's length from your horse. The centurion at its head looks at you. He is very young. "Who are you," he asks in Latin, "to stop the Ninth?" You tell him your name, and your king. He looks at you for a long time. Then he raises his hand in salute. "Rome is gone," he says. "Britain is yours now. Guard it well." The legion fades, rank by rank, into the dusk. The drover is staring at you with his mouth open.

partial.body: The column stops, an arm's length from your horse. The centurion looks at you, and does not speak, and then the legion marches round you, and on. You feel the cold of them as they pass.

failure.body: The column does not stop. It marches through you, rank upon rank, and every one of them is cold as ice. When it has passed, you fall out of the saddle.

entries.body: "I will help you," you say. "But not in his sleep." Emrys's face hardens. "Why not? He is not a knight. He is a murderer." You shake your head. "We are not."

resolutions.label: challenge Sir Breuse and fight him openly

success.body: You find Breuse at dawn, in a black pavilion by a river. He comes out laughing and mounts, and charges you with a lance tipped with steel. You meet him head-on, and on the second pass, you throw him. He lies in the grass and calls for quarter, and Emrys, beside you, lifts his master's sword. For a long moment the boy stands over Breuse, shaking. Then he lowers the sword. "Go and tell everyone," he says, "that a squire spared you." Breuse flees, and his name is a joke in every hall by winter.

failure.body: You find Breuse at dawn, in a black pavilion by a river. He comes out laughing and mounts, and on the first pass his steel-tipped lance throws you out of the saddle. You lie in the grass. Breuse wheels his horse and comes back to finish you, and Emrys leaps from the bushes, and takes the blow meant for you. Breuse flees. Emrys dies in your arms.

resolutions.label: ambush Breuse with Emrys in the night

success.body: You go with Emrys after all. At midnight, you creep into Breuse's pavilion together and tie him hand and foot while he sleeps. He wakes up to Emrys's sword at his throat. "I could kill you," says the squire. "I will not. I will take you to the High King, and you will hang." And so he does. You feel, at the hanging, that justice was done. You also feel that you did not do it as a knight should.

failure.body: You go with Emrys after all. At midnight, you creep toward Breuse's pavilion, but Breuse is no fool, and has set traps. You step in one, and the snare hoists you into the air by your ankle, and Breuse comes out of his pavilion with a torch and a grin. You and the squire both spend a very bad week in his cellar.

entries.body: You ride to the gate of Benwick under a white branch. They let you in. The queen's champion's kinsmen, Sir Bors and Sir Lionel and Sir Ector de Maris, meet you in the courtyard, grave and grey.

resolutions.label: carry a secret peace between the old king and Benwick

success.body: You speak to them all night. You tell them what the old king said: that he does not want this war. They tell you what they want: to go home, and for the queen to be safe. At dawn, you ride out of Benwick with terms: the house of Benwick will go into exile for a year, and pay for the masses of Gareth and Gaheris, and the old king will call off the siege. The old king reads them and puts his face in his hands. "Yes," he says. It is the only peace anyone makes in those last years. It holds long enough for him to go home.

failure.body: You speak to them all night, but in the morning, the great knight of Orkney hears that you have been inside Benwick, and calls you a traitor before the whole army. The peace is dead before it is born.

resolutions.label: carry the peace by the old right of a herald

success.body: You take a herald's white tabard and a herald's white staff and ride to the gate of Benwick, and demand entry by the law that no knight on either side will break. They let you in. Sir Bors and Sir Lionel and Sir Ector de Maris meet you in the courtyard, grave and grey, and you talk all night. At dawn, you ride out with terms. The old king reads them and puts his face in his hands. "Yes," he says. It is the only peace anyone makes in those last years.

failure.body: You ride to the gate as a herald, and the great knight of Orkney sees you do it, and calls you a traitor before the whole army. The peace is dead before it is born.

entries.body: You enter the lists in your own name. Rhiannedd watches you ride out onto the field with a look of dawning horror.

resolutions.label: win the tournament and claim the lady's hand

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You beat Sir Harry, and Sir Brian, and Sir Ywain the Poor, whose lance shakes in his hand. The crowd cheers you to the echo. When you ride to the stand to claim your prize, Rhiannedd looks at you for a long, long moment. "You are famous," she says at last, slowly. "And you are not sixty. And you do not beat squires." She sighs. "Very well." Sir Ywain writes a twelfth song, which is very sad.

partial.body: You beat Sir Harry and Sir Brian, and then Sir Ywain the Poor, whose lance shakes. But when you ride to claim your prize, Rhiannedd has gone, and so has Sir Ywain, and so has his one horse. Her father is purple. You are given a silver cup instead.

failure.body: You beat Sir Harry, but Sir Brian beats you, and goes on to win. Rhiannedd weeps. You do not feel that you have covered yourself in glory.

entries.body: "Wait here a little longer," you say. "I will look for her." The girl nods seriously.

resolutions.label: search the ruins for the child's mother

success.body: You search all day. At dusk, in a wood two miles from the town, you find a camp of survivors, and among them a woman who has been weeping for a month. When you say "a girl with a rag doll", she screams. You bring her back to the cellar. The girl looks up. "You were a long time," she says reproachfully, and her mother laughs and weeps and clutches her. You leave them in the ruins, holding each other, with the doll between them.

failure.body: You search all day, and find the survivors' camp, and ask about a girl with a rag doll. A woman looks at you, and then away. "Her mother," she says, "stayed behind to lead the Saxons off." You go back to the cellar. You do not know how to tell her.

resolutions.label: ask among the survivors in the woods

success.body: You ride to the survivors' camp in the wood and go from fire to fire asking about a girl with a rag doll. At the fifth fire, a woman who has been weeping for a month looks up and screams. You bring her back to the cellar. The girl looks up. "You were a long time," she says reproachfully, and her mother clutches her. You leave them in the ruins, holding each other.

failure.body: You go from fire to fire asking about a girl with a rag doll. Everyone has lost a girl. Everyone thinks you have found theirs. You ride back to the cellar with nothing, and cannot tell her.

entries.body: You rise from your place. "King Pellam," you call, "a knight at your table strikes your guests from behind. By the law of hospitality, I ask you to make him show himself."

resolutions.label: shame the invisible knight into the open

success.body: The hall goes silent. King Pellam frowns. Then he lifts his hand. "Garlon," he says. "Show yourself, brother." For a long moment, nothing happens. Then a knight in black appears beside Balin, red with anger. The king looks at him with disgust. "Go to your chamber," he says, "and do not come to my table again." Garlon goes. Balin sits down, shaking. King Pellam sends you a cup from his own table, and bids you visit again. You feel, under your feet, that something has been turned aside.

failure.body: The hall goes silent. King Pellam frowns. "My brother," he says, "does as he pleases in my hall." Garlon laughs, invisible, and strikes you across the face. You are put out of the castle. Behind you, you hear Balin draw his sword.

resolutions.label: unmask the invisible knight with flour from the kitchen

success.body: You slip out to the kitchens and come back with a sack of flour, and when the next invisible blow falls on Balin, you throw the whole sack at the empty air behind him. There, white from head to foot, sputtering, stands a knight in black. The whole hall roars with laughter. King Pellam looks at his brother with disgust. "Go to your chamber," he says. Garlon goes, leaving white footprints. Balin sits down, shaking.

failure.body: You throw a sack of flour at the empty air behind Balin. It covers King Pellam. The feast is over. So is your welcome.

entries.body: You sit down with your back against the stone. "Tell me," you say.

resolutions.label: hear Merlin's visions from inside the stone

success.body: He tells you. He sees the knights on the quest, one by one: which are close, and which are lost, and which are dead in ditches. He sees a white ship, and a castle, and a knight so pure he shines. He sees the vessel going east, over the sea, and never coming back. He sees the Round Table, emptier every year. He talks until dark. When he is finished, he says, "Thank you for listening. Nobody listens any more." You ride away knowing more than any knight in Britain, and wishing you did not.

failure.body: He tells you, but his voice is muffled by the stone, and you cannot make out most of it. At the end, he says, "Did you hear that last part? It was important." You did not.

resolutions.label: keep Merlin company through the long dark

success.body: You do not ask to hear his visions. You sit with your back against the stone for three days and nights, talking to him about nothing: the weather, the price of hay, the young knights at court. He laughs, sometimes. He tells you his visions anyway, a few at a time, when he wants to. At the end, he says, "Thank you. Nobody talks to me about hay." You ride away knowing more than any knight in Britain.

failure.body: You sit with your back against the stone for three days. On the second, a storm comes, and you have to go. Merlin, inside, sighs. "They always go," he says.

entries.body: You walk through the arch. The music rises round you. A lady with silver hair takes your hand and leads you to a seat at the golden table.

resolutions.label: feast with the fay and come back again

success.body: You eat and drink and dance, and it is the most wonderful night of your life. At dawn, the lady with the silver hair leads you back to the arch. "You ate, and you may leave," she says. "Because you laughed at our jokes." You step through. It is the same morning you went in. In your pocket, you find a silver apple. It never rots.

failure.body: You eat and drink and dance, and when you come back through the arch, the leaves have turned. It has been three months. Your horse is gone.

resolutions.label: trade jests with the fair folk and win your leave

success.body: You laugh at their jokes, which are very old and very strange, and then you tell one of your own, about a bishop and a goat. The fair folk have never heard it. The silver-haired lady laughs until she weeps. At dawn, she leads you back to the arch. "You made us laugh," she says, "so you may leave." It is the same morning you went in. In your pocket is a silver apple that never rots.

failure.body: You tell them the joke about the bishop and the goat. They have heard it. They told it to the bishop. You come back through the arch three months later.

entries.body:
As you walk your horse through the crooked streets of London in the Grail year, you see a crowd of pilgrims queuing at a low door in the side of Saint Paul's churchyard. A monk is letting them in two at a time. "The Shrine of the Hidden Light," says a woman in the queue. "Down in the old caves. There is a monk there who saw the Grail pass through Camelot, and his eyes have shone ever since."

The pilgrims coming up the steps are pale and trembling. One old man is weeping with joy. Another is weeping with something else. A young priest standing apart from the queue catches your arm. "It is a fraud," he says urgently. "I am sure of it. He takes their money in the dark and gives them a candle and a lie."

responses.label: You may go down into the cave-shrine to see the shining monk for yourself.
You may help the young priest expose the shrine as a fraud.

entries.body: You ride into a walled town in the Grail year and find a castle on its hill with every shutter closed and a black banner flying. At the gate, a knight in black armour bars your way. "The custom of this castle," he says, "is that every maiden who passes must give a dish of her blood for our lady. She is sick of a leprosy, and a wise man told her that only the blood of a pure maiden will heal her." Behind him, you see a line of frightened girls in the courtyard, with bandaged arms. Some of them are very pale. "Many have died," he adds, "but she has not been healed. We will keep trying."

responses.label: You may challenge the knights of the castle and end their custom.
You may go in to the sick lady and seek another cure.

entries.body:
You ride into Wells in the Grail year and find the cathedral doors wide open and the whole town crowded in the square outside, whispering. Inside, lying on the stone floor before the high altar, is a unicorn. It is white as milk, with a horn like twisted ivory, and it will not move.

The bishop comes out, wringing his hands. "It walked in at Matins," he says. "It lay down and it will not leave. We cannot say Mass. The canons say it is a sign. The huntsmen say its horn is worth a kingdom and cures all poisons." He lowers his voice. "The Earl of Somerset's huntsmen are outside now, with nets. They say they will take it tonight."

responses.label: You may protect the unicorn from the Earl's huntsmen.
You may approach the unicorn and learn why it has come.

entries.body:
You ride into a market town in the middle of a thunderstorm and find the whole town crowded in the square in the pouring rain, listening to a preacher on the church steps. He is tall and gaunt, in a sackcloth robe, and his voice carries over the thunder.

"The Grail has left us!" he cries. "Because of our sins! This storm is God's judgement! Bring out your gold, bring out your rings, lay them here at my feet as a sacrifice, and God will spare this town!" A pile of jewellery is already heaped on the steps. As you watch, lightning strikes the church tower above him, and the crowd screams and throws more.

A young woman pulls at your sleeve. "He has done this in three towns," she whispers. "Each time, he leaves in the night. With the gold."

responses.label: You may expose the false prophet before the crowd.
You may preach to the crowd yourself and calm their fear.

entries.body:
You ride into Glastonbury in the Grail year and find it crowded with pilgrims come to pray at the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. At the edge of the town, a band of monks in brown habits are offering to guide pilgrims up the Tor, for a small fee, to see the spot where Joseph planted his staff.

You notice that the monks have very large hands, and scars, and that one of them has a cutlass hanging under his habit. A pilgrim woman comes running down the path, weeping. "They took everything," she sobs. "At the top of the Tor. They pushed my husband down the slope."

responses.label: You may climb the Tor and catch the false monks in the act.
You may warn the pilgrims and guide them up the Tor yourself.

entries.body:
You are walking late at night through the cellars of Camelot, looking for a quiet place to pray, when you see a light under a door and hear two voices. One is sharp and dry. The other is soft and courteous.

"The queen was seen in the garden again on Tuesday," says the dry voice. "I have written it down." You recognise Sir Agravain. "Good," says the soft voice. "Keep writing." That is Mordred. "One day my father will have to listen. And we will be ready." Mordred laughs gently. "Is someone there?" The door opens. Mordred looks at you with his warm grey eyes. "Friend," he says. "Come in. We have been hoping you would join us."

responses.label: You may join Mordred and Agravain in their secret council.
You may refuse Mordred and warn the High King.

entries.body:
You ride into a small city in the Grail year and find a crowd outside a ruined church, whose roof fell in a hundred years ago. A family of beggars has been living in the ruins, and the bishop's men are trying to drive them out. "This is holy ground!" the bishop's steward is shouting. "Joseph of Arimathea rested here with the Grail, on his way to Glastonbury! The bishop will rebuild it as a shrine, and pilgrims will come!"

The beggar woman, a gaunt, fierce woman with four children, stands in the doorway. "We have lived here seven years," she says. "Nobody cared about the holy ground until the Grail came back into fashion."

responses.label: You may defend the beggars' right to stay.
You may search the ruined church for any sign of the Grail.

entries.body:
You ride into Winchester in the Grail year on the feast of Saint Swithun, and find the city in a riot. The monks of the cathedral were carrying their saint's bones in procession when the monks of the rival abbey across the river blocked their way with their own saint. Now both processions are fighting in the market square, with staves and censers, and the townsfolk have joined in on both sides.

In the middle of the square, the two reliquaries have fallen in the mud, and the bones are spilling out. An old bishop is trying to stop the fight, and is being trampled.

responses.label: You may wade into the riot and rescue the old bishop.
You may shame both sides into stopping the fight.

entries.body:
You are a guest at a feast given by Queen Guinevere in London in the Grail year, to show that the court still stands while so many knights are away on the quest. It is a fine feast. At its height, a young knight, Sir Patrise of Ireland, takes an apple from the queen's own dish, bites it, and falls down dead.

The hall erupts. Sir Mador de la Porte, the dead man's cousin, leaps to his feet. "Poison!" he cries. "The queen gave that feast! The queen chose those apples! I accuse the queen of murder!" The queen goes white. She looks round the hall for a champion, and none of her own knights meet her eye.

responses.label: You may stand as the queen's champion against Sir Mador.
You may find the true poisoner before the trial.

entries.body:
As you ride through the forest in dappled sunlight, you hear someone singing a psalm behind a waterfall. You dismount and push through the curtain of water into a cave. A knight in a hair shirt is kneeling on the bare rock, with his sword laid before him and his armour in a heap. His back is raw from a scourge.

"Sir Melias," he says, without turning. "I was on the Grail quest. I came to a crossroads and a crown lay in the road. I took it. It was not mine. A knight came out of the trees and struck me down, and a hermit told me that the crown was my pride, and the knight was my sin." He lifts the scourge. "So I am doing penance. Until the Grail forgives me."

He is very thin. There are blood-stains on the rock that are weeks old.

responses.label: You may kneel beside Sir Melias and help him complete his penance.
You may persuade Sir Melias that his penance is done.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dappled sunlight, you come upon a castle of white stone. The gate is open. In the courtyard, the flagstones are black and white squares, and on them lie thirty-two knights in old armour, all dead, all perfectly preserved, as though they fell a moment ago.

In a high chair at the end of the courtyard sits an old lord in a black tabard, with a white beard to his knees. "Guivret," he says. "Once lord of this castle. Once very proud of my games." He points at the dead knights. "They played for me every night for forty years, and I never let one go. When the Grail passed over this land, they all died at once. I am waiting to die too. But God will not have me until someone forgives me."

responses.label: You may hear the old lord's confession.
You may lay the dead knights to rest.

entries.body: "You will not keep vigil alone tonight," you say, and kneel down on the other side of the tomb. Ceinwen looks at you for a long moment. Then she bows her head. Around midnight, you hear footsteps on the hill.

resolutions.label: drive off the grave-robbers

success.body: There are six of them, with spades and a lantern, and they are expecting one grieving girl. They are not expecting you. You drive them back down the hill with the flat of your sword, and they run, and do not come back. At dawn, Ceinwen stands up for the first time in forty days. "I think he can rest now," she says. She takes the gilded helm from the wall and gives it to you. "He would want it used," she says, "by someone who would guard it."

failure.body: There are six of them, with spades and a lantern, and they are more than you expected. You fight hard, but a spade catches you across the head, and when you come to, they are gone, and so are the helm and the shield. Ceinwen is sitting beside the broken tomb. She does not weep. That is somehow worse.

resolutions.label: shame the grave-robbers into leaving

success.body: When the six men come over the brow of the hill with their spades and their lantern, you stand up in the chapel door with a candle in your hand and speak to them in a loud, clear voice, about their mothers, and their priests, and the Day of Judgement, and the dead who will sit up in their graves to accuse them. They stop. One of them crosses himself. Then, one by one, they turn and go back down the hill. Ceinwen stares at you in wonder. "They will not come back," she says. "I think you have frightened them all to church."

failure.body: When the six men come over the brow of the hill, you stand up in the chapel door and speak to them of the Day of Judgement. The biggest of them laughs and knocks the candle out of your hand. In the darkness, they pull down the helm and the shield and run, and one of them shouts over his shoulder that the Day of Judgement can come and find him.

entries.body: You dismount and seek out the late king's physician, an old man hiding in his house with the shutters closed. There is not much time.

resolutions.label: uncover the truth before the fire is lit

success.body: The physician is terrified, but you talk to him gently, and at last he shows you what Cadell ordered him to burn: the dead king's cup, with a white crust in the bottom that smells of almonds. It was poison, not witchcraft, and the cup was Cadell's gift. You run to the square with it as the torches are being lit. When you hold it up before the crowd, Cadell draws his sword and flees, and the townsfolk run him down in the road. The queen is freed. She gives you the dead king's own ring.

failure.body: The physician is terrified and will not speak. You search his house and find nothing. By the time you give up, the sun is on the hills, and you can hear the crowd. You reach the square as the fire catches. The queen looks at you through the smoke, and she does not look angry. She only looks tired.

resolutions.label: examine the dead king's body for the marks of poison

success.body: You go to the chapel where King Rhodri lies and look closely. His lips are blue, his nails are grey, and there is a smell of bitter almonds in his beard that no fever ever made. You run to the square with the priest behind you and show them. The crowd goes silent. Prince Cadell draws his sword and flees, and the townsfolk catch him at the gate. The queen is unchained. She gives you the king's own ring.

failure.body: You go to the chapel and look at the dead king. You see nothing but an old man who died. By the time you give up, the sun is on the hills, and you hear the crowd. You reach the square as the fire catches.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dappled sunlight, you hear a sound like thirty couple of hounds baying, coming from inside something that runs. The Questing Beast crashes out of the bracken ahead of you, with its serpent's head held low. It stops in the path and looks at you.

If you have Story Token #2, turn immediately to [[1156]].

Behind it, a young knight on a grey horse comes crashing after, with the arms of the Isles on his shield. "Did you see it?" he calls. "I am Lamorak, son of Pellinore. My father hunted it all his life. The Orkney brothers killed him, and now it is mine to hunt." His face is grim. "Help me take it, and I will give you a share of the glory."

The beast looks at you. The baying in its belly has stopped.

responses.label: You may help Sir Lamorak hunt down the Questing Beast.
You may let the Questing Beast go.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dappled sunlight, the sky turns black and a storm breaks over the trees. You find shelter in a woodcutter's hut, where two others are already sitting by the fire: an old hermit, and a knight in grey armour with a wound in his side that has soaked his surcoat red.

The storm roars all night. Near midnight, the wounded knight begins to talk, feverish, to no one. "I killed him," he says. "At a crossroads. He asked me which way to the Grail and I told him wrong on purpose, because I wanted to find it first. And he rode into a bog. I heard him. I did not go back." He turns his burning eyes on you. "I cannot die with that on me. I cannot."

The hermit looks at you. "He will not live till morning," he says quietly.

responses.label: You may help the dying knight make his confession.
You may ride out into the storm to find the bog he spoke of.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dappled sunlight, you come to a great oak with a clearing beneath it, where a band of outlaws is robbing a party of pilgrims. The outlaws are thin and ragged, and so are their children, watching from the trees. Their leader, a tall man with a knight's belt, is taking the pilgrims' purses one by one, and weeping as he does it.

"Sir Hervi de Rivel," he says, when he sees you. "I swore I would only rob the rich. But the harvest failed, and the Baron's men burned our stores, and there are no rich men on the roads any more. Only pilgrims." He looks at the purse in his hand. "My children have not eaten in three days. God forgive me."

responses.label: You may stop the robbery and feed the outlaws another way.
You may let the robbery go on and ride away.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest at midnight, you see a ring of torches under a hollow oak. Four figures in crowns sit on four stones around a fire: four queens. One is in black, one in white, one in red and one in kingfisher blue. You recognise the last. It is Morgan le Fay.

"The scabbard," she is saying. "My brother's scabbard. Whoever wears it cannot bleed. I will have it, and then my brother will bleed like anyone else." The Queen of Northgalis laughs. "And then?" she asks. "And then," says Morgan, "we will see who the Grail was really for." She turns her head and looks straight at you through the trees. "Come in, little knight," she says. "We know you are there."

responses.label: You may join the four queens' plot.
You may break up the queens' meeting and warn Camelot.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dappled sunlight, you come upon a ruined temple in a clearing, with a ring of broken columns and no roof. When the wind blows through the columns, it makes a sound like voices singing. You stop, and realise they are singing a psalm.

A young hermit is kneeling in the middle of the temple, weeping. "I came here to drive out the old goddess," he says. "I built an altar to the true God in her temple. And the voices changed. They sing psalms now." He looks up at you with frightened eyes. "But they sing them in her voice. Is it a blessing? Or a mockery? I cannot tell."

responses.label: You may pray in the ruined temple with the hermit.
You may listen closely to the voices to learn what they are.

entries.body: You step your horse off the road and let the column pass, and then fall in behind it, at a distance.

resolutions.label: follow the ghost legion without being taken

success.body: You follow them all night along the old road, and at dawn, they march into a hill and are gone. When you look at the hillside where they vanished, you see the outline of an old ditch and rampart, and in the grass, glinting, a bronze eagle, very old, green with age. You take it. The drover, when you show it to him, crosses himself. "The Ninth's eagle," he says. "It has been lost for four hundred years."

failure.body: You follow them along the old road, and at some point in the night, you find that you are marching in step with them, and cannot stop. You march until dawn. When the legion fades, you are thirty miles from where you started, and very footsore.

resolutions.label: ride alongside the legion as one of its escort

success.body: You bring your horse up beside the column and ride with it, as a mounted scout rides with foot, never falling into step. The centurion looks at you, once, and nods. You ride with them all night. At dawn, they march into a hill and are gone, and in the grass where they vanished, something bronze glints: an eagle, green with age. The drover crosses himself. "The Ninth's eagle," he says. "Lost four hundred years."

failure.body: You ride beside the column, and at some point in the night your horse falls into step with them, and so do you. You march until dawn, thirty miles, and your horse is lame at the end of it.

entries.body:
You come upon two knights fighting in a clearing in a forest, hammering at each other with swords, both of them exhausted, both of them bleeding. Neither wears a surcoat, and their shields are plain. One is in white armour. One is in red.

As you watch, the knight in white falls, and the knight in red stands over him, raising his sword. "Yield!" he cries. "I will not," gasps the knight in white. "I am on the Grail quest. I yield to no one." The knight in red hesitates. "So am I," he says.

Neither knows who the other is. Their helms are closed.

responses.label: You may stop the fight before the knight in red strikes.
You may let the fight run its course.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dappled sunlight, you come to a stone arch standing alone in a clearing. Through it, you see not a fay revel but a long wooden table under an oak, where a crowd of beggars, lepers, cripples and pilgrims is sitting down to a feast of bread and fish. An old man in a plain brown robe is breaking the bread and passing it round, and however much he breaks, there is always more.

"Come in," he says, looking up at you. "There is always room. I am only a hermit. I do not know where the bread comes from. It started when the Grail left Camelot." He smiles. "Perhaps it went looking for the hungry."

responses.label: You may sit down and share the hermit's bread.
You may serve the hungry at the hermit's table.

entries.body:
You come to a cave high on a mountainside, where the rocks around the entrance are carved with crosses and the air smells of beeswax. A path of white pebbles leads into the dark. From inside, you hear breathing, long and slow, like a sleeper.

An old nun, climbing the path behind you with a basket, stops to catch her breath. "Saint Collen," she says. "He went into that cave to pray two hundred years ago and fell asleep. He has not woken. We bring him bread every day, and every day it is gone." She smiles. "They say he will wake when a knight of the Grail asks him the way. Many have tried. Would you like to?"

responses.label: You may go into the cave and ask the sleeping saint the way to the Grail.
You may ask the old nun to tell you the saint's story.

entries.body:
You come upon a castle on a crag that turns. Slowly, all day and all night, the whole castle revolves on its rock like a millstone, and its gate comes round once every hour. A hermit sits at the foot of the crag, watching it. "The Turning Castle," he says. "Its lord was a knight who swore he would find the Grail before any other. He locked himself in and set the castle turning so nobody could reach him until he was ready. That was ten years ago. Nobody has seen him since." He looks up. "Sometimes, when the gate goes by, you can hear him singing."

The gate comes round. You hear, faintly, a man's voice singing a psalm, very badly.

responses.label: You may leap for the gate as it passes and enter the Turning Castle.
You may stop the castle turning.

entries.body: "Follow me," you say, though you are not at all sure where you are going. Owain and his huntsmen fall in behind you gratefully.

resolutions.label: find the way out of the moving wood

success.body: You do not trust your eyes. You trust your nose, and follow the smell of woodsmoke. You trust your ears, and follow the sound of running water. When the trees seem to lean in front of you, you walk straight at them, and they lean away. At sunset, the whole party comes out of the wood onto a hillside above Owain's own castle. He whoops. His huntsmen cheer. The white hart watches from the edge of the trees, and then it is gone. Owain gives you a ring with a lion on it.

failure.body: You do not trust your eyes. You follow the smell of woodsmoke, and it leads you to a charcoal-burner's hut, and the charcoal-burner is very old and very strange and will not let you leave until you have played a game of chess with him. You lose. When you come out, it is two days later, and the huntsmen are gone.

resolutions.label: keep the frightened huntsmen together

success.body: You get the huntsmen dismounted and roped together, each to the next, so that no one wanders off. Then you set one hound loose at a time and follow it, and when a hound comes back to the clearing, you know that way is closed. The sixth hound does not come back. You follow its tracks, all of you roped together, and come out of the wood at nightfall. Owain says it is the best-organised hunt he has ever been on, and the only one where he did not catch anything.

failure.body: You get the huntsmen dismounted and roped together. It works until one of the hounds spots the white hart and bolts, dragging its handler after it, who drags the next man, who drags the next. When you have picked yourselves up, you are all in a different clearing, no better off than before.

entries.body:
You come upon an eagle sitting on a crag on the top of Snowdon, so old that its feathers are white and its beak is worn down to a stub. It turns its head as you climb up to it, and speaks.

"I am the Eagle of Gwernabwy," it says. "I have sat on this rock so long that I have pecked the stars from the sky at night and watched them grow back. There was a hill here once, and I wore it down to this with my claws." It blinks slowly. "Everyone who climbs up asks me where the Grail is. I do not know. But I know older things. Ask me one of those."

responses.label: You may ask the ancient eagle what it knows of the oldest things.
You may ask the eagle to carry you somewhere no one else can reach.

entries.body:
You come upon a party of pilgrims trapped on a narrow ledge on a mountainside, in a storm. The path above them has been swept away by a landslide, and the path below is a torrent of water. They are huddled together, twenty of them, singing a psalm to keep their courage up. Their leader, an old abbess, calls down to you. "We were going to the shrine at Saint David's to pray for the Grail's return. God has tested us. Can you help?"

The rain is getting heavier. More stones are falling.

responses.label: You may climb up to the ledge and lead the pilgrims down.
You may pray with the pilgrims for the storm to pass.

entries.body:
You come to a mountain pass where a band of brigands has set up camp in a ruined chapel. They are drinking and dicing on the altar, and hung on the chapel wall is a painted cross, very old, with gold leaf. Before it, on the altar, among the dice, is a small gold casket.

An old monk is sitting by the road, weeping. "They took the Rood of Bromholm from our abbey," he says. "A piece of the True Cross. The Grail left us, and now the Rood has gone too. They mean to sell the casket in Chester." He looks up at you. "They do not know what is inside. If they open it and throw the wood away…"

responses.label: You may attack the brigands and take back the holy relic.
You may trick the brigands into giving up the relic.

entries.body:
You come upon a cave high on a mountain where seven hermits sit around a single candle, with their hoods over their heads, in silence. When you come to the entrance, one of them looks up. "Come in," he says. "We have been waiting for a knight. We are the seven hermits of the Grail. Every knight on the quest has come to one of us, to have his dreams read." He gestures at the others. "We meet once a year to compare what we have seen. This year, we have all dreamed the same dream."

"A plain," says another. "A king and his son. Ravens." The seven look at you. "We cannot tell the king," says the first. "Kings do not listen to hermits. Will you?"

responses.label: You may carry the hermits' warning to the High King.
You may ask the hermits to read your own dreams.

entries.body:
You come upon a ruined monastery on a mountainside, its roof long gone, where snow drifts through the empty windows of the church. In the ruined scriptorium, you find an old monk, the last of his brothers, sitting at a desk under the open sky, copying a book by the light of the snow.

"The Gospel of Joseph," he says, without looking up. "The only copy. It tells where the holy vessel came to rest in this island. The Saxons burned the monastery sixty years ago. I saved the book. I have been copying it ever since, so there will be two." He looks up. His fingers are black with cold. "I will not finish before the winter. Unless someone helps me."

responses.label: You may help the old monk finish copying the book.
You may carry the old monk and his book down the mountain to safety.

entries.body: "I will help you look, my lord," you say. Mark's eyes narrow, then brighten. "At last," he says. "A knight with sense." He gives you a list of names, most of them crossed out, and a description of the man that would fit half the knights in Britain.

resolutions.label: search the carts and the countryside with the king's men

success.body: You spend a hard week on the moors with Mark's soldiers. You find no lover, but you do find a band of wreckers who have been lighting false beacons on the cliffs. Mark is delighted to hang somebody, and for a while he forgets his wife. He gives you a purse of Cornish silver and calls you the only honest knight in Britain. You are not sure you want to be his favourite, but the silver spends well.

failure.body: You spend a hard week on the moors with Mark's soldiers, and find nothing at all. On the seventh day Mark decides that your failure is suspicious, and that a knight who cannot find a lover must be hiding one. You leave Cornwall by night, with his soldiers hunting the moor behind you.

entries.body:
You come upon a battlefield on a mountainside in the Grail year, where a lord's army was destroyed a week ago by a band of reivers. Nobody has buried the dead. The crows are thick. In the middle of the field, an old priest is digging a grave alone, with a spade too big for him.

"Three hundred," he says, when you ride up. "I have buried eleven. The lord who led them has fled. The families have not come. They are afraid of the reivers." He leans on his spade. "Last night, I saw the dead men standing. All of them. Looking at me. They want to be buried before the Grail passes this way. I do not know why they think it will."

responses.label: You may help the old priest bury the dead.
You may ride to the villages and bring the families to bury their dead.

entries.body:
You climb to a monastery on the top of a mountain on Easter morning in the Grail year, and find the monks sitting down to their first meal after the Lenten fast. It is a very plain feast: bread, eggs, a little cheese. But they are laughing and singing, and they make room for you at once.

The abbot, a tiny old man, leans over. "We have eaten nothing but bread and water for forty days," he says. "It makes an egg taste like the Grail itself." He points to the end of the table, where a young monk sits alone, not eating. "Brother Idwal. He will not break his fast. He says he will not eat until he has seen the Grail. He has not eaten in sixty days."

responses.label: You may persuade Brother Idwal to break his fast.
You may keep vigil with Brother Idwal in his fast.

entries.body:
You come upon a crowd of pilgrims on a wide plain, gathered round a well with a stone cross beside it. They are lowering a bucket, drawing it up and passing the water from hand to hand. The water is red.

"Joseph's Well," a friar tells you. "They say Joseph of Arimathea rested here on his way to Glastonbury, and washed the holy vessel in it, and the water has run red ever since, like wine. It cures anything." He looks worried. "But since the Grail left Camelot, the water has been getting fainter. There is a cave at the bottom. Someone should go down and see."

responses.label: You may climb down the well to the cave below.
You may pray at the well for its healing to return.

entries.body:
You come upon a castle on a wide plain in a land gone to dust. The fields around it are grey and dead, and the moat is dry. In the gatehouse sits a knight in rusted armour, with his hands on the pommel of his sword. He does not move as you approach. "The Castle Mortal," he says. "King Pellam's brother lives here. He wounded his own brother with the spear that bleeds, and made the land waste, and he is proud of it." His voice is empty. "I am his porter. I have not eaten in a year. Nothing here eats. Nothing here dies."

From the keep, you hear someone laughing, a thin, cruel laugh.

responses.label: You may challenge the lord of the Castle Mortal.
You may give the starving porter food and pray for the castle.

entries.body:
You come upon a fight on a wide plain: a lion and a great serpent, locked together. The serpent has wound itself round the lion's body and is crushing it, and the lion is roaring, and its roars are growing weaker. The grass is torn up all around them.

A hermit is watching from a rock, telling his beads. "Every day they fight," he says. "Every day at noon. The lion is the soul. The serpent is sin. So the preachers say." He shakes his head. "I think it is only a lion and a serpent. But I have never seen the lion lose before."

responses.label: You may help the lion kill the serpent.
You may leave the beasts to their battle and pray over them.

entries.body:
You come upon a village on a wide plain as a hailstorm smashes its harvest flat. When the storm has passed, the villagers are standing in their ruined fields, and a crowd of them is dragging an old woman out of her cottage. "Witch!" they are shouting. "She did this! She was out on the heath last night, muttering!"

The old woman is thin and frightened. "I was praying," she cries. "I was praying for the Grail to come back. I pray on the heath every night. It is quieter there."

The crowd has a rope.

responses.label: You may defend the old woman from the mob.
You may prove what truly brought the storm.

entries.body:
You come upon a bishop's baggage train drawn up on a wide plain, surrounded by a band of brigands on horseback. The bishop himself, a fat man in purple, is standing on a cart shouting anathemas at them. The brigands are laughing. "Your gold, my lord bishop," their leader calls. "Or your life. The Grail has gone, and God has stopped listening."

The bishop's guards have fled. His chaplain, a thin young priest, is standing in front of the bishop with his arms spread. "Take me," he says. "Not him."

responses.label: You may ride to the bishop's defence.
You may shame the brigands with the young chaplain's courage.

entries.body:
You come upon a ring of standing stones on a wide plain at dusk, where a nun in a grey habit and a knight in grey armour are standing together, not touching, in the middle of the circle. They turn as you approach, and the nun pulls her veil across her face.

"Do not be alarmed," the knight says. "I am Sir Ector de Maris. This is Sister Eleri. We were betrothed before she took the veil and I took the Grail quest. We meet here once a year, and talk, and pray, and part. We have never broken our vows." He looks tired. "But her abbess has heard of it, and says she must be walled up as an anchoress. Tomorrow."

responses.label: You may help Sister Eleri escape the abbess's punishment.
You may speak for the two of them before the abbess.

entries.body:
You come upon a ruined chapel on a wide plain, its roof fallen in, with a single tomb inside. On the tomb lies the carved figure of a knight, and on its side is an inscription in old letters: *Here shall lie the knight who will see the vessel bare. Let no other lie here.* The tomb is empty. Its lid lies beside it, pushed aside.

A young knight is standing beside the empty tomb, trembling. "I was going to lie in it," he says. "To see if it was me. My friend dared me." He looks at you. "Should I? If it is not me, they say, the lid falls and crushes you."

responses.label: You may dissuade the young knight from lying in the tomb.
You may test the tomb yourself.

entries.body: "What has the abbot done?" you ask. "Besides calling you hags." The witches look at each other. "He burned our sister," says the eldest. The cackling stops.

resolutions.label: brew the witches' curse

success.body: You tell them of your own villainies while they stir, and they listen with delight, and ask for more. By dawn, the curse is ready: the Abbot of Crowland will itch, all over, for a year. The witches thank you and give you a bone charm that will turn a blade once. "You are one of us," says the one-eyed witch, fondly. You find this less flattering than she means it.

partial.body: You tell them of your villainies. The witches are unimpressed. "Is that all?" says the eldest. But they let you stir.

failure.body: You tell them of your villainies. The witches laugh at you until the raven falls off. "A saint!" cries the eldest. "We have a saint at our fire!" They throw you in the bog.

entries.body:
You come upon a tournament on a wide plain at Winchester in the Grail year, where the High King has called a great melee to bring home the knights of the quest. Many have come. Many have not. They fight in disguise, with plain shields, so that no man may know who he fights. It is a strange, sad tournament. Knights who were brothers break lances on each other without knowing it.

A herald comes up to you. "The High King asks every knight to fight without his arms," he says, handing you a plain white shield. "So that the quest may be forgotten, for one day." He lowers his voice. "The king is lonely. He wants his knights home."

responses.label: You may fight in the disguised melee for the High King's pleasure.
You may seek out the High King and speak with him.

entries.body:
You come upon a village on a wide plain in the wasted land, where there has been no harvest since the Grail left Camelot. The fields are dust. But the villagers are setting out a harvest feast anyway, on bare tables, with empty bowls and empty cups, and they are singing the old harvest songs.

The reeve, an old woman, sees your face. "We keep the feast," she says, "because if we stop, we will forget how. And when the harvest comes back, we will need to remember." She hands you an empty cup. "Will you sit with us?"

responses.label: You may sit down at the empty feast and keep it with them.
You may ride out and find the villagers food for their feast.

entries.body:
You come to an island of firm ground in a wide bog, where a cave opens under a hump of rock. Water has flooded the cave to the height of a man's waist. Standing in the water, up to his chest, is an old hermit, with his arms raised in prayer. His lips are blue with cold.

"Do not come in," he says, through chattering teeth. "I am Brother Gwrgant. I have vowed to stand here until the waters go down or God takes me. The bog rose at Candlemas when the Grail left the land. The rivers are wrong everywhere now." He shivers violently. "I thought, if one man would stand in the flood and pray, God might send it back."

The water in the cave is still rising.

responses.label: You may pull the hermit out of the flooded cave.
You may find the cause of the flood and drain the cave.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a bog at dusk, you see a faint light shining across the water. It comes from a castle on stilts over the marsh, with one lantern burning in a high window. A bell rings as you approach, and a voice calls from the window: "Unclean! Unclean! Come no closer!"

A man looks down at you. His face is bandaged, and his hands. "I am Sir Hervis," he says. "I was a knight of the Round Table. I have the leprosy. I came here so as not to shame my brothers. I have lived here alone for eight years." His voice is quite calm. "I only wanted to ask you one thing. They say the Grail has been seen. Is it true?"

responses.label: You may go up into the leper-knight's castle and sit with him.
You may tell Sir Hervis all you know of the Grail from where you stand.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a marsh at dusk, a little blue flame rises from the reeds ahead of you and dances away across the water. Then another, and another, until the marsh is full of them, bobbing and weaving. A voice calls from somewhere among them: "Help! Help me! This way!"

You see, far off across the marsh, a pilgrim in a grey hood, following the lights. He is walking straight toward deep water. "The Grail!" he cries. "I see it! It is leading me!"

responses.label: You may chase down the pilgrim before he drowns.
You may follow the will-o'-the-wisps to see where they lead.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a marsh in the Grail year, a storm rises out of nowhere, and the rain comes down black and stinking. In the middle of it, standing on a tussock, is a hag with green skin and long teeth, cackling, stirring the air with a stick. "Sin!" she shrieks. "The Grail is gone, and the sin comes up out of the bog! I am the bog's own daughter, and I am free!"

As she stirs, the rain grows heavier, and you see the marsh villages on the edges of the bog beginning to flood.

responses.label: You may drive the bog-hag back into the marsh.
You may bargain with the bog-hag to calm her storm.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through the fens in the Grail year, you hear the sound of a sanctus bell in the reeds, and find a chapel on an island, where a priest is saying Mass to a congregation of fen-folk. At the end of the Mass, the priest turns and looks at you, and you see that he is wearing a sword under his vestments. So are his congregation.

"Father Ulf," he says. "Once an outlaw. Now a priest. These are my old band. We gave up robbing when the Grail came to Camelot, and built this chapel." He looks troubled. "But since the Grail left, some of them want to go back to robbing. There is a merchant's barge coming down the river tomorrow. I cannot stop them. Perhaps you can."

responses.label: You may keep the reformed outlaws from returning to their old ways.
You may join the raid on the merchant's barge.

entries.body:
You come upon a fire on an island in a marsh at midnight, where a woman in kingfisher blue is sitting with a man in rags. The man has a great wound in his thigh that will not close. You recognise the woman. It is Morgan le Fay. You do not recognise the man, until he looks up, and you see that he is a king, and that his eyes are full of an old, old pain.

"This is King Pellam's brother," says Morgan, without surprise. "The one who struck the Dolorous Stroke. He came to me for healing. I am a very good healer." She smiles. "I will heal him if he tells me the way to Corbenic. I want to see this Grail everyone talks about. And then I want to see what happens if I take it." The wounded man looks at you in despair.

responses.label: You may take the wounded man away from Morgan.
You may bargain with Morgan for the wounded man's healing.

entries.body: As you pick your way through a marsh, you come upon a ruined tower on an island, black and cracked, with a light burning in its highest window. At its foot, a young man is sitting on a rock, weeping. "My master," he says. "Master Blaise. He was a great scholar. He was Merlin's teacher, they say. He shut himself in the tower to find the Grail by magic, instead of prayer. That was a year ago. He will not come down, and he will not let me up." He points at the window. "Sometimes I hear him laughing. Sometimes screaming."

responses.label: You may climb the ruined tower to confront the old sorcerer.
You may break the enchantment that holds the tower.

entries.body: You spur after the knight in black. "Sir Brun!" you call. "That motley belongs to a fool. I will fight you for it." Brun turns in the saddle and laughs. "Fight a knight for a fool's coat?" he says. "Very well."

resolutions.label: joust with Sir Brun for the motley

success.body: You meet him in the road with lances, and on the first pass, you put him into a hedge. He comes out with leaves in his hair. "For a coat?" he says wonderingly. "For a coat," you say. He hands it over. You ride back to Hwfa and toss him his motley and his cap and his bauble, and he puts them on right there on the milestone, and does a handspring, and falls over. "*I am a fool again!*" he cries. "Thank God!"

failure.body: You meet him in the road with lances, and on the first pass, he puts you into a hedge. He rides on laughing, with two trophies now: a fool's cap and a knight's pride. Hwfa helps you out of the hedge. "*We are both fools now,*" he says gloomily.

resolutions.label: shame Sir Brun into giving back a fool's coat

success.body: You ride alongside him. "A knight," you say, "who hangs a fool's coat in his hall and says he won it in single combat. The heralds will enjoy that." Brun opens his mouth to answer, and then imagines the heralds. He goes very red. He unties the motley and throws it at you. "It is only a coat," he says. You ride back to Hwfa, who puts it on and does a handspring and falls over.

failure.body: You tell Sir Brun what the heralds will say. Brun laughs. "Let them," he says. "Every herald in Britain already calls me worse." He rides on, jingling.

entries.body:
You come upon a battle in the marshes in the Grail year, where a lord's army is fighting a band of men in white robes, the followers of a hermit who has declared himself the Grail's prophet and seized a monastery. The white-robed men are fanatics, and they fight with a terrible, joyful courage, singing hymns. Many of them are boys.

The lord's captain, a hard-faced man, sees you and waves you over. "Help us break them," he says. "They have killed forty of my men. They will not surrender." Across the marsh, a white-robed boy of fourteen is standing on a hummock, singing, with a spear in his hand.

responses.label: You may help the lord's men break the fanatics.
You may find the false prophet and end the battle another way.

entries.body:
You come upon an island in a marsh in the Grail year, where a great hall stands among apple trees, and a feast is laid in it for a hundred people, and there is nobody there. The food is hot. The candles are lit. The wine is poured.

A little girl is sitting on the steps of the hall, swinging her legs. "It is the King's feast," she says. "King Pellam of Corbenic's. It gets laid every night, but nobody comes. He is wounded, so he cannot. And the knights all go looking for his castle instead of here." She looks up at you. "You can eat, if you like. But you have to ask a question first. That is the rule."

responses.label: You may ask the girl a question and eat at the king's feast.
You may ask the girl why nobody comes to the feast.

entries.body:
As you ride along a cliff-top at dusk, you hear bells ringing from beneath the sea. The sound comes from a sea-cave at the foot of the cliff, deep and slow, like a church calling people to Mass. Kneeling on the rocks outside the cave, a fisherman is crossing himself over and over.

"The drowned church of Llys Helig," he says. "The sea took it, and the town, a hundred years ago, for their sins. When the Grail was at Camelot, the bells were quiet. Since it left, they ring every night." He shivers. "And there is a voice. A woman singing in the cave. My son went in to see her a week ago. He has not come out."

responses.label: You may go into the sea-cave to find the fisherman's son.
You may pray for the drowned town so that its bells can rest.

entries.body:
As you sail along a rocky coast in the grey dawn, you see a castle on a rock in the sea, with a single lamp burning in its highest window. A woman is standing at the window, looking out to sea, and she has been standing there, the fishermen tell you, every night since Pentecost.

"The Lady Amide," says the fisherman who is rowing you. "Her husband, Sir Bleheris, went on the Grail quest. He sailed from this castle on a white ship with no sails. He said he would be back in a year. It has been two." He lowers his voice. "The lamp has never gone out. She says if it does, he will die."

responses.label: You may search the sea for word of the lady's husband.
You may go to the lady and help her keep her vigil.

entries.body: You push past the crew to the wheel, where the captain has left it swinging. "The sea wants nothing," you say. "It is only the sea."

resolutions.label: steer the ship through the storm

success.body: You take the wheel and shout orders: reef the sail, man the pumps, lash the cargo. The crew obeys, because someone is shouting orders, and there is no time to throw anyone overboard while you are bailing. You steer into the waves all night. In the morning, the ship limps into Waterford with its sail in rags and everyone on board. The young woman walks down the gangplank with her head high. The captain buys you a drink and does not meet your eye.

failure.body: You take the wheel, but you are no sailor, and a great wave takes the ship broadside. The mast goes. You are all in the sea, clinging to wreckage, until a fishing boat picks you up the next morning.

entries.body:
As you sail west in the Grail year, looking for islands that are not on any map, you come upon an island with no trees and no rocks, only smooth black ground and a little chapel. A dozen monks are standing on it, singing Mass. Their abbot waves to your ship. "Come ashore!" he calls. "We have been here since Easter! We are waiting for Pentecost!"

As you row closer, the island shivers, and a great spout of water shoots up from its far end. The monks do not seem to notice. The sailors do. "That is no island," the helmsman whispers. "That is a whale."

responses.label: You may go ashore and join the monks' Mass on the whale.
You may warn the monks and bring them off before the whale dives.

entries.body:
You are at sea when a storm drives your ship far off its course, into a strange grey sea where the water is flat as glass and there is no wind at all. Floating before you is a ship unlike any you have seen, very old, of white wood, with no sail and no oars and no crew. Painted on its side, in letters of gold, are the words: *You who come aboard, beware that you are full of faith, for I am nothing but faith.*

Your sailors refuse to go near it. On its deck, you can see a bed hung with white silk, and on the bed lies a sword, half-drawn from its scabbard.

responses.label: You may go aboard the ship of faith.
You may pray and wait to see what the ship will do.

entries.body:
You are sailing along the coast of Cornwall at night when you see a light on the cliffs, like a beacon. Your captain turns toward it, relieved. "Saint Ia's lighthouse," he says. Then he frowns. "No. Saint Ia's is further west." But it is too late. The ship strikes a rock.

As the ship grinds and groans, you see men coming down the cliff with lanterns and axes. Wreckers. They light false beacons to lure ships onto the rocks, and kill the crews, and take the cargo. "In the Grail year," your captain says bitterly, "even the Cornish have stopped fearing God."

responses.label: You may fight the wreckers on the shore.
You may save the ship's crew from the rocks and the sea.

entries.body: You are sailing to the Holy Land in the Grail year, aboard a pilgrim ship, when you see the captain meeting secretly at night with a hooded passenger in his cabin. You overhear them through the planks. "The relic is in the hold," says the hooded man. "A thorn from the Crown. Stolen from Glastonbury. The Emperor in Constantinople will pay a king's ransom for it." The captain laughs. "And the pilgrims?" "Sell them in Tunis," says the hooded man. "Who will ever know?"

responses.label: You may take control of the pilgrim ship.
You may find the stolen relic and keep it safe.

entries.body:
As you sail north along the coast in the Grail year, you come upon a ruined monastery on an island, where the Saxons burned the monks a hundred years ago. Its walls are black and roofless. But there is a light in the library.

You row ashore and find a young woman sitting among the ruins with a great book on her knees, reading by candlelight. "Sister Hild," she says. "I came here to find this. The monks hid it in the wall when the Saxons came." She shows you the book: pages of gold and blue and red, illuminations so beautiful they seem to glow. "It is the Book of the Grail. It tells where the vessel goes when it leaves a land." She looks up. "But the pages are rotting. And there is a storm coming."

responses.label: You may help Sister Hild save the book from the storm.
You may help Sister Hild read the book before it rots.

entries.body: You draw your sword. The sergeant sighs. "Always one," he says.

resolutions.label: drive off the band of deserters

success.body: They are soldiers, but they are tired and drunk and have lost the heart to fight. You cut down the sergeant, and the rest scatter across the plain. You help the woman and her children gather what the deserters dropped: a pot, some blankets, a sack of flour. It is not much. It is more than they had. She thanks you with dry eyes.

failure.body: They are soldiers, and there are a dozen of them. You are beaten and left in the ashes beside the woman. She binds your head with a strip of her shift.

entries.body:
You are at sea in the Grail year when you come upon a strange sea battle: a ship of monks from Iona, attacked by a pirate ship, and the monks are defending themselves with oars and psalms. The pirates are winning. As you watch, a monk falls overboard.

Your captain wants to sail on. "Not our business," he says. "Pirates are pirates. Monks are monks."

responses.label: You may attack the pirates and save the monks.
You may pull the drowning monks out of the sea.

entries.body:
You are sailing west in the Grail year when you come to an island that is one great garden, where the fruit on the trees is gold and the grass is soft as silk. On the shore, a feast is laid on a white cloth: fruits, honey, bread, wine. Nobody is there.

Your sailors fall on it at once. You notice, as they eat, that they are growing sleepy, and happy, and slow. An old man in a white robe appears beside you. "The Island of Delight," he says. "Whoever eats here never wants to leave. Many knights of the quest have stopped here. They are still here." He points. In the trees, you see men sleeping, with smiles on their faces, and grass growing through their armour.

responses.label: You may drag your sailors back to the ship before they fall asleep.
You may ask the old man how to wake the sleeping knights.

entries.body: You sit down under the thorn tree. The old man settles back, delighted. "You first," he says.

resolutions.label: match wits with the old beggar

success.body: You give him the best riddle you know. He laughs aloud and answers it, but he has to think first, which pleases him enormously. "Now mine," he says. "*I taught a girl everything I knew, and she used it to put me in a box. What am I?*" You think for a long time. "A fool," you say at last. The old man's grin fades. "Yes," he says quietly. "Yes, I suppose I am." He stands, and for a moment he is very tall and not a beggar at all. "Remember that answer," he says. "One day, someone will need it." He is gone. His bowl is full of gold.

failure.body: You give him the best riddle you know. He answers it at once, and yawns. "Now mine," he says. "*I taught a girl everything I knew, and she used it to put me in a box. What am I?*" You guess, and guess again, and cannot get it. He laughs, but his eyes are sad. "No," he says. "Nor could I, when I was your age. Keep it. Perhaps you will guess it later." When you look up, he is gone, and there is an apple peel curled on the grass.

entries.body: "Hag," you call. "What do you want?" She stops stirring and looks at you with her little red eyes. "Want?" she says. "Nobody ever asks the bog what it wants."

resolutions.label: strike a bargain with the bog's daughter

success.body: It turns out she wants the villages to stop cutting peat from her bog without asking. You wade to the nearest village and tell them. They agree, very quickly, to leave an offering at the edge of the bog every spring, and to cut only from the western side. The hag grumbles, and stirs once more, and the storm drifts away. "The western side," she mutters, sinking. "Only the western side."

failure.body: It turns out she wants a husband. She looks at you very hopefully. You flee, and the storm follows you for three days.

entries.body: You ride into the besiegers' camp under a white branch and ask to see King Claudas. He is a lean, fox-faced man with a gold chain on his chest. "Peace?" he says. "I have ten thousand men and he has three hundred."

resolutions.label: broker a peace between King Claudas and King Ban

success.body: You tell him that the young British king has sworn to defend King Ban, and that he is young and angry and has just beaten eleven kings in a single summer. You tell him how much a war across the sea would cost, and how little Benwick is worth, compared to the friendship of a young king who will one day rule half the world. Claudas listens, with his fox's face very still. At the end, he sends a herald to the walls. Benwick keeps its old king. Claudas keeps his men. You are given gifts by both sides, which is the best sort of peace.

failure.body: You tell him the young British king has sworn to defend King Ban. Claudas laughs. "Then let him come," he says, "and find Benwick in ashes." He has you escorted out of the camp. Benwick falls a month later.

resolutions.label: meet King Claudas's champion to decide the siege

success.body: You offer Claudas a bargain: single combat, his champion against you, and whoever loses, his king's army goes home. Claudas laughs and accepts, because his champion is a giant of a man from the Desert Land. You fight him on the bridge before Benwick's gate, with both armies watching. It is the hardest fight of your life. At the end, the champion yields. Claudas, to his credit, keeps his word. You are given gifts by both sides.

failure.body: You fight Claudas's champion on the bridge before Benwick's gate. He throws you off it into the moat. Benwick falls a month later.

entries.body: You bring your boat alongside and climb up the rocks. The king falls on your neck. "Can you steer an island?" he asks. You have no idea.

resolutions.label: steer the drifting island to shore

success.body: You treat it like a ship. You rig the castle's banners as sails from the tallest tower and set the king's household to haul on ropes tied to the trees, and you steer by the sun, shouting orders from the battlements. The king thinks you are marvellous. Very slowly, over three days, the island drifts back across the bay, until it grounds on a sandbank off Gwynedd. The king steps off onto his own shore and kisses it, and the island drifts away again without him, and nobody minds.

failure.body: You rig the castle's banners as sails and shout orders from the battlements. The island turns very slowly and drifts faster toward Ireland. You land in Wexford with the King of Gwynedd, who is not pleased, and it takes you a month to get home.

resolutions.label: read the currents and let the island drift home

success.body: You do not try to steer. You watch the sea for a day, and the weed, and the birds, and you find the current that runs back toward Gwynedd, a mile south. You get the king's household to paddle the island toward it with every oar and door they have. On the third day, the current takes it, and the island drifts gently back across the bay and grounds on a sandbank. The King of Gwynedd kisses the shore.

failure.body: You watch the sea for a day and find a current, and paddle the island into it. It is the wrong current. You land in Wexford with the King of Gwynedd, who is not pleased.

entries.body: "I will find them," you say. The dwarf nods briskly. "Comfrey by the stream. Yarrow on the hillside. The water-avens you will find in a marsh, if you are lucky. Hurry."

resolutions.label: find the healing herbs in time

success.body: You find comfrey by the stream and yarrow on the hillside, and in a marsh two miles away you find the water-avens, its red flowers nodding. You ride back with your arms full. The dwarf grins. "You have a good eye," he says. He works fast, and by nightfall the knight's fever has broken. The knight, who turns out to be Sir Sagramore, says he owes you his leg. Meddyg says he owes you nothing, but teaches you the names of twenty herbs on the way to the next town.

failure.body: You find comfrey by the stream and yarrow on the hillside, but you cannot find the water-avens. You search every marsh for miles. When you ride back at dusk, the dwarf is sitting beside the knight, who is very still. He shakes his head.

resolutions.label: draw the poison out with a healer's charm

success.body: You kneel beside the knight and lay your hands on the wound and speak the old charm for poison, the one that begins *Wound, wound, give it back*. The dwarf watches with his eyebrows raised. The black flesh round the wound slowly reddens. The knight's breathing eases. "Salerno," says the dwarf, "does not teach that." He cleans the wound, and the knight lives, and Meddyg makes you teach him the charm on the way to the next town.

failure.body: You lay your hands on the wound and speak the charm for poison. The dwarf watches, then pushes you aside. "Charms later," he says. "Comfrey now." By the time you have found the comfrey, the leg cannot be saved.

entries.body: "The old king," you say, "is not dead." The messenger's face goes white. He draws his sword.

resolutions.label: take the treasure from Mordred's man

success.body: He is no fighter. After three passes, his sword is in the bog and he is on his knees. You let him run. Then you look at the chests: coin, and plate, and a golden altar cross from Glastonbury. You take the cross to Glastonbury, where the monks weep. The coin you give to a village on the edge of the bog, which has had its cattle stolen by both sides. You keep one chest. It seems fair.

failure.body: He is no fighter, but his friends are. They come out of the cave behind him, three of them, and you are driven back across the causeway into the bog. By the time you have struggled out, they have moved the treasure somewhere else.

resolutions.label: trick the messenger into showing you the rest

success.body: "The old king is dead," you say, "and I serve Mordred too. But I was sent to check your hiding places. The king does not trust bogs." The messenger, relieved, shows you everything: the chests in the cave, and the other three sunk in a pool behind it. Then you draw your sword. He runs. You take the altar cross to Glastonbury and the coin to a village that has lost its cattle to both sides.

failure.body: "I serve Mordred too," you say. The messenger narrows his eyes. "Then you know the watchword," he says. You do not. He runs, and so does the treasure, before you can find it.

entries.body: You wait until night, and row alone to the cove below Tintagel, where the Saxon ships are drawn up on the beach.

resolutions.label: burn the Saxon ships in the cove

success.body: The Saxons are feasting in the ruins above. You set fire to their ships, one by one, and slip back into your boat. By the time they see the flames, the fleet is burning. They run down to the cove, and the fishermen, who have been waiting in the dark, are on them. By dawn, the Saxons have surrendered. The Cornish are very proud of you.

failure.body: You set fire to the first ship, but a Saxon on watch sees you, and raises the alarm. You escape back to your boat, but the other ships are saved.

resolutions.label: cut the Saxon ships loose on the ebb

success.body: You do not burn them. You swim out on the ebb and cut their mooring lines one by one, and the tide does the rest, carrying the longships quietly out of the cove and away round the headland in the dark. At dawn, the Saxons come down to their ships and find the cove empty. The fishermen are waiting on the cliff. The Saxons surrender by noon.
