failure.body: You cut the mooring lines, and the ebb carries the ships out, and then the flood carries them back in again, and the Saxons, who have seen your wet footprints on the rocks, are waiting.

entries.body: You ride your horse into the square, scattering monks like chickens.

resolutions.label: pull the bishop out of the riot

success.body: You ride through the melee to the bishop, lift him bodily onto your saddle, and ride out of the square. The monks, seeing their bishop carried off by a knight, stop fighting in astonishment. In the sudden quiet, the bishop, from your saddle, tells both processions exactly what he thinks of them. It takes a long time. At the end, both sets of monks are on their knees in the mud, picking up the bones together.

failure.body: You ride into the square, and a flying censer hits your horse, and it bolts. You come off in the middle of the riot and are trampled by monks.

resolutions.label: bring the two abbots to a truce in the mud

success.body: You do not fight monks. You dismount in the middle of the riot, pick up both fallen reliquaries, one under each arm, and walk to where the two abbots are shouting at each other, and hand one to each. "Your saints," you say, "are lying in the mud together. Perhaps they want you to carry them together." The abbots look at the bones. The riot, round them, falters and stops. Both saints go home in the same cart.

failure.body: You pick up both reliquaries and walk to the abbots. Each one grabs the wrong reliquary. The riot starts again, worse.

entries.body: "Gareth," you say, "was the gentlest knight I ever knew. Would he have wanted this?" The grey-bearded knight's face twists.

resolutions.label: persuade the Orkney knights to lay down their vengeance

success.body: You talk to them of Gareth: his kitchen year, his pastry, his kindness to squires. You make them laugh, and then weep. You remind them that the High King is at Benwick already, and that more blood will only make the war longer and the realm weaker, with Mordred at home. At the end, the grey-bearded knight lays his sword down on the ground. "For Gareth," he says. "Not for Benwick. For Gareth." They ride home to Orkney. It is not the end of the war. It is the end of their part in it.

failure.body: You talk to them of Gareth, and his kindness, and the grey-bearded knight listens, and then says, "Yes. And they killed him." You have only made it worse.

resolutions.label: remind them of what the High King needs of Orkney

success.body: You do not speak of Gareth. You speak of Mordred, who holds the old king's crown, and the Saxons, who hold the east, and of what the old king's army will be without the men of Orkney. "Benwick is over the sea," you say. "Mordred is at Canterbury." The grey-bearded knight is silent a long time. Then he sheathes his sword. "Mordred first," he says. "Benwick after." They ride south to the old king's standard.

failure.body: You speak of Mordred and the Saxons. The grey-bearded knight spits. "Mordred is Orkney's son too," he says. You have said the wrong thing to the wrong men.

entries.body: "I do not play games with people," you say, and draw your sword. Guivret's face darkens. "Then you will play with my knights," he says, and the black pieces draw their swords.

resolutions.label: cut your way to the lord of the castle

success.body: The black knights are only painted people, frightened and unwilling, and most of them throw down their swords when you come at them. You reach Lord Guivret's chair and put your sword to his throat. "Release them," you say. He does. The travellers flee the castle, and so do you. When you look back from the edge of the wood, there is no castle, only a clearing with a chessboard of black and white flowers.

failure.body: The black knights are painted people, but they fight well. You are taken, and set on the board as a white pawn. You spend three days in the front rank before you are captured and released.

entries.body: "Heal me," you say. The eldest sister nods, and the nine of them lead you up through the orchard to a spring in a hollow, where the water is so clear it is almost invisible.

resolutions.label: submit to the healing of Avalon

notes: Lose all unwanted Status Cards

success.body: They lay you in the spring, and sing, and the water closes over you, and it is like being born. When you rise, every scar you have ever had is gone, and every sorrow is lighter, and you are hungry in a way you have not been since you were a child. The sisters feed you apples and send you back across the water, and you sleep the whole way.

notes: You may remove 1 unwanted Status Card

partial.body: They lay you in the spring, and sing, and the water is warm. When you rise, your wounds are healed, though not your sorrows. "Some things," says the eldest, "you must carry a little longer."

failure.body: They lay you in the spring, and the water is cold as winter, and you come up gasping. "It will not take you," says the eldest sister, sadly. "Not yet. There is too much you have not finished."

entries.body: "My lord," you say, "the man you seek is not in a cask of wine." Mark laughs, a short, ugly laugh. "You have not met him," he says.

resolutions.label: reason with the jealous king

success.body: You ask him what he will do when he finds the man. Mark opens his mouth and shuts it. You ask him what his queen will think of a king who stops wool carts at bridges. You ask him who will buy Cornish wool next year. By the end, he is staring at the slashed bales as if he has just woken. "Put it back," he mutters to his captain. "Pay them." He rides away without looking at you. The carters kiss your hands, and the weeping woman presses a length of fine blue cloth on you.

notes: Lose 1 Treasure, if possible

failure.body: You ask him what he will do when he finds the man. "Hang him from this bridge," Mark says at once, and smiles, and you realise he has thought of little else for years. When you try to argue, he decides you are too interested in the matter and has you searched as well. His soldiers take your purse "for the investigation". You ride on lighter and wiser.

resolutions.label: shame the king before his own soldiers

success.body: You get down from your horse, pick the priest's vestments out of the mud, and hold them up. "Is this what Cornwall's king makes war on?" you ask, loudly enough for every soldier to hear. The men look at their feet. The captain, a grey-bearded man named Andred, quietly orders them to repack the carts. Mark rages, but his men have stopped listening, and at last he rides off alone. Captain Andred thanks you under his breath. "I have wanted someone to do that for a year," he says.

failure.body: You get down from your horse, pick the priest's vestments out of the mud, and hold them up. "Is this what Cornwall's king makes war on?" Mark looks at you with pure hatred. "It is what Cornwall's king makes war on today," he says. "Tomorrow it may be you." His soldiers throw you into the river to cool your piety, and your horse bolts. By the time you have caught it, the search has moved on.

entries.body: "Tell her," you say. "It will be hard. The truth is always better than the lie found out." Piran stares at you. "She will hate me." "She may," you say. "She will not hate you for long."

resolutions.label: help Piran tell her the truth

success.body: The Lady Elidan arrives at the tavern the next morning, bright-eyed, and finds a squire with ink on his fingers kneeling before her. Piran tells her everything. For a long time she says nothing. Then she takes the sheaf of letters out of her sleeve, all of them, and holds them out. "Read me the first one," she says, "in your own voice." Sir Sagramore, when he hears, roars with laughter and gives Piran his blessing and a horse. "I never liked writing," he says.

failure.body: The Lady Elidan arrives the next morning and finds a squire kneeling before her. Piran begins to tell her everything, but he stammers and cannot find the words, and she grows angrier with every stammer. "You wrote so beautifully," she says, "and speak so badly." She leaves. Piran does not write another word for a year.

entries.body: You sit down with the shepherds and take a leg of mutton. The High King winks at you.

resolutions.label: join the shepherds' dancing and keep the secret

success.body: You dance with a shepherdess, and wrestle the smith, and lose, and sing songs you did not know you knew. The young king dances beside you, badly, and nobody guesses. At dawn, as you walk down the mountain together, he says, "Thank you. I wanted one night of being nobody." He gives you his shepherd's crook, which he carved himself. It is very crooked.

failure.body: You dance with a shepherdess, and wrestle the smith, and at some point, far too drunk, you raise your cup and toast *the king*, looking straight at him. The shepherds fall silent. The young king sighs. The feast is not the same after that.

entries.body: You look at the two young kings, and at their secret peace, and you think of the High King, who will want to know.

resolutions.label: carry word of the meeting to Camelot

success.body: You ride down the mountain and to Camelot in two days. The High King hears of the meeting, and smiles, and sends Merlin himself to bless it. The two young kings are furious at first, and then flattered. The peace is signed at Camelot, before the Round Table, and the High King is its guarantor, and all Wales knows it.

failure.body: You ride down the mountain to Camelot, but the young kings, finding you gone, assume the worst. When the High King's messenger arrives, the peace is broken, and they each blame the other for the leak.

resolutions.label: keep watch over the meeting from the crags

success.body: You say nothing about Camelot. You climb to the crags above the meadow and watch the pass, and at noon you see what the young kings have not: two dozen men from the northern king's own council creeping up the valley to break the meeting. You come down on them from above, shouting. They scatter. The young kings clasp hands at sunset. Both send you gifts at Michaelmas, and neither says why.

failure.body: You climb to the crags and watch the pass, and see nothing all day. At dusk, the young kings ride down the mountain in a fury. The meeting was broken by a quarrel about cattle.

entries.body: You look at the basket, and at the Munster men in the harbour, and you make up your mind. Orlaith sees it in your face. "Ah," she says, and her hand goes to her gutting-knife.

resolutions.label: seize the crown from the queen

success.body: You catch her wrist before the knife comes up and take the crown from the basket. She spits at you in Irish. The Munster sergeant pays you a bag of silver and a gold cup for the crown, and has Orlaith led away. You hear, later, that she escaped on the way to Munster and has sworn to have your ears. You keep them covered in Irish company.

failure.body: You reach for the crown, but her knife is quicker, and the gutting-knife opens your arm from wrist to elbow. By the time you have bound it, the queen has gone, and so has the basket. The Munster men laugh at you. "She did the same to our king," says the sergeant.

resolutions.label: switch the crown for a gilded basket-lid

success.body: You help her gut herring for an hour, and admire the crown, and when she turns to serve a customer, you swap it for a round lid from a creel, gilded with the paint from a tavern sign. You sell the crown to the Munster sergeant for a bag of silver and a gold cup. Orlaith sails for Ireland with a painted basket-lid under her fish. You do not want to be in Ireland when she finds out.

failure.body: You help her gut herring and admire the crown, and when she turns away you reach for it. She does not turn round. "My mother," she says, "was a fishwife. My grandmother too. We can hear a thief breathe." She has her knife at your wrist before you have lifted it.

entries.body: "Bring us alongside," you say. The captain curses, but he does it.

resolutions.label: drive off the pirates from the monks' ship

success.body: You leap onto the pirates' deck from behind, and they turn in surprise, and the monks take heart and come at them from the front. The pirates are caught between a knight and forty monks with oars. They surrender. The abbot of the monks blesses you, and asks what you would like as a reward. You ask for a prayer. He gives you three, and a small silver cross.

failure.body: You leap onto the pirates' deck, but you slip, and fall between the ships. You are pulled out by the monks, who are losing.

resolutions.label: rally the monks themselves against the pirates

success.body: You shout across to the monks: oars together, in a line, like pikes. They do it. You bring your ship alongside the pirates and leap aboard from behind, and the pirates, caught between a knight and forty monks presenting oars like a shield-wall, surrender. The abbot blesses you and asks what you would like as a reward. You ask for a prayer. He gives you three, and a small silver cross.

failure.body: You shout across to the monks to form a line with their oars. They do, very bravely, facing the wrong way. The pirates come at them from behind, and you leap aboard into the middle of it all, and it is a long, confused fight before the pirates take the monks' ship anyway.

entries.body:
As you walk your horse through the half-empty streets of London, now under Mordred's banner, you hear a knocking from beneath the cobbles: three knocks, a pause, three knocks. A woman selling turnips looks away quickly. When you kneel by a drain, a voice comes up through it. "For the love of God, who is there?"

"We are knights of the old king," the voice says. "Mordred's men brought us down here from the Tower. There are thirty of us in the caves under the city. They have left us no water for three days." A pause. "There is a way in through the crypt of Saint Martin's. There are guards."

responses.label: You may break into Mordred's cave-prison and free the captive knights.
You may find a way to get water and food to the prisoners.

entries.body:
You ride into London under a sky black with smoke. Mordred's banners hang from every tower but one: the great white Tower by the river, where the High King's own dragon still flies. The Tower is besieged. Mordred's men have siege engines in the streets.

A washerwoman pulls you into a doorway. "The queen is in there," she whispers. "When Mordred said he would marry her, she said she must go to London to buy her wedding clothes. Then she went into the Tower with every loyal man she could find and shut the gates. She has held it for a month." The washerwoman lowers her voice further. "She needs someone to carry word to the king across the sea. And the food is running out."

responses.label: You may fight your way into the Tower to help defend the queen.
You may slip a message out of London to carry to the king.

entries.body: You hold out your hand. The pedlar hesitates, then gives you the letter. The young man is still asleep.

resolutions.label: read the secret letter without waking its bearer

success.body: You ease the seal with a hot knife. The letter is from King Lot to a baron in the south, promising him land if he rises against Arthur at Michaelmas. You copy it by firelight onto a scrap of your own parchment, reseal it and slip it back into the satchel. In the morning, the young man rides away none the wiser. You ride to Camelot. The pedlar, it turns out, is one of Merlin's spies. She is very annoyed that you read it first.

failure.body: You ease the seal with a hot knife, and it cracks. The young man wakes at the sound and sees the letter in your hand. He draws his knife. In the struggle, the letter goes into the fire. The young man flees into the storm. The pedlar looks at the ashes. "Well," she says. "That was a waste."

resolutions.label: take the letter by force and bind the messenger

success.body: You wake the young man with your sword at his throat and tie his hands with his own belt. The letter is from King Lot to a baron in the south, promising land for a rising at Michaelmas. You take messenger and letter to Camelot through the storm. The High King reads it and gives you the messenger's horse. The pedlar, who is one of Merlin's spies, is very annoyed that you took all the credit.

failure.body: You wake the young man with your sword at his throat, and he is quicker than he looks. He rolls into the fire, throws the letter into it and is out of the door into the storm before you can stop him.

entries.body:
You ride into Carlisle as it burns. Mordred's men have taken half the town, and the old king's men hold the castle. In the streets between, among the fires, something is roaring. A lion runs past the end of the lane, and then another, a lioness, with blood on her jaws.

A boy in the red livery of the royal menagerie is hiding in a doorway. "The king's lions," he gasps. "The fighting smashed their cage. They are terrified. They are killing anything that moves. They were the old king's own lions. He fed them with his own hands." He looks up at you. "They will be shot. Unless someone can get them back into the stable."

responses.label: You may hunt down the frightened lions before they kill again.
You may try to calm the lions and lead them to safety.

entries.body:
You ride into Canterbury in the teeth of a gale on the night before Mordred's coronation. The cathedral is hung with his red and black banners, and his soldiers are on every street corner. But the Archbishop, a thin old man who crowned the old king forty years ago, has refused to crown the new one. He has been locked in his own palace.

A monk with a lantern finds you sheltering in a doorway. "They will make him crown Mordred tomorrow," he says, "or they will kill him and find a bishop who will." He shivers. "The storm will cover us tonight. The guards have gone inside. If someone could get him out, over the wall, to the river, there is a boat."

responses.label: You may rescue the Archbishop from his palace in the storm.
You may stay and disrupt Mordred's coronation.

entries.body:
You ride into the cathedral town of Worcester, which has been left without a garrison since the war began, and find the cathedral doors smashed in. A band of brigands, deserters from both armies, are carrying the cathedral's plate out to a line of carts. The townsfolk watch from their doorways, too frightened to move.

An old priest is kneeling in the cathedral porch, bleeding from the head. "The relics," he says, as you ride up. "They have taken the bones of Saint Oswald from the altar. They mean to sell the reliquary and throw away the bones." He grips your stirrup. "The silver does not matter. The saint does."

responses.label: You may attack the brigands and save the cathedral treasure.
You may follow the brigands and recover the saint's bones.

entries.body:
You are hiding in London, which Mordred holds, when a baker slips a note into your loaf. *The Bell and Anchor, midnight. Come alone.* At midnight, in the back room of the tavern, you find a dozen men and women: a goldsmith, two monks, a sergeant of the watch, a laundress. "Friends of the old king," the goldsmith says. "When his army comes to London, we mean to open the Ludgate for him." He looks at you. "We need a knight to lead us on the night. And we need to know you are not one of Mordred's."

If you have Story Token #12, turn immediately to [[1491]].

responses.label: You may lead the loyalists in opening the city gate.
You may betray the loyalists to Mordred's men.

entries.body:
You ride into the ruins of Silchester, a Roman town that Saxons burned a month ago. The walls still stand, but inside them, everything is ash. There is nobody. Then you hear, from a cellar under the old basilica, a sound like a child singing.

You find her in the dark: a girl of seven or eight, filthy, thin, sitting on a pile of sacks, singing to a rag doll. "Everyone went away," she says. "The men with axes came, and my mother put me down here and said wait. I have been waiting." She looks up at you. "Is she coming back?"

responses.label: You may search the burned town for the girl's mother.
You may take the girl to safety.

entries.body:
You ride into Winchester and find it under attack. Mordred's army has come to take it, and the townsfolk are defending their walls with whatever they have. The old king's garrison is a dozen men. The townsfolk are everyone else: bakers, tanners, monks, women with pots of boiling water.

An old woman with a pitchfork shouts at you from the wall. "Up here, knight! They are bringing a ram to the Westgate! If it breaks, they will burn the city!"

responses.label: You may join the townsfolk on the walls.
You may ride out and attack the ram from outside the walls.

entries.body:
You ride into London and find Mordred holding a great feast in the old king's hall, to celebrate his crowning. The guests are Mordred's lords, and three Saxon kings in gold torcs, and a great many wolfhounds. At the head of the table, Mordred sits in his father's chair, smiling, pouring wine for the Saxon kings with his own hand. There is an empty chair beside him. "For the queen," he says, "when she comes out of her tower."

You are in the hall disguised as a servant, with a jug of wine. You are close enough to Mordred's cup to touch it.

responses.label: You may learn what you can of Mordred's plans from the feast.
You may spoil the feast and shame Mordred before his guests.

entries.body:
As you ride through the forest in dim sunlight, with smoke drifting through the trees from a village burning somewhere to the east, you hear groaning behind a waterfall. You dismount and push through the curtain of water into a cave. It is full of wounded men.

There are twenty of them, lying on the bare rock in bloody bandages, and a single young woman going from one to the next with a bucket. "Saxons burned Cilgerran yesterday," she says. "These are the men who held the bridge so the women could get away. I brought them here." She wipes her forehead. "I have no more bandages, no more food, and the Saxons are searching the woods. If they find the waterfall, they will kill them all."

Outside, faintly, you hear a horn.

responses.label: You may lead the Saxons away from the waterfall.
You may help the woman tend the wounded and hide the cave.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dim sunlight, with the sound of a battle somewhere to the south, you come upon a castle of white stone, half fallen down. The gate hangs on one hinge. In the courtyard, the flagstones are black and white squares, cracked and overgrown with weeds, and on one of the white squares lies a wounded knight in the old king's colours, with a sword in his hand.

"Water," he croaks. "For the love of God." Then, as you kneel beside him, he grips your arm. "There are Mordred's men in the woods. I led them here, away from the king's baggage train. Five of them. They will come in a moment." He tries to get up and falls back. "I cannot fight again."

You hear voices at the gate.

responses.label: You may hold the gate against Mordred's men.
You may carry the wounded knight to safety.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dim sunlight, with the smoke of the war drifting between the trees, you find a great beast lying in a clearing. It has the head of a serpent, the body of a leopard, the haunches of a lion and the feet of a hart. It is very old, and very still, and an arrow is sticking out of its side.

If you have Story Token #2, turn immediately to [[1139]].

It lifts its serpent's head and looks at you. From its belly comes a faint sound, like one tired hound baying, far away. Across the clearing, a Saxon archer is nocking another arrow.

responses.label: You may drive off the Saxon archer and tend the wounded beast.
You may finish the Questing Beast yourself, and take its head.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dim sunlight, a storm breaks over the trees, cold and bitter. You find shelter in a woodcutter's hut, where a family is already huddled by the fire: a woman, three children, an old man. And in the corner, a young man in a Saxon's leather jerkin, with no weapons, shaking.

"He came in an hour ago," the woman whispers. "He says he has run away from the Saxon host. He says he was forced to fight. He does not want to fight any more." The old man has a knife in his hand. "He is a Saxon," he says. "They burned our village."

The young Saxon looks at you, and says something in his own tongue. You catch only one word, which is *please*.

responses.label: You may protect the Saxon deserter from the family's anger.
You may take the Saxon prisoner and deliver him to the old king's men.

entries.body: As you ride through a forest in dim sunlight, you come to a great oak with a clearing beneath it, where a band of outlaws is gathered round a fire. There are Saxon heads on spears at the edge of the clearing. The outlaws' leader is an old man with a knight's belt and a grey beard. "Sir Hervi de Rivel," he says. "We used to rob the Baron of Arden. The Saxons killed the Baron. So now we rob the Saxons." He grins, showing broken teeth. "A Saxon war-band is camped at the ford tomorrow night. Forty men. We are twenty. We need someone who knows how to fight a battle."

responses.label: You may lead Sir Hervi's outlaws against the Saxon war-band.
You may use the outlaws to spy on the Saxons for the old king.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest at midnight, you see a ring of torches under a hollow oak. Two men sit on a log, talking in low voices. One wears Mordred's red and black. The other is a tall, fair-haired Saxon, with a gold torc round his neck. Between them, on the log, is a map, and a bag of gold.

"Kent," the Saxon is saying, in heavy British. "And Sussex. And the Isle of Wight. Those are my king's terms." Mordred's man nods. "And your king will bring his fleet to the Medway at midsummer," he says, "and hold it against the old king's ships." They clasp hands over the map.

Neither has seen you.

responses.label: You may seize the map and the gold.
You may follow the Saxon envoy back to his fleet.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dim sunlight, you come upon a ruined temple in a clearing, and hear drums. A band of Saxons have made it a shrine to their own god, Woden. There is a great wooden idol in the middle of the broken columns, and before it, tied to a stake, are three British captives. A Saxon priest in a wolfskin is sharpening a knife.

"Midsummer," one of the captives calls to you, desperately. "They offer three to Woden at midsummer. It is midsummer tomorrow."

There are twenty Saxons. They are feasting, and drunk.

responses.label: You may attack the Saxon shrine and free the captives.
You may burn the Saxons' idol to break their courage.

entries.body:
You come upon an ambush in a forest: a supply train of the old king's army, twenty carts of bread and arrows, stopped on the road by a fallen tree, and Saxons swarming out of the trees on both sides. The carters are fighting with whips. The escort, six men, is already down.

A young carter, his face bloody, sees you. "The bread!" he shouts. "The army has not eaten in three days! If they take the carts, the king's men will starve!"

responses.label: You may fight off the Saxons and save the supply train.
You may clear the fallen tree so the carts can escape.

entries.body:
As you ride through a forest in dim sunlight, you come to a stone arch standing alone in a clearing. Through it, you see a feast, but it is a sad one. The fair folk are sitting at their golden tables in silence, with their heads bowed. The music is a lament.

A small man with pointed ears is standing by the arch. His face is wet. "The last feast," he says. "The fair folk are leaving Britain. When the old king falls, there will be no more room for us here. We are going west, over the sea, to the Summer Country." He looks at you. "We would like one mortal at our last feast. To remember us."

responses.label: You may join the fair folk's last feast.
You may ask the fair folk to stay and help the old king.

entries.body:
You come to a cave high on a mountainside, with a great iron door half-hidden by ferns and a bronze bell hanging from a chain beside it. The air is still and cold, and from behind the door comes a sound like many men breathing in their sleep.

A shepherd boy is sitting on a rock nearby. "The Sleepers," he says. "My grandfather told me. There are a thousand knights asleep in there, with their horses and their swords, and they will wake when the bell is rung and Britain has most need." He looks east, where the smoke of the war hangs over the valleys. "Britain has need now, does it not? The Saxons are everywhere." He looks at the bell. "My grandfather said never ring it. He said if it is rung too soon, they will wake, and see it is not time, and go back to sleep forever."

responses.label: You may ring the bell and wake the Sleepers.
You may go in quietly and look at the sleeping knights without waking them.

entries.body: You come upon a castle on a crag, flying a Saxon banner, with a line of heads on spears along its walls. Below it, in a valley, a village has been burned, and the survivors are sitting in the ashes. An old woman comes up to you. "They took our children," she says. "Twelve of them. They will sell them over the sea as slaves when the next ship comes." She points at the castle. "That is Cynric's hold. He is the son of the Saxon king. He has two hundred men."

responses.label: You may climb into the castle by night and free the children.
You may go to Cynric and bargain for the children's lives.

entries.body: You lower your visor and look only at the ground in front of your horse. You can see the beast's feet, and nothing else.

resolutions.label: slay the catoblepas without looking at it

success.body: You ride toward the sound of its breathing, with your eyes on the grass, until you see its feet. It grunts and begins to lift its enormous head. You drive your lance in under the heavy neck before the head can come up. It falls with a groan that shakes the plain. When you dare to look, its eyes are closed. The cowherd kisses your stirrup. The Earl sends you a cow.

failure.body: You ride toward the sound of its breathing with your eyes on the grass. The beast lifts its head. You feel its gaze on the top of your helmet like a cold hand, and everything goes dark. You wake an hour later behind the gorse bush, where the cowherd dragged you. You cannot see properly for a week.

resolutions.label: ward your sight with the old words and look it in the eye

success.body: You speak the old words for a gaze that cannot be taken, over your own eyes, three times. Then you ride up to the beast and wait. It lifts its enormous head, slowly, slowly, and looks at you, and you look back. Nothing happens. The catoblepas, astonished, looks away. You drive your lance in under its neck. The cowherd kisses your stirrup, and the Earl sends you a cow.

failure.body: You speak the words over your own eyes and ride up to it. It lifts its head and looks at you. The words do not hold. You wake behind the gorse bush, where the cowherd dragged you, and cannot see properly for a week.

entries.body: You step into the little room. On the table is a book, full of dates and times and places in Agravain's crabbed hand. Mordred pours you a cup of wine.

resolutions.label: win Mordred's confidence

success.body: You sit with them long into the night. You laugh at Mordred's jokes and nod at Agravain's lists, and you tell them one or two things you have seen, true things, small things. By dawn, Mordred has taken you by the hand. "A friend," he says. "I knew it. We will not forget you." He gives you a ring from his own finger. You go out into the grey morning and wonder what you have done.

failure.body: You sit with them long into the night, but Agravain watches you with his cold eyes the whole time, and when you leave, he whispers something to Mordred. From then on, you notice, Mordred greets you with great warmth, and you are never again told anything.

resolutions.label: let Mordred read in you whatever he wishes

success.body: You sit with them long into the night, and you do not pretend to be good. You tell Mordred of the things you have done that you would not tell a priest, and he listens with his warm grey eyes, delighted. "At last," he says, "someone honest." By dawn he has taken you by the hand, and given you a ring from his own finger. You walk out into the grey morning and wonder what you have done.

partial.body: You tell Mordred a few of your worse deeds. He nods politely. "Small sins," he says. "We all have those." He pours you more wine, and tells you nothing.

failure.body: You tell Mordred of your wicked deeds, and he laughs, very kindly. "Oh, friend," he says. "You are much too good for us." You are never told anything again.

entries.body:
You come upon a column of refugees struggling up a mountain pass in the rain: women, children, carts, goats. They are fleeing the fighting in the valleys. Halfway up, the column has stopped. On a rock above the pass crouches a wyvern, black and leathery, with a barbed tail, eating a goat.

"It came down this morning," says a woman carrying a baby. "It took two goats and a boy. It will not let us through. The Saxons are behind us." She looks back down the valley, where smoke is rising. "We cannot go back."

responses.label: You may drive the wyvern away from the pass.
You may lead the refugees over the mountain by another way.

entries.body:
You come upon a man lying in the snow on a mountain pass in a blizzard, half-frozen, with a leather satchel clutched to his chest. He wears the red and black of Mordred's household. When you turn him over, he opens his eyes. "Letters," he croaks. "For the Saxon kings. From King Mordred. Promising them Kent." His lips are blue. "I will die if you leave me."

The blizzard is thickening. You could carry him down, or you could take the satchel and leave him. Either way, you must move fast.

responses.label: You may carry Mordred's messenger down the mountain to safety.
You may take the letters and leave the messenger in the snow.

entries.body:
You come to a mountain pass in the north where a war-band of painted Picts, come down from beyond the Wall now that the old king's armies are away, has taken the road. They have a dozen captives roped together, a village's worth of young men and women, and they are driving them north.

A shepherd hiding in the heather beside you whispers, "They will sell them in the Orkneys as thralls." He points at the Picts' leader, a huge man with blue tattoos all over his face. "That is Drust. They say he has never lost a fight."

responses.label: You may challenge Drust to single combat for the captives.
You may follow the war-band and free the captives at night.

entries.body:
You come upon a camp on a mountainside at dusk, where a dozen knights in the black and gold of Orkney are gathered round a fire, swearing an oath on a sword. They are grim, hard men. Their leader, a grey-bearded knight, is speaking. "Gareth and Gaheris, unarmed, cut down at the stake," he says. "By Benwick's hand. We swear we will not rest until the house of Benwick is ash."

He sees you. "You," he says. "Were you there? At the burning? Whose side were you on?" The Orkney knights turn, their hands on their swords.

If you have Story Token #17, turn immediately to [[1089]].

responses.label: You may swear the Orkney oath of vengeance with them.
You may try to turn the Orkney knights from their vengeance.

entries.body:
You come upon the ruins of an old fort on a mountaintop, where a dozen of the old king's soldiers have taken refuge. They are ragged and wounded and starving. Their captain, a young knight with a bandaged head, is standing on the broken wall, looking down at the valley, where a Saxon war-band is camped. "They have been there a week," he says. "They know we are here. They are waiting for us to starve."

"There is a way down the back of the mountain," says an old soldier. "A goat-path. But the wounded cannot climb it."

responses.label: You may lead the fit men down the goat-path to fetch help.
You may stay and hold the fort with the wounded.

entries.body:
You come upon a battle in a mountain pass, where a small band of the old king's men is holding the pass against a Saxon host coming up from the valley. They are forty. The Saxons are four hundred. Their captain, an old knight you recognise as Sir Bedivere, is standing in the narrowest part of the pass with his back to a rock, holding a shield in his one good hand.

"The king's army is retreating through the valley behind us," he says. "If the Saxons get through this pass before nightfall, they will fall on the king's rear." He looks at you with tired, calm eyes. "We need to hold until dark. Another sword would help."

responses.label: You may stand with Sir Bedivere in the pass.
You may ride to the king's army and bring back help.

entries.body:
You climb to an old fort on the top of a mountain, where the last of the old king's garrison is holding a feast. There are forty of them, grey-bearded veterans, and they have killed the last of their cattle and broached the last barrel. Tomorrow, the Saxons will come up the mountain, and there are four hundred Saxons.

The old captain, a one-eyed knight called Sir Brian of the Isles, waves you to a seat. "A guest!" he cries. "Welcome to the last feast of the Garrison of Carn Fadryn. We have decided to eat everything tonight, so the Saxons get nothing." He hands you a cup. "Will you drink with us? Or will you ride down the other side of the mountain while you can? Nobody would blame you."

responses.label: You may drink and feast with the doomed garrison.
You may use the night to lead the garrison to safety.

entries.body:
You come upon a family hiding in a hollow on a wide plain, crouched beside a hole in the chalk that drops away into darkness. There are a dozen of them: old people, women, children. Behind you, on the horizon, smoke rises from a burning village.

"Saxons," says an old man. "They came at dawn. We ran. There are old caves under the plain, the dene-holes, where our grandfathers hid in the Pictish wars. We were going to go down. But the ladder is rotten." He looks up. "Riders."

A troop of Saxon horsemen is coming over the rise.

responses.label: You may hold off the Saxon riders while the family climbs down.
You may help the family down into the caves and hide with them.

entries.body:
You come upon a castle on a wide plain, besieged. Mordred's red and black banners fly over a camp of a thousand men around it, and the castle flies the dragon of the old king. You can hear the siege engines thudding.

A herald in Mordred's colours rides up to you. "Knight!" he calls. "King Mordred offers land and gold to any knight who will join his host. Or are you the old king's man?" He points at the castle. "They are starving in there. They will fall within the week. It is only a matter of which side you want to be on when they do."

responses.label: You may join Mordred's host besieging the castle.
You may slip into the castle to help its defenders.

entries.body:
You come upon a great horse running wild across a wide plain after a battle, among the dead. It is a black destrier in the old king's caparison, torn and bloody, and it is screaming and lashing out at anyone who comes near. A dozen soldiers from both sides stand in a ring round it, not daring to go closer.

"That is Llamrei," says an old groom. "The old king's own mare. She threw her rider in the charge. She will not let anybody near. The Saxons want to kill her before she kills someone. Mordred's men want to catch her and give her to Mordred." He looks at you pleadingly. "She has carried the king for twenty years."

responses.label: You may tame the old king's mare.
You may fight off the soldiers who want the mare for Mordred.

entries.body:
You come upon the old king's army camped on a wide plain on the night before a battle, as a great storm breaks over it. Lightning strikes the king's own tent-pole, and his banner falls in the mud. All through the camp, men are muttering. "An omen." "God is against us." "The king is old." Some of them are packing their bundles.

A grizzled captain comes up to you. "They will run in the night," he says, "half of them. I have seen it before. If someone does not put heart into them, there will be no army in the morning."

responses.label: You may raise the fallen banner and rally the frightened army.
You may go among the soldiers and tell them what omens really mean.

entries.body:
You come upon a burned farmhouse on a wide plain, where a band of deserters is dividing the loot: a dozen men in the scraps of both armies' colours, some red and black, some the old king's dragon. A woman sits in the ashes of the house, with two children. "They were our own soldiers," she says. "Both sides. They are the same now."

The deserters see you and stand up. Their leader, a scarred sergeant, grins. "No sides here, knight," he says. "The war is lost for everyone. Join us or ride on."

responses.label: You may fight the deserters and drive them away.
You may shame the deserters back to their duty.

entries.body:
You come upon a ring of standing stones on a wide plain in the west. Inside the ring, under a white flag, two heralds are meeting: one in the old king's colours and one in Mordred's. Between them, on a stone, is a parchment. They look up as you ride in.

"A parley," says the old king's herald. "Tomorrow, on the plain beyond. The king and Mordred will meet, each with fourteen men, to make terms. Every other man on both sides will stand back." He looks at you gravely. "The king has given one order: no man is to draw a sword while the parley is on, for any reason, or the armies will fall on each other." Mordred's herald nods. "The same order," he says, "from my king."

Both heralds are uneasy. "We need a witness," says the old king's herald, "who will carry the order to the troops, and see that it is obeyed."

responses.label: You may carry the order not to draw swords to the old king's army.
You may carry the order to Mordred's army.

entries.body:
You come upon a village on a wide plain that has been burned to the ground. The church is a shell. The houses are ashes. In the square, a handful of survivors are digging graves. "Mordred's men," says an old man, leaning on his spade. "Because the lord of the manor would not send his sons to the war. They burned the manor, and the church, and hanged the lord from his own gate."

A young woman is kneeling beside the burned church, pulling stones out of the rubble with her bare hands. "The priest," she says. "He is under here. I heard him yesterday. I have not heard him today."

responses.label: You may dig the priest out of the ruined church.
You may track the raiders who burned the village.

entries.body: You walk past the stone into the valley. The mist closes round you. You hear music, faint and sweet.

resolutions.label: walk through the valley with a true heart

success.body: You walk through the meadow among the dancers, and the music pulls at you, and you do not dance. On the far side of the valley, you find the way out, and as you step through it, the mist behind you tears like cloth, and all the dancers stop, and blink, and look round, and begin to walk out after you. Two hundred knights come out of the Valley of No Return that day. Morgan, on her rock, stops eating cherries. "Well," she says. "Someone was true." She does not sound entirely displeased.

partial.body: You walk through the meadow, and the music pulls at you, and you nearly dance, but you do not. You come out on the far side. The dancers do not follow.

failure.body: You walk into the meadow, and the music takes you, and you dance. You dance for a month, until a stranger walks through and breaks the spell.

entries.body:
You come to Salisbury Plain in May, where two armies face each other across the heather under a sky full of ravens. On one side, the dragon banner of the old king. On the other, the red and black of Mordred. Between them, a pavilion, where the old king and Mordred are meeting with fourteen men each, to make terms. Every man on both sides has been ordered not to draw his sword, for any reason.

If you have Story Token #12, turn immediately to [[1772]].

You are standing in the old king's front rank. It is very quiet. A lark is singing. Then, from the heather near the pavilion, an adder slides out and strikes a knight in the heel. The knight cries out and draws his sword to kill it. The sun catches the blade. Across the plain, ten thousand men see a sword drawn at the parley.

responses.label: You may charge with the old king's army.
You may run to the pavilion and try to stop the battle.
You may fight your way to Mordred and seek him out.

entries.body:
You come upon a wake on a wide plain after a battle: a hundred soldiers of the old king's army, sitting round fires among the graves of their comrades, drinking and telling stories of the dead. It is a strange feast, full of laughter and tears. An old sergeant sees you and waves you over. "Sit," he says. "Drink. Tell us about someone. Everybody tells about someone."

A young soldier sitting apart is not drinking. He is staring at a fresh grave. "My brother," the sergeant whispers. "He has not said a word since."

responses.label: You may tell the soldiers a tale of someone you have lost.
You may sit with the young soldier by his brother's grave.

entries.body:
You come to an island of firm ground in a wide bog, where a cave opens under a hump of rock. There are fresh hoofprints on the causeway, and the marks of something heavy being dragged. In the mouth of the cave, a man in the black and red of Mordred's household is sitting on an iron-bound chest, eating an apple.

He jumps up when he sees you. "Stand off!" he says. "This is the king's business." His voice is shaking. "The king's treasure. King Mordred's. He sent me to hide it until the war is won." He looks at you uneasily. "You are not from the old king, are you? Everyone says the old king is dead."

Through the cave mouth, you see three more chests, and a great deal of church plate.

responses.label: You may seize Mordred's treasure.
You may help the messenger hide the treasure for Mordred.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a bog at dusk, with the sound of distant fighting rolling across the marsh, you see a light shining across the water. It comes from a castle on stilts, crowded with people. There are women and children on every walkway, old men on the roofs, cattle on a raft below. Refugees.

A young priest with a sword at his belt meets you at the end of the causeway. "Father Idris," he says. "These are the people of four villages. The armies of the old king and Mordred are fighting over the high ground, and whichever wins will come through the marsh. Either side will take our food." He looks at you. "Some of the men want to go and fight for one side, so that side will protect us. I think we should hide. What do you think?"

responses.label: You may help the refugees hide from both armies in the marsh.
You may lead the refugees' men to join the old king's army.

entries.body: You look up at the fair lady on the tower. "I am sorry," you say. "I cannot love you, to save you or anyone." The ladies scream.

resolutions.label: hold to your vow as the ladies fall

notes: Lose all Ranks of Villainy

success.body: They jump. All twelve of them, in white, falling. You do not look away. And as they fall, they change: their white gowns turn black, their faces become the faces of demons, and they burst into smoke before they reach the ground, with a howl that shakes the tower. When the smoke clears, the courtyard is empty. The old hermit is on his knees, weeping. "You held," he says. "Sir Bors held, and you held." He blesses you with a relic of Benwick, a scrap of the Shield of Evalach, which once turned every blow.

partial.body: They jump, and as they fall, they turn to smoke and demons, and are gone. You held, but only just. Your hands are shaking.

failure.body: They jump, and you cry out and look away, and when you look back, the courtyard is empty, and you do not know what you saw. You do not sleep for many nights.

entries.body: "A third," you say, "and I look stern." Hob claps his hands. "You were born for commerce," he says.

resolutions.label: sell crossbows to both sides without being caught

success.body: For a month you ride with Hob, and look stern at Cardigan on Monday and at Pembroke on Thursday, and the crossbows sell and sell. Nobody notices. At the end of the month, Hob divides the money and gives you a third, and a crossbow of your own. "The war will end next spring," he says, "when they run out of salmon. Then I will go north. There is a very promising quarrel in Lothian." He tips his cap and drives away.

failure.body: For a week you ride with Hob, looking stern. Then, in Cardigan, you meet a knight whom you last met in Pembroke, buying crossbows. He looks at you, and at the cart, and turns it round. You and Hob leave town very quickly, without the cart.

resolutions.label: drive the cart between the two camps at speed

success.body: You take the reins yourself, and turn the cart so that its Cardigan side faces Cardigan and its Pembroke side faces Pembroke, and drive it between the two camps at a gallop, dealing from both sides at once. It is the best day's trade Hob has ever had. He divides the money fairly and gives you a crossbow of your own. "There is a very promising quarrel in Lothian," he says.

failure.body: You drive the cart between the two camps at a gallop, and take a corner too fast, and the cart overturns in the middle of the salmon weir, both signs showing. Both lords come to look. You and Hob leave on foot, quickly.

entries.body:
You come upon a marsh where the ravens are gathering. Hundreds of them. They sit on every dead tree and every tussock, black and silent, looking east, toward the war. In the middle of them stands a raven taller than a man, with eyes like red coals, and it turns its head and looks at you.

"Knight," it says, in a voice like tearing cloth. "I am the Raven of Owain. I and my kin will feed well this year. We are waiting for the great battle." Its beak opens in something like a smile. "I can tell you where and when it will be. For a price. Or you can go away and let us wait in peace."

responses.label: You may bargain with the great raven for its knowledge.
You may drive the ravens from the marsh.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a marsh in a storm at night, you see lanterns by the edge of a deep pool, and soldiers in Mordred's red and black. They are pushing bound men into the water, one at a time. The storm drowns their screams.

You count: ten soldiers, and a line of fifteen prisoners in the old king's colours, roped together, waiting their turn. The officer in charge is laughing. "The king said no prisoners," he says. "He did not say how."

responses.label: You may attack the soldiers and free the prisoners.
You may cut the prisoners loose in the dark and lead them away.

entries.body: As you pick your way through the fens during the war, you find a village of reed huts burning, and the fen-folk fleeing into the marsh. A band of Mordred's soldiers is rounding up the young men. "Conscripts," says an old woman, spitting. "They take the boys for Mordred's army. They will put them in the front rank, to die first." She looks at you. "My grandsons are there."

responses.label: You may attack the recruiting party and free the conscripts.
You may help the young men hide in the fens.

entries.body:
You come upon a fire on an island in a marsh at midnight, where a dozen soldiers in the old king's colours are sitting in a huddle, whispering. You hear the word *captain*. You hear the word *knife*. A young soldier stands up as you approach, his hand on his sword. "Who goes?"

When they see you are alone, they relax a little. Their spokesman, a scarred sergeant, speaks. "Our captain, Sir Grummore, has led us into three battles and lost them all. He hangs a man a day for cowardice. He will get us all killed. Tonight," he says, very quietly, "we are going to kill him, and go home." He looks at you. "Are you with us?"

responses.label: You may join the soldiers' mutiny against their captain.
You may talk the soldiers out of murder.

entries.body:
As you pick your way through a marsh during the war, you come upon a ruined fort on a causeway, held by a single old soldier in the old king's colours. He is sitting on the gate with a spear, and he has been there, he says, for a month. "I was told to hold the causeway until relieved," he says. "Nobody has relieved me."

Behind him, you hear horses. Mordred's men are coming down the causeway.

"There are thirty of them," he says calmly. "I have held it against ten before. Not thirty."

responses.label: You may stand with the old soldier to hold the causeway.
You may persuade the old soldier that his duty is done.

entries.body: You leap from your horse and throw yourself between them. "Hold!" you cry. "Take off your helms!"

resolutions.label: persuade the knights to unhelm

success.body: They are both too tired to argue. The knight in red lowers his sword, and they unlace their helms. They stare at each other. They are brothers: Sir Aglovale and Sir Dornar, sons of King Pellinore, who have not seen each other in two years. They fall on each other's necks and weep. "I nearly killed you," says one. "I nearly let you," says the other. They ride on together. The quest, they say, can wait a day.

failure.body: They are both too proud. "Stand aside," says the knight in red. You do not, and he strikes you with the flat of his sword, and you fall, and they fight on. When it is over, they unhelm, and they are brothers, and one of them is dead.

resolutions.label: strike both their swords down at once

success.body: You do not argue. As the red knight's sword comes down, you meet it with your own, and turn it, and with the same stroke knock the white knight's blade out of his hand. They stare at you. "Now," you say, "unlace your helms." They are too astonished to refuse. They are brothers: Sir Aglovale and Sir Dornar, sons of King Pellinore. They fall on each other's necks and weep.

failure.body: You meet the red knight's sword with your own, and the white knight, seeing a new enemy, strikes at you too. You spend a very bad quarter of an hour fighting both of them before they unhelm.

entries.body:
You come upon a battle in the Fens during the war, where the old king's men and Mordred's are fighting over a causeway, the only road across the marsh. Neither side can win. They have been fighting for three days, and the causeway is covered in dead. The fen-folk watch from their reed-boats, waiting to loot whoever loses.

A fen-man in a flat-bottomed boat paddles up beside you. "There is another way across," he says. "A way only we know. For a price, I will show it to one side or the other." He grins. "Whoever pays most."

responses.label: You may pay the fen-man to show the hidden way to the old king's men.
You may break the deadlock on the causeway by force.

entries.body:
You come upon a feast in a marsh-lord's hall during the war, where Mordred's allies are celebrating: a dozen lords of the marshes, drinking to Mordred's victory and dividing up the lands of those who fight for the old king. You are there as a guest, because the marsh-lord does not know which side you are on. He is a fat, jolly man with small eyes.

"Drink!" he cries. "To King Mordred! And to Salisbury Plain, where the old man will fall!" He looks at you over his cup. "You are drinking, friend? Or are you one of the old king's?"

responses.label: You may drink Mordred's health and learn the marsh-lords' plans.
You may refuse the toast and shame the marsh-lords.

entries.body:
As you ride along a cliff-top in the grey light of dawn, you see smoke rising from a sea-cave at the foot of the cliff, and the prow of a longship with a carved dragon's head just visible inside it. Saxons. You count their voices: twenty, perhaps more. They are singing and roasting sheep.

A girl comes running along the cliff-path toward you. "They landed last night," she gasps. "They hide in the cave by day and raid by night. They burned Porthgwarra. Tonight it will be us." She points down the coast, to a little fishing village. "Our men are all gone to the war."

responses.label: You may attack the Saxons in their sea-cave.
You may prepare the village to defend itself tonight.

entries.body:
As you sail along the coast of Kent in a fleet of fishing boats, you see the castle of Dover on its white cliff, with Mordred's banners on its towers. Behind you, the sea is full of ships: the old king's fleet, come back from over the sea. On the beach below the castle, Mordred's army is drawn up in its thousands.

The captain of your boat, a grizzled old fisherman, spits over the side. "They say the old king's nephew, the lord of Orkney, will lead the landing," he says. "They say Mordred's men will cut them to pieces in the surf." He looks at you. "We could land further up the coast. Or we could land here, now, with them."

responses.label: You may land with the first wave on Dover beach.
You may land further up the coast and take the castle from behind.

entries.body: Igraine is quiet for a long while. "My husband Gorlois was fighting Uther," she says at last. "He left me at Tintagel, which cannot be taken. And that night he came home. He came up the stair in his own armour and his own face, and he was very gentle, and he left before dawn." Her hands tighten on the case. "In the morning they told me that Gorlois had been killed at midnight in another castle ten miles away. I had been with Uther. Merlin had given him my husband's face." She looks at you with dry eyes. "I have been told that my son is a great king. I have been told that the price was fair. I have never been asked." She rides on beside you in silence to the next crossroads, and there she blesses you and turns toward Camelot.

As you stand on a beach looking out at the sea, with the old king's army embarking in boats behind you, a white horse comes up out of the waves and walks toward you across the sand. It is beautiful, with a mane of foam and eyes like the sea. It kneels in front of you.

An old fisherman grabs your arm. "Do not touch it," he says. "It is a kelpie. It will carry you into the sea and drown you." The horse looks at you. It speaks, in a voice like the tide. "I will carry you across to the king's camp faster than any boat. The war will not wait for boats."

responses.label: You may ride the kelpie across the sea.
You may bind the kelpie with a bridle and make it serve you.

entries.body:
You are at sea with the old king's fleet, sailing back to Britain from the war over the sea, when a storm scatters the ships. In the lightning, you see one of them, a big troop-ship, foundering on a reef, with men clinging to its rigging and the waves breaking over it.

Your own captain shakes his head. "We cannot go near the reef," he says. "We will go down with them." But from the troop-ship, you can hear men screaming.

responses.label: You may take your ship to the reef to save the drowning men.
You may take a small boat alone to the reef.

entries.body:
You are sailing along the east coast during the war when you see a Saxon longship beached in a cove, and on the beach, Saxon raiders dragging captives down to it: villagers, and among them, a nun in a grey habit, fighting and kicking. "Sister Wenna of Lindisfarne," your helmsman says. "They say she healed half the wounded in Northumbria. They will sell her in Frisia."

The Saxons are nearly finished loading. Their ship will sail on the next tide.

responses.label: You may attack the Saxon ship before it sails.
You may sink the Saxon longship where it lies.

entries.body:
You are sailing along the coast of Kent in the war when you see two ships meeting in the mouth of the Thames at dusk. One is a Saxon longship, dragon-prowed. The other flies Mordred's red and black. As you watch, a rowing boat crosses from Mordred's ship to the Saxon, carrying a man in a fine cloak and a heavy chest.

"Gold for the Saxon king," says your captain grimly. "Mordred is paying them to fight. If that chest reaches the Saxon king, he will bring another thousand men."

responses.label: You may intercept the rowing boat and take the gold.
You may follow the Saxon longship back to its fleet.

entries.body:
As you sail along the coast of Cornwall during the war, you see the ruins of Tintagel on its rock, where the old king was born. Smoke is rising from the ruins. Saxons. A war-band has landed there and is using the old castle as a base, raiding the villages on the coast.

A fisherman rowing beside you spits. "They want to take the old king's birthplace," he says, "and hold it, to shame him. And to have a harbour."

responses.label: You may lead the fishermen in an attack on Tintagel.
You may slip into Tintagel and burn the Saxons' ships.

entries.body: You look across the heather to the red and black, and to the figure at its heart. If Mordred falls, the battle ends.

resolutions.label: cut your way through the host to Mordred

success.body: You fight across the plain all day, toward Mordred, and at dusk, you reach him. He is on foot, exhausted, surrounded by the dead. He looks at you, and smiles. "Friend," he says. "Is it you, then?" You cross swords. He is very good. At the end, he is on his knees, and your sword is at his throat, and he laughs. "My father should do this," he says. Before you can answer, the old king is there, with his spear. You step aside. You will remember that you did, for the rest of your life.

failure.body: You fight across the plain toward Mordred, but the battle is too thick. At dusk, you are still a hundred yards from him when you see the old king's spear go through him, and his sword come down on the old king's head.

entries.body:
You are at sea with the old king's fleet off the mouth of the Medway, where Mordred's ships and the Saxon fleet have come out to stop the old king landing. It is the greatest sea battle Britain has ever seen: three hundred ships locked together in the estuary, fighting deck to deck.

Your ship is next to the old king's own. You see Mordred's flagship, its red and black sails, bearing down on the old king's ship to ram it.

responses.label: You may put your ship between the old king's and Mordred's flagship.
You may board Mordred's flagship before it can ram.

entries.body:
You are sailing along the coast when you come upon a great ship at anchor, hung with black, where a funeral feast is being held on deck for an old sea-king of the Orkneys, who lies on a bier of oak with his sword on his chest. His people are feasting round him, and drinking, and singing his deeds. In the morning, they will set the ship alight and send it out to sea.

His daughter, a tall grey-eyed woman, calls across to your ship. "Come aboard! My father would want every warrior at his last feast. He fought for the old king at Badon." She lowers her voice. "And I would ask a favour. My father's sword. He wanted it to go to the old king, not to the sea. But my brothers say it must burn with him."

responses.label: You may join the funeral feast and honour the old sea-king.
You may carry the old sea-king's sword to the old king.

entries.body: "You will not need a burr," you say, "if we can find the cup." Pebin snorts. "They will have hidden it."

resolutions.label: find the cup and prove the saddler's innocence

success.body: You go into the castle as a guest, and at supper you watch Sir Hugh's knights. One of them, a young man with a loud voice, drinks from a silver cup and keeps it by his hand all evening. You ask him, admiringly, where he got it. He tells you, drunkenly, that it was the one they said the dwarf stole, and wasn't that a fine joke. Sir Hugh's steward hears it too. In the morning, Pebin is released and paid for his saddle, twice over. The young knight goes to the stocks. Pebin makes him a very fine saddle afterwards, with no burr in it at all.

failure.body: You go into the castle as a guest and watch Sir Hugh's knights at supper, but you see no cup, and when you ask about it, the knights laugh and say the dwarf must have melted it. Pebin sits in the stocks for another three days.

resolutions.label: follow the knights and learn where the cup went

success.body: You wait by the castle gate at dusk until one of the laughing knights rides out alone, and follow him to a tavern in the next village, where he sells a silver cup to the landlord for two marks. You buy it back for three. The next morning, you set it on the table before Sir Hugh, and the landlord beside it. Pebin is out of the stocks by noon, and paid for his saddle twice over.

failure.body: You follow one of the knights at dusk, and he rides to a tavern, and drinks, and rides home. You have spent a night and learned only that he likes ale. Pebin sits in the stocks for three more days.

entries.body: You stand up in your stirrups and shout at the top of your voice.

resolutions.label: stop the riot with a righteous rebuke

success.body: "The Grail has left Camelot," you shout, "and you are fighting over bones!" The riot stops, a little at a time, as people hear you. You go on. You tell them what the Grail looked like, covered in white, passing down the hall. You tell them it did not choose between abbeys. By the end, there is silence in the square, and then an old monk from one side goes and helps an old monk from the other side up out of the mud. Both saints go home together, in the same cart.

failure.body: You stand up in your stirrups and shout. Nobody listens. A monk with a face like a turnip swings his stave at a rival and catches you across the head instead. When you come to, the riot is over, the bones are back in their boxes, and both abbots are blaming you.

entries.body: You pick up one of the swords. "Good people," you say, "this sword is made of tin." Master Pym glares at you. "It is made," he says, "of legend."

resolutions.label: prove the swords worthless

success.body: You take the sword by the hilt and bring it down on the edge of the stall. It bends double. The crowd gasps. You take another and bend it round your knee. The crowd begins to shout. Master Pym grabs his cashbox and runs, and the crowd runs after him, waving tin swords. The little boy holds his up to you. "Is mine real?" he asks. You tell him that it is as real as he makes it, which he seems to find satisfactory.

failure.body: You take one of the swords by the hilt and bring it down on the edge of the stall. It does not bend. It is, astonishingly, a perfectly good sword. The crowd laughs at you. Master Pym sells twelve more on the strength of it.

resolutions.label: trick Master Pym into drawing the "true" sword

success.body: You ask Master Pym, very loudly, to prove the sword is Excalibur by driving it into a stone and drawing it out again, as the king did. The crowd loves this idea. They find a stone. Master Pym hammers the sword into a crack and then cannot, for all his heaving, get it out again. "Then you are not the rightful king of Britain!" cries a woman in the crowd. "And neither is my husband," says another, "and he bought three!" Master Pym is last seen leaving town in a hurry, and the sword is still in the stone.

failure.body: You ask Master Pym to prove the sword is Excalibur by driving it into a stone and drawing it out again. He does, easily, because the stone is soft sandstone, and the crowd cheers. You buy a sword, just to save face.

entries.body: You wait until the carts have left, and follow them at a distance, keeping off the road.

resolutions.label: track the looters and steal back the relics

success.body: The brigands camp that night in a wood. When they are drunk on the cathedral's wine, you creep into the camp and find the reliquary, and take it, and slip away. In the morning, they find it gone, and blame each other, and fight. You bring Saint Oswald home to Worcester at noon. The old priest lays him on the altar again, and the whole town kneels.

failure.body: You follow the brigands into the hills, but they have a lookout, and he sees you. You are ambushed in a gully. You escape, but the relics do not.

resolutions.label: ride the carts down on the open road

success.body: You wait until the carts are strung out along the high road across the downs, where there is nowhere to hide, and ride down on them from the ridge at a gallop, shouting. The drivers jump down and run. You take the last cart, which has the saint's reliquary lashed to the tailboard, and turn it for home. At noon you bring Saint Oswald back to Worcester. The whole town kneels.

failure.body: You ride down on the carts from the ridge, and the drivers do not run. They have bows. You turn and gallop back up the ridge with arrows behind you.

entries.body: "Then let us find your players," you say. Dagonet brightens. "*A knight to guard a fool,*" he says, "*is an unusual rule.*" Sarum is two days away, and the players are rough men.

resolutions.label: win Dagonet a place among the players

success.body: The players at Sarum are suspicious of a court fool, but you persuade them to let Dagonet do one turn in the market square. He is wonderful. He juggles, and sings, and falls off a barrel, and makes a pig do a sum. The crowd throws so many pennies that the players take him on at once. As you leave, Dagonet catches your sleeve. "*If ever you are sad,*" he says, "*come find the fool you had.*" You hear, a month later, that the High King rode to Sarum himself to see the famous new fool, and brought him home.

failure.body: The players at Sarum are rough men, and they do not like a court fool. They laugh at Dagonet's riddles, and not kindly, and then they throw him in the river. You fish him out. He sits on the bank, dripping, jingling faintly. "*Home again,*" he says, "*home again.*"

resolutions.label: trick-ride in the players' show beside him

success.body: You offer the players a knight's turn as well as a fool's. In the market square at Sarum, you ride your horse round the square standing on the saddle while Dagonet juggles on your shoulders. It is a disaster, very nearly, several times, and the crowd adores it. The players take Dagonet on at once and try to take you too. A month later, the High King rides to Sarum himself to see the famous fool, and brings him home.

failure.body: You offer the players a knight's turn. In the market square, you stand on your saddle with Dagonet on your shoulders, and the horse sneezes. Dagonet lands in a fish-cart. The players do not take him on, and they do not take you either.

entries.body: "Where are the letters?" you ask. Brother Hugh leads you into his hut and lifts a floorboard. Beneath it are thirty years of letters, tied in bundles with river-weed.

resolutions.label: hide the letters from the bishop's men

success.body: You pack the letters into an empty barrel labelled *Pickled Herring* and roll it into the nunnery's cellar with the abbess's help, among forty other barrels of pickled herring. When the bishop comes, he searches both hut and nunnery from top to bottom, and finds nothing but herring. He leaves disappointed and faintly nauseated. The next Wednesday, you see a wooden bowl floating downstream with a letter in it, and on the far bank, among the apple trees, an old woman waving.

failure.body: You pack the letters into a barrel labelled *Pickled Herring* and roll it into the nunnery cellar. When the bishop comes, he is hungry, and asks for herring. They open the wrong barrel. Brother Hugh is sent to a monastery in the north. The abbess, you hear, weeps for a month.

resolutions.label: hide the letters among the abbey's beehives

success.body: You pack thirty years of letters into three old skeps and set them among the abbess's beehives, where the bees soon move in on top. When the bishop comes, he searches both hut and nunnery from top to bottom, and nobody searches a beehive. He leaves with a sting on his nose. The next Wednesday, you see a wooden bowl floating downstream with a letter in it.

failure.body: You pack the letters into old skeps among the beehives. The bees object. The whole nunnery hears the screaming, including the bishop, who comes to see what is the matter and finds you surrounded by bees and love letters.

entries.body: You draw your sword and ride into the ruined chapel. The brigands leap up from their dice.

resolutions.label: drive the brigands from the ruined chapel

success.body: You ride your horse straight up the nave, and the brigands scatter like pigeons. One of them grabs the casket and runs. You ride him down in the doorway. He drops it. You pick it up, and it is warm in your hand. You carry it back to the old monk, who opens it with trembling fingers: a splinter of dark wood, wrapped in silk. He weeps. The abbey rings its bells for three days when you bring it home.

failure.body: You ride your horse up the nave, but the chapel floor is broken, and your horse stumbles. The brigands are on you. You get out of the chapel, but not with the casket.

resolutions.label: shame the brigands out of the holy place

success.body: You walk into the ruined chapel, past the drinking brigands, straight up to the altar, and kneel, and begin to pray aloud before the painted cross. The dicing stops. Then, one by one, men who were baptised in chapels like this one begin to shuffle their feet. The oldest of them takes off his cap. "Take the box," he says hoarsely, "and go." You carry the Rood back to the old monk, who opens it with trembling fingers.

failure.body: You kneel at the altar and pray aloud. The brigands watch you for a while, then one of them tips his ale over your head. They go back to dicing. You leave without the box.

entries.body: You leave the battle and ride round the marsh to the monastery, where the false prophet is watching from the tower.

resolutions.label: unmask the false prophet before his followers

success.body: You climb the tower and find him: a thin, feverish man, who believes every word he says. You do not argue with him. You ask him to describe the Grail. He does, at length. When he has finished, you ask him why, if he has seen it, he is sending boys to die for it. He opens his mouth, and closes it. Then he goes to the window and tells his followers to put down their spears. They do. He weeps. You take him to a hermit who can help him.

failure.body: You climb the tower and find him, and try to reason with him, but he calls you a demon and his guards throw you down the stair.

resolutions.label: cut your way to the tower and take the prophet

success.body: You go in through the monastery's back gate, past two white-robed guards who are more used to singing than fighting, and up the tower stair. The prophet is at the window, preaching. You take him by the collar and walk him down the stair and out into the courtyard in plain view, and his followers see their prophet held by a stranger. The singing stops. They put down their spears.

failure.body: You go in through the back gate, and the white-robed guards are more used to fighting than you thought. You are thrown out of the gate.

entries.body: The old king's army surges forward, and you go with it, into the heather, toward the red and black.

resolutions.label: fight in the last battle for the old king

success.body: You fight all day. You do not remember most of it afterwards. You remember a Saxon axe, and a boy in Mordred's colours who could have been your son, and the ravens coming down. At dusk, there are almost none left standing. You see the old king, on foot, with a spear, and Mordred coming at him. You see them strike each other. You reach the old king as he falls, with Sir Bedivere and Sir Lucan, and you help carry him from the field to a chapel by the water. He looks at you, and knows you. "You stayed," he says.

failure.body: You fight all day, and at noon, a blow on your helm puts you down in the heather among the dead. When you wake, it is dark, and it is over, and the plain is silent except for the ravens and the looters. You never know how it ended until the others tell you.

entries.body: "They have lain here long enough," you say. The old lord looks at you, surprised. "You would bury them? All of them?"

resolutions.label: bury the thirty-two dead knights

success.body: You dig for three days in the castle orchard, and carry the knights out one by one, and lay each in his own grave. The old lord watches from his chair. On the third evening, when the last grave is filled, he gets up for the first time in years, walks into the orchard, and lies down on the grass beside the graves. In the morning, he is dead. You bury him too. The castle is gone when you ride away.

failure.body: You dig for three days in the castle orchard, but the ground is full of roots and stones, and by the end, you have buried eleven knights and cannot lift a spade. You leave the rest where they lie, and the old lord watching them.

resolutions.label: lay the dead to rest with the words for the dead

success.body: You do not dig. You walk among the thirty-two dead knights on their black and white squares and close each one's eyes, and speak over each the old words that send the dead where they should go. As you speak, each body crumbles into white dust on its square. When the last is gone, the old lord gets up from his chair for the first time in years, walks onto the empty board, and lies down on it. In the morning, he is dust too.

failure.body: You walk among the dead knights and speak the old words, and one of them sits up. You do not finish. You leave the castle very fast.

entries.body: You walk down the lane to the reeve. "Your children are sick," you say. "It is time to put this right." The reeve scowls. "He is an old fool," he says. "There was silver."

resolutions.label: persuade the reeve and villagers to rebuild the chapel

success.body: You talk to the villagers, and they talk to each other, and slowly it comes out: there was no silver. The reeve's own debts were the reason. The villagers turn on him, and then they turn to the ruins. They rebuild the chapel in a fortnight, stone by stone, working all day. On the last day, the reeve is made to kneel in it. Brother Cynan comes to the door, looks at the reeve for a long time, and lifts his hand in blessing. That night, the wells run clear.

failure.body: You talk to the villagers, but the reeve is a powerful man in that village, and nobody dares speak against him. The children go on coughing. You ride on, and the black water stays black.

resolutions.label: rebuild the chapel with your own hands

success.body: You do not argue. You roll up your sleeves, find a trowel, and start laying stones. By the end of the first day, three villagers have come to help you, out of shame. By the end of the week, the whole village is there. The reeve holds out for ten days, and then even he comes, and carries stones, and at the end, he kneels in the rebuilt chapel without being asked. Brother Cynan lifts his curse. He lifts it, he says, for you.

failure.body: You roll up your sleeves and start laying stones. Nobody comes to help you. At the end of a week, you have built a wall knee-high, and the villagers are laughing at you from the lane. You ride on with blistered hands.

entries.body:
