You come across the still water in a boat that no one rows, to an island where it is always the end of summer. Apple trees heavy with fruit grow down to the shore. The air smells of honey and woodsmoke. On the beach, nine women in grey are waiting for you, each with an apple in her hand. The eldest steps forward. Her hair is white and her face is young.

"This is Avalon," she says. "We are the nine sisters who keep it. We heal the wounds that cannot be healed, and we make the things that cannot be made anywhere else. The young king's sword was quenched in our spring." She holds out her apple. "Every mortal who comes here may ask us one thing. Choose well. We do not give twice."

Behind her, on a slipway among the trees, you see a ship being built of white wood, so light and fine it seems to float on the air.

responses.label: You may ask the nine sisters to heal you of all your hurts.
You may ask the nine sisters for a gift from their workshops.
* You may ask the youngest of the nine sisters to walk with you in the orchard.

entries.body:
You come to Benwick across the sea, in the Golden Age, and find its white walls besieged. King Claudas of the Desert Land has come with ten thousand men to take the castle from old King Ban, who has ruled here for forty years. On the walls, King Ban's banner is still flying, but you can see smoke inside.

At the gate of the besiegers' camp, a herald of Claudas stops you. "Knight of the young British king?" he asks. "King Claudas offers you land in Benwick, when it falls, if you will stand aside. He knows your king is King Ban's ally. But he does not think your king will come across the sea for an old man."

From the walls, far off, you hear a horn: King Ban's horn, calling for help.

responses.label: You may fight your way into besieged Benwick to aid King Ban.
You may go to King Claudas and try to make peace.
You may accept King Claudas's offer and stand aside.

entries.body:
You come across the sea to the island of Lewis at midsummer, to the great stones of Callanish, which stand in a cross on a hill above a grey loch. At dawn, as the sun rises over the hills, a figure walks down the long avenue of stones toward the centre of the circle: a tall man in a cloak of feathers, shining.

The islanders are gathered at the edge of the circle, silent. An old woman whispers to you. "The Shining One. He walks the avenue every midsummer dawn. Whoever stands in the centre of the circle when he arrives is given a gift. But whoever stands there with a lie in them is turned to stone." She points at the stones. "Those were all liars, once."

responses.label: You may stand in the centre of the circle to meet the Shining One.
You may ask the islanders to teach you the songs of the stones.

entries.body:
You come to Camelot on the day the Round Table arrives from Cameliard, the wedding gift of King Leodegrance. It fills the great hall: a circle of oak so big that a hundred and fifty knights can sit at it, and no seat is higher than any other. Merlin is walking round it with his staff, touching each seat, and as he touches them, names appear on their backs in letters of gold.

The whole court is crowded round, watching for their names. The young king stands at one side with his bride. Merlin stops at a seat, and touches it, and your name appears. The hall goes quiet.

If you have Story Token #1, turn immediately to [[2572]].

Merlin looks at you. "Sit," he says. "Or do not. It is the same to the table." Across the circle, one seat has no name, and it is draped in black.

responses.label: You may take your seat at the Round Table.
You may ask Merlin about the seat draped in black.
You may sit in the black seat, the Siege Perilous.

entries.body:
You come to Corbenic, the castle of King Pellam, on the night of a great feast. The hall is hung with gold, and the king sits at the high table, old and stately, with a bleeding spear hung on the wall behind him in a silver bracket. Beside you at the lower table sits a haggard knight with two swords at his belt. You know him: Sir Balin, whom they call the Knight of Two Swords.

If you have Story Token #19, turn immediately to [[1683]].

If you have Story Token #15, turn immediately to [[1377]].

As the meat is served, a knight you cannot see strikes Balin across the face, and laughs. "Garlon," Balin hisses. "The king's brother. He rides invisible. He has killed two men I swore to protect." His hand is on his sword. "I will kill him here, at his own brother's table."

responses.label: You may restrain Sir Balin before he draws.
You may challenge the invisible knight yourself, by the old law of hospitality.

entries.body:
You come to Morgan's castle, a tower of white marble on an island in a lake, where the swans are black and the water is warm. The gate opens before you knock. In the hall, Morgan le Fay sits on a silver throne, with four knights kneeling in chains before her. She is laughing.

"Little knight!" she cries. "Welcome. These are four of my brother's best. I have told them they may go free if one of them will be my lover. None of them will." She pouts. "They are very dull."

If you have Story Token #13, turn immediately to [[2724]].

The four knights look at you with desperate eyes.

responses.label: You may challenge Morgan to free the four knights.
* You may offer Morgan your company in place of the captives.

entries.body:
You come across the cold sea to Orkney, to King Lot's hall of grey stone on a green island full of sheep and wind. The hall is loud with feasting. King Lot sits at the high table with his queen Morgause, laughing, and round them play their young sons, wild red-haired boys, wrestling on the rushes.

If you have Story Token #1, turn immediately to [[2632]].

King Lot looks at you with his grey wolf's eyes. "A knight of the beardless boy," he says. "Come to spy on me? Or to fight me?" Queen Morgause laughs and pats the bench beside her. "Or to dine," she says. "Sit, knight. My husband's bark is worse than his bite." Lot does not look as though his bite is very gentle either.

responses.label: You may try to persuade King Lot to make peace with the young High King.
You may accept King Lot's challenge to wrestle his champion.
* You may sit with Queen Morgause and court her favour.

entries.body:
You come to the great stones on Salisbury Plain at sunset in the Golden Age, and find Merlin sitting on the altar stone, eating an apple, with a harp across his knees. The stones glow faintly in the dusk, as though they had been warmed all day.

"Ah," he says. "You. I thought you would come." He plays a single note on the harp. The stones answer it, humming. "I brought these from Ireland," he says, "for Uther's grave, and his brother Aurelius's, and every British lord the Saxons murdered at the peace-feast. The stones sing, if you know how to play them." He holds out the harp. "Would you like to try? Or would you rather I told you your future? I have been told I am quite good at that."

responses.label: You may try to play the stones with Merlin's harp.
You may ask Merlin to tell you your future.

entries.body:
You come across the Irish Sea to the Abbey of Kells, a ring of round huts and a stone church inside an earth bank, where monks sit in the sunshine copying books. In the church, the abbot is standing between two furious men: a thin, fierce young monk clutching a book to his chest, and an old abbot from another house, red in the face, with a crowd of his own monks behind him.

"He borrowed my psalter," the old abbot is shouting, "and copied it by night, without asking! The copy is mine!" "The words are God's," the young monk shouts back, "and God does not ask permission!" The King of Meath has been sent for to judge between them, and he has just given his judgement: *To every cow belongs its calf. To every book belongs its copy.* The young monk's kinsmen, you are told, are gathering their spears. "There will be a war," the abbot of Kells whispers to you, "over a book."

responses.label: You may plead before the King of Meath for a better judgement.
You may help the young monk hide his copy and keep the peace.

entries.body:
You come to a cave in a hillside in Wales, whose mouth is hidden by a hawthorn tree, and when you push through the hawthorn, you find yourself in a hall of books. Shelves climb into the dark above you, crammed with scrolls and books and jars and bones and stuffed birds. In the middle, at a table covered in maps, sits Merlin, writing, with an owl on his shoulder.

If you have Story Token #3, turn immediately to [[1663]].

"You found it," he says, without looking up. "Clever. Or lucky. It is always hard to tell the difference." He puts down his pen. "Since you are here, you may make yourself useful. There is a book on the top shelf, at the very back, that I need, and my knees are old. Or you may sit down and ask me a question. I will answer one, truthfully. Most people regret it."

responses.label: You may climb to the top shelf to fetch Merlin's book.
You may sit down and ask Merlin a question.

entries.body:
You come through a wild wood in the north on a winter morning to a green mound beside a rushing stream, with a door in its side, overgrown with moss. From inside, you hear the sound of a great axe being ground on a whetstone. A voice calls out, deep and courteous. "Who is there? Come in, if you have business with me."

If you have Story Token #14, turn immediately to [[1625]].

It is the Green Knight. He comes out of the mound with his axe on his shoulder, and his green face breaks into a smile. "A guest!" he says. "I have a castle nearby, and a wife, and a very good cook. Stay three days. Each day, I will go hunting, and you will stay at home, and in the evening, we will exchange whatever we have won. A game." His eyes glint. "My wife will keep you company."

responses.label: You may accept the Green Knight's game of exchanges.
* You may accept the company of the Green Knight's lady.

entries.body:
You come to the shore of a great lake at dawn, and a lady in white samite rises out of the water and walks toward you across it, as if it were a floor. She takes your hand, and leads you down into the lake, and you find you can breathe. Beneath the water, there is a palace of white stone and green glass, full of light, where ladies in white move silently among gardens of waterweed.

If you have Story Token #16, turn immediately to [[1672]].

"You are welcome in my house," says the Lady of the Lake. "I gave the young king his sword. It was forged here, in our furnace under the water, which burns with a cold fire." She smiles. "You may see it, if you like. Or you may stay and dine with us. We do not often have guests who breathe air."

responses.label: You may ask to see the forge where Excalibur was made.
You may dine in the Lady of the Lake's palace.

entries.body:
You come across the still water in the Grail year, and find Avalon changed. The apple trees are bare, as if it were winter. The nine sisters are gone. In their place, on the shore, a monk in a white habit is digging in the frozen ground beside an old stone cross.

"The sisters have gone west," he says, without looking up. "When the vessel left the land, they went after it. They left me to keep the island." He leans on his spade. "I am digging for Joseph. The old men say he is buried here, with two cruets of the Lord's blood and sweat. If I find him, perhaps the vessel will come back." He looks up at you. "Or perhaps it will not. Would you dig, or would you pray? I have been doing both, and neither is working."

On the hill above, a single thorn tree is in flower, though everything else is bare.

responses.label: You may help the monk dig for the grave of Joseph of Arimathea.
You may climb the hill and pray beneath the flowering thorn.

entries.body:
You come to Benwick across the sea in the Grail year, and find the white castle quiet. Its young lords are away on the quest. In the courtyard, a tall white tower stands, and on its top, twelve ladies in white are standing at the very edge, looking down at you.

"Knight!" calls the fairest of them. "I love you. I have loved you since I saw you ride in. If you will not love me in return, I will throw myself from this tower, and all my ladies with me, and our deaths will be on your soul." The other ladies weep and wring their hands. They lean further out.

An old hermit is sitting at the foot of the tower. "It happened to Sir Bors," he says quietly, "on this very spot. He would not break his vow. They jumped." He looks up at the ladies. "They are not what they seem. But I cannot prove it."

responses.label: You may refuse the lady's love and let them do as they will.
You may pray for a sign that will show the ladies' true nature.
* You may climb the tower and accept the lady's love to save their lives.

entries.body:
You come across the sea to Callanish in the Grail year, and find the stones white with frost in midsummer. The loch is frozen. An old hermit lives in a hut at the foot of the avenue, and he is waiting for you at his door.

"I have been counting," he says. "The stones are a calendar. They tell the turnings of the sun and moon. And they tell the turnings of the Grail." He shows you a slate covered in scratched marks. "It comes to Britain every five hundred years. It came with Joseph. It came to Camelot. It is going now, and I know when it will come back." He looks at you. "But the frost has come early. Something is wrong with the stones. They are not singing."

responses.label: You may help the hermit find what has silenced the stones.
You may ask the hermit when the Grail will return.

entries.body:
You come to Camelot in the Grail year and find it half empty. The great hall is silent. The Round Table stands with more empty seats than full ones. The High King sits alone at it, in his own seat, with a cup of wine going warm in his hand. Queen Guinevere is in her solar. Mordred and Agravain are playing chess in a corner, watching.

The High King looks up when you come in. "Another come to say goodbye?" he asks. "Or have you come back?" He sighs. "They go out to find the Grail, and half of them never come back, and the other half come back so holy they cannot bear to look at me." He gestures at the empty seats. "Sit, if you like. There is plenty of room."

responses.label: You may sit with the High King and keep him company.
You may ride out from Camelot on the quest of the Grail.
You may challenge Mordred and Agravain about their game.

entries.body:
You come to Corbenic in the Grail year, across a land that has turned to dust. The castle stands on a rock above a dry river. Its gate is open. In the hall, an old king lies on a litter by the fire, with a wound in his thighs that bleeds and bleeds and never stops. He greets you with great courtesy and bids you sit.

If you have Story Token #15, turn immediately to [[2172]].

As you eat, a procession passes through the hall. A squire carrying a spear with a drop of blood running down its point. Two squires with golden candlesticks. And a maiden carrying something covered in white samite, so bright that the candles go pale. It passes you, and goes out of the far door, and nobody speaks. The old king watches you, waiting. Everyone is waiting.

responses.label: You may keep a courteous silence as the procession passes.
You may ask the old king about the bleeding spear.
You may kneel and pray as the covered vessel passes.

entries.body:
You come to Morgan's country in the Grail year, and find it has become a valley ringed with mist. At its entrance, a stone says: *The Valley of No Return. Whoever has been false in love shall not leave.* Inside the valley, through the mist, you see knights dancing in a meadow, round and round, with blank faces. Some of them have been dancing for years.

Morgan sits on a rock at the valley's mouth, eating cherries. "My brother's knights," she says, "have been so busy with their holy quest that they have forgotten their ladies. So I made this for them." She spits out a stone. "You may go in, if you like. If you have always been true, you may walk out again. If not…" She shrugs.

If you have Story Token #13, turn immediately to [[2644]].

responses.label: You may walk into the Valley of No Return.
You may try to break Morgan's enchantment on the valley.

entries.body:
You come across the cold sea to Orkney in the Grail year, and find the grey hall in uproar. Queen Morgause is dead. She was found in her bed at dawn with her throat cut, and Sir Lamorak, who was with her, fled naked through the window. Her son Sir Gaheris is sitting on the steps of the hall with a bloody sword across his knees, staring at nothing.

If you have Story Token #17, turn immediately to [[1523]].

"She shamed us," Gaheris says, when he sees you. "She shamed us all. I meant to kill him. I killed her." His voice is empty. "My brothers will come. They will kill Lamorak. And then, perhaps, they will kill me." He looks up at you. "What would you do?"

responses.label: You may take Gaheris to answer for his mother's death before the High King.
You may help Sir Lamorak escape from Orkney before the brothers come.

entries.body:
You come to the great stones on Salisbury Plain in the Grail year, and find a crowd of pilgrims camped among them. In the middle of the circle, the altar stone has cracked in two, and from the crack, a light is coming up, pale and steady.

"It cracked on Pentecost," an old pilgrim tells you, "the moment the vessel passed through Camelot. The light has come up out of it ever since." She looks at you. "They say that under the altar stone is buried Aurelius, Uther's brother, the first king to fight the Saxons. They say the light is his soul, waiting for the vessel to pass this way." She lowers her voice. "Some of the young men want to lift the stone and see."

responses.label: You may lift the altar stone and look beneath it.
You may keep the pilgrims from disturbing the king's grave.

entries.body:
You come across the Irish Sea to the Abbey of Kells in the Grail year, and find the monks gathered round a great book open on the altar of the church. They are silent. On the page, in the middle of a picture of the Last Supper, the painted cup on the table is glowing, and the ink around it is moving, slowly, like water.

"It began at Pentecost," the abbot whispers. "When the vessel appeared in your king's hall. The page has been changing ever since. We think it is telling us where the vessel has gone." He looks at you. "None of us can read it. It is not in any language we know. Perhaps a knight of the quest can."

That night, you hear, a thief has been seen near the abbey: a man who deals in relics, who would sell a page like this for a king's ransom.

responses.label: You may keep vigil before the glowing page and try to read it.
You may guard the book from the relic-thief.

entries.body:
You come to a cave in a hillside in Wales, hidden by a hawthorn tree, and find it sealed. Where the mouth of the cave was, there is solid rock, smooth as glass. Pressed into the rock, as if into wax, is the shape of an old man's hand. As you stand there, a voice comes out of the stone, faint and muffled.

"Is someone there? It is Merlin. Nimue has shut me in. I taught her the spell myself." The voice sighs. "I knew she would. I knew the day and the hour. It does not help, knowing."

If you have Story Token #3, turn immediately to [[2822]].

"I cannot get out," the voice goes on. "Nothing can open this stone but the one who closed it. But I can still see. I can see the vessel, and the knights chasing it. Would you like to know what I see? Or you could try to open the stone. People have tried. It is quite entertaining."

responses.label: You may try to break the stone and free Merlin.
You may listen to what Merlin sees from inside the stone.

entries.body:
You come through a wild wood in the north in the Grail year to a green mound by a rushing stream, and find it overgrown with holly, so thick that the door is hidden. Holly berries lie on the snow like drops of blood. Out of the holly, the Green Knight steps, with no axe, only a sprig of holly in his hand.

If you have Story Token #14, turn immediately to [[1063]].

"Knights of the quest," he says. "Every week, one of them comes through my wood, looking for the vessel. I ask each of them one question. None of them has answered it." He looks at you, gravely. "What will you give up, to find it?"

responses.label: You may answer the Green Knight's question honestly.
You may offer the Green Knight a game instead of an answer.

entries.body:
You come to the shore of a great lake in the Grail year, and the Lady of the Lake rises out of the water to meet you, and she is weeping. She takes you down into her palace under the water. In its great hall lie a hundred knights, on biers of white stone, as if asleep.

If you have Story Token #16, turn immediately to [[2889]].

"Knights of the quest," she says. "Drowned in rivers and lakes, crossing water in their hurry. The water brings them to me." She looks at them. "I can send one back. Only one. Whichever you choose. Or you may take something from my treasury instead, for yourself. I will not blame you."

You walk along the rows. You know some of the faces.

responses.label: You may choose one drowned knight to return to life.
You may take a treasure from the Lady's treasury.

entries.body:
You come to the edge of a great lake at dawn, after the last battle, with the mist lying on the water. On the shore, among the reeds, the old king lies on a cloak, grey-faced, with his crown beside him and a great wound in his head. Sir Bedivere is kneeling beside him, weeping. Sir Lucan lies dead a little way off.

If you have Story Token #16, turn immediately to [[1549]].

Out on the water, a black barge is coming toward the shore through the mist, with no oars and no sail. In it sit three queens in black, with their faces veiled.

The old king opens his eyes and sees you. "Take my sword," he whispers. "Excalibur. Throw it into the water. Do not keep it." Sir Bedivere is holding the sword. He looks at it, and at you, and you can see that he cannot bear to throw it.

responses.label: You may take Excalibur and throw it into the lake.
You may carry the old king down to the black barge.
You may keep Excalibur for yourself.

entries.body:
You come to Benwick across the sea in the last years, and find the old British king's army camped round its white walls. Arthur is besieging the castle where the queen's champion and his kin have taken refuge since the burning. It is a bitter, joyless siege. Every morning, a great knight of Orkney rides up to the gate and calls out for the queen's champion to come and fight him, for the deaths of his brothers. Every morning, the champion comes, and every morning, he wounds the Orkney knight and will not kill him.

The old king sits in his pavilion, grey and tired. "I do not want this war," he says to you. "My nephew of Orkney wants it. The house of Benwick does not. And Mordred is at home, with my crown." He looks at you. "Tell me what to do."

responses.label: You may fight in the siege for the old king.
You may carry a secret offer of peace into Benwick.
You may urge the old king to go home and deal with Mordred.

entries.body:
You come across the sea to Callanish in the last years, and find the stones surrounded by people: islanders, and old priests in white, and refugees who have fled the war on the mainland in fishing boats. They have come to the stones, they say, because the stones are singing, all day and all night, a long low note like a lament.

The eldest of the old priests, a woman with a face like bark, takes your hand. "The stones sing for the passing of kings," she says. "They sang for Uther. They sang for Vortigern. Now they sing for Arthur." She looks south, toward Britain. "It is not over yet. The stones can hold the moment a little longer, if enough people sing with them. But they cannot hold it forever."

responses.label: You may sing with the stones to hold back the old king's fate.
You may take the refugees' boats back to Britain to fight for the old king.

entries.body:
You come to Camelot on a grey morning in the last years, and find the whole city gathered in the meadow outside the walls, where a stake has been driven into the ground and faggots piled round it. Queen Guinevere stands chained to it, in a white shift, very pale and very straight. The High King sits on a horse, facing away. He cannot watch.

Round the stake stand the knights of the king's guard. Among them, in plain clothes, unarmed, because they refused to bear arms against the house of Benwick, stand Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris. The executioner is lighting his torch.

If you have Story Token #12, turn immediately to [[1277]].

If you have Story Token #7, turn immediately to [[1295]].

In the distance, from the woods, you hear horses: many horses, coming fast.

responses.label: You may stand guard at the stake for the king's law.
You may help the rescue and free the queen.

entries.body:
You come to Corbenic in the last years, across a land that is green again. The castle stands above a river full of water. Its gate is open. There are no guards. In the hall, an old king lies in a bed by the fire, very old and very peaceful, with no wound. It is Pellam. His people are gathered round his bed.

"The vessel has gone," he says, when he sees you. "It went over the sea to Sarras, with the knight who found it. My land is healed. My wound is healed. And now I may die, which I have wanted for a long time." He smiles at you. "But the spear is still here." He points at the wall, where a spear hangs, clean and bright, no longer bleeding. "The High King is going to his last battle. He will need it. Or perhaps he will not. I cannot decide."

responses.label: You may keep the deathwatch with King Pellam.
You may ask King Pellam for the spear to carry to the High King.

entries.body:
You come to Morgan's castle in the last years, and find it hung with black. On the shore of the lake, a black barge is being made ready, with black sails and no oars. Morgan le Fay is standing on the shore, directing her women, and she is weeping.

"He is going to die," she says, when she sees you. "My brother. On the plain, in a week. I have seen it in every water in this castle." She wipes her eyes, fiercely. "I have hated him all my life. I have tried to kill him four times. And now I am going to carry him to Avalon, and heal him if I can, and I do not know why." She looks at you. "You have come to ask what I am doing. Well. I am doing this."

If you have Story Token #13, turn immediately to [[2868]].

responses.label: You may help Morgan make the barge ready.
You may warn Morgan that you do not trust her with the king.

entries.body:
You come across the cold sea to Orkney in the last years, and find the grey hall hung with black. There is nobody at the high table. In the hall, an old woman is sitting by the fire, spinning, alone. She was the nurse of Queen Morgause's sons, when they were boys.

If you have Story Token #17, turn immediately to [[1911]].

If you have Story Token #7, turn immediately to [[2872]].

"All gone," she says, when she sees you. "Agravain killed in the queen's chamber. Gaheris and Gareth killed at the burning, with no swords in their hands. My eldest boy at Benwick, fighting, and they say he will not come home." She stops spinning. "Four boys I raised. Wild red-haired things." She looks at you. "Tell me something about them. Anything. Nobody comes here any more to tell me anything."

responses.label: You may tell the old nurse what you know of her boys.
You may carry the old nurse's words to her last son at Benwick.

entries.body:
You come to Salisbury Plain on the night before the last battle, and find the old king's army camped among the great stones. It is very quiet. In the old king's tent, in the middle of the circle, a single lamp is burning. You are on watch. Near midnight, the old king comes out of his tent, alone, in his nightshirt, and sits down on the altar stone.

"I dreamed," he says, to you, as though you were an old friend. "I dreamed I sat on a great wheel, in fine clothes, high up, and below me was black water full of serpents. And the wheel turned, and I fell. And then my nephew of Orkney came to me, who died at Dover, with a crowd of ladies, and told me not to fight tomorrow. To make any treaty. Wait a month, he said, and the house of Benwick will come to help you." The old king looks at you. "It was only a dream. What do you think?"

responses.label: You may counsel the old king to heed the dream and make a treaty.
You may counsel the old king to fight tomorrow and trust his sword.

entries.body:
You come across the Irish Sea to the Abbey of Kells in the last years, and find it crowded with refugees: Britons who have fled the war in fishing boats, with nothing but what they could carry. They are camped in the fields round the abbey, and the monks are feeding them from their own stores, which are running out.

At the abbey gate, a band of Irish warriors on horseback is shouting at the abbot. "These foreigners are eating our grain," their chief says. "Send them back across the sea, or we will send them ourselves." The refugees huddle together. The abbot, a small grey man, stands in the gate alone.

responses.label: You may defend the refugees and the abbey.
You may persuade the Irish chief to let the refugees stay.

entries.body:
You come to Merlin's cave in the last years, and find a young woman sitting on the rock where the cave mouth used to be, with her knees drawn up, weeping. It is Nimue. She has grown older. She is the Lady of the Lake now, since her mistress died.

"He is talking," she says, without looking up. "Inside the stone. He has been talking for three days. The king is going to die, he says. In a week. On the plain." She wipes her face. "I put him in there so I would be free of him, and now I cannot bear the silence when he stops." She looks at you. "He wants to speak to someone who is going to the battle. He says he has something to say."

If you have Story Token #3, turn immediately to [[1619]].

responses.label: You may put your ear to the stone and hear Merlin's last words.
You may persuade Nimue to open the stone at last.

entries.body:
You come through a wild wood in the north in the last years to a green mound by a stream, and find the Green Knight sitting on the mound in the snow with his axe across his knees, looking south, toward the war. His green has faded. He looks almost grey.

If you have Story Token #14, turn immediately to [[2187]].

"The land is dying," he says, when he sees you. "My wood. Your king. They are the same, you know. When he falls, the green goes out of Britain for a very long time." He turns his axe over in his hands. "I have been thinking of a game. My head, for a season. If you strike it off, as you would have once, the green goes into the land, and the land lives a little longer. A spring, perhaps. A summer." He holds out the axe. "But I will not pick it up again this time."

responses.label: You may take the Green Knight's axe and strike the blow for Britain.
You may refuse the Green Knight's sacrifice.

entries.body:
You come to the shore of the great lake after the last battle, with the mist lying on the water, and wait. Behind you, on the plain, the ravens are thick. At the water's edge, a one-handed knight is standing with a great sword in his hand, weeping, unable to throw it. Sir Bedivere.

If you have Story Token #16, turn immediately to [[2975]].

He sees you. "The king told me to throw it in," he says. "Twice I have hidden it, and told him I did it, and twice he has known I lied." He holds it out to you. "I cannot. It is the last thing of him. Of all of it." The sword Excalibur lies across his one palm, shining in the mist.

responses.label: You may take Excalibur from Sir Bedivere and throw it into the lake.
You may help Sir Bedivere find the strength to throw it himself.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You put yourself between the old man's knife and the young Saxon. "He has no weapon," you say. "Nor do the children. Let it be."

resolutions.label: calm the old man's hatred

success.body: You talk to the old man about his village, and what he has lost. You talk to the young Saxon, in the few words you share, about his. By the end of the night, the old man has put down his knife. In the morning, the Saxon helps the family carry their few things to the next village. The woman says he may stay and work their land, since her husband is dead and her sons are at the war. Years later, you hear that he married her daughter.

failure.body: You talk to the old man, but he will not listen. In the night, while you sleep, he does what he wanted to do. In the morning, the young Saxon is gone, and there is blood on the floor, and the old man will not meet your eyes.

resolutions.label: pray with them all for the dead on both sides

success.body: You kneel on the floor of the hut between the old man and the young Saxon and begin to pray aloud for the dead of the burned village, by name, as the woman tells them to you. Then you pray for the Saxon's dead, whose names he gives you in his own tongue. Somewhere in the prayer, the old man puts down his knife. In the morning, the young Saxon helps the family carry their things to the next village.

failure.body: You begin to pray for the dead on both sides. At the Saxon names, the old man stands up and walks out into the storm. In the morning, he has not come back, and neither has the Saxon.

entries.body: "The adventure is yours, my lord," you say. "I only mean to hold your horse." Bagdemagus beams and rolls up his list. The copper tower turns out to be a mill with a green copper roof, and the lady in the cage turns out to be a very large parrot. Its owner, Sir Hebes the miller-knight, comes out with a flail and a face like thunder.

resolutions.label: keep the peace between the king and the miller

success.body: Sir Hebes swears the bird is his, bought honestly from a Genoese sailor. Bagdemagus swears the pedlar's list cannot lie. You step between them before the flail and the sword meet. "My lord," you say to the king, "a king who frees parrots will be laughed at. A king who buys one for the queen at Camelot will be remembered." The king considers this, pays the miller twice what the bird is worth, and rides away with it on his wrist. It learns to say "Bagdemagus" before sundown. "Not a seat at the Table," he says, "but a start."

failure.body: Sir Hebes swears the bird is his, bought honestly from a Genoese sailor. Bagdemagus swears the pedlar's list cannot lie. You step between them and suggest they split the bird's price, which offends both men at once. The miller's flail catches you across the shoulder, and the king rides off with his list in a sulk. You rub your shoulder and resolve to choose your compromises more carefully.

resolutions.label: stand as the king's champion against the miller-knight

success.body: Sir Hebes will not hear a word. He swings his flail, and you take it on your shield and drive him back against his own millwheel until he yields. Bagdemagus claps so hard his circlet falls off. "Well struck! Well struck for Gore!" The miller sulkily hands over the parrot and a sack of flour besides. The king insists on telling the whole story at the next inn, and in his version he did most of the fighting. You let him.

failure.body: Sir Hebes will not hear a word. He swings his flail, you raise your shield too slowly, and the next thing you know you are lying in the millrace looking up at the parrot. "Yield," it says. Bagdemagus hauls you out and pays the miller for his trouble. You squelch away, having learned a great deal about flails.

entries.body: Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
Refer to physical Book of Tales for this passage.
You follow the roars through the burning streets, spear in hand.

resolutions.label: hunt the escaped lions through the burning town

success.body: You corner the lioness in a smithy yard and bring her down with your spear. It is terrible to see. The lion you find in the church, lying before the altar, bleeding from a soldier's arrow. He does not rise when you come in. You kneel beside him and end it, quickly. The boy from the menagerie weeps. The townsfolk come out of their houses and thank you, and the old king's men in the castle send you a gift, and you do not feel as if you have done anything worth thanks.

failure.body: You corner the lioness in a smithy yard, and she comes at you like a thunderbolt. You wake in the smithy with your arm in a sling. The lions are gone, somewhere in the smoke.

entries.body: "You will not ride unguarded while I have a sword," you say. The nuns look relieved. Igraine only nods, as if she expected nothing less. The road to Camelot runs through the Forest of Arroy, and the forest is full of masterless men.

resolutions.label: guard the old queen through the forest

success.body: On the second night, six men with cudgels come out of the trees. You put the nuns and the queen behind a fallen oak, set their mules in a ring, and hold the gap between them until the robbers lose heart. At Camelot, Igraine is brought into the hall. Arthur rises from the high table. For a long moment neither of them moves. Then the old queen opens her case and holds up a tiny linen gown, and the High King of Britain comes down from his dais and kneels at her feet.

failure.body: On the second night, six men with cudgels come out of the trees. You drive them off, but in the confusion one of them snatches the leather case and runs. You chase him to a stream, where he throws it in, and the baby gown and the lock of hair go sailing away into the dark. Igraine says nothing at all for the rest of the journey. You resolve to guard what matters, not just who.

resolutions.label: take the old paths round the forest where robbers do not go

success.body: You leave the road and lead the little party by sheep-tracks and drove roads along the forest's edge, where there is nothing to steal and nobody to steal it. It takes two days longer. On the last evening, from a hilltop, you see the smoke of the robbers' fires on the main road below. At Camelot, the old queen opens her case in the great hall and holds up a tiny linen gown, and the High King comes down from his dais and kneels.

failure.body: You leave the road for the sheep-tracks, and the sheep-tracks lead into a bog, and one of the mules goes in to its belly. It takes all day to get it out. Igraine says nothing, but she prays very loudly all the rest of the way.

entries.body: "Hang him, my lord," you say, "or the next king who rebels will know he risks nothing." Arthur grimaces, but he nods. "Kay says the same. So does Merlin, though Merlin says it more politely."

resolutions.label: argue for justice before the king and his drovers

success.body: The drovers join in. They have lost cattle to Nentres's raids, and a brother, and a barn. By the end of the evening Arthur knows exactly what the rebellion cost the people who never saw a battlefield. "Then he will not hang," the king says at last, "but he will pay. Every cow, every barn." It is not quite what you asked for, but it is justice, and the drovers carry you home on their shoulders.

failure.body: The drovers turn on you. They want the war over, not another hanging, and they think a hanged king means another rebellion from his sons. By the end of the evening you have been shouted down by an ox-driver, and Arthur is laughing at you both. "You see?" he says. "Eleven answers." You leave with your ears ringing.

resolutions.label: show the king what another rebellion would cost in blood

success.body: You take a handful of barley and a handful of salt from the table and lay them out like armies. Here is Nentres. Here are his sons. Here are the passes into Garlot, and the harvest that will burn if they rise again. Arthur watches, and so do the drovers. At last the king sweeps the barley into his palm. "Then he stays in prison until his sons are grown," he says, "and learns patience." It is a hard answer, and a sensible one.

failure.body: You lay out the barley and the salt like armies, but you put a pass in the wrong valley, and a drover from Garlot points it out, loudly. The whole alehouse laughs. Arthur laughs loudest. You resolve to learn the map of Britain before you draw it for a king.

entries.body: You get down from your horse and take the spade from the old priest's hands.

resolutions.label: bury the dead of the mountain battle

success.body: You dig for a week, from dawn until dark, and the old priest says the words over each grave. On the seventh night, as you lie exhausted by the fire, you see them: three hundred men standing in rows on the hillside, looking at you. Then they turn, all together, and walk away over the mountain, and are gone. In the morning, the old priest is smiling. "They thanked you," he says. "I saw it."

failure.body: You dig for three days, and on the fourth, you fall ill with the smell of the field. The old priest nurses you. The dead go unburied.

resolutions.label: speak the old words that settle the unquiet dead

success.body: You walk the field at dusk, from one end to the other, and speak over it the old words for the dead who have not been sung home: the words the grandmothers still say at crossroads. That night, you see them: three hundred men standing on the hillside, looking at you. Then they turn, all together, and walk away over the mountain. In the morning, the old priest is smiling. "They can wait for the spade now," he says.

failure.body: You walk the field and speak the old words. That night, three hundred men stand on the hillside, and they do not walk away. They walk toward you.

entries.body: You catch up with Sir Brun at the next inn. "I hear you dice," you say, and put down a silver penny. "I will play you for the fool's motley." Brun's eyes gleam. He sets down his dice.

resolutions.label: win the motley back at dice

success.body: His dice are loaded. You know it by the second throw, because they fall with a heavy little thump, and you have your own. When he is not looking, you switch his dice for yours. You win the coat, and the cap, and the bells, and the bauble, and, as Brun grows desperate, his second-best horse. Hwfa is overjoyed. He does a handspring and falls over. Sir Brun, when he finds the switched dice, says nothing at all, because to complain he would have to admit his own were loaded.

failure.body: His dice are loaded, and you know it by the second throw. You try to switch them for your own, but Brun sees you do it and seizes your wrist. "A cheat," he says loudly, to the whole inn. You are thrown out into the yard. Hwfa is waiting there, in his plain grey, and helps you up.

entries.body: "Tell me your idea," you say. Robin grins. "We bring the goose to court," he says, "and put it on trial."

resolutions.label: stage the trial of the goose

success.body: It takes a week to arrange. You ride to the Earl and persuade him, with some difficulty, to lend you his goose. Then, before the whole court, the goose is tried for trespass, with Robin as the prosecutor and you as the goose's defender. You argue that the goose was only following its nature, and that the barley was very good barley. The goose bites the prosecutor. The king laughs so hard he has to be carried from the hall. The next day, he invites the Earl to dinner, and they eat the goose together.

failure.body: It takes a week to arrange. You ride to the Earl and ask to borrow his goose, and the Earl, suspicious, refuses, and sends his men to guard it. The trial is held with a borrowed goose, which the king recognises at once as one of his own. He is not amused. The army marches the next day.

entries.body: You draw your sword. "The custom ends today," you say. The black knight calls over his shoulder, and nine more come out of the gatehouse.

resolutions.label: break the knights' cruel custom by force

success.body: You fight them at the gate, one at a time, as custom demands, because not even these knights will break that. You unhorse the first, and the second, and the fourth. By the seventh, they are looking at one another. The black knight, their captain, rides against you last, and when he goes down, he stays down, and says, "Enough. God forgive us. Enough." The maidens are sent home. You go in to see the lady, and find her in a dark room, weeping, and alone.

failure.body: You fight them at the gate, one at a time. You unhorse three. The fourth unhorses you. They carry you into the courtyard and lay you beside the pale maidens, and you watch them bleed until your wounds let you ride.

resolutions.label: shame them by the vows of the Grail quest

success.body: You do not draw. You speak to the black knight and his nine of the Grail, which asks for clean hands, and of the maidens in the courtyard whose blood is on theirs. You ask them how many have died, and whether their lady is any better. The black knight tries to answer and cannot. At last he takes off his helm. "God forgive us," he says. "Enough." The maidens are sent home. You go in to see the lady, and find her alone in the dark, weeping.

failure.body: You speak to them of the Grail and of clean hands. The black knight laughs. "The Grail has left us," he says. "We keep our own customs now." He closes the gate.

entries.body: You bow to the king and go out into the courtyard. There must be a marvel somewhere.

resolutions.label: find a true marvel for the Pentecost feast

success.body: You ride out into the forest, and within the hour, you find it: a white stag with a golden collar, drinking at a stream. You do not kill it. You drive it, gently, all the way back to Camelot, and through the gate, and into the great hall, where it stands among the tables, looking at the king. The whole court gasps. The king rises. "A marvel," he says. The stag bows its head, and trots out again. Sir Kay falls on the swan.

failure.body: You ride out into the forest and search all afternoon, and find nothing but a very cross badger. When you get back, a damsel has already brought a marvel, and the swans are eaten.

resolutions.label: conjure a small marvel from the old craft

success.body: You go out into the courtyard and gather what you need: a bowl of water from the well, a feather, the king's own candle. You come back into the hall and set the bowl before the young king and speak over it, and the water clouds, and clears, and shows the king his own hall as it will be in ten years, with every seat at the table full. The court gasps. Merlin, at the king's elbow, raises an eyebrow. The king eats. So does Sir Kay.

failure.body: You set a bowl of water before the young king and speak over it. It shows the king a very clear picture of Sir Kay eating the swan in the kitchen. The court laughs. It is not quite a marvel.

entries.body: You climb up into the hayloft and sit down beside him. "What does this town need?" you ask. Gwilym stops giggling. He thinks for a long time. "The bridge," he says. "The lord has been promising to mend it for five years. A child fell through it last winter."

resolutions.label: draft a decree the lord cannot undo

success.body: You draft it together, very carefully: *By order of the Lord of Kidwelly, the bridge shall be mended at the Lord's cost, and the Lord's name shall be carved upon it forever in thanks.* The heralds read it out. The townsfolk cheer. By the time the lord returns, the masons are already at work, and his name is half-carved on the parapet, and every man in town is thanking him. He cannot undo it without looking a fool. He is furious, and very proud of his bridge. Gwilym returns the seal to his lord's desk that night, and nobody ever proves a thing.

failure.body: You draft it together, very carefully, but you forget that the seal must be pressed right side up. The heralds notice. They also notice the handwriting. By the time the lord returns, you and Gwilym are both sitting in the pillory beside the steward.

entries.body: You walk round the foot of the crag, watching the castle turn, looking for what turns it.

resolutions.label: find the mechanism that turns the castle

success.body: It is not a mechanism. Carved into the rock at the foot of the crag, where the castle's shadow falls at noon, is a circle of words in an old tongue. You read them aloud, backwards, and the castle groans and slows and stops, with its gate facing you. The singing inside stops too. After a long while, an old man comes to the gate, blinking, and says, "Is it Pentecost already?" You tell him it is not.

failure.body: You find the circle of words and read them aloud. The castle does not stop. It speeds up. You have to lie flat on the rock while the wind of it roars over you, until the hermit comes and reads them properly.

entries.body:
You climb onto the cart. The hangman lets you. Nentres raises an eyebrow. "A priest in armour," he says. "Well. Why not."

He tells you of battles he won and lost, of a wife in Garlot who is King Lot's sister-in-law, and of a son he has not seen in two years. He tells you that he burned a church at Caerwent in the war, with no one in it, and has been sorry ever since. At the end he asks you to carry his ring to his son and tell the boy to keep the peace. At noon, they hang him. He does not laugh at the end.

The ring is heavy in your pocket all the way to Garlot. When you give it to the boy, he looks at you with his father's eyes and says nothing at all.

Merlin touches the seat, and your name begins to appear in gold, and then it fades, and the seat is blank. The court murmurs. Merlin looks at you over his staff, with his old bright eyes.

"You rode with Lot," he says. "The table knows. The table always knows." He moves on to the next seat.

Nobody says anything to you for the rest of the feast. The young king does not look at you. At the end of the evening, as you leave the hall, Merlin is waiting in the doorway. "Do something," he says quietly, "that the table will want to remember. Then come back." He gives you nothing. He does not have to.

notes: Lose Story Token #1

entries.body: You ride down the valley and find the three knights camped by the river, polishing their armour and boasting. "A knight of Arthur's court!" says their leader, a young man called Sir Aglovale le Bel. "Come to join the hunt? There is a giantess up the valley."

resolutions.label: shame the knights for what they have done

success.body: You ask them what the goat-herd had done. They look at each other. You ask them what they will tell the High King, when he asks at Pentecost what their greatest deed was. "A sleeping shepherd," you say, "and his widow." The youngest of them goes red to the ears. Sir Aglovale throws his wine in the fire. The next morning, they ride away the other way. You carry word to Morfran. She does not thank you, but she stops weeping, and lays one more stone.

failure.body: You ask them what the goat-herd had done. Sir Aglovale laughs. "Been a giant," he says. "What more is needed?" His companions laugh too. The next morning, they ride up the valley. You follow, but they are three and you are one.

resolutions.label: challenge the three knights to meet you instead

success.body: "If you want glory," you say, "win it from me." They cannot refuse without shame. You joust with all three, one after another, by the river, with the whole valley watching from the hills. You unhorse them all. The last, Sir Aglovale, lies in the river and laughs, ruefully. "Well," he says, "that will make a better story than a giantess." They ride away with their lances broken. Morfran watches from the hilltop, and when you ride up to her, she hands you a goat.

failure.body: "If you want glory," you say, "win it from me." They joust with you, one after another, and the second of them puts you in the river. They ride up the valley, laughing. You follow on foot, soaking, and far too late.

entries.body: You look at Mordred in his father's chair, and at the empty chair beside him, and you cannot bear it.

resolutions.label: shame Mordred before the Saxon kings

success.body: You set down your jug, throw off your servant's apron and stand before the high table. "That chair," you say, loudly, to the whole hall, "belongs to a king who is still alive. And the lady you are waiting for would rather burn." There is a terrible silence. The Saxon kings look at Mordred. Mordred smiles. But the oldest Saxon king gets up and leaves the hall, and takes his men with him. You escape in the uproar. By morning, all London knows what you said.

failure.body: You throw off your apron and stand before the high table. Mordred looks at you with his warm grey eyes. "Friend," he says. "Seize him." You spend a month in the Tower.

entries.body: "Come," you say gently. "Let us find your kin." Angharad looks at you with bewildered eyes and takes your arm.

resolutions.label: trace Angharad's family through the parish

success.body: The priest has an old book of baptisms, and you sit with him for an afternoon, following names from father to son and mother to daughter. By evening, you have found her kin: the old woman in the crowd, and her grandchildren, and a great-great-niece who has Angharad's own red hair. They take her in. The old woman sits with her by the fire, and they talk about the yew tree that was cut down, and the smithy that burned. When you leave, Angharad is holding a baby and laughing.

failure.body: The priest has an old book of baptisms, but the old pages have been eaten by mice, and you cannot find the names. The villagers are frightened of Angharad and do not want her. In the end she walks out of the village toward the hill, and does not look back.

resolutions.label: persuade the frightened villagers to take her in

success.body: The villagers are frightened of her. You talk to them about their own great-grandmothers, and about how any of them might dance too long on a May Eve. The old woman speaks up for her. At last a farmer's wife says she could use another pair of hands, and that is how Angharad stays. She marries, in the end, and her children are said to be very lucky, and to hear music in the hills that nobody else can hear.

failure.body: The villagers are frightened, and when you speak for her, they become more frightened of you. A stone is thrown. You ride away with Angharad on your saddle and leave her at the next convent. You never learn what became of her.

entries.body: You bow. "I would be honoured to dine," you say. The Lady of the Lake smiles and leads you to a hall where the table is laid with fish and fruits and wine that tastes of rain.

resolutions.label: dine with the Lady of the Lake with perfect courtesy

success.body: You eat, and talk, and listen to the ladies sing, and you are careful to thank each dish and each singer, as they do in the old courts. The Lady watches you with approval. At the end, she gives you a single pearl. "When you are in the greatest danger of your life," she says, "throw it in any water, and I will come." You keep it in your purse, and you never throw it. It is a comfort, all the same.

failure.body: You eat, and talk, and at the end of the meal, you forget to thank the singers. The Lady says nothing. But when you come up out of the lake, it is a day later than you went in.

resolutions.label: match the Lady's ladies in song at the feast

success.body: At the end of the meal, the ladies sing, and then they turn to you, as a guest must be turned to. You sing an old song of the lakes, and as you sing, the water of the palace glows round you, which it does not do for everyone. The Lady watches you with approval. She gives you a single pearl. "When you are in the greatest danger of your life," she says, "throw it in any water, and I will come."

failure.body: You sing an old song of the lakes, and the water round you goes dark. The Lady says nothing. But when you come up out of the lake, it is a day later than you went in.

entries.body: "Take us in," you say. The captain stares at you. Then he spits, and turns the wheel.

resolutions.label: command the ship through the rescue at the reef

success.body: You bring your ship in on the lee side of the reef, where the troop-ship's hull breaks the waves, and throw lines across. Men come along the lines one by one, hand over hand, over the boiling water. It takes all night. Your ship's hull scrapes the reef twice. At dawn, the troop-ship breaks up and goes under, but a hundred and twenty men are on your deck, soaked and shaking and alive. The captain drinks a whole bottle of wine and then embraces you.

failure.body: You bring your ship in toward the reef, and a wave throws it on the rocks. Now there are two ships foundering. By dawn, a third ship from the fleet has come and taken off most of the men from both. Many are lost.

resolutions.label: read the reef and bring the ship in on the lee

success.body: You watch the breakers by the lightning and see where the water is darker and smoother: a channel through the reef, on the lee side. You shout it to the helmsman, and he takes the ship through it, scraping, into the calm water behind the wreck. You throw lines across. Men come along them, hand over hand. At dawn, a hundred and twenty men are on your deck, alive.

failure.body: You see a channel through the reef and call it, and it is not a channel. The ship grinds on the rocks, and now there are two ships foundering. By dawn, a third ship has taken off most of both crews.

entries.body: You look at the Lady Tangwystl. She is very lovely. Pwca, following your gaze, goes pale. "Oh," he says, in a small voice. "Oh, no."

resolutions.label: win the tournament and the lady's kiss

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You ride in the lists and win every course. When you ride to the stand to claim your kiss, the Lady Tangwystl gives it gracefully and asks you to sup with her. She is charming and witty, and she laughs at all your stories. Late in the evening, she says, "You know, I have a fool who loves me. He thinks I do not know." She sighs. "But a lady cannot marry a fool." You find Pwca afterwards, sitting on the fence. He does not speak to you.

partial.body: You win two courses and lose the third. The Lady Tangwystl kisses the winner, who is fat and fifty. She catches your eye across the field and shrugs.

failure.body: You are thrown on your first course. As you lie in the dust, you hear a jingle of bells, and see Pwca doing cartwheels along the barrier to make the lady laugh. She does.

entries.body: "Who is your best wrestler?" you ask. The crowd parts, and a young woman built like an ox steps forward. "Megan the Miller," says the lord, delighted.

resolutions.label: wrestle the champion of the fair

success.body: Megan the Miller throws you three times, and you throw her twice, and on the sixth fall, you pin her, and hold her, and she laughs and taps the ground. The crowd cheers. Megan kisses you, hard, on the mouth. "Six years," she says. "Six years, nobody." She gives you a sack of flour and challenges you to a rematch next year.

failure.body: Megan the Miller throws you six times in a row. The crowd is weeping with laughter. Megan helps you up, very kindly, and gives you a sack of flour anyway. "For the bruises," she says.

resolutions.label: charm the champion into a friendly draw

success.body: You bow to Megan the Miller as if she were a duchess, and tell her you have heard of her from three counties away, and would count it an honour to be thrown by her. She laughs so hard she has to sit down on the grass. You wrestle anyway, and she throws you once, gently, and you throw her once, and then she calls it a draw before the whole fair and kisses you on the mouth. She gives you a sack of flour.

failure.body: You bow to Megan the Miller as if she were a duchess. She suspects mockery. She throws you six times in a row.

entries.body: You walk across the causeway and climb the ladder to his door. Sir Hervis draws back. "You must not," he says. "You will take it." "Then I will take it," you say.

resolutions.label: sit with the leper-knight without fear

notes: Lose all Ranks of Villainy

success.body: You sit with him through the evening, and share his bread, and tell him everything you know of the Grail. At the end, he takes off his bandages, slowly, and lets you see his face. Then he puts his ruined hand in yours. In the morning, when you wake, he is gone, and there is a smell of roses in the room, and the bandages are lying empty on the bed. You do not take the leprosy. You do not know what you have taken instead, only that you feel it, warm, under your ribs.

failure.body: You sit with him through the evening, and share his bread. But when he takes off his bandages, you cannot help it; you flinch. He sees it. He puts the bandages back on, and thanks you for coming, and asks you to go.

entries.body: "There is doubt," you say. "Where there is doubt, the High King's law gives mercy." The crowd murmurs. The widow's lip tightens.

resolutions.label: persuade the crowd to spare the squire

success.body: You speak of the High King's oath and of doubt and of the long life ahead of a boy of sixteen. You speak slowly, and the crowd listens, and when you finish, the reeve takes the rope off the squire's neck. "Exile," he says. "He goes to the Holy Land and does not come back." Iolo kisses your hand. The widow looks at you for a long moment, then gets into her litter and is carried away. Something in her look makes you think you have spared the right person, for the wrong reasons.

failure.body: You speak of the High King's oath and of doubt, but the crowd wants a hanging, and they have had a long morning waiting for one. They shout you down. The squire hangs. As you ride away, you see the widow watching you from her litter with something that might be amusement.

resolutions.label: call on the crowd to fear God's judgement

success.body: You do not argue the law. You ask the crowd whether any of them would like to stand before God on the last day with an innocent boy's blood on their hands, if innocent he is. You ask it quietly. One by one, they look away. The reeve takes the rope from the squire's neck and sends him on pilgrimage instead. As you ride away, you see the widow watching from her litter, and she is not smiling.

failure.body: You ask the crowd whether they would stand before God with innocent blood on their hands. The widow answers for them. "Nor would I," she says, "with my husband's." The crowd roars agreement, and the squire hangs.

entries.body: You look at the beast's great drooping head. It is not wicked. It is only what it is.

resolutions.label: drive the beast gently away from the village

success.body: You ride in a wide circle round behind it, shouting and clattering your sword on your shield. The catoblepas lumbers away from you, its head dragging in the grass, too heavy to lift while it walks. You herd it for a whole day, across the plain and into the marshes to the south, where there are no villages. It lies down in the reeds with a groan of contentment. The cowherd tells everyone that you drove the catoblepas like a cow.

failure.body: You ride round behind it, shouting. The catoblepas stops. Then, very slowly, it begins to lift its head. You gallop away across the plain without looking back.

entries.body: You look at the queen and then at her son on the road. "My lady," you say, "I am sorry." Morgause's face goes very still. "Ah," she says. "One of those."

resolutions.label: tell Gaheris everything, and try to prevent bloodshed

success.body: You ride to meet Gaheris and tell him everything, but you make him swear on his sword first that he will not harm his mother. He swears, grinding his teeth. At the woodcutter's hut, Lamorak comes out with his hands empty, and the two men stare at each other. Nobody draws. Morgause goes home to Orkney with her son that same day. You have kept the peace, but you do not think it will last.

failure.body: You ride to meet Gaheris and tell him everything. He does not wait to hear the rest. He spurs into the wood, and by the time you catch up, the woodcutter's hut is on fire, Lamorak is gone, and Morgause is sitting on the stile weeping. Gaheris will not look at either of you. You have made an enemy of Orkney's queen, and you are not sure you made a friend of her son.

entries.body: You follow the monk through the dark, wet streets to the palace wall, where the rain is coming down so hard that no guard would see you.

resolutions.label: spirit the Archbishop out through the storm

success.body: You climb the wall with a rope and find the Archbishop in his chapel, praying. He comes with you without a word, an old man in a wet cloak, down the rope and through the streets and down to the river, where the boat is waiting. As he steps into it, he turns and blesses you. "Tell the king," he says, "that I would not." In the morning, there is no Archbishop to crown Mordred. He is crowned by the Bishop of Rochester instead, and the whole country knows why.

failure.body: You climb the wall with a rope, and the rope is wet, and it slips. You fall into the palace garden among Mordred's dogs. You get away, but the guards are awake now, and the Archbishop is moved to a tower with no windows.

resolutions.label: ride him out at the gallop through the storm

success.body: You take the Archbishop up behind your saddle in the palace garden and put your horse at the low wall where it has fallen. It clears it. You gallop through the flooded streets, and the rain is so loud that the guards at the gate do not hear you until you are past them. By dawn you are ten miles away, and the old man is laughing into your back. In the morning, there is no Archbishop to crown Mordred.

failure.body: You put your horse at the fallen wall, and it refuses, and you both go into the palace fishpond. The guards hear that.

entries.body: At night, you creep to the river and swim to the water-gate of the Tower, where the guards on the wall let down a rope when you give the old king's password.

resolutions.label: help the queen's garrison hold the Tower

success.body: You spend a month on the walls. You show the garrison how to drop fire on the siege engines and how to dig a counter-mine under the wall. When Mordred's men storm the gate at last, you are standing on it with the queen's household knights. They break. The queen herself comes down to the walls afterwards and gives you her hand to kiss. She is thinner and older than you remember, and very calm. "We will hold," she says. "Until he comes." You believe her.

failure.body: You spend a month on the walls. When Mordred's men storm the gate, you are there, and a stone from a siege engine brings down the wall beside you. You are carried inside with a broken arm. The Tower holds, but you are no use to it any more.

entries.body:
You dream of an island where it is always the end of summer, where apple trees grow down to the water and nine women in grey stand on the shore, waiting. One of them lifts her hand and beckons. When you wake, there is an apple on your pillow, still warm from the sun, and the smell of honey in the air.

You know, without knowing how, that the boat will come for you if you go down to the water.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Avalon

entries.body: A herald in the colours of Benwick finds you at a crossroads, dusty from the road. He carries a letter sealed with a white castle on blue. "From the lords of Benwick, across the sea," he says. "They have heard your name. They would be glad to receive you in their hall." He bows and rides on before you can ask him how they heard.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Benwick

entries.body: You dream of a hill above a grey loch in the far north, where tall stones stand in a cross. In the dream, the stones are singing, one long low note, and they are singing your name. When you wake, you can still hear it, faintly, if you hold your breath. A fisherman at the next port tells you the way to Lewis without being asked.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit the Callanish Stones

entries.body: A royal messenger in the dragon livery rides up to you on a lathered horse. "From the High King," he says, and hands you a letter with the great seal. It is short: the king has heard of your deeds and would see you at Camelot, at the next feast, at his table. The messenger grins. "He wrote it himself," he says. "You can tell by the spelling."

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Camelot

entries.body: You dream of a castle on a rock above a dry river, and a procession passing through its hall: a spear that bleeds, two candles, and something covered in white. In the dream, an old king on a litter looks at you and opens his mouth to speak. You wake before he does. For a whole day afterwards, everything you eat tastes of bread and wine.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Corbenic

entries.body: A black swan lands on the water beside you as you water your horse, and in its beak is a letter sealed with green wax. It is written in a fine, amused hand. *Little knight. Come and see me. I promise I will only be a little wicked. M.* The swan waits until you have read it, and then eats the letter, and flies away.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Morgan's Castle

entries.body: A grizzled sea-captain finds you in a harbour tavern and sits down across from you uninvited. "I sail for Orkney on the morning tide," he says. "The queen there has heard of you. She says you are to come, and I am to bring you, and not to take no." He looks at you shrewdly. "I would not say no to her myself."

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Orkney

entries.body: You dream of a ring of great stones on a plain at sunset, glowing faintly, humming like a harp-string that has just been plucked. An old man sits on the altar stone eating an apple, and waves you over. When you wake, you find that you know the road to Salisbury Plain, though you have never taken it.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit Stonehenge

entries.body: A travelling monk in a grey habit shares your fire one night, and before he sleeps, he shows you a single page from a book, painted in gold and blue and red so bright it seems to glow. "From Kells," he says. "Across the water. They would like to meet the knight who sat with a stranger and did not ask for his story." In the morning, he is gone, and the page is under your saddle.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit the Abbey of Kells

entries.body: An owl lands on your saddle-bow at dusk and looks at you for a long time with its round yellow eyes. Then it says, very clearly, in an old man's voice, "Hawthorn. Hillside. Wales. Do not bring a crowd." It flies away. You are not sure you heard it. You are quite sure you did.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit the Cave of Merlin

entries.body: You wake one winter morning to find a sprig of holly lying on your chest, with the berries bright as blood. Tied to it with a green thread is a scrap of birch bark, on which someone has written, in a large, courteous hand: *The chapel in the north. When you are ready. There is no hurry, and there is every hurry.*

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit the Green Chapel

entries.body: As you ride along the shore of a great lake, a hand in white samite rises out of the still water, and beckons, once, and sinks. The water where it was is perfectly still. You stand there for a long time. When you ride on, your cloak is damp at the hem, though you did not go near the water.

notes: Keep this Location card. You may now visit the Underwater Palace

entries.body: You climb the hill. The thorn tree is covered in white flowers, and it smells of snow and honey. You kneel beneath it.

resolutions.label: pray beneath the Holy Thorn

success.body: You pray for a long time. The wind blows petals over you. Toward sunset, you hear a voice, very quiet, like an old man speaking from the next room. It says your name. It says, *Not here. Not me. Go on.* When you come down the hill, the monk looks at your face and stops digging. "You heard him," he says. "Then I can stop." He gives you a sprig of the thorn, still in flower. It does not fade.

failure.body: You pray until dark. The thorn drops its petals on you. You hear nothing but the wind. When you come down, the monk is still digging.

resolutions.label: keep the winter vigil under the thorn through the night

success.body: You kneel beneath the thorn and do not rise when the sun goes down. The frost comes. Your knees freeze to the ground. Near midnight, you hear a voice, very quiet, like an old man speaking from the next room. It says your name. It says, *Not here. Not me. Go on.* When you come down the hill at dawn, the monk looks at your face and stops digging. He gives you a sprig of the thorn, still in flower.

failure.body: You kneel beneath the thorn through the night, and near midnight you cannot feel your hands, and the monk comes up the hill and carries you down to his fire. You hear nothing but the wind.

entries.body: You find a boatman who still loves the old king, and at night, he rows you under the Tower wall, where a hand lets down a letter on a string. It is sealed with the queen's own seal.

resolutions.label: carry the queen's letter through Mordred's lines

success.body: You go down the river by night, lie up in the marshes by day, and walk to Dover through the woods, avoiding every road. At Dover, you find a fishing boat that will take you over the sea, and in the High King's camp before Benwick, you put the letter into Arthur's own hand. He reads it. His face goes grey. "We sail tomorrow," he says. You sail with him.

failure.body: You go down the river by night, but at the estuary, Mordred's patrol boats are waiting. You swim for it. The letter, in its oilcloth, sinks. You reach the shore alive, and nothing else.

resolutions.label: ride the letter out through the gate in a carter's clothes

success.body: You borrow a carter's smock and a cart of cabbages, sew the queen's letter into the lining of the horse's collar, and drive out of the Ludgate at dawn with the market carts. The guards poke the cabbages with spears. Nobody looks at the horse. Ten miles out, you unharness it, and ride it bareback to Dover. In the High King's camp before Benwick, you put the letter into Arthur's hand.

failure.body: You drive a cart of cabbages out of the Ludgate, and a guard who has been bored all night decides to search the horse. He finds the letter. You leave the cabbages and run.

entries.body: You stay. In the morning, the storm is still blowing, and the cathedral is full of Mordred's lords, and Mordred himself kneels at the altar, pale and handsome in red.

resolutions.label: cause an uproar at Mordred's coronation

success.body: You do not need to do much. When the Bishop of Rochester lifts the crown, you stand up at the back of the nave and ask, in a clear voice, where the Archbishop is. The whole cathedral goes quiet. Mordred turns and looks at you. His face does not change. Then the storm blows open the great west door, and every candle in the cathedral goes out at once. In the dark, you slip out. The story of the coronation in the dark is told across Britain within the week.

partial.body: You stand up at the back of the nave and ask where the Archbishop is. There is a murmur, and a few lords look uneasy, and Mordred's soldiers march you out. The coronation goes on.

failure.body: You stand up and ask where the Archbishop is. Nobody listens. The organ is too loud and the lords are too frightened. Two of Mordred's soldiers take you by the elbows and throw you into the street, and you hear the cheering begin behind the closed doors.

entries.body: You climb down the rope ladder into the dark. At the bottom, a tunnel runs away under the town, lit here and there by candle-stubs stuck in old Roman brickwork.

resolutions.label: creep through the tunnels and bring the girl out

success.body: You follow the voices through the tunnels, keeping to the shadows, until you find a vault where a dozen thieves are melting silver over a brazier. The girl is tied in a corner. You wait until they are arguing over the shares, then slip in, cut her loose and lead her out by the way you came. She is up the ladder before the thieves notice she is gone. The boy hugs her until she squeaks. The bishop, when he hears where his candlesticks went, sends you a reward.

failure.body: You follow the voices through the tunnels, but the tunnels branch and branch again, and your candle gutters out. You wander in the dark for hours before you find daylight, through a grating in the fish market. The girl, you learn later, was let go the next morning, frightened into silence.

resolutions.label: fight your way to the girl through the thieves

success.body: You go straight down the tunnel toward the voices and burst into a vault where a dozen thieves are melting silver. They are not fighters. You scatter them with the flat of your sword, and a small, rat-faced man in a velvet hat flees down a side passage, squeaking orders. You untie the girl and carry her out. The watch, finally roused, comes down behind you and finds a whole church's worth of silver in the vault.

failure.body: You go straight at the voices and burst into the vault, but there are more thieves than you counted, and one of them knocks over the brazier. In the smoke and molten silver, you are burned and driven back. You climb out empty-handed.

entries.body: "A beard for gold," you say. "Agreed." Rience roars with delight. You ride away with a purse of expenses and a plan that becomes more foolish the more you think about it.

resolutions.label: deliver the king a beard that is not Arthur's

success.body: In a village three days away you find a goatherd with a magnificent red beard and pay him a silver penny for it. You bring it back to Rience, wrapped in a silk cloth, and describe at length how you crept into the king's chamber. Rience weighs it on a scale, pays you in gold, and sews it onto his mantle himself. When word reaches Camelot, Arthur laughs so hard he has to be helped from the table. "My beard is brown," he says, "but let him have it."

failure.body: In a village three days away you find a goatherd with a magnificent red beard and pay him a silver penny for it. You bring it back to Rience, who holds it up to the light and then to his nose. "This," he says, "smells of goat." His guards throw you down his front steps, and Rience keeps your purse. You resolve to wash your forgeries next time.

resolutions.label: steal into Camelot and cut a lock of the king's own beard

success.body: You climb the kitchen wall at Camelot on a moonless night and creep up to the royal chamber past a sleeping page. Arthur sleeps on his back, snoring. You cut a single lock from his chin with your knife and slip away. Rience pays you its weight in gold, which is very little gold, and sews it onto his mantle in pride of place. You never tell anyone, and Arthur never notices. But from then on you cannot look him in the eye.

failure.body: You climb the kitchen wall at Camelot on a moonless night. Halfway up, a hand closes on your ankle. It belongs to Sir Kay, who is out raiding the larder. "Well, well," says Kay. By dawn you are in the king's own dungeon, explaining yourself. Arthur, when he hears the story, laughs until he cries, and then leaves you there for a week anyway.
