entries.body: You get down from your horse and roll up your sleeves. Father Mabon looks at you and says nothing. He hands you a cloth for your face.

resolutions.label: tend the sick through the worst of the plague

success.body: You stay a fortnight. You boil water and burn rushes and bathe fevered faces and carry bowls. You learn which herbs cool a fever and which ease a cough. Of the thirty sick, twenty-two live. On the last day, Father Mabon sits down in the straw beside you, with a child asleep on his lap. "I could not have done it alone," he says. When you ride away, the whole village is at the doors to watch you go, and some of them are weeping.

failure.body: You stay a week. You do everything Father Mabon tells you. But on the fifth day, you wake up shivering, and by the seventh, you are lying in the straw among the others. You live. Many do not. When you ride away, you are weak and thin, and you carry the sickness with you for a long time.

resolutions.label: pray over the sick through the long nights

success.body: You kneel in the barn every night with Father Mabon, moving from pallet to pallet, praying over each of the sick by name. Some of them ask you to hold their hands. You do. On the tenth night, the fever breaks in the youngest child, and then in her mother, and then, one by one, in almost all of them. Father Mabon sits down in the straw and weeps. "I thought I was the only one still praying," he says.

failure.body: You kneel in the barn every night and pray. On the fifth night, you feel the fever start in your own blood. You pray on, shivering, until you are lying among the others.

entries.body: You turn your horse to face the sound of the riders.

resolutions.label: hold off Lot's riders in the moonlit wood

success.body: You meet them on the path, six riders in Orkney colours, and you ride through them and scatter them among the trees. While they are finding their horses, the chant behind you rises and falls, and ends. When you ride back to the oak, the old priests are gone, and the white bull is standing alone, garlanded, eating grass. The old woman's voice comes out of the dark: "The old gods thank you. They let the bull go. They liked your fighting better."

failure.body: You meet them on the path, and there are too many. You are driven back into the circle, and the rite is broken, and the priests flee. Lot's men take the bull.

resolutions.label: cast a mist over the wood to hide the rite

success.body: You speak the old words for mist, which the old priests themselves taught your grandmother, and white fog rises out of the grass all round the hollow oak. Lot's riders come into it and lose each other, and their way, and at last their nerve. The chant behind you rises and falls, and ends. When the mist lifts, the priests are gone, and the white bull is standing alone, garlanded, eating grass.

failure.body: You speak the words for mist, and the mist rises, and Lot's riders ride straight through it to the torches, which are the only light in the wood. The rite is broken. The priests flee.

entries.body: "Where is this well?" you ask. Pedr's wife points up the valley. "An hour's walk," she says. "But she will not come."

resolutions.label: persuade the witch at the well to lift the curse

success.body: The witch at the well is a bent old woman with a face like a crab-apple and a sharp tongue. You bow very low and do not make a single joke. You tell her that Pedr is sorry, and that he has a wife who loves him, and that he has learned his lesson. She hears you out. "He called me a withered old bat," she says. "I am a withered old bat," she adds, "but he did not have to say it." At last she nods, and draws a sign in the air. Down the valley, you hear the laughing stop. When you get back, Pedr is asleep.

failure.body: The witch at the well is a bent old woman with a face like a crab-apple. You bow very low and begin to plead for Pedr. Halfway through, you notice she has a wart on her nose shaped exactly like a pear, and something in your face gives you away. She points at you. "You too," she says. You laugh all the way back down the valley, and for three days after.

resolutions.label: bring the witch a gift of rare herbs

success.body: You do not go empty-handed. You spend the morning in the woods and bring old Nest's sister a basket of the things a witch cannot easily find: wood-sorrel, and moonwort, and a mandrake root that you dig with your dagger at noon so it cannot scream. The witch at the well looks in the basket and cackles with pleasure. She draws a sign in the air. Down the valley, the laughing stops.

failure.body: You bring the witch a basket of herbs. She looks in it and snorts. "Common hemlock," she says, "and dock, and nettles. Do you think I am a cow?" She points her finger at you. You laugh all the way down the valley.

entries.body: You put your finger to your lips and kneel beside the chain. It is old iron, rusted, and the ring is set deep in the rock.

resolutions.label: break the chain and slip away before the tide

success.body: You work at the ring with your dagger and your bare hands, while the snoring rumbles above you and the tide creeps up the causeway. Your fingers bleed. At last the ring comes out of the rock with a crack. You lift the old woman onto your back and wade across the causeway with the water up to your chest. Behind you, the snoring stops. A great voice roars. But the tide is in, and the giant cannot swim. On the shore, the old woman kisses your hands and tells you her name is Dame Gwenhael, and that she will pray for you every day she lives.

failure.body: You work at the ring with your dagger, but it will not come out of the rock, and the tide is rising. At last the old woman pushes you away. "Go," she says. "Go, or he will have you too." You wade back across the causeway alone, with her weeping behind you.

resolutions.label: loosen the chain with a charm of opening

success.body: You lay your hand on the iron ring and whisper the old words for opening, which work on locks and gates and, sometimes, on stones. The ring grinds in the rock and slides out into your hand. The old woman stares at it, and at you. You lift her onto your back and wade across the causeway as the tide rises. Behind you, the giant wakes and roars, but the tide is in. On the shore, she tells you her name is Dame Gwenhael, and prays for you.

failure.body: You lay your hand on the iron and whisper the words for opening. Up in the cave, the giant's eyes open. You have opened the wrong thing. You flee across the causeway with the tide at your waist and the old woman weeping behind you.

entries.body:
King Lot rises from his seat when he sees you, and comes down the hall, and embraces you in front of everyone. "My friend!" he roars. "My knight! Who rode with me to Bedegraine!" He sits you at his right hand, and pours your wine himself, and tells the whole hall how you fought. Queen Morgause looks at you with new interest. The young red-haired boys stare at you in awe.

Before you leave, Lot takes you aside. "I will rise again," he says. "Next spring. Will you ride with me?" You tell him you will think about it. He gives you a gold arm-ring, and a horse, and a promise that Orkney does not forget its friends.

notes: Lose Story Token #1

entries.body: You get down from your horse. "Give the pilgrims back their purses," you say. "I will find your children bread."

resolutions.label: feed the starving outlaws

success.body: You take the outlaws into the deep forest and show them what can be eaten there: hazelnuts, beechmast, mushrooms, the roots of the burdock. You set snares for rabbits with them. You shoot a deer, and damn the king's forest law. By nightfall, there is a stew bubbling, and the children are eating. The pilgrims, who have followed you, share their own bread, and Sir Hervi kneels among them and asks their pardon. They give it.

failure.body: You take the outlaws into the deep forest to find food, but it is the wrong season, and you find nothing but a few sour berries. The children go hungry. Sir Hervi does not rob the pilgrims, but the next day, he robs someone else.

resolutions.label: hunt deer enough to feed the band

success.body: You take the outlaws' best archer and go into the deep forest, and by dusk you have two deer and a boar, and damn the king's forest law. There is roast meat enough for every child in the band. The pilgrims, who have followed you, share their bread, and Sir Hervi kneels among them and asks their pardon. They give it.

failure.body: You go into the deep forest to hunt, and the deer have gone east with the frost. You come back with a hare. Sir Hervi looks at it, and at his children, and does not rob the pilgrims, but he robs someone else the next day.

entries.body: You walk across the circle to the black seat. The court gasps. Merlin does not move to stop you.

resolutions.label: dare to sit in the Siege Perilous

success.body: You sit down. For a moment, nothing happens. Then the black drape slides off the seat, and a light comes up through the wood, and you feel it burning, not your body, but something inside you. You stand up at once. You are alive. On the back of the seat, for a moment, letters of gold appear: *Not you. But worthy to try.* Then they fade. Merlin is laughing. "The first to live," he says. "The table likes you." The young king comes round the table and embraces you.

partial.body: You sit down, and the seat burns you, and you leap up with your hands scorched. You are alive. The court is silent. Merlin says, "Foolish. But alive."

failure.body: You sit down, and the seat burns like a furnace. You are dragged out of it by Sir Kay, smoking. You spend a month in bed, and a year being laughed at.

entries.body: "You are robbing your own master," you say. Hywel shrugs. "I am keeping the inn paid," he says, "and myself fed."

resolutions.label: prove Hywel's thefts before the town reeve

success.body: You go with the reeve to every buyer in the market and find each of Sir Brastias's horses, with the knight's brand on its hindquarters. Hywel is put in the stocks. The horses are returned, most of them grumbling. When the reeve asks what should be done with the squire, you say he should be made to sit by his master's bed and wait until he wakes. You hear, much later, that Brastias did wake, and forgave the boy, and beat him soundly.

failure.body: You go with the reeve to every buyer in the market, but the buyers are unwilling to give up good horses cheaply bought, and they all swear the brand is different. Hywel smiles at you from beside the reeve. "An honest mistake," he says. You leave town knowing you have been outplayed by a boy with a winning smile.

resolutions.label: track down every horse he sold

success.body: You go from farm to farm across the county with the knight's brand drawn on a scrap of parchment, and find all four horses, one pulling a plough, one in a baker's cart and two in a lord's stable. You bring them back to the inn in a string. Hywel's smile finally slips. The reeve puts him in the stocks. Sir Brastias, when he wakes, is very surprised to find his horses so well travelled.

failure.body: You go from farm to farm across the county and find one horse, pulling a plough, and the farmer will not give it up. By the time you come back, Hywel has sold the knight's hawks as well.

entries.body: You take up the white shield and ride into the melee.

resolutions.label: win glory in the melee without a name

success.body: You fight all day. You unhorse seven knights. At the end, when the heralds call for the knight of the white shield to come and be named, you ride up to the royal stand, and the High King himself leans down to lift your visor, and when he sees your face, he smiles for the first time that day. "Welcome home," he says. You are given the prize, a silver cup, and a seat at the king's side at the feast.

failure.body: You fight all day, and in the afternoon, a knight with a plain black shield unhorses you and rides away. You never learn who he was. That night, you think you see him at the feast, and then you are sure you do not.

resolutions.label: fight on foot in the thick of the melee

success.body: When your lance breaks in the first charge, you do not ride back for another. You dismount in the middle of the melee and fight on foot with your plain white shield, and it is the best fighting of the day: nobody knows who you are, and nobody holds back. When the heralds call for the knight of the white shield, the High King himself lifts your visor, and smiles for the first time that day. "Welcome home," he says.

failure.body: You dismount and fight on foot in the melee, and a knight with a plain black shield beats you to your knees and walks away. You never learn who he was.

entries.body: You leave your horse and creep through the reeds on your belly to the end of the line of prisoners.

resolutions.label: free the prisoners by stealth

success.body: You cut the rope at the back of the line, and the last man looks round, and you put your finger to your lips. You cut the next, and the next. They slip away into the reeds, one by one, while the soldiers are busy at the front of the line. By the time the officer notices his line has got shorter, eleven men are gone into the storm. You lead them through the marsh all night. At dawn, you reach the old king's lines.

failure.body: You cut the rope at the back of the line, but the man there cries out in surprise, and the lanterns swing round. You run. A few of the prisoners run too. You do not know how many get away.

entries.body:
Morgan stops eating cherries. "You," she says. "You owe me." She points into the valley with a cherry stem. "There is a knight in there who was false to me, a long time ago. Sir Accolon. He is not dancing. He is sitting by the stream, weeping. Bring him out to me."

You walk into the valley. The mist closes round you. You find Accolon by the stream, and bring him out, and Morgan looks at him for a long time. Then she touches his face, very gently, and he wakes from his weeping and looks at her, and they walk away into the mist together without a word to you. On the rock, she has left the cherries, and a note: *Quits.*

notes: Lose Story Token #13

entries.body:
You look at the children in the trees, and at the pilgrims with their purses. It is not your quarrel.

You ride on. Behind you, you hear Sir Hervi weeping, and a pilgrim saying, quite gently, "Take it. We are going to pray for the Grail. You need it more than we do." You do not look back.

You walk back down the line to the shouting man. He is a well-fed merchant with rings on every finger. "It's a trick!" he says. "She makes you shame yourself before a hundred people and then gives you well-water. I have a cough. I will pay for my cure."

resolutions.label: talk the merchant round

success.body: You ask him about his cough, and his trade, and his wife. It comes out, slowly, that he has cheated his partner out of a warehouse in Chester, and that the cough started the week after. You do not say anything. You do not need to. The merchant goes quiet, then red, then white. He walks up to the well without another word and kneels before the old queen. When he comes back, he is not coughing. He presses a purse into your hand without meeting your eye.

failure.body: You ask him about his cough, and his trade, and his wife. He tells you to mind your own business and shoves you, and his servants join in. By the time the pilgrims have pulled you apart, you have a bloody nose and the merchant has ridden off, shouting that the well is a fraud to everyone he passes. You resolve to know when a man does not want to be helped.

resolutions.label: test whether the well truly heals

success.body: You watch the well for a whole day, speaking with pilgrims before and after. A boy with a withered hand. A woman whose eyes were clouded. A soldier who had not slept in a year. You see enough to know the truth, and you tell the merchant so. "It is no fraud," you say. "But it is a hard cure." The merchant scowls, but he stays, and the next morning you see him at the front of the line, confessing in a very small voice.

failure.body: You watch the well for a whole day, speaking with pilgrims before and after. Some seem healed. Some do not. You cannot tell which is which, or why. By evening you are no wiser than the merchant, and he rides off laughing. The old queen watches you go. "Some things," she calls after you, "you do not learn by watching."

entries.body: You follow Gwion back into the inn. "Good people," you say, "before your hero goes out, I think he has something to tell you." Gwion looks at you with pure terror.

resolutions.label: persuade Gwion to tell the truth, and the village to forgive him

success.body: Gwion confesses. It is the best song he has ever sung: halting, honest, and full of real fear. The villagers are angry, then disgusted, then, as he describes hiding under a hay-cart from a goose, helpless with laughter. By the end, they have forgiven him. "But the wolf is still there," says the old farmer. You go and kill it the next morning, and the village pays you instead, and Gwion writes a song about it that makes you sound twice as brave as you were.

failure.body: Gwion confesses, and the villagers are angry, and then very angry, and then they take him outside and throw him in the horse pond. They throw you in after him, for good measure, for bringing him there in the first place. The wolf takes three more sheep that night.

entries.body: "Chains," you say. "And a very large bait." The old woman looks at you doubtfully.

resolutions.label: trap the afanc with chains and cunning

success.body: You borrow every chain in the village and the smithy's anchor, and build a snare on the bank, baited with a whole sheep. At midnight, the afanc comes out of the water, sniffing. When it seizes the sheep, you pull the pin, and the chains fall on it, and the whole village hauls on the ropes. It thrashes all night. In the morning, it is lying on the bank, exhausted and furious and very securely chained. They find the boy in its den, alive. The villagers sell the afanc to a lord in Gwent who keeps a menagerie.

failure.body: You build a snare on the bank baited with a sheep. The afanc comes out of the water, and looks at the sheep, and at the chains, and at you. Then it takes you instead, and drags you into the lake. You get away, but not your dignity.

entries.body: You kneel at the edge of the well among the pilgrims and pray.

resolutions.label: pray for the holy well to run red again

success.body: You pray for the well, and for the pilgrims, and for the Grail, wherever it has gone. You pray for a long time. The pilgrims fall silent around you. Toward evening, an old woman with a crippled arm lowers the bucket and draws it up, and the water in it is red as wine, and when she drinks it, she lifts her arm above her head for the first time in ten years. The pilgrims fall on their knees. The friar looks at you strangely. "It was not me," you say. He does not believe you.

failure.body: You pray for the well until dark, and the water that comes up is as pale as ever. The pilgrims drift away one by one. The friar sits beside you. "Sometimes," he says, "he is only waiting for someone else."

entries.body: "I will take you," you say. "A herald should not be blamed for his message." Tudwal looks at you with gratitude. "You would be surprised," he says, "how often he is."

resolutions.label: present the herald before the High King's court

success.body: At Camelot, the court is outraged by the message before Tudwal has finished reading it. Sir Kay reaches for his sword. You step forward and remind them all that the herald is under your protection and the law of heralds. The High King, to his credit, laughs. "Tell your king," he says to Tudwal, "that my beard is too young to be worth sending. And give this herald a good dinner and a new tabard that fits." Tudwal leaves Camelot the next morning with a full belly and a tabard that does not trail. He gives you his old silver trumpet.

failure.body: At Camelot, the court is outraged by the message, and before you can speak, Sir Kay has knocked Tudwal off his mule. The High King rebukes Kay, but the damage is done. Tudwal rides home with a black eye, and King Ryons, you hear, is delighted to have a new grievance.

resolutions.label: advise the herald how to deliver it without changing a word

success.body: On the road, you work it out together. The words must stay the same; that is the herald's law. But the manner of reading them is his own. At Camelot, Tudwal reads King Ryons's demand in a voice of such exaggerated pomposity, with such flourishes on his silver trumpet, that the whole court is laughing before he reaches the word *beard*. The High King laughs loudest. Tudwal leaves with a new tabard and gives you his old trumpet.

failure.body: You advise him to read it in a pompous voice. He does. Unfortunately, the High King is in a bad mood that day, and thinks the herald is mocking him. Tudwal is thrown out of the hall.

entries.body: You climb up the mountain by the long path, and come out on the ledge beside the nest. The griffin turns her head and looks at you with one great golden eye.

resolutions.label: calm the angry griffin

success.body: You do not look her in the eye. You sit down on the ledge with your back to her, as you would with an angry hawk, and wait. After an hour, she stops hissing. After two, she comes over and looks at you. You offer her a leg of mutton from your pack. She takes it. By sundown, she has settled on her eggs again, and the villagers can hear her crooning. The Lord of Dinas's huntsmen do not come back. You hear, a year later, that two young griffins have been seen over the mountain, and that the village is very proud of them.

failure.body: You sit down on the ledge with your back to her. The griffin picks you up by your belt, carries you down to the valley, and drops you in the village pond.

entries.body: "You were told to hold until relieved," you say. "I am relieving you." The old soldier looks at you suspiciously.

resolutions.label: persuade the old soldier to leave his post

success.body: You tell him, formally, in the old king's name, that he is relieved, and that his duty is done. The old soldier stands up and salutes you. Then he walks away down the causeway, and you walk with him, and the horses come on behind you to an empty gate. Nobody holds a causeway nobody guards. You find him a place by a fire, and he talks about his wife for three hours.

failure.body: You tell him he is relieved. The old soldier looks at you. "By whom?" he asks. "I do not know you." He turns back to the causeway and lowers his spear. You cannot leave him. You cannot stay.

resolutions.label: relieve him formally, as an officer would

success.body: You draw yourself up and speak to him as a captain speaks to a sentry: the watchword, the name of his commander, the order that relieves him, and the place he is to report. He knows all the old forms. So do you. At the end, he salutes, and shoulders his spear, and marches off down the causeway with you, and the horses come on to an empty gate. You find him a place by a fire.

failure.body: You speak to him as a captain speaks to a sentry, and give him the watchword. It is last year's. He lowers his spear at you.

entries.body: "The old king," you say, "would want the sword of a man who fought at Badon." The daughter looks at you with gratitude.

resolutions.label: persuade the sea-king's sons to part with his sword

success.body: You speak to the brothers, big fierce men, and tell them about the old king: that he is grey and tired and fighting his last war, and that he remembers the men who fought beside him at Badon. You tell them that a sword from Badon, at Salisbury, would mean something. They are silent a long time. Then the eldest lifts the sword from his father's chest and puts it in your hands. You carry it to the old king. He holds it a long time, and weeps.

failure.body: You speak to the brothers. The eldest takes offence. "It is our father's," he says, "not the old king's." You are asked to leave the ship.

resolutions.label: win the sword in fair combat with the eldest son

success.body: The eldest son says the sword goes to the sea, unless a better warrior than he claims it. You accept. You fight him on the deck of his father's funeral ship, before the bier, with the Orkneymen striking their shields. It is a long, fair fight. At the end, he lowers his blade, and lifts the sword from his father's chest himself, and puts it in your hands. The old king holds it a long time, and weeps.

failure.body: You fight the eldest son on the deck before the bier, and he is better. The sword goes to the sea.

entries.body: You climb the rock and sit beside her without speaking. She goes on counting. After a while, you ask her what her sons' names were.

resolutions.label: draw Queen Anna out of her madness

success.body: She tells you. Brude and Talorc. She tells you how Talorc could not swim and Brude went back for him. She tells you about her husband's laugh, which could be heard across a hall. Somewhere in the telling, she stops counting. The soldiers, one by one, put down their whips and wade out of the sea. When she has finished, the queen stands and looks at the water. "Tell them to stop," she says, though they already have. She gives you her own mourning ring.

failure.body: She tells you. Brude and Talorc. Then, halfway through, she looks at you and sees that you pity her, and her face hardens. "Get off my rock," she says. "Four hundred and twelve." You go back to your horse with the sound of whips in your ears.

resolutions.label: tell her a story of someone who lost as much and lived

success.body: You tell her of a widow in Carleon who lost four sons in the Saxon wars and went on to found a hospital for sailors. Anna listens. "Sailors," she says. "The sea took hers too?" "Two of them," you say. The queen is quiet for a long time. Then she stands and calls her men out of the water. "We will build a tower on this headland," she says, "with a light in it, so no more ships are lost here." It is standing still, many years later.

failure.body: You tell her of a widow in Carleon who lost four sons in the Saxon wars. "And did she whip the sea?" Anna asks. "No," you admit. "Then she was a fool," says the queen, and turns back to her count. You have misjudged her grief, and you leave the beach knowing it.

entries.body: You sit down beside the High King. He pours you wine.

resolutions.label: lift the lonely king's heart

success.body: You do not talk about the Grail. You talk about the old days: Badon, and the eleven kings, and the young king climbing onto his table at Pentecost. You make him laugh. By midnight, he is telling you stories you never heard, about Sir Ector's pig and Merlin's temper. At dawn, he stands up and stretches, and looks like a younger man. "I needed that," he says. "More than any Grail." He gives you a spear from the wall of the hall, which he says his father carried. It is called Rhongomyniad.

failure.body: You try to cheer him, but every story you tell reminds him of someone who has gone. By midnight, he is weeping into his wine. You leave him there, alone, with the empty seats.

resolutions.label: take the king out hawking as in the old days

success.body: You do not sit at the empty table. You tell him that his hawks have not flown in a month, and take him out onto the downs with a falcon on his fist, and nobody else. You fly the hawks all afternoon. He laughs when his falcon misses a heron. He tells you stories of Sir Ector's pig and Merlin's temper. At dusk, he looks like a younger man. He gives you a spear from the wall of his hall, which his father carried.

failure.body: You take him out hawking, and his falcon flies off and does not come back. He stands on the downs looking at the empty sky for a long time. You ride back in silence.

entries.body: You watch the dancing lights. There is something in them, a pattern, like a hand beckoning.

resolutions.label: follow the lights without losing your way

success.body: You follow them, carefully, speaking the old charm against false fire under your breath. They lead you deeper and deeper into the marsh, to a little island with a ruined chapel on it, and in the chapel is the pilgrim, sitting on the floor, alive, staring at the wall. On the wall, painted by some long-dead monk, is a picture of a cup. The lights hover over it, and then go out. The pilgrim looks at you. "It was only a painting," he says. But he is smiling.

failure.body: You follow the lights, and they lead you round and round the marsh, until dawn, when you find yourself back where you started, soaked and freezing. The pilgrim is never seen again.

resolutions.label: pray against the false fire as you follow

success.body: You follow the lights with the Paternoster on your lips, and each time you reach the Amen, one of the little flames goes out, until only one is left, leading you. It brings you to an island with a ruined chapel on it, and in the chapel, the pilgrim sits staring at a painting of a cup on the wall. The last flame hovers over the painting and goes out. "It was only a painting," the pilgrim says. But he is smiling.

failure.body: You follow the lights praying, but the lights do not care for prayers. They lead you round the marsh until dawn. The pilgrim is never seen again.

entries.body: You stand up and look at the priest. "Who says she should be burned?" you ask. The priest glances toward the churchyard gate, where men are gathering with torches, though it is broad daylight.

resolutions.label: turn the mob away from the churchyard

success.body: You go out to meet them. They are frightened men, not wicked ones, and you talk to them about the fever, which has killed half the valley, and about their own daughters. At last the blacksmith, who seems to lead them, puts down his torch. "If she is a revenant," he says, "she is a very quiet one." They go home. Before you leave, you persuade Tegwen's mother to come to the churchyard. That is a harder thing, but when she sees her daughter singing in the sun, she weeps, and goes to her.

failure.body: You go out to meet them, but they are frightened men, and frightened men do not listen. They push past you into the churchyard. You fight them off, and in the struggle, a torch falls onto the dry grass. When the smoke clears, Tegwen is gone. You search for her for a day, and do not find her.

resolutions.label: take her away from the valley before the mob comes

success.body: You lift Tegwen onto your saddle, shroud and all, and ride out through the back of the churchyard just as the torches come in at the front. She laughs all the way. "I have never ridden a horse," she says. "Do the dead ride horses?" You take her to a convent three valleys away, where the nuns have seen fevers before and are not frightened. After a month, she writes you a letter. *I have decided I am alive after all*, it says. *It is more interesting.*

failure.body: You lift Tegwen onto your saddle and ride out through the back of the churchyard, but your horse takes fright at her shroud and throws you both into a ditch. The mob catches up. They take Tegwen away, and you do not know where, and nobody will tell you.

entries.body: You gather up the mantle. It is warm to the touch, and very light. "Good," says Morgan. "Now I owe you." She kisses her fingertips and blows the kiss at you, and you feel it land on your cheek like a snowflake.

resolutions.label: carry the mantle to Camelot and deliver it

success.body: It is a long ride, and the mantle grows heavier every mile. At night it whispers. You keep it wrapped in sacking and do not unwrap it. At Camelot, you lay it before the king, and as he stoops to lift it, the Lady of the Lake, who is visiting court, puts out her hand. "Let the bearer wear it first," she says. You shake your head. "I carried it," you say, "I did not make it." The Lady drapes it over a tree in the courtyard, and the tree burns to ash. Arthur embraces you. Morgan, you hear later, laughed when she heard.

failure.body: It is a long ride, and the mantle grows heavier every mile. At night it whispers, and on the fourth night you unwrap it to see what it says. You wake the next morning in a ditch with blistered hands and no mantle, and your horse is standing at a distance, trembling. Somewhere, you are sure, Morgan is laughing.

resolutions.label: ward the mantle with salt and prayer as you ride

success.body: You wrap the mantle in sacking and sprinkle it with salt every night, and say the old words over it, and it stops whispering. At Camelot, you lay it down and tell the High King exactly what you did, and why. The Lady of the Lake, who is at court, unwraps it with a stick and throws it into the fire, and the fire leaps to the rafters. The High King gives you a horse. Morgan, you hear, is furious that the salt worked.

failure.body: You wrap the mantle in sacking and sprinkle it with salt, but on the fourth night the salt runs out, and the mantle whispers until dawn. In the morning, your hands are blistered where you touched it, and your horse will not come near you.

entries.body: You ride to the castle gate and ask to see the Lady Ettarde. She receives you in her hall with her ladies about her. She is very lovely and very bored. "Pelleas," she says, before you can speak. "You have come about Pelleas. Everyone does."

resolutions.label: speak for Pelleas with honesty and grace

success.body: You do not praise Pelleas. You tell her plainly that he is a fool, and that he has lain in the wet grass for a month for her sake, and that most ladies go their whole lives without being loved so badly. Ettarde laughs, despite herself. "So badly," she repeats. She goes to the window and looks down at him for a long time. "Tell him," she says at last, "that he may come to supper. Once. And if he brings that circlet back, I may wear it." You are not sure that you have done Pelleas a kindness. He is sure.

failure.body: You praise Pelleas's courage and his skill and his devotion, and with every word Ettarde's lip curls further. "If he is so fine," she says, "why does he need a stranger to say so?" Her knights escort you out, and that night they beat Pelleas harder than ever.

resolutions.label: win Ettarde for him with a love-charm

success.body: You go down to the stream at dusk and gather the herbs an old woman once told you about, and bind them with a thread from Pelleas's surcoat, and leave them on the lady's windowsill. In the morning, Ettarde looks out of her window at the man in the grass, and something in her face softens. She sends her maid to bring him in. You are not sure you have done a good thing. Pelleas is sure.

failure.body: You gather the herbs and leave them on the lady's windowsill. In the morning, Ettarde looks out of her window and falls deeply in love with the first man she sees, who is her steward. Pelleas is heartbroken all over again.

entries.body: You slip down the cellar stairs in your stockinged feet and crouch behind a row of barrels.

resolutions.label: overhear the traitors' plot unseen

success.body: You hear it all: Sir Maldred is to leave the postern gate of Carleon unbarred on Midsummer Night, and King Lot's men will come through it and seize the young king in his bed. The steward is to be paid a hundred marks and a castle in Lothian. You creep back up the stairs and ride for Camelot. On Midsummer Night, King Lot's men come through the postern, and find it guarded by a hundred of the king's knights. Maldred flees north. The High King thanks you in person.

failure.body: You crouch behind the barrels, but you knock one with your elbow, and it rolls. Every man in the cellar draws his sword. You flee up the stairs and out into the night, and you have heard nothing worth hearing.

resolutions.label: read the traitor's face at the tavern door

success.body: You do not go down. You sit by the cellar door with your ale and watch each man as he comes up, and listen to what they say on the stairs when they think the room is empty. By midnight you have it: the postern gate, Midsummer Night, a hundred marks for Sir Maldred. You ride for Camelot. On Midsummer Night, King Lot's men come through the postern and find a hundred of the king's knights waiting.

failure.body: You sit by the cellar door and watch each man come up. Sir Maldred watches you back. By the time you leave, he has two men following you.

entries.body: "There is a king," you say, "and there is a fool. It is not for us to decide which is which." The steward looks relieved. "The flask," he says. "The flask came from a pedlar at the fair."

resolutions.label: find the cure for the enchanted flask

success.body: You find the pedlar at the next fair and persuade him, with some difficulty, to tell you what was in the flask. It was a love potion, badly made. The cure is to drink from the flask again, both at once, looking the other way. You bring the flask back and make the king and the fool drink from it back to back. They wake up in their right minds, in each other's clothes. The king is appalled. The fool is sorry. But the king, you notice, does not raise the taxes again. "I have had a lesson," he says, "in being a fool."

failure.body: You find the pedlar at the next fair, but he will not tell you what was in the flask, and he sells you another one instead, which he swears is the cure. It is not. When the king and the fool drink it, they both think they are the Bishop of Hereford, and the steward will not speak to you again.

resolutions.label: turn the flask's enchantment back on itself

success.body: You ask for the flask and sniff it: sweet, and green, and wrong. You pour water into it and speak over it the words for undoing, and make the king and the fool each take a sip from it, back to back, at midnight. They wake in their right minds and in each other's clothes. The king is appalled. The fool is sorry. But the king does not raise the taxes again. "I have had a lesson," he says, "in being a fool."

failure.body: You speak the words for undoing over the flask and make them each take a sip. In the morning, the king thinks he is a goose. The fool still thinks he is king. The steward will not speak to you.

entries.body: You look at the stone, and the mist, and at Morgan. "Your spell," you say, "is cruel." "Yes," she says. "Try to break it."

resolutions.label: unmake the Valley of No Return

success.body: You kneel at the stone and read its words, and read them again, and find the flaw: *whoever has been false in love*. You call out into the mist the name of every knight you know is dancing there, and remind each one of the lady he left, and why. One by one, they stop dancing, and weep, and walk out. The mist thins, and tears, and is gone. Morgan watches, with a cherry halfway to her mouth. "That," she says, "was not how it was meant to be broken." She gives you a green sash, woven with her own hands, and tells you to go away.

failure.body: You kneel at the stone and try to read its spell, and the words crawl on the stone like ants, and you cannot. The mist reaches out and takes you. You dance for a week.

resolutions.label: walk the valley's edge and call each dancer home by name

success.body: You do not try to unmake the spell. You walk round the edge of the valley, outside the mist, and call into it, one by one, the names of the knights you know are dancing there, and with each name, the name of the lady he left, and why he should go back to her. One by one, they stop dancing, and weep, and walk out. The mist thins, and tears, and is gone. Morgan watches. "That," she says, "was not how it was meant to be broken." She gives you a green sash and tells you to go away.

failure.body: You walk round the valley calling names, and the mist reaches out and takes you. You dance for a week.

entries.body: You take Tegau aside where the carter cannot hear. "The king means to propose," you tell her. "He is kind, but he is old, and I think your heart lies elsewhere." She glances at the carter, then back at you. "It does," she says, "and if I refuse a king, my father will lose the mill."

resolutions.label: help Tegau and her carter find a way out

success.body: Between you, you hatch a plan. When the king arrives on his reluctant horse, he finds Tegau with her hair full of flour and her teeth blacked with soot, cackling at nothing. He goes very pale, makes his excuses and flees. A week later Tegau marries her carter, and the king, much relieved, sends them a wedding gift of a cartwheel with silver spokes. "Poor mad girl," he tells everyone. "I was lucky to escape." Tegau sends you a loaf every Easter for the rest of your life.

failure.body: Between you, you hatch a plan. When the king arrives, he finds Tegau with her hair full of flour and her teeth blacked with soot, cackling at nothing. Unfortunately, the carter bursts out laughing in the middle of it. The king looks from one to the other and then at you, and understands everything. "In the romances," he says stiffly, "the knight does not lie to the king." He rides off. You are left with a carter, a sooty miller's daughter and a lesson in keeping a straight face.

resolutions.label: persuade the king to give up the match

success.body: You ride back to Leodegrance and tell him, gently, that Tegau loves another man. "She fears you, my lord," you say, "because you are a king. If you release her, she will bless your name." The old king is silent for a long moment. Then he takes off his tight new doublet with a sigh of relief. "Tell her I release her," he says, "and that I will stand godfather to her first child." He fetches out a flagon of good wine, and the two of you drink it on the roadside while his horse finally kneels, of its own accord, to eat the grass.

failure.body: You ride back to Leodegrance and tell him that Tegau loves another man. The old king goes purple. "A carter? A carter?" He mounts his horse at the first attempt, which surprises you both, and gallops off to the mill. By the time you catch up, the carter is locked in the village stocks and Tegau is in tears. You spend a long day talking the king down, and he releases the man at last, but nobody in that village thanks you.

entries.body: You slip away from the uproar and go to the kitchens, where the apples came from.

resolutions.label: uncover the true poisoner

success.body: The cook remembers that one knight came into the kitchen that morning and asked to see the apples: Sir Pinel le Savage. You find Sir Pinel packing his saddlebags in a hurry. Under his shirt, you find a phial with a few drops of a grey liquid. He meant the apple for another knight, he confesses, who killed his cousin. Not for poor Patrise. He weeps. You bring him before the court, and the queen is cleared. Sir Mador asks her pardon on his knees.

failure.body: You go to the kitchens, but the cook is terrified and will not talk. By the time you find anything, Sir Pinel has fled. The queen goes to trial with no champion and no proof.

resolutions.label: find the poison's name in the apple itself

success.body: You take the bitten apple from the table before anyone thinks to throw it away, and cut it open. There is a grey powder packed into a hole bored by the stalk. You smell it: wolfsbane, ground fine. Only one knight at the feast keeps wolfsbane, for the wolves on his lands in the north: Sir Pinel le Savage. You find him packing his saddlebags in a hurry. The queen is cleared. Sir Mador asks her pardon on his knees.

failure.body: You cut the apple open and find a grey powder, and do not know what it is. By the time a physician tells you, the knight who keeps wolfsbane has fled.

entries.body: You take her hand. It is cool and light, like a leaf. "I accept," you say. Tryamour's smile, for a moment, is quite real.

resolutions.label: keep faith with the fay lady's condition

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: It is the sweetest year of your life. She comes to you whenever you are alone. The purse never empties. But at a feast at Camelot, a lady mocks you for having no sweetheart, and you nearly speak, nearly, and bite your tongue until it bleeds. You say nothing. That night, Tryamour comes to you and kisses your bleeding mouth. "That," she says, "is why I chose you." She gives you a ring to remember her by, because she is going home under the hill. "You kept it," she says. "Nobody keeps it."

failure.body: It is the sweetest month of your life. Then, at a feast, a lady mocks you for having no sweetheart, and before you can stop yourself, you say, "I have a love more beautiful than any queen." You know as soon as you have said it. That night, she does not come. The purse is empty. The horse is lame.

entries.body: You grin. "There is an old trick," you say. "The fair folk cannot bear the smell of iron."

resolutions.label: outwit the fair folk

success.body: That night, you help Brother Fychan nail horseshoes to every corner of his cell, and put an iron pot over the chimney. In the morning, the cell is exactly where he left it, and there are tiny angry footprints all round it in the dew. The hermit is delighted. For good measure you hang a string of iron nails across the door. The fair folk leave him alone after that. They do not, however, leave you alone, and for a week you keep finding your boots on the wrong feet.

failure.body: That night, you help Brother Fychan nail horseshoes to every corner of his cell. In the morning, the cell is exactly where he left it. The meadow is not. You wake up, both of you, in the cell, on top of a mountain three counties away.

entries.body: You dismount and walk up the pass toward the wyvern, with your shield up and your sword drawn.

resolutions.label: fight the wyvern on the mountain pass

success.body: The wyvern drops its goat and comes at you, stinging and snapping. You take the sting on your shield, and the barb goes through it and stops a finger's width from your arm. You cut off its tail. It screams and takes to the air, and flies away over the mountain, trailing black blood. The refugees file past you, one by one, and every one of them touches your arm as they go. You find the boy on the far side of the rock, alive, clinging to a ledge.

failure.body: The wyvern drops its goat and comes at you. Its sting goes through your shield and into your arm. You fall, and the poison burns. The refugees drag you back down the pass. You are sick for a week, and they have to go back into the valley.

resolutions.label: shoot the wyvern from cover as it feeds

success.body: You leave your horse and creep up through the rocks with a borrowed bow until you are thirty paces from the wyvern, which is busy with its goat. Your first arrow takes it in the eye. It screams and flaps into the air, lurching, and flies away over the mountain, trailing black blood. The refugees file past you one by one, and every one touches your arm. You find the boy on a ledge, alive.

failure.body: You creep up through the rocks with a bow, and a stone rolls under your foot. The wyvern looks round. Your arrow bounces off its hide, and its sting does not.

entries.body: You step into the bower and bow to the Fay Queen. "Your majesty," you say, "a fine creature. But does he sing?" Titania smiles dreamily. "Like a nightingale," she says. The weaver brays.

resolutions.label: persuade the Fay Queen to part with her donkey

success.body: You tell her that a creature so fine needs a proper stable, with a trough of best hay and a mortal wife to groom him, and that there is one waiting just outside the wood. You describe the stable in such glowing detail that the Queen, enchanted as she is, becomes quite anxious for his comfort. She sends him out of the wood with a garland round his neck. His wife is waiting. By the next morning, the spell has worn off, and he is a weaver again, and he says he had the most wonderful dream.

failure.body: You tell her that a creature so fine needs a proper stable. The Fay Queen agrees completely, and asks you to be his stable-boy. It is three days before she tires of you, and you are allowed to go, smelling strongly of hay.

entries.body: You take the bucket out of Crach's hands. "Not today," you say. Crach glares at you. "Oh, very well," he says. "You tell him, then. See if he thanks you."

resolutions.label: warn Sir Kay and turn the joke

success.body: You find Kay in the buttery and tell him, and Kay turns purple, and then he thinks. "Crach," he says. "Still bitter about the boots." He is silent a moment. "They were very good boots." At the feast, Kay steps up to carve the swan, and then, instead, he calls Crach up to carve it for him, in front of the High King. Crach walks up, sees the grease too late, and sits down in the swan. The hall roars. Kay helps him up and gives him his old position back. "You are a better fool," he says, "than the bishop deserves."

failure.body: You find Kay in the buttery and tell him about the grease. Kay does not believe you. "Crach is in Winchester," he says, "and you are wasting my time." At the feast, Kay sits down in the swan. Afterwards, somebody tells him you knew. He does not speak to you for a year.

entries.body: You unbuckle your sword and kneel beside him on the rock. He looks at you in surprise. "You have no need," he says. "Everyone has need," you say.

resolutions.label: share the knight's vigil and penance

success.body: You pray beside him for three days and nights, without food. On the third night, the sound of the waterfall changes, and there is a light in the water like a lamp behind a curtain, and a smell of roses. Sir Melias drops his scourge. Neither of you sees anything. Neither of you needs to. In the morning, he puts on his armour, very slowly, and thanks you, and goes back to the quest. You feel light and clean, and very hungry.

failure.body: You pray beside him for three days. On the third day, you faint from hunger, and when you wake, Sir Melias is feeding you broth and looking at you with great pity. "It is not for everyone," he says. You ride away ashamed.

entries.body: You sit down beside Queen Morgause. She pours you wine, and looks at you over the rim of her cup with laughing eyes.

resolutions.label: court the Queen of Orkney

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You talk with her all evening, and she laughs at your jokes, and tells you stories about the old Orkney kings that make you blush. King Lot does not seem to mind; he is busy with his wine and his sons. At the end of the evening, Morgause gives you a brooch from her gown. "Come back to Orkney," she says, "when my husband is away." You are not sure whether she means it. You are not sure you want to find out.

partial.body: You talk with her all evening, and she is amused, but only just. "You are sweet," she says, and turns to talk to someone else.

failure.body: You talk with her all evening, and King Lot notices. He does not seem to mind until the end, when he throws you out of his hall.

entries.body:
Morgan stops laughing. "Ah," she says. "You. You carried my mantle once. You owe me a favour." She holds out a sword in a jewelled scabbard. It looks exactly like Excalibur. "My brother's sword is at Camelot. Take this one there, and put it in its place, and bring the real one to a knight called Accolon, at the Fountain of the Two Sycamores. That is all. Then we are quits."

She is still smiling. The four knights are watching you.

resolutions.label: decide how to pay Morgan's debt

notes: Lose Story Token #13

success.body: You look at the false sword. Then you look at Morgan. "No," you say. "Ask me for anything else." Her face goes still. For a long moment you think she will kill you. Then she laughs, and throws the false sword into the lake. "Very well," she says. "I will ask you for something else. One day." She frees the four knights, because she is bored of them, and sends you away. You are not quits. But you are not a traitor either.

notes: Lose Story Token #13

partial.body: You take the false sword and ride away, and throw it in the first river you come to. Morgan will know. You will be paying for it for a long time.

notes: Lose Story Token #13

failure.body: You take the false sword to Camelot, and make the exchange, and carry Excalibur to Accolon. You do not know, until the High King nearly dies fighting Accolon with a sword that breaks, what you have done.

entries.body: You take an egg and go and sit beside the young monk. He does not look at you.

resolutions.label: persuade the starving monk to eat

success.body: You do not tell him to eat. You tell him about the Pentecost feast at Camelot, when the Grail passed through the hall, and how every knight found before him the food he loved best. "The Grail feeds," you say. "It does not starve." Brother Idwal looks at you for a long time. Then he looks at the egg. He takes it, and eats it, and weeps, and the whole table cheers.

failure.body: You tell him about the Pentecost feast, and the food. He listens, and then he turns away. "It fed them," he says, "because they had earned it." He does not eat.

entries.body: You kneel on the stone. Heledd waits, ladle in hand. The pilgrims fall silent to listen.

resolutions.label: confess your deeds openly and honestly

notes: You may remove 1 unwanted Status Card

success.body: You tell her the truth, all of it: the deeds you are proud of and the ones you are not. It takes a long time. When you finish, the old queen hands you the ladle. The water is cold enough to hurt your teeth, and it tastes of iron and moss. You feel every ache you have gathered on the road simply leave you. Heledd nods. "That was well done," she says. "It is harder than fighting." Behind you, several of the pilgrims who had turned to go come back to the line.

failure.body: You tell her the truth, but not all of it. There is one deed you leave out, and you think nobody notices. Heledd hands you the ladle. The water tastes of nothing at all. "The well knows," she says quietly, "even when I do not." You rise and leave the line, and the pilgrims part to let you through.

entries.body: You pull him up across your saddle and lead your horse down the pass, into the teeth of the blizzard.

resolutions.label: bring the freezing messenger down through the blizzard

success.body: You walk all night, leading your horse, with the messenger across the saddle and your own feet going numb. At dawn, you reach a shepherd's hut, and build a fire, and rub his hands and feet until he screams with the pain of them warming. He lives. He looks at you for a long time. Then he gives you the satchel. "Take them," he says. "I will not carry them again. I will tell Mordred the snow took them." You take them to the old king's men.

failure.body: You walk all night, leading your horse, with the messenger across your saddle. Near dawn, he stops shivering. When you reach the shepherd's hut, he is dead. You take the letters. They are small comfort.

resolutions.label: find shelter from the blizzard before you both freeze

success.body: You do not try to go down. You look for the shepherd's signs instead: the lie of the snow, the stunted rowan that grows beside rocks, the smell of old smoke. Within the hour, you find a stone hut half-buried in snow. You get the messenger inside and build a fire and rub his hands and feet until he screams. He lives. In the morning, he gives you the satchel. "I will not carry them again," he says.

failure.body: You look for the shepherd's signs, and the snow hides them all. You walk in circles until dawn. The messenger does not wake.

entries.body: "Every beast has a bane," you say. "Find me a weasel." The frightened face stares at you. "A weasel?" "And a cockerel," you say.

resolutions.label: use the old lore to trap the basilisk

success.body: The bestiaries say that the basilisk dies at a cockerel's crow and fears the weasel above all things. You lower the weasel down the well in a basket and set the cockerel on the well-head. At noon, the cockerel crows, and something in the well screams, and the weasel comes up in the basket, very pleased with itself, and the basilisk does not come up at all. The three stone men turn back into men. You give the weasel to the mayor's daughter, who names it after you.

failure.body: You lower a weasel down the well in a basket and set a cockerel on the well-head. At noon, the cockerel does not crow. It looks at the well, and turns to stone. So does the weasel. You decide the bestiaries were written by men who never met a basilisk.

entries.body: "Let the man go," you say. Grace looks at you for a long moment. "And have him bring the sheriff?" she says. "I think not."

resolutions.label: rescue the customs man from the sea-cave

success.body: You go back up the cliff as if you are leaving, and come down again by a goat-path at the far end of the beach, where the tide is still out. The back of the cave is dark. You find the customs man tied to a post and cut him free, and lead him out the back way, round the rocks, just as the tide turns. He is a small, frightened man called Master Colley. He is very grateful. You make him promise to take only a tenth next time. He promises. You think he might even mean it.

failure.body: You come down by a goat-path at the far end of the beach and creep into the back of the cave. But the tide comes in faster than you expected, and by the time you have cut the customs man loose, the only way out is through the smugglers. Grace grins at you. "Evening again, sir knight," she says.

resolutions.label: claim the customs man's life as a knight's due

success.body: "Mistress Penhale," you say, "I am a knight, and I have seen your faces, and I have seen your wine. I will forget both, if you give me the customs man. Or I will remember both, at the sheriff's." Grace looks at you for a long moment, then laughs. "An honest bargain," she says. She sends the customs man out blindfolded, and gives you a barrel for your forgetting. You make him promise to take only a tenth next time.

failure.body: You offer Grace your silence for the customs man. She thinks about it. "Or," she says, "I could have two customs men." You are tied up next to him until the tide goes out.

entries.body: You ride between the hound and the hare and scoop the trembling beast up in your arms. Kay splutters with rage. "That is my squire!" he says. "And my supper!"

resolutions.label: break the fay spell on the boy

success.body: You carry the hare to the well where Madoc insulted the fay lady, and set him down on the edge of it, and call politely for her to come. She comes, in a ripple of water, and looks at the hare with some satisfaction. You apologise on the boy's behalf with every courtesy you know. The fay lady laughs and tips water from the well over the hare's head, and Madoc sits there, dripping and naked, and begins to apologise for himself. Kay rides off in disgust, calling for a new supper.

failure.body: You carry the hare to the well where Madoc insulted the fay lady, and call for her. She comes, in a ripple of water, and looks at you and at the hare. "Your friend called me a milkmaid," she says. "What will you call me?" You call her *lady*, which is the wrong answer. When you ride away from the well, you are wearing long brown ears, and they are not coming off until morning.

resolutions.label: plead with Sir Kay for his squire's life

success.body: You remind Kay that Madoc has been his squire for five years, and polished his armour, and fetched his wine, and laughed at his jokes. "Somebody has to," you say. Kay snorts. But he looks at the hare for a long moment. "Oh, very well," he says. "I suppose I should be sorry if the dogs got him." He sends for a wise woman instead, who turns Madoc back with a bowl of milk and a great deal of scolding. Kay pretends not to care, and is gruffly kind to the boy for a whole week.

failure.body: You remind Kay that Madoc has been his squire for five years. "Yes," says Kay. "And he has been a hare for one week, and a better hare than squire." He lets the dogs go. You never find out whether the wizards were right, because the hare outruns them all and vanishes into the wood. Kay is furious with you for the rest of the summer.

entries.body: "My lord," you say, "you are a great king. That is why the young king needs you." Lot laughs. "Needs me? He needs a nursemaid. Go on, then. Tell me why I should kneel."

resolutions.label: persuade Lot that a united Britain needs him

success.body: You talk long into the night, by the fire outside his pavilion. You speak of Saxon ships on the east coast, of the Irish in the west, and of Orkney's sons, who will inherit whatever Lot leaves them. At that, the king goes quiet. "My boys," he says. "They would like him, I think. They like everyone." He does not agree to kneel, but he agrees to hold his army back until after harvest. You carry his terms to Camelot, and for one summer, at least, no one dies.

failure.body: You talk long into the night, by the fire outside his pavilion. But every time you mention the young king, Lot hears Uther's name, and his temper rises. At last he throws his cup into the fire. "Get out," he says, "before I remember that you came here as his friend." You leave with the whole camp jeering at your back.

resolutions.label: remind Lot of Merlin's prophecy of his death

success.body: "Merlin says," you tell him, "that the king who rises against the boy will die at the hand of a king who keeps a beast." Lot laughs, but his laugh is too loud. He knows the prophecy. Everyone does. You talk quietly, of his sons and his lands and his long life, and of how little a crown helps a dead man. At the end, Lot sends his levies home for the winter. "Not because of your wizard," he says. "Because of my boys."

failure.body: "Merlin says," you tell him, "that the king who rises against the boy will die." Lot's face goes cold. "Then Merlin can come and kill me himself," he says, "instead of sending messengers." You leave the camp to the sound of axes being sharpened.

entries.body: You take the sword from Sir Bedivere's hands. It is heavier than any sword you have ever held. You walk to the water's edge.

resolutions.label: throw Excalibur into the lake

success.body: You look at the sword for a long moment. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen. Then you throw it, with all your strength, out over the water. It wheels in the air, flashing. An arm in white samite rises from the lake and catches it by the hilt, and brandishes it three times, and draws it under. When you turn round, the old king is smiling. "Well done," he says. "The first time." The three queens lift him into the barge, and it goes out into the mist.

failure.body: You look at the sword, and you cannot. You hide it in the reeds and come back. "What did you see?" asks the old king. "The wind on the water," you say. His face twists with grief. "You have lied to me," he says. In the end, Sir Bedivere throws it. The hand rises and takes it. The old king does not look at you again.

resolutions.label: throw it true with a strength not your own

success.body: The sword is so heavy that you can barely lift it above your head, and your arms are shaking from the battle. You pray, once, and throw. It wheels out over the lake, flashing, farther than any man could throw it, and an arm in white samite rises out of the water and catches it by the hilt, and brandishes it three times, and draws it under. When you turn round, the old king is smiling. "Well done," he says. "The first time."

failure.body: The sword is so heavy you can barely lift it. You throw, and it falls in the reeds at the water's edge. Sir Bedivere wades in and throws it for you. The arm rises and takes it. The old king does not look at you.

entries.body: "Further up," you say. "Let me see what they have left behind." The old fisherman grins and turns the boat north, round the headland, to a cove under the cliff.

resolutions.label: climb the cliff and take Dover castle from behind

success.body: You climb the chalk cliff with a dozen fishermen behind you, by a smugglers' path the old man knows, and come out at the top behind the castle. Its garrison is on the walls, watching the beach. You open the postern gate from inside, and Mordred's flag comes down, and the old king's dragon goes up, and the army on the beach sees it and cheers. Mordred's men, finding their castle taken behind them, fall back from Dover in disorder.

failure.body: You climb the chalk cliff with the fishermen behind you, but halfway up the path crumbles and two men fall. By the time you reach the top, the garrison is waiting. You flee back down the cliff, and watch the landing from the cove.

entries.body:
You rein in at the edge of the clearing. It is not your quarrel.

The knight in red strikes. The knight in white falls. The knight in red unlaces his dead opponent's helm, and cries out, and falls to his knees. They were brothers. He is still kneeling there when you ride away.
"I will fetch a physician," you say. Father Mabon nods. "The nearest is the Abbey of Saint Asaph," he says. "Three days' ride. Two, if you do not sleep."

resolutions.label: ride to the abbey and back without rest

success.body: You ride through the night, and the next day, and the next night. At the abbey, you drag the infirmarian out of his bed and put him on a fresh horse, and you ride back. It takes you four days in all. When you arrive, Father Mabon is still on his feet, but only just. The infirmarian knows what to do. Of the thirty sick, eighteen live. The infirmarian says it would have been none, without you.

failure.body: You ride through the night, and at dawn, your horse falls, exhausted, and cannot get up. You walk the rest of the way. By the time you reach the abbey and return with the infirmarian, it has been a week, and there is nobody left in the barn to cough.

entries.body: You stand before the high table. The hall goes quiet. You take a breath.

resolutions.label: hold the court spellbound with your tale

success.body: You tell them of your adventures, and you tell them well: the fights and the fair ladies and the strange things on the roads. You leave out nothing that is true, and add nothing that is not. The hall listens with its mouth open. When you finish, the young king claps his hands, and the whole court cheers, and Sir Kay falls on the swan. The king calls you to sit at his right hand for the feast.

partial.body: You tell them of your adventures. The court listens politely. It is not quite a marvel, the king says, but it will do. Sir Kay falls on the swan.

failure.body: You tell them of your adventures. The court yawns. Halfway through, the doors fly open and a damsel on a white palfrey rides into the hall with a real marvel, and nobody listens to you any more.

entries.body: "You have tried to kill him four times," you say. "Why should I trust you with him now?" Morgan's face goes very still.

resolutions.label: test the truth of Morgan's grief

success.body: You ask her questions, and she answers them. Why now? Because he is dying, and she does not want him to die. Why Avalon? Because it is the only place where he might live. What does she want? Nothing. She wants nothing. You look into her face for a long time, and you believe her. "Go, then," you say. "I will tell no one." She laughs, a little brokenly. "Nobody would believe you," she says.

failure.body: You ask her questions, and she answers them, and you do not believe a word. She sees it. "Then go," she says, "and tell them all. And when he dies on the plain, and there is no barge, remember it was you."

resolutions.label: ask her to swear on something she loves

success.body: "Swear it," you say, "on something you love." Morgan looks at you for a long time. Then she says, very quietly, "On my brother." You believe her. "Go, then," you say. "I will tell no one." She laughs, a little brokenly. "Nobody would believe you," she says. When you leave, the barge is ready, and she is sitting on the shore beside it, alone.

failure.body: "Swear it," you say, "on something you love." Morgan laughs. "I love nothing," she says. "You know that." You ride away, and you do not know whether she lied.

entries.body: You kneel beside Iddo and look into the trough. There is nothing in it but water and a drowned beetle. "Tell me exactly what you saw," you say.

resolutions.label: judge the truth of the vision

success.body: You question him closely, and his answers are strange and simple: not what a boy would invent. The light was not gold but white. There was no voice. He did not see a cup, only a covering of white cloth. You turn to the hermit. "Did you see it covered," you ask, "or bare?" The hermit stops shouting. After a long moment, he kneels down beside the squire and begins, very quietly, to weep. The villagers put down their stones. Iddo gives you his hand. "Thank you for believing me," he says.

failure.body: You question him closely, and his answers become more confused the more you ask. Did the light speak? Perhaps it did. Was the vessel gold? It might have been. In the end, even Iddo does not know what he saw. The hermit is triumphant, and the villagers drive the squire out of the village with sticks. You cannot tell, riding away, whether you have helped a liar or failed a saint.

resolutions.label: keep vigil with Iddo by the trough through the night

success.body: You and the squire kneel by the trough all night, while the village sleeps. Nothing happens until the first grey light. Then, for a single breath, the water shines white, and the beetle is gone, and there is a scent of roses. The hermit, who has stayed to watch you, falls on his face. In the morning, the village builds a little shrine over the trough. Iddo will not stay to be made a saint. He rides away with his master, saying nothing, looking very happy.

failure.body: You and the squire kneel by the trough all night. Nothing happens. At dawn Iddo looks into the water, then at you, and his face crumples. "It was real," he says. "It was." You ride away with his grief in your ears, and do not know whether you were unworthy to see it, or whether there was nothing to see.

entries.body: "How do they wake?" you ask. The old man smiles. "When someone reminds them," he says, "what they were looking for."

resolutions.label: wake the sleeping knights of the quest

success.body: You walk among the sleeping knights and kneel beside each one and speak into his ear. You speak of the Grail, and of the hall at Pentecost, and the oath they swore. One by one, they stir, and open their eyes, and look round in horror. Twelve knights come with you to your ship. Some of them have been asleep for three years. They go on with the quest. They thank you all the way.

partial.body: You walk among the sleeping knights and speak into their ears. Three of them wake. The rest smile, and turn over, and sleep on.

failure.body: You walk among the sleeping knights and speak into their ears. None of them wake. The fruit smells very good. You leave quickly.

entries.body: You stay aboard and sail out toward the Sands with every lantern lit.

resolutions.label: guide the fleet away from the Sands

success.body: You sail up and down the edge of the Sands all night, with every lantern blazing and your crew shouting through speaking-trumpets. The Calais fleet sees you and steers clear. At dawn, every ship is past the Sands. The fishermen of Dover tell the story for years.

failure.body: You sail up and down the edge of the Sands, but the tide takes you onto them yourself. By dawn, you are aground, and so are two of the Calais ships.

resolutions.label: pilot the fleet round the Sands by your own lore

success.body: You know the Goodwins. You bring your ship to the edge of the Sands and anchor it there, with every lantern lit, and send the ship's boat round to each of the Calais ships in turn with a man who knows the channel. By dawn, every ship is past. The fishermen of Dover tell the story for years.

failure.body: You anchor at the edge of the Sands with every lantern lit, and the anchor drags. By dawn, your ship is aground, and so are two of the Calais ships.

entries.body: "Your brother," you say. Bors closes his eyes for a moment. "God keep him," he says, and wheels his horse toward the maiden. You ride hard down the left-hand road.

resolutions.label: charge the two knights and free Sir Lionel

success.body: You come on them in a clearing and ride straight through them, scattering them into the bracken. Lionel is bruised and bloody and half-conscious, but alive. When he can speak, he asks where his brother is. You tell him. Lionel's face darkens. "He left me," he says, "for a stranger." You get him home, and Bors comes back that evening with the maiden safe. The two brothers do not speak. But Lionel lives, and the maiden lives, and that is two more than the crossroads meant to allow.

failure.body: You come on them in a clearing and charge, but your horse stumbles on a root, and you go down in the bracken. By the time you are up, the two knights have gone, and Lionel with them. You follow their track until it is dark and lose it in a stream. When you find Bors, he has saved the maiden. He looks at your face and asks nothing.

resolutions.label: track them into the wood and free Lionel by stealth

success.body: You follow the trail of broken thorn to a charcoal-burner's hut, where the two knights have tied Lionel to a post and are arguing over his ransom. You wait until they are drunk, cut through the back wall of the hut with your dagger, and bring Lionel out on your shoulder. When Bors comes to find you, the brothers embrace. "God sent you," says Bors, and Lionel, for once, does not argue.

failure.body: You follow the trail of broken thorn to a charcoal-burner's hut. But the two knights have left a man on watch, and he sees you coming. You fight him, but by the time he is down, the other two have fled with their prisoner into the dark. You resolve to watch a camp longer before you go in.

entries.body: "Can it be unmade?" you ask. The dwarf shakes his head. "Not unmade. But perhaps quieted."

resolutions.label: quench the sword's voice

success.body: You and the dwarf work through the night. You tell him what you know of the old words for binding and quenching, and he heats the sword white-hot, and at midnight you plunge it together into a trough of water from a holy well, while you speak the binding. There is a scream of steam, and then silence. The sword lies in the trough, grey and plain and perfectly quiet. The dwarf lifts it out and weighs it in his hand. "Still sharp," he says. He gives you a dagger from the same steel, and it never sings at all.

failure.body: You and the dwarf work through the night, and at midnight you plunge the sword into a trough of holy water. There is a scream of steam, and then the sword is singing louder than ever, and now it knows your name.

resolutions.label: work the forge all night to reforge the blade

success.body: You and the dwarf work through the night at the forge. You pump the bellows until your arms are dead, and he hammers the blade flat, and folds it, and hammers it again, and the song grows fainter with every fold. At dawn, it is silent, and very sharp. The dwarf lays it on the anvil and weeps. "My best work," he says, "and it will never say a word." He gives you a dagger from the same steel.

failure.body: You pump the bellows all night, but near dawn your strength fails, and the fire cools, and the blade cracks in the quench. It sings one last time, a terrible note, and is silent. The dwarf does not speak to you.

entries.body: "You are not ready to go home," you say gently. "Not yet." Marrok growls, but he does not attack you. You think, perhaps, he knows you are right.

resolutions.label: draw the last of the wolf out of him

success.body: You build a fire of rowan wood and sit with him through a long night, burning dock leaves and speaking the old words over him that a wise woman once taught you. Toward dawn he shudders violently, and something grey and shadowy slips out of him and runs away into the trees. Marrok's eyes are brown. He weeps for a long while. Then he says, "I think I will not go home after all. I think I will go to the Round Table instead," and he does.

failure.body: You build a fire of rowan wood and sit with him through a long night, speaking the old words over him. Toward dawn he shudders violently, and something grey and shadowy slips out of him and runs straight into you. You spend the next three days snarling at your own horse. Marrok, now fully a man, nurses you through it, and is very apologetic.

resolutions.label: keep him in the woods until he is himself

success.body: You camp with him in the woods for a week. You hunt together, and he is a better hunter than you. You cook the meat, and after the first day, he eats it cooked. By the end of the week he no longer drinks from streams, and his eyes have faded from yellow to hazel. "I am ready," he says. When he goes home, he does not break down the door. He knocks.

failure.body: You camp with him in the woods for a week. On the fourth night the moon is full, and Marrok is gone when you wake. You follow his tracks to his manor, and from a distance you hear the screaming. You ride away without learning how it ended.

entries.body: "You need a priest, not a stag," you say. "There is a hermitage at the edge of this forest." Eustace looks doubtful, but he goes with you.

resolutions.label: persuade the forester to make his peace

success.body: The hermit is a sharp old woman named Mother Tanwen, who was once a nun at Amesbury. She listens to Eustace's story and then asks him about every deer he has ever killed. It takes three days. At the end of it, Eustace is lighter than he has been in years. "I think I will be a gamekeeper," he says, "and not a hunter." Mother Tanwen nods. "That," she says, "is the right answer." She gives you her blessing for bringing him.

failure.body: The hermit is a sharp old woman who listens to Eustace's story and then says it was a trick of the light. Eustace is furious. He storms off into the old forest after the stag, and you never learn what he found.

resolutions.label: confess beside him, so he is not alone

success.body: At the hermitage, you kneel first, and make your own confession in front of him, and it is not a short one. Eustace listens with his mouth open. When you have finished, he kneels too, and tells the hermit about every deer he ever killed. It takes three days. At the end of it, he gives you his bow. "I will not need it," he says. "I am going to be a gamekeeper."

failure.body: At the hermitage you kneel first and begin your confession. Halfway through, Eustace gets up and walks out. "If a knight has done all that," he says, "what hope is there for me?" You have made it worse.

entries.body: You call the fishing boats together and tell them your plan.

resolutions.label: retake Tintagel from the Saxons

success.body: You come in at dawn, on the tide, with twenty fishing boats and a hundred angry Cornishmen. You land on the causeway, and the Saxons, who were expecting the villages to be frightened, find the villages coming for them. It is a hard fight in the ruins. By noon, the Saxons are in their ships, rowing away. The Cornishmen raise a cheer that echoes off the cliffs, and plant the old king's dragon on the highest wall.
