failure.body: You come in at dawn with twenty fishing boats, but the Saxons are waiting on the causeway with a shield-wall. The fishermen are brave, but not soldiers. You fall back to the boats.

resolutions.label: retake Tintagel by the sea-cave the Saxons do not know

success.body: An old fisherman knows the way: a sea-cave under the rock that climbs up into the castle's old cellar. You take twenty Cornishmen through it at low tide in the dark, and come up inside the walls while the Saxons are watching the causeway. By noon, the Saxons are in their ships, rowing away. The Cornishmen plant the old king's dragon on the highest wall.

failure.body: You take twenty Cornishmen through the sea-cave at low tide, and the tide turns faster than the old fisherman said. You come out half-drowned in the cellar, into the arms of a Saxon sentry.

entries.body: You look up at the shelves. They go up into the dark, and they sway slightly, and there is no ladder.

resolutions.label: climb Merlin's shelves to the book he needs

success.body: You climb, shelf by shelf, with books sliding out under your feet and stuffed owls staring at you. At the very top, at the very back, you find a small book bound in green leather. You climb down with it in your teeth. Merlin takes it and opens it and laughs. "My recipe for plum cake," he says. "I have been looking for this for eleven years." He cuts you a slice of plum cake that has been in a jar since the reign of Vortigern. It is very good. He also gives you a book of your own, from the bottom shelf. "You will want this," he says, "later."

failure.body: You climb, shelf by shelf, and halfway up, the shelf gives way, and you come down in an avalanche of books and bones and one very indignant owl. Merlin sighs. "I will get it myself," he says.

resolutions.label: find the book by magic rather than climbing

success.body: You do not climb. You stand at the foot of the shelves and speak the old words for finding what is lost, and a small book bound in green leather slides out of the dark at the very top and drops into your hands. Merlin stares at you, and then laughs. "My recipe for plum cake," he says. "Eleven years." He cuts you a slice that has been in a jar since Vortigern. He gives you a book of your own from the bottom shelf. "You will want this," he says.

failure.body: You speak the old words for finding, and every book on every shelf slides out at once. Merlin sighs. "I will get it myself," he says, "when you have put those back."

entries.body: "The forge," you say. The Lady nods, and leads you down, deeper, to a cavern where a great cold fire burns blue under the water.

resolutions.label: learn at the cold forge under the lake

success.body: The smiths are old women with arms like men's, and they are forging a sword. They let you work the bellows. The fire is cold as snow and burns like the sun, and as you pump, you feel the old words go into the metal. At the end of the day, the blade is finished: not Excalibur, but its little sister, a dagger, plain and very sharp. The eldest smith gives it to you. "For the day when the sword goes back," she says. You do not understand her.

failure.body: The smiths let you work the bellows, but the cold fire freezes your hands, and you drop the bellows, and the fire gutters. The eldest smith is very cross. You are sent back up to the shore.

resolutions.label: work the bellows at the cold forge until the blade is done

success.body: The smiths are old women with arms like men's, and they are forging a sword. They let you work the bellows. The fire is cold as snow and burns like the sun, and you pump until your arms are dead and your hands are blue. At the end of the day, the blade is finished: not Excalibur, but its little sister, a dagger. The eldest smith gives it to you. "For the day when the sword goes back," she says. You do not understand her.

failure.body: You pump the bellows, and the cold fire freezes your hands, and you drop the handle, and the fire gutters. The eldest smith sends you back up to the shore.

entries.body: "For eleven songs," you say, "I will lose with pleasure." Rhiannedd claps her hands. The herald enters your name, and you ride out onto the field.

resolutions.label: unhorse the two rivals and fall convincingly to Ywain

success.body: You unhorse Sir Harry on the first pass, which is not hard, and Sir Brian on the third, which is. Then you ride against Sir Ywain the Poor. He is so nervous that his lance is shaking. You angle your shield, just so, and his lance strikes it, and you throw yourself backwards off your horse with a tremendous clatter. The crowd roars. Ywain stares at you in astonishment. Rhiannedd runs out onto the field and kisses him. As you are being helped up, she winks at you over his shoulder.

failure.body: You unhorse Sir Harry on the first pass. But Sir Brian's lance takes you under the arm on the second, and you go over your horse's tail in earnest. Sir Brian goes on to beat Sir Ywain the Poor into the mud. Rhiannedd does not look at you as you are carried off.

resolutions.label: persuade her father to let the poor knight have her

success.body: Instead of entering, you take Rhiannedd's father aside, a plain, worried old lord, and tell him plainly what his daughter wants. He is surprised. "Nobody asked her," he says. "It never occurred to me." He watches Sir Ywain the Poor, who has just been thrown for the third time and is climbing back into the saddle for the fourth. "He does not give up, does he?" says the old lord. By sundown he has cancelled the final joust and announced the betrothal. Sir Harry is relieved. Sir Brian is not.

failure.body: Instead of entering, you take Rhiannedd's father aside and tell him what his daughter wants. He is furious. "My daughter," he says, "does not choose her husband. She chooses her gown." He has you escorted from the field. Sir Brian wins the tournament.

entries.body: You ride between the soldiers and the boy. "The High King swore mercy to any who ask it," you say. "He is asking."

resolutions.label: stay the soldiers' vengeance

success.body: The soldiers glare at you. But you are a knight, and they are soldiers, and the High King's oath is fresh in everyone's mind. At last they lower their spears. You take the boy with you, and at the end of the battle, you give him to the High King's own priest. Years later, you hear that a Saxon monk called Brother Eadric has founded an abbey in the Forest of Celidon, and prays every day for the knight who spared him.

failure.body: The soldiers glare at you. One of them spits, and they go, but when you turn round, the boy has run. You hear a scream from further in the forest. You do not know if it was him.

resolutions.label: ask the soldiers to pray for their dead with the boy

success.body: You kneel in the leaves between the soldiers and the Saxon boy, and ask the soldier whose brother was killed what his brother's name was. Then you pray for him, aloud, by name, and pray for the boy's dead too. After a while, the soldier kneels. Then the others. The boy kneels last. When you rise, nobody is holding a spear. Years later, a Saxon monk founds an abbey in the Forest of Celidon.

failure.body: You kneel and begin to pray for the soldier's brother. The soldier looks at the boy, and at you praying, and walks away without a word. When you look up, the boy has run.

entries.body: You take the pot from her gently and pour the hemlock out on the rock. Eluned cries out and tries to stop you. "It is not the way," you say. "Let me go to him."

resolutions.label: challenge Sir Loholt before his own household

success.body: You walk into the steward's feast and throw your gauntlet down among the dishes. "You sold a maiden to a giant for a hundred sheep," you say, loudly, so every guest can hear. The steward goes pale and calls for his sword. You fight him in the middle of his own hall, and when he falls, his household does not lift a hand for him. Then, with Eluned beside you, you go up into the hills. The giant Carnwen, it turns out, has married Eluned's sister, and is very sorry about the whole business. The sisters are reunited, weeping, in the giant's kitchen.

failure.body: You walk into the steward's feast and throw your gauntlet down among the dishes. Sir Loholt does not fight you. He shouts for his guards, and six men pile on you at once. You spend the next week in his dungeon. Eluned, you hear later, found another pot of hemlock.

resolutions.label: climb to the giant's hall and rescue the sister yourself

success.body: The giant's hall is on a crag three hours' hard climb above the castle. You make it, with Eluned beside you, by dusk. The giant Carnwen opens the door. He is very large and very worried, and Eluned's sister, standing behind him with a ladle, is not a captive at all. "He has been ever so kind," she says. "I only wanted to send word." The two sisters fall on each other's necks. Eluned throws her pot of hemlock off the crag. The steward, when he learns he has lost his hundred sheep, is inconsolable.

failure.body: The giant's hall is on a crag three hours' hard climb above the castle. Halfway up, the rock gives way under your hands, and you fall twenty feet onto a ledge. By the time you have got your breath back, it is dark, and Eluned has gone back down the mountain with her pot.

entries.body: "Lead on, my lord," you say. Pellinore's face creases into a delighted smile. "Splendid!" he cries. "Bellerus, we have a companion!" The horse does not seem pleased.

resolutions.label: chase the Questing Beast through the forest

success.body: You ride all day, through thickets and over streams, following the baying. Twice you see the beast ahead of you, and twice it vanishes. At dusk, you corner it at last in a ravine. It turns and looks at you with sad, intelligent eyes, and the baying stops. Then it leaps the ravine in one bound and is gone. Pellinore sits on his horse, breathless and grinning. "Closest I have been in three years," he says. "You have the gift. Same time next year?" He gives you a hunting horn with a questing beast carved on it.

failure.body: You ride all day, following the baying. At noon, your horse puts its foot in a rabbit hole and goes down, and you go over its head into a bramble bush. By the time you are out, Pellinore is a speck on the horizon. You hear his voice, very faint, calling "Left! Always left!"

resolutions.label: track the beast to its lair

success.body: While Pellinore gallops off after the baying, you look at the ground. The beast's feet are a hart's feet, and harts go to water at dusk. You find the pool where it drinks, and you and Pellinore wait in the rushes. At sunset it comes, and drinks, and lifts its serpent's head and looks straight at you. Pellinore does not move. After a while he whispers, "I do not want to catch it, you know. Not really. What would I do then?" The beast finishes drinking and pads away. Pellinore wipes his eyes and shakes your hand.

failure.body: While Pellinore gallops off after the baying, you look at the ground. You find hart's tracks, and follow them all afternoon, and at dusk you find a hart. An ordinary one. It looks at you in surprise and bounds away. Somewhere far off, the baying goes on.

entries.body:
You drop a coin in his bowl. "I have no riddles, old man," you say. "Only this." The beggar looks at the coin, and then at you, and his grin softens.

"No riddle? No bargain? Nothing?" He shakes his head. "They all want something. Arthur wanted a sword. Uther wanted a woman. Lot wanted a crown." He picks up the coin and turns it in his fingers. "I will give you something anyway. *A lady by a lake will ask you to hold a door. Do not.*" He stands up, and for a moment, he is very tall, and his cloak is not grey but midnight blue. "That is the riddle. You may not understand it for years." Then he is only a beggar again, limping away down the road, and your coin is back in your purse.
"I accept," you say. The Green Knight claps you on the shoulder. "Splendid!" he says.

resolutions.label: keep faith in the game of exchanges

success.body: Three days. Each day, the Green Knight goes hunting, and each day, his wife comes to your room and kisses you, once, then twice, then three times, and gives you a green sash that she says will keep you from harm. Each evening, the Green Knight gives you a deer, a boar, a fox, and you give him the kisses, one, two, three. On the third evening, you give him the sash too, though you want to keep it more than anything. He looks at it, and at you, and laughs until the rafters ring. "Nobody," he says, "has ever given back the sash." He gives it back to you. "Keep it," he says. "You earned it by giving it."

failure.body: Three days. On the third day, the lady gives you a green sash that she says will keep you from harm, and in the evening, you give the Green Knight the kisses, but not the sash. He looks at you for a long time. "You kept something back," he says. He does not say it angrily. That is the worst of it.

resolutions.label: match the Green Knight at his own hunting

success.body: You do not stay home with his lady. You ride out with the Green Knight every morning instead, and hunt beside him: the deer, the boar, the fox. Each evening, you exchange what you have won, and you have won as much as he has. On the third evening, he looks at you across the table and laughs until the rafters ring. "Nobody," he says, "has ever come hunting." He ties his own green sash round your waist. "You earned it on horseback," he says.

failure.body: You ride out hunting with the Green Knight every morning, and every evening he has won more than you. On the third, he pats your shoulder kindly. "Perhaps," he says, "you should have stayed at home."

entries.body: "I will ride with you," you say. The dwarf beams. He climbs up behind your saddle, bell and all, and you start up the pass.

resolutions.label: bring the pilgrim safe through the robbers' pass

success.body: The robbers are waiting at the top of the pass: eight men with cudgels and one with a crossbow. You charge the crossbowman first, and the rest scatter up the slopes. As they flee, Brother Ifan rings the bell. It is only a little sound, but every one of the robbers stops and turns and looks back, and one of them, the youngest, comes slowly down the slope and kneels in the road. He asks the dwarf to hear his confession. Brother Ifan does, sitting on your saddle. When you part at the far side of the pass, he rings the bell once for you.

failure.body: The robbers are waiting at the top of the pass. You charge them, but there are too many, and the crossbowman shoots your horse. In the confusion, one of them snatches the bell from the dwarf's hands. Brother Ifan sits in the road afterwards and says nothing for a long time. Then he says, "Well. It will ring for them now, I suppose."

resolutions.label: take him over the mountain by the goat track

success.body: You leave the road and lead the dwarf up a goat track that the robbers do not watch, because no robber would climb it. It takes all day, and the bell rings softly in its cloth at every step. At the top, you see the robbers far below, waiting at the pass for pilgrims who never come. On the far side, Brother Ifan rings the bell once for you, and it sounds like water.

failure.body: You lead him up the goat track, and the goat track ends at a cliff, and you have to come down the long way, through the pass, at dusk. The robbers are waiting. You get through, but the bell does not.

entries.body: You go and sit beside the young monk, and do not eat either. He looks at you in surprise.

resolutions.label: fast with the young monk until he is ready

success.body: You fast with him for three days, in the chapel, praying. On the third night, you both see it: not the Grail, but a light, very small, in the dark of the chapel, like a candle, with a smell of fresh bread. Brother Idwal laughs aloud. "It is enough," he says. "It is enough." In the morning, you eat together. It is the best breakfast of your life.

failure.body: You fast with him for three days, and on the third day, you faint. The monks carry you out. Brother Idwal stays in the chapel.

entries.body: You leave the queens in their glade and ride hard up the valley. Sir Breunor is in his orchard, trimming a pear tree. He listens to your warning with growing horror. "Three of them?" he says. "All together? I thought they did not speak."

resolutions.label: persuade Sir Breunor to make amends to the queens

success.body: "Return the horses," you tell him, "and go on your knees. And bring them pears." Breunor, who is not a bad man, only a foolish one, does exactly that. You ride with him down the valley and watch him kneel in the glade with a basket of pears and three horses on a string. The queens make him wait a long time before they forgive him. Afterwards, the Queen of Northgalis tells you that you are wasted on errantry. "You should be a steward," she says. It is a compliment, you think.

failure.body: "Return the horses," you tell him, "and go on your knees." Breunor considers this for a long moment and decides it is simpler to go to Ireland. He is gone by nightfall. When the queens hear who warned him, they send their knights after you, and you spend an uncomfortable week avoiding them.

resolutions.label: ride back with the stolen horses before the queens miss them

success.body: "Where are the horses?" you ask. Breunor points, shamefaced, at his paddock. You take all three on a leading rein and ride them back down the valley at a gallop, and lead them into the glade just as the queens are finishing their cherries. The Queen of the Out Isles claps her hands. "He is sorry!" she cries. "Look, he sent the horses!" They forgive him. You do not tell them he did not send them.

failure.body: You take all three horses on a leading rein, and at the ford, they all decide to go different ways. You arrive at the glade with one horse and no dignity. The queens laugh at you, and then send their knights after Breunor anyway.

entries.body: "Hide," you say. "This is not your war." Father Idris lets out a long breath. "Thank God," he says. "Then help us."

resolutions.label: hide the castle and its people in the marsh

success.body: You show them how to cut the causeway and float the planks away, and how to put out every light at night, and to hang reeds from the walkways so that from a distance the castle looks like a heap of drowned trees. When the armies come through the marsh, first one, then the other, they pass within a mile and do not see it. The priest holds a mass of thanksgiving on the roof. You are asked to be godparent to three babies at once.

failure.body: You show them how to cut the causeway and put out every light. But a baby cries on the second night, and a patrol of Mordred's men hears it. They take the cattle and half the food, and they leave laughing. It could have been worse. It was bad enough.

resolutions.label: make both armies think the marsh is full of plague

success.body: You have the refugees hang rags on poles along every approach to the castle, the red rags that mark a plague house, and dig false graves along the causeway and paint crosses on the doors. When the scouts of both armies come through the marsh, they take one look and turn back, holding their noses. Neither army comes within a mile. Father Idris holds a mass of thanksgiving on the roof.

failure.body: You hang red rags and paint crosses, and it works too well. Mordred's captain decides to burn the plague-castle to stop the sickness spreading. You get the people out in boats as it burns.

entries.body: You stand in the middle of the ring of columns and ask your question aloud. The wind rises. The voices murmur.

resolutions.label: understand the answer of the wind

success.body: The voices speak all at once, and then one at a time, and at last you understand. It is not the answer you expected. It is better. You thank the temple. The old woman nods. "It likes you," she says. "It does not usually." She gives you a little bronze arrowhead from the temple floor, for luck.

failure.body: The voices speak all at once, and you cannot make out a word. The old woman laughs. "Too many questions in you," she says. "Come back when you have only one."

resolutions.label: ask your question with an offering of the hunt

success.body: The old woman nods at the bow on your saddle. "She is a goddess of the hunt," she says. You go into the wood and come back at dusk with a hare, cleanly killed, and lay it on the temple step. Then you ask. The wind rises in the columns, and the voices answer, one at a time, and you understand. It is not the answer you expected. It is better. The old woman gives you a bronze arrowhead for luck.

failure.body: You go into the wood to hunt an offering and come back with nothing but a scratch. When you ask your question, the voices speak all at once, and none of them to you.

entries.body: You ride through the old king's camp from end to end, telling every captain: no man is to draw a sword while the parley is on. For any reason.

resolutions.label: make every man in the old king's host understand

success.body: By dawn, every man in the old king's host has heard it from your own mouth. You have told them why: that this is the last chance, and that one drawn sword could end everything. The next day, you stand in the ranks and watch the parley in the distance. You watch an adder slide out of the heather. You watch a knight lift his sword to strike at it. You are already running. You reach him before the sword is clear of the scabbard, and seize his wrist. Across the plain, the armies stand still. The parley goes on.

failure.body: By dawn, you have told every captain. The next day, you watch the parley in the distance. You see an adder slide out of the heather. You see a knight lift his sword to strike at it. You are too far away. The sunlight catches the blade. Both armies see it. Both armies charge.

resolutions.label: set the old king's knights to guard the front rank

success.body: You do not trust the order to reach ten thousand men by word. You go to the old king's oldest knights, Bedivere and Lucan and the rest, and set one of them every fifty paces along the front rank, with orders to hold any sword that moves. The next day, when the adder strikes and a young knight's hand goes to his hilt, Sir Lucan's hand is already on his wrist. The blade never clears the scabbard. The parley goes on.

failure.body: You set the old knights along the front rank, but the pavilion is in the middle of the plain, and the fourteen men beside the king are the ones who matter. When the adder strikes there, nobody is close enough.

entries.body: You ride through the chaos shouting for the knights to rally to you. A few of them turn.

resolutions.label: command the knights to put out the fire

success.body: You form them into a line from the river to the stand, passing helmets full of water, and send the strongest to pull down the burning timbers. It is a strange sight: the flower of chivalry passing buckets. The fire is out within the hour, and every lady is safe. The knights, soaked and blackened, cheer you, and the prize of the tournament, a silver horse, is given to you by acclaim.

failure.body: You shout for the knights to rally, but in the storm nobody hears you. By the time the fire is out, it has burned itself out. Three ladies are badly hurt.

resolutions.label: turn the river into the lists by breaking its bank

success.body: You see what nobody else has: the lists are built on the flood-meadow, below the river. You gallop to the bank with six knights and hack through the turf where the river runs highest, and the water pours through the gap and across the meadow and into the burning stand. It goes out in a great cloud of steam. The ladies come out wet and furious and alive. The prize, a silver horse, is given to you by acclaim.

failure.body: You break the river's bank, and the water pours across the meadow, and into the pavilions, and the horse-lines, and the kitchens, and not the stand, which is on a little rise. The fire burns itself out.

entries.body: You ride down the mountain to the villages where the dead men came from, and knock on every door.

resolutions.label: persuade the villagers to bury their own

success.body: They are frightened of the reivers. You promise to stand guard while they dig. They come, slowly, a few at a time, then a whole village, then three. They bury their sons and husbands and fathers on the mountain, and weep, and the old priest says the words. The reivers do not come. You stand guard all week. At the end, a woman gives you her dead husband's sword. "He would want a knight to have it," she says.

failure.body: They are frightened of the reivers, and will not come. You ride back up the mountain alone. The old priest keeps digging.

resolutions.label: stand guard while the villagers bury their dead

success.body: You tell the villagers they will not dig alone. You set a watch on the pass, and walk the ridge yourself every hour, with your sword drawn, so that they can see you from below. They come, a few at a time, then a whole village, then three. The reivers see a knight on the ridge and do not come. At the end of the week, a woman gives you her dead husband's sword.

failure.body: You set a watch on the pass and walk the ridge. On the third night, the reivers come by the other pass. The villagers scatter. The dead go unburied.

entries.body: "Come back with me," you say. "I will speak to Sir Kay." Dagonet looks at you as though you have offered to speak to a thunderstorm. "*He will not care what you say,*" he murmurs. "*He'll kick you too, then, and I'll stay.*"

resolutions.label: stand up to Sir Kay on the fool's behalf

success.body: You find Kay in the great hall and tell him, in front of everyone, that a man who kicks a fool down the stair is a smaller man than the fool. The hall goes silent. Kay goes red, then white. Then, to everyone's astonishment, he laughs. "Fair," he says. "That was fair." He turns to Dagonet. "Come back, then. I will not kick you." He pauses. "Much." The High King, who has been listening from the dais, calls you over and fills your cup with his own hand.

failure.body: You find Kay in the great hall and tell him that a man who kicks a fool is a smaller man than the fool. Kay looks at you for a long moment. Then he picks up a jug of water and pours it over your head. The whole hall laughs, and Dagonet laughs loudest of all, because it is better than being kicked.

resolutions.label: make Kay the butt of the fool's best joke

success.body: You and Dagonet plan it together on the road. At supper, Dagonet stands up and tells the court a long, rambling tale about a seneschal who was so proud of his cooking that he ate it all himself, and grew so fat he could not fit through the door of his own buttery. It is not about Kay, of course. Everyone knows it is about Kay. The High King laughs until he has to hold the table. Kay is furious, but he cannot kick a fool for telling a story the king laughed at. Dagonet is safe for a year.

failure.body: You and Dagonet plan it together. At supper, Dagonet stands up and tells the court the tale of the seneschal who ate all his own cooking. Nobody laughs. Kay, it turns out, has been ill for a week and can eat nothing. The High King frowns. Dagonet is sent to the kitchens, and you are not invited to dine at the high table again that season.

entries.body: "What would you take," you ask, "to heal him without the Grail's road?" Morgan looks at you with interest. "Oh," she says, "I like you."

resolutions.label: strike a bargain with Morgan le Fay

success.body: You bargain with her all night. At the end, she heals the man's wound, not fully, but enough for him to walk, in return for a promise from you: that you will bring her one thing, one day, when she asks. She does not say what. The wounded man goes on his way, weeping with relief. Morgan kisses you on the forehead. "Do not forget," she says. You will not.

failure.body: You bargain with her all night. At the end, she heals the man's wound, and he tells her the way to Corbenic, and she laughs, and is gone. You have given her what she wanted.

resolutions.label: match Morgan's price with a better one

success.body: You tell her what you can offer: not a promise, but a service, and you tell her what you have done in the past to show that you will do it. Morgan listens with growing delight. "Oh," she says, "you are one of us." She heals the man's wound, not fully, but enough to walk, and does not ask him the way to Corbenic at all. She kisses your forehead. "I will call on you," she says.

partial.body: You offer her a service. Morgan considers it, and laughs, and heals the man only a little. "That is all you are worth," she says.

failure.body: You offer her a service. "From you?" says Morgan. She heals the man, and he tells her the way to Corbenic.

entries.body: You take the slice. It is very good. "Share and share alike," you say. Tom laughs. "A knight after my own heart," he says. "Now help me get the rest of it home before the verderer comes by."

resolutions.label: smuggle the deer past the king's foresters

success.body: You wrap the deer in your cloak, sling it over your saddle, and ride through the forester's lodge with Tom walking at your stirrup, chatting to the foresters about the weather. Nobody questions a knight. At Tom's cottage, his wife and six children fall on the venison with cheers. Tom presses a purse of silver on you, which he says was a gift from a gentleman who did not know he was giving it. You do not ask.

failure.body: You wrap the deer in your cloak and ride past the forester's lodge. Unfortunately, the deer's hind leg slips out from under the cloak and dangles there, with the king's brand clearly visible. The foresters are very interested. Tom escapes into the trees. You do not.

resolutions.label: ride the deer out through the forest at speed

success.body: You sling the deer across your saddle, pull Tom up behind you, and gallop through the forest by the rides the foresters use, straight past their lodge, waving. Nobody stops a knight at a gallop. At Tom's cottage, his wife and six children fall on the venison. Tom presses a purse of silver on you that he says came from a gentleman who did not know he was giving it.

failure.body: You sling the deer across your saddle and gallop through the forest, and at the foresters' lodge your horse shies at a dog, and the deer slides off in front of the verderer. Tom escapes. You do not.

entries.body: You fold the poem carefully. "I will see it reaches the right hands," you say. As soon as Kay has gone, you head for the great hall, where Sir Dinadan is holding court among the young knights.

resolutions.label: have the poem read aloud at the high table

success.body: Dinadan sets the poem to the tune of a drinking song, and at supper he sings it before the whole court, with the young knights joining in on the chorus: *as starch'd, as starch'd*. Kay goes purple. The High King laughs until he cries. Then Nest the laundress stands up at the back of the hall, and walks the whole length of it, and kisses Kay full on the mouth in front of everybody. "That," she says, "was the best poem anyone ever wrote me." The court is silent. Kay is speechless. You are not sure whether the joke is on him or on you.

failure.body: Dinadan sets the poem to the tune of a drinking song, but he has had too much wine before supper, and when he stands up to sing, he points at you and announces that you wrote it. The court roars. Nest the laundress stands up at the back of the hall and says loudly that it is the worst poem she has ever heard, and that she would not walk out with its author for a sack of silver. Kay laughs at you for a month.

entries.body: "Tell your king's champion," you say, "that there is a knight at this crossroads who answers for the High King." Tudwal's eyes light up. "Oh, splendid," he says. "Nobody ever answers."

resolutions.label: meet King Ryons's champion at the crossroads

success.body: The champion arrives two days later: a huge knight called Sir Maleger, on a horse covered in black bearskin. He takes one look at you and laughs. You meet him at the crossroads, with Tudwal blowing his trumpet as judge, and on the second pass, you put him into a gorse bush. Tudwal writes a new message on the back of the old one: *Arthur's knight has answered, and the champion is in a gorse bush. Please send another.* He rides home with it, whistling.

failure.body: The champion arrives two days later on a horse covered in black bearskin. He puts you in a gorse bush on the first pass. Tudwal sighs, and writes a new message: *Arthur's knight answered, and is in a gorse bush.* You help him spell *gorse*.

resolutions.label: fight the champion on foot when his lance breaks

success.body: The champion's lance shatters on your shield on the first pass, and so does yours, and you both come off your horses. You meet him on foot among the gorse. He is big and slow and angry. You are quicker. By the end, he is on his back in a gorse bush, and Tudwal is writing a message on the back of the old one: *Arthur's knight has answered.* He rides home with it, whistling.

failure.body: The champion's lance and yours both shatter, and you meet him on foot. He is bigger than you thought and not slow at all. You end up in the gorse bush. Tudwal helps you spell *gorse*.

entries.body:
"Wait," says the voice. "I know you. You are the one with the answer." A long pause. "A fool," Merlin says. "Yes. You knew, and I did not listen." The stone under your hand grows warm. "Well. I cannot come out. But because you knew, I can give you something."

A crack opens in the stone, no wider than a finger, and through it, something falls into your hand: a small silver key, very old. "It opens any lock," Merlin says, "once. Keep it for when it matters." The crack closes. From inside the stone, faintly, you hear him laughing. "A fool," he says. "A fool."

notes: Lose Story Token #3

entries.body:
"Why does nobody come?" you ask. The girl sighs.

"Because they are all too busy looking for the Grail," she says, "to eat what the Grail has laid for them. They think it must be far away and very hard to find. So they ride past." She swings her legs. "The king lays the feast every night, in a different place. Once it was a peasant's hut. Once it was a leper's cave. Once it was here." She looks at you. "You are the first to stop and ask. That is better than most." She hands you an apple from the table. It is warm. When you take a bite, you understand, just for a moment, why they all keep looking.
"My lord," you say, "the war that matters is not here. It is at home. Mordred has your crown."

resolutions.label: persuade the old king to abandon the siege

success.body: You tell him everything you have heard of Mordred: the letters, the Saxons, the coronation. The old king listens with his head bowed. At last he lifts it. "You are right," he says. "I have been fighting the wrong war." He calls his captains. The next morning, the army strikes its tents and marches for the coast, and the defenders of Benwick come out onto their walls to watch it go, in silence. The old king gives you his helm, Goswhit, to carry before him on the march.

failure.body: You tell him about Mordred. The old king listens, and then shakes his head. "My nephew of Orkney will not leave," he says, "and I will not leave him." The siege goes on. You go home alone.

resolutions.label: ride home ahead of the army to show the king what Mordred has done

success.body: You do not argue. You take ship at night, ride through Kent in three days, see Mordred's banners on every tower and the Saxon ships in every creek, and ride back to the coast and take ship again. You walk into the old king's pavilion with mud to your waist and tell him what you have seen with your own eyes. He listens with his head bowed. "I have been fighting the wrong war," he says. He gives you his helm, Goswhit, to carry before him on the march.

failure.body: You take ship and ride through Kent, and Mordred's men catch you at Rochester. By the time you escape, the old king has heard the news from someone else.

entries.body: "Keep it by you," you say. "Do not put it near the fire. I will go to the hill." The woman grips your hand. The changeling watches you go.

resolutions.label: bargain with the fair folk under the hill for the child

success.body: At midnight, the fay fort on the hill stands open, and you walk in. There is a feast in the great hall, and in a golden cradle by the fire lies a fat, rosy human baby, surrounded by adoring fay women. You speak to the queen of the fort for a long time, with every courtesy you know. At last she sighs. "He is a very fine baby," she says. "But our old Grandsire Crab is missing his pipe." She lets you carry the baby out. When you get back to the cottage, the changeling is gone from its cradle, and the mother is weeping over her own son.

failure.body: At midnight, the fay fort on the hill stands open, and you walk in, and there is a feast, and you sit down at it. You mean only to taste one thing. When you walk out, it is a week later, and the changeling is still in the cradle.

resolutions.label: win the child back with a guest's perfect courtesy

success.body: At midnight you walk into the fay fort as a guest, and eat nothing, and drink nothing, and praise the queen's feast and her music and her baby, without once asking for him. The fay queen is enchanted. At dawn, she says, "What gift would you like?" You ask for the baby. She sighs. "That was clever," she says, and lets you carry him out. When you get home, the changeling is gone and the mother is weeping over her own son.

failure.body: You walk into the fort and praise everything and eat nothing. At dawn, the fay queen asks what gift you would like, and you ask for the baby too eagerly. She laughs. "No," she says, "not that." You walk home empty-handed.

entries.body: You look at the oak, and at the forester's face. "I will help you," you say. Cadfan nods once, and climbs back into the tree.

resolutions.label: ambush Lord Fulk's party from the trees

success.body: Fulk rides into view with four men-at-arms and a hawk on his wrist. Cadfan's arrow takes him in the throat before he has seen the oak. His men draw their swords, but you come out of the trees at them, and they flee. Cadfan climbs down and stands over the dead lord for a long time. Then he takes the rope that hangs from the oak, which has hung there since his brother died, and drapes it over Fulk's body. "Now it is finished," he says. He gives you Fulk's hawk, and vanishes into the forest.

failure.body: Fulk rides into view with four men-at-arms, and one of them sees the forester in the tree. Cadfan's arrow goes wide. The men-at-arms come at you both, and you are dragged to Chester in chains. Fulk is very pleased to see you. So is the hangman.

entries.body: You ride out through the postern gate and come round behind Mordred's army, to where the ram is being wheeled toward the Westgate.

resolutions.label: charge the ram and its crew

success.body: You come out of a lane at a gallop, straight at the ram's crew, and they scatter. You set fire to the ram's roof with a torch you brought from the wall, and ride away before Mordred's knights can reach you. The ram burns in the road. The townsfolk on the walls cheer. Mordred's army has no other ram, and marches away after a week of sulking.

failure.body: You come out of a lane at a gallop, but Mordred's knights are guarding the ram. You are driven back. The ram reaches the gate.

resolutions.label: burn the ram with fire-arrows from the church tower

success.body: You do not ride out. You climb the tower of Saint Swithun's, which overlooks the road, with a bow and a pot of pitch, and when the ram comes up the road, you put an arrow into its roof, and another, and another, until the whole thing is burning. The crew flee. The townsfolk on the walls cheer. Mordred's army has no other ram.

failure.body: You climb the tower with a bow and pitch, and your first fire-arrow lands on the thatch of a Winchester baker's house. The townsfolk are not pleased. The ram reaches the gate.

entries.body: You put your hand on Balin's sword-arm. "Not here," you say. "Not at the king's table. It is death to draw at a feast."

resolutions.label: hold Balin back from his vengeance

success.body: You talk to him quietly while the hall laughs and eats around you. You remind him of his brother, and of the curse he carries, and of what happens to knights who break the peace of a king's hall. At last, trembling, he lets go of his sword and gets up and walks out of the hall and into the night. Garlon's laughter follows him. You do not know what you have prevented. You feel, as you ride away from Corbenic the next day, as though the ground under you has sighed with relief.

failure.body: You talk to him quietly, but Garlon strikes him again, invisibly, and Balin tears his arm from your grip and draws. What follows, you will remember all your life: the invisible knight falling, the king's rage, Balin fleeing unarmed through the castle, and then a stroke that shakes the world. You escape Corbenic as the walls fall.

resolutions.label: take Balin out of the hall before he can draw

success.body: You do not argue with him. You take him by the belt and the sword-arm, as if he were drunk, and walk him out of the hall between the tables, laughing loudly for the benefit of the guests, while he struggles. Garlon's laughter follows you both. Outside, in the cold, Balin stops struggling and weeps. You put him on his horse and send him away from Corbenic. You feel, riding away the next day, as though the ground under you has sighed with relief.

failure.body: You take Balin by the sword-arm to walk him out, and he throws you across a table. What follows, you will remember all your life: the invisible knight falling, Balin fleeing through the castle, and a stroke that shakes the world.

entries.body:
You rein in and do not follow. Lamorak stares at you, then gallops on alone. The beast lingers a moment longer, looking at you with strange, intelligent eyes. Then it turns and goes, and the baying starts again in its belly, fading into the trees.

You sit in the quiet forest for a long time. You do not know why, but you feel that you have been thanked.
"You must answer for it," you say. "Before the High King. Not before your brothers." Gaheris looks at you for a long time.

resolutions.label: bring Gaheris to the High King's justice

success.body: He comes with you. He does not speak all the way across the sea, and all the way to Camelot. Before the High King, he tells everything. The High King, who was his mother's brother, listens with his face grey. At last, he banishes Gaheris from court for a year, and sends him on pilgrimage to Rome. It is a mercy, and a hard one. Gaheris kneels to you before he goes. "Thank you," he says, "for not letting me run." Lamorak is not killed, that year.

failure.body: He comes with you as far as the shore, and then he turns and walks away across the island, and you cannot stop him. When his brothers come, they find Lamorak three weeks later, on a road in the south, and kill him. The feud begins.

resolutions.label: stand guard over Gaheris against his brothers' ships

success.body: You do not take him anywhere. You stay, and you set his few loyal men to hold the harbour, and when his brothers' ships come in, you stand on the quay with your sword drawn and tell them that Gaheris will answer to the High King's justice, not to Orkney's. They look at you, and at the High King's colours on your shield. They do not come ashore. Gaheris goes on pilgrimage to Rome. Lamorak lives, that year.

failure.body: You stand on the quay with your sword drawn. His brothers come ashore anyway, a little way along the beach. The feud begins.

entries.body: "I will stay," you say. The young captain nods. "Then we will hold," he says.

resolutions.label: hold the ruined fort against the Saxons

success.body: The Saxons come on the third night. You have used the time well: stones piled on the walls, the gate blocked with rubble, the wounded men set where they can throw spears without standing. The Saxons come up the hill in the dark, and the fort fights back from every stone. By dawn, the Saxons have gone back down the mountain, carrying their dead. They do not come again. A week later, the old king's men find you, and bring bread.

failure.body: The Saxons come on the third night, and they are too many. The fort falls. You and three others escape down the goat-path. You do not know what became of the rest.

resolutions.label: hold the gate by strength of arm alone

success.body: The fort's gate is a gap in the rubble a single man wide. You stand in it. When the Saxons come on the third night, they come one at a time, and you meet each one. The wounded men throw stones over your head. By dawn, the gap is full of dead Saxons, and the survivors are going back down the mountain. A week later, the old king's men find you, and bring bread.

failure.body: You stand in the gap. The Saxons come one at a time for an hour, and then they stop coming one at a time. You and three others escape down the goat-path.

entries.body: "Tell the princess," you say to the herald, "that I can sail." The herald grins.

resolutions.label: spirit the princess away from her wedding ship

success.body: At midnight, when the whole wedding party is drunk, the princess climbs down a rope into your boat, and you sail away into the dark. At dawn, you land her at Dublin, where she has an aunt who does not like the King of Man either. She kisses you on both cheeks. "Now," she says, "I will choose my own husband." The King of Man, you hear, is quite relieved.

failure.body: At midnight, the princess climbs down a rope into your boat, but the rope breaks, and she falls into the sea, and the whole wedding party wakes up. You are arrested for piracy. It takes a week to explain.

resolutions.label: sail her away by night through the reefs

success.body: You take her down the rope into your own small boat at midnight and do not run for open water, where the wedding ship could chase you. You slip in among the reefs off the Irish coast, reading the white water by moonlight, where the big ship cannot follow. At dawn, you land her at Dublin, where she has an aunt who does not like the King of Man either. She kisses you on both cheeks.

failure.body: You take her in among the reefs by moonlight, and the moon goes behind a cloud. You spend the rest of the night on a rock, with the princess, waiting for the tide. She is not pleased.

entries.body: "Seven years," you say. "Your brothers are dead. Your dogs are dead. What will the comb give you?" Iddawg looks at you blankly, as though you have spoken in a foreign tongue.

resolutions.label: talk Iddawg back to himself

success.body: You sit with him by the stream all night. You ask about his brothers. You ask about his father. You ask about his dogs, one by one, and their names. He tells you. Some time before dawn, he stops watching the far bank. At sunrise, the boar comes down to drink, and Iddawg watches it and does not reach for his spear. "It is only a pig," he says wonderingly. "It is only a very big pig." He walks away from the stream and does not look back. You take the great spear and hang it in the nearest church.

failure.body: You sit with him by the stream all night, talking. At dawn the boar comes down to drink, and Iddawg is on his feet and across the water before you can stop him. You hear the fight, and then you hear nothing.

resolutions.label: learn the boar's ways so that Iddawg can let it go

success.body: You spend a day watching the boar with Iddawg, and you show him things he never noticed: how it limps from an old wound, how it lies down beside a sow in the bracken, how it has three piglets. "It is not a king," you say. "It is only an old boar with a family." Iddawg watches the piglets tumbling in the mud for a long time. Then he puts down his spear. "Seven years," he says. "I never looked." He leaves the forest that evening.

failure.body: You spend a day watching the boar with Iddawg, and you try to show him how old and tired it is. But the boar smells you, and charges out of the bracken, and you are knocked flat. Iddawg is already running after it, shrieking with joy.

entries.body: "Helm hard over!" you shout. Your captain stares at you, and then turns the wheel.

resolutions.label: take the ram meant for the old king

success.body: Your ship swings across the old king's bow just as Mordred's flagship strikes. The ram takes your ship amidships, and it begins to sink. But the old king's ship is untouched. You and your crew leap onto Mordred's flagship from your sinking deck, and fight. By the end of the day, the Medway is the old king's, and the old king himself sends a boat to bring you aboard. "You gave me your ship," he says. "I will give you another."

failure.body: Your ship swings across the old king's bow, and the ram strikes it, and it sinks. You are pulled from the sea, half-drowned. The old king's ship is saved. Yours is not.

resolutions.label: steer across the ram's path by the run of the tide

success.body: You do not throw your ship in the way. You watch the tide, which is running hard across the estuary, and turn your ship so that it drifts, fast, across the flagship's bow at the last moment, and the ram strikes you a glancing blow and slides off into open water. Mordred's flagship is swept past the old king's ship by the same tide, with its ram in the air. The old king lifts his sword to you.

failure.body: You watch the tide and turn your ship to drift across the flagship's bow. The tide turns first. The ram takes you amidships.

entries.body: You look at the bucket. You think of every time Kay has been rude to you. "Show me which flagstone," you say. Crach's grin spreads from ear to ear.

resolutions.label: grease the flagstone without being seen

success.body: You slip into the great hall while the servants are laying the tables, and while Crach distracts the butler with a riddle, you tip goose fat onto the flagstone in front of the high table and rub it in with your boot. At the feast, Kay steps up to carve the swan, and his feet go out from under him, and he sits down in the swan. The High King laughs until he weeps. So do the ambassadors from Rome. Kay looks round the hall for the culprit, and his eyes rest on Crach, and then, thoughtfully, on you.

failure.body: You slip into the great hall and tip goose fat on the flagstone. Unfortunately, Queen Guinevere comes down from the dais before Kay does, to greet the Roman ambassadors, and steps on it. She does not fall. Sir Bedivere catches her. But the High King is not laughing, and Crach, you notice, has vanished.

entries.body: You look at the causeway, and the dead, and the two exhausted armies. There must be a way.

resolutions.label: break the deadlock on the causeway

success.body: You wait until dusk, when both sides are too tired to watch. Then you ride straight down the causeway, alone, at a gallop, over the dead, shouting the old king's war-cry. Mordred's men, seeing a knight charge out of the dusk, think the whole army is behind you. They break. The old king's men follow you, roaring. By dark, the causeway is taken.

failure.body: You ride down the causeway at a gallop, alone. Mordred's men are not too tired to watch. Your horse is killed under you. You crawl back.

entries.body: You wait at the foot of the crag, watching the gate come round. When it is level with you, you run.

resolutions.label: leap into the turning castle

success.body: You gallop at the gate and your horse leaps, and you are through, into a courtyard where the walls spin past and the sky wheels overhead. In a chapel at the heart of the castle, the only thing that does not turn, you find the lord, an old man with a long beard, singing to an empty altar. He looks up. "Is it found?" he asks. You tell him the truth: not yet, and not by him. He weeps, and then he laughs, and he stops the castle, and walks out with you into the sunlight for the first time in ten years.

failure.body: You gallop at the gate, and your horse leaps, and misses, and you fall back down the crag in a shower of stones. The hermit bandages you. "Most miss," he says. "Some several times."

resolutions.label: climb the turning wall by its ivy

success.body: You do not leap for the gate. You wait for the ivy on the castle's side to come round, grab it, and hold on, and are swept up and away as the castle turns, clinging on, round and round, until you can climb to a window. In the chapel at the heart of the castle, you find the lord singing to an empty altar. You tell him the truth: not yet, and not by him. He stops the castle and walks out with you into the sunlight.

failure.body: You grab the ivy and are swept up and away, round and round, until the ivy tears. You fall into the heather at the hermit's feet. "Most fall," he says, and bandages you.

entries.body: "I will carry you both," you say. You lift her onto your horse's saddle, dish and all, and lead the horse into the water. The current is strong, and cold as death.

resolutions.label: bring the maiden across the flood without spilling the dish

success.body: Halfway across, your horse loses its footing and goes under. You catch the maiden by the arm and swim, one-handed, for the far bank, while she holds the dish above her head. When you crawl out onto the green grass, gasping, the cloth is still dry. Anfelise laughs through her tears. "You did not look," she says. "You could have. It was right in front of you." She lifts one corner of the cloth, and a light comes out of it like the sun on water, and you are warm, and dry, and not tired at all. "Now you know what he needs," she says. "Remember to ask."

failure.body: Halfway across, your horse loses its footing and goes under. You grab for the maiden and the dish, and the cloth slips, and for an instant you see what is under it. You cannot say afterwards what it was. You wake on the far bank with the maiden gone and your eyes streaming, and for many days you cannot look at the sun.

entries.body: You push your horse through the crowd to the foot of the cart. "Sheriff," you say, "the High King swore to give mercy to any who ask it. Has anyone asked?"

resolutions.label: argue that the High King must hear the case himself

success.body: The sheriff sweats. You speak of the king's oath, of the king's honour, and of what the king will say if he returns to find a fellow king hanged in his absence without a hearing. The crowd begins to murmur. At last the sheriff gives way and orders the rope taken off. "Three days," he says. "If the High King does not send word in three days, I hang him and you with him." Word comes on the second day: Nentres is to be spared. The captive king shakes your hand. "I owe you a life," he says.

failure.body: The sheriff sweats. You speak of the king's oath and the king's honour, but Nentres interrupts to call the sheriff a fat coward, and the crowd laughs, and the sheriff's face sets like stone. "Noon," he says. They hang Nentres at noon. He dies laughing. You ride away without looking back, and the laugh stays with you.

resolutions.label: invoke the High King's law to stay the hanging

success.body: You draw your sword, reverse it and hold it up like a cross. "I claim the right of any knight of Logres," you say, "to stand surety for a prisoner until his king returns. If he runs, hang me." The crowd goes silent. The sheriff has never heard of any such right, but he has never heard of it not existing either. He takes the rope off Nentres and puts it around your wrist instead. Nentres does not run. When the High King returns, he hears the story and pardons you both.

failure.body: You draw your sword, reverse it and hold it up like a cross. "I claim the right of any knight of Logres to stand surety for a prisoner." The sheriff consults a clerk, who consults a book, who finds no such right. They take you into custody for disturbing the king's peace. Nentres hangs at noon while you watch from the gaol window. You learn, too late, that fine words need a law behind them.

entries.body: "Sir Griflet," you say, "no one at court remembers that squire. But they have missed you." Griflet looks doubtful. "Do you think so?" he asks.

resolutions.label: convince Griflet his honour is restored

success.body: You tell him that nine knights in fair joust is more than most of the Round Table manage in three years. You tell him the queen's ladies have been asking after him, which may be true. You tell him that a vow kept so faithfully is kept, even if the number is short by one. Griflet's face brightens with every word. By the end, he is packing his tent. "Nine," he says. "Nine is a good number. Nine is a holy number, isn't it?" He rides for Camelot with a light heart.

failure.body: You tell him that nine is nearly ten. Griflet's face falls. "A vow is a vow," he says stiffly, and goes back to charging his post. You leave him there, missing it.

resolutions.label: swear yourself to his vow and ride with him to find the tenth

success.body: "Then I will ride with you," you say, "until we find the tenth." Griflet is overjoyed. You ride together for a week, and on the seventh day you meet a proud knight at a bridge who refuses to let anyone pass. Griflet rides him down on the first pass. He is so happy afterwards that he weeps. You ride back to Camelot together, and at the gate he says, "I would never have done it alone." He is wrong, but you do not say so.

failure.body: "Then I will ride with you," you say, "until we find the tenth." You ride together for a week, and on the seventh day you meet a proud knight at a bridge, who takes one look at Griflet's rusty armour and laughs. Griflet charges him and is thrown into the river. You haul him out. He sits on the bank, dripping. "Eight," he says miserably.

entries.body: "Forty nights is a long vigil," you say gently. "He would not want you to spend your life in this chapel." Ceinwen's hands tighten on her knife.

resolutions.label: persuade Ceinwen to leave the tomb

success.body: You sit down beside her and talk about her Brangor, and she tells you about him: his laugh, his terrible singing, the hawk he was so proud of. After a while, she is almost smiling. You ask her if Brangor would want her to die for a gilded helm. "No," she says slowly. "He would say it was a very ugly helm, and I should let them have it." She comes away with you. The grave-robbers find the helm is painted wood. Brangor's cousin, you hear, is not pleased.

failure.body: You sit down beside her and talk about her Brangor, but she does not want to talk. "You do not understand," she says. "If I leave, he will be alone." You leave her there. At dawn, you hear from a shepherd that there was fighting at the chapel in the night.

resolutions.label: offer to bring the cousin to justice instead

success.body: "The helm does not matter," you say. "His cousin does. He killed Brangor and he sends robbers to his grave. Let me take him before the High King's justice." Ceinwen looks at you, and slowly, her face changes. She stands. "Yes," she says. "Yes. Take me with you." You ride together to Camelot, and before the whole court she tells her story. The cousin is sent on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, barefoot. Ceinwen enters the queen's household.

failure.body: "Let me take his cousin before the High King's justice," you say. Ceinwen laughs bitterly. "His cousin," she says, "is the High King's sheriff." She turns back to the tomb. You ride away feeling you have made a promise you had no means of keeping.

entries.body:
Morgan looks at you across the black barge. "You still owe me," she says. "Here is what I want. When you see him fall, do not stay to fight. Come to the lake. Help me lift him into the barge. I cannot do it alone. I will not ask any of my women to see him like that."

You nod. You do not trust yourself to speak. Morgan looks away. "Then we are quits," she says. "And more than quits." She presses something into your hand: a skein of grey thread. "For crossing," she says. "Water, or anything else. Use it once."

notes: Lose Story Token #13

entries.body: "Who was the lady?" you ask. Dicon points up at the hills. "She was very tall," he says. "And her dress was made of leaves. I should have known."

resolutions.label: bargain with the fay lady for the thief's life

success.body: You take Dicon up to the hill at dusk and call on the lady politely by all the names you can think of. At last she comes, tall and green-gowned and very angry. You speak for Dicon, and offer her an apology, and a new purse of your own, and a promise that he will never cut another purse again. The fay lady considers. Then she laughs, and the green purse unties itself from Dicon's belt and floats to her hand. "Never," she says to him. "Never again." He never does. He becomes, of all things, a baker.

failure.body: You take Dicon up to the hill at dusk and call on the lady. She comes, and she is very angry, and when you try to bargain with her, she only laughs and points at you. The purse unties itself from Dicon's belt and ties itself to yours. It screams all the way down the hill, and for three days after, until you bury it in a churchyard.

resolutions.label: return the purse with a knight's full apology

success.body: You go up the hill alone and kneel at its foot, and lay the screaming purse on the grass, and apologise, not as a thief, but as a knight whose friend has wronged a lady. You take it on yourself. The hill is quiet a long while. Then a hand comes out of the turf, takes the purse and pats your head, once, like a dog. Dicon never sees the little people again. You see them, sometimes, at the edges of your eyes, but they are smiling.

failure.body: You kneel at the foot of the hill and apologise on Dicon's behalf. The hill is quiet. Then the purse leaps up and ties itself to your own belt. It screams for three days, until you bury it in a churchyard.

entries.body:
You sit down by the old nurse's fire. "I knew Gareth," you say. "On the road, when he was Beaumains, with Lynette. In his kitchen apron."

The old woman puts down her spinning. "Tell me," she says.

You tell her everything: the bridge, the pastry, the rusty sword, the slow smile. You tell her how he ate. She laughs until she weeps. When you finish, she gets up, slowly, and goes to a chest, and brings out a little wooden sword, very worn. "His," she says. "He made it when he was six. He always said he would be a knight without anyone knowing whose son he was." She puts it in your hands. "You knew him," she says. "Keep it."

notes: Lose Story Token #7

entries.body: "I am no friend of the old king," you say. The messenger sags with relief. "Then help me," he says. "There are more chests coming, and I am alone, and the bog is full of the old king's men."

resolutions.label: hide Mordred's treasure in the bog

success.body: You help him sink the chests in a pool at the back of the cave, tied to stakes, where only someone who knew would find them. It takes all night. At dawn, the messenger gives you a purse of gold from the last chest and a letter with Mordred's seal. "The king will reward you," he says, "when he is king of all Britain." You look at the seal for a long time. It is a very good seal.

failure.body: You help him sink the chests in a pool at the back of the cave. As you are tying the last one, a band of the old king's men comes across the causeway with torches. The messenger runs. You are caught with your hands full of Mordred's gold.

entries.body: You kneel at the edge of the toadstools and wait for Huw to dance past. The music is loud in your ears, and the pale dancers turn to look at you, smiling.

resolutions.label: pull the dancer from the ring without being drawn in

success.body: Huw whirls past, and you plunge your arm into the ring and seize his smock and haul. For a moment, you are pulled toward the ring, and the music roars, and you feel your knee cross the line of toadstools. You throw yourself backward with all your strength, and Huw comes with you, and you both land in the bracken outside the ring. The music stops. The dancers are gone. Huw lies on his back, gasping, a year older, with his feet in ribbons. His sister falls on him weeping. "Was it only an hour?" he keeps asking. "Was it only an hour?"

failure.body: Huw whirls past, and you plunge your arm into the ring and seize his smock. He does not want to come. He fights you, laughing, and the pale dancers take his other arm, and pull, and the music roars, and you let go. When the music stops at dawn, you are sitting outside the ring with his sister, and your feet are bleeding, though you do not remember dancing.

resolutions.label: break the ring with cold iron

success.body: You draw your dagger, which is iron, and drive it into the ground at the edge of the ring, where the toadstools meet. The music screams and stops. The pale dancers stumble and cry out and are gone, like mist, and in the middle of the empty ring, Huw falls to his knees. He is a year older and his feet are in ribbons, but he is himself. His sister falls on him weeping. "Was it only an hour?" he keeps asking.

failure.body: You drive your dagger into the ring's edge, and the music stops, and the pale dancers turn and look at you. They take Huw with them when they go. Your dagger is lying in the grass, bent into a knot.

entries.body: "I will ride with him, my lady," you say. "And I will see that he listens." Gromer looks at you with loathing. The maiden he wronged, a miller's daughter named Tanwen, is standing among the queen's ladies. She does not look at him at all.

resolutions.label: seek the answer to the queen's riddle

success.body: You ride through a long year, asking. Some say gold, some say beauty, some say a husband, some say none. Then, in a cottage on the edge of a moor, an old woman with a face like a walnut gives you the answer. "Their own way," she says. "In all things. The same as men." When Gromer speaks it at Camelot, the queen is silent for a moment. "That is the answer," she says. "Now you know it. Remember it." Tanwen is given his lands in recompense. Gromer is given his life and nothing else.

failure.body: You ride through a long year, asking. You collect a hundred answers and cannot choose between them. At Camelot, Gromer guesses "flattery", and the queen's ladies laugh aloud. "Then you have learned nothing," says the queen. He hangs the next morning, and you watch, knowing that you did not help him learn.

resolutions.label: teach Sir Gromer what the riddle means

success.body: You do not give Gromer the answer. You make him earn it. You make him carry water for a widow, and dig a ditch for a nun, and listen to Tanwen's mother tell him exactly what he has done, for an hour, without answering back. By the end of the year he is thinner and quieter. When he stands before the queen, he gives no clever answer. "Their own will," he says, "which I took from Tanwen. I cannot give it back." The queen studies him for a long while. "No," she says. "But you may try." She lets him live.

failure.body: You do not give Gromer the answer. You try to make him earn it. He escapes in the night in the third week, stealing your horse, and is never seen again. The queen is not pleased. "I asked you to see that he asked honestly," she says. "Not to lose him." You resolve to watch a prisoner as closely as you would guard a friend.

entries.body: "I will ride for King Mordred," you say. The herald grins. "A wise choice," he says. "Come. The captain will want to meet you."

resolutions.label: lead the final assault for Mordred

success.body: You look at the walls and see what the captain has not: a postern gate on the north side, half-hidden by a collapsed cart, where the ground is soft enough to mine. You lead a party of sappers under it by night. At dawn, the wall falls, and Mordred's host pours in. The castle is taken. The captain gives you the castellan's own sword and a manor in the valley. "King Mordred remembers his friends," he says. You wonder, looking at the defenders being led away in chains, what you will be remembered for.

failure.body: You lead a party of sappers under the north wall. The defenders hear you digging and flood the mine. You are dragged out half-drowned, and the captain curses you for losing him twenty men.

resolutions.label: talk the garrison into opening the gate

success.body: You ride to the castle under a white branch and tell the castellan, very sadly, that the old king is dead over the sea, and that Mordred has promised mercy to any who open their gates by Sunday. You show him a letter you have written yourself. He believes it, because he wants the siege to end. The gate opens on Sunday. Mordred's captain gives you the castellan's sword and a manor. You try not to look at the castellan's face.

failure.body: You ride to the castle under a white branch with your false letter, and the castellan reads it and laughs. "The old king's army landed at Dover yesterday," he says. "Tell your master." Mordred's captain is not pleased that you told him first.

entries.body: "Your eldest is alive," you say. "Give me a message for him, and I will carry it across the sea."

resolutions.label: carry the nurse's message to Benwick

success.body: She thinks for a long time. Then she says, "Tell him to come home. Tell him his old nurse says the vengeance is not worth it. Tell him I am waiting." You carry it across the sea to the siege of Benwick, and find the great knight of Orkney in his tent, with his wounds, and tell him. He weeps like a child. He does not come home. He dies at Dover, landing with the king. But before he dies, he writes a letter to the queen's champion, asking forgiveness. You never know if the nurse's words were why.

failure.body: You carry her message across the sea to Benwick, but the great knight of Orkney will not see you. "Tell her," he sends out, "that I will come home when they are all dead." You do not go back to Orkney to tell her.

resolutions.label: write the nurse's words in a letter he cannot refuse to read

success.body: You do not trust the great knight of Orkney to see you. You write her words down, in her own way of speaking, and have her make her mark, and you send it into his tent at Benwick by his own squire. He reads it alone. He does not come home. But before he dies, landing at Dover, he writes a letter to the queen's champion, asking forgiveness. You never know if the nurse's words were why.

failure.body: You write her words down and send them into his tent. The squire brings back the answer: "Tell her I will come home when they are all dead."

entries.body:
The Lady of the Lake takes your hand. "You helped Nimue," she says. "So I will give you more than I give others." She looks at the rows of drowned knights. "Choose three," she says. "Three may go back."

You choose. You walk along the rows for a long time, and choose the youngest, and the one with the most children, and the one whose face you remember from a road long ago. They wake, and sit up, and look round in wonder. You lead them up out of the lake into the sunlight. They will tell your name in three different halls for the rest of their lives.

You tie your own rope to a stone and lower the children down one at a time, then the women, then the old men. Then you send your horse galloping away across the plain, and climb down after them, pulling the rope in behind you.

resolutions.label: keep the family hidden and silent in the caves

success.body: The caves are cold and dark and full of old bones. You sit in the dark with twelve frightened people for a day and a night, with your hand over a baby's mouth when the Saxons ride past overhead. Nobody makes a sound. When you climb out the next evening, the Saxons are gone. The old man embraces you. Your horse, to your surprise, is grazing a mile away, waiting for you.

failure.body: The caves are cold and dark. In the night, a child begins to cry, and will not stop, and you hear the Saxons stop overhead and laugh. They drop burning straw into the hole. You get the family out through a side passage, coughing, but you lose two of the old men to the smoke.

entries.body: You ride into Mordred's camp under a white branch, and are taken to his captains, and tell them: no man is to draw a sword while the parley is on.

resolutions.label: persuade Mordred's captains to keep the truce

success.body: Mordred's captains are hard, suspicious men, and they do not trust you. But you speak to them of their own lives, and of the Saxons who will take everything if the British kill each other. You tell them that no one on either side wants to die tomorrow. At the end, a grizzled old captain nods. "No swords," he says. "I will see to it." You do not know, riding away, whether the old king's men will be as careful. You hope so.

failure.body: Mordred's captains listen to you in silence. Then one of them says, "And who will tell the adders?" and they all laugh. You do not understand the joke until the next day.

resolutions.label: warn Mordred's captains against his own treachery

success.body: You speak to Mordred's captains not of peace, but of Mordred: that he has promised Kent to the Saxons, and will pay them with his captains' lands. You show them the proof. The grizzled old captain reads it, and is silent. "No swords," he says at last. "Not for him. Not tomorrow." You do not know whether the old king's men will be as careful. You hope so.

failure.body: You speak to Mordred's captains of his treachery. One of them is his cousin. You are escorted out of the camp at spear-point.

entries.body: You nod and smile, and agree to everything. Then, at dawn, you go to Mordred's steward at the palace.

resolutions.label: sell the loyalists to Mordred

success.body: The steward listens, and smiles, and pays you in gold. The next night, the Bell and Anchor is raided. The goldsmith and the laundress and the rest are taken away. You do not ask where. Mordred himself sends for you, and thanks you, and calls you *friend*. It is a very warm word, in his mouth.

failure.body: The steward listens, and smiles, and asks how he can know you are not lying. He has you held while the tavern is searched. It is empty. The loyalists were warned. You are held for a week and let go, empty-handed and despised by both sides.

resolutions.label: seize the loyalists yourself for Mordred's reward

success.body: You do not go to the palace. You wait until the night they meet, and walk into the back room of the Bell and Anchor with Mordred's sergeants behind you, and draw your sword. The goldsmith looks at you. He does not say anything. You take them all to the Tower. Mordred himself sends for you, and thanks you, and calls you friend.

failure.body: You walk into the back room with your sword drawn. The laundress throws a pot of hot fat at your face. The loyalists are over the wall before you can see again.

entries.body: "Go, my lady," you say. "I will speak with your son." Morgause blows you a kiss and vanishes into the trees. The rider comes up: a lean young man in Orkney colours, his face pinched with anger. "Have you seen a woman in a hooded cloak?" he demands.

resolutions.label: keep Sir Gaheris talking

success.body: You have seen, you tell him, a party of pilgrims, a pedlar, a woman with geese and a monk with a limp. Gaheris wants to know about all of them. You describe each in great detail, especially the geese. By the time he realises the geese are not relevant, the rain has washed out every track on the road. He curses you and rides back toward Carlisle. Two days later, a basket of Orkney apples arrives for you at the next inn with no note.

failure.body: You tell him of pilgrims and pedlars and geese. Gaheris narrows his eyes. "You have seen her," he says, "and you are lying for her." He pushes past you into the wood. You hear him shouting his mother's name long after you have ridden on, and you do not know whether he found her.

resolutions.label: bar the road to Sir Gaheris

success.body: You draw your sword and stand in the road. "You shall not pass this way today," you say. Gaheris does not ask why. He draws and comes at you, and you fight in the mud for a long, grim quarter-hour, until his sword flies out of his hand into the hedge. He stares at you, panting. "Who are you?" he asks. "Nobody who wishes you harm," you say. He goes back to Carlisle. You never learn if he guessed.

failure.body: You draw your sword and stand in the road. Gaheris does not ask why. He draws and comes at you, and he is faster than he looks. The fight ends with you on your back in the mud and his sword at your throat. "You are protecting her," he says, "and I know who from." He leaves you lying there and rides into the wood.

entries.body: You seize the nearest sailor and haul him toward the boat. He struggles, laughing.

resolutions.label: haul your crew off the Island of Delight

success.body: You drag them one by one, kicking and laughing, back to the boat, and row them out to the ship, and throw them aboard. By the time you have the last one, you are exhausted, and the smell of the fruit is making you sleepy too. You bite your own hand until it bleeds, to stay awake, and row. When the island is out of sight, the sailors wake, and weep, and thank you.

failure.body: You drag the first two sailors back to the boat, and then you sit down to rest for a moment on the soft grass. You wake a month later, when another ship finds you.

resolutions.label: break the island's spell over your crew

success.body: You bite your own hand until it bleeds, to keep your head, and walk among your sleeping sailors speaking the old words that break a glamour of the senses, and dash sea-water in each face. One by one, they wake, and look at the golden fruit in their hands with horror, and drop it. By dusk, every man is back aboard. When the island is out of sight, they weep and thank you.

failure.body: You walk among your sleeping sailors speaking the old words, and the fruit smells so very good. You sit down to rest for a moment on the soft grass. You wake a month later.

entries.body: You push through to the stocks. "Wait," you call out. "If the clock is sorcery, then show me. Let him open it." The crowd hesitates. The priest scowls.

resolutions.label: reveal the workings of the clock to the crowd

success.body: They bring the clock out of the church and set it on a cart, and you help the dwarf, with his hands still bound, to open its back. Inside are wheels and weights and a long pendulum swinging. He shows them how the wheels turn, and how the figures are only painted wood on a lever. The crowd presses close to look. A blacksmith, who knows what a wheel is, begins to laugh. The priest's brother drops his torch. By sundown, the clock is back in the church, and the dwarf is sitting in the tavern, and people are buying him ale.

failure.body: They bring the clock out and open it. But inside, among the wheels, is a tiny carved figure of a horned man, which the dwarf says is only a joke. The crowd does not find it funny. You are lucky to get out of the square.

entries.body: "Your cause is just," you say. "Let the High King hear it." Sir Hervi laughs bitterly. "The High King," he says, "has never heard of me."

resolutions.label: plead the outlaw knight's case at Camelot
