success.body: You ride to Camelot with Sir Hervi, under your protection, and ask for a hearing. It takes a week, but the High King hears you, and sends for the Baron of Arden and his books. The books do not add up. The Baron is fined, and the land is given back to Sir Hervi, and the tenants return to their farms. The outlaws come out of the forest in a long, blinking procession. Sir Hervi gives you his father's sword.

failure.body: You ride to Camelot with Sir Hervi, but the Baron of Arden gets there first, with gifts. Sir Hervi is arrested as an outlaw. You spend a month getting him out.

resolutions.label: find the forged debts in the Baron's own books

success.body: Before you go to Camelot, you go to the Baron's steward, who is an honest man and unhappy, and ask to see the accounts. The debt Sir Hervi is said to owe was entered in a different ink, on a scraped page. You take the page to Camelot. The High King sends for the Baron and his books. Sir Hervi gets his land back, and the outlaws come out of the forest in a long, blinking procession.

failure.body: You ask the Baron's steward to show you the accounts. He does, and then he shows them to the Baron, who has you thrown out. Sir Hervi laughs bitterly.

entries.body: "Come," you say. "Your new king needs you more than your old one does." Llew looks at the tomb. "*That is what the old king said,*" he says, "*in his will.*"

resolutions.label: help the fool break through the new king's grief

success.body: You go to the new king's hall together. You do not let Llew tell jokes. Instead, you ask the new king, quietly, what his father's favourite joke was. He does not want to answer. Then, very reluctantly, he tells you: the one about the bishop and the goat. He tells it badly. Llew, at the back of the hall, laughs aloud, and the king hears the laugh, and remembers his father laughing, and his face crumples, and he laughs and weeps at once. Afterwards, the fine is abolished. Llew is made the king's fool, and the king gives you his father's cup.

failure.body: You go to the new king's hall together, and Llew tells his best joke. The new king does not laugh. He fines Llew a shilling for the attempt, and you a shilling for bringing him, and has you both put out of the hall. Llew goes back to the tomb.

resolutions.label: hold a requiem where laughter is allowed

success.body: You go to the priest and ask for a Mass for the old king's soul, and ask that, at the end, his fool be allowed to tell one jest at the tomb, as the old king would have wished. The priest is doubtful, and then he laughs. The whole court comes. At the end, Llew tells the jest about the hedgehog. There is a terrible silence. Then the new king laughs, and weeps, and laughs. The fine is abolished that afternoon.

failure.body: You ask for a Mass with a jest at the end. The priest refuses, very firmly. The new king hears of the request and fines you a shilling for impiety.

entries.body: "This way, my lady," you say. Morgause laughs and takes your arm. "I knew I could trust a face like yours," she says. "You will not tell anyone? Not a soul?"

resolutions.label: lead the queen through the woods by a path no rider can follow

success.body: You lead her down a deer track and through a stream, and at the woodcutter's hut a huge, cheerful knight bursts out of the door and lifts the queen off her feet. "Lamorak," says Morgause, "this knight saved my life." Lamorak crushes your hand in his. "Then I owe you mine," he says. As you leave them, you hear them laughing. You hope, for their sakes, that Gaheris is a poor tracker.

failure.body: You lead her down a deer track and through a stream, and straight into a bog. The queen loses both of her slippers and most of her temper, and it is dark by the time you reach the hut. Lamorak has gone, leaving a note. Morgause reads it, crumples it, and says something about knights that is not suitable for a queen.

resolutions.label: ride with the queen pillion by the fast road

success.body: You pull Morgause up behind your saddle and gallop past her son on the road before he knows who is under the hood. She laughs in your ear the whole way. At the woodcutter's hut, a huge, cheerful knight bursts out of the door and lifts her down. "Lamorak," says Morgause, "this knight has the finest horse in Britain." Lamorak gives you a silver bit for it, and his undying thanks.

failure.body: You pull Morgause up behind your saddle and gallop past her son, but her hood blows back, and Gaheris sees the red-gold braids. He gives chase. You lose him in the end, but not before he has seen your face as well.

entries.body: You lift the shield from the cart. It is heavier than it looks. "Tell me where he went," you say. The queen points north. "To the pavilions at the Red Ford," she says. "He boasts of it there."

resolutions.label: challenge the nameless knight at the Red Ford

notes: Place a Hunting Skill Marker on your Accompanied Status Card

success.body: You find him drinking outside a pavilion at the Red Ford, on a tall grey horse that is not his. When he sees the silver fish on your shield, he goes pale and calls for his lance. You meet him on the ford itself, with the water splashing to your stirrups, and on the third pass you put him into the river. He gives up the horse and his name, which is Sir Garlon, and you lead the grey back to the black cart. The queen buries her husband at last, with the shield on his breast, and gives you his hound.

failure.body: You find him drinking outside a pavilion at the Red Ford. When he sees the silver fish on your shield, he laughs and calls for his lance. You meet him on the ford, and on the first pass his lance shatters your shield, fish and all, into three pieces. You ride back to the black cart with the pieces in your hand. The queen takes them without a word.

resolutions.label: track the nameless knight and win the horse back by stealth

success.body: You follow the grey horse's hoofprints across the moor to a pavilion at the Red Ford, where the nameless knight lies snoring off a great deal of wine. You slip the grey's tether, lead it away through the shallows, and leave the silver fish shield propped against his tent-pole where he will see it when he wakes. The queen weeps when you lead the horse up to the black cart. "He will know," she says, "that he was not forgotten."

failure.body: You follow the grey horse's hoofprints across the moor to a pavilion at the Red Ford. You are halfway to the tether when the grey horse whinnies at you, loudly and happily. The nameless knight comes out of his tent with a sword in his hand, and you spend the next hour running across a bog with his men behind you.

entries.body: "Rest," you say. "I will fight him." Balin looks up at you, astonished. "It is not your curse," he says. "No," you say. "That may help."

resolutions.label: meet the red knight on the causeway

success.body: The red knight fights hard, but he does not fight like a man trying to kill you. After a long, grim bout on the narrow stones, you beat down his guard, and he yields and unlaces his helm. He is a young man with Balin's face. "I am Balan," he says. "I was told my brother was dead." Balin, on the shore, makes a sound you will never forget. He runs across the causeway to his brother, and the ladies on the battlements are silent. You have turned a curse aside, for once.

failure.body: The red knight fights hard, and he fights like a man with nothing to lose. His sword finds the joint of your armour, and you go down on the stones. Before he can strike again, Balin has run across the causeway and thrown himself between you. You are carried to the tower. From a window, bleeding, you watch the two knights fight to the death on the causeway. Afterwards, when they unlace their helms, they are brothers. You close your eyes.

resolutions.label: ride against him along the narrow causeway

success.body: You mount, and he mounts, and you ride at each other along the narrow stones with the water on either side. Your lance takes him on the shield and lifts him out of the saddle into the lake. When you drag him out and unlace his helm, he is a young man with Balin's face. "I am Balan," he says. On the shore, Balin cries out. You have turned a curse aside, for once.

failure.body: You ride at each other along the narrow stones, and his lance takes you into the lake. Before he can finish you, Balin has run across the causeway. From the water, you watch the brothers fight, and die, and learn each other's names.

entries.body: "What share?" you ask. Master Pym beams. "A third," he says, "and you tell them you watched the king draw it yourself, and this is the very blade."

resolutions.label: sell the false swords as a knight of the High King's court

success.body: You are very good at it. In the next town, you tell the story of the sword in the stone with such feeling that grown men weep, and then you sell them tin swords. In the town after that, you sell the rest. Master Pym gives you your third and a sword of your own, a real one, with a plain hilt. "In case anyone asks for their money back," he says.

failure.body: You tell the story of the sword in the stone to the crowd in the next town. At the back of the crowd is a tall, heavy man in a plain brown cloak, listening with great interest. When you finish, he comes up and asks to buy a sword, and he asks you to describe the king, and you do, and he laughs. It is Arthur himself. He does not have you arrested. He only takes a sword, and pays for it, and walks away, still laughing. You feel smaller than you have ever felt.

resolutions.label: stage a mock joust to sell the swords

success.body: In the next town, you ride up and down the market with one of Pym's swords, and challenge a friend of Pym's to a mock combat, and cut his wooden shield in half with a great flourish. The crowd gasps. Nobody notices that the shield was sawn through beforehand. By sundown, every sword is sold. Pym gives you your third and a real sword of your own.

failure.body: You ride up and down the market and strike the sawn shield with a great flourish, and the tin sword bends double. The crowd laughs, and then gets angry. You and Pym leave town very fast.

entries.body: "Wait here," you say. You ride up to the gallows in plain view, as if you have every right to be there. From the gatehouse, you see a soldier stand up and peer out.

resolutions.label: cut her down under the eyes of the gatehouse

success.body: You call up to the gatehouse, in your most lordly voice, that you have come from the bishop, who is displeased that a Christian soul should hang unburied on a feast day. The soldier has no idea whether it is a feast day, and neither do you. He waves. You cut the chains, and carry Alis to Hob, who takes her in his arms. You bury her together in the churchyard of a village two miles away, and the priest asks no questions. Hob gives you a silver cup, which he says he came by honestly. You do not believe him.

failure.body: You call up to the gatehouse that you have come from the bishop. The soldier calls back that the bishop is dining with the sheriff tonight, and would you care to join them? You cut the chains anyway and flee with the body across your saddle, with half the garrison behind you. You and Hob bury her in the woods, in the dark, with no priest.

resolutions.label: cut her down and fight off the guard

success.body: You cut the chains in full view of the gatehouse. Six soldiers come running down the hill. You put your horse between them and the gallows while Hob carries his wife away, and you hold them off with your sword until he has disappeared into the trees. Then you ride after him. The sheriff puts a price on your head, but it is not a very large one, and you bury Alis in a quiet churchyard by the river.

failure.body: You cut the chains in full view of the gatehouse, and six soldiers come running. You fight, but they are six, and one of them has a crossbow. You wake up in the sheriff's cellar. Hob, you hear later, got his wife away while they were busy with you.

entries.body: You catch the pedlar's wrist. The young man wakes and sees her hand in his satchel. He draws his knife.

resolutions.label: keep the peace in the woodcutter's hut

success.body: You get between them before any blood is spilled, and make them both sit down. By the fire, it all comes out: she is a spy of Merlin's, he is a messenger of King Lot's, and both of them are very frightened of what will happen to them if they fail. You make them share the last of the bread and wait out the storm. In the morning, the young man rides north and the woman rides south, and you do not know which of them to warn.

failure.body: You get between them, but the young man's knife catches your arm, and the pedlar slips out into the storm with the letter. By morning, the young man is gone too.

resolutions.label: disarm them both before blood is spilled

success.body: The young man's knife comes out, and so does the pedlar's, and you knock both out of their hands in a single stroke and stand between them with your sword on the table. "Sit," you say. They sit. By the fire, it all comes out: a spy of Merlin's and a messenger of Lot's, both frightened. In the morning, they ride off in opposite directions. You ride to Camelot, faster than either.

failure.body: You knock the young man's knife away, but the pedlar's catches your arm, and while you are cursing, both of them are out in the storm, still fighting over the letter.

entries.body: You ride at the boar, shouting, and wheel away as it charges, drawing it after you into the trees.

resolutions.label: lure the boar away and lose it in the forest

success.body: The boar chases you for a mile, and you let it get close enough to smell your horse, and then you lead it into a bog, and it sinks to its belly and bellows. You ride back to the oak and help Rhodri down and put him across your saddle and take him home. That night, he and his sons go out with spears to the bog. They bring back enough meat for the whole village.

failure.body: The boar chases you into the trees, and it is faster than your horse. It catches you in a thicket, and your horse screams and throws you and bolts. You climb a tree. Now there are two of you up trees, a mile apart, shouting at each other.

resolutions.label: lay a false scent to draw the boar off

success.body: You kill a hare and drag it on a string through the forest, laying a trail of blood. The boar lifts its snout, snorts, and trots off after the scent. By the time it has found the hare, you have Rhodri down from the tree and are riding away with him. His family welcomes you like a lost son.

failure.body: You kill a hare and drag it through the forest, but the boar is not interested in hares. It is interested in you. You spend the afternoon up a tree, beside Rhodri, listening to him describe the other boars he has known.

entries.body: You sit down across from her. Morgan cuts the pear in half and gives you the bigger piece. "So," she says. "Tell me why I should like you."

resolutions.label: win the enchantress's favour

notes: If you are Betrothed, gain 1 Rank of Villainy

success.body: You tell her of your deeds of love and daring, and Morgan listens with her chin on her hand, laughing in the right places. When you finish, she looks at you for a long moment. "Better than my brother's knights usually manage," she says. She forgets entirely about the mantle. You spend the afternoon in her company, and when she leaves she presses a ring into your palm. "For when you are bored of Camelot," she says.

partial.body: You tell her of your deeds, and Morgan listens politely. "Charming," she says, and pats your hand, and sends you on your way with a kiss on the cheek and nothing else. You feel as if you have been sized up and found to be a size too small.

failure.body: You tell her of your deeds, such as they are. Morgan yawns. "Oh, little knight," she says. When she has gone, you find you cannot stop thinking about her, which is exactly what she intended.

entries.body: You thank the herald, ride away and circle round the camp by night to the castle's river side, where a rope hangs down the wall.

resolutions.label: get food and hope into the besieged castle

success.body: You swim the river three nights running with sacks of flour tied to your back, bought from a miller who remembers the old king. On the fourth night, you bring a message instead: the old king's army has landed at Dover. The castellan reads it aloud from the walls, and a cheer goes up that the besiegers can hear a mile away. Mordred's host breaks camp two days later. The castellan embraces you on the steps of his hall. "You fed us," he says, "and then you gave us something better."

failure.body: You swim the river with a sack of flour on your back, and the current takes you, and the flour, and you are washed up a mile downstream, in Mordred's camp. They do not know who you are. You spend a very frightening day pretending to be one of them.

resolutions.label: slip in by the reeds on the river side

success.body: You leave your horse and crawl through the reeds below the castle on the river side, where the besiegers' watch is thinnest, and swim the last stretch under the water-gate. The defenders haul you up. You bring them word, and then you go back out the same way and bring them flour, three nights running. On the fourth night, you bring them news that the old king's army has landed. Mordred's host breaks camp two days later.

failure.body: You crawl through the reeds below the castle, and a heron gets up beside you with a great clatter. The besiegers' watch looks round. You spend the night lying in the river up to your nose.

entries.body: You walk round the foot of the tower, looking for the spell that holds it.

resolutions.label: unmake the sorcerer's tower-spell

success.body: You find it: a ring of runes carved in the stones at the tower's foot, a spell of binding, turned inward, so that the old man cannot leave. He has bound himself. You scratch out one rune, and the whole tower shudders, and the light in the window goes out. A moment later, the old scholar comes stumbling out of the door, blinking in the daylight, and falls into his pupil's arms.

failure.body: You scratch out one rune, and the tower shudders, and a crack runs up its side, and it falls, slowly, into the marsh. The old man and his pupil are saved, but the books are lost.

resolutions.label: talk the old scholar down from his tower

success.body: You stand at the foot of the tower and call up to the window, and talk to him. You talk about Merlin, his pupil, who was also too clever. You talk about his own pupil, sitting on a rock outside, weeping. You talk about lunch. After an hour, the light in the window goes out, and a moment later, the old scholar comes stumbling out of the door, blinking in the daylight, and falls into his pupil's arms.

failure.body: You stand at the foot of the tower and call up to him. The window opens. A book comes out of it and hits you on the head.

entries.body: You wait until the breathing is slow and steady. Then you slip off your boots and creep into the cave on your stockinged feet.

resolutions.label: steal from the sleeping dragon's hoard

success.body: The dragon is asleep on a heap of gold, with its tail curled round it like a cat. You fill your helmet with coins and cups and a jewelled collar that once belonged to a horse, and creep out again. At the entrance, you look back. One yellow eye is open, watching you. The dragon yawns, and closes it again. You have the strangest feeling that it does not mind. You find out why, later, when you learn that dragons count their gold every hundred years, and this one has ninety to go.

failure.body: The dragon is asleep on a heap of gold. You fill your helmet with coins, and one of them slips out and rings on the rock like a bell. The dragon wakes. You run. You get out of the cave with your life and without your helmet, and the shepherd has to lend you his hat.

resolutions.label: creep in by the smoke-hole in the hill above

success.body: There is a crack in the hillside above the cave where the dragon's smoke comes out. You wait until it is only a thin grey thread, then climb down through it on a rope, hand over hand, into the hot dark, right above the hoard. You fill a sack and climb back up. The dragon sleeps on. You wonder, later, whether it counts its gold. You hope not.

failure.body: You climb down through the smoke-hole on a rope, and the dragon breathes out in its sleep. The rope burns through. You land on the hoard. The dragon wakes.

entries.body: "I will pay your toll," you say, "if you will guide me across." Aelfgifu considers this. "The toll," she says, "is a story. We have heard all ours."

resolutions.label: pay the fen-toll with a story worth hearing

success.body: You sit on a tussock among the fen-outlaws at dusk and tell them the story of the sword in the stone, and the boy who pulled it out. They have never heard it. They listen with their mouths open. When you finish, they ask for another, and another. By dawn, you are across the fens, and Aelfgifu is telling the sword story to her own children, very badly. She gives you a necklace of river-pearls.

failure.body: You tell them the story of the sword in the stone. They have heard it. They yawn. You go in the bog, and it is a long night.

entries.body: You kneel on the cold stones beneath the window. Mother Elen waits. You can hear her breathing, slow and quiet.

resolutions.label: open your heart to the anchoress

notes: While you hold Story Token #22, you may discard it at any time to lose one unwanted Status

success.body: You tell her. It comes out slowly at first, and then all at once. When you are done, there is a long silence. Then the white hand comes out of the window and rests on your head. It is warm. Mother Elen speaks a blessing so simple that a child could have said it, and something you have carried for a very long time is lifted from you. "Keep this," she says, and presses a small wooden cross into your hand. "When you are in great trouble, give it away, and your trouble will go with it."

failure.body: You tell her, but when you come to the thing you most need to be forgiven for, you find you cannot say it. You say something smaller instead. The hand on the ledge is still. "That is not it," says Mother Elen gently. "Come back when you can say it." The shutter closes.

entries.body: You climb up to the cave and bang your sword on your shield. The snoring stops. Something as big as a house comes out of the dark, blinking, with a club in its hand made from a whole tree.

resolutions.label: fight the mad giant of the Mount

success.body: He is huge and mad and very strong, and he swings the club so hard the wind of it knocks you flat. You get up. You keep moving, round and round the fire, until he is dizzy and roaring, and then you run in under his arm and strike at his knee, and he falls, and the whole island shakes. It is a long, grim business after that. When it is over, you free the old woman, and carry the duchess down to the shore, and bury her there with the old woman singing. The Duke of Brittany, when he hears of it, sends you a gift fit for a king.

failure.body: He is huge and mad and very strong, and he swings the club so hard the wind of it knocks you flat. You get up. He knocks you down again. The third time, you do not get up, and he picks you up by one leg and looks at you, puzzled, and throws you into the sea. The tide carries you back to the shore, half-drowned.

resolutions.label: trap him with fire and falling rock

success.body: You do not wake him at once. You spend an hour levering loose the great stones above the cave mouth and piling brushwood from the beach against them. Then you bang your shield. The giant comes out roaring, into a wall of fire, and you knock the props from under the rocks. When the dust clears, the giant of the Mount is buried to the waist, raging, and it is easy after that. You free the old woman and bury the duchess by the shore.

failure.body: You spend an hour levering stones and piling brushwood, and the smoke from your fire drifts into the cave before you are ready. The giant comes out coughing and furious, and finds you standing on the rocks with a lever in your hands. It goes badly after that.

entries.body: You cannot free thirty men alone. But you can keep them alive until someone else can.

resolutions.label: smuggle water to the prisoners through the drains

success.body: For a week, you crawl through the city's drains every night, dragging skins of water and bags of bread through filth to the grating above the caves. You hear the prisoners weeping when the first skin comes through. On the eighth night, a band of the old king's men takes the city gate, and the prisoners are freed. They come up out of the caves into daylight, blinking, and every one of them asks for the knight who crawled through the drains. You are, by then, very ill.

failure.body: You crawl through the city's drains with a skin of water, but the drains are a maze, and you cannot find the right grating. You come out at dawn, filthy and exhausted, by the river. The knocking goes on for two more days, and then it stops.

resolutions.label: bribe the gaolers to carry the water down themselves

success.body: You find out which of Mordred's gaolers drinks, and which has a sick child, and which owes money to the wrong man. By the end of the week, all three are carrying water and bread down to the caves every night, for different reasons, and none of them knows about the others. On the eighth night, the old king's men take the city gate. Thirty knights come up out of the caves alive.

failure.body: You find the gaoler who drinks and pay him to carry water down. He drinks your money and tells his captain. You leave London the same night, over the wall.

entries.body: "Your father is worried for you," you say. "He would want you home." Gwenllian's hand goes to the knife at her belt. "He would want me married to the Earl's steward," she says. "That is what worries him."

resolutions.label: bring the girl back to her father's men

success.body: She fights you, but she is no match for you, and at last she lets you disarm her and take her down into the next valley, where her father's men pay you the reward in silver. She does not speak to you once. As they take her away, she turns and says, "If my brother dies on that field, it is on your head." You do not ask whether he did.

failure.body: She fights you, and she is quicker than you expected. Her knife nicks your wrist, and while you are cursing, she is gone into the dusk. You spend the night searching for her and find only the crows. Her father's men laugh at you when you come to them empty-handed.

resolutions.label: let her run, then follow and bring her in when she tires

success.body: You shrug and let her go. She runs into the dusk. You follow at a distance, keeping to the dead ground, and at midnight you find her asleep in a hayrick, exhausted. You carry her down to her father's men without waking her. They pay you in silver. When she wakes on a cart going home, she says nothing to you at all. You find you cannot meet her eye.

failure.body: You let her run and follow at a distance, but she is a hunter's daughter, and she doubles back through a stream. You lose her in the dark. Her father's men laugh at you when you come in empty-handed.

entries.body: "I will bring you his shield," you say. The Queen of Northgalis tosses you a cherry. "Upside down," she says. "Remember."

resolutions.label: challenge Sir Breunor at his gate

success.body: Sir Breunor comes out to meet you in fine armour, with a shield painted with three silver hearts, which you think is a little much. He fights well, but he fights like a man who has always won, and when you drive him back against his own gatehouse he yields in astonishment. "The queens sent you," he says bitterly. "I was going to give the horses back." You bring the shield to the glade. The three queens hang it upside down from a branch and pelt it with cherry stones, and pay you handsomely.

failure.body: Sir Breunor comes out to meet you with a shield painted with three silver hearts. He fights like a man who has always won, and it turns out that he usually has. When you come to, he is sitting on the grass beside you, polishing his shield. "Tell the ladies I am sorry," he says, "and that I will send the horses back." The three queens are not pleased with your message.

resolutions.label: steal the shield from Sir Breunor's hall

success.body: You go to the castle dressed as a travelling tinker, offering to mend pans. Breunor's steward lets you into the kitchen. By nightfall you have mended three pans and stolen one shield painted with silver hearts, and are well down the valley before anybody notices. The queens are delighted. "Upside down!" cries the Queen of Northgalis, and hangs it herself, and the Queen of Eastland kisses you on both cheeks.

failure.body: You go to the castle dressed as a travelling tinker. Breunor's steward lets you in, watches you mend a pan very badly, and calls the guard. They throw you into the moat. Breunor comes to the wall to watch you climb out. "The queens sent you," he calls. "Tell them I am very sorry and the horses are coming." You go back to the glade dripping, and the queens laugh for a quarter of an hour.

entries.body: At dusk, you go to the stump of the hawthorn and call, courteously, on the King of the Fay. For a long while nothing happens. Then there is a tall man standing beside you in a cloak of leaves, with a crown of thorns. "Oberon," he says. "You called."

resolutions.label: plead with Oberon for the farmer's family

success.body: You do not argue. You apologise, on the farmer's behalf, fully and without excuses. You tell Oberon that the farmer has children, and that they did not cut the tree. You tell him that you will see a new thorn planted, and watered, and protected, as long as you live. Oberon listens with his head on one side. At last he says, "The children may live. The cattle stay dead. A thorn for a thorn." He is gone. By the morning, the children have stopped coughing. The farmer weeps on your shoulder.

failure.body: You apologise on the farmer's behalf, and then you make the mistake of pointing out that the tree was on the farmer's land. Oberon's face goes cold. "The land," he says, "was ours before your kind came. And now so is your luck." He vanishes. The next morning, your horse is lame.

resolutions.label: answer the Fay King's riddle of the thorn

success.body: Oberon looks at you. "Tell me," he says, "what a thorn is for." You think a long time. "To keep things out," you say, "and to keep things safe." Oberon smiles, very slightly. "Your farmer cut a door in my wall," he says. "Let him build me another." The farmer plants a hedge of hawthorn round the whole field. The children stop coughing. The cattle, being dead, stay dead.

failure.body: Oberon asks you what a thorn is for. "For firewood," you say, without thinking, and remember whom you are talking to. The next morning, your horse is lame.

entries.body: You go from fire to fire through the camp, where the frightened men are huddled.

resolutions.label: turn the men's fear with wise words

success.body: At every fire, you tell them a story: of the storm before the battle of Badon, when lightning struck the king's standard and he won anyway; of the Roman general who fell on his face as he landed in Britain and said, *I have taken hold of this land*. You make them laugh. You make them angry. By midnight, the talk at the fires has changed. In the morning, the army stands. You do not know if what you told them was all true. It was true enough.

failure.body: You go from fire to fire, telling them stories of omens that meant nothing. But at the fourth fire, a soldier asks you, quietly, why the lightning struck the king's tent and nobody else's. You have no answer.

entries.body: You ride in. The porter takes your name and gives you a lance of white ash. Your first opponent is a knight in silver who seems to be made of moonlight.

resolutions.label: joust in the moonlit lists

success.body: You ride three courses against the silver knight, and on the third, you lift him out of the saddle, and he falls, and becomes a shower of light on the sand. The crowd cheers. The lord of the castle, a tall man with a crown of stars, gives you a prize: a silver bridle. "Your horse will never tire," he says. When you ride out at dawn, the castle is gone, and your horse is prancing as if it were a colt.

failure.body: You ride three courses against the silver knight, and on the third, he lifts you out of the saddle, and you fall into the moonlight. You wake in the castle, where it is always night, and the music never stops, and it is a month before the moon is full again and you can ride out.

entries.body: Anfelise sits down on a stone, holding the dish in her lap. "Corbenic is the castle of King Pellam," she says. "He was wounded long ago, through both thighs, with a spear that bleeds. He cannot die, and he cannot heal. The land is wounded with him. That is why the grass on your side is brown." She looks at the dish. "Every night the vessel passes through his hall, and every knight who has been brought there has sat and watched and eaten, and said nothing. They are too courteous. They think it would be rude to ask." She lowers her voice. "There is a question. If a knight asks it, the king will be healed. I am not supposed to tell anyone." She hesitates. Then she leans close and whispers it in your ear. It is so simple that you laugh. She smiles. "Yes," she says. "That is why nobody asks."
You sit down at the bare table with the empty cup. The villagers sing. After a while, you sing too.

resolutions.label: keep the empty feast with faith

success.body: You sing the harvest songs with them until the stars come out. Then, at the end of the last song, an old man lifts his empty cup to his lips, and stops, and looks into it. It is full of milk. Up and down the table, the cups are filling, and the bowls, with bread and apples and honey. Nobody speaks. The reeve looks at you, and at the sky. "It was never us," she says. "We only kept the table laid."

failure.body: You sing the harvest songs with them until the stars come out. The cups stay empty. You ride away hungry, with the singing following you across the dust.

entries.body: You walk out to the Irish chief and bow. "My lord," you say, "these people have lost everything. Surely Ireland has room for a few more farmers."

resolutions.label: win the Irish chief's mercy for the refugees

success.body: You talk to him about his own grandfather, who came from Britain, as half the Irish chiefs' grandfathers did. You talk to him about the war, and what it has done. You offer to work his fields yourself, for a season, in payment. He laughs at that, but he is touched. At last, he gives the refugees a valley in the hills, empty since a plague, and tells them to farm it. He makes you swear to come back and help with the harvest. You do.

failure.body: You talk to him about his grandfather, but he is not interested in his grandfather. He is interested in grain. The refugees are sent back across the sea.

resolutions.label: show the chief that his own land needs these farmers

success.body: You ride with the Irish chief across his own land, and point out, as you go, the empty valleys where the plague took the farmers, the fields gone back to rush, the cattle with no one to herd them. You do not mention the refugees. You do not need to. At the end of the day, he is quiet. "That valley," he says, pointing, "has been empty ten years." He gives it to them. He makes you swear to come back and help with the harvest.

failure.body: You ride with the chief across his land and point out the empty valleys. "Empty," he says, "and I like them that way." The refugees are sent back across the sea.

entries.body: You go aboard and take a cup of mead, and stand before the bier.

resolutions.label: honour the dead sea-king at his funeral feast

success.body: You speak of him, though you never knew him, because you know what it means to fight at Badon. The Orkneymen listen, and nod, and at the end, they strike their shields. The daughter embraces you. At dawn, you watch the burning ship go out to sea, with the old man on it, and his sword on his chest. It is right. You know it is right. His daughter stands beside you on the shore, and does not weep.

failure.body: You speak of him, but halfway through, you get his name wrong. The Orkneymen go silent. His daughter looks at you with her grey eyes and says nothing at all. You leave the ship before dawn, and you resolve never again to praise a man you did not know.

entries.body: You climb the steps up the rock to the castle. The Lady Amide does not turn from the window when you come in. "Do not ask me to rest," she says. "Everyone asks me to rest."

resolutions.label: keep the vigil beside the lady

success.body: You do not ask her to rest. You take the other side of the window and keep watch with her, all night, and in the morning, you trim the lamp while she sleeps for an hour. You do this for a week. On the seventh night, far out on the water, you both see a white light moving, like a ship with no sails. It comes no nearer. It dips, once, like a bow, and is gone. The lady weeps and weeps, and then she sleeps for a whole day. When she wakes, she thanks you, and lets the lamp burn down.

failure.body: You take the other side of the window and keep watch with her. On the third night, you fall asleep, and the lamp burns low, and she wakes you screaming. You fill it just in time. She will not let you watch again.

entries.body: You ride up to the brigands' leader, slowly, with your sword sheathed. "Look at him," you say, pointing to the chaplain. "Is that a man God has stopped listening to?"

resolutions.label: turn the brigands' hearts with the priest's example

success.body: The brigand leader looks at the thin young priest standing in front of his bishop with his arms spread. The priest looks back. After a long moment, the brigand lowers his sword. "No," he says. "No, I suppose not." He turns his horse. His men follow. The bishop splutters. The young chaplain sits down on the grass very suddenly, shaking. "I did not think it would work," he says.

failure.body: The brigand leader looks at the priest, and laughs. "Brave," he says. "Now move." He knocks the priest aside and takes the gold. You fight them, but they are too many.

entries.body: "It is winter soon," you say. "You should not be cold." Mother Elen laughs, a small dry sound. "I am always cold," she says. "But I would not say no to firewood."

resolutions.label: gather food and firewood for the anchoress

success.body: You spend two days in the wood below the hill, cutting and hauling timber, and a day in the village persuading the miller to part with a sack of flour. At the end of it, the ledge beside her window is piled high. Mother Elen puts her hand out and touches the logs. "Nobody has done this for thirty years," she says. "They bring bread. They never think of wood." She blesses you and your journey. That winter, you hear, she is the only soul in the parish who does not have a cough.

failure.body: You spend two days in the wood below the hill, cutting timber, and on the second day, the axe-head flies off the handle and cuts your foot. You limp back to the cell with half a load. Mother Elen thanks you kindly, but you know you have done her little good.

resolutions.label: find the wood and herbs that will see her through the winter

success.body: You do not cut green wood. You find a fallen ash, dry and seasoned, and split it, and you gather feverfew and coltsfoot and elder from the hedges, the herbs for a winter cough. You tie them in bundles and hang them by her window. Mother Elen puts her hand out and touches them. "Nobody ever thinks of the herbs," she says. That winter she is the only soul in the parish who does not have a cough.

failure.body: You gather herbs from the hedges and hang them by her window. One of them, it turns out, is foxglove. Mother Elen, who knows her herbs better than you, thanks you very politely and throws it away when you are gone.

entries.body: "Running will not make you happy," you say. "It will make you afraid. Let me speak to your father." The young woman laughs bitterly. "My father," she says, "does not listen."

resolutions.label: persuade Lord Maelwas to let his daughter choose

success.body: Lord Maelwas does not listen, at first. But you tell him about the stone circle, and the full moons, and how the young woman looked when she held the shepherd's hand. You ask him whether his own wife chose him. He is silent a long time. "She did," he says. "Her father hated me." In the end, he does not give his daughter to the shepherd. But he does not give her to the Earl, either. And he gives Cian a farm.

failure.body: Lord Maelwas does not listen. He sends his men to the stone circle that night. Cian is not hanged. He is sent to the Holy Land. The young woman does not speak to you, or anyone, for a year.

resolutions.label: show her father the girl he has forgotten she is

success.body: You do not argue with Lord Maelwas. You ask him instead what his daughter likes to read, what songs she sings, what she was afraid of as a child. He does not know. He tries to answer, and cannot. He is silent a long while. Then he goes up to her chamber, alone. In the end, he does not give her to the shepherd. But he does not give her to the Earl, either, and he gives Cian a farm.

failure.body: You ask Lord Maelwas what his daughter likes to read. "Nothing," he says, "if I have anything to do with it." He sends his men to the stone circle that night.

entries.body: You sit down beside the giant. "Gogyrfan," you say, "have you ever thought about the giantess who lives across the valley?" The giant blinks. "Angharad?" he says. "She is very loud."

resolutions.label: play matchmaker between the giants

success.body: You spend a day carrying messages across the valley, which is a long way for a small knight, and you tell each giant what the other has said, only nicer. Angharad the giantess, it turns out, has been watching Gogyrfan for years. She leaves him a boulder. He leaves her a tree. By the end of the week, they are sitting together on the hilltop, being very loud. Elin the miller's wife gets her washing dry at last. The miller sends you a sack of flour.

failure.body: You spend a day carrying messages across the valley. Unfortunately, you get the messages mixed up, and Angharad the giantess receives a message meant for the miller's wife, which compares her to a pretty little bird. She is very insulted. She throws a boulder across the valley. It lands on the mill.

resolutions.label: teach the giant how to court properly

success.body: You teach Gogyrfan about flowers, and how one flower is better than a tree, and how to bow, and how to take no for an answer. At the end of it, he goes down to the millyard with a single daisy held very carefully between his finger and thumb, and bows so low his nose touches the ground, and gives it to Elin. She laughs, and takes it, and thanks him kindly. "Now," you say, "that is how it ends." Gogyrfan sighs. But he goes home content, and he never leaves another cow.

failure.body: You teach Gogyrfan about flowers. He goes down to the millyard and gives Elin a flower. Unfortunately, he pulls it up by the roots, and it is an apple tree. The miller comes out with a pitchfork.

entries.body: "I will play," you say. Cormoran rubs his hands together. "Excellent," he says. "Nobody plays any more. They all bring cheese."

resolutions.label: outwit the cheese-giant

success.body: "Is this your bridge?" you ask. "Yes," he says proudly. "And you are very fond of cheese?" "Yes," he says, licking his lips. "Then you will surely want to know where the best cheese in all Britain is to be found?" Cormoran opens his mouth, stops, thinks very hard, and then cannot help himself. "Yes!" he cries. You tell him: a dairy in Caerphilly. He is so pleased that he carries you across the bridge himself, and sets off for Caerphilly that same afternoon, and is never seen at the bridge again.

failure.body: "Is this your bridge?" you ask. "No," he says, grinning. "It is the king's. I only mind it." You try again. "Are you fond of cheese?" "Fond?" he says. "I am fonder of knights." You do not wait for the third question. You jump off the bridge into the river and swim for it.

entries.body: You let the rowing boat reach the longship, and then follow the longship, with no lanterns, keeping far behind.

resolutions.label: track the Saxon longship to its fleet

success.body: The longship leads you north, round the coast, to a creek in the marshes where two hundred Saxon ships lie at anchor, waiting. You count them, and mark the creek on your chart, and turn for the old king's camp. The old king's admirals send fire-ships into the creek on the next spring tide. It is the greatest victory at sea in the war.

failure.body: You follow the longship through the night, but at dawn, you see that it has led you straight into the middle of the Saxon fleet. You turn and run, and just escape.

resolutions.label: follow the longship under cover of a sea-mist

success.body: You speak the fishermen's words for mist, and it comes up off the water round your ship like wool, and the longship ahead never sees you. You follow its oars' sound through the night to a creek in the marshes where two hundred Saxon ships lie waiting. You mark it and turn for the old king's camp. The fire-ships go in on the next spring tide.

failure.body: You speak the words for mist, and it comes up so thick you lose the longship, and then the coast, and then your bearings.

entries.body: You walk through the arch. A lady with silver hair offers you a golden cup. You bow and decline.

resolutions.label: refuse the fay food without giving offence

success.body: "Lady," you say, "I am under a vow not to eat until I have done a great deed. Perhaps you know of one?" The fay lady laughs, delighted. "A vow!" she says. "How very mortal. How very charming." She tells you of a real deed to be done, and a real enemy, and you dance with her instead of eating. At dawn, she lets you go. "Come back when the deed is done," she says. "Then you may eat."

failure.body: You bow and decline the cup. The fay lady's face goes cold. "Our food is not good enough?" she says. The music stops. You are thrown back through the arch, and you wake in the clearing with a donkey's ears, which last a day.

entries.body: "She has lost her husband," you say. "She need not lose him twice." Grugyn looks at you doubtfully. "But what shall I say?"

resolutions.label: craft a tale that honours the dead man

success.body: You work it out together on the road. Sir Madoc met five outlaws at a ford, and rode at them to draw them away from a party of pilgrims, and they caught him in the water. It is almost true: there were pilgrims on the road that day, and Madoc's flight did draw the outlaws away from them, though he did not mean it to. Lady Nest weeps and adds a verse to her song. Grugyn is quiet afterwards. "It is not a lie," he says. "It is only what he should have done." He gives you the dead knight's spurs.

failure.body: You work out a tale together on the road. But Grugyn is a poor liar, and when he tells it to the widow, he stumbles over the number of outlaws, and then over the ford, and then he bursts into tears and tells her the truth. She looks at you over his head. You have made it worse.

entries.body: You take your shield, which is polished bright, and walk backwards toward the well, watching it in the shield's face.

resolutions.label: strike the basilisk by its reflection

success.body: At noon, a head rises from the well: a cockerel's comb, a serpent's neck, eyes like hot coals. You see it in your shield. You strike backwards over your shoulder, blind, and feel the blade bite. There is a scream like a hen being strangled, and a splash, and silence. When you dare to turn round, there is a dead thing floating in the well, and the three stone men are blinking and stretching and asking what time it is. The mayor pays you his hundred marks.

failure.body: At noon, a head rises from the well. You see it in your shield and strike backwards, and miss. The basilisk hisses. For a moment, out of the corner of your eye, you glimpse it directly. Your arm goes grey and heavy to the elbow. You stagger away. The feeling comes back, slowly, over a month.

resolutions.label: ward your eyes against its gaze and strike face to face

success.body: You bind your eyes with a strip of linen soaked in rue and vervain, and speak the old words for sight that cannot be taken, and walk to the well blind. At noon, you feel its gaze on you like cold water, and it does not stop your heart. You strike at the sound of its hissing. There is a scream like a strangled hen, and a splash, and silence. When you take off the linen, the three stone men are stretching and asking the time.

failure.body: You bind your eyes with linen and herbs and walk to the well. At noon, its gaze falls on you, and the herbs are not enough. Your arm turns grey to the elbow. It is a month before the feeling comes back.

entries.body:
The water in front of you ripples, and a young woman rises out of it: Nimue, who is the Lady of the Lake now. She looks at you across the water, and at Bedivere, weeping, with the sword.

"Take it," she says to you. "You helped me once, when I was running. Now help me again. Bring it to me."

You take the sword from Bedivere's hand. He lets you. You walk out into the lake, up to your waist, up to your chest, and Nimue meets you in the water, and takes the sword from your hands, and holds it up, three times, flashing, over the lake, so that everyone on the shore can see. Then she kisses your forehead and sinks with it into the water.

Behind you, you hear the old king laugh, once, from where he lies on the shore. "Well done," he says. "The first time."

notes: Lose Story Token #16

entries.body: You put on a pilgrim's cloak over your armour, pay the false monks their fee, and follow them up the Tor.

resolutions.label: trap the false monks on the Tor

success.body: At the top of the Tor, in the ruined chapel, the false monks turn on you and the other pilgrims with cudgels. You throw off your cloak. They stare at your armour, and at your sword, and at the pilgrims, who, seeing a knight, have found their courage. It is a short fight. The false monks are marched down the Tor with their hands tied with their own rope girdles. The Abbot of Glastonbury is so grateful he lets you touch the Holy Thorn.

failure.body: At the top of the Tor, the false monks turn on you with cudgels, and there are more of them than you thought. You are knocked down, robbed of your purse and your cloak, and rolled down the slope. The real monks find you at the bottom.

resolutions.label: meet the false monks at the summit with steel

success.body: You climb the Tor ahead of them by the steep side and wait in the ruined chapel. When they come up with their pilgrims, you step out with your sword drawn. The false monks draw cudgels from under their habits. It is a short fight in the ruins. The pilgrims, seeing a knight, find their own courage. The false monks go down the Tor with their hands tied with their own girdles.

failure.body: You wait in the ruined chapel and step out with your sword drawn. There are eight false monks, not four. You are rolled down the Tor with the pilgrims.

entries.body:
"Tell me of Joseph," you say. The old king's face lights up, and you realise nobody has asked him in a hundred years.

"He was a rich man, and he gave his own tomb for the Lord's body," Evelake says. "Afterwards they put him in a prison without windows, and he did not starve, because the vessel fed him. Forty years he was in that place. When they let him out he thought it had been three days." He laughs, a papery sound. "We came over the sea on his shirt. He spread it on the water and we stood on it, a hundred of us, and it carried us here. You do not believe me. No matter. The one who comes after you will believe it." He tells you of the lance that bleeds, the maimed king who guards the vessel, and the castle that can only be found by those who are not looking for it. When he falls asleep in the middle of a sentence, the abbot shows you out and gives you his blessing.
"They will not find you alone," you say. Morfran looks at you for the first time, with red, disbelieving eyes. "You would fight your own kind?" she asks. "For a giant?" "For a widow," you say.

resolutions.label: defend the giantess from the knights

success.body: You set her on the hilltop behind the cairn, with a pile of boulders to hand, and you take the narrow path below. When the three knights come riding up at dawn, they find a knight barring their way and a giantess above them with a stone the size of a cart. They come on anyway. You fight the first, and Morfran drops a boulder in front of the other two, and their horses bolt. The three knights ride away, much less eager for glory. Morfran lays the last stone on her husband's cairn and asks you to say a prayer over it.

failure.body: You set her on the hilltop and take the path below. But the knights do not come up the path. They come round the back of the hill, and by the time you hear her roar, it is too late to reach her. You find them gone and the giantess wounded, sitting beside her husband's cairn, and she will not let you near her.

resolutions.label: meet the three knights on the road before they reach her

success.body: You do not wait for them. You go down the valley at night and find their camp, and loose their horses, and cut their saddle-girths, and take their lances and throw them in the river. In the morning, three knights on foot, with no lances and saddles that slide off their horses, decide that the giantess is not worth the walk. Morfran lays the last stone on her husband's cairn and asks you to say a prayer over it.

failure.body: You go down the valley at night to their camp, and step on a dry stick. Three knights wake at once. You get away, but now they know someone is protecting her, and they come up the valley at dawn in a very bad temper.

entries.body: You go into the ruins with the beggar children, who know every corner. "Is there anything strange here?" you ask them. The smallest nods. "The warm stone," she says.

resolutions.label: find what lies beneath the warm stone

success.body: The children show you a flagstone in the floor of the old chancel that is always warm, even in winter. You lift it. Under it is a small stone chamber, empty except for a ring worn into the floor, as if something round had stood there for a very long time. There is a faint smell of roses. You put the flagstone back. You tell the bishop's steward nothing, and the beggar woman everything, and she keeps it secret for the rest of her life, and the children sleep on the warm stone every winter.

failure.body: The children show you a warm flagstone, and you lift it, and find nothing but earth and worms. The bishop's steward, who has been watching, has the family thrown out for hiding things.

resolutions.label: feel for the warmth of holy ground

success.body: You kneel on the floor of the ruined chancel and put your palms flat on the flagstones, one after another, as a dowser does, until one of them is warm. Beneath it is a small stone chamber with a ring worn into its floor, as if something round had stood there a very long time, and a faint smell of roses. You put the stone back. You tell the beggar woman, and nobody else, and the children sleep on the warm stone every winter.

failure.body: You kneel and feel the flagstones for warmth, and every one of them is cold, and the bishop's steward is watching you from the doorway.

entries.body: "You should not be walking alone," you say. "Let me carry it." Morfudd hands it over gratefully. The sword is very heavy, much heavier than it should be. By the time you have gone a mile, you are sure it is getting heavier.

resolutions.label: carry the sword to the next town

success.body: You carry it the whole way, though your arms ache and your back aches and your horse will not let you put it across the saddle. At the town, Morfudd thanks you and asks every knight in the tavern to try the sword. None of them can. At the end of the evening, she comes to sit by you. "You did not try," she says. "Why not?" "I did not need to," you say. She smiles for the first time. "That," she says, "is a better answer than any of them."

failure.body: You carry it a mile, then two, then your arm gives out, and the sword falls in the road. When you try to pick it up again, you cannot lift it. Morfudd picks it up with one hand and walks on. "It does that," she says. "It does not like being carried by people who might want it."

resolutions.label: calm the restless sword with a charm

success.body: You stop in the road and lay the sword across your knees, and speak to it as you would to a horse that shies, in the old words for rest and quiet. The weight goes out of it. You carry it the rest of the way as easily as a walking stick. Morfudd watches you with wide eyes. "It has never let anyone do that," she says. That evening, she tells you where it came from, which she has told no one else.

failure.body: You lay the sword across your knees and speak to it, and it grows heavier and heavier until it pins you to the road. Morfudd has to lift it off you. "It does not like to be spoken to," she says, too late.

entries.body: You walk across the plain. The old king's men watch you go. Nobody stops you. When you reach Mordred's lines, he is waiting, smiling. "Friend," he says, and embraces you.

resolutions.label: fight at Mordred's side on the last day

notes: Lose all Ranks of Divinity

success.body: Then the adder strikes, and the sword is drawn, and the armies charge. You fight at Mordred's side all day. At dusk, there are almost none left standing on either side, and Mordred rides out alone across the plain toward the old king. You do not follow. You watch the spear go through him. You watch him drag himself up the shaft to strike his father. You walk away across the plain in the dusk, with Mordred's gold on your arm and no one left alive to give you anything else.

partial.body: Then the adder strikes, and the sword is drawn, and the armies charge. Mordred's line breaks against the old king's, and you are swept away from his side in the first hour. You never see him again.

failure.body: Then the adder strikes, and the armies charge, and Mordred's men, who have watched you walk over, do not trust you. They put you in the front rank, where it is worst.

entries.body: You look at the deserters, and at their colours. "You wore the dragon," you say to one of them. "You wore the king's colours. Is this what he fought for?"

resolutions.label: remind the deserters of their oaths

success.body: You speak to each of them in turn. You ask the old soldiers where they fought, and the young ones who their fathers were. You remind them of the oath at Pentecost, and the king who swore it with them. One by one, they put down the loot. The sergeant is the last. "The king is dead," he says. "Then fight for his memory," you say. At dawn, eight of them ride with you to the old king's camp. The other four go home to their farms. The woman gets her pot back.

failure.body: You speak to them of oaths. The sergeant laughs in your face. "Oaths," he says, "are what got us here." They beat you and take your horse.

resolutions.label: order them into ranks as their captain would

success.body: You do not plead. You bark at them, as a sergeant barks, and they are soldiers still: "Fall in! Dress your ranks! Who is the senior man?" The scarred sergeant is on his feet before he knows it. You march them up and down the ashes until they remember what they were. At dawn, eight of them ride with you to the old king's camp. The woman gets her pot back.

failure.body: You bark at them to fall in. The sergeant looks at you, amused. "Whose army?" he asks. Nobody falls in. They take your horse.

entries.body: You lean down from your saddle. "What share?" you ask. Cadoc beams. "A third," he says, "and you stand beside me looking holy and warlike, and swear you were healed by the saint of a lance wound at Carleon."

resolutions.label: play the healed knight for Brother Cadoc's crowds

success.body: You travel with Brother Cadoc for a fortnight, village to village. You are very good at being healed. You limp in, touch the knuckle, throw away your crutch and weep. The pennies pour in. At the end of it, Cadoc divides the money fairly and gives you a lead badge as a keepsake. "Stamped from a bishop's roof," he says proudly. "You have a gift, my son. If you ever tire of the sword, come and find me."

failure.body: You travel with Brother Cadoc for a week. In the fifth village, you throw away your crutch with such enthusiasm that it hits the reeve on the head. The reeve is not in a forgiving mood. He has Brother Cadoc and you put in the stocks, and the villagers throw rotten turnips until sundown.

resolutions.label: preach beside him with learned words

success.body: You stand beside Brother Cadoc on his bucket and speak to the crowd of Saint Petroc's life and miracles, with dates and places and a good deal of Latin. You know a great deal about Saint Petroc, it turns out. The crowd is deeply impressed. The pennies pour in. At the end of a fortnight, Cadoc divides the money fairly and weeps a little. "You could have been a bishop," he says.

failure.body: You stand beside Brother Cadoc and preach of Saint Petroc, and a real monk in the crowd asks you which Petroc, since there were three. You do not know. The crowd turns ugly. You and Cadoc leave town in a hurry.

entries.body:
The Grail is gone from Britain, and more than half the knights who went looking for it never came home. Those who did are changed. They pray more and laugh less, and they watch one another.

On a grey May morning, Sir Agravain and Sir Mordred stand before the king in his own hall and accuse the queen of treason. Agravain reads the charges from a list he has kept for years. Mordred only says, softly, "I am sorry, Father. Someone had to tell you." The law is the law, and Arthur made it. Guinevere is sentenced to burn.

On the day of the burning, the queen's champion of the house of Benwick and his kinsmen cut their way through the guard around the stake and carry her away. In the crush, two unarmed knights of Orkney are struck down. They are Sir Gareth, whom everyone loved, and his brother Sir Gaheris. The house of Orkney swears it will have blood for blood. Arthur, grey and heavy now, takes ship with his host to besiege Benwick across the sea, and leaves Mordred to rule Britain in his absence.

Within the month, letters are read in every market cross saying the king is dead in France. Mordred has had himself crowned at Canterbury. Saxon ships are beaching on the eastern shore, and the men who crew them say they were invited.

Each Knight chooses where their loyalty lies:

Those who swear to hold the realm for Arthur and restore Camelot's glory gain 1 Rank of Divinity.

Those who ride to protect what good has already been done, the villages, the abbeys and the people they love, gain 1 Rank of Romance.

Those who ride to Canterbury to kneel to King Mordred gain 1 Rank of Villainy.

notes: Every Knight gains Destiny equal to their highest Rank of Renown
Every Knight with 3 or more Ranks of Villainy may gain 1 Treasure

entries.body:
The last battle is over. On Salisbury Plain the dead of both hosts lie together in the rain, and no herald can tell you any longer who fought for whom. Mordred is dead by his father's spear. Arthur has been carried to the water's edge, where a black barge waited with three queens in it, and none of those who watched it go into the mist can agree on what they saw.

Every Knight adds Destiny equal to their total Ranks of Renown. The Knight with the most Destiny is remembered longest. Then the table counts which kind of Renown all the Knights together have gathered most, and reads the ending that matches it.

**If Divinity is greatest:** Word spreads among the abbeys that the king is not dead but sleeping, and that he will wake when Britain has most need of him. The knights who survive give away their horses and take up the habit. For a hundred years the chapels on the old roads are kept by men and women who were once feared in the lists, and travellers are never turned away from them.

**If Romance is greatest:** The songs begin before the grass has grown back on the plain. Minstrels carry them to every court in Christendom, and the deeds grow larger with every telling. Ladies who were never at Camelot swear they danced there. In a hundred halls, young knights who were not yet born when the Round Table broke kneel before a king who is not Arthur and swear an oath they learned from a song.

**If Villainy is greatest:** The Saxon kings divide Logres like a joint of meat, and those knights who helped them take their share. The castles are handed to new masters. The Round Table itself is chopped up for firewood by a steward who does not know what it is. Somewhere, perhaps, a sword lies at the bottom of a lake. Nobody goes to look for it.
